The success came from focusing on necessary conditions rather than surface similarity. In similar problems, I should continue converting definitions into a checklist and eliminate choices that fail even one required element. A transferable rule is: when applying a formal definition, test every option against each defining criterion separately, and do not accept an option that matches only the general idea while missing the category or context.

item.context: Solving the problem of aging population requires the joint efforts of the government, society and families. To a large extent, it is the duty of children to support the elderly in traditional China.Rather than the responsibility of the government, this concept will not only increase the burden of the younger generation, but also affect the optimal allocation of human resources, but also the mermaid, people-oriented value orientation.Bringing the problem of providing for the aged into the scope of social coordination and government responsibility will not only benefit the elderly population, but also lighten the burden of the younger generation.In this regard, some developed countries have explored successful experiences that can be used for reference. As early as the 1980s, Japan has formulated an outline of social countermeasures for longevity on the basis of the National annuity Law, the Welfare Law for the elderly and the Law on Health Care for the elderly. It has been committed to building a dynamic longevity society.
item.question: Which of the following is the author is main point of view?

choices.label: A
choices.text: We should formulate a complete system of laws and regulations to deal with the problem of population aging

choices.label: B
choices.text: There are disadvantages in the traditional Chinese pension model of emphasizing children's obligations

choices.label: C
choices.text: The solution of the pension problem in China needs to emphasize social and government responsibility

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is a big gap between China's pension model and developed countries

response:
Reasoning: The passage argues that relying mainly on children in the traditional model increases burdens and is not ideal. It emphasizes that elderly care should be brought into social coordination and government responsibility, with developed countries like Japan as reference. So the main point is stressing society and government responsibility.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach: identify the author’s thesis, then treat supporting points and examples as secondary. The key factor was the contrast between the traditional model centered on children’s duties and the author’s repeated claim that elder care should be incorporated into social coordination and government responsibility. My success came from recognizing that the discussion of burdens on the younger generation and Japan’s experience were evidence supporting that broader claim, not separate main points. For similar questions, first locate the passage’s central recommendation or judgment, then eliminate choices that capture only a problem, an example, or a supporting detail.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s central thesis, not just a supporting detail or one example. That was the right frame, because the paragraph presents several claims but organizes them around one policy conclusion. My strategy was to identify the contrast structure: the author first criticizes the traditional model centered on children’s duty, then proposes a broader model involving social coordination and government responsibility, and finally cites Japan as support. That approach was appropriate because main-point questions are usually resolved by tracking the author’s problem–critique–solution sequence. The key evidence I used was the passage’s evaluative language about the burden on the younger generation and its explicit endorsement of bringing elderly care into the scope of society and government. I also correctly treated the discussion of Japan as illustrative evidence rather than the main point itself.  

An important assumption I avoided was equating the first criticism of the traditional family model with the entire thesis; that criticism is only one step in the argument. I also distinguished between “legal system” and “government/social responsibility,” since the mention of laws in Japan supports a broader policy direction rather than making legislation the sole focus. One alternative I needed to consider was whether the passage mainly compared China with developed countries, but the comparison clearly functioned as reference material, not the thesis. The reasoning succeeded because I prioritized the author’s conclusion over background, examples, and partial claims. In similar problems, I should keep asking: which statement subsumes the others rather than merely appearing in one sentence? A useful general rule is that the main point is usually the most inclusive claim that explains why the author included criticisms, examples, and consequences.

item.context: Emotional education means that the educational attitude and behavior of educators must cause positive emotional reactions in the hearts of teenagers. It has no fixed pattern and includes almost all means of education, including rigor, discipline and even punishment. Not exactly equivalent to the education of love, but obviously operational.
item.question: Which of the following is the main argument supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a kind of education with the emotional infection of the educator as the main form.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the main way of family education.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a kind of education for young people, but there is no fixed model.

choices.label: D
choices.text: is a combination of strict and love.

response:
Reasoning: The passage emphasizes two key points: emotional education targets teenagers’ positive emotional responses, and it “has no fixed pattern,” covering many educational means. It does not say its main form is emotional infection, nor that it is mainly family education, and “strict + love” is too narrow.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an elimination approach, focusing on explicit phrases like “no fixed pattern” and “includes almost all means of education,” and chose the option that repeated those surface details. The key factor I underweighted was the definition’s core mechanism: educators’ attitudes and behaviors are meant to trigger positive emotional reactions, which points to emotional influence as the central form. My mistake was treating a secondary descriptive feature as the main argument instead of identifying the passage’s defining characteristic. For similar problems, first separate the core definition or essence from supporting modifiers, and choose the option that captures that central function rather than a broad incidental detail.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the most explicitly stated feature of emotional education, so I focused on the phrase “has no fixed pattern” and selected the option that repeated that wording. That interpretation was incomplete, because the task was to identify the main argument or central characterization, not just a true descriptive detail. My strategy was essentially keyword matching: I compared each choice to surface statements in the passage and chose the one with the strongest verbal overlap. That was inappropriate here because the passage had a definitional structure, and the core idea was about what kind of education this is, while the “no fixed pattern” claim was only a secondary attribute. I used the evidence that emotional education includes many means and is not identical to love-based education, but I underweighted the opening statement that educators’ attitudes and behaviors should produce positive emotional reactions. I implicitly assumed that the broadest-sounding option was most likely the main point, which caused me to miss the passage’s emphasis on emotional influence as the defining mechanism. I also dismissed the “emotional infection” language too quickly instead of testing whether it summarized the causal process described. I should have considered which option captured the passage’s organizing principle, rather than which one reproduced a supporting detail. The specific error was confusing a subsidiary property with the thesis statement. In similar problems, I should separate definition, mechanism, and auxiliary qualifiers before mapping them to answer choices. A transferable rule is: when a passage defines a concept and then lists its features, the correct “main argument” usually matches the defining mechanism, not a later limitation or elaboration.

item.context: A certain country's economy is dominated by agriculture. In 2001, it suffered a severe drought that was unprecedented in a century. International organizations called on the people of all countries to extend a helping hand to the country.
item.question: Which of the following options can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The country's agricultural productivity is low

choices.label: B
choices.text: The country is an economically developed country

choices.label: C
choices.text: The country has a low national income and a low standard of living

choices.label: D
choices.text: The country's economy is greatly affected by the climate

response:
Reasoning: If an economy is dominated by agriculture, a severe drought would strongly reduce output and livelihoods. The aid appeal after an unprecedented drought suggests climate has a major impact on the economy. The other options are not necessarily implied.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a causal inference approach: starting from the premise that agriculture dominates the economy, then linking drought to agricultural disruption and, therefore, broad economic impact. The key factor was the dependence of the national economy on agriculture, because that makes climate events especially consequential. The successful step was distinguishing what is directly supported from what is merely plausible; the prompt supports climate sensitivity, but not low productivity, low income, or developed status. For similar problems, first identify the core dependency in the scenario, then choose only the option that follows necessarily from that dependency rather than adding unstated socioeconomic assumptions.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the strongest inference supported directly by the given facts, not a broadly plausible description of the country. That was the right framing, because inference questions depend on necessity or strong support rather than stereotype. My strategy was to connect the structure of the economy with the event described: if agriculture dominates the economy, then a severe drought would disrupt the main productive sector. I also used the added detail that international organizations appealed for help as evidence that the drought’s effects were not minor or isolated. That combination supported a conclusion about economic vulnerability to climate, which is exactly the kind of relationship the prompt emphasized.

The key evidence I used correctly was the causal link between drought and agricultural output, and between agricultural output and overall economic performance in an agriculture-dominated country. I avoided overreaching to claims about productivity, development level, or living standards, because those require additional data not provided in the prompt. A tempting shortcut would have been to associate an agriculture-based economy with poverty, but that would rely on a generalization rather than an inference from the stated facts. I should still note that other options might sound plausible in the real world, so eliminating them requires asking whether they are logically entailed. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on direct dependency rather than background assumptions. A transferable rule is: when evaluating inference questions, prefer conclusions that follow from explicit causal relationships in the prompt, and reject answers that introduce unstated socioeconomic attributes.

item.context: Professor Smith published a paper arguing that a chemical found in minute quantities in most drinking water had an adverse effect on the human nervous system. Existing scientific theory held that no such effect was possible because there was no neural mechanism for bringing it about. Several papers by well-known scientists in the field followed, unanimously purporting to prove Professor Smith wrong. This clearly shows that the scientific establishment was threatened by Professor Smith' s work and conspired to discredit it.
item.question: Which one of the following is the central flaw in the argument given by the author of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The author fails to mention whether or not Professor Smith knew that the existence of the alleged new effect was incompatible with established scientific theory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The author passes over the possibility that Professor Smith had much to gain should Professor Smith's discovery have found general acceptance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The author fails to show why the other scientists could not have been presenting evidence in order to establish the truth of the matter.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The author fails to indicate what, if any, effect the publication of Professor Smith's paper had on the public's confidence in the safety of most drinking water.

response:
Reasoning: The argument infers conspiracy from the fact that many scientists published papers criticizing Smith. But that reaction could simply reflect ordinary scientific efforts to test and refute a claim they believed false. The author gives no reason to rule out sincere truth-seeking rather than a coordinated attempt to discredit him.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an alternative-explanation approach: I tested whether the cited evidence uniquely supported “conspiracy” or whether a normal scientific explanation also fit. The key clue was that the opposing papers merely “purported to prove” Smith wrong, which is exactly what scientists might do when a claim conflicts with established theory and they are evaluating its truth. My success came from spotting that the argument jumps from criticism to threatened collusion without excluding ordinary truth-seeking behavior. For similar flaws, I should always ask whether the evidence could be explained by a non-nefarious, routine motive before accepting an accusation of conspiracy or bias.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the argument’s main logical defect, not whether the conclusion might possibly be true. That was the right framing, because flaw questions hinge on the gap between the evidence offered and the conclusion drawn. My strategy was to identify the author’s inference pattern: from widespread criticism by established scientists, the author concluded there was a threatened establishment and a conspiracy to discredit. That strategy was appropriate because the core issue is whether the same facts could be explained by a non-conspiratorial alternative. I focused on the key missing link: criticism in science is often an attempt to test, challenge, or refute a claim on the merits, especially when it conflicts with accepted theory. The argument never established that the responding scientists were motivated by fear or self-protection rather than by a genuine effort to determine truth.

I did not rely on irrelevant side issues such as Smith’s motives, public reaction, or Smith’s awareness of existing theory, which helped avoid attractive but noncentral distractors. A tempting shortcut in these problems is to treat “many experts disagree” as evidence of bad faith, but that assumption is precisely what needed support. I also recognized that “conspired” is a much stronger claim than “responded critically,” so the burden of proof was high. The reasoning succeeded because I tested the conclusion against plausible alternative explanations and chose the answer that exposed that failure directly. In similar problems, I should explicitly ask: what innocent or ordinary explanation fits the same evidence? A general rule is that when an argument infers hidden motive or coordinated suppression from mere opposition, the flaw is failing to eliminate straightforward substantive disagreement as an alternative explanation.

item.context: Risk avoidance refers to the elimination of risks or conditions under which risks occur through planned changes, and to protect targets from the impact of risks. Risk avoidance does not mean completely eliminating risks, but avoiding the losses that risks may cause. The first is to reduce the occurrence of losses. This is mainly to take pre-control measures and to reduce the degree of loss, which mainly includes pre-control and post-remediation.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following options is not risk avoidance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A foreign language training organization has developed rapidly in the past two years, but lacks supporting capital investment. Therefore, the organization chooses to raise funds through the channel of listing and issuing stocks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An advertising company implemented many incentive mechanisms to reduce employee turnover, including providing more training opportunities, increasing bonuses, and increasing insurance coverage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Xiao Li likes financial management in his spare time. His financial products in the bank involve many types, including bonds, short-term and long-term funds. He thinks this way of financial management is more stable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A shopping website has a special storage warehouse, which usually supplies stablely, but often exceeds supply during the holidays. For this reason, the company has formulated a series of plans to control cargo storage and logistics management.

response:
Reasoning: Risk avoidance means taking measures to prevent risks or reduce their occurrence/losses. A, B, and D all involve preventive organizational measures. C is mainly diversifying investments to spread risk, which is risk dispersion, not risk avoidance.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a classification-by-definition approach: I checked whether each option described planned measures to prevent a risk from occurring or to reduce the resulting loss. The key clue I focused on was the distinction between direct prevention/loss reduction and other risk-management methods, which led me to treat diversification as outside the definition. My mistake was not testing the same standard carefully against A: raising capital through listing is more like solving a financing need through expansion/financing strategy, not a clear pre-control or post-remediation measure aimed at avoiding loss from a defined risk. For similar problems, I should map each option to every element of the definition and reject choices that address a business problem indirectly rather than explicitly preventing or reducing risk losses.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the definition too loosely and focused only on whether an action was generally “good risk management,” rather than whether it specifically fit the definition’s structure: planned changes aimed at preventing losses from a risk or reducing the impact of that risk. My strategy was to classify the options by familiar business concepts, and I quickly mapped investment diversification to “risk dispersion,” which was reasonable but incomplete. The key evidence I used correctly was that several options involved pre-control measures, such as stabilizing staffing or preparing logistics plans before predictable problems occurred. However, I missed an important distinction: the financing choice was not a measure that prevented a risk event or reduced loss severity; it was a growth or capital-acquisition decision responding to a resource shortage. I assumed that because raising funds addresses a business problem, it must count as avoiding risk, but the definition requires a direct connection to risk prevention or loss reduction. By contrast, diversification can still fit the definition because it reduces exposure and limits potential loss, even if it is also describable under another risk-management label. I should have compared each option against the exact causal chain in the definition: risk source, preventive/remedial measure, and reduced probability or reduced damage. I also should have considered whether an option addresses operational uncertainty versus merely improving business conditions. The specific cause of my error was substituting category labels from finance for the narrower definitional test in the prompt. A transferable rule is: when a definition question distinguishes among related management concepts, evaluate each option by the definition’s operative mechanism, not by the option’s familiar textbook category.

item.context: Today, China's higher education is quite professional. Engineering students generally do not need to study literature courses, and history students generally do not need to study mathematics courses. In this case, it should be difficult for school graduates to change their majors, According to common sense, when employing personnel, an organization should pay attention to whether a person's major is consistent with the work he will be engaged in. However, in fact, it is quite common for college graduates to change their major and study is not used, use is not learned. This is especially true for graduates of some agricultural and forestry colleges.
item.question: Accordingly, we can consider that:

choices.label: A
choices.text: There are obvious problems in the structure of higher education in China

choices.label: B
choices.text: Graduates of colleges and universities have quite strong adaptability

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many units do not pay much attention to whether the candidate's major is appropriate when selecting candidates

choices.label: D
choices.text: Over specialized education is not conducive to students' development of broad interests and general adaptability

response:
Reasoning: The passage contrasts the expectation that specialized education should lock majors to matching jobs with the reality that many graduates work outside their majors. The most direct conclusion is that employers often do not strictly value major-job consistency when hiring.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a “most direct inference” approach and focused narrowly on the hiring sentence, treating the mismatch between study and work as mainly evidence about employer behavior. The key clue I over-weighted was the statement that organizations “should” consider major-job consistency, which led me to infer that many do not. My mistake was ignoring the broader argumentative structure: the passage emphasizes highly specialized education and then points out widespread major-job mismatch to criticize the education-employment setup itself, not just recruiters. In similar problems, identify the author’s overall evaluative target first, then choose the option that best captures the passage’s main conclusion rather than a single local inference.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question too narrowly as asking for the most immediate explanation of the observed mismatch between majors and jobs, rather than the broader evaluative conclusion the passage was guiding toward. My strategy was to identify the sentence closest to a direct inference: if many graduates work outside their majors, then employers may not insist on major-job alignment. That inference is plausible, but it treats one phenomenon in the passage as the endpoint of reasoning instead of asking what the author wants us to think about the education system as a whole. I used the contrast between “common sense” and “in fact” as evidence, but I underused the opening description of highly specialized higher education and the final emphasis on the mismatch being especially common in certain institutions. Those details were not merely background; they framed the mismatch as a sign of a deeper systemic issue.

A key assumption that misled me was treating employer behavior as the main causal factor. I should also have considered that the passage criticizes the way education is organized, not just hiring practices. Another missed alternative was distinguishing between a local inference (“some employers ignore majors”) and a global conclusion (“the educational arrangement itself is problematic”). The specific error was choosing a statement that explained the symptom rather than the author’s broader judgment. In similar problems, I should first identify whether the prompt asks for a direct factual inference or an overall argumentative takeaway. A transferable rule is: when a passage juxtaposes an expected consequence with a widespread contrary reality, the strongest conclusion often targets the underlying system that produced the mismatch, not just one participant’s behavior within it.

item.context: It is often said that people should be rewarded for doing a given job in proportion to the effort it costs them to do it. However, a little reflection will show that this is, in fact, a very bad idea, since it would mean that those people with the least skill or natural aptitude for a particular task would be the ones given the most incentive to do it.
item.question: Which one of the following argumentative strategies is used above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: stating a general principle and then presenting reasons in favor of adopting it

choices.label: B
choices.text: showing that, in practice, the principle under consideration could not be uniformly applied

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrating that a consequence that had been assumed to follow from the principle under consideration need not follow from it

choices.label: D
choices.text: attempting to undermine a general principle by arguing that undesirable consequences would follow from it

response:
Reasoning: The argument attacks the principle “reward effort proportionally” by claiming it leads to an undesirable result: the least skilled people would get the most incentive to do the job. That is undermining a general principle via bad consequences.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a consequence-based reasoning approach: I identified the claim under attack as a general principle and then looked for how the passage tried to reject it. The key factor was that the argument did not test feasibility or consistency; it said the principle was a “bad idea” because it would lead to an undesirable outcome. What helped was distinguishing “this leads to a bad result” from other common LSAT patterns like “this can’t be applied uniformly” or “the stated consequence doesn’t actually follow.” For similar problems, first classify whether the argument supports a principle, questions its application, or attacks it by tracing its consequences.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the argument’s method, not whether the principle itself was true or false. That distinction mattered, because the task was to classify the argumentative strategy used in the passage. My strategy was to identify the conclusion about the principle, then look at how the author tried to support that conclusion. I noticed that the author begins with a general principle about rewarding people in proportion to effort, then rejects it by pointing to what would happen if it were adopted. The key evidence was the claimed consequence: people with the least skill or aptitude would receive the greatest incentive to perform the task. That consequence is presented as undesirable, and the undesirability is used to attack the principle itself.

I did not get distracted by whether the consequence was realistic, because the answer choices focused on argumentative form. I also correctly ruled out choices about supporting a principle, showing it cannot be uniformly applied, or denying that a supposed consequence follows. An important assumption in my reasoning was that “very bad idea” signaled normative criticism based on outcomes, which fit the consequence-based pattern. What made the reasoning successful was matching the structure “principle → bad result → reject principle” to the answer choice. In similar problems, I should explicitly map premise and conclusion roles before comparing answer choices. General rule: when an argument challenges a rule by citing harmful results of adopting it, classify it as undermining the rule through undesirable consequences.

item.context: A television commercial argued as follows: both the product advertised and its competitor contain the same active ingredients, but the product advertised contains them in higher concentrations; tests show that the higher concentrations are completely safe; since a product that provides faster relief is always preferable, one should use the product advertised.
item.question: The television commercial's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that the product with the higher concentration of active ingredients provides faster relief than its competitor

choices.label: B
choices.text: attempts to manipulate the emotions of potential customers of the advertised product rather than presenting logically sound reasons for preferring the product advertised

choices.label: C
choices.text: attempts to establish its conclusion on the basis of evidence that is in principle impossible to disprove

choices.label: D
choices.text: dismisses its competitor's claims because of their source rather than their content

response:
Reasoning: The ad shows only that both products share active ingredients, the advertised one has higher concentrations, and those concentrations are safe. It then concludes it should be preferred because faster relief is always better, but never establishes that higher concentration actually causes faster relief.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-gap approach: I compared the stated premises with the conclusion and looked for the unstated link needed to make the argument work. The key factor was that the ad established sameness of ingredients, higher concentration, and safety, but then relied on a preference for faster relief without proving that higher concentration actually leads to faster relief. My answer was correct because I identified that missing causal/comparative connection rather than getting distracted by weaker flaws like emotional manipulation. For similar arguments, I should explicitly test whether every term in the conclusion is supported by the premises, especially when the argument shifts from “more” or “safe” to “better” or “faster.”
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the flaw in the commercial’s reasoning, not whether the conclusion might happen to be true. That interpretation was correct, because flaw questions hinge on whether the premises actually support the conclusion. My strategy was to map the argument into premises and conclusion: same ingredients, higher concentration, safety of higher concentration, and a principle that faster relief is preferable. Then I checked whether the conclusion followed from those premises. The key missing link I identified was that the ad never established that a higher concentration leads to faster relief, so the “preferable if faster” principle was never activated. That was the decisive relationship, and recognizing the gap made choice A the best criticism.

I also correctly ignored tempting but irrelevant alternatives such as emotional manipulation, since the argument was presented as a straightforward chain of reasons rather than as a purely emotional appeal. I did not assume that “more of the active ingredient” automatically means “works faster,” which is exactly the unsupported assumption the ad relied on. A weaker approach would have been to react to the realism of the medical claim rather than to the logical structure. The success came from testing each conclusion term against the premises and asking, “Where was that established?” In similar problems, I should continue translating arguments into explicit conditional links and checking whether any necessary bridge premise is missing. A general rule is: when an argument applies a value judgment to an outcome, verify first that the argument has actually shown the outcome will occur.

item.context: A civil servant is a staff member who performs public functions in accordance with the law, is included in the administrative establishment of the state and is financed by the state for wages and benefits.
item.question: Which of the following belongs to the civil servant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mr. Zhang is a university teacher. He has been working in the university for 30 years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Xiao Wang is a temporary driver employed by the District Judicial Bureau.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Li has been working as a cleaner in the personnel office since he was laid off.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mr. Chen has been offered the position of deputy director of the Traffic Department.

response:
Reasoning: Civil servants must perform public duties, be on the state’s administrative establishment, and receive state-funded pay. University teachers are usually public institution staff, not civil servants; temporary drivers and cleaners are not on establishment. A deputy director of a government traffic department is a civil service post.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option against all required elements of civil servant status rather than focusing on job titles alone. The key factor was the three-part constraint that the person must perform public functions, be within the state’s administrative establishment, and receive state-funded compensation in that official capacity. The successful step was eliminating options that only seemed government-related but lacked establishment status or were institution/service roles instead of administrative posts. For similar problems, apply every condition in the definition to each choice systematically and reject any option that fails even one required criterion.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking which person satisfies all three defining conditions of a civil servant: performing public functions under law, being included in the state administrative establishment, and receiving state-funded compensation. That interpretation was correct because the stem gave a legal-style definition with multiple necessary elements, so the task was to test each option against all of them rather than rely on job titles alone. My strategy was to eliminate options that clearly failed one of the criteria, especially the “administrative establishment” requirement, which is often the decisive distinction in these classification questions. This was appropriate because several choices involved people who may work in or around public institutions but do not hold formal civil-service status. I used the important fact that university teachers are generally staff of public institutions rather than administrative civil servants, and that temporary or support-service workers are typically outside the formal establishment. I also recognized that a leadership role inside a government department strongly indicates a civil-service post. One assumption I made was that an “offered position” in such a department implies entry into the qualifying post rather than merely an informal appointment; in this context that was reasonable. I should still note that status questions depend on legal classification, not social prestige, length of service, or workplace proximity to government. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on institutional status instead of surface features like “works for the state” or “has served many years.” In similar problems, I should systematically map each option to every element in the definition and reject any option missing even one required condition. A transferable rule is: when a concept is defined by multiple legal or formal criteria, classify cases by necessary-and-joint conditions, not by title, seniority, or intuition.

item.context: A survey by the World Health Organization pointed out that sugar addiction is more harmful than smoking, and long-term consumption of foods with high sugar content will significantly shorten people's lifespan. In recent years, Chinese consumption of sugar has remained high, especially among children. According to survey data, 10 years ago, children in my country drank 715 ml of beverages per day, which has doubled 10 years later. Most beverages currently on the market contain 8% to 11% sugar, and a 500ml bottle of beverage contains between 40g and 55g of sugar. Medical experts recommend that the daily intake of added sugars for adults should not exceed 50 grams, preferably less than 25 grams. Children should not consume more than 25 grams of added sugars per day. However, the amount of added sugar in just 1 drink already exceeds the bottom line of recommended values. As everyone knows, while we are feasting and eating sugar, sugar is quietly eating our health.
item.question: Which of the followings is the best title for this text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sweet temptation, irresistible

choices.label: B
choices.text: Action to reduce sugar consumption is urgent

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sugar addiction is more harmful than smoking

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low-sugar diet for health

response:
Reasoning: The passage stresses the harm of excessive sugar intake, especially in sugary drinks and among children, using data and expert recommendations to call attention to a serious public-health problem. The main purpose is to urge reduction of sugar consumption, not just describe temptation or compare with smoking.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea/title approach, trying to identify the author’s overall purpose from the examples about beverages, children, and recommended sugar limits. The key factor that drove my choice was the passage’s strong emphasis on excessive intake and the implied call to cut sugar consumption. My mistake was treating the supporting details and concluding warning as the central title, while underweighting the opening sentence, which states the passage’s headline claim and frames everything that follows. For similar title questions, first test whether the first sentence presents the core thesis, and prefer the option that most directly matches that thesis over one that reflects the passage’s recommendation or consequence.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s overall communicative purpose, and I treated the best title as the one that captured the author’s practical takeaway. That led me to focus on the repeated evidence about children’s intake, beverage sugar percentages, and expert limits, which made the passage sound like a warning meant to promote reduced sugar consumption. This strategy was partly reasonable, because title questions often reward identifying the main idea rather than a single supporting fact. However, I over-weighted the implied recommendation and under-weighted the passage’s opening claim, which framed the whole text with a strong comparison designed to attract attention. In headline selection, the leading thesis sentence often functions as the organizing center, especially when the rest of the paragraph mainly elaborates or proves that claim. I assumed that because the passage ended with a health warning, the title should be action-oriented, but that was a shortcut from “author’s intention” to “best title.” I should also have compared how broad each option was relative to the text’s actual wording, not just its practical implication. The error came from choosing a title that summarized the consequence or call to action rather than the passage’s stated focal assertion. In similar problems, I should separate three levels: topic, evidence, and headline thesis. General rule: when choosing a title, prefer the option that matches the text’s explicit central claim and rhetorical frame, not an inferred recommendation unless the passage directly foregrounds that recommendation.

item.context: When astronomers observed the comet Schwassman - Wachmann 3 becoming 1, 000 times brighter in September 1995, they correctly hypothesized that its increased brightness was a result of the comet' s breaking up -- when comets break up, they emit large amounts of gas and dust, becoming visibly brighter as a result. However, their observations did not reveal comet Schwassman-Wachmann 3 actually breaking into pieces until November 1995, even though telescopes were trained on it throughout the entire period.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent conflict in the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The amount of gas and dust emitted steadily increased during the period from September through November.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gas and dust can be released by cracks in a comet even if the comet is not broken all the way through.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Comets often do not emit gas and dust until several weeks after they have begun to break up.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reason comets become brighter when they break up is that the gas and dust that they emit refract light.

response:
Reasoning: The conflict is between brightness indicating breakup in September and visible pieces not appearing until November. If cracks can release gas and dust before the comet fully separates, then astronomers could correctly infer breakup had begun even though distinct pieces were not yet observable.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a discrepancy-resolution approach: identify the two claims that seem inconsistent, then look for a choice that allows both to be true at different stages of the same process. The key factor was distinguishing between a comet beginning to break up and the later point at which separate pieces become observable. My success came from recognizing that the evidence of gas and dust did not require full physical separation yet, only structural cracking. For similar problems, explicitly separate an underlying process from its visible endpoint and prefer answers that introduce an intermediate stage linking the two observations.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a resolve-the-paradox problem: the evidence suggested breakup in September, but direct observation of separate pieces did not occur until November. My strategy was to identify the exact tension and look for an answer that allowed both statements to be true without rejecting either one. That is the right approach for apparent-conflict questions, because the goal is not to weaken one side but to supply a missing mechanism or timeline distinction. I focused on the causal link given in the stimulus: breakup leads to gas and dust emission, and that emission causes increased brightness. The key fact I used was that visible brightening does not necessarily require fully detached fragments if some earlier stage of structural failure could already release gas and dust. Choice B supplied precisely that intermediate stage by distinguishing cracking from complete separation.  

I avoided less useful answers by checking whether they actually connected the two observations rather than merely restating one of them. For example, an answer about brightness continuing to increase would not explain why pieces were unseen earlier, and an answer about light refraction would explain the brightness mechanism without addressing the timing gap. The successful part of my reasoning was treating “breaking up” as potentially gradual rather than instantaneous. A transferable rule is: in paradox questions involving timing, look for an option that separates an early indicator of a process from the later point at which the process becomes directly observable.

item.context: American philosophers Cohen and Arato divide modern society into three parts. On the one hand, they distinguish civil society from a political society composed of parties, political organizations and political public bodies. On the other hand, they distinguish civil society from an economic society composed of production and distribution organizations. When discussing China's social transformation, we should also choose the theoretical framework of modern society as the coordinate.
item.question: From the above words, which of the following can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: China's social transformation needs to play the role of cooperative organizations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The government should consistently carry out economic restructuring.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The social transformation of contemporary China is to bid farewell to the planned society.

choices.label: D
choices.text: China's social transformation is related to political organizations, enterprises and citizens.

response:
Reasoning: The passage frames social transformation using three parts of modern society: civil society, political society, and economic society. Applied to China, this implies transformation involves political organizations, economic organizations (enterprises), and civil society (citizens), not specifically cooperatives, restructuring, or only leaving the planned system.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a structural mapping approach: I identified the three-part framework in the passage—civil, political, and economic society—and then matched the options to that full structure. The key factor was that the text explicitly says China’s social transformation should be discussed using this modern-society coordinate, so any valid inference had to involve all three domains rather than a single policy claim. The successful step was resisting options that introduced new specifics like cooperatives, restructuring, or planned economy, none of which were stated. For similar inference questions, I should prefer the choice that restates the passage’s full conceptual framework and avoid answers that add unsupported details or narrow it to one aspect.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as an inference problem: I needed to determine what follows from applying Cohen and Arato’s three-part framework of modern society to China’s social transformation. That interpretation was correct because the passage did not ask for a policy recommendation or a historical judgment, only a conclusion supported by the stated framework. My strategy was structural mapping: identify the three social spheres named in the passage and see which option corresponded to those spheres when translated into concrete actors. That was appropriate because the text itself is conceptual and categorical rather than causal or evaluative.

The key evidence I used was that modern society is divided into civil society, political society, and economic society, and that China’s transformation should be analyzed within that same coordinate system. From this, I connected political society to political organizations, economic society to production and distribution organizations such as enterprises, and civil society to citizens or social actors. I also correctly rejected choices that introduced extra claims not licensed by the text, such as emphasizing cooperatives, prescribing government restructuring, or reducing transformation to departure from a planned system. An important assumption I made was that “civil society” can be reasonably represented by citizens, which fits standard usage in this kind of question. I should still note that this is a paraphrase, so it was important to check that no option mirrored the framework more directly.

What made the reasoning successful was sticking closely to the passage’s explicit categories instead of importing background knowledge about China’s reforms. In similar problems, I should continue to distinguish between “supported by the text” and “plausible in the real world.” A useful general rule is: when a passage provides a classification framework, the safest inference is the option that preserves that structure without adding new causal, normative, or historical content.

item.context: Each of the elements of Girelli' s recently completed design for a university library is copied from a different one of several historic libraries. The design includes various features from Classical Greek, Islamic, Mogul, and Romanesque structures. Since no one element in the design is original, it follows that the design of the library cannot be considered original.
item.question: Which one of the following is a reasoning error made in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: concluding that an unknown instance of a phenomenon must have all the properties of the known instances

choices.label: B
choices.text: deriving a factual conclusion from evidence derived from reports of aesthetic preferences

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizing illegitimately from a few instances of a certain kind to all instances of that kind

choices.label: D
choices.text: assuming that because something is true of each of the parts of a whole it is true of the whole itself

response:
Reasoning: The argument says each individual element is unoriginal, so the entire design is unoriginal. That is the fallacy of assuming what is true of the parts must be true of the whole; a novel combination of old elements can still be original.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used structural flaw analysis: I identified the conclusion and checked whether it improperly transferred a property from components to the overall design. The key clue was the move from “no one element is original” to “the design cannot be original,” which treats originality as if it must belong independently to every part rather than possibly arising from their arrangement. My success came from recognizing the classic part-to-whole fallacy. For similar problems, explicitly test whether the disputed property could emerge at the whole level even when none of the individual parts has it.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the flaw in the argument’s reasoning, not whether the conclusion about originality was plausible in ordinary conversation. My strategy was to map the structure: each element of the design is copied, therefore the whole design is not original. That was the right approach because LSAT flaw questions usually turn on identifying the gap between premises and conclusion at the level of logical form. The key evidence I used was the shift from claims about individual components to a claim about the complete design. I correctly recognized that originality can be an emergent property of how borrowed parts are combined, so the argument treated a property of the parts as if it automatically transferred to the whole.  

A useful assumption I avoided was equating “made of copied parts” with “not original overall,” which would have accepted the argument’s hidden premise without scrutiny. I also implicitly ruled out the other choices by checking whether the argument involved unknown cases, aesthetic reports, or hasty generalization; it did not. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the composition relationship rather than getting distracted by the subject matter of architecture or art. In similar problems, I should continue abstracting the argument into a form like “each part has property P, so the whole has property P.” The transferable rule is: when an argument moves from properties of individual components to a property of the aggregate, test whether that property is preserved under combination rather than assuming it is.

item.context: After all the cold dishes of a banquet table are served, there are a total of 7 hot dishes. Among them, 3 Sichuan dishes: K, L, M: 3 Cantonese dishes: Q, N, P: one Shandong cuisine: X. Only one hot dish is served at a time, and the order of serving must meet the following conditions: (1) Sichuan cuisine and Cantonese cuisine cannot be served continuously. (2) P cannot go before Q unless the second goes on Q. (3) P must go before X. (4) M must go before K, and K must go before N.
item.question: Which of the following lists the order of serving from first to seventh, and which one is eligible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Q, M, P, L, X, K, N

choices.label: B
choices.text: Q, M, X, P, K, N, L

choices.label: C
choices.text: L, P, M, Q, X, K, N

choices.label: D
choices.text: M, Q, K, L, P, X, N

response:
Reasoning: Interpret (1) as no two consecutive dishes can be of the same cuisine type among Sichuan or Cantonese. Check options: A satisfies alternation, P after Q, P before X, and M before K before N. B violates P before X. C violates “if P before Q, Q must be second.” D has K and L consecutive (both Sichuan).
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used direct constraint checking: translate each rule into an ordering or adjacency test, then scan each option for violations. The key factor was interpreting the cuisine rule correctly as forbidding consecutive Sichuan/Cantonese dishes from those two groups, while separately enforcing the chain constraints \(M<K<N\) and \(P<X\), plus the conditional relation between \(P\) and \(Q\). The successful step was eliminating choices by a single decisive violation rather than trying to construct the whole sequence from scratch. For similar problems, convert each condition into a quick checklist and test answer choices systematically, prioritizing hard-order constraints and “if/then” rules first.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a constrained ordering problem: test each proposed sequence against all four rules and identify the one that satisfies every condition. That interpretation was correct, and the most appropriate strategy was direct elimination, since the answer choices already provided complete candidate orders. My key step was correctly reading rule (1) as forbidding consecutive dishes when both are from the Sichuan/Cantonese groups, which means I had to track cuisine categories, not just individual dish names. I also used the precedence constraints effectively: one relation between two Cantonese dishes, one relation involving the Shandong dish, and one chain relation among three dishes. 

The strongest part of my reasoning was combining local checks efficiently: adjacency restrictions, then order constraints, then the special conditional rule about one dish relative to another. I did not rely on unnecessary reconstruction of all possible schedules, which would have been slower and more error-prone. One assumption I handled correctly was that the “unless” clause creates a conditional exception, so the relative order is allowed only in a very specific position. I also correctly noticed that a violation can occur either by reversed precedence or by adjacency of same-category dishes, so different rules operate in different ways. 

What made the reasoning successful was treating each option as a full candidate and systematically falsifying bad ones with a specific rule. For similar problems, I should continue translating each verbal condition into a precise test: adjacency, precedence, conditional precedence, or chained precedence. General rule: in sequencing problems with multiple constraints, classify each constraint by type and check candidates in a fixed order so no condition is forgotten or misapplied.

item.context: A report on acid rain concluded, most forests in Canada are not damaged by acid rain. Critics of the report insist that this conclusion must be changed to, most forests in Canada do not show obvious symptoms of being damaged by acid rain, such as abnormal leaf loss, slower growth or higher mortality.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, provides the most logically strong justification for critics' insistence on changing the conclusions of the report?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some forests in Canada are being damaged by acid rain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acid rain may be causing damage whose symptoms are not yet obvious

choices.label: C
choices.text: The report does not compare the damage caused by acid rain to forests in Canada with the damage caused by acid rain to forests in other countries

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the past 15 years, all forests in Canada have been exposed to acid rain

response:
Reasoning: Critics want weaker wording because lack of obvious symptoms does not prove lack of damage. If acid rain can cause damage before visible signs appear, then saying forests are “not damaged” is too strong; only “do not show obvious symptoms” is justified.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a gap-analysis approach, comparing the report’s strong claim about actual absence of damage with the critics’ weaker claim about absence of visible symptoms. The key factor was the distinction between “not damaged” and “not showing obvious symptoms,” since those are not logically equivalent. My success came from identifying the assumption needed to justify the critics: damage could exist before it becomes observable. For similar problems, test whether the conclusion confuses underlying reality with observable evidence, and prefer the choice that shows why the stronger statement is not warranted.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the strongest justification for weakening a conclusion from a claim about actual absence of damage to a claim about absence of observable symptoms. The key logical issue was the gap between “not damaged” and “not showing obvious symptoms,” which is a classic distinction between an underlying condition and the evidence used to detect it. My strategy was to look for an answer choice that exposed this gap directly, rather than one that merely made acid rain seem relevant or widespread. That was appropriate because the critics were not disputing that forests are exposed to acid rain; they were disputing what the report was entitled to conclude from the evidence. I used the fact that visible indicators like leaf loss, slow growth, and mortality are symptoms, and symptoms can fail to appear even when a condition is present. The crucial relationship was that absence of observed symptoms does not entail absence of the phenomenon itself. I avoided assuming that the report had direct measures of internal damage, since the revised conclusion suggests it relied on observable signs. I also correctly rejected alternatives that were too weak, too indirect, or irrelevant to the logical revision the critics wanted. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the evidentiary standard behind the wording change rather than on the topic of acid rain generally. In similar problems, I should keep testing whether an answer choice attacks the inference itself or merely adds background facts. A transferable rule is: when a conclusion moves from “no observable evidence” to “no underlying condition,” the strongest objection is evidence that the condition can exist without being observable.

item.context: The researchers conducted the following study to study the relationship between sleep and memory. They were tested for sleep and memory at age 21 and 75 respectively. The subjects were tested for word memory before falling asleep at night. The results showed that older people had about 25 percent worse word memory than younger people. During sleep, the researchers used electroencephalograms to detect sleep and brainwave activity in subjects, and older adults slept 75 percent less slow-wave sleep than younger people on average. The day after eight hours of sleep, the researchers again tested memory of previous words. The results showed that older people had a 55 percent worse score in word memory the next day than younger people. As a result, researchers believe that shorter slow-wave sleep times are key to affecting memory in older adults.
item.question: Which of the following options, if correct, would challenge the above view?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The quality of sleep depends on the length of slow-wave sleep and the length of fast-wave sleep

choices.label: B
choices.text: Slow-wave sleep can help transfer newly acquired information from the hippocum region where memories are stored for a short period of time to the prefrontal cortex, where memories are stored in the long term

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most older adults have reduced brain function and memory loss, making it difficult to improve memory even if they sleep longer in slow waves

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the experiment, some older people with shorter slow-wave sleep remembered more words than those who slept longer in slow-wave

response:
Reasoning: The claim is that less slow-wave sleep causes poorer memory in older adults. A and B support or are neutral. C offers an alternative explanation, but D directly contradicts the proposed relationship by showing shorter slow-wave sleep can coincide with better memory in older adults.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a weakening-by-counterexample approach, looking for an option that directly broke the observed correlation between sleep stage length and memory performance. The key clue I focused on was the researchers’ causal claim that shorter slow-wave sleep is the key factor affecting older adults’ memory, so I chose the option that showed an apparent exception within older adults. My mistake was treating a few contrary cases as stronger evidence than an option that attacked causation more fundamentally by offering an alternative limiting factor. For similar problems, I should prefer choices that undermine the claimed causal mechanism or show the proposed cause would not change the outcome, rather than isolated exceptions.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for evidence that weakens a causal claim: that reduced slow-wave sleep is a key factor driving poorer memory in older adults. That interpretation was broadly correct, but my mistake was in treating any counterexample to correlation as the strongest challenge, rather than asking which option most directly undermines the proposed causal mechanism. My strategy was to look for an option showing that less slow-wave sleep does not always correspond to worse memory, which led me to favor the within-group variation described in one choice. However, I underweighted the difference between noisy individual exceptions and a stronger alternative explanation that makes the proposed cause less important or ineffective. The key evidence I should have focused on was the phrase “key to affecting memory,” which invites a challenge to causal centrality, not merely to perfect consistency. I assumed that showing some older individuals with shorter slow-wave sleep performed better would significantly weaken the claim, but isolated variation can coexist with an overall causal trend. I should also have considered whether an option implies that even increasing slow-wave sleep would not materially improve memory, since that would more directly attack the researchers’ conclusion. The error came from preferring a correlation-based rebuttal over a mechanism-based rebuttal. In similar problems, I should rank weakening choices by how directly they reduce explanatory power, not by how superficially contradictory they seem. General rule: when evaluating causal conclusions, the strongest challenge is often evidence of an alternative cause or of causal irrelevance, not merely evidence of imperfect correlation.

item.context: In the 1950s, my country's forest coverage rate was 19%, in the 1960s it was 11%, in the 1970s it was 6%, and in the 1980s it was less than 4%. With the decrease in forest coverage year by year, the vegetation was greatly destroyed, which weakened the land's impact on rainwater. The effect of arresting, a heavy rain, the water rolls and the sand rolls down, making the floods serious year by year. It can be seen that the destruction of forest resources is the cause of the floods.
item.question: Which of the following uses the most similar method to the above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cotton is a plant fiber, loose and porous, and can keep warm. Snow is formed by the freezing of water, with 40% to 50% of the air gap, and it is also loose and porous, which can keep heat. It can be seen that loose and porous are the reason for heat preservation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Divide a group of chickens into two groups. One group is fed with polished white rice. The chickens have a disease, their feet are weak and cannot walk, and the symptoms are similar to human beriberi. The other group is fed with hulled rice, and the chickens must not have this disease. It is speculated that some things that are not in the polished white rice contained in the hulled rice are the cause of beriberi. Further research found that this kind of thing is vitamin B1

choices.label: C
choices.text: The minefield in Italy repeatedly carried out an experiment. Put meat and fish in 4 large-mouth bottles, and then covered with a lid or gauze. Flies could not get in, and there was no maggot. In the other 4 large-mouth bottles, put them in. The same meat and fish, open the bottle door, flies fly in and lay eggs, and the rotten meat and fish quickly become full of maggots. It can be seen that the flies lay eggs are the cause of the rotten maggots of the fish

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bell is energized in the glass cover with air. As the amount of air extracted changes, the ringtone becomes smaller and smaller. If the air is completely extracted, the ringtone will not be heard at all. It can be seen that the sound is transmitted by air

response:
Reasoning: The stem infers causation from correlated changes in one factor and one result over time/degree, without a strict controlled comparison. D uses the same “change one condition, observe corresponding change in outcome, then infer cause” method. B and C are controlled experiments; A is analogy.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a method-of-argument comparison, focusing on the structure of the inference rather than the subject matter. The key factor was that the stem links a gradual change in one condition with a gradual change in an outcome, then draws a causal conclusion without using a true controlled two-group experiment. My success came from separating that pattern from options like B and C, which rely on stronger experimental control, and from rejecting A as mainly analogical reasoning. For similar problems, first classify each argument by its evidence pattern—correlated variation, controlled comparison, analogy, or mechanism—and then match the pattern, not the topic.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stem as asking for a match in argumentative structure, not in subject matter, so the key task was to identify the reasoning pattern behind the flood claim. The passage does not present a controlled experiment; instead, it tracks one factor and one outcome changing together over time, then treats that co-variation as evidence of causation. My strategy was therefore to classify each option by method: analogy, controlled comparison, direct intervention, or correlated variation. That was appropriate because “most similar method” questions are about logical form, not factual correctness.

The crucial evidence I used was that the stem relies on gradual change in a condition and a corresponding gradual change in an effect. I also noticed that some options introduced stronger causal evidence than the stem, such as comparison groups or exclusion of alternative causes, which made them methodologically different even if they also reached causal conclusions. A shortcut that helped was asking, “Does this option manipulate a single factor continuously and observe the outcome vary with it?” I correctly rejected the analogy option because shared properties are not the same as causal co-variation. I also rejected the controlled-test options because they depend on experimental comparison rather than temporal or degree-based variation. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the evidential structure, not on whether the conclusion itself was scientifically sound. In similar problems, I should continue separating argument type from topic and from truth. General rule: when matching reasoning methods, identify the exact evidence-to-conclusion pattern—correlation, analogy, controlled experiment, or elimination—not merely the presence of a causal claim.

item.context: A scientist made three observations: (1) in the world' s temperate zones, food is more plentiful in the ocean than it is in fresh water; (2) migratory fish in temperate zones generally mature in the ocean and spawn in fresh water; and (3) migratory fish need much nourishment as they mature but little or none during the part of their lives when they spawn. On the basis of those observations, the scientist formulated the hypothesis that food availability is a determining factor in the migration of migratory fish. Subsequently the scientist learned that in the tropics migratory fish generally mature in fresh water and spawn in the ocean.
item.question: Which one of the following would it be most helpful to know in order to judge whether what the scientist subsequently learned calls into question the hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: whether in the tropics food is less plentiful in the ocean than in fresh water

choices.label: B
choices.text: whether any species of fish with populations in temperate zones also have populations that live in the tropics

choices.label: C
choices.text: whether in the world's temperate zones, the temperatures of bodies of fresh water tend to be lower than those of the regions of the oceans into which they flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: whether there are more species of migratory fish in the tropics than there are in temperate zones

response:
Reasoning: The hypothesis ties migration direction to where food is more plentiful during maturation. In temperate zones, fish mature where food is abundant. To see if the tropical pattern challenges this, we need to know whether tropical fresh water has more food than the ocean. If yes, the hypothesis still fits; if no, it is undermined.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a consistency test: I matched the hypothesis’s causal claim to the new tropical migration pattern and asked what background fact would determine whether the pattern supports or weakens that claim. The key factor was the relationship between where fish mature, where they need the most nourishment, and which environment has greater food availability. The successful step was focusing on the one missing comparative fact in the tropics rather than getting distracted by species counts or temperature. For similar problems, identify the hypothesis’s core causal variable and ask which new fact would directly test whether that variable still predicts the observed pattern in the new setting.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking not which option explains migration in general, but which additional fact would best test whether the new tropical observation weakens the scientist’s food-availability hypothesis. My strategy was to identify the core causal claim in the hypothesis: fish mature where nourishment is most available and spawn where little nourishment is needed. That was the right framework because the new information only matters insofar as it matches or conflicts with that predicted relationship. I used the key evidence appropriately: in temperate zones, ocean food abundance aligns with ocean maturation, and spawning occurs in fresh water where feeding matters less. The crucial missing fact for the tropics, then, was the relative food supply in tropical ocean versus fresh water, since that determines whether the reversed migration pattern is consistent or inconsistent with the hypothesis. I avoided being distracted by answer choices about species counts, overlapping populations, or temperature, because those do not directly test the stated causal variable. One assumption I made was that “food availability is a determining factor” means it should predict the maturation habitat across regions; that assumption was justified by the structure of the scientist’s original reasoning. A weaker approach would have treated the new tropical pattern as automatically disconfirming, without checking whether the environmental food pattern also reverses. What made the reasoning successful was matching the needed evidence to the exact variable named in the hypothesis rather than to loosely related biological facts. In similar problems, I should first restate the hypothesis as a conditional relationship, then ask what new fact would most directly confirm or threaten that relationship. General rule: when evaluating whether new evidence challenges a causal hypothesis, seek the missing information about the hypothesized cause in the new setting, not peripheral differences between the cases.

item.context: A school has seven outstanding students G, H, L, M, U, W and Z. During the summer vacation, the school will send them to England and the United States to study. Only these seven students from the school took part in the activity, and each of them happened to go to one of the two countries. Considering the specialty of each student, the following conditions must be met in this activity: (1) if G goes to the England, then H goes to the United States. (2) if L goes to England, then both M and U go to the United States. (3) the country where W goes is different from that of Z. (4) the country where U goes is different from that of G. (5) if Z goes to the England, H also goes to the England.
item.question: Which of the followings can be true if both M and W go to the England?

choices.label: A
choices.text: G and L both go to the England

choices.label: B
choices.text: G and U both go to the United States

choices.label: C
choices.text: H and Z both go to the England

choices.label: D
choices.text: L and U both go to the United States

response:
Reasoning: Since W goes to England, Z must go to the United States.  
A: L in England would force M to the U.S., impossible.  
B: G and U both in the U.S. violates “U different from G.”  
C: Z cannot be in England.  
D: Let M,W,G go to England; H,L,U,Z go to the U.S. All conditions hold.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a constraint-propagation approach: start from the added condition that M and W go to England, then apply each rule to eliminate impossible options and test the remaining one with a full assignment. The key factor was noticing that W in England forces Z to the United States, which immediately rules out any option requiring Z in England and simplifies the other conditions. The successful step was checking the surviving choice by constructing a concrete arrangement rather than assuming it worked abstractly. For similar problems, first derive all forced placements from the strongest given conditions, then verify any remaining candidate with an explicit complete scenario.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task correctly as a “could be true” question under an added condition, so the goal was not to prove one option must happen but to eliminate options that create contradictions and find one option consistent with all rules. My strategy was to start with the extra premise that both M and W go to England and immediately propagate forced consequences from the conditional rules. That was appropriate because these problems are best handled by chaining implications from the strongest fixed placements before testing answer choices. The key fact I used first was that W and Z must be in different countries, so W in England forced Z to the United States; this single deduction ruled out any option requiring Z in England. I also used the rule that U and G must be in different countries, which directly eliminated any option placing them together. For the option involving L in England, I correctly noticed that this would force both M and U to the United States, which conflicts with the fixed condition that M is already in England. My successful step on the remaining option was to construct one full assignment and verify each rule rather than relying on partial intuition. A potential risk would have been assuming that once an option avoids one contradiction it must work; instead, I checked every condition systematically. The general lesson is: in conditional-assignment problems, first derive all consequences of the given setup, then reject options by contradiction, and for any surviving “can be true” candidate, confirm it with a complete consistent model.

item.context: In the face of the current complex international and domestic situation, China's future industrial development will gradually present two major grasps: one is to adapt to the changing trend of demand structure and speed up the technological transformation of traditional industries; the second is to scientifically judge the future market demand changes and technological development trends, and speed up the development of strategic emerging industries. At present, the pattern of global economic competition is undergoing profound changes, scientific and technological development is giving birth to new revolutionary breakthroughs, and the development of strategic emerging industries has become a major strategy for major countries in the world to seize the commanding heights of the new round of economic and scientific and technological development.
item.question: Which of the following is the most likely content of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: China should promote the progress of science and technology and enhance the ability of independent development

choices.label: B
choices.text: China should seize the commanding heights of the new round of economic and scientific and technological development

choices.label: C
choices.text: China should promote the technological transformation of traditional industries

choices.label: D
choices.text: China should speed up the development of strategic emerging industries

response:
Reasoning: The passage mentions two “grasps,” but it focuses especially on judging future demand/technology trends and says developing strategic emerging industries is a major global strategy. So the most likely main content is accelerating strategic emerging industries, not just traditional-industry upgrading or a broader slogan.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach: I compared the passage’s overall emphasis with each option and looked for the choice that matched the author’s central focus rather than a side point. The key factor was that, although the passage mentions two tasks, it gives much more explanatory support to the second one by discussing global competition, technological breakthroughs, and the strategic importance of emerging industries. My success came from weighting emphasis, not just counting topics mentioned. For similar problems, identify which idea the passage develops most fully and choose the option that captures that emphasis rather than a broader or merely partial statement.
