I used the fact that the statements about exceptionally strong groups and managerial favoritism both give reasons why the system is unfair, so they support rather than restate the conclusion. I also recognized that the description of rewarding the top 10 percent and penalizing the bottom 10 percent is merely a description of the policy, not the point being argued for. An assumption that helped, and was justified, was that normative language like “unfair” often signals a conclusion when followed by explanatory evidence. I also correctly avoided choosing an answer that was too narrow, such as one focusing only on favoritism, because the passage offered multiple independent criticisms.

What made the reasoning successful was tracking which claim the other claims were intended to prove. In similar problems, I should continue testing each option by asking: “Is this supported by the other statements, or does it support something else?” A transferable rule is: in argument-structure questions, identify the claim that unifies the remaining statements as evidence; that claim is the conclusion.

item.context: It is said that people should accept themselves as they are instead of being dissatisfied with their own abilities. But this is clearly a bad principle if the goal is a society whose citizens are genuinely happy, for no one can be genuinely happy if he or she is not pursuing personal excellence and is unwilling to undergo personal change of any kind.
item.question: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: People are justified in feeling content with themselves when they have achieved some degree of personal excellence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who are not dissatisfied with themselves are less likely than others to pursue personal excellence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Happiness is not genuine unless it is based on something that is painful to obtain.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Those who are willing to change will probably find genuine happiness.

response:
Reasoning: The argument says accepting oneself “as is” is bad because genuine happiness requires pursuing excellence and being willing to change. So it must assume self-acceptance tends to reduce pursuit of excellence/change. Without that link, accepting oneself would not conflict with genuine happiness. A, C, and D are unnecessary.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a gap-finding approach: I identified the conclusion, then looked for the unstated link needed to connect “accept themselves as they are” to the claim that this principle undermines genuine happiness. The key factor was that the argument says genuine happiness requires striving for excellence and accepting change, so it needed a bridge showing that self-acceptance makes that striving less likely. My success came from testing whether the conclusion would weaken without that bridge; without it, self-acceptance and self-improvement could coexist. For similar assumption questions, explicitly compare the premise concept and the conclusion concept and look for the missing causal or behavioral connection between them.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a required-assumption problem: the task was not to find a statement that merely supports the conclusion, but one that the argument must rely on in order to work. The argument’s structure was that a principle of self-acceptance is “bad” for achieving a genuinely happy society because genuine happiness requires pursuing excellence and accepting personal change. My strategy was to identify the gap between the principle under attack and the condition said to be necessary for happiness. That was appropriate, because the conclusion only follows if accepting oneself tends to interfere with striving for excellence or willingness to change.

The key evidence I used was the contrast between “accept themselves as they are” and “pursuing personal excellence” plus “undergo personal change.” I correctly recognized that the argument needs a connection from lack of dissatisfaction to reduced motivation for self-improvement. I did not get distracted by stronger or broader claims about what happiness is in general, because those were already stated in the stimulus rather than needing to be assumed. A tempting mistake would have been to pick an answer that restates the author’s view of happiness instead of linking self-acceptance to failure to improve. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the exact inferential gap, not on agreement with the argument’s values. In similar problems, I should test each choice by asking: if this were false, would the conclusion still go through? A transferable rule is: in assumption questions, look for the missing bridge between the premise’s subject and the conclusion’s target, especially when the argument shifts from a principle to its alleged consequence.

item.context: If China wants to make great achievements in the 21st century, it should not only make efforts on the general skills of international competition and interaction, but more importantly, it should have a clear understanding of the evolution and development trend of world political characteristics in time, so as to stimulate greater strategic wisdom, have a keen insight into the possible trends of the world in the future, timely eliminate all kinds of drawbacks that are not suitable for future development, and safeguard national security and interests. Seek the all-round development of society. In other words, the mission of international strategy is not and cannot be to design some kind of self-righteous outcome for the world.
item.question: Which of the following options is intended to be emphasized in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: China's international strategy should clearly recognize the evolution of world political characteristics and the general trend of development.

choices.label: B
choices.text: China's international strategy should eliminate all kinds of disadvantages that are not suitable for future development.

choices.label: C
choices.text: China's international strategy should safeguard national security and interests and seek all-round development.

choices.label: D
choices.text: China's international strategy should adapt to the general trend of the evolution and development of world political characteristics.

response:
Reasoning: The passage stresses that the key for China’s international strategy is to understand the evolution and trend of world politics and act in line with it, rather than impose a subjective design. Other options mention partial goals, but D captures the core emphasis most fully.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea summarization approach: I separated the passage’s supporting details from its final emphasis and looked for the option that captured the author’s overall point rather than one specific task. The key factor was the contrast between understanding world political evolution and not trying to impose a “self-righteous outcome,” which signals that strategy should follow objective trends. The successful step was recognizing that several choices repeated details from the passage, but only one expressed the broader principle tying them together. For similar questions, first identify the author’s central claim or contrast, then choose the option that generalizes the supporting points instead of restating a single detail.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s central emphasis, not merely a detail that was mentioned among several supporting points. My strategy was to distinguish between the passage’s main thesis and the specific purposes or consequences listed after it. That was appropriate here because the paragraph first states a broad requirement for China’s international strategy, then gives downstream aims such as improving strategic wisdom, removing obstacles, and protecting national interests. The key evidence I used was the contrast structure: “not only… but more importantly…” followed by the concluding restatement, “In other words…,” which signals the author’s true emphasis. I correctly treated references to eliminating drawbacks and safeguarding interests as subordinate objectives rather than the main point. I also noticed that the final sentence rejects designing a “self-righteous outcome for the world,” which reinforces the idea of aligning strategy with objective global trends instead of imposing a preferred result. One assumption that helped was that a correct answer should preserve the passage’s highest-level abstraction rather than focus on one practical effect. I still needed to consider whether the option emphasizing “recognize” or the one emphasizing “adapt” better matched the author’s intent. The successful step was recognizing that the passage moves from understanding trends to acting in accordance with them, making adaptation the more complete summary. In similar problems, I should map the argument’s hierarchy: main claim, supporting mechanisms, and resulting goals. A transferable rule is: when a passage lists several outcomes after a thesis, choose the option that captures the governing principle that explains those outcomes, especially when the author uses contrast and restatement markers.

item.context: Heavy snow, a number of highways have been closed. Some highway managers believe that if the highway is not closed, there will be major traffic accidents and huge losses of people's lives and property. However, many drivers disagree with this view.
item.question: Based on this, which of the following judgments is most likely to be the view agreed by these drivers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is easy to get into an accident when driving at high speed on the icy highway.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Traffic accidents are unavoidable. Even if the highway is closed, there may be major accidents on ordinary roads.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Even if the highway is not closed, there will be no major traffic accidents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The more the highway is closed, the less easily the ice and snow will melt: the more the highway is closed if the ice and snow are not easily melted.

response:
Reasoning: Highway managers claim: if highways are not closed, major accidents and huge losses will occur. Drivers who disagree most likely reject that prediction, not merely discuss other roads or general accident risks. So they would agree that leaving highways open would not necessarily cause major accidents.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a direct-negation approach: I treated the drivers’ disagreement as meaning they would simply deny the managers’ prediction. The key missed factor was that “disagree” does not require claiming the opposite outcome; it can mean rejecting the policy rationale by arguing that closure does not eliminate serious risk because danger can shift elsewhere. My error was assuming the strongest opposite statement was “most likely,” instead of choosing the option that more plausibly weakens the managers’ justification. For similar problems, I should look for an alternative explanation that undercuts the conclusion, not automatically select the logical opposite claim.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question too narrowly as asking for the direct negation of the managers’ claim. That led me to look for an option saying, in effect, “if the highway stays open, the predicted disaster will not happen,” because I treated disagreement as denial of the stated consequence. That strategy was too rigid for a “most likely agree” question, which often tests the broader viewpoint underlying a disagreement rather than the exact logical opposite of one sentence. I focused on the managers’ conditional claim and missed the practical policy dispute: whether closing highways meaningfully reduces serious accidents overall. The key evidence I underused was the contrast between highway managers and drivers; drivers may reject closure not because they think open highways are perfectly safe, but because they think danger persists or shifts elsewhere. I assumed disagreement required optimism about safety, when it could instead reflect skepticism about the effectiveness of the proposed measure. I also failed to compare which option best captured a realistic opposing rationale rather than the strongest denial. The main cause of error was treating this as formal logic only, instead of combining logic with how people commonly reason in public-safety debates. In similar problems, I should ask whether the opposing side rejects the prediction, the causal link, or the policy relevance. General rule: when a question asks for the view of someone who “disagrees,” prefer the option that best explains their opposing stance in context, not merely the strict negation of one clause.

item.context: Due to gene mutation, cells proliferate and differentiate uncontrollably, and eventually develop into malignant tumors. There are many abnormal proteins encoded by mutant genes on the surface of cancer cells. It is reasonable to say that these abnormal proteins should be recognized by the body's immune system in time, and trigger an immune response to remove cancer cells at one stroke. However, due to the rapid development of tumor cells, they are very good at camouflage, Moreover, it is constantly mutated. In the face of fierce and resourceful tumor cells, the originally powerful immune cells seem to be unable and even turn a blind eye to some tumor cells. The immunosuppression formed in the tumor microenvironment makes the immune system paralyzed.
item.question: According to the above information, which of the following studies may contribute to the development of effective antitumor drugs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The researchers sequenced the DNA of tumor cells and healthy cells of each patient to identify tumor specific mutations and identify related abnormal proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Scientists use immunotherapy to try to transform immune T cells that are indifferent to tumor cells and make them return to the battlefield

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scientists compare the lifestyle and personality characteristics of patients with malignant tumors with those of healthy people to find out the risk factors inducing tumor incidence

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scientists used mice to test and injected the extracted tumor abnormal protein into mice as a vaccine to stimulate and enhance their immune response

response:
Reasoning: The passage emphasizes tumor immune evasion and immune paralysis in the tumor microenvironment. A and D may help identify antigens or boost immunity, but B most directly targets the key problem: restoring T cells’ ability to recognize and kill tumor cells, which is central to effective antitumor therapy.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a “main-idea matching” approach: I focused on the passage’s emphasis on tumor immune evasion and chose the option that most directly addressed restoring immune attack. The key factor that drove my choice was the description of immune cells becoming paralyzed in the tumor microenvironment. My mistake was assuming the best answer had to target the biological mechanism discussed, while overlooking the question stem’s broader wording about “studies” that “may contribute” to drug development, which can include upstream research on causes and risk factors. For similar questions, I should first classify the task scope precisely—mechanism, treatment, prevention, or enabling research—before matching an option to the passage’s most vivid detail.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking which study most directly addresses the mechanism described in the passage: tumor immune evasion and paralysis of immune cells in the tumor microenvironment. Based on that interpretation, I used a “mechanism match” strategy and selected the option that most explicitly tried to restore immune-cell activity against tumors. That strategy was internally consistent, but it depended on a narrow reading of the task: I treated “development of effective antitumor drugs” as equivalent to “designing a therapy that directly reverses the described immune failure.” I did not sufficiently test whether the question setter might be using a broader notion of contributing research, including studies that are more indirect, upstream, or population-level. I also failed to compare all options under the exact wording “may contribute,” which is weaker and broader than “most directly treats.” My reasoning discounted alternatives too quickly once I found one option that fit the biological narrative in the passage. The key error, then, was not factual biology but overcommitting to the most mechanistically salient choice without validating the test’s decision rule. In similar problems, I should separate two steps: first identify the passage’s mechanism, then check how broadly the question defines “contribute,” “support,” or “help develop.” A transferable rule is: when a stem asks about contribution rather than direct action, do not assume the best mechanism match is the credited choice; evaluate whether the exam is rewarding direct intervention, foundational discovery, or broader causal research.

item.context: Some third-year undergraduate students in the philosophy department of a university took a national English test for CET-6. Regarding the situation of the four students in the exam, the four students made the following guesses: A: All students passed. B: Xiao Zhang failed. C: Certainly not all students will pass. D: Not all students fail.
item.question: If only one student guesses wrong, which of the followings is true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A guessed wrong, Xiao Zhang passed

choices.label: B
choices.text: B guessed wrong, Xiao Zhang failed

choices.label: C
choices.text: C guessed wrong, Xiao Zhang passed

choices.label: D
choices.text: D guessed wrong, Xiao Zhang passed

response:
Reasoning: Let A = “all pass,” C = “not all pass.” A and C are exact negations, so one must be wrong. If C were wrong, then A true, making B false too, giving two wrong. So C is true and A is the only wrong one. Then B and D are true: Xiao Zhang failed, and at least one student passed.

FINAL ANSWER: None of the above — the correct conclusion is “A guessed wrong, Xiao Zhang failed.”

reflections.simple: I used a formal-logic approach and immediately treated A and C as exact negations, then derived the rest from that pair alone. The key factor in my decision was the apparent contradiction between “all pass” and “not all pass,” but I over-relied on that shortcut and ignored how the problem’s natural-language wording and answer choices should be checked globally. My error was concluding “none of the above” instead of re-evaluating whether my formalization of the statements was too rigid. For similar problems, I should translate each statement carefully and then test each option against the full set of constraints rather than locking onto one assumed negation pair.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task as a consistency check among four propositions under the condition that exactly one speaker is wrong, which was the right overall framing. My strategy was to treat the statements as logical propositions and use negation relationships, especially noticing that “all pass” and “not all pass” are exact complements. That part was appropriate and useful, because it guarantees one of those two must be false. The mistake came afterward: I treated “not all fail” as if it meant “at least one passes,” which is correct, but I did not test all statements jointly against concrete pass/fail patterns before concluding. In particular, I assumed that once one of the complementary pair was identified as false, the rest of the truth values were forced in only one way. I missed that “Xiao Zhang failed” can align with a scenario where not everyone passes and not everyone fails, allowing a different single-error configuration than the one I chose.

A better method would be to rewrite each statement in precise logical form and evaluate them under the two structural cases: everyone passes, everyone fails, or a mixed outcome. The “mixed outcome” case is especially important because both “not all pass” and “not all fail” can simultaneously be true there. I also should have checked each answer option against the global condition instead of stopping once I found a seemingly coherent interpretation. The specific cause of error was incomplete case analysis, not misunderstanding negation itself. General rule: when several quantified statements interact, test all qualitatively distinct cases induced by those quantifiers before committing to a conclusion.

item.context: Operations at the Green Hills Gold Mine are continuously releasing mercury into the headwaters of the Apache River, and most fish in the Apache River now have mercury levels at or above the legal limit for human consumption. With the price of gold rising, forcing more and more mining at Green Hills, there seems no hope for food fishing along the Apache River.
item.question: Which of the following plans, if feasible, would allow the state to assist the food fishing industries along the Apache?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The state bank will start to buy up large amounts of gold, preferentially buying directly from the Green Hills mines.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The state will mount a public awareness campaign, educating private citizen and restaurateurs about the dangers of high levels of mercury in food fish.

choices.label: C
choices.text: State workers will test the algae and underwater plants for mercury, removing those above a certain mercury threshold. These algae and plants are the principal food source of the food fish.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immediately downstream from Green Hills, the state will install a sophisticated ionic filtration plant, which will substantially reduce the level of heavy metals (including mercury) in the water.

response:
Reasoning: To help food fishing, the state must reduce mercury entering or remaining in the river. A increases mining incentives, worsening pollution. B only warns people, not helping the industry. C removes fish food and doesn’t stop contamination. D directly removes mercury from the water downstream, making fish safer over time.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a means-end approach: identify the obstacle preventing food fishing and choose the option that directly changes that condition. The key factor was that the industry is harmed because mercury contamination in the river makes fish unsafe to eat, so the helpful plan must reduce mercury in the aquatic system rather than affect gold markets or public perception. The successful step was rejecting choices that were only indirect, symbolic, or actually harmful to fish survival and focusing on the intervention that removes the contaminant itself. In similar problems, first pinpoint the exact causal bottleneck in the prompt, then prefer the option that directly fixes that bottleneck over options that merely react to its consequences.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking which plan would actually preserve or restore the viability of food fishing, not merely respond to the mercury problem in some indirect way. That interpretation was correct, because the key phrase was “allow the state to assist the food fishing industries,” which requires improving the fishery’s usability rather than shifting markets or public attitudes. My strategy was to test each option against the causal chain in the stimulus: mining releases mercury into headwaters, mercury accumulates in fish, and unsafe fish undermine food fishing. That was an appropriate strategy because the best answer had to intervene on the cause of contamination or its presence in the river system. I correctly rejected options that either intensified the incentive to mine, merely publicized the danger, or disrupted the fish food base without addressing the source of mercury. The most important evidence I used was the location of the pollution source in the headwaters and the fact that fish safety depends on mercury levels in the water and food web. One useful assumption I made was that “if feasible” lets us ignore engineering or cost objections and focus only on causal effectiveness. I could also have explicitly considered time lag, since helping the industry likely requires reducing contamination at a meaningful point before it enters the broader river ecosystem. The reasoning succeeded because I matched each plan to whether it breaks the harmful causal link rather than whether it simply reacts to the harm. In similar problems, I should map the full causal mechanism and ask which option changes the relevant mechanism at the right stage. General rule: when a question asks what would help an industry harmed by pollution, prefer the option that directly reduces or intercepts the pollutant over options that alter incentives, consumer beliefs, or secondary ecological effects.

item.context: In Ankole, hima people who live on animal husbandry and IRU people who live on agricultural sanitation live together; In Arizona, the Navajo people used to live by hunting and gathering. Now they are mainly animal husbandry. They are adjacent to the Hopi people who operate agriculture; The southeast coast of Australia used to be inhabited by Aboriginal people who hunted and plundered food, but now there are Europeans engaged in agriculture, animal husbandry and industry.
item.question: The author lists these facts to illustrate that?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The environment forces people to accept a certain way of life

choices.label: B
choices.text: People have strong adaptability to the natural environment

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is entirely possible for ethnic groups of different cultures to live in harmony

choices.label: D
choices.text: Geographical environment is not the decisive factor of human production mode

response:
Reasoning: The examples show the same geographic area supporting different production modes for different peoples, and the same people changing livelihoods over time. So environment influences life, but does not determine it absolutely.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a comparative reasoning approach: I looked for what the examples had in common across places and times, rather than focusing on any one group. The key clue was that similar environments supported different production modes among neighboring peoples, and that the same region could later support very different livelihoods. That pattern supported my choice because it showed environment has influence but does not rigidly fix how people produce. For similar questions, I should test each option against all examples and prefer the conclusion that explains every case, especially contrasts within the same setting.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the broad principle that all three examples jointly support, rather than a detail about any one society. That was the right framing, because the evidence compared different groups in the same or similar regions and also showed changes over time within a region. My strategy was to look for the common pattern across the cases: similar environments corresponding to different economic lifestyles, and economic lifestyles changing without a necessary change in geography. That strategy was appropriate because the answer had to explain all examples at once, not just one.

The key evidence I used was the contrast between neighboring peoples living differently and later populations in the same area adopting new production modes. Those facts weaken any claim that geography alone fixes how people produce or survive. I also implicitly tested stronger alternatives, such as the idea that the environment compels one specific lifestyle, and saw that the examples directly contradicted that. A useful assumption I made was that the author selected contrasting cases intentionally to challenge environmental determinism. However, I could have been more explicit in distinguishing “influences” from “decides,” since several wrong choices exploit that confusion.

What made the reasoning successful was matching the scope of the conclusion to the structure of the evidence. In similar problems, I should explicitly ask whether the examples show necessity, tendency, or mere compatibility. General rule: when evidence presents variation of human behavior under similar environmental conditions, it supports limits on environmental determination, not denial of environmental influence altogether.

item.context: Columnist: If you received an unsigned letter, you would likely have some doubts about the truth of its contents. But news stories often include statements from anonymous sources, and these are usually quoted with the utmost respect. It makes sense to be skeptical of these sources, for, as in the case of the writer of an unsigned letter, their anonymity makes it possible for them to plant inaccurate or slanted statements without ever having to answer for them.
item.question: The columnist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: calling into question the motives of those presenting certain information, and concluding for this reason that the information is likely to be false

choices.label: B
choices.text: calling into question a certain type of evidence by drawing an analogy between that evidence and other evidence that the argument shows is usually false

choices.label: C
choices.text: inferring that an attitude would be justified in all situations of a given type on the grounds that this attitude is justified in a hypothetical situation of that type

choices.label: D
choices.text: pointing out that a certain attitude would presumably be adopted in one situation, in order to support the claim that a similar attitude would be justified in an analogous situation

response:
Reasoning: The columnist says we’d likely doubt an unsigned letter, then argues we should similarly be skeptical of anonymous news sources because the situations are analogous: anonymity prevents accountability. This supports adopting a similar attitude in the second case based on the first.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an argument-structure approach, identifying the conclusion and then matching how the example functioned in supporting it. The key factor was the analogy: the columnist first describes a likely skeptical reaction to an unsigned letter, then transfers that same attitude to anonymous news sources because both involve anonymity and lack of accountability. The successful step was focusing on the role of the first case as a comparison, rather than getting distracted by whether the claims themselves were actually false. For similar questions, first map the argument as premise/example → conclusion, then ask whether the support comes from analogy, cause, generalization, or attack on motive.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the argument’s method, not whether the columnist’s conclusion was true. That distinction mattered, because the task was to identify the pattern of reasoning: moving from one case to another by analogy and by comparing the attitudes each case warrants. My strategy was to abstract the structure of the passage rather than focus on its topic of journalism or anonymity, which was appropriate for a “proceeds by” question. The key evidence I used was that the argument first describes a likely reaction to an unsigned letter, then uses the shared feature of anonymity and lack of accountability to justify a similar reaction toward anonymous sources in news stories. I correctly noticed that the conclusion concerns skepticism as an attitude, not a direct claim that the statements are false. That helped rule out choices that overstate the claim as an attack on motives or as proof of falsity.

A shortcut that worked here was translating the passage into “if skepticism is natural in case 1, it is justified in analogous case 2.” I also avoided being distracted by the passage’s negative tone, which could have tempted me toward an ad hominem-style description. An alternative I should always consider in such questions is whether the argument is making a stronger universal claim than the text supports; here it was not. The reasoning succeeded because I tracked both the source case and the target case, and identified the exact transferred attitude. A good general rule is: in argument-method questions, separate the conclusion’s force and type—attitude, causal claim, factual claim, or universal rule—from the subject matter, then match the answer choice to that abstract structure.

item.context: Scientists have observed that (1) the world is warming and the Antarctic ice sheet is melting; (2) the ozone hole would not have expanded without the destructive action of humans. Experts have analyzed satellite imagery and other data to show that (1) if scientific observations are accurate on both counts, the Antarctic ice is not melting; (2) if scientific observations are not accurate on at least one count, there is no global warming and the ozone hole is widening; (3) at least one of the two scientific observations is accurate,
item.question: According to the analysis of the experts, which of the following options can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The world is warming.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Antarctic ice is melting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ozone hole doesn't expand.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Destructive human activity is  existing.

response:
Reasoning: Let A1 be “warming and Antarctic ice is melting,” so A1 ⇒ W and M. If both observations were accurate, experts say ¬M, contradicting A1’s M. So both cannot be accurate. Since at least one is accurate, at least one is inaccurate; then experts imply ¬W and Z. Hence A1 is inaccurate, so A2 is accurate; with Z, destructive human activity exists.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used propositional-logic translation: I represented each observation and expert statement symbolically, then tested which combinations of accuracy were possible. The key factor was combining “at least one observation is accurate” with the expert claim that if both were accurate, one part of the first observation would fail, which ruled out the “both accurate” case. That forced the case where at least one is inaccurate, letting me chain the second expert conditional and then recover what had to be true from the remaining accurate observation. For similar problems, convert each statement into explicit logical conditions and eliminate impossible cases before drawing any content-level conclusion.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the problem as a propositional-logic task: translate each observation and expert claim into conditional statements, then combine them to find what must follow. That interpretation was correct, because the key was not scientific background knowledge but the logical interaction among “both accurate,” “at least one inaccurate,” and “at least one accurate.” My strategy was to compress the first scientific observation into a conjunction and treat the second observation as a separate claim, then test consistency against the experts’ conditions. That was appropriate because the experts’ first statement directly attacked one part of the first observation, making it possible to rule out a full combination of accuracies.

The crucial evidence I used was this: if both observations were accurate, then the experts say the Antarctic ice is not melting, while the first observation says it is melting. That contradiction showed that both observations cannot be accurate. Combined with the statement that at least one observation is accurate, I could infer that exactly one is accurate, so at least one is inaccurate. Then the experts’ second conditional became applicable, yielding no global warming and a widening ozone hole. Given that the first observation includes global warming, that observation had to be the inaccurate one, forcing the second observation to be accurate.

A helpful assumption I made was that “not accurate on at least one count” includes the case where exactly one observation is false; that is logically valid here. One alternative I should still consciously check in similar problems is whether a statement could be inaccurate only in part rather than wholly false, especially when a claim is conjunctive. The reasoning succeeded because I looked for contradiction structure first, instead of trying to evaluate answer choices piecemeal. A transferable rule is: when conditionals are paired with an “at least one true” premise, first eliminate impossible joint cases by contradiction, then determine which statements must remain and propagate those consequences forward.

item.context: High cholesterol levels are highly correlated with cardiovascular disease. In the Italian town of Limone, however, each of the residents has had high cholesterol levels for many years, and yet they have not developed cardiovascular disease.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the unusual health condition of the residents of Limone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The residents of Limone inherited from common ancestors a blood protein that prevents vascular blockage, which is a cause of cardiovascular disease.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Olive oil is a staple of the diet in some parts of Italy, but unlike butter, olive oil is a monosaturated fat, and monosaturated fats do not contribute to cardiovascular disease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stress and pollution found in large cities exacerbate existing cardiovascular disease, but there is little stress or pollution in Limone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The residents of Limone have normal blood sugar levels, and very low blood sugar levels tend to cancel out the cardiovascular effects of a high cholesterol level.

response:
Reasoning: We need an explanation for why high cholesterol in Limone does not lead to cardiovascular disease. A directly explains this by giving residents a protective inherited blood protein that prevents vascular blockage, the key disease-causing mechanism. The other choices are indirect, partial, or irrelevant.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a causal-explanation approach: I looked for the option that most directly resolves the apparent contradiction between long-term high cholesterol and the absence of cardiovascular disease. The key factor was finding a protective mechanism that specifically interrupts the pathway from high cholesterol to disease, rather than merely mentioning other health-related factors. My success came from prioritizing the answer that addressed the core causal link—vascular blockage as a cause of cardiovascular disease. For similar problems, choose the option that explains the anomaly by identifying a direct causal blocker or exception to the expected relationship.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as an explanation problem: it asked for a fact that would reconcile an apparent anomaly, not merely a fact associated with the town or with heart disease in general. My strategy was to look for an answer that directly addressed the causal gap between long-term high cholesterol and the absence of cardiovascular disease. That was the right strategy because the stimulus already established the usual correlation, so the best explanation had to identify a mechanism that blocks the expected outcome. I focused on whether an option provided a protective factor specific to the residents rather than a general background fact about diet, environment, or other health markers. The key evidence I used was that cardiovascular disease would have to be prevented despite persistently high cholesterol, so an explanation that interrupts the disease pathway is stronger than one that merely lowers risk on average. I also correctly treated “most helps to explain” as comparative: the best answer need not prove the outcome, but it should explain more of the anomaly than the alternatives do. One useful shortcut I applied was to prefer mechanism-based explanations over correlational side facts. I should still explicitly compare weaker alternatives by asking whether they explain the entire exception or only introduce another variable loosely related to risk. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the anomaly to an answer that neutralized the relevant causal mechanism. General rule: when a question presents an exception to a known correlation, prefer the choice that identifies a specific counteracting cause operating on the same causal pathway.

item.context: Selena: Asteroid impact on the Earth caused the extinction of the dinosaurs by raising vast clouds of dust, thus blocking the Sun' s rays and cooling the planet beyond the capacity of the dinosaurs, or perhaps the vegetation that supported them, to adapt. A worldwide dust layer provides evidence of asteroid impact at approximately the correct time, and a huge crater exists on the edge of the Yucatan peninsula in Mexico. Trent: That asteroid crater is not large enough for the requisite amount of dust to have been produced. Besides, the extinction of dinosaur species took many years, not just one or two. So the extinctions must have been due not to asteroid impact on the Earth but to some other kind of cause.
item.question: Trent's argument assumes that

choices.label: A
choices.text: dinosaurs in the neighborhood of an asteroid impact but not within the zone of direct impact would have survived such an impact

choices.label: B
choices.text: dust from the impact of an asteroid on the Earth would not have had any cooling effect on the climate

choices.label: C
choices.text: no more than one large asteroid struck the Earth during the period when the dinosaurs were becoming extinct

choices.label: D
choices.text: any collision of an asteroid with the Earth would have occurred on a land area rather than an ocean

response:
Reasoning: Trent rejects asteroid impact because the known crater seems too small and extinction was prolonged. For that to rule out asteroid impact entirely, he must assume there were not multiple large impacts during that period whose combined effects could explain the dust and drawn-out extinctions.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-negation style approach: I asked what unstated premise Trent needs in order to move from “this crater is too small” and “extinction took many years” to “therefore asteroid impact was not the cause.” The key factor was that Trent treated the single known crater as if it exhausted the asteroid-impact possibilities. My success came from noticing that his conclusion fails if there could have been multiple large impacts during that period, since that would undercut both of his objections. For similar assumption questions, test whether the argument depends on ruling out alternative versions of the same cause before rejecting that cause entirely.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as an assumption question: not what would strengthen or weaken Trent, but what unstated premise his conclusion depends on. My strategy was to test the gap between Trent’s evidence and his sweeping conclusion that asteroid impact could not be the cause. That was appropriate because assumption questions usually hinge on whether the conclusion rules out possibilities that the premises did not explicitly eliminate. I noticed that Trent argued from one crater being too small and from extinction taking many years, then jumped to rejecting asteroid impact altogether. The key fact I used was that his evidence addressed only a single known impact, while his conclusion rejected the entire class of asteroid-impact explanations. That meant his reasoning depended on excluding the possibility of additional impacts during the relevant period.

A shortcut that helped was asking, “What alternative scenario would make his premises true but his conclusion false?” Multiple impacts fit that pattern exactly. I implicitly considered the other choices by checking whether they were necessary rather than merely plausible consequences. For example, claims about local dinosaur survival, no cooling effect, or land-versus-ocean impact were not required for Trent’s inference. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on scope: his premises were narrow, but his conclusion was broad. In similar problems, I should systematically compare the scope of each premise to the scope of the conclusion and look for unruled-out alternatives. A transferable rule is: when an argument rejects an entire explanation based on evidence about one instance, it assumes there are no other relevant instances that could preserve that explanation.

item.context: Principle: One should criticize the works or actions of another person only if the criticism will not seriously harm the person criticized and one does so in the hope or expectation of benefiting someone other than oneself. Application: Jarrett should not have criticized Ostertag' s essay in front of the class, since the defects in it were so obvious that pointing them out benefited no one.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, justifies the above application of the principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jarrett knew that the criticism might antagonize Ostertag.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jarrett hoped to gain prestige by criticizing Ostertag.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jarrett did not expect the criticism to be to Ostertag's benefit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jarrett knew that the defects in the essay were so obvious that pointing them out would benefit no one.

response:
Reasoning: The application concludes Jarrett should not criticize because pointing out obvious defects would benefit no one. To justify applying the principle, we need a fact showing Jarrett knew no one would benefit from the criticism. That is exactly what choice D states.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a principle-application matching approach: identify the rule’s necessary conditions for permissible criticism, then find the choice that directly shows one of those conditions fails. The key factor was that the application hinges on “benefited no one,” so the best support had to connect Jarrett’s criticism to an absence of expected benefit, not merely possible harm or motive. My success came from focusing on the exact language of the principle and selecting the option that mirrored it most closely. For similar problems, translate the principle into required conditions and test which answer explicitly establishes that at least one required condition is not met.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task correctly as a principle-application question: the goal was not to judge the criticism directly, but to identify the additional fact that would make the stated application follow from the principle. My strategy was to match the negation conditions in the principle to the conclusion that Jarrett should not have criticized. The principle allows criticism only when two conditions hold: it does not seriously harm the target, and it is done with the hope or expectation of benefiting someone other than oneself. Since the application said the criticism benefited no one, I focused on the second condition as the likely point of failure. That was appropriate because if no one could benefit, then the required expectation of benefiting someone else is missing.

The key evidence I used was the application’s statement that the defects were so obvious that pointing them out benefited no one. I correctly recognized that to justify the application, the answer choice had to connect Jarrett’s own knowledge or expectation to that fact, not merely describe a possible side effect such as antagonizing Ostertag. I also avoided being distracted by self-interest language, because hoping for prestige would matter only if the principle’s “benefiting someone other than oneself” condition were otherwise met. The successful step was noticing that a justification answer must bridge the principle’s mental-state requirement to the application’s factual claim. In similar problems, I should systematically identify each necessary condition in the principle and ask which answer explicitly shows one of them fails. General rule: when a principle depends on an agent’s intention, hope, expectation, or knowledge, a valid justification usually requires evidence about that mental state, not just external circumstances.

item.context: Ordinary consumers are limited by the status of professional and vulnerable groups and cannot effectively identify false or distorted negative information. Even if companies try to clarify, in the current public opinion dissemination environment of good things don't go out, bad things spread thousands of miles, the strong memory effect will It makes it difficult for people who pursue risk aversion to change their original misconceptions, and they will still use it as a guide for consumer decision-making for a long time in the future, which makes it difficult to clarify the injustice of some law-abiding companies, and also gives Businesses have suffered serious losses.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, would most weaken the above argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The media popularize professional knowledge to the society by taking advantage of its convenience and easy compatibility with the public cognitive structure

choices.label: B
choices.text: The regulatory department establishes credit files for enterprises and provides consumers with a dynamic panorama of the company's situation

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is difficult for those companies that have a conviction but try to rehabilitate to return to the normal trading track

choices.label: D
choices.text: Once a bad reputation becomes a collective memory of the society, it will have a strong stickiness in the public perception

response:
Reasoning: The argument says consumers can’t distinguish false negative information and clarifications are ineffective, harming innocent firms. If regulators create enterprise credit files and give consumers dynamic, authoritative information, consumers can verify claims more accurately, which directly weakens that conclusion.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a weakening approach: first identify the conclusion that false negative information causes long-term harm because consumers cannot reliably correct misconceptions, then look for an option that breaks that chain. The key factor was whether consumers gain a credible, accessible way to verify company information despite misleading public opinion. My success came from targeting the argument’s central assumption—that consumers lack effective correction mechanisms—rather than picking a choice that merely restated reputation effects. For similar problems, map the causal chain in the argument and choose the option that directly blocks a necessary link in that chain.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as a weaken-the-argument task aimed at identifying a fact that would reduce the force of the claim that consumers cannot correct false negative impressions and that innocent firms therefore remain harmed. That interpretation was correct because the passage’s core conclusion is not merely that rumors spread quickly, but that clarifications are ineffective in changing consumer decisions over time. My strategy was to isolate the mechanism of the argument: consumers lack expertise, negative information spreads widely, memory and risk aversion preserve misconceptions, and firms suffer despite attempts to clarify. For a weakening question, the right move is to look for an intervention that breaks one of those links, especially the link between misinformation and persistent consumer belief. I focused on whether any option gives consumers a credible, accessible, ongoing source of verification, because that would directly undermine the claim that they cannot effectively identify distortion. That made the regulatory credit-file option especially strong, since it supplies authoritative information and changes the information environment rather than merely commenting on it. I also implicitly rejected options that simply restated or reinforced the persistence of bad impressions, since those would strengthen the passage. One useful assumption in my reasoning was that consumers trust official, dynamic records enough to update beliefs; here that assumption was reasonable because the option directly addressed the informational deficiency described. An alternative I needed to keep checking was whether media education might also help, but that option is more indirect and less clearly sufficient to overcome entrenched misconceptions. The reasoning succeeded because it targeted the argument’s causal structure rather than matching keywords. A transferable rule is: in weaken questions, identify the specific causal bottleneck supporting the conclusion and prefer the choice that introduces a reliable mechanism that disrupts that bottleneck most directly.

item.context: At present, Chinese people who often go abroad are obviously feeling a huge gap: on the one hand, China's economy is getting stronger and stronger, on the other hand, the cultural image and public image of some Chinese people are falling.
item.question: Which of the following options can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Let's not sell ourselves short

choices.label: B
choices.text: Let's not be conceited

choices.label: C
choices.text: We need moral construction

choices.label: D
choices.text: We need economic change

response:
Reasoning: The statement contrasts rising economic strength with declining cultural/public behavior image of some Chinese people abroad. This suggests the problem is not the economy, but people’s conduct and civility, so the needed response is strengthening ethics and moral quality.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the most reasonable implication of a contrast, not for a slogan that merely sounds compatible with the passage. The key structure was “on the one hand… on the other hand…,” which signaled that the inference had to address the gap between material rise and image decline. My strategy was to identify what variable was improving and what variable was deteriorating, then look for an option that directly targets the deteriorating side. That was appropriate because inference questions often hinge on mapping each clause to the response that resolves the tension.

The evidence I used was the distinction between economic strength and the cultural/public image of citizens abroad. From that, I correctly concluded that the issue is not economic capacity but behavior, values, or civic quality. I implicitly rejected options about self-esteem or arrogance because they are attitudes about national self-perception, whereas the passage focused on external public image caused by conduct. I also rejected economic reform because the passage explicitly said the economy is already becoming stronger. A possible shortcut in my reasoning was treating “cultural image” and “public image” as indicators of ethics and civility; here that was justified by the contrast and answer set. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the remedy to the deficient dimension rather than the successful one. In similar problems, I should first classify each option as addressing cause, symptom, tone, or distraction. General rule: when a statement contrasts progress in one domain with decline in another, the strongest inference usually points to strengthening the declining domain, not the improving one.

item.context: Most plants have developed chemical defenses against parasites. The average plant contains about 40 natural pesticides -- chemical compounds toxic to bacteria, fungi, and other parasites. Humans ingest these natural pesticides without harm every day. Ttherefore, the additional threat posed by synthetic pesticides sprayed on crop plants by humans is minimal.
item.question: Each of the following, if true, weakens the argument EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: The synthetic pesticides sprayed on crop plants by humans usually have chemical structures similar to those of the natural pesticides produced by the plants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Natural plant pesticides generally serve only as defenses against specific parasites, whereas synthetic pesticides are often harmful to a wide variety of organisms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The concentrations of natural pesticides in plants are typically much lower than the concentrations of synthetic pesticides in sprayed crop plants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Natural plant pesticides are typically less potent than synthetic pesticides, whose toxicity is highly concentrated.

response:
Reasoning: The argument assumes natural and synthetic pesticides are similarly harmless. B, C, and D undermine that by showing synthetic pesticides may be broader, more concentrated, or more potent. A instead supports the analogy by saying synthetic pesticides usually have similar chemical structures to natural ones, so it does not weaken.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an argument-structure approach: identify the conclusion, find its supporting analogy, and test which choice fails to attack that analogy. The key factor was that the argument depends on treating natural and synthetic pesticides as relevantly similar in their effects on humans. My success came from separating choices that introduce meaningful differences—such as scope, concentration, or potency—from the one choice that reinforces similarity instead of undermining it. For similar weaken-EXCEPT questions, first pinpoint the core assumption, then classify each option as either challenging that assumption or supporting it.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as an “EXCEPT” weakening problem: identify the one option that does not undermine the conclusion. The argument’s core move was an analogy from natural pesticides humans routinely ingest to synthetic pesticides added by spraying, so the main task was to test whether that analogy held. My strategy was to look for answer choices that exposed a relevant difference between natural and synthetic pesticides, because any such difference would weaken the inference that the added threat is minimal. That was the right strategy for this argument type. I used the key relationships well: if synthetic pesticides are broader in effect, present at higher concentrations, or more potent, then harmless exposure to natural pesticides does not justify dismissing synthetic risk. I also correctly noticed that similarity in chemical structure tends to strengthen, or at least preserve, the analogy rather than attack it. One assumption I implicitly evaluated was that “chemical similarity” is evidence of similar biological effects; while not conclusive, it clearly does not weaken the argument in context. I did not need to consider every remote possibility, only whether each choice created a meaningful disanalogy. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the argument’s hidden premise: natural and synthetic pesticides are relevantly alike in risk. For similar problems, I should explicitly identify the conclusion, the support, and the exact bridge assumption before evaluating choices. General rule: when an argument infers safety from an analogy, weakening answers usually show a risk-relevant difference, while non-weakeners preserve or reinforce the analogy.

item.context: The kite is constantly in line is an artistic concept put forward by Wu Guanzhong around the 1980s, which has had an important impact on the history of contemporary Chinese art. It seems that this is an elaboration on the internal relationship between formal beauty and abstract beauty, but in fact it emphasizes that no matter how creative artistic creation is, no matter how self-flying, we cannot stay away from real life. Abstract painting is like a flying kite. A kite is a work, which is an art form abstracted from materials and feelings from life by the author using subtraction, division or other methods, and the audience is the sky. To make a kite fly into the sky, the artist must have a line in his hand to connect the source of work and life. Only when the kite is constantly in line, can art have a foundation. To maintain communication with the audience.
item.question: Which of the following ideas is in line with the concept of the kite is constantly in line?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Art comes from life and is higher than life.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first purpose of art is to reproduce reality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Artistic creation should be based on life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Art loses its soil when it leaves the people.

response:
Reasoning: The concept stresses that however abstract or innovative art becomes, it must remain connected to real life, which is its source and foundation. This matches the idea that artistic creation should be grounded in life, not merely imitate reality or only emphasize “the people.”
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a paraphrase-and-match approach: I identified the metaphor’s core claim, then compared each option to that claim. The key factor was the “line” connecting the kite to life, which signals that even abstract, highly creative art must stay rooted in lived reality rather than sever itself from its source. The successful step was rejecting choices that added extra claims like “higher than life,” “reproduce reality,” or “the people,” because they narrowed or shifted the original idea. For similar problems, first extract the exact principle from the passage, then choose the option that restates it most directly without adding new conditions.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the option that most precisely captured the core claim of the “kite is constantly in line” metaphor, rather than the option that was merely related to art and life in a broad sense. That interpretation was correct, because the passage explicitly explained the metaphor: art may become abstract and “fly,” but it must remain tethered to life as its source. My strategy was to extract the governing principle from the metaphor and then test each choice against that principle. This was appropriate because the answer depended more on conceptual matching than on background knowledge about aesthetics. I used the key textual constraints that art is “abstracted from materials and feelings from life” and that without the “line,” art loses its foundation and connection. I also correctly noticed that the passage did not argue for simple realism or literal reproduction, so any option equating art with copying reality was too narrow. One useful distinction I made was between “based on life” and stronger or different claims like “higher than life” or “for the people,” which add ideas not directly stated. The success came from choosing the option that matched the passage at the right level of generality without importing extra doctrine. In similar problems, I should keep separating the passage’s necessary claim from answer choices that are adjacent but embellished. A transferable rule is: when a metaphor is explained in the prompt, map answers to the explicit explanation, not to broader familiar slogans in the same topic area.

item.context: Economist: In general, several apprentices working together produce about the same amount in an hour as a single more highly trained worker. Hence the more highly trained worker can usually command several times the hourly wage of an apprentice. Thus if the apprentice wage is increased, the hourly wages of more highly trained workers will generally rise by a proportionate amount. Ttherefore the reason that more highly trained workers favor an increased apprentice wage is that it would increase their own wages.
item.question: The economist's reasoning is flawed because the economist takes for granted that

choices.label: A
choices.text: an increase in the apprentice wage would benefit only highly trained workers

choices.label: B
choices.text: if a policy change that people support would work in their favor, that is why they support it

choices.label: C
choices.text: the wages of highly trained workers will usually not increase unless the apprentice wage increases

choices.label: D
choices.text: if one event causes another event, then the first event occurs whenever the second event occurs

response:
Reasoning: The argument moves from “higher apprentice wages would raise skilled workers’ wages” to “that is why skilled workers support higher apprentice wages.” That assumes a favorable consequence is the motive for support, ignoring other possible reasons.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-flaw approach: I traced the argument from its economic premise about wage relationships to its final claim about workers’ motives and looked for the unstated bridge. The key factor was the shift from “this policy would benefit them” to “this benefit is the reason they support it,” which is a classic move from effect to motive. My success came from spotting that the conclusion was not about wages themselves but about why people hold a view. For similar problems, I should explicitly compare the evidence’s subject matter to the conclusion’s subject matter and test whether the argument is illegitimately inferring motive from mere self-interest.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the hidden assumption that makes the economist’s conclusion about motive go through, not for a factual weakness about wages themselves. That was the correct framing, because the argument’s last step shifts from an economic effect to an explanation of why certain workers favor that policy. My strategy was to isolate the conclusion—an explanation of support—and then compare it with the evidence, which only showed that the policy would likely increase those workers’ wages. That gap signaled a classic motivation assumption: moving from “this benefits them” to “this is their reason for supporting it.”

The key evidence I used was the distinction between causal/economic relationships and psychological/explanatory claims. I correctly recognized that the premises established possible self-interest but did not establish actual motivation. The crucial assumption was that when a policy would work in someone’s favor, that benefit explains their support for it. I did not get distracted by answer choices about whether only highly trained workers benefit or about whether wage increases require apprentice wage increases, because those do not address the motive inference. I also avoided the common trap of reversing causation in the wage relationship, which was irrelevant to the conclusion actually drawn. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the argument’s final inferential leap rather than on the topic area. General rule: whenever an argument concludes “X supports policy P because P benefits X,” check whether it unjustifiably equates personal benefit with actual motive.

item.context: Many people of insight often point out that if a country, nation and culture want to flourish, they need not only the high level of material development, but also the support of progressive faith. Human beings should always be beyond the limits of ordinary animals, with more wisdom, faith, willpower and other spiritual things.
item.question: Which of the following options can be  inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For a country, a nation and a person, spirit and faith are indispensable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Spirit is more important than material.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spirit is wisdom, faith and willpower.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Material and spirit are two aspects of the same problem.

response:
Reasoning: The passage says flourishing requires not only material development but also progressive faith and spiritual qualities. This supports that spirit/faith are necessary for countries, nations, and people. It does not say spirit is more important than material, define spirit exactly, or claim material and spirit are the same problem.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a direct inference approach: identify the author’s main claim, then test each option against what is explicitly supported versus what would require an extra leap. The key clue was the “not only … but also …” structure, which shows that material development alone is insufficient and that spiritual support is presented as necessary for flourishing. My success came from rejecting stronger or distorted claims such as superiority, strict definition, or equivalence. For similar questions, isolate whether the passage states necessity, comparison, definition, or identity, and choose only the option that matches that exact logical relationship.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the strongest statement that must follow from the passage, not merely a statement that sounds compatible with it. That was the right framing, because “can be inferred” requires comparing the exact strength and scope of each option against what the text explicitly supports. My strategy was to extract the core claim of the passage: flourishing requires both material development and a form of spiritual support, and human beings should possess spiritual qualities beyond animal existence. That strategy was appropriate because the passage contrasts material conditions with faith and other inner qualities, making necessity the key relationship.

The main evidence I used was the phrase “not only… but also…,” which signals that material development alone is insufficient and that faith or spirit is also needed. I also used the second sentence to extend the importance of spiritual qualities from countries and cultures to human beings as individuals. I correctly rejected the option claiming superiority of spirit over material, because the passage argues for addition, not ranking. I also rejected the definition option because the list of wisdom, faith, and willpower functions as examples of spiritual things, not a complete definition. Another good move was rejecting the claim that material and spirit are “two aspects of the same problem,” since the passage never frames them that way.

What made the reasoning successful was respecting the difference between necessity and comparison, and between examples and definitions. In similar problems, I should continue testing each choice for whether it is strictly entailed, overstated, or merely plausible. A transferable rule is: when a passage says X is needed “not only” with Y, infer joint necessity, but do not infer that X is less important, identical to Y, or exhaustively defined by nearby examples.

item.context: The so-called urban disease refers to a series of social problems caused by the excessive concentration of population in big cities. It is mainly manifested in the blind expansion of urban planning and construction to the surrounding area, a large amount of cultivated land is occupied, and the contradiction between man and land is more acute. .
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings does not belong to the specific manifestation of urban disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pressure of employment is increasing

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is a shortage of housing for citizens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Citizens travel with traffic jams

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lead to a decline in the city's economic strength

response:
Reasoning: Urban disease is mainly about problems from excessive urban population concentration and sprawl, such as employment pressure, housing shortages, and traffic congestion. “Decline in the city's economic strength” is not a typical direct manifestation; big cities usually remain economically strong despite these problems.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option against the stated features of problems caused by excessive urban population concentration and spatial overexpansion. The key factor was distinguishing direct social manifestations of urban crowding—like jobs, housing, and transportation stress—from a broader or indirect economic outcome. My answer was correct because I focused on whether the option fit the definition’s concrete symptoms rather than whether it might happen in some cities. For similar problems, first extract the definition’s core attributes, then eliminate any option that describes a downstream consequence instead of a defining manifestation.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the option that falls outside the definition’s listed manifestations of “urban disease,” not the option that is merely undesirable or loosely related to cities. That interpretation was correct because the definition emphasized social problems caused by excessive population concentration, especially land pressure, spatial expansion, and resulting urban living problems. My strategy was to compare each choice against the core features implied by the definition: overcrowding, strain on land use, and pressure on urban systems. This was appropriate because a definition-based multiple-choice question is best handled by checking whether each option is a direct manifestation, an indirect consequence, or unrelated.

The key evidence I used was that employment pressure, housing shortage, and traffic congestion are standard capacity-strain effects of overconcentration. I also used a category distinction: the definition focuses on social and spatial dysfunctions of urban growth, not on a city’s aggregate macroeconomic performance. One assumption that helped was treating “manifestation” as a direct symptom rather than a possible long-term downstream effect. That assumption was justified here, but in similar questions I should explicitly test whether an option is direct, indirect, or opposite in tendency. I should also consider whether a choice sounds plausible only because it is negative, rather than because it matches the definitional features. The success came from mapping the wording of the definition to the level of consequence each option described. A transferable rule is: in definition-matching questions, classify each option by necessary attributes of the definition and reject options that are merely associated outcomes without the defining characteristics.

item.context: As the only South American team to stay in the World Cup, Brazil will face England, who eliminated Denmark, in the next game. Scolari, the Head coach of Brazil, would not talk about how to play against England. And his players keep a clear head. The first thing that's on my mind right now is to relax Scolari said with relief after beating the tenacious Belgian.
item.question: According to the above information, which of the following options cannot be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Brazil will never play South American teams again in this World Cup

choices.label: B
choices.text: Scolari is reluctant to talk about the match against England because he is not well

choices.label: C
choices.text: The game against Belgium was tough, so Scolari was relieved after the game

choices.label: D
choices.text: England must beat Denmark before the game against Brazil

response:
Reasoning: The passage says Brazil, the only South American team left, will next face England, who eliminated Denmark. It also says Scolari “would not talk” about playing England and felt relieved after beating tenacious Belgium. Nothing suggests he was unwilling to talk because he was unwell. So B cannot be inferred.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a direct textual-inference approach: I checked each option against what the passage explicitly stated or strongly implied. The key factor was the cause behind Scolari’s silence about England: the passage only says he “would not talk” and wanted to relax, not that he was sick or unwell. The successful step was separating a supported observation from an invented explanation. For similar problems, I should test each choice by asking whether the passage supports both the claim and its stated cause, and reject options that add a new causal reason not grounded in the text.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task correctly as an inference question asking which option was not supported by the passage, rather than which option was false in the real world. My strategy was to compare each choice directly against explicit statements in the text and check whether the choice followed from them or introduced new causal information. That was appropriate here because the passage was short and inference depended on close textual grounding, not outside knowledge about soccer. I used three key facts: Brazil was the only South American team remaining, England had eliminated Denmark, and Scolari was relieved after beating a “tenacious” Belgian side while declining to discuss the next match. The decisive point was that the passage gave no health-related reason for his silence, so any explanation based on illness added an unsupported cause. I implicitly applied the rule that a statement may match the situation superficially yet still fail as an inference if it invents motive or explanation not present in the text. I also checked that the other options were tied more closely to explicit wording or straightforward tournament structure. One assumption that helped was treating “tenacious” and “relief” as evidence that the prior match was difficult. The reasoning succeeded because I distinguished between what the passage said happened and why it happened. In similar problems, I should systematically test whether each option is a direct consequence, a reasonable paraphrase, or an unjustified causal leap. A transferable rule is: reject answer choices that introduce new intentions, causes, or conditions unless the passage explicitly or necessarily implies them.

item.context: Although high cholesterol levels have been associated with the development of heart disease, many people with high cholesterol never develop heart disease, while many without high cholesterol do. Recently, above average concentrations of the blood particle lipoprotein(a) were found in the blood of many people whose heart disease was not attributable to other causes. Dietary changes that affect cholesterol levels have no effect on lipoprotein(a) levels. Hence, there is no reason for anyone to make dietary changes for the sake of preventing heart disease.
item.question: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It presents but ignores evidence that, for some people, high cholesterol contributes to heart disease.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It provides no evidence for a link between lipoprotein(a) and heart disease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It fails to consider the possibility that lipoprotein(a) raises cholesterol levels.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It fails to consider the possibility that poor diets cause some people to develop health problems other than heart disease.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion is too broad.
