Even if diet does not affect lipoprotein(a), the passage itself indicates high cholesterol is associated with heart disease, and some people’s heart disease may still be caused or worsened by cholesterol. So dietary changes could still help prevent heart disease for some people.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a scope-and-relevance approach: I compared the broad conclusion against the evidence and checked whether the argument ruled out all remaining ways diet could matter. The key clue was that the stimulus itself says high cholesterol has been associated with heart disease, even if not in every case, so introducing lipoprotein(a) does not eliminate cholesterol as a contributing cause for some people. My success came from noticing that the argument treated a new possible cause as if it displaced an existing one entirely. For similar problems, test whether a conclusion about “no reason for anyone” improperly ignores evidence that supports a benefit for at least some subset.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the stimulus as an argument-structure question asking for the logical flaw, not a factual question about medical causation. The key task was to compare the evidence given with the scope of the conclusion and ask whether the conclusion ruled out more than the premises supported. My strategy was to track each causal claim separately: high cholesterol is associated with some heart disease, lipoprotein(a) appears in many cases not explained by other causes, and diet affects cholesterol but not lipoprotein(a). That was an appropriate method because flaw questions often turn on whether an argument illegitimately substitutes one cause for another or treats a partial explanation as a complete one. The crucial evidence I used was that the passage itself allowed cholesterol to remain relevant in at least some cases, since it never denied that dietary changes could reduce a risk pathway involving cholesterol. I correctly noticed that “diet does not affect lipoprotein(a)” does not imply “diet cannot help prevent heart disease at all.” One assumption I avoided was treating “many” as “all,” which would have made the conclusion seem stronger than the premises warranted. I also implicitly rejected distractors that focused on missing proof of lipoprotein(a)’s role, because the argument’s flaw was broader than evidentiary sufficiency on that point. What made the reasoning successful was identifying that the author ignored one live causal route while drawing a universal recommendation. A transferable rule is: when an argument concludes that an intervention is pointless because it does not affect one cause, check whether the premises still leave other causally relevant pathways that the intervention could influence.

item.context: Some scientists believe that 65 million years ago an asteroid struck what is now the Yucatan Peninsula, thereby causing extinction of the dinosaurs. These scientists have established that such a strike could have hurled enough debris into the atmosphere to block sunlight and cool the atmosphere. Without adequate sunlight, food sources for herbivorous dinosaurs would have disappeared, and no dinosaurs could have survived a prolonged period of low temperatures. These same scientists, however, have also established that most debris launched by the asteroid would have settled to the ground within six months, too soon for the plants to disappear or the dinosaurs to freeze.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy between the scientists' beliefs and the scientists' results, as described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dinosaurs were susceptible to fatal respiratory problems caused by contamination of the air by asteroid debris.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A cloud of debris capable of diminishing sunlight by 20 percent would have cooled the earth's surface by 7 to 10 degrees Celsius.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of the herbivorous dinosaurs would have deprived the carnivorous dinosaurs of their food source.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dinosaurs inhabited most landmasses on the planet but were not especially abundant in the area of the asteroid strike.

response:
Reasoning: The discrepancy is that debris would not stay aloft long enough to kill dinosaurs via darkness/cold. The best resolution is that the asteroid could still have caused extinction through a different rapid effect. Choice A provides that: debris-contaminated air could have killed dinosaurs within months.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a discrepancy-resolution approach: identify the scientists’ proposed mechanism, then find the new fact that allows both their extinction claim and their short debris-duration finding to be true. The key factor was that the original mechanism required a long period of darkness and cold, but the evidence said the debris settled too quickly for that pathway to work. The successful step was looking for an alternative lethal effect caused by the same debris on a shorter timescale. For similar problems, when evidence undermines a proposed causal chain, look for an answer that preserves the overall conclusion by supplying a different mechanism consistent with all stated constraints.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a discrepancy-resolution problem: the scientists’ causal story required long-lasting atmospheric effects, but their own findings suggested the debris would fall too quickly for that mechanism to work. My strategy was to look for a new fact that would allow both claims to remain true at once, rather than attacking either side of the discrepancy. That is the right approach for “resolve the apparent discrepancy” questions, because the goal is not to choose the strongest cause in general, but the fact that makes the two seemingly inconsistent statements compatible. I focused on the timing constraint as the key evidence: six months was too short for prolonged darkness to eliminate plants or for extended cold to kill dinosaurs. From that, I inferred that the best answer would introduce a faster lethal pathway triggered by the same debris.

That reasoning was successful because it preserved the asteroid hypothesis while explaining why extinction could still occur despite the short debris duration. I correctly rejected answer types that merely restated downstream effects, quantified cooling, or discussed geographic distribution without addressing the timing problem. A hidden assumption in my reasoning was that “fatal within months” is enough to bridge the gap, which fit the structure here. In similar problems, I should explicitly identify the exact point of tension—here, duration—and test each option for whether it directly repairs that tension. General rule: when two statements conflict because a proposed mechanism seems too weak, too slow, or too limited, prefer an answer that supplies a different mechanism matching the limiting condition.

item.context: Traditional Chinese painting pays attention to knowing the white and keeping the black, which means that the black is the painting and the white is the blank. The blank  left on the picture should be valued as much as the image of the painting. In other words, the blank  should be reasonable and conform to the composition rules. The most taboo is the same size and shape of the blank, the most taboo is the blank like round, square, the most taboo is the blank scattered like stars. Good blanks are large and small, are irregular triangles and the blanks left are complete and unified.
item.question: Which of the following options is intended to be explained in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The characteristics of traditional chinese painting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The composition principle of traditional chinese painting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The angle of appreciating traditional chinese painting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ink skills of traditional Chinese painting.

response:
Reasoning: The passage focuses on how blank space should be arranged in a painting—balanced, reasonable, unified, and not repetitive in shape. This is about compositional use of emptiness, not appreciation, general characteristics, or ink technique.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach: I identified the repeated concept in the passage and matched it to the choice that best captured that focus. The key factor was that nearly every sentence discussed how blank space should be arranged—reasonable, varied, unified, and consistent with composition rules. My answer was correct because I focused on the organizing principle of the passage rather than being distracted by broader choices like general characteristics or technique. For similar questions, first track the passage’s repeated subject and purpose, then choose the option that matches that scope most precisely.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the main idea or explanatory purpose of the passage, not just a detail it mentioned. That was the right framing because the passage did not define a broad art tradition, teach brushwork, or discuss how viewers should respond; it explained a specific design principle. My strategy was to identify the dominant topic by tracking repeated terms and constraints, especially the repeated discussion of “blank” space, its shapes, proportions, and unity within the picture. That strategy was appropriate because multiple-choice main-idea questions are usually settled by the passage’s organizing focus rather than by isolated keywords.

The key evidence I used was that the passage gave normative rules: blank areas should be reasonable, conform to compositional rules, avoid uniform shapes, and remain complete and unified. Those are structural directives about arrangement within an artwork. I implicitly rejected options about appreciation and ink technique because the passage never shifted to audience response or brush/material handling. A possible shortcut I used was equating any discussion of visual arrangement with composition, but here that shortcut was justified by the explicit mention of “composition rules.” I still should have considered whether the passage was presenting a general characteristic of the tradition, since it began with a broader statement about traditional painting. What made the reasoning successful was distinguishing between a broad opening frame and the narrower explanatory target developed by the rest of the paragraph. In similar problems, I should map each answer choice to the passage’s function: definition, technique, evaluation, appreciation, or organizing principle. General rule: when a passage repeatedly gives rules about placement, balance, proportion, and spatial relations, the best label is a compositional principle rather than a general characteristic or technical method.

item.context: One name-brand cereal manufacturer is about to reduce wholesale prices for its cereals by 20 percent because consumers have been switching from its cereals to cheaper store brands. The success of this strategy relies on the assumption that supermarkets will pass on all of the savings by lowering the prices they charge consumers for the manufacturer' s cereals. Although supermarkets usually pass on such savings, in this case it is likely that supermarkets not do so because__.
item.question: Which of the following most logically completes the passage below?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the average price per box of name-brand cereals has increased significantly in the last 10 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: several other name-brand cereal manufacturers are about to reduce the wholesale prices of their cereals

choices.label: C
choices.text: supermarkets make far more profit on sales of store-brand cereals than on sales of name-brand cereals

choices.label: D
choices.text: the current prices of the manufacturer's cereals are comparable to the prices of name-brand cereals produced by other cereal manufacturers

response:
Reasoning: The manufacturer’s strategy works only if lower wholesale prices reduce consumer prices. Supermarkets would be less likely to pass along those savings if they prefer customers to keep buying store brands. If store-brand cereals yield much higher profit, supermarkets have an incentive to keep name-brand prices relatively high.  
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an incentive-based reasoning approach: identify what must happen for the strategy to work, then ask what would make the intermediary choose not to do it. The key factor was the supermarket’s profit motive, since supermarkets control retail prices and will only pass along wholesale savings if doing so helps their own bottom line. The successful step was focusing on the actor mentioned in the conclusion gap—the supermarkets—and looking for a choice that gave them a reason to keep prices high. For similar problems, trace the plan through each decision-maker and select the option that changes that decision-maker’s incentives in the opposite direction.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as an assumption-based completion problem: it asked for the fact that best explains why supermarkets would likely not pass the wholesale savings on to consumers in this particular case. My strategy was to identify the incentive structure of the supermarkets, since the passage turns on whether retailers will choose to lower shelf prices. That was the right approach because the conclusion is not about what usually happens, but about what motive could override the usual practice. I focused on the relationship between retailer profit and consumer switching behavior: if consumers are moving to store brands, supermarkets may benefit from that trend rather than resist it. The key evidence I used was that the manufacturer is cutting wholesale prices specifically to stop customers from switching to cheaper store brands. From that, I inferred that any answer increasing supermarkets’ incentive to preserve store-brand demand would weaken the expectation that savings get passed through.

I avoided weaker alternatives because they did not directly address supermarket incentives. For example, facts about long-term cereal prices or other manufacturers’ pricing do not by themselves explain why this supermarket behavior would change. The successful part of my reasoning was matching the blank to the causal mechanism required: a reason supermarkets would prefer not to reduce consumer prices. In similar problems, I should explicitly ask, “What actor’s incentives determine whether the stated assumption holds?” A transferable rule is: when a passage depends on one party passing along a benefit, the best challenge often shows that party earns more by withholding the benefit.

item.context: Scientist: Venus contains a hot molten core, like that of Earth. Also like Earth, Venus must expel the excess heat the core generates. On Earth, this occurs entirely through active volcanos and fissures created when tectonic plates separate. Yet Venus has neither active volcanos nor fissures caused by the movement of tectonic plates.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, does the most to resolve the apparent discrepancy described by the scientist?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The atmosphere of Venus is significantly hotter than that of Earth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rock on the surface of Venus remains solid at much higher temperatures than does rock on Earth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Though Venus lacks active volcanoes and heat- diffusing fissures, it has surface movement somewhat like that of Earth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The surface of Venus is relatively thin, allowing internally produced heat to radiate into space.

response:
Reasoning: The discrepancy is how Venus releases internal heat without Earth-like volcanism or plate-created fissures. Choice D provides an alternative mechanism: if Venus’s surface is thin, heat can radiate into space directly, so it need not rely on volcanoes or tectonic fissures.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a discrepancy-resolution approach: identify the conflict, then look for an option that provides an alternative mechanism making both facts compatible. The key factor was that Venus still needed some way to release internal heat even without Earth’s specific heat-loss processes, so the best choice had to explain heat escape directly. The successful step was focusing on the function that needed to be replaced—heat dissipation—rather than superficial similarities to Earth. For similar problems, first isolate the exact causal gap, then prefer the choice that supplies a new pathway that fulfills the missing role.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a discrepancy-resolution problem: the stimulus claimed Venus must release internal heat, then denied the Earth-style mechanisms that do that on Earth. The task, therefore, was not to prove a general fact about Venus, but to find a new fact that makes both claims compatible. My strategy was to identify the missing link in the causal chain: if Venus cannot use volcanism or tectonic fissures, it must have some alternative path for heat escape. That was the right strategy for this type of LR question because the best answer should directly supply an overlooked mechanism rather than merely add background detail.

The key evidence I used was the contrast between “must expel excess heat” and “has neither active volcanos nor fissures.” I correctly recognized that an answer resolving the discrepancy had to address heat transfer, not just temperature, rock properties, or superficial similarities to Earth. I implicitly applied the useful constraint that any strong resolver must explain Venus specifically, not Earth, and must bear directly on the heat-release problem. I also avoided a common bad assumption: that if Earth uses one method, every similar planet must use the same method. I did briefly rely on a shortcut—looking for an “alternative mechanism” answer choice—but here that shortcut was justified by the structure of the stimulus. The other possibilities should be screened by asking whether they explain how heat gets out, rather than whether they merely sound geologically relevant. What made the reasoning successful was matching the contradiction to a missing causal route. A general rule to transfer is: when resolving an apparent discrepancy, identify the exact process that seems blocked and prefer the choice that introduces a specific alternative pathway allowing both stated facts to remain true.

item.context: Though Earth' s human population is increasing, it currently uses only a relatively small fraction of the supply of fresh water. Thus, claims that water shortages will plague humankind in the near future unless population growth trends change are simply mistaken.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The percentage of fresh water used for agriculture is likely to grow more quickly than is the percentage used for industry.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Not all of Earth's population will adopt water conservation methods in the near future.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Population growth trends are notoriously hard to predict with reasonable accuracy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The amount of fresh water available to meet the needs of Earth's population varies significantly from region to region.

response:
Reasoning: The argument assumes that because humans use only a small fraction of total fresh water, shortages cannot occur soon. But if usable fresh water is unevenly distributed, many regions could face serious shortages despite abundant global supply. That directly weakens the conclusion.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-testing approach: I looked for the gap between “small fraction of total fresh water” and “therefore no near-future shortages.” The key factor was the distinction between global supply and actual availability where people live, since shortages can occur locally even when the overall total seems ample. My success came from identifying that the argument treats fresh water as if it were uniformly accessible, which is not guaranteed. For similar problems, I should test whether the argument illegitimately moves from a broad aggregate fact to a conclusion about all places or cases.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the answer choice that most undermines the argument’s move from a global fact to a broad dismissal of near-future water shortages. The key structure was: humans currently use only a small fraction of total fresh water, therefore warnings about shortages are mistaken. My strategy was to look for a hidden assumption linking total worldwide supply to actual human access and local scarcity. That was appropriate because weakening questions often turn on whether the conclusion depends on an overly simple measure, here total fresh water rather than available fresh water where people live.

The crucial fact I used was that shortages can occur even when total supply is large if that supply is not evenly available. I recognized that a mismatch between aggregate quantity and distribution would directly challenge the argument’s inference. I did not rely on whether population growth is predictable or whether conservation will occur, because those points do not attack the core assumption as directly. I also correctly set aside choice A, since changing sectoral use does not by itself show that warnings are not mistaken. The successful part of my reasoning was identifying the argument’s scope shift from global abundance to universal adequacy. In similar problems, I should explicitly test whether the author confuses total amount with accessible amount, average condition with local condition, or present fraction used with future practical sufficiency. A transferable rule is: when an argument dismisses shortage claims by citing a large overall supply, check whether distribution, accessibility, timing, or infrastructure could break the link between total resource volume and actual availability.

item.context: Raising the humidity of a room protects furniture, draperies, and computers from damage caused by excessively dry air. Further, it can make people feel warmer, helps the body' s defenses against viruses, and alleviates some skin rashes.
item.question: Each of the following is supported by the information above EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dry air can feel cooler than humid air of the same temperature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased humidity can be beneficial to the skin.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Humidity can be bad for computers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The human immune system can benefit from humidity.

response:
Reasoning: The passage says increased humidity protects computers from damage caused by dry air, not that humidity is harmful to computers. The other choices are directly supported: humid air can feel warmer, can help skin rashes, and can aid defenses against viruses.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a direct evidence-matching approach: I checked each choice against the exact claims in the passage and looked for the one that was not supported. The key factor was the distinction between “protects from damage caused by dry air” and a statement claiming humidity itself is harmful; that reverses the relationship given. My success came from comparing wording carefully instead of relying on background assumptions about electronics and moisture. For similar problems, translate each option into the passage’s exact causal claim and reject any choice that changes the direction, cause, or scope of that claim.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as an “EXCEPT” item, so the task was to find the one choice not supported by the passage rather than the one directly stated. My strategy was to map each answer choice to a specific sentence or implication in the passage and then look for the option that reversed or exceeded what was actually said. That was appropriate here because the passage was short and each claim corresponded fairly directly to one of the listed benefits of humidity. I used the explicit statements that humidity can make people feel warmer, help the body’s defenses against viruses, and alleviate some skin rashes, which supported three of the choices. I also noticed the passage said raising humidity protects computers from damage caused by excessively dry air, which is importantly different from saying humidity itself harms computers. The key relationship I handled correctly was distinguishing “protection from X” from “caused by X,” rather than collapsing them into a vague association with computers and humidity. A common shortcut in these questions is to treat any mention of a topic as support for any nearby claim about that topic; I avoided that mistake. I should still remember to check whether an answer is a direct restatement, a valid implication, or a contradiction. In similar problems, I should test each option against the exact direction of causation or comparison in the text. General rule: when evaluating support, preserve the passage’s polarity and causal structure; do not infer the converse, reverse, or opposite of a stated relationship.

item.context: Until fairly recently, classroom computers were considered a luxury. Today, educators argue that students who have not had training in computer skills will lack the skills necessary to compete in the global marketplace . However, studies show that schools emphasizing computer technology spend more time teaching computer skills but less time developing students' basic math and reading skills.
item.question: Which one of the following propositions is best illustrated by the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Schools cannot emphasize the teaching of computer skills without neglecting other skills.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A complete rethinking of traditional academic subjects is required in order to keep pace with global developments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attempting to keep pace with recent educational developments can result in neglecting basic skills in favor of other skills.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A knowledge of the latest technologies is no more valuable than a knowledge of the fundamental academic disciplines .

response:
Reasoning: The passage says schools stress computer skills to meet modern demands, but this can reduce time spent on basic math and reading. That best illustrates that trying to keep up with new educational developments may cause neglect of fundamental skills. It does not prove this must always happen or that computer knowledge is equally/unimportant.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a pattern-matching approach: I identified the passage’s structure as a tradeoff between adopting a newer priority and reducing attention to foundational skills, then matched that pattern to the most general answer choice. The key factor was the contrast between the push for computer training to stay competitive and the evidence that this emphasis takes time away from math and reading. My success came from rejecting stronger claims like “cannot” or broader value judgments that the passage did not establish. Lesson: for “best illustrated” questions, abstract the passage to its core relationship and choose the option that matches that relationship without adding necessity, exclusivity, or unsupported evaluation.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the broader principle exemplified by the passage, not for a restatement of every detail. That was the correct framing, because “best illustrated” questions require abstraction from the specific case of computers in schools to a more general proposition. My strategy was to identify the tension in the passage: schools adopt computer instruction to meet modern economic demands, but that shift is associated with reduced attention to math and reading. From that pattern, I looked for an answer choice that captured possibility and tradeoff rather than certainty or value judgment.

The key evidence I used was the contrast between “spend more time teaching computer skills” and “less time developing students’ basic math and reading skills.” I also noticed that the passage said this happens in schools “emphasizing” technology, which supports a conditional tendency, not an absolute rule. That helped me reject stronger alternatives that used language like “cannot” or implied an inevitable exclusion of other skills. I also avoided the trap of treating the passage as making a comparative claim about the value of technology versus basic disciplines, since it only described consequences of emphasis, not relative worth.

What made the reasoning successful was matching the strength and scope of the answer choice to the evidence in the stimulus. In similar problems, I should continue testing each choice for modality: does the passage show “can,” “must,” or “should”? A transferable rule is: when a stimulus presents a concrete example of an unintended tradeoff, choose the option that generalizes that tradeoff at the same level of certainty, without adding stronger necessity or new evaluative claims.

item.context: Traditionally, students at Kelly University have evaluated professors on the last day of class. But some professors at Kelly either do not distribute the paper evaluation forms or do so selectively, and many students cannot attend the last day of class. Soon, students will be able to use school computers to evaluate their professors at any time during the semester. Ttherefore, evaluations under the new system will accurately reflect the distribution of student opinion about teaching performance.
item.question: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Professors who distribute the paper evaluation forms selectively distribute them only to students they personally like.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dissatisfied students are in general not more likely than satisfied students to submit a computerized evaluation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students can wisely and insightfully assess a professor's performance before the end of the semester.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nearly all professors who fail to distribute the paper evaluation forms do so because they believe the students will evaluate them unfavorably.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion claims the new system will accurately reflect the distribution of student opinion. That requires assuming the new method will not systematically skew who chooses to respond. If dissatisfied students were more likely than satisfied students to submit evaluations, results would be biased. The other choices are not necessary.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a necessary-assumption approach: identify the conclusion, then ask what must be true for that conclusion to hold. The key factor was the shift from a limited in-class paper process to a voluntary computerized process; even if access improves, the argument still needs the respondent pool not to be systematically biased. My success came from focusing on representativeness rather than the specific flaws of the old system, since the conclusion was about accurately reflecting the distribution of opinion. For similar problems, test whether a new method could introduce self-selection bias and check whether the argument requires that such bias not distort the sample.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the argument correctly as a required-assumption question: the author moved from fixing access problems in the old paper system to claiming that the new computerized system would accurately represent overall student opinion. My strategy was to test what must be true for that representativeness claim to hold, rather than what might merely strengthen it. That was appropriate because the conclusion was specifically about the distribution of opinions, so I focused on whether the new system could introduce a new participation bias. The key evidence I used was that the old system suffered from selective distribution and absence on the last day, while the new system allows evaluation at any time; this removes some barriers but does not by itself guarantee an unbiased sample. I recognized that if one type of student were more likely to respond under the new system, the resulting evaluations could still misrepresent the true distribution. That is why the response-rate balance between dissatisfied and satisfied students was the critical missing condition. I also correctly rejected choices about professors’ motives or about students’ ability to assess performance early, because those are not necessary for the claim about representativeness. One assumption I implicitly used was that “accurately reflect the distribution” depends on comparable likelihood of participation across opinion groups. A useful alternative to consider in such problems is whether the new system solves only the old flaw while creating a different flaw. The transferable lesson is: when an argument claims a new measurement method is accurate, check whether the method avoids systematic selection effects among the groups being measured.

item.context: In today's world, devices are highly interconnected, and people attach great importance to security and privacy. In the future when the brain can be interconnected, these two issues will only become more critical. Mental security researchers need to develop highly secure communication protocols to minimize the risk of brain communication. Policy makers also need to pass relevant laws, minimize the abuse of technology. Can the benefits of brain communication outweigh its risks? How will this technology change the trajectory of human evolution? Will society get better because of it? Maybe it's time to discuss these issues.
item.question: Which of the following is mainly explained in the above text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The possible negative effects of brain communication technology should be paid attention to.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Security and privacy are the most noteworthy issues in brain communication technology.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Society may not necessarily become better because of the application of brain communication technology.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Brain communication technology is a double-edged sword.

response:
Reasoning: The passage focuses on concerns and precautions about brain communication—especially security, privacy, legal regulation, and possible abuse. It raises questions about benefits, risks, and social impact, urging discussion of its negative side effects rather than mainly arguing both sides equally.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach, tracking what the passage emphasized rather than giving equal weight to every sentence. The key factor was that most of the text focused on risks, including security, privacy, abuse, and the need for laws and discussion, while the possible benefits were only mentioned as open questions. My answer was correct because I prioritized the passage’s emphasis and tone instead of being distracted by broader but less supported choices. For similar problems, I should identify which idea receives the most concrete development and treat brief rhetorical questions as secondary unless the passage actually elaborates on them.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s main explanatory focus, not just a detail mentioned within it. That distinction mattered, because the text mentions security and privacy specifically, but only as examples within a broader warning-oriented discussion. My strategy was to identify the passage’s overall tone and rhetorical purpose: it emphasizes risks, abuse, regulation, and the need for discussion before widespread adoption. That was an appropriate approach for a “mainly explained” question, since such questions require synthesis rather than selecting the most vivid detail.

The key evidence I used was the clustering of cautionary elements: minimizing risk, preventing abuse, passing laws, and questioning whether society will improve. I also noticed that the text does not actually argue a balanced pros-and-cons analysis in equal depth, so the “double-edged sword” framing was too broad and too symmetrical. One useful restraint in my reasoning was avoiding the trap of choosing the option that repeated the most concrete nouns from the passage, since “security and privacy” were important but not the full main idea. I also correctly recognized that the sentence about whether society will get better was posed as an open question, not the central claim. The reasoning succeeded because I prioritized authorial emphasis over isolated content. In similar problems, I should continue testing each option against scope: detail-level, balanced-theme, and main-purpose are not interchangeable. A transferable rule is: for main-idea questions, choose the option that best captures the passage’s dominant purpose and scope, not the option that merely echoes its most specific terms.

item.context: The proportion of fat calories in the diets of people who read the nutrition labels on food products is significantly lower than it is in the diets of people who do not read nutrition labels. This shows that reading these labels promotes healthful dietary behavior.
item.question: The reasoning in the argument above is flawed in that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: illicitly infers a cause from a correlation

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on a sample that is unlikely to be representative of the group as a whole

choices.label: C
choices.text: confuses a condition that is necessary for a phenomenon to occur with a condition that is sufficient for that phenomenon to occur

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the intentions of a group of people based solely on data about the consequences of their behavior

response:
Reasoning: The argument observes a correlation: label readers consume a lower proportion of fat calories. It then concludes that reading labels causes healthier eating. But people who already care about health may be more likely to read labels, so causation is not established.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a causal-flaw approach: I looked for whether the evidence only showed an association while the conclusion claimed one factor produced the other. The key clue was the comparison between two groups—label readers and non-readers—which establishes correlation but does not rule out self-selection or a third variable, such as prior health consciousness. My success came from noticing that the argument jumped from “these traits occur together” to “one promotes the other.” For similar problems, I should explicitly test any causal conclusion by asking whether the evidence eliminates reverse causation and confounding alternatives.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the stimulus as asking for the flaw in moving from an observed difference between two groups to a claim about what produced that difference. That interpretation was correct, because the key issue was not whether lower fat intake is healthier, but whether the evidence justified attributing that outcome to label reading itself. My strategy was to identify the argument’s structure: a comparison between label readers and nonreaders, followed by a causal conclusion. That was the right strategy for flaw questions, since these often hinge on whether the conclusion goes beyond the evidence type provided. I used the crucial fact that the stimulus gave only a correlation between two traits—reading labels and consuming less fat—not an experiment, temporal sequence, or control for confounds. I also recognized an omitted-variable possibility: people already motivated to eat healthfully may be more likely both to read labels and to choose lower-fat diets. That alternative explanation was the central evidence needed to evaluate the flaw. I did not rely on irrelevant answer patterns such as sampling problems, necessity/sufficiency confusion, or claims about intentions, because nothing in the wording supported those structures. What made the reasoning successful was matching the conclusion type (causal) against the evidence type (observational comparison). In similar problems, I should explicitly ask whether the evidence rules out reverse causation or a common cause. General rule: when an argument infers that one behavior produces another outcome from a mere group difference, treat the inference as suspect unless the evidence establishes causation rather than association.

item.context: Taylor: From observing close friends and relatives, it is clear to me that telepathy is indeed possible between people with close psychic ties. The amazing frequency with which a good friend or family member knows what one is thinking or feeling cannot be dismissed as mere coincidence.
item.question: Taylor's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: appeals to a premise one would accept only if one already accepted the truth of the conclusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: is based on too small a sample to yield a reliable conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that one can never know what a stranger is thinking or feeling

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to address a highly plausible alternative explanation for all instances of the observed phenomenon

response:
Reasoning: Taylor infers telepathy from cases where close friends/family seem to know each other’s thoughts, but ignores a strong alternative: people who know each other well can predict feelings and thoughts from familiarity, shared experiences, and subtle cues. That unexplored explanation weakens the argument most.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an argument-flaw approach: identify the conclusion, note the evidence offered, and ask what assumption is needed to move from the observations to that conclusion. The key factor was that the observed “mind reading” among close friends and relatives can be explained by familiarity, behavioral cues, and shared context, so the evidence does not uniquely support the claimed cause. The success came from testing whether a plausible non-telepathic explanation could account for the same data and seeing that the argument never addressed it. For similar problems, I should systematically ask whether the evidence could be fully explained by an ordinary alternative before accepting a more extraordinary conclusion.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the main logical flaw in Taylor’s argument, not whether telepathy is true or false. The key task was to identify how the conclusion was supported and what weakness most directly undermined that support. My strategy was to compare the observed phenomenon—close friends and relatives often seeming to know each other’s thoughts or feelings—with the answer choices to see which flaw best matched the structure of the reasoning. That was appropriate because flaw questions depend on diagnosing the gap between evidence and conclusion, not disputing the topic itself.

The most important evidence in the argument was that the people involved were close, familiar, and emotionally connected. I used the fact that such closeness naturally creates a plausible non-telepathic explanation: shared background knowledge, pattern recognition, and sensitivity to subtle behavioral cues. That made the alternative-explanation choice the strongest fit. I also implicitly rejected the small-sample answer because the argument’s deeper problem was not just quantity of observations, but the failure to rule out a better causal account of those observations. I avoided assuming the argument said anything about strangers, so I correctly set aside that distractor. I also recognized that the argument was not circular, since the premise did not already presuppose telepathy outright.

The reasoning succeeded because I focused on causal inference: when an argument explains an event by an extraordinary cause, test whether ordinary causes have been excluded. A transferable rule is: when evidence is consistent with both a remarkable hypothesis and a common alternative, the argument is weakest if it treats the remarkable hypothesis as established without eliminating the common alternative.

item.context: Some people have been promoting a new herbal mixture as a remedy for the common cold. The mixture contains, among other things, extracts of the plants purple coneflower and goldenseal. A cold sufferer, skeptical of the claim that the mixture is an effective cold remedy, argued, Suppose that the mixture were an effective cold remedy. Since most people with colds wish to recover quickly, it follows that almost everybody with a cold would be using it. Ttherefore, since there are many people who have colds but do not use the mixture, it is obviously not effective.
item.question: Each of the following is an assumption required by the skeptical cold sufferer's argument EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mixture does not have side effects severe enough to make many people who have colds avoid using it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enough of the mixture is produced to provide the required doses to almost everybody with a cold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There are no effective cold remedies available that many people who have colds prefer to the mixture.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mixture is powerful enough to prevent almost everybody who uses it from contracting any further colds.

response:
Reasoning: The argument needs assumptions that an effective remedy would be widely used: no severe side effects (A), enough supply (B), and no preferred effective alternatives (C). Whether the mixture prevents future colds (D) is irrelevant to whether current cold sufferers would use it now.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a necessary-assumption test: I looked for what must be true for the skeptic’s inference from “effective remedy” to “almost everybody with a cold would use it” to work. The key factor was that the argument depends on likely uptake among current cold sufferers, so assumptions about side effects, availability, and competing preferred remedies all matter because they affect whether people would actually use it. My success came from separating conditions that influence present usage from a statement about preventing future colds, which does not support that uptake inference. For similar problems, identify the argument’s critical link, then negate each choice and ask whether the reasoning collapses; if not, that choice is not required.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as an “assumption EXCEPT” problem: identify which option is not necessary for the skeptic’s reasoning to work. My strategy was to reconstruct the argument’s core conditional chain: if the remedy were effective, then nearly everyone with a cold would use it; many do not use it; therefore it is not effective. That made the task one of testing what must be true for “effective” to imply “almost universally used.” I correctly focused on factors that could block widespread use even if the remedy worked, such as deterrent side effects, insufficient supply, or competition from other remedies people would choose instead. Those are all genuine gap-fillers because, without them, nonuse would not undermine effectiveness.

The successful part of my reasoning was distinguishing between assumptions about use and assumptions about the remedy’s additional properties. I noticed that preventing future colds concerns long-term prophylactic power, not whether current sufferers would adopt the remedy in the first place. I did not assume that every beneficial feature matters; I asked whether the conclusion depends on that feature. That dependency test is exactly the right method for required-assumption questions. In similar problems, I should continue mapping the argument’s causal or behavioral link and checking whether each choice is necessary to preserve that link. The transferable rule is: for “assumption EXCEPT,” isolate the argument’s key inference and reject any option that describes a merely helpful, stronger, or tangential claim rather than a condition required for the inference to hold.

item.context: Commentator: many historians assert that their own discussion of historical issues, like any natural scientist, is objective and rarely influenced by ethical or aesthetic preconceptions. We obviously cannot accept what these historians say, because it is easy to find some wrong historical works that show the author's preconceived ideas or other aspects.
item.question: The commentator's reasoning is flawed because he

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mistakenly believe that many historians who emphasize methodology intend to completely eliminate preconceptions

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is taken for granted that the requirements for objectivity put forward by natural scientists should be applicable to other fields

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is inappropriate to think that all ideological historical works are wrong

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is taken for granted that some historical works with preconceptions are written by historians who claim to be objective

response:
Reasoning: The commentator rejects “many historians” claims by citing “some wrong historical works” showing bias. But that only undermines the claim if those biased works were written by the same historians who claim objectivity. That link is assumed, not shown.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-identification approach by matching the conclusion’s target group with the evidence’s source group. The crucial clue was the shift from “many historians who claim objectivity” to merely “some wrong historical works showing preconceptions,” without establishing that those works were produced by the same historians making the claim. My success came from spotting this unsupported linkage between the example and the group being criticized. For similar problems, I should explicitly test whether the evidence actually comes from the population or category the conclusion is about, especially when quantifiers like “many” and “some” appear.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the argument as attacking a broad self-description made by many historians and looked for the gap between that broad claim and the evidence offered against it. That was the right framing, because the flaw question turned on whether the evidence actually targeted the group whose claim was being rejected. My strategy was to trace the quantifiers and group references: “many historians” make a claim, but the commentator cites only “some wrong historical works” showing preconceptions. The key evidentiary issue was that the argument never established that those flawed works were produced by members of the self-described objective group. Without that connection, the example could come from different historians entirely, so the rebuttal would miss its target. I did not rely on outside facts about history or science; I focused on the internal structure of the argument, which was appropriate for this type of logical criticism. A tempting but weaker alternative would have been to focus on whether objectivity requires total absence of preconceptions, but the argument’s more immediate defect was the missing link between the sample and the claimants. The reasoning succeeded because I treated the flaw as a mismatch between population and evidence rather than as a dispute about objectivity itself. In similar problems, I should continue mapping who is making the claim, who the evidence concerns, and whether the evidence is representative of or even connected to that group. General rule: when an argument refutes a claim about a class by citing counterexamples, verify that the examples are actually members of the class under discussion.

item.context: Breaking up is not only psychological pain, but also physical pain. U.S. researchers recruited 40 volunteers who were forced to break up by their spouses in the past six months and still mind being rejected.The researchers used functional magnetic resonance imaging to observe the brain activity of volunteers. The results show that the brain parts that respond to social rejection such as breakup coincide with those that respond to physical pain, so social rejection such as breakup will cause their physical pain.
item.question: What are the implied assumptions when we get the above conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Individual's feeling of pain is closely related to social stress events

choices.label: B
choices.text: Functional magnetic resonance imaging is a common method for brain localization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Changes of individual emotion and other psychological processes can affect their physiological response

choices.label: D
choices.text: Physiological and psychological reactions can be related through the brain

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion moves from “the same brain areas are active” to “social rejection causes physical pain.” That requires assuming psychological and physiological responses are connected through brain activity. B is irrelevant, A is close to the conclusion, and C is broader but less directly required.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-analysis approach: I identified the gap between the evidence (“overlapping brain regions activate”) and the conclusion (“social rejection causes physical pain”). The key factor was that the argument relies on treating shared neural activation as meaningful evidence that psychological and physical reactions are linked, rather than merely coincidental. My success came from focusing on the bridge principle required by the inference, not on statements that were true but merely supportive or descriptive. For similar problems, I should explicitly ask: “What unstated rule must be true for this evidence to justify this exact conclusion?”
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task as an assumption question: identify the hidden bridge needed to move from an observed correlation in brain activation to a causal claim about physical pain from social rejection. That interpretation was correct, because the argument’s key move was not about the imaging method itself, but about what shared neural activation is supposed to mean. My strategy was to look for the gap between evidence and conclusion, which is the right approach for assumption problems. The evidence given was that certain brain regions activated by rejection overlap with those activated by physical pain; the conclusion inferred that rejection therefore produces physical pain. To justify that inference, the argument needed a principle connecting psychological and physiological responses via shared brain mechanisms.

I correctly rejected the answer about imaging methodology because technical reliability of localization does not establish the conceptual link needed by the conclusion. I also correctly noticed that the option about pain and social stress was too close to the conclusion, making it more like a restatement than a necessary assumption. One subtle risk in my reasoning was not explicitly distinguishing correlation, overlap, and causal interpretation; that should always be stated more clearly. I should also test assumptions by negation: if psychological and physiological reactions could not be linked through the brain, the conclusion would collapse. In similar problems, I should identify the exact inferential leap and ask what general principle makes that leap possible. General rule: when an argument infers a real-world connection from a shared indicator, the needed assumption is the rule that makes that indicator evidentially meaningful, not a restatement of the conclusion or a detail about the measurement tool.

item.context: Principle: A government should reduce taxes on imports if doing so would financially benefit many consumers in its domestic economy. There is a notable exception, however: it should never reduce import taxes if one or more of its domestic industries would be significantly harmed by the added competition. Conclusion: The government should not reduce taxes on textile imports.
item.question: Which one of the following is a statement from which the conclusion can be properly drawn using the principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The domestic textile industry faces significant competition in many of its export markets.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reducing taxes on textile imports would financially benefit some consumers in the domestic economy but would not benefit the domestic textile industry.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The added competition produced by any reduction of taxes on imports would significantly harm the domestic textile industry.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The domestic textile industry and consumers in the domestic economy would benefit less from reductions in taxes on textile imports than they would from other measures.

response:
Reasoning: The principle says never reduce import taxes if added competition would significantly harm a domestic industry. If reducing taxes on textile imports would significantly harm the domestic textile industry, then the government should not reduce those taxes. Only C states this directly.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a direct conditional-matching approach: I translated the principle into a rule with an exception and looked for the choice that triggered the exception strongly enough to force the conclusion. The key factor was the “should never reduce import taxes if” clause, which makes significant harm to a domestic industry sufficient to justify not reducing the tax, regardless of consumer benefit. My success came from focusing on the exact condition tied to the conclusion rather than being distracted by weaker statements about competition, limited consumer benefit, or relative usefulness. For similar problems, isolate the sufficient condition in the principle that guarantees the conclusion and choose the option that explicitly satisfies that condition.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task correctly as a principle-application question: identify the statement that, when combined with the given rule, is sufficient to justify the conclusion that the government should not reduce taxes on textile imports. My strategy was to focus on the exception in the principle, because the conclusion was negative and the exception gives a direct route to “should not reduce.” That was appropriate because the principle’s structure is effectively: reduce taxes when many consumers benefit, unless a domestic industry would be significantly harmed, in which case do not reduce them. I used the key conditional relationship that significant harm to even one domestic industry blocks any tax reduction, regardless of consumer benefit. The crucial evidence was the phrase “one or more of its domestic industries would be significantly harmed by the added competition,” and I matched that to the textile industry specifically. I did not rely on weaker ideas such as mere lack of benefit to the domestic textile industry or comparisons to alternative policies, because those are not part of the stated rule. I also correctly rejected irrelevant considerations like competition in export markets, since the principle concerns harm from added import competition in the domestic economy. The success came from treating the exception as decisive rather than balancing all factors loosely. In similar problems, I should continue translating principles into clear sufficient conditions and exceptions before evaluating choices. A general rule is: when a principle contains an explicit override or exception, any answer that triggers that override is stronger than answers that mention only peripheral benefits, disadvantages, or comparisons.

item.context: Recently, we conducted a survey on insurers of insurance companies. The results show that the performance of insurers with better working environment is 25% higher than those with poor working environment. The objective criteria for evaluating work performance include workload and complexity of work. This shows that improving the artificial environment will improve their labor productivity.
item.question: So, which of the followings is the most unlikely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Workers with higher productivity do not work more hours than their less productive colleagues

choices.label: B
choices.text: Generally, workers with high labor productivity are rewarded with a pleasant working environment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compared with a pleasant working environment, an unpleasant environment will reduce workers' work motivation

choices.label: D
choices.text: On average, low productivity workers spend less time on the job than their high productivity colleagues

response:
Reasoning: The survey shows correlation, not causation. The conclusion assumes the environment causes higher productivity. Option B offers the strongest reverse-causation explanation: productive workers may be given better environments as a reward, so improving environment itself may not raise productivity.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a causal-reasoning approach, checking whether the conclusion improperly inferred causation from a reported association. The key factor was that the survey only showed that better environments and higher performance occurred together, while the conclusion claimed that changing the environment would itself raise productivity. My success came from identifying a reverse-causation alternative: productivity could influence who gets the better environment, which directly undermines the inference. For similar problems, I should test any causal claim against at least three alternatives—reverse causation, omitted variables, and mere correlation—before accepting the conclusion.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the option that is least compatible with the argument’s conclusion, not simply the one that sounds false in the real world. The passage moved from an observed association between working environment and performance to a causal claim that improving the environment will raise productivity, so the key reasoning task was to test that causal inference. My strategy was to look for an option that would undermine the direction of causation most directly, because “most unlikely” here functions like “least supported if the argument is valid.” That was appropriate, since the argument’s weak point is the jump from correlation to causation.

The critical fact I used was that the survey only established that better environments and higher performance occur together; it did not establish which causes which, or whether both are caused by something else. Option B introduced a reverse-causation explanation: high-productivity workers might receive better environments as a consequence of their productivity. If that were true, then the argument’s conclusion about improving the environment increasing productivity would be much less credible. I did not need to rely on the workload criterion in detail, because it mainly framed how performance was measured rather than securing causation. I also correctly avoided treating options about hours worked or motivation as equally damaging, since they do not directly challenge the causal direction. The success came from identifying the exact inferential gap rather than comparing options superficially. In similar problems, I should explicitly separate observational evidence from causal claims and ask what alternative causal structures fit the same data. General rule: when an argument infers causation from correlation, first test reverse causation and common-cause explanations before accepting the proposed direction.

item.context: Every new play that runs for more than three months is either a commercial or a critical success. Last year, all new plays that were critical successes were also commercial successes. Ttherefore, every new play that ran for more than three months last year was a commercial success.
item.question: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most new restaurants require either good publicity or a good location in order to succeed. But most restaurants with a good location also receive good publicity. Hence, a restaurant that has a good location is guaranteed to succeed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All students at the Freeman School of Cooking study either desserts or soups in their second year. This year, all Freeman students studying soups are also studying desserts. Ttherefore, every second-year student at Freeman is studying desserts this year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every catering service in Woodside Township will accept both residential and business catering assignments. Peggy's Fine Foods is a catering service that will not accept business catering assignments. Hence, Peggy's Fine Foods is not in Woodside Township.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every best-selling cookbook published last year is both well written and contains beautiful photographs. The cookbook Cynthia Cleveland published last year is well written and contains beautiful photographs. Ttherefore, Cleveland's cookbook is a best seller.

response:
Reasoning: The argument has form: A → (B or C); C → B; therefore A → B. Option B matches: second-year student → (desserts or soups); soups → desserts; therefore second-year student → desserts. The others use different structures or invalid reversals.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a structural analogy approach, translating the stimulus into conditional form and then comparing each option’s logical pattern rather than its subject matter. The key relationship was: if something falls into either of two categories, and one of those categories is entirely contained within the other, then everything in the original group must be in the broader category. My success came from explicitly mapping the argument as \(A \rightarrow (B \text{ or } C)\), \(C \rightarrow B\), therefore \(A \rightarrow B\), which made the matching option stand out. For similar problems, first rewrite each argument into abstract conditional symbols and compare the exact inference pattern before considering wording.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stimulus as a pure argument-form question, so the key task was to abstract the logical structure rather than focus on the subject matter about plays. I read the premises as: if a play ran more than three months, then it was either commercially successful or critically successful; and last year, any critical success was also a commercial success. From those two premises, the conclusion followed by subsuming one branch of the disjunction into the other, yielding a single required outcome. My strategy was therefore appropriate: translate the argument into symbolic form, compare each answer choice to that template, and reject choices that introduced quantifier shifts, converse errors, or different conditional patterns.

The crucial relationship I used was the pattern \(A \rightarrow (B \lor C)\), \(C \rightarrow B\), therefore \(A \rightarrow B\). I also correctly noticed that the “last year/this year” timing detail in the parallel choice had to match the restricted scope of the second premise, rather than be treated as irrelevant decoration. One assumption that helped, and was justified, was treating “either … or …” as inclusive, since the conclusion does not depend on exclusivity. I should still be alert in other problems to whether “either/or” is intended inclusively or exclusively, because that can change validity. I properly considered alternatives by checking whether any choice merely reversed a conditional or concluded too much from “most.” What made the reasoning successful was focusing on formal structure instead of plausibility. A transferable rule is: when one premise gives a disjunction and another premise makes one disjunct imply the other, collapse the disjunction before comparing answer choices.

item.context: Self-efficacy: refers to people's belief in their ability to produce a certain level of behavior that can affect their own life events.
item.question: Which of the following is not related to self-efficacy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The company leaders strictly require Xiao Dong to answer the phone every day, respect customers, and not play computer games during work

choices.label: B
choices.text: Xiaochang always treats difficult tasks as challenges to be conquered rather than threats to be avoided. He often sets challenging goals for himself and keeps his commitment to the goals

choices.label: C
choices.text: Xiao Cai's image in everyone's mind is: he likes to attribute failure to insufficient effort or lack of available knowledge and skills

choices.label: D
choices.text: Xiao Guo of Xinglong Industrial Co., Ltd. never forgets his shortcomings, will encounter obstacles and various unfavorable results, but does not carefully consider how to act successfully

response:
Reasoning: Self-efficacy is about one’s own belief in handling tasks and challenges. B and C reflect typical high self-efficacy traits. D describes low self-efficacy-related thinking. A is external company management requirements, not a person’s self-belief.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option to the core idea of self-efficacy as a person’s belief about their own ability to act effectively. The key factor was whether the description showed an internal belief pattern about handling challenges, effort, and success, versus an external rule or management demand. The successful step was separating personal cognition from outside control, which made the non-related option stand out. For similar problems, I should first restate the defining feature of the concept, then test each choice for direct fit with that feature rather than picking the one that merely sounds less positive.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking which option does not describe a person’s belief about their own capability to organize and carry out behavior. That interpretation was correct, because self-efficacy concerns internal judgments of competence, not simply any behavior or outcome-related statement. My strategy was to compare each option against core indicators of self-efficacy: challenge orientation, persistence, causal explanations for failure, and confidence in managing obstacles. That was an appropriate strategy because the concept is defined by perceived personal agency, so options reflecting beliefs, attributions, or coping tendencies are relevant even if they describe high or low self-efficacy. I used the fact that treating difficult tasks as challenges and attributing failure to effort or skills are classic self-efficacy-related patterns. I also recognized that even negative self-referential patterns can still be related to self-efficacy if they describe how someone evaluates their ability to act effectively. The key distinction was between internal belief structures and external control or organizational rules. A possible shortcut I used was assuming that any statement about management requirements is automatically unrelated, but here that shortcut was justified because the option contained no self-appraisal element. I should still consider whether an externally described behavior might imply internal belief before excluding it. The specific reason the reasoning succeeded is that I classified the options by psychological construct, not by whether the behavior seemed desirable. General rule: when identifying examples of a construct, test whether each option contains the construct’s defining mechanism rather than merely a surrounding context or consequence.

item.context: Studies have shown that people who rarely take antibiotics have a stronger immune system than those who take antibiotics regularly. However, there is no evidence that taking antibiotics weakens the immune system.
item.question: Which of the followings, if correct, can best reconcile the inconsistencies between the above information?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some people often take antibiotics because their doctors prescribe antibiotics for both viral and bacterial infections.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People with strong immunity are rarely infected with diseases that people usually treat with antibiotics.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although antibiotics can have many side effects, some people still use them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If people with poor immunity do not take antibiotics, it is difficult to recover from bacterial infectious diseases.

response:
Reasoning: The correlation can be explained by reverse causation: people with stronger immune systems get fewer infections, so they rarely need antibiotics. Thus, rare antibiotic use is a result of strong immunity, not the cause, which reconciles the statements.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a causal-reconciliation approach: instead of assuming antibiotics affect immunity, I looked for an explanation in which immune strength influences antibiotic use. The key factor was the need to explain a correlation without contradicting the statement that there is no evidence antibiotics weaken the immune system. My success came from identifying reverse causation: people with stronger immunity get sick less often and therefore take antibiotics less often. For similar problems, test whether the observed association can be explained by a third factor or reversed direction of causality before accepting a direct causal link.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for an explanation that removes an apparent contradiction between a correlation and a denial of causation. The key was to notice that the passage says people who rarely take antibiotics tend to have stronger immune systems, but also says there is no evidence that antibiotics themselves weaken immunity. My strategy was to look for a third-factor or reverse-causation explanation rather than a direct causal mechanism. That was appropriate because “best reconcile” questions usually require showing how both statements can be true at once.

The central fact I used was that stronger immunity can reduce the frequency of infections, which in turn reduces the need for antibiotics. This preserves the observed association without implying that antibiotic use causes weaker immunity. I correctly avoided assuming that correlation implies causation, which is the main trap in the stimulus. I also implicitly checked whether the choice explained why low antibiotic use and strong immunity appear together, rather than merely adding background information.

The alternatives were weaker because they discussed prescribing habits, side effects, or recovery difficulty without directly linking immune strength to antibiotic frequency. What made the reasoning successful was identifying the direction of dependence: immunity level can influence antibiotic use, not necessarily the reverse. In similar problems, I should explicitly test at least three causal structures: X causes Y, Y causes X, or a third factor causes both. General rule: when two statements conflict only if a causal interpretation is assumed, prefer an answer that explains the correlation through selection effects, reverse causation, or a common cause.

item.context: Product liability means that the product is defective, there is a danger that may endanger personal and property safety, and causes the personal or other direct property losses of the consumer, user or other third party of the product, the producer and seller of the defective product should bear legal liability of tort.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following victims can claim compensation for infringement damages due to product liability?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bought a new car, and when he drove out with his friend Wang, the car spontaneously ignited due to circuit quality problems, causing Wang to be burned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: B bought a coat. There was no washing sign and ingredient description on the coat, and the salesperson did not tell how to wash it. The coat shrank seriously after washing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: C bought a new mobile phone, and it turned off automatically due to quality problems and could not be turned on. As a result, C missed the customer's call and lost a large order.

choices.label: D
choices.text: D's TV set has been in use for 20 years, and just a few taps when the image is not clear. Once D was tapping the TV, the TV exploded and injured Ding. After inspection, it was found that it was caused by the aging of the picture tube.

response:
Reasoning: Product liability tort requires a defective product that threatens safety and causes personal injury or direct property loss. A fits: a car defect caused Wang’s burns. B is only damage to the product itself, C is indirect economic loss, and D resulted from aging after long use, not a product defect.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used definition matching: I broke the rule into required elements—product defect, safety danger, and personal injury or direct property loss to a consumer, user, or third party—and checked each option against them. The key factor was distinguishing compensable tort harm from non-covered losses, especially separating personal injury/direct property damage from damage to the product itself or purely economic loss. The successful step was noticing that only one scenario clearly involved a defective product causing physical injury to another person. For similar problems, convert the definition into a checklist of necessary elements and eliminate any option missing even one required element.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the definition as setting out three cumulative elements: a product defect, a safety-threatening danger, and resulting personal injury or direct property loss to a consumer, user, or third party. That interpretation was correct, and it guided me to test each option against all elements rather than just asking whether the product had a quality problem. My strategy was to classify the harms by type: personal injury, direct property damage, damage only to the product itself, and indirect economic loss. That was appropriate because product liability in the definition is not triggered by every breach of quality or performance; it is limited to safety-related tort harm.

The key facts I used well were that one scenario involved bodily injury to a third party, one involved only shrinkage of the purchased item itself, one involved lost business profits after malfunction, and one involved an old product failing from aging after very long use. I also correctly treated “other direct property losses” as excluding consequential losses like missed commercial opportunities. An important assumption I made was that “defective product” refers to a defect existing in the product, not deterioration caused by ordinary aging after decades of use; that assumption fits the legal framing here.
