I interpreted the argument as a conditional logical inference: the premises described who the shoe factory employs relative to all other businesses, and the conclusion shifted to how many **Centerville residents** in that employment category would lose jobs if the factory closed. The key issue was whether the employment comparison in the premises matched the resident-based population in the conclusion. My strategy was to look for the missing bridge between “people employed by the factory” and “residents of Centerville with full-time unskilled jobs in Centerville.” That was the right strategy because assumption questions often hinge on a category shift between premise and conclusion.

The crucial fact I used was that the premise only guaranteed the factory employed more unskilled full-time workers than all other businesses combined; by itself, that does not guarantee a majority of **residents** would be affected. I recognized that if many of the factory workers were nonresidents, the conclusion about residents could fail. That made the residency link the decisive hidden assumption. I did not rely on irrelevant background facts like total employment, skilled versus unskilled population balance, or the number of factories, which was appropriate because those facts do not address the category shift.

What made the reasoning successful was identifying the exact term introduced in the conclusion but unsupported in the premises: “residents of Centerville.” In similar problems, I should systematically compare the noun groups in premises and conclusion and ask whether any subgroup, location, or time frame has changed. A transferable rule is: when a conclusion quantifies over a narrower group than the premises, the necessary assumption often states that the broader group in the premises is contained within that narrower group.

item.context: Spiritual support: In family life, children understand, respect, care, consider their parents, and try their best to meet their spiritual needs.
item.question: Which of the following does not belong to spiritual support?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lao Sun recently bought an LCD TV and installed it in his parents' room, so that the two old men can watch their favorite shows, and he also bought multiple Peking Opera CDs for them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although Lao Wu did not live with his parents, he has developed the habit of visiting every day for many years, taking care of their lives meticulously, and the elderly are very pleased.

choices.label: C
choices.text: As the Spring Festival is approaching, Dean Li of the Sunset Red Nursing Home invited the Little Red Flower Paradise of Chaoyang Primary School. The laughter and wonderful programs of the children brought endless happiness to the elderly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lao Jiang's mother is in her 70s, but she still refuses to accept her old age. She signed up for a ballroom dancing training class. In order to prevent the elderly from getting angry and to ensure their safety, Lao Jiang quietly followed behind every time her mother went to class.

response:
Reasoning: Spiritual support focuses on emotional comfort, respect, companionship, and enriching elders’ mental life. A, C, and D all support the elderly’s interests or happiness. B mainly emphasizes daily life care and practical support, not specifically spiritual support.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a category-matching approach: I compared each option to the definition’s core elements—children understanding, respecting, caring for, and considering their parents’ spiritual needs. The key clue I underweighted was the subject constraint: this is specifically about support provided by children within family life, not just any activity that makes older people happy. My error was focusing too much on whether an act was emotional versus practical, and not enough on who provided the support and whether it fit the parent-child family context. For similar problems, first check all definitional conditions—actor, recipient, relationship, and type of support—before comparing examples.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the prompt as asking which option failed to count as “spiritual support,” meaning support that comes from family members’ understanding, respect, consideration, and efforts to satisfy parents’ emotional or psychological needs. My overall strategy was to classify each option as either emotional/spiritual care or practical/material care, which was a reasonable starting point. However, I focused too narrowly on the phrase “spiritual support” and not enough on the definitional context “in family life” and “children” meeting “their parents’” needs. That missing relational constraint was decisive. I treated any action that made elders happy as qualifying, even if it was provided by an institution and schoolchildren rather than by the elders’ own children within family life.  

The evidence I used correctly was that several options involved companionship, respect for interests, or emotional consideration. The evidence I missed was the subject of the support: the definition was not just about the type of benefit, but also who provides it and in what context. I also assumed that “taking care of their lives meticulously” made one option primarily material support, but I overlooked that frequent visits over many years can itself be a form of emotional companionship. I should have compared options on all definitional elements, not just one feature. The specific cause of error was reducing a multi-part definition to a single dimension. A transferable rule is: when a concept is defined by both content and relationship, test every answer choice against each required condition before excluding one.

item.context: Some anthropologists believe that humans could not have survived in prehistoric times without the ability to cope with various natural environments. However, there is considerable evidence that Australopithecus, a prehistoric species related to early humans, was as tenacious as prehistoric humans in a variety of natural environments, but eventually became extinct. Therefore, the above view of anthropologists is wrong.
item.question: Which of the following is similar to the loophole in the above reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Big Zhang realized that gambling is harmful, but he just can't change it. Therefore, the conclusion that if you do not recognize mistakes, you cannot correct them is not valid.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Evidence of operational error has been found to prove that the Acer mine disaster was caused. Therefore, the speculation that the Acer mine disaster is caused by aging equipment and disrepair is not valid.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dali bought this pair of sneakers cheaply and they were worn out after a few days. Therefore, it is unreasonable to suspect that there is no good thing to be cheap.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Since there is no doubt that Xiao Zhao may be admitted to the university, there is no reason to worry that Xiao Zhao may not be admitted to the university.

response:
Reasoning: The argument attacks a necessary-condition claim by giving a case showing the condition is not sufficient. A does the same: recognizing mistakes may be necessary for correction, but Big Zhang shows it is not sufficient, which doesn’t refute the original claim.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a conditional-logic approach, identifying the original argument as attacking a necessary condition by offering a case that only shows the condition is not sufficient. The key clue was the structure: “could not survive without X” means X is necessary, while the evidence cited only shows that having X does not guarantee survival. My success came from matching that exact flaw in the option, rather than focusing on topic similarity. For similar problems, first translate the claim into necessary vs. sufficient form, then check whether the counterexample actually targets the same direction of the condition.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the original argument as attacking a necessary-condition claim: the anthropologists’ view says a certain ability was required for survival, not that possessing that ability guaranteed survival. My strategy was to compare the logical form of the stimulus with each option rather than focus on subject matter, which was appropriate for a “similar loophole” question. The key relationship I used was the distinction between necessity and sufficiency: showing that one species had the ability yet still went extinct only shows the ability was not enough by itself, not that it was unnecessary. That same pattern appeared in my chosen option, where an example showed that recognizing a mistake does not always lead to correcting it, which fails to challenge the claim that recognition is required for correction.

A crucial part of the success was not being distracted by the plausibility of the claims themselves and instead tracking the direction of the conditional reasoning. I implicitly tested whether the counterexample matched the statement being attacked: to refute a necessary condition, the example would need success without the condition, not failure despite the condition. I also considered the alternatives by checking whether they involved different flaws, such as weak causal inference or dismissing a concern without justification. The main risk in problems like this is to treat “necessary for X” and “enough for X” as interchangeable, which would collapse two distinct logical structures. In similar questions, I should explicitly restate the claim as “without A, not B” or “if B, then A” before evaluating the rebuttal. General rule: a counterexample only refutes a conditional claim if it contradicts the exact direction of that claim, not its converse.

item.context: A student in a class did a good deeds without leaving a name. Four teachers, including A, B, C, D, etc. expressed their opinions to the four students in the class. A said: If this thing wasn't done by Zhang San, it would definitely be Zhao Liu did it. B said: If Zhang San did this thing, then Li Si or Wang Wu will do it too. C said: If Li Si doesn't do this thing, Wang Wu will not do it either. ;Zhao Liu would not be the one who did this. Ding said: This thing must have been done by Zhang San, and neither Li Si nor Wang Wu would do it.
item.question: Afterwards, I learned that only one of the four teachers'views was correct. Based on this, it can be concluded that which of the following students did a good thing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Zhang San

choices.label: B
choices.text: Li Si

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wang Wu

choices.label: D
choices.text: Zhao Liu

response:
Reasoning: Let only one student have done it.  
A: ¬Zhang → Zhao.  
B: Zhang → (Li or Wang).  
C: (¬Li → ¬Wang) and ¬Zhao.  
D: Zhang and not Li and not Wang.

Test options:  
- Zhang: A,C,D true.  
- Li: B,C true.  
- Wang: only B true.  
- Zhao: A,B true.  
So only Wang fits.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a case-by-case truth-table approach, translating each teacher’s statement into implications and then testing each student as the sole doer. The key factor I relied on was the “only one teacher is correct” constraint, but I combined it with an unstated extra assumption: that exactly one student did the good deed. That assumption distorted the implications, especially statements about whether other students “would do it too,” which only make sense if multiple students could have done good deeds. For similar problems, I should first verify whether exclusivity is explicitly given; if not, evaluate each statement under all allowed combinations instead of forcing a single-actor model.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the problem as a pure propositional-logic puzzle, and that general approach was appropriate, but I locked into one formalization too quickly. I translated each teacher’s remark into a single compound statement and then evaluated those statements under the extra assumption that exactly one student performed the deed. That assumption was a major shortcut: the prompt asks who did the deed, but the wording does not explicitly guarantee the exclusivity condition I imposed, so my model may already have diverged from the intended one. More importantly, I treated the awkwardly translated statement from C as an unquestioned conjunction, without checking whether the punctuation indicated one opinion, two separate claims, or a different scope. I also accepted the English rendering of A, B, C, and D at face value instead of asking whether any implication was intended as a stronger biconditional-style claim in the original wording. My evidence use was therefore mechanically consistent but linguistically fragile. The error was not in truth-table execution; it was in formalizing ambiguous natural language without validating the formalization. In similar problems, I should first list all plausible logical readings of each sentence before testing cases. If different formalizations lead to different outcomes, that is a signal to revisit the language rather than trust the first symbolic version. A transferable rule is: when a logic puzzle is translated or punctuated awkwardly, correctness depends first on semantic parsing, and symbolic deduction is only as reliable as that parse.

item.context: It is popularly believed that a poem has whatever meaning is assigned to it by the reader. But objective evaluation of poetry is possible only if this popular belief is false; for the aesthetic value of a poem cannot be discussed unless it is possible for at least two readers to agree on the correct interpretation of the poem.
item.question: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aesthetic evaluation of literature is best accomplished through discussion by more than two readers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If two readers agree about the meaning of a given poem, that ensures that an objective evaluation of the poem can be made.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discussion of a poem is possible only if it is false that a poem has whatever meaning is assigned to it by the reader.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A given poem can be objectively evaluated only if the poem's aesthetic value can be discussed.

response:
Reasoning: The argument moves from “aesthetic value cannot be discussed unless readers can agree on interpretation” to “therefore objective evaluation is possible only if that belief is false.” This requires assuming that objective evaluation depends on discussing the poem’s aesthetic value. Without that link, the conclusion does not follow.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a bridge-assumption approach: I identified the premise about when a poem’s aesthetic value can be discussed and the conclusion about when objective evaluation is possible, then looked for the missing link connecting those two ideas. The key factor was that the argument shifts from “discussion of aesthetic value” to “objective evaluation,” so it needs a principle saying evaluation depends on such discussion. My success came from noticing that this was not a direct restatement of the premise but a necessary dependency the conclusion relies on. For similar problems, explicitly map premise terms to conclusion terms and test what connecting condition must be true for the conclusion to follow.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stimulus as an argument about a necessary-condition chain: if objective evaluation of poetry is possible, then the popular belief must be false, because discussion of aesthetic value requires shared interpretation. That interpretation was correct because the conclusion was not claiming sufficiency, only what must be true for objective evaluation to occur. My strategy was to identify the gap between the premise about discussability and the conclusion about objective evaluation, then look for the missing bridge. That was appropriate because assumption questions often hinge on linking a premise-level requirement to the conclusion’s target concept. The key evidence I used was that the premise spoke only about when aesthetic value can be discussed, while the conclusion spoke about when objective evaluation is possible. I therefore inferred that the argument needed a principle connecting objective evaluation to the discussability of aesthetic value.

A possible shortcut I avoided, correctly, was confusing “agreeing on interpretation” with “guaranteeing objective evaluation,” which would have been too strong. I also properly ignored choices that shifted the issue from evaluation to discussion generally or introduced claims about “best” methods, since those were outside the argument’s scope. What made the reasoning successful was tracking the exact logical role of each claim rather than matching surface keywords. For similar problems, I should continue mapping the argument into conditional links and test whether the answer supplies a missing necessary connection. General rule: when a conclusion uses a concept not fully supported by the premises, the required assumption often links that concept to a premise condition without adding extra strength.

item.context: Undifferentiated Marketing: it means that the enterprise does not consider the characteristics of each sub market, but only pays attention to the commonness of the market, decides to launch only a single product, uses a single marketing combination, and strives to meet the needs of as many customers as possible to a certain extent.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings is Undifferentiated Marketing:

choices.label: A
choices.text: After market investigation, a cosmetics company found that no one produced medium and low-grade cosmetics with whitening characteristics, so it developed a cosmetics with whitening characteristics and promoted it in the market

choices.label: B
choices.text: An enterprise found that the health care products produced by some enterprises could make high profits, so it imitated them and produced similar products

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although the scale of a multinational company is very large, it only produces one beverage, and uses the same packaging and advertising in all regions of the world

choices.label: D
choices.text: After market analysis, an enterprise found that people in country A also prefer to drink instant coffee, so it sold a large number of instant coffee originally planned to be sold domestically to country a, and the packaging and price of coffee are exactly the same as those sold at home

response:
Reasoning: Undifferentiated marketing uses one product and one marketing mix for the whole market, ignoring segment differences. C clearly states one beverage with the same packaging and advertising worldwide. A targets a niche, B is imitation, and D is market transfer rather than a full undifferentiated strategy.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used direct definition matching: I extracted the core criteria from the definition—single product, single marketing mix, and no attention to submarket differences—and checked each option against all of them. The key factor was whether the company treated the entire market uniformly rather than identifying or exploiting a particular segment. My reasoning succeeded because I compared every option to the full definition instead of latching onto just “same product” or “same packaging” alone. For similar problems, I should turn the definition into a short checklist of necessary conditions and reject any choice that misses even one required element.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the option that matches a specific marketing strategy definition, not merely one that shares a few surface features like selling one product. That interpretation was correct because the definition included several linked conditions: ignoring submarket differences, emphasizing common demand, offering a single product, and using a single marketing mix. My strategy was to compare each option against all elements of the definition rather than matching on a single phrase. That was appropriate because definition questions often include distractors that satisfy one condition but fail others.

The key evidence I used was the combination of “single product” and “same packaging and advertising,” which maps directly to a unified marketing mix applied broadly. I also correctly rejected the niche-targeting case because it focused on a specific underserved segment, which is the opposite of treating the market as homogeneous. I recognized that simple imitation is not enough; copying a profitable product says nothing about whether the firm ignores segment differences or uses one common marketing program. I also distinguished exporting the same product to another country from a full undifferentiated strategy, because the scenario did not clearly establish a whole-market orientation.

What made the reasoning successful was checking necessary conditions cumulatively instead of relying on intuition. In similar problems, I should continue testing every option against each clause of the definition. General rule: when applying a formal definition, require that the chosen example satisfy the core mechanism and all essential features, not just a familiar outcome.

item.context: Relevant studies have shown that mobile phones are more harmful than computers. Because of the small screen of it, people are more focused when playing mobile phones, so it hurts the eyes even more. When using computers, people's limbs can move, but people who addicted to playing with mobile phones often have little activity, which is more detrimental to their physical and mental health.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, weakens the above view most?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When the computer is in use, the display will emit electromagnetic and ionizing radiation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The background light of the computer is more likely to cause the user's vision loss and headaches than the mobile phone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scientific research shows that the use of mobile phones has nothing to do with the incidence of brain tumors and cancer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: People who use computers for a long time are prone to computer diseases such as mouse hands and cervical spondylosis.

response:
Reasoning: The claim says mobile phones harm eyes and health more than computers. The strongest weakening is evidence that computers actually cause greater eye-related harm. B directly states computer backlight is more likely to cause vision loss and headaches than mobile phones, most directly undermining the comparison.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a direct comparative-weighing approach: identify the claim’s core comparison, then choose the option that most directly shows the opposite side may be more harmful. The key factor was that the argument focused heavily on eye strain and overall harm, so evidence that computers are more likely to cause vision loss and headaches struck at the same dimension of harm. My success came from matching the weakening choice to the argument’s main comparative premise rather than picking a merely harmful fact about computers. For similar problems, first isolate the exact comparison being made, then prefer the option that reverses or undercuts that comparison on the same criterion the argument uses.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a weakening task aimed at the comparative claim that mobile phones are more harmful than computers overall. The key was not to find a statement showing phones have some harmless aspect, but one that most directly undercuts the reasons given for the comparison. My strategy was to identify the argument’s main support: stronger eye strain from phone use and worse physical/mental health due to less movement. Then I looked for an option that attacked one of those central supports by showing computers may actually be more damaging on a relevant dimension. Choice B fit because it directly reverses the eye-harm comparison, which is one of the argument’s explicit pillars.

The reasoning succeeded because I focused on comparative relevance rather than isolated harm. For example, A mentions radiation from computers, but without tying it to greater harm than phones in the argument’s terms, it is less targeted. C is about brain tumors and cancer, which the argument never used, so it weakens little. D gives harms from prolonged computer use, but it does not directly answer the specific comparison as sharply as B does. A useful lesson is: in weaken-the-argument questions, target the premise that carries the comparison, and prefer evidence that reverses the exact dimension the author relies on rather than introducing a new issue.

item.context: Zhang Nan is a staff member of a research institute, and his friends are all doctors or professors. Wang Xiao is a staff member of the research institute, and Zhao Lin is a middle school classmate of Zhang Nan.
item.question: If the above information is true, which of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wang Xiao is Zhang Nan's friend

choices.label: B
choices.text: Zhao Lin is not Zhang Nan's friend

choices.label: C
choices.text: If Wang Xiao is a doctor, then Wang Xiao is Zhang Nan's friend

choices.label: D
choices.text: If Zhao Lin is Zhang Nan's friend, then she is a PhD or professor

response:
Reasoning: Premise: all of Zhang Nan’s friends are doctors/PhDs or professors. This does not imply every doctor is his friend, nor that Zhao Lin is or isn’t his friend. But if Zhao Lin is his friend, then she must fit that category.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a conditional-logic approach: translate the statement “all of Zhang Nan’s friends are doctors or professors” into a one-way rule about friendship implying professional status. The key factor was recognizing that the premises give a necessary condition for being Zhang Nan’s friend, not a sufficient condition for someone with that status to be his friend. The successful step was testing each option against that direction of implication and rejecting choices that reversed it or added unsupported facts. For similar problems, explicitly rewrite statements of the form “all X are Y” as “if X, then Y” and check whether an option preserves that exact direction.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for a statement that is logically guaranteed by the premises in every possible case, not merely something plausible. My strategy was to translate the key premise into a conditional: “If someone is Zhang Nan’s friend, then that person is a doctor or professor.” That was the right approach because “must be true” questions depend on necessity, so the safest method is to identify direct logical consequences rather than infer extra social relationships. I correctly noticed that being a staff member of the same research institute does not imply friendship, so choice A lacked support. I also correctly rejected the temptation to infer anything definite about Zhao Lin’s friendship status from the fact that she is a former classmate; that fact alone neither confirms nor denies friendship, so B was not forced.  

The crucial evidence was the one-way nature of the premise: it restricts Zhang Nan’s friends, but it does not describe all doctors or professors. That distinction let me dismiss C, which tries to reverse the direction of implication by suggesting that being a doctor could make Wang Xiao a friend. My reasoning succeeded because I preserved the conditional structure instead of converting it into its converse. An assumption I avoided, correctly, was treating common workplace or school ties as evidence of friendship. In similar problems, I should continue converting statements like “all X are Y” into “if X, then Y” and then test each option against that exact direction. A general rule is: from “all X are Y,” you may infer statements about any confirmed X being Y, but you may not infer that any Y is X or that any non-X is excluded.

item.context: It is generally believed that the sports level and endurance of a professional athlete at the age of 45 are significantly lower than those at the age of 30. but the result of a marathon between retired and serving professional footballers was that there was no difference between 45-year-old retired footballers and 30-year-old serving players. Therefore, it is wrong to think that the sports level and endurance of a professional player will be significantly reduced by the age of 45.
item.question: Which of the following is true and can best strengthen the above argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The above investigation and analysis is carried out by scientific research institutions specializing in the physical fitness of football players

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sports level and endurance of active professional footballers around the age of 30 are higher than those of the previous generation of professional footballers

choices.label: C
choices.text: The retired professional players in the above survey are all long-term football coaches

choices.label: D
choices.text: The increase of age within a certain limit does not necessarily lead to a decline in exercise level and endurance

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion claims age 45 does not significantly reduce a professional player’s athletic level/endurance, based on footballers’ marathon results. The best support is the general principle that aging within a certain range does not necessarily cause decline, which directly backs the inference. A only supports credibility; B weakens comparability; C introduces a confounder.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a strengthen-the-argument approach by identifying the conclusion and asking which option most directly supports the move from one observed comparison to a broader claim. The key factor was that the argument depends on linking the marathon result to a general principle about age and athletic decline, rather than merely improving the study’s credibility. The successful step was distinguishing evidence that reinforces the inference itself from evidence that is only background or potentially introduces new variables. For similar problems, I should choose the option that closes the gap between the specific evidence and the general conclusion.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a strengthen-the-argument task, not a request for the most plausible standalone statement. The argument moved from one observed comparison in a marathon to a broader claim about whether athletic level and endurance necessarily decline by age 45, so the key was to find a choice that supported that generalization rather than merely praising the study. My strategy was to identify the gap between the evidence and the conclusion: a single empirical result needs a principle connecting age and performance to make the inference more credible. That was appropriate because strengthen questions are usually solved by locating the argument’s weakest inferential step and supplying support there.

I correctly noticed that one option only increased source credibility, which is weaker than adding substantive support to the claim itself. I also used the fact that another option introduced a cohort comparison across generations, which would undermine comparability rather than strengthen the age-based conclusion. I recognized that a further option created an alternative explanation by suggesting the retired athletes might retain fitness for reasons unrelated to age. An important assumption in the argument was that marathon performance is an acceptable indicator of sports level and endurance for the purpose of the conclusion. The selected choice worked because it supplied a general rule under which the observed result becomes less surprising and more probative.

What made the reasoning successful was distinguishing evidence-strengthening from authority-strengthening and from confounder-adding information. In similar problems, I should continue testing each option by asking: does it support the link from premises to conclusion, or does it only affect credibility, comparability, or alternative causes? General rule: in a strengthen question, prefer the option that directly reinforces the argument’s missing bridge over options that merely describe the study, the source, or background facts.

item.context: The researchers used genetic manipulation to enable the experimental mice to metabolize glucose and fatty acids, but not acetic acid, and then compared the physical conditions of these experimental rats and normal experimental rats when they were fed bait and fasted for 48 hours. In the state of being forced to go on a hunger strike for a long time, the body temperature and endurance of the experimental mice that cannot metabolize acetic acid are significantly reduced. Acetic acid is the basic substance in life, and the body structure of the experimental mice is very close to the human body.
item.question: Which of the followings can be inferred from these?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetic acid plays a vital role in maintaining the body's energy supply.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acetic acid can be used as an energy source for the human body that does not increase blood sugar levels.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adenosine triphosphate produced by metabolism is the source of energy for life activities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: During prolonged exercise, fatty acids and ketone bodies are the main sources of ATP.

response:
Reasoning: Fasting mice unable to metabolize acetic acid showed much lower body temperature and endurance than normal mice. This supports that acetic acid is important for sustaining energy supply during prolonged starvation. The other options add claims not supported by the experiment.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an elimination-based inference approach: I matched the experimental result to the weakest claim directly supported by the evidence and rejected choices that introduced extra mechanisms or human-specific conclusions. The key clue was the contrast during 48-hour fasting: mice that could not metabolize acetic acid had sharply reduced temperature and endurance, showing that this metabolic pathway matters when energy is limited. The successful step was distinguishing a broad supported inference from stronger claims about blood sugar, ATP, or prolonged exercise that were not tested. For similar problems, infer only what the experiment directly compares, and avoid answer choices that extend from animal data to untested mechanisms or species.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the strongest conclusion supported directly by the experiment, not for a broad biology fact or a claim about humans in general. That was the right framing, because the passage described a manipulation, a comparison group, and an observed physiological decline under fasting conditions. My strategy was to match the observed difference—reduced body temperature and endurance in animals unable to metabolize acetic acid—to the most conservative causal role supported by the data. This was appropriate because the experiment isolated acetic-acid metabolism while leaving glucose and fatty-acid metabolism available, so the additional impairment during prolonged fasting pointed to a distinct energetic contribution from acetic acid. The key evidence I used was the contrast between normal and modified mice specifically after 48 hours of fasting, when stored glucose is limited and alternate fuels matter more. I also noticed that the statement about similarity to humans was too weak to justify a direct claim about human treatment or blood sugar effects. That helped eliminate options that extrapolated beyond the experiment. A shortcut that worked here was preferring the answer that stayed closest to the measured outcomes rather than introducing extra mechanisms like ATP details or exercise physiology not tested in the study. The success came from respecting the boundary between “supported by the experiment” and “plausible background knowledge.” In similar problems, I should explicitly ask which answer merely restates the experimental implication with the fewest added assumptions. General rule: when drawing inferences from an experiment, choose the option that is causally consistent with the manipulated variable and observed outcomes, while avoiding answers that extend to untested mechanisms, contexts, or species.

item.context: Job burnout: Refers to the phenomenon that the job itself requires excessive personal abilities, energy, and resources, which causes workers to feel emotionally exhausted and worn out.
item.question: According to this definition, which of the following does not belong to burnout of teacher?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Teacher Xiao Wang feels it is difficult to complete the additional teaching tasks assigned by the school

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many students are very naughty now, and some young teachers are struggling to cope

choices.label: C
choices.text: Teacher Li can't keep up the energy in class these days because he often works overtime recently

choices.label: D
choices.text: Teacher Xiao Zhang has always been frowning at work recently because of the tension with her husband

response:
Reasoning: Burnout here must be caused by excessive job demands consuming ability, energy, or resources. A, B, and C are all due to teaching workload or classroom pressures. D is caused by marital/family tension, not the teaching job itself, so it does not belong to teacher burnout.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option against the requirement that the exhaustion must come from the job itself demanding too much ability, energy, or resources. The key factor was the source of the strain—whether it was work-related or caused by something outside the job. The successful step was separating symptoms shown at work from causes rooted in work demands. For similar problems, explicitly test each option against every part of the definition, especially the causal source, rather than judging only by the surface appearance of stress or fatigue.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a definition-matching task: identify which scenario fails the causal condition in the definition of teacher burnout. That interpretation was correct because the key phrase was that the exhaustion must come from the job itself demanding excessive ability, energy, or resources. My strategy was to test each option against that causal criterion rather than against a vague feeling of stress or unhappiness. That was appropriate because several choices described fatigue or difficulty, but only some linked those experiences directly to teaching work.

The decisive evidence I used was the source of the teacher’s emotional depletion. In three options, the pressure came from added school tasks, difficult students, or overtime work, all of which are job-related demands. In the remaining option, the negative mood originated in a personal relationship outside work, so it failed the definitional constraint. A potential shortcut I avoided was equating any bad mood at work with burnout; the definition required occupational causation, not merely workplace presence. Another possibility I correctly ruled out was that reduced classroom energy automatically excludes burnout; the cause still mattered more than the symptom.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on necessary conditions in the definition, especially the phrase “the job itself.” In similar problems, I should continue separating symptom, setting, and cause before matching examples. General rule: when a concept is defined by a specific causal source, classify cases by the origin of the condition, not by superficial similarity in behavior or emotion.

item.context: It is generally believed that early music training can enhance an individual's musical sound and speech processing ability. But some psychologists doubt this. Researchers investigated 1211 pairs of identical twins and 1358 pairs of fraternal twins born between 1959 and 1985, recorded their music practice time and evaluated their music ability. They found that, Practicing for a longer time does not show better musical ability. For example, a pair of identical twins with the same gene have 20228 hours of musical practice time difference, but their musical ability is exactly the same. These researchers believe that without the correct gene, it is meaningless to practice for 20000 hours, and the musical ability is determined by the gene.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, most refutes the researcher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Musical ability assessment uses fingers to simulate fast-paced music, and finger flexibility is genetically affected

choices.label: B
choices.text: Individuals with genetically superior auditory skills may choose to become musicians themselves and practice longer

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is usually telepathy between identical twins, which affects the performance of individuals in music ability tests

choices.label: D
choices.text: People with poor musical ability underestimate their practice time in order to maintain psychological balance

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion attributes equal musical ability among twins to genes, not practice. If identical twins influence each other’s test performance through telepathy, then similar scores need not come from genes alone, undermining the study’s key evidence. A and B support genetic explanations; D doesn’t clearly explain away the result.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a weaken-the-argument approach: identify the researchers’ main inference and look for an alternative explanation for the evidence they treat as proof of genetic determination. The key factor was that their conclusion depended heavily on identical twins showing the same measured ability despite very different practice time, so anything that could make twins score similarly for a non-genetic reason would undercut that inference. My success came from targeting the link between evidence and conclusion rather than debating whether practice usually helps. For similar problems, I should isolate the study’s critical comparison and ask what hidden factor could create the observed pattern without supporting the claimed cause.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a weaken-the-conclusion problem: the task was not to explain the data, but to identify a fact that most undermines the researchers’ jump from correlation within twin pairs to a strong genetic-determinism claim. My strategy was to locate the key inferential link in the argument, namely that equal performance among genetically identical twins despite different practice histories proves practice is meaningless and genes determine ability. That was the right strategy because the best refutation would attack either the validity of the test scores or the inference from twin similarity to genetic causation. I focused on the possibility that the observed similarity in ability could arise from something other than genes, which directly challenges the researchers’ main evidence. I also correctly recognized that some options merely made the genetic account more plausible rather than weakening it. In particular, I rejected alternatives that described genetically influenced traits or self-selection into music practice, because those do not undercut the conclusion’s evidential basis. One assumption in my reasoning was that a flaw affecting the measurement of ability is more damaging than a competing causal story about practice time, and here that assumption was appropriate. The reasoning succeeded because I distinguished between facts that support heredity and facts that expose a confound in the study’s interpretation. For similar problems, I should continue identifying the exact causal or inferential step being claimed and then prefer answers that introduce an alternative explanation for the crucial evidence rather than answers that merely comment on side details. A good transferable rule is: when an argument claims “X proves Y,” the strongest refutation often shows that the observed evidence for Y could be produced by some factor other than X.

item.context: A researcher believes that human language originally came directly from birds and primates, because if we re-examine modern human language, we can see how human communication evolved from the ancient communication mode system of birds and other primates; From other primates, we got the practical content of language. Sometime in the past 100000 years, these abilities eventually evolved into the human language we know today.
item.question: Which of the following premises should the above conclusions be based on?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Human communication is more similar to that of other animals than we generally think

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human language consists of two different levels: the expressive level related to the variable structure of sentences and the lexical level expressing the core content of sentences

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human language communication has changed little in the past and now

choices.label: D
choices.text: Birds and mammals other than humans have their own communication language

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion depends on linking parts of human language to two ancestral sources: birds for expressive structure and primates for practical content. That requires assuming human language has two separable levels matching those functions, which is exactly what B states.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a structural-mapping approach: I looked for a premise that mirrored the argument’s division of human language into components and chose the option that best matched that internal structure. The key clue I focused on was the claim that birds contributed one aspect of language while primates contributed another, which made the two-level description seem necessary. My mistake was confusing a helpful explanatory detail with a required assumption; the argument first needs the more basic premise that those nonhuman species actually have communicative systems that could serve as sources. In similar assumption questions, I should test each choice by asking whether the conclusion could even get started without it, and prefer foundational prerequisites over elaborating mechanisms.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument as needing a premise that explains how two different animal sources could map onto two components of human language. That interpretation was partly reasonable, but I focused too quickly on a detailed mechanism instead of identifying the minimum assumption required for the conclusion to get off the ground. My strategy was to look for a premise that mirrored the argument’s structure, so I chose the option that divided human language into two levels and seemed to align with “birds” and “primates.” That was an overfit: I treated an attractive explanatory model as if it were a necessary premise. The argument’s conclusion only needs a basic bridge showing that those nonhuman groups actually possess communication systems from which human language could plausibly descend. I missed the difference between a premise that enriches the theory and a premise that must be true for the theory even to be considered.

A key assumption behind my wrong choice was that the passage had already committed to a two-part architecture of language, when it had not. I should also have tested each option with a necessity check: if the option were false, would the conclusion collapse? Under that test, my chosen option was not essential, but the more basic existence claim was. The specific error was confusing “matches the story well” with “is required by the story.” In similar problems, I should first identify the weakest indispensable premise before considering more specific supporting details. General rule: when asked for a required premise, prefer the most fundamental enabling condition over a more elaborate explanatory framework.

item.context: Four randomly chosen market research companies each produced population estimates for three middle-sized cities; the estimates of each company were then compared with those of the other companies. Two of the cities had relatively stable populations, and for them estimates of current population and of projected population in five years varied little from company to company. However, for the third city, which was growing rapidly, estimates varied greatly from company to company.
item.question: The passage provides the most support for which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is more difficult to estimate the population of middle-sized cities than of smaller cities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The market research companies are likely to be equally reliable in estimating the population of stable cities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Estimates of a city's future population are likely to be more accurate than are estimates of that city's current population.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rate of change in population of rapidly growing cities does not fluctuate.

response:
Reasoning: The companies’ estimates for the two stable cities “varied little from company to company,” which supports that the companies were likely similarly reliable for stable cities. Nothing compares middle-sized to smaller cities, says future estimates are more accurate, or implies growth rates do not fluctuate.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used an inference-by-elimination approach: I matched the passage’s direct comparison of agreement across companies to the option that stayed closest to that evidence. The key factor was that for the two stable cities, both current and five-year estimates “varied little,” which supports similar reliability across companies in that context. What helped was distinguishing between what the passage explicitly supports and what would require extra assumptions, such as comparisons to smaller cities or claims about accuracy. For similar problems, choose the answer that restates the strongest supported relationship in the stimulus and reject options that introduce new comparisons, stronger claims, or unsupported causal ideas.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the answer choice most strongly supported by the comparative pattern in the passage, not the one that was definitively proven. My strategy was to track the contrast the passage emphasized: low variation among companies for the stable cities versus high variation for the rapidly growing city. That was appropriate because the stimulus gave no direct accuracy data, only agreement patterns, so the key was to infer what agreement among estimators reasonably suggests. I used the fact that similar estimates across companies for the stable cities supports a claim about comparable reliability there, especially relative to the city where estimates diverged. I also correctly noticed that the other choices introduced unsupported comparisons or stronger claims than the evidence allowed. For example, one option compared city sizes even though the passage only discussed middle-sized cities, and another claimed something about future versus current accuracy that the passage never established. An important assumption in my reasoning was that low inter-company variation is evidence of roughly equal reliability, even if it does not guarantee actual correctness. That assumption was justified because the question asked for “most support,” not certainty. What made the reasoning successful was matching the strength of the conclusion to the strength of the evidence and rejecting answer choices that went beyond the passage. In similar problems, I should continue distinguishing between agreement, accuracy, and causation rather than treating them as interchangeable. General rule: when a passage reports variation among observers or estimates, infer only what that variation directly bears on, and avoid conclusions that require external comparisons or stronger causal claims.

item.context: Despite all the evils of man, we must not forget the great and honorable qualities that his art forms reveal in science, the pursuit of truth, the creation of beauty and the concept of justice. Whenever we utter the words man or humanity, we touch on a great mystery; If we become unconscious of this mystery, then we have succumbed to spiritual death.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following fits the word mystery?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The man who possesses art, seeks science, truth and justice is guilty

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sinful human beings are associated with art, science, beauty and justice

choices.label: C
choices.text: Man, with all his well-known SINS, still has great and honorable qualities

choices.label: D
choices.text: Forget man's spiritual SINS, but never his great and lovable qualities

response:
Reasoning: The passage says that despite human evil, we should remember humanity’s noble qualities shown in art, science, truth, beauty, and justice. “Mystery” refers to this profound paradox of flawed yet honorable human nature. Option C expresses that best.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a paraphrasing and elimination approach: I restated the passage’s main idea as a paradox about human nature and then looked for the option that preserved that contrast. The key factor was the phrase “despite all the evils of man,” paired with “great and honorable qualities,” which shows that “mystery” refers to the coexistence of moral flaws and nobility in humanity. My success came from focusing on the overall relationship between the two halves of the passage rather than isolated words like art or justice. For similar problems, I should first identify the passage’s central contrast or structure, then choose the option that restates that full relationship most faithfully.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the best paraphrase of the passage’s use of “mystery,” not a literal definition like “unknown” or “secret.” That was the right framing, because the passage presents “mystery” as the profound coexistence of human evil with humanity’s noble capacities. My strategy was to identify the central contrast in the passage: human wrongdoing on one side, and art, science, truth, beauty, and justice on the other. That strategy was appropriate because the answer choices were not technical definitions; they were interpretive restatements. The key evidence I used was the opening concession, “Despite all the evils of man,” followed by the insistence that we “must not forget” the honorable qualities revealed in human achievements. I also noted that “mystery” referred to the whole paradox of humanity, not to just one trait such as guilt, spirituality, or beauty alone. A shortcut that helped, and happened to be valid here, was eliminating options that distorted the passage’s tone by adding claims like guilt or by telling us to forget sin. I should still recognize that paraphrase questions can hide traps through emotionally similar wording. Other possibilities to test were whether “mystery” referred to spiritual death or to artistic achievement alone, but the passage clearly tied it to the dual nature of humanity. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the answer to the passage’s structure of contrast rather than isolated vocabulary. A useful general rule is: when a passage defines an abstract term through contrast, choose the option that preserves the full relationship between opposing ideas, not one that exaggerates, moralizes, or drops one side of the contrast.

item.context: In 2018, 70.3 percent of families in A city had the habit of reading books with their children, with the number of books read by parents increasing by 1.8 percentage points compared with 2017, and the length of books read by parents also increasing compared with last year. However, the number of books read per child in the city was only 4.72 in 2018, down 0.6 percentage points from 2017.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, best explains this phenomenon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In recent years, children's school load is heavy, and many people are willing to spare time for extracurricular reading.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most of the parents born in the 1980s and 1990s are highly educated and pay more attention to the significance of parent-child reading

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many children are accustomed to listening to books in parent-child reading, which was not counted in 2018

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electronic reading by parents on mobile phones and computers has not been included in children's book reading

response:
Reasoning: The puzzle is: parent-child reading participation rose, parents read more and longer, yet children’s per-capita books fell. This is best explained if many children mainly “listened” to books during parent-child reading, and those were not counted as children’s book reading in 2018. That reconciles both facts.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a reconciliation approach: identify the apparent contradiction, then look for an option that makes both trends true at the same time. The key factor was the mismatch between increased parent-child reading activity and a lower measured number of books per child, which suggests a change in what was being counted rather than a real drop in reading exposure. My success came from focusing on the measurement gap implied by “not counted,” which directly explains why participation and parental reading could rise while the child metric fell. For similar problems, first separate behavior changes from measurement changes and prefer the choice that resolves the discrepancy by addressing the exact metric being reported.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for a causal explanation of an apparent mismatch: parent-child reading activity became more common and more intensive, yet the measured number of books read per child declined. That interpretation was correct because the task was not to identify a generally positive statement about reading, but to resolve a statistical-looking inconsistency. My strategy was to look for an answer that separated “more parent-child reading” from “more books counted as read by children,” which is the right framework for this kind of explanation question. I focused on the measurement issue: if part of the increased reading activity took a form that was excluded from the child-book count, then both trends can coexist without contradiction. The key fact I used was that the child metric was specifically “books read per child,” while the stimulus described parents reading more and for longer, which does not necessarily imply more counted books for children.

I correctly rejected options that only strengthened the idea that parents value reading, because those choices did not explain the decline in the child measure. I also implicitly distinguished between behavior change and accounting change, which was important here. One assumption behind my reasoning was that “listening to books” can increase parent-child reading time without increasing the recorded number of books children are considered to have read. I should continue to test each option against all parts of the stimulus, especially when the question asks to explain a seeming paradox. A transferable rule is: when trends appear inconsistent, prefer an option that identifies a definitional, counting, or category mismatch linking both trends rather than one that merely supports one side of the data.

item.context: Business reputation undoubtedly refers to credit and reputation, which refers to the social evaluation given by the public on the economic ability and credit status of specific commercial subjects. In criminal law, not all damage business reputation will constitute a crime. If the business subject has its own problems and its credit falls sharply and reputation is discredited after media exposure, such damage is actually brought about by the subject's own problems. The exercise of media supervision by public opinion is not illegal, but should be protected by law.
item.question: Which of the following is emphasized in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is not illegal for the media to expose businesses that do not keep their business reputation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Business problems caused by their own reputation damage is not protected by law

choices.label: C
choices.text: The law is very careful about the identification of acts that damage business reputation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Laws should be introduced to protect the media from public opinion supervision of businesses

response:
Reasoning: The passage stresses that not every act causing harm to a business’s reputation is criminal. If the harm comes from the business’s own misconduct exposed by lawful media supervision, it is not illegal. So the focus is on cautious legal determination of reputation-damaging acts.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an abstraction-heavy approach: I summarized the passage into a broader legal principle about cautious criminal identification instead of tracking what consequence the passage emphasized. The key clue was the contrast between unlawful reputation damage and losses caused by a business’s own misconduct after truthful media exposure. My error was choosing the more general legal framing rather than the passage’s concrete point that self-caused reputational harm is not entitled to legal protection. For similar questions, I should identify the sentence stating who is or is not protected, and match that specific claim before selecting a broader summary.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the passage as asking for the broad legal principle it highlighted, and I focused on the sentence saying that not all harm to business reputation constitutes a crime. That interpretation captured part of the passage, but I missed that the question asked what was emphasized most, not merely what was mentioned. My strategy was to abstract upward to a general legal rule, which is often useful, but here it caused me to overlook the passage’s more specific concluding point about lack of legal protection when reputational harm is self-caused. I used the contrast between unlawful defamation and lawful media supervision, but I underweighted the causal claim: when exposure reveals a business’s real defects, the resulting loss is attributed to the business itself. I also treated “not illegal” and “should be protected by law” as support for a general cautionary principle, instead of asking which answer best matched the passage’s target of protection or non-protection. A key assumption that misled me was that a more general statement is usually the main idea; in fact, the passage used the general rule only as setup for a narrower normative conclusion. I should have compared the answer choices by checking which one captured both causation and legal consequence together. I also should have rejected choices that merely paraphrased one sentence while ignoring the passage’s final evaluative emphasis. The specific error was selecting an option that summarized background reasoning rather than the author’s main takeaway. A transferable rule is: when a passage presents a general principle and then applies it to a concrete scenario, the emphasized point is usually the application or conclusion, not the introductory principle.

item.context: Place phobia is mainly manifested as fear of certain specific environments, such as high places, squares, objective environments, and crowded public places. It often starts with a spontaneous panic attack, and then produces anxiety about expectations and the behavior of avoidance, and finally becomes conditioning. Some clinical studies have shown that, patients with place phobia are often accompanied by panic attacks. However, some experts believe that the first panic attack is a necessary condition for the onset of  place phobia, and therefore claims that  place phobia is the consequence of the development of panic attacks and should be involved into the category of panic disorder.
item.question: Which one of the followings, if true, can most question the above experts' opinion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The course of place phobia often fluctuates, and many patients may improve or even alleviate in a short time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Place phobia may be related to heredity and panic disorder.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The study found that the onset of place phobia was mostly in people's 40s, and the course of disease tended to be chronic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The study found that some patients' place phobia appeared before panic attack.

response:
Reasoning: The experts claim a first panic attack is necessary for place phobia, so place phobia is just a result of panic disorder. If some patients develop place phobia before any panic attack, that directly contradicts the “necessary condition” claim.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a direct necessary-condition test: the experts’ claim depends on panic attack occurring first for place phobia to arise, so I looked for an option that breaks that causal/temporal requirement. The key factor was the phrase “necessary condition,” which means even one genuine counterexample is enough to seriously undermine the claim. My success came from focusing on order of onset rather than on background associations, severity, or course of illness. For similar problems, isolate whether the argument asserts necessity, sufficiency, or correlation, and then choose evidence that directly violates that exact logical relationship.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as an argument-weaken task, not a medical knowledge task. The experts’ core claim had two linked parts: first, that an initial panic attack is a necessary condition for the phobia’s onset, and second, that the phobia should therefore be classified as a consequence of panic disorder. My strategy was to identify the strongest way to attack a necessary-condition claim: find a case where the supposed effect occurs without the alleged prerequisite. That was appropriate because if even some cases begin before any panic attack, the experts’ causal and classificatory inference is undermined at its foundation.

The key evidence I focused on was the temporal order between the two conditions. I correctly recognized that timing matters more here than background correlations, severity, age of onset, or disease course. I did not get distracted by tempting but weaker alternatives that merely describe fluctuation, heredity, or chronicity, none of which directly bears on whether the first panic attack is required. My reasoning relied on a strict logical relationship: “necessary condition” means no occurrence without it. Because I tested the claim against a direct counterexample, the reasoning succeeded.

For similar problems, I should continue isolating the argument’s exact logical form before evaluating answer choices. A transferable rule is: when an argument asserts that X is necessary for Y, the strongest challenge is evidence of Y occurring without prior or accompanying X.

item.context: Research shows that 90% of people with severe insomnia like to drink strong tea. Lao Zhang likes drinking strong tea, so he is likely to have serious insomnia.
item.question: Which of the followings best points out the loopholes in the above argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It ignores the possibility that Lao Zhang belongs to 10% of those who don't have serious insomnia.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It ignores other causes of severe insomnia.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It ignores that drinking strong tea may also cause other adverse consequences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The argument it relies on does not involve the proportion of people who have severe insomnia among those who love strong tea.

response:
Reasoning: The argument reverses the conditional. From “90% of people with severe insomnia like strong tea” it does not follow that “people who like strong tea likely have severe insomnia.” We need the proportion of severe-insomnia cases among strong-tea drinkers, not vice versa.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a conditional/probabilistic reasoning approach, checking whether the statistic given actually supports the conclusion drawn. The key factor was the direction of the percentage: it described how common strong-tea drinking is among people with severe insomnia, but the conclusion needed information about how common severe insomnia is among strong-tea drinkers. My success came from noticing this reversal of conditional probability, a classic flaw in arguments based on percentages. For similar problems, I should explicitly match the denominator in the evidence to the denominator required by the conclusion before accepting the inference.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the flaw in an argument that infers a likely condition from a statistic stated in the opposite direction. That interpretation was correct, because the key issue was not whether tea and insomnia are related at all, but whether the cited percentage supports the conclusion drawn about Lao Zhang. My strategy was to compare the population described in the premise with the population required by the conclusion. The premise gives the proportion of strong-tea drinkers among people with severe insomnia, while the conclusion needs the proportion of severe insomnia among strong-tea drinkers. That distinction is exactly the relevant evidential gap.

The most important fact I used was that conditional-looking statistical claims cannot be inverted without additional information. I did not get distracted by causal possibilities, such as whether tea causes insomnia, because the argument’s flaw appears even before any causal analysis. I also correctly avoided choice A, which sounds plausible but misidentifies the problem as an exception case rather than a mismatch in statistical direction. The success came from focusing on base-rate structure rather than surface wording. An alternative I should always consider in similar problems is whether the conclusion requires the reverse conditional, a converse probability, or a missing denominator. The transferable rule is: when an argument moves from “most A are B” to “if B, then probably A,” check whether it has illegitimately reversed the reference class.

item.context: Last year, Jingwei Automobile Store raised the proportion of marketing performance rewards for marketers. Manager Li of the store plans to continue to implement the reward rate in the new year, as the store's car sales increased by 16% last year compared with the year before. Deputy Manager Chen is skeptical about this. She points out that their competitors have not adjusted the proportion of rewards for marketers, but there has been a similar increase in the past year.
item.question: Which of the following best summarizes the questioning method of Deputy Manager Chen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use a counterexample to negate Manager Li's general conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use a counterexample to show that Manager Li's argument is not in line with the facts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A counterexample is used to show that although Manager Li's argument is valid, it is not enough to draw a conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is pointed out that Manager Li's argument is wrong in the understanding and application of a key concept.

response:
Reasoning: Li infers that raising reward rates caused sales growth. Chen cites competitors with similar growth despite no reward-rate change, showing Li’s evidence does not sufficiently establish the causal conclusion, not necessarily that the facts are false or a concept is misused.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an argument-structure approach, identifying Li’s claim as a causal inference and Chen’s reply as a competing-case objection. The key factor was the competitor example: I treated it as merely weakening the sufficiency of Li’s evidence, so I classified it as “not enough to conclude.” My mistake was drawing too fine a distinction between “insufficient support” and “counterexample showing the claimed factual basis doesn’t fit reality as presented”; the option set wanted the latter. For similar problems, first match the rebuttal to the test-maker’s category by asking whether the example directly conflicts with the claimed factual linkage, not just whether it weakens causation.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the flaw in Chen’s rebuttal to Li’s causal inference, and that part was mostly right. My strategy was to classify the objection at a high level: I saw Chen presenting a comparison case where the supposed cause was absent but the same result occurred, so I treated it as undercutting causal sufficiency. That strategy is often useful on weakening questions, but here the task was more specific: identify the *questioning method* in the answer-choice taxonomy, not merely the logical weakness. I focused on the idea that Li’s evidence was “insufficient,” which led me to the option about a valid argument that cannot support the conclusion. The missed point is that Chen’s comparison was being framed not as a subtle criticism of evidential adequacy, but as a concrete counterexample showing that Li’s inference conflicts with observed facts. I assumed that because Li’s premises could still be true, the objection must be about non sequitur rather than factual mismatch; that was too abstract for the wording of the choices. I also failed to distinguish between “showing the cause is not established” and “showing a cited pattern is contradicted by comparable cases.” I should have tested each option against the exact rhetorical function of the competitor example, not my preferred causal-analysis template. In similar problems, I need to map the rebuttal to the answer choices using the source of attack: premise fact, inference link, or concept definition. General rule: when a respondent cites a parallel case with the key factor absent but the same outcome present, first check whether the test is classifying that move as a factual counterexample rather than as a mere claim of insufficient support.

item.context: A company has a six-story office building. The company's finance department, planning department, administration department, sales department, human resources department, R & D department and other six departments work here, each department occupies one floor. It is known that: (1) the floors of the human resources department and the sales department are not adjacent; (2) the finance department is on the lower floor of the planning department; (3) the floor of the administration department is above the planning department, but below the human resources department.
item.question: Which of the followings may be the two departments on the first floor and the second floor, respectively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Finance department, sales department

choices.label: B
choices.text: Planning department, sales department

choices.label: C
choices.text: R & D department, sales department

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sales department, planning department

response:
Reasoning: Since administration is above planning and below HR, we need \(P<A<H\). If “finance is on the lower floor of planning” means immediately below, then B and D are impossible, A is impossible, and C works: 1-R&D, 2-Sales, 3-Finance, 4-Planning, 5-Administration, 6-HR.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a constraint-satisfaction approach: I translated the statements into an order chain, especially the vertical relation among planning, administration, and human resources, and then tested each option against those constraints. The key factor was recognizing the strict ordering \(P < A < H\), which forces planning low enough to leave room above it, while also keeping human resources nonadjacent to sales. My success came from constructing a concrete valid arrangement for the remaining feasible option rather than only eliminating others abstractly. For similar problems, first convert every verbal condition into explicit positional inequalities/order chains, then verify a choice by building one full arrangement that satisfies all constraints.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task correctly as a “may be” question: I only needed to find one answer choice that could fit all the constraints, not determine the full floor assignment uniquely. My strategy was to translate the verbal conditions into order relations, especially the key chain \(P < A < H\), and then test each option for whether it could participate in some complete arrangement. That was an appropriate approach because the problem is fundamentally about relative ordering rather than exact placement from the start. The main evidence I used was that administration must be strictly above planning and strictly below human resources, which forces three distinct floors in that order, and that human resources cannot be adjacent to sales. I also used the condition that finance is below planning, but I made a risky assumption by treating “on the lower floor of” as “immediately below.” In this case the assumption did not change the final choice, but it was not justified by the wording and could easily have caused an error on a different problem. I should have considered both interpretations explicitly and preferred the weaker, standard one unless “immediately” is stated. Another successful part of the reasoning was constructing a full feasible example for the selected option, which is the strongest way to confirm a “may be” answer. The reason the solution still succeeded is that the valid option remained feasible even under my stricter reading. In similar problems, I should first formalize each statement with the least restrictive interpretation, then eliminate options only when they violate those exact constraints. General rule: in ordering problems, convert each clue into precise inequalities, avoid strengthening a condition without textual support, and verify a “possible” answer by building one complete consistent arrangement.

item.context: Environmentalist: The commissioner of the Fish and Game Authority would have the public believe that increases in the number of marine fish caught demonstrate that this resource is no longer endangered. This is a specious argument, as unsound as it would be to assert that the ever-increasing rate at which rain forests are being cut down demonstrates a lack of danger to that resource. The real cause of the increased fish-catch is a greater efficiency in using technologies that deplete resources.
item.question: The environmentalist's statements, if true, best support which of the following as a conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is possible to determine how many fish are in the sea in some way other than by catching fish.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Marine fish continue to be an endangered resource.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Modern technologies waste resources by catching inedible fish.
