choices.label: D
choices.text: The proportion of marine fish that are caught is as high as the proportion of rain forest trees that are cut down each year.

response:
Reasoning: The environmentalist directly argues that higher catches do not show safety; instead, improved technology can increase catch while still depleting the resource. So the supported conclusion is that marine fish are still endangered. The other options introduce claims not stated or supported.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a weaken-the-commissioner / infer-the-environmentalist’s-main-point approach: identify the claim being attacked, then ask what conclusion the environmentalist is trying to establish instead. The key factor was the causal distinction between increased catch and increased abundance; the passage says higher catches can result from more efficient depletion technology, so catch numbers are not reliable evidence of recovery. My success came from treating the rain-forest comparison as an analogy showing why the commissioner’s evidence is misleading. For similar problems, first separate the observed outcome from its possible causes, then choose the conclusion that follows from rejecting the bad causal inference.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the conclusion most strongly supported by the environmentalist’s own statements, not for a flaw in the commissioner’s reasoning or a broader policy claim. My strategy was to identify the environmentalist’s main point by contrasting the commissioner’s evidence with the alternative explanation the environmentalist provided. That was appropriate because the passage explicitly argues that increased catch numbers are not reliable evidence of recovery. The key evidence I used was the analogy to rain forests: a rising rate of extraction can coexist with, and even indicate, ongoing endangerment rather than safety. I also used the final sentence, which gives a causal account—improved harvesting technology can raise catches while depleting the underlying resource. That causal explanation is crucial because it undercuts the commissioner’s inference from “more caught” to “less endangered.”

A potential shortcut would have been to equate “the commissioner is wrong” with every strong opposite claim, but I avoided that by checking whether the environmentalist positively supported a conclusion. I correctly rejected options that introduced new issues, such as wasteful bycatch, direct fish-population measurement methods, or quantitative comparisons with rain forests, because the stimulus did not establish those. The success came from distinguishing between evidence about extraction rates and evidence about resource abundance. In similar problems, I should keep separating “attacks on a piece of evidence” from “support for a conclusion” and track whether the speaker offers an alternative cause. General rule: when a passage shows that an observed increase is caused by improved extraction efficiency, do not infer resource health from output levels alone.

item.context: Speculation: refers to the purchase of goods in order to sell (or temporarily sell) goods in the future, in order to profit from changes in their prices.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following belong to the category of speculation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 10 years ago, Lao Zhang contracted 15 acres of orchards that no one wanted in the village, and now he relies on fruit trees to make his fortune

choices.label: B
choices.text: Xiao Liu bought a pair of leather shoes recently, and sold them to friends because they didn't like the style

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lao Yang bought 2000 shares at 10.03 yuan and sold them at 11.00 yuan

choices.label: D
choices.text: Teacher Wang bought a house for self-occupation. After the house price rose, Mr. Wang teacher a profit from selling the house

response:
Reasoning: Speculation requires buying with the intent to later sell for profit from price changes. A is production/operation, B is casual resale not for price gain, D was bought for self-use rather than resale intent. Only C fits.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I broke the concept into necessary conditions—buying something, intending to sell later, and seeking profit specifically from price changes—then tested each option against all parts. The key factor was distinguishing speculative intent from other motives like production, personal use, or convenience resale. My success came from treating “profit from price changes” and “purchase for future resale” as both required, which ruled out tempting but incomplete cases. For similar problems, first convert the definition into a checklist of required elements and reject any option that fails even one element.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as a definition-matching task: identify the option that satisfies both the action pattern and the motive described in the definition. My strategy was to decompose the definition into necessary elements: a purchase, a later sale or temporary sale, and a profit motive tied specifically to price changes rather than use or production. That was the right approach because in definition problems, each option must be tested against all required conditions, not just one prominent feature. I used the key distinction between earning through market price fluctuation and earning through labor, production, or incidental resale. This helped me reject the orchard case as investment in productive activity rather than buying goods to resell based on price movement. It also helped me reject the shoes case because the resale was prompted by dislike of the style, not an attempt to gain from changing prices. For the house case, I correctly focused on original intent: buying for self-occupation does not meet the speculative motive even if a later sale earns money. A shortcut that worked well here was treating “intent at time of purchase” as central, because speculation is defined by purchase for resale profit. An alternative I still needed to keep in mind was whether the definition allowed accidental profit, but the wording about buying “in order to profit” ruled that out. The reasoning succeeded because I checked motive, timing, and source of profit together rather than relying on surface similarity. A transferable rule is: when applying a definition, convert it into a checklist of necessary conditions and reject any option that misses even one condition, especially when intent is part of the definition.

item.context: In recent years, spaghetti has been given a bad reputation for obesity, so many people have a mixture of hate and love in the face of this Mediterranean diet. However, a study of 23000 people by the Mediterranean Institute of Neurology in Italy found that spaghetti does not lead to weight gain as many people think. Moreover, instead of causing obesity, spaghetti can have the opposite effect-reducing body fat. The results show that spaghetti is good for people's health if they eat in moderation and eat a variety of foods.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, can best support the above discussion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The carbohydrates contained in noodles are an important factor leading to obesity

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is no research showing that pasta will increase the obesity rate in the population

choices.label: C
choices.text: Olive oil used in the Mediterranean diet has great health benefits

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eating spaghetti appropriately can maintain people's ideal body fat percentage

response:
Reasoning: The passage argues spaghetti, when eaten in moderation, does not cause weight gain and may reduce body fat. The best supporting option directly reinforces that moderate spaghetti consumption helps maintain healthy body fat. A weakens, B is too indirect, and C is irrelevant to spaghetti itself.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a direct argument-matching approach: I identified the conclusion that moderate spaghetti consumption does not cause weight gain and may even reduce body fat, then looked for the option that most directly reinforced that claim. The key factor was relevance and strength—only one choice linked appropriate spaghetti consumption to a healthy body-fat outcome, which mirrors the passage’s central point. The successful step was rejecting options that were indirect, irrelevant, or actually pointed the other way. For similar problems, first isolate the exact claim being supported, then choose the option that most directly strengthens that claim rather than one that is merely related.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the option that most directly strengthens the passage’s central claim about spaghetti’s effect on weight and body fat. That interpretation was correct because the task was not to find a merely related fact, but the strongest support for the stated conclusion. My strategy was to identify the conclusion first—moderate spaghetti consumption is not fattening and may even reduce body fat—and then compare each choice by how directly it confirmed that claim. This was an appropriate strengthening approach because support questions reward evidence that matches the exact causal or correlational statement in the passage.

The key evidence I used was the passage’s emphasis on moderation, health, and reduced body fat, so I favored the choice that mirrored those points most closely. I also correctly rejected alternatives by type: one choice contradicted the claim, one was only indirectly supportive because absence of evidence is weaker than positive evidence, and one discussed another food component rather than spaghetti itself. A useful assumption in my reasoning was that the best support would mention both spaghetti and a favorable weight-related outcome, which held here. I should still note that I relied on semantic alignment, not on deeper methodological issues such as whether the cited study proved causation. In similar problems, I should continue separating direct support from peripheral relevance and from mere lack of disconfirming evidence. A general rule is: in strengthen questions, prefer the option that most specifically reinforces the passage’s exact conclusion using the same subject, condition, and outcome.

item.context: For a long time, the biggest challenge encountered in the inheritance of traditional opera is the loss of audience, especially the young audience is getting fewer and fewer. One of the important factors is that the opening way of traditional opera is still relatively monotonous and can not meet the needs of contemporary people. What kind of open way can attract people? One of the secrets is to fit into life. As an excellent traditional culture, opera represents the way of life in the past, now the times are changing, although some lifestyles have been out of touch with people, but some elements can still be used by people. the first set of Opera broadcast Gymnastics was broadcast at the CCTV Opera Spring Festival Gala, and many people are eager to learn, precisely because this set of broadcast gymnastics meets the physical exercise needs of modern people, while at the same time taking into account the experience of artistic charm.
item.question: This passage is intended to emphasize that the inheritance of traditional opera should be:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Which of the followings is the emphasis of this passage on the inheritance of opera?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pay attention to the dissemination of excellent culture

choices.label: C
choices.text: Try to integrate into people's lives

choices.label: D
choices.text: Give consideration to both nationality and cosmopolitanism

response:
Reasoning: The passage says traditional opera loses audience because its presentation is monotonous. It stresses that a way to attract people is to “fit into life,” using modern needs like exercise while preserving artistic charm. So inheritance should integrate opera into everyday life.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach: identify the problem, track the author’s proposed solution, and match that solution to the option that best generalizes it. The key factor was the repeated emphasis on “fit into life,” reinforced by the example of opera broadcast gymnastics meeting modern exercise needs while preserving artistic experience. My success came from distinguishing the passage’s central prescription from broader but less supported ideas like cultural dissemination. For similar questions, first locate the author’s explicit solution or recommendation, then choose the option that restates that idea at the right level of generality.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the author’s main prescription for how traditional opera should be inherited, not merely the problem it faces or a side benefit of inheritance. That interpretation was correct because the passage moves from identifying audience loss to proposing a specific remedy. My strategy was to track the passage’s structure: problem, cause, guiding question, and then the author’s answer supported by an example. This was appropriate for a “main idea/intended to emphasize” question, where the conclusion usually appears after the explanatory setup. The key evidence I used was the repeated claim that one secret is to “fit into life,” plus the example of opera broadcast gymnastics satisfying modern exercise needs while preserving artistic appeal. I correctly treated the example as evidence for a broader principle rather than as the main point itself. I also avoided being distracted by general but weaker ideas like promoting excellent culture, which appear in the passage but are not the author’s central recommendation. A possible trap was to choose an option that sounded lofty or comprehensive without matching the passage’s concrete emphasis. The reasoning succeeded because I prioritized repeated causal and prescriptive language over background description. In similar problems, I should continue distinguishing between context, diagnosis, and the author’s proposed solution. General rule: in main-purpose questions, identify the claim that the examples are supporting, not the topic they merely discuss.

item.context: A worldwide ban on the production of certain ozone-destroying chemicals would provide only an illusion of protection. Quantities of such chemicals, already produced, exist as coolants in millions of refrigerators. When they reach the ozone layer in the atmosphere, their action cannot be halted. So there is no way to prevent these chemicals from damaging the ozone layer further.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The coolants in refrigerators can be fully recovered at the end of the useful life of the refrigerators and reused.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In modern societies, refrigeration of food is necessary to prevent unhealthy and potentially life-threatening conditions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Even if people should give up the use of refrigeration, the coolants already in existing refrigerators are a threat to atmospheric ozone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is impossible to measure with accuracy the quantity of ozone-destroying chemicals that exist as coolants in refrigerators.

response:
Reasoning: The argument says a production ban is useless because existing chemicals in refrigerators will inevitably keep damaging ozone. If those coolants can be recovered and reused instead of escaping into the atmosphere, then further damage can be prevented, so the ban is not merely an illusion.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-weaken approach: I identified the conclusion that “there is no way to prevent further damage” and looked for a choice that attacked the inevitability in that claim. The key factor was the argument’s hidden assumption that the chemicals currently inside refrigerators must eventually escape and reach the atmosphere. My reasoning succeeded because I focused on the causal pathway, not on side issues like the usefulness of refrigeration or measurement problems. For similar problems, isolate the step that makes the harm seem unavoidable and test whether any option introduces a feasible intervention that breaks that chain.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the argument correctly as attacking the conclusion, not the background issue of ozone damage itself. The core claim was that a production ban would be only symbolic because chemicals already inside refrigerators would inevitably continue harming the ozone layer, making further prevention impossible. My strategy was to look for an answer choice that breaks the step from “already produced” to “unavoidable future damage,” which is the argument’s main logical bridge. That was the right strategy for a weakening question, because the strongest weakener does not need to disprove every premise; it only needs to show that the conclusion overreaches. The key fact I used was that the chemicals matter only if they eventually escape and reach the atmosphere, so a method of capturing them before release undercuts the inevitability claim. I avoided being distracted by choices about the social value of refrigeration or the difficulty of measurement, since those do not address whether damage can be prevented. One assumption I correctly challenged was the author’s unstated idea that all existing coolant stocks must eventually enter the atmosphere. I also implicitly recognized that “no way to prevent” is an extreme conclusion, so any credible prevention mechanism is powerful. The reasoning succeeded because it targeted necessity and inevitability rather than the broader policy debate. A general rule is: when an argument concludes that harm is unavoidable, test whether it has ignored any intervention that could block the causal path from existing conditions to the predicted outcome.

item.context: Public empowerment: it refers to the active participation of the public in the formulation, implementation, evaluation and supervision of public policies, and the full expression of their own interests, so as to promote the democratization and scientific process of public policies.
item.question: Which of the following is Public empowerment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: On the eve of the Tomb-sweeping Day, some social figures in the city's civilization office under the support of the creation of a civilized worship website, called on people to worship when not set off firecrackers, do not burn paper money, instead of virtual flowers, electronic candles and other green ways

choices.label: B
choices.text: After being elected as a representative of the municipal People's Congress, express little brother Xiao Li submitted a proposal on how to protect the rights and interests of express workers and promote the healthy development of the express industry on the basis of extensive visits and full research

choices.label: C
choices.text: A city is about to hold a public hearing on the adjustment of natural gas prices, and the relevant departments require all the streets and neighborhood committees under their jurisdiction to do a good job in publicity and mobilization, and elect citizen representatives according to the quota assigned to ensure openness, fairness and justice

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the process of formulating the development plan for the next five years of a county, the county party committee and the county government have solicited many valuable opinions by holding resident symposiums and expert hearings

response:
Reasoning: Public empowerment means the public directly participates in public policy making and expresses interests. D best matches this: during formulation of a county’s five-year plan, the government actively solicits residents’ and experts’ opinions. A is advocacy, B is a representative’s action, C is more administrative organization than genuine broad participation.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option against the full concept of public empowerment, especially participation in policy formulation and expression of public interests. The key factor was whether the public was directly involved in a public policy process, not merely being guided, represented indirectly, or administratively selected. My success came from distinguishing genuine consultation in policymaking from publicity campaigns and top-down mobilization. For similar problems, I should test each option against every element of the definition and prefer the one that satisfies the core mechanism most directly and completely.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which option best exemplified the definition’s key structure: ordinary members of the public actively participating in a public policy process, especially at the stages of formulation, evaluation, or supervision, while expressing their interests. That interpretation was correct, and it kept my attention on whether the case involved policy participation rather than general civic behavior or government publicity. My strategy was to compare each option against the definition’s components one by one: who participates, what process they are participating in, and whether the activity is genuinely tied to public policy. This was an appropriate elimination method because the options were similar on the surface but differed in whether public participation was direct and substantive.

The most important evidence I used was that one option described government decision-making on a formal development plan and included resident symposiums and expert hearings, which clearly connected citizens’ input to policy formulation. I correctly ruled out the advocacy example because promoting green mourning practices is social guidance, not public participation in policy design. I also distinguished the representative-submitted proposal from direct public empowerment, since action through an elected official is not the same as the public itself participating. For the hearing example, I noticed that the emphasis was on administrative mobilization and quota assignment rather than authentic, broad, self-expressive participation. A shortcut that helped was asking, “Is the public shaping policy, or is the government simply informing, organizing, or being petitioned?” I should continue using definitional decomposition in similar problems, especially when distractors contain public-facing language. A transferable rule is: when a concept includes multiple required elements, test each option against every element explicitly instead of matching on one attractive keyword.

item.context: Since the outbreak of the global financial crisis in 2008, the United States, Japan, Europe and other developed economies have fallen into the dilemma of weak economic growth, and their economic growth has always been significantly lower than the pre-crisis level. According to the secular stagnation theory, this is because the equilibrium real interest rate continues to decline and has fallen into the negative range. The central bank is constrained by the zero zero limit and it is difficult to lower the real interest rate to the equilibrium real interest rate. Therefore, the relatively high real interest rate leads to the continuous suppression of aggregate demand (especially investment demand). That is why, even with zero interest rates in the US, Japan and Europe, output gaps remain negative and recovery is hard to achieve. According to this theory, some argue that China's economy also faces a lack of investment demand and a prolonged period of stagnation.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, refutes the above conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: China's lack of investment demand is mainly reflected in the sharp decline in private investment demand

choices.label: B
choices.text: China's real interest rate has a wider range of adjustment and is therefore easier to fall to the equilibrium real rate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Even if the stagnation theory were true, China's equilibrium real interest rate is still greater than zero

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sharp decline in China's investment growth is at odds with the theory's emphasis on deficient investment demand

response:
Reasoning: Secular stagnation requires the equilibrium real interest rate to be negative so the zero lower bound prevents policy from reaching it, suppressing demand. If China’s equilibrium real rate is still above zero, that key mechanism does not apply, so the conclusion is undermined.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a mechanism-matching approach: I focused on the secular stagnation chain of logic and looked for an option that would break a necessary link in that chain. The key factor I prioritized was the zero lower bound requiring the equilibrium real interest rate to be negative, so I chose the statement denying that condition. My mistake was treating the argument as if it had to rely strictly on the full original theory, instead of asking which option most directly weakens the conclusion about China by showing the observed investment weakness can be explained within the theory rather than contradicting it. For similar questions, first identify the exact conclusion being challenged, then test each option for whether it weakens the conclusion itself versus merely disputing one theoretical detail.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which option would break the causal chain of secular stagnation when applied to China. My strategy was to identify the theory’s core mechanism—an equilibrium real interest rate below zero combined with a zero lower bound—and then select the option that seemed to deny that mechanism most directly. That strategy was partly appropriate, but I treated the argument too narrowly as a pure theoretical syllogism and not as an application claim about China’s actual economic conditions. I focused on whether one necessary condition of the theory held, but I did not ask which option most strongly weakens the conclusion that China therefore faces insufficient investment demand and prolonged stagnation.

The key fact I underused was that the conclusion concerns “investment demand,” and the best refutation can come from showing that the observed pattern is compatible with something other than economy-wide demand deficiency. I implicitly assumed that disproving one technical feature of secular stagnation was stronger than distinguishing the type of investment weakness actually present. I also failed to compare options by explanatory relevance: one option directly reframes the decline as concentrated in a specific sector, which weakens the inference from aggregate stagnation theory to China. Another mistake was treating a theoretical inconsistency as sufficient, even though the argument said “some argue,” making the target an applied analogy rather than a formal proof. In similar problems, I should test each choice against the exact conclusion and ask whether it attacks mechanism, evidence, or scope most effectively. General rule: when an argument transfers a macro theory from one context to another, the strongest refutation often shows a mismatch in the underlying structure of the cases, not merely a partial failure of one abstract condition.

item.context: Before the French arrived in North America, this land was already inhabited by the indigenous peoples of North American Indians. It is said that as early as 30,000 to 10,000 years ago, their ancestors came to live in the region of non frozen soil of Alaska and Yukon through the area bordering North America in the northeast corner of Asia (the Bering Strait now). And some people continued to expand to the southeastern part of North America to the Atlantic coast and the tip of South America. It is generally believed that the earliest indigenous people here belonged to the Mongolian race in Asia. At that time, Asia was during the Stone Age, which can be corroborated by the stone tools and weapons excavated from contemporary Canada.
item.question: Which one of the followings does here in the above paragraph refer to?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atlantic coast

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alaska

choices.label: C
choices.text: Canada

choices.label: D
choices.text: America

response:
Reasoning: “Here” refers to the place discussed throughout the paragraph before the French arrived and where stone tools were excavated from “contemporary Canada.” The paragraph is about the land of present-day Canada, not all of America or only Alaska/Atlantic coast.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a local-reference approach, looking for the nearest concrete place name and anchoring “here” to the later mention of present-day Canada. The key clue that misled me was the phrase about stone tools excavated from contemporary Canada, which I treated as defining the whole passage’s setting rather than as supporting evidence. My error was narrowing the scope too quickly instead of tracking the broader discourse: the paragraph describes migration across North America and down to South America, so “here” referred to the larger landmass under discussion. In similar pronoun-reference questions, I should first identify the passage’s overall topic scope before choosing the nearest geographic noun.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the nearest concrete place name that “here” could point to, and I anchored too strongly on the final sentence about stone tools excavated from contemporary Canada. That strategy was too local: I treated “here” as if it had to refer to the most recent geographic mention, rather than the larger discourse topic of the paragraph. The paragraph begins with a broad setting—North America and the migration of indigenous peoples across the hemisphere—so the pronoun was more likely tied to that wider frame than to one later example. I used one supporting clue correctly, namely that “contemporary Canada” is presented as evidence, but I misused it by turning an evidentiary example into the paragraph’s main referent. I also overlooked that Alaska, the Atlantic coast, and Canada appear as stages or subregions within a much larger migration narrative, not as the central entity under discussion. My main assumption was that the sentence-final phrase controlled the pronoun’s meaning, but pronouns in passages often inherit the global topic instead of the nearest noun. I should have compared all answer choices by asking which one best matches the scope of the whole paragraph. Another missed alternative was the broad continental referent implied by movement from Alaska through North America and down to South America. The specific cause of error was a scope mismatch: I selected a regional example when the passage was framed at a continental level. A transferable rule is: when resolving a pronoun in a passage, identify the discourse-level topic first, then prefer the referent whose scope best fits the surrounding sentences, rather than defaulting to the nearest place name.

item.context: Viewers surveyed immediately after the televised political debate last year between Lopez and Tanner tended to think that Lopez had made the better arguments, but the survey respondents who reported that Lopez' s arguments were better may have been biased in favor of Lopez. After all, Lopez eventually did win the election.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lopez won the election over Tanner by a very narrow margin.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most of the viewers surveyed immediately prior to the debate said that they would probably vote for Tanner.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most people in the live audience watching the debate who were surveyed immediately afterward said that they thought that Tanner was more persuasive in the debate than was Lopez.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The people who watched the televised debate were more likely to vote for Tanner than were the people who did not watch the debate.

response:
Reasoning: The argument suggests post-debate viewers favored Lopez because they were already biased toward the eventual winner. But if, immediately before the debate, most of those viewers said they would probably vote for Tanner, that strongly shows they were not biased toward Lopez beforehand. That most undermines the claim of pro-Lopez bias.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple:
I used a weakening approach: identify the argument’s causal assumption and look for a fact that directly breaks it. The key factor was that the argument explains the post-debate pro-Lopez responses by claiming those viewers were already biased toward Lopez because Lopez later won. The strongest counter was evidence about those same viewers’ pre-debate preferences, showing they initially leaned the other way, which directly undercuts the alleged source of bias.  

A useful rule for similar problems is: when an argument claims survey results are explained by prior bias, test that claim by looking for evidence about respondents’ attitudes before the event, not just general facts about the outcome afterward.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stimulus as making a causal challenge to the survey result: the claim was not that the respondents were wrong about the debate, but that their judgment might be explained by prior favoritism toward the eventual election winner. That means the key task was to find information that weakens the allegation of preexisting pro-Lopez bias among the surveyed viewers. My strategy was to identify the argument’s hidden assumption: that because Lopez later won the election, many respondents were likely already disposed to favor Lopez when they judged the debate. That was the right strategy because weakening questions often turn on attacking the link between the evidence offered and the conclusion drawn from it.

The crucial evidence I focused on was timing. The survey about debate performance happened immediately after the debate, while the election result came later, so the argument was inferring earlier bias from a later outcome. The strongest underminer would therefore show that the surveyed viewers were not initially leaning toward Lopez at all. I correctly treated prior voting intention as more probative than later election success, because it directly measures baseline preference in the same population. I also implicitly rejected weaker alternatives that discussed margins of victory, audience reactions, or comparisons with nonviewers, since those facts do not directly test the alleged bias of the surveyed respondents. The reasoning succeeded because it matched the weakening evidence to the argument’s exact causal assumption. In similar problems, I should explicitly ask: “What assumption about this group’s prior state must be true for the author’s explanation to work?” A transferable rule is: when an argument attributes a judgment to bias, the best rebuttal is evidence about that group’s attitudes before the event being judged.

item.context: Based on the above questions, two additional conditions are added: (1) the players of the Chinese go team who draw Hongta Mountain in any match hold the folding fan at the same time; (2) the players of the Chinese go team do not hold the folding fan in the NEC match.
item.question: Which of the following options can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the NEC Kuaiqi match, every player of the Chinese go team smokes Ashima cigarettes

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the NEC Kuaiqi match, some Chinese go team players play Hongta Mountain smoke

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the NEC Kuaiqi match, every player of the Chinese go team does not smoke during the match

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the NEC Kuaiqi match, if the players of the Chinese go team smoke during the match, they must smoke Ashima cigarettes

response:
Reasoning: Added condition (1) says anyone who draws Hongta Mountain must also hold the folding fan. Condition (2) says in the NEC match, Chinese team players do not hold the folding fan. So in NEC, they cannot draw Hongta Mountain. Therefore, if they smoke, it must be the other brand, Ashima.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a constraint-combination approach: I linked the new conditional rule about Hongta Mountain with the separate restriction on folding fans in the NEC match, then eliminated one smoking possibility. The key factor was the one-way implication that drawing Hongta Mountain requires holding the folding fan; once NEC forbids folding fans, Hongta Mountain becomes impossible there. The successful step was translating the conditions into an exclusion chain rather than treating them as unrelated facts. For similar problems, explicitly connect conditionals across the same setting and use forbidden consequences to eliminate answer choices.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking what new conclusion becomes logically necessary after adding two extra conditions to the original setup. That interpretation was correct, because the task was not to identify what is merely plausible, but what must follow in the NEC match. My strategy was to chain the two new conditions together: one condition linked a specific cigarette brand to holding a folding fan, and the other banned folding fans in the NEC match. That was an appropriate conditional-reasoning strategy because the problem is about eliminating possibilities through implications and contradictions.

The key evidence I used was the one-way implication: smoking that specific brand implies holding the fan. Combined with the NEC restriction, this blocks that brand in that match. I then used the remaining binary structure of the smoking options from the original setup to infer that any smoking that still occurs must involve the other brand. A crucial assumption, which was justified by the original framework, was that the only smoking possibilities under consideration were those listed brands rather than some unspecified third option. I also correctly distinguished between “cannot smoke one brand” and “cannot smoke at all,” which rules out overreaching to a stronger claim.

An alternative I needed to check was whether the new conditions implied universal non-smoking, but they did not. The reasoning succeeded because it respected directionality: from brand to fan, then fan prohibition to brand prohibition, not the reverse. In similar problems, I should explicitly test whether each conditional supports a necessary conclusion or only excludes one option. A transferable rule is: when a condition says P → Q and a scenario gives not-Q, you may infer not-P, but only conclusions consistent with the remaining option structure are warranted.

item.context: Traditional social moral education in my country has always emphasized obedience and obligation. If what is required under the traditional society and planned economy system is to perform obligations and obey the common people, then modern society and the market economy require everyone to actively participate in the public Live, citizens who dare to own power.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following options is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The primary goal of education in the new era is to cultivate students' civic awareness and improve the quality of citizens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Facts have proved that traditional obedience and compulsory education are not suitable for modern society

choices.label: C
choices.text: The traditional moral education is in conflict with the moral education of the new era

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modern society and market economy require citizens to participate more in public life and public affairs

response:
Reasoning: The statement contrasts traditional obedience/obligation with modern society’s need for active participation in public life and public affairs. Only D directly matches this definition; A, B, and C add judgments or conclusions not stated.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a direct text-matching approach: I compared each option against what the passage explicitly stated rather than drawing broader implications. The key factor was the contrast in the passage between traditional moral education focused on obedience and modern society’s need for active participation in public life and public affairs. The success came from rejecting choices that added evaluation or policy conclusions not supported by the text, and selecting the one that restated the core claim. For similar problems, I should first separate explicit statements from inferred opinions, then choose the option that most closely paraphrases the original passage without adding new claims.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the prompt as a definition-matching question: identify the option that restates the core claim of the passage without adding new evaluation or policy conclusions. That interpretation was correct, because the stem asked what follows “according to the above definition,” which usually means selecting the statement most directly supported by the text. My strategy was to compare each option against the passage and reject any choice that introduced stronger claims than the original language justified. That was appropriate here because the passage made a descriptive contrast between two social models rather than arguing for an educational reform program or declaring one model wholly invalid.

The key evidence I used was the contrast structure: traditional moral education emphasized obedience and obligation, while modern society requires active public participation and a sense of rights. I correctly noticed that one option closely paraphrased this second clause, while the others moved beyond the text. In particular, I rejected options that turned the passage into a judgment that tradition is “not suitable,” a policy claim about the “primary goal” of education, or a broad claim of “conflict” between old and new moral education. Those choices relied on assumptions of implication rather than explicit support. I should continue using this distinction between paraphrase and inference in definition questions. A transferable rule is: when a prompt asks what accords with a stated definition, prefer the option that preserves the passage’s scope and wording, and eliminate choices that add evaluation, causation, or policy not directly stated.

item.context: Crowdfunding refers to the collection of funds through the Internet to publish projects, implement programs, and return on investment. The elements of crowdfunding include originators who are creative but lack funds, supporters interested in the stories or returns of the fund-raisers, internet platforms that connect the two.
item.question: Which of the following is crowdfunding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: After the earthquake, the city Red Cross made use of its official website, Weibo, wechat and other online platforms to timely release information about the disaster and appeal to the public for donations to help the victims rebuild their homes. It quickly raised large amounts of money and relief supplies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After graduating from university, Xiao Tao returned to his hometown to start a business, but his funds are insufficient. He posted his idea on the Internet to get financial aid from people from all walks of life. With the help of netizens, he pulled through the difficulty quickly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: After a middle school student fell ill with leukemia, the school launched an online fund-raising campaign, raising tens of thousands of yuan within two days. After the post is reprinted, more and more donations are coming from all over the world.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In order to hold a solo exhibition, a young artist used the network to raise a large amount of start-up funds. After the successful completion of the exhibition, one by one to allow investors to enjoy the collection of promises.

response:
Reasoning: Crowdfunding typically involves a project initiator lacking funds, raising money online from supporters, and giving supporters some return/reward. A and C are online charity donations; B is vague online aid. D matches best: a creator raises funds online for an exhibition and gives investors promised returns.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option against the stated elements of crowdfunding rather than focusing on surface similarities like “raising money online.” The key factor was that crowdfunding requires not just internet fundraising, but also a project originator, supporters, and some story/return structure tied to the project. The successful step was separating charity-style donation appeals from project-based financing with promised benefits to backers. For similar problems, I should turn the definition into a checklist of necessary elements and eliminate any option that misses even one core condition.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the option that matches the definitional structure of crowdfunding, not merely any online fundraising. That interpretation was correct because the stem specified three elements: an originator with a project but insufficient funds, supporters connected through the Internet, and some story/return mechanism rather than simple charitable giving. My strategy was to compare each option against the definition element by element, which was appropriate for a concept-classification question. The key evidence I used was the distinction between funding a specific creative or entrepreneurial project and making donations for relief or medical aid. I also used the phrase about “return on investment” to separate true crowdfunding from pure philanthropy. That helped eliminate the disaster-relief and illness cases, since those are online charitable appeals rather than project-based financing. I noted that the entrepreneurship example had an initiator and internet fundraising, but it did not clearly include a platform-based supporter relationship or any return/reward, so it was weaker. The successful part of the reasoning was focusing on all required conditions instead of matching only the superficial feature “raising money online.” A shortcut that worked here was treating “reward or promised return” as a strong discriminator when options looked similar. In similar problems, I should continue testing each choice against every definitional component and reject options that satisfy only part of the definition. A useful general rule is: when identifying an example of a defined concept, classify by necessary features, not by broad family resemblance.

item.context: Scientific and technological discoveries have considerable effects on the development of any society. It follows that predictions of the future condition of societies in which scientific and technological discovery is particularly frequent are particularly untrustworthy.
item.question: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is not as difficult to predict scientific and technological discoveries in a technologically more advanced society as it is in a technologically less advanced society.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The development of a society requires scientific and technological discoveries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Predictions of scientific and technological discoveries or predictions of their effects have harmful consequences in some societies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Forecasts of scientific and technological discoveries, or forecasts of their effects, are not entirely reliable.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion only follows if future discoveries, or their societal effects, cannot be predicted reliably. Otherwise, even frequent discoveries could be incorporated into forecasts of a society’s future condition. So the argument assumes such forecasts are not fully reliable.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a necessary-assumption approach: I asked what must be true for the move from “discoveries strongly affect society” plus “discoveries are frequent” to “predictions about society are untrustworthy” to work. The key factor was that frequent change only undermines social predictions if the discoveries themselves, or their effects, cannot be forecasted well enough to build into those predictions. The successful step was testing whether the conclusion could still hold if those forecasts were reliable; if so, the argument would fail, which isolated the needed assumption. For similar problems, explicitly negate each candidate assumption and check whether the argument’s conclusion collapses.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the stimulus as a necessary-assumption question: the author moved from “discoveries strongly affect social development” plus “some societies have many discoveries” to the conclusion that predictions about those societies are less trustworthy. That interpretation was correct because the key task was to identify what must be true for that inferential step to work. My strategy was to test the gap between premise and conclusion by asking what would prevent frequent discovery from making forecasts unreliable. That was appropriate, because if discoveries and their effects could themselves be forecast reliably, then frequent discovery would not undermine prediction. The critical evidence I used was the causal role of discoveries in shaping society and the comparative claim that more frequent discoveries make social forecasts especially untrustworthy. I correctly focused on predictability rather than on whether discoveries are beneficial, necessary for development, or harmful when forecast. One assumption I effectively rejected was that mere importance of a factor automatically makes outcomes harder to predict; that is only true if the factor itself is not reliably predictable. I also implicitly considered an alternative possibility: a society could change rapidly yet still be forecast well if the drivers of change were known in advance. The reasoning succeeded because it identified the hidden dependence of the conclusion on uncertainty about future discoveries or their consequences. In similar problems, I should continue translating the argument into a conditional gap analysis: “What missing condition turns these premises into this conclusion?” A transferable rule is: when an argument says a major influence makes prediction unreliable, check whether the argument must assume that the influence itself, or its effects, cannot be predicted well.

item.context: There is a well-known investment philosophy, that is, invest in a company with a moat. The general idea is that a company must have sufficient competitive advantages to resist the encroachment of other competitors on its own profitability. Investors can only invest in this way. Companies are likely to bring excess returns. However, moats often have traps, and the most common trap is market share. A higher market share is usually regarded by investors as the moat of the company, but practice has proved that this is not the case. Unreliable. Market share only illustrates the company's past performance, not the future. If there is not enough ability to resist foreign invasion, the company will have to maintain market share through price wars, and the result must be a sharp decline in profitability.
item.question: According to this text, which of the following statements is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Understanding competitive advantage as market share is one-sided

choices.label: B
choices.text: The market share reflects the size of the company's competitive advantage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Investors should consider both the profit margin and the company's market share

choices.label: D
choices.text: The moat of a company does not guarantee investors' excess returns

response:
Reasoning: The passage says market share is a common “moat” trap: it shows past performance, not future competitiveness, and high share without defense leads to price wars and lower profits. So equating competitive advantage with market share is incomplete/one-sided. B contradicts the text; C is unsupported; D contradicts “likely to bring excess returns.”
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used elimination grounded in the passage’s main claim: it warns that treating market share as a company’s “moat” is a trap because share reflects past performance rather than durable protection against competitors. The key factor was the contrast between true competitive advantage and mere market share, especially the point that firms may defend share through price wars that destroy profitability. My success came from matching that caution directly to the option that framed market share as only a partial view of competitive advantage, while rejecting choices that overstated or added unsupported criteria. For similar questions, identify the author’s explicit caution or qualification and prefer the option that preserves that nuance rather than extending the claim beyond the text.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which option is most directly supported by the passage, not which option sounds generally reasonable in investing. That was the right framing, because the passage makes a specific argumentative move: it criticizes a common investor shortcut, namely treating market share as evidence of a “moat.” My strategy was to identify the author’s conclusion and then test each choice against that conclusion. That approach was appropriate here because the passage contrasts a valid concept of competitive advantage with an invalid proxy for it.

The key evidence I used was that market share “only illustrates the company's past performance, not the future,” and that without the ability to resist competitors, a firm may preserve share only through price wars that reduce profitability. Those details directly support the idea that equating competitive advantage with market share is incomplete. I also correctly rejected options that went beyond the text: one choice tried to make market share measure competitive advantage, and another introduced a recommendation about jointly considering profit margin and market share that the passage never states. A useful assumption I avoided was treating “high market share” as automatically equivalent to “strong moat,” which is exactly the trap the author warns about.

What made the reasoning successful was distinguishing between a historical indicator and a durable causal advantage. In similar problems, I should keep separating what the author endorses from what the author critiques. A transferable rule is: when a passage attacks a commonly used indicator as unreliable, the supported answer will usually deny equivalence between the indicator and the underlying concept, not merely qualify it slightly.

item.context: In a recent study of more than 400 North American men and women whose previous heart attack put them at risk for a second heart attack, about half were told to switch to a Mediterranean-type diet -- one rich in fish, vegetables, olive oil, and grains -- while the other half were advised to eat a more traditional Western diet but to limit their fat intake. Those following the Mediterranean diet were significantly less likely than those in the other group to have a second heart attack. But the Mediterranean diet includes a fair amount of fat from fish and olive oil, so the research suggests that a diet may not have to be extremely low in fat in order to protect the heart.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some cardiologists believe that the protection afforded by the Mediterranean diet might be enhanced by drugs that lower blood-cholesterol levels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Studies suggest that the kinds of oils in the fat included in the Mediterranean diet may protect the heart against potentially fatal disruptions of heart rhythms and other causes of heart attacks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many people who have had heart attacks are advised by their cardiologists to begin an exercise regimen in addition to changing their diet.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patients who consumed the Mediterranean diet enjoyed the food and continued to follow the diet after the experiment was concluded.

response:
Reasoning: The argument infers that the Mediterranean diet’s heart protection occurs despite its fat content, so fat itself need not be extremely low. This is strengthened if the specific fats in that diet are actually protective. B directly explains why a higher-fat diet could still reduce second heart attacks.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a causal-strengthening approach: I identified the conclusion that a diet need not be extremely low in fat to protect the heart and looked for a choice that would make the study’s result more supportive of that inference. The key factor was the apparent tension between “contains a fair amount of fat” and “still lowers heart-attack risk,” so the best support had to explain how the fat in that diet could be compatible with protection. The successful step was focusing on the type of fat rather than the mere amount of fat. For similar problems, isolate the exact gap in the argument and prefer an answer that directly links the evidence to the conclusion by explaining the mechanism or relevant distinction.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a strengthening task aimed at the argument’s final inference, not merely at the study result itself. The core claim was that because the Mediterranean group had better outcomes despite consuming a meaningful amount of fat, very low fat intake is not necessary for heart protection. My strategy was to identify the gap between the evidence and the conclusion: the study showed a beneficial diet containing fat, but the argument needed support for why that fact undermines the idea that fat must be minimized. I focused on whether any choice connected the presence of fat in that diet to the observed protection, rather than introducing side issues.

The key evidence I used was the distinction between quantity of fat and type of fat. That distinction matters because the conclusion is not that all fat is harmless, but that a protective diet need not be extremely low in fat. I implicitly rejected choices that discussed drugs, exercise, or enjoyment because they do not explain the diet’s heart-protective effect in a way relevant to the conclusion. One assumption in my reasoning was that a causal explanation can strengthen an argument better than a mere correlation when the question asks why an apparent exception is plausible. That assumption was appropriate here because the argument needed a mechanism reconciling fat intake with protection. A weaker alternative would have been to favor long-term adherence, but that would support practicality more than the specific nutritional inference. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the answer choice to the exact inferential gap. A transferable rule is: in strengthen questions, identify the conclusion’s most vulnerable link and prefer evidence that directly explains why the cited evidence supports that conclusion rather than merely adding related facts.

item.context: Although the world is splendid by invention, individual inventors often struggle lonely in adversity. The market only recognizes products with direct consumer value, and few people will pay the bill for the ideals of inventors. There are professional teachers in the world. And scientists, because people recognize the importance of education and science to mankind, teachers and scientists can nurture students and explore the universe without worry; however, there is no occupation of inventor in the world, and no one pays inventors to inventors.
item.question: Which of the following is the main purpose of this text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The development and progress of the world is inseparable from invention

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inventors are in a tougher position than scientists, etc

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inventions usually have no direct consumer value

choices.label: D
choices.text: Society should provide more protection for inventors

response:
Reasoning: The passage contrasts inventors with teachers/scientists to show inventors lack institutional and social support despite their importance. It highlights their hardship not just to compare status, but to imply society should better support and protect them.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a purpose-focused reading approach: I looked at how the passage framed the problem and what conclusion or implication it was pushing toward. The key factor was the contrast between inventors and recognized professions like teachers and scientists, especially the claim that no one “pays inventors to invent,” which signals a lack of social support rather than a neutral description. My answer was correct because I moved beyond the surface fact of inventors’ hardship and identified the author’s implied advocacy. For similar questions, first separate supporting evidence from the author’s ultimate aim, and choose the option that captures the implied call, judgment, or recommendation.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the author’s communicative goal, not merely the topic or a factual summary. That distinction mattered because the passage does more than describe inventors’ hardship; it builds toward a normative implication about what society fails to provide. My strategy was to track the passage’s structure: first, inventors are described as isolated and unsupported; then teachers and scientists are presented as examples of socially funded roles; finally, inventors are singled out as lacking any comparable institutional position. This comparison signaled that the text was arguing from contrast, which is often used to imply a need for reform rather than to make a neutral observation.

The key evidence I used was the emphasis on who “pays” for socially valued work and the claim that no one pays inventors to invent. That language points to missing social support, not just personal difficulty. I avoided a common shortcut of picking the option that repeated the most surface details; instead, I looked for the answer that captured the passage’s rhetorical direction. I also correctly rejected choices that were too broad, too descriptive, or contradicted the text’s premise about invention’s importance. One alternative I needed to consider was whether the passage was mainly comparative, but the comparison functioned as support for a broader claim. The reasoning succeeded because I identified the author’s implied conclusion rather than stopping at the explicit complaint. A general rule is: when a passage contrasts one group’s institutional support with another group’s lack of it, infer the author may be advocating a remedy, not merely describing inequality.

item.context: A fuel-efficient car of a certain brand is priced at 270,000 yuan, while another is priced at 170,000 yuan. According to the current gasoline price and the test data of the fuel consumption per 100 kilometers of the two cars, people who buy this fuel-efficient car need to complete 300,000 kilometers to make up the price difference higher than that of buying a normal car. If the oil price rises in the future, the mileage required to make up the purchase price of the car will also increase accordingly.
item.question: Which of the following statements most points out the flaw in the above argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arguments and conclusions are contradictory

choices.label: B
choices.text: Arguments do not adequately support its conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: The argument does not take into account the possibility of future oil price cuts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arguments that use unproven assumptions as arguments

response:
Reasoning: If gasoline becomes more expensive, the fuel-efficient car saves more money per kilometer compared with the normal car. So the distance needed to recover the higher purchase price should decrease, not increase. The conclusion contradicts the logic of the premises.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a causal/quantitative consistency check: compare how a change in fuel price affects per-kilometer savings and then infer how that should affect the break-even mileage. The key factor was the inverse relationship between savings per kilometer and required recovery distance: if fuel becomes more expensive, a more efficient car saves more each kilometer, so the break-even distance should move in the opposite direction. My success came from testing the conclusion against the premise’s own logic and spotting that they pointed to conflicting outcomes. For similar problems, explicitly trace how each variable change affects the intermediate quantity and then verify that the stated conclusion follows that direction.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a flaw-identification task: determine what is wrong with the relationship between the premises and the final claim, not whether the numerical estimate itself is realistic. That interpretation was correct, because the key issue was the direction of the effect of fuel prices on the break-even mileage. My strategy was to isolate the economic mechanism: the higher-priced car has lower fuel consumption, so its advantage comes from savings per kilometer. From that, I compared how a rise in gasoline prices changes those per-kilometer savings and therefore the distance required to offset the upfront price gap. This was an appropriate strategy because the argument’s conclusion depended on a monotonic relationship, not on missing data or an unsupported background assumption.

The crucial fact I used was that when fuel prices rise, the monetary value of each unit of fuel saved also rises. I did not need to compute exact numbers; I only needed the directional relationship between fuel price and break-even distance. A possible shortcut I used was assuming the fuel-efficient car truly consumes less fuel, but that assumption was licensed by the setup. I also correctly rejected distractors about insufficient support or unproven assumptions, because the stronger flaw was internal inconsistency. What made the reasoning successful was testing the conclusion against the premise-driven model rather than paraphrasing the argument. In similar problems, I should explicitly map each variable’s direction of change before evaluating answer choices. General rule: when an argument predicts how one quantity changes with another, check whether the stated conclusion matches the causal or mathematical direction implied by the premises.

item.context: State secrets refer to matters related to national security and interests, determined in accordance with legal procedures and known only to a certain range of personnel within a certain period of time.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following statements does not contain state secrets?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wang works in state organs, and some documents are related to national security and interests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The legal procedure of the court at trial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Li's unit stipulates that he shall not contact with a certain range of personnel within a certain period of time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some of the business contents of Zhang's unit are not allowed to be disclosed.

response:
Reasoning: State secrets must be matters related to national security/interests, legally determined, and restricted to certain people for a time. C only says Li cannot contact certain personnel for a period; it is a personnel rule, not a secret matter.  
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach, checking each option against all required elements: relation to national security/interests, legal determination, and limited circulation. The key factor I focused on was whether the statement described a “secret matter” itself rather than just a rule or circumstance around people. My error was narrowing too quickly to the option that looked least like a secret, while overlooking that one choice described an open legal process that is generally procedural and public, so it failed the definition more clearly. In similar problems, I should compare every option against each clause of the definition and prefer the one that directly contradicts a necessary condition, not just the one that seems vague or incomplete.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the definition as requiring three elements simultaneously: relation to national security/interests, formal legal determination, and limited circulation among specific people for a specific time. That interpretation was broadly correct, but I applied it too narrowly to only one option instead of systematically testing all four against every element. My strategy was elimination by spotting an option that obviously failed the definition, but I stopped once I found one plausible mismatch. That shortcut was inappropriate because multiple options could appear weak, and the task asked for the one statement that does not contain state secrets, so I needed comparative evaluation rather than first-fit elimination.

The key evidence I used was that a restriction on contacting certain personnel is a personnel-management rule, not itself a secret matter. However, I missed a more decisive distinction elsewhere: some statements may describe ordinary legal or institutional procedures rather than confidential content, even if they sound formal or governmental. I also assumed that because one option lacked explicit mention of secrecy, it must be the best answer, without checking whether another option was even further from the definition. I should have considered whether each option referred to content, rules about people, or public procedures, since the definition concerns secret matters, not merely restrictions or official settings. The error came from evaluating one option in isolation instead of ranking all options by fit with the full definition. In similar problems, I should build a checklist from the definition and apply it to every choice before deciding. General rule: when a concept is defined by multiple necessary conditions, reject any answer choice only after comparing all options against all conditions, not after identifying the first apparent mismatch.

item.context: To face danger solely because doing so affords one a certain pleasure does not constitute courage. Real courage is manifested only when a person, in acting to attain a goal, perseveres in the face of fear prompted by one or more dangers involved.
item.question: Which one of the following statements can be properly inferred from the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A person who faces danger in order to benefit others is acting courageously only if the person is afraid of the danger.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A person who must face danger in order to avoid future pain cannot properly be called courageous for doing so.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A person who has no fear of the situations that everyone else would fear cannot be said to be courageous in any situation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A person who experiences fear of some aspects of a dangerous situation cannot be said to act courageously in that situation.

response:
Reasoning: Courage requires persevering toward a goal despite fear caused by danger. So if someone acts courageously to benefit others, that person must be afraid of the danger. The other choices either deny possible courage where it could exist or contradict the role of fear in courage.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a definitional reasoning approach: I translated the stimulus into necessary conditions for courage and then checked which option matched those conditions without adding new ones. The key factor was that courage requires both pursuing a goal and persisting despite fear caused by danger, while acting solely for the pleasure of danger does not qualify. My success came from recognizing that “only when” sets a necessary condition, so any courageous action must include fear of the danger. For similar problems, first convert terms like “only,” “solely,” and “real” into clear conditional requirements, then eliminate choices that go beyond or negate those requirements.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stimulus as giving a necessary condition for courage, not a full definition of every admirable action. The key structure was: facing danger for pleasure alone is not courage, and courage appears only when someone persists toward a goal despite fear caused by the danger. My strategy was to translate that into a conditional test: if an action counts as courageous, then it must involve both a goal and fear in the face of danger. That was the right approach because inference questions depend more on logical entailment than on plausibility.

The evidence I used correctly was the phrase “only when,” which signals a necessary condition. I also used the contrast between “solely for pleasure” and “to attain a goal,” recognizing that pleasure-seeking alone is excluded but goal-directed action under fear can qualify. One assumption that worked was treating “benefit others” as a kind of goal, which fits the general wording of the stimulus. I properly rejected options that tried to make courage impossible in broader classes of cases, because the passage did not justify such sweeping exclusions. The main reason the reasoning succeeded is that I tracked necessity carefully and did not confuse it with sufficiency. In similar problems, I should keep converting restrictive phrases like “only when” into explicit conditional rules before comparing choices. General lesson: when a statement defines something with “only if” or “only when,” valid inferences usually preserve that requirement rather than broaden it.

item.context: The ability to analyze genomes - sequences of DNA - has grown more and more sophisticated. Scientists are able to examine the biological past in finer detail and with greater accuracy. A new analysis of the genetic links between early humans and chimpanzees has led to a hypothesis that the two species diverged more recently than previous estimates indicated. This gives credence to a very startling new theory: the ancestors of humans and chimpanzees might have hybridized to produce the lineage from which modern humans eventually developed.
item.question: What can be inferred from the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Political and religious pressures will affect the course of future research.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hybridized species combine the best of both lineages.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Earlier genome analysis established genetic links between early humans and chimpanzees.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human DNA is more complex than that of chimpanzees.

response:
Reasoning: The passage says a “new analysis of the genetic links between early humans and chimpanzees” refined earlier estimates, which implies those genetic links had already been established by previous genome analysis. Nothing supports claims about politics/religion, “best” traits in hybrids, or DNA complexity.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an inference-based elimination approach: identify what the passage explicitly supports, then reject choices that introduce new topics or stronger claims than the text warrants. The key clue was the phrase “a new analysis of the genetic links,” which implies those links were already known and are now being examined with improved methods. The successful step was noticing that “new analysis” suggests prior analysis rather than a first-time discovery. For similar problems, anchor each option to a specific phrase in the passage and prefer the choice that is most directly implied, not one that requires extra assumptions.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as an inference task: identify what must be supported by the passage, not what might be true in the real world. That interpretation was correct, because the answer had to come from implications of the wording, especially the contrast between a “new analysis” and “previous estimates.” My strategy was to compare each option against the passage and ask whether it was directly supported, contradicted, or unsupported. That was appropriate for a reading-inference multiple-choice problem, where elimination of unsupported claims is often more reliable than chasing the most interesting idea.

The key evidence I used was that scientists conducted a new analysis of genetic links and that this analysis revised earlier divergence estimates. From that, it follows that some earlier analysis had already identified those links, which aligns with the chosen option. I also correctly rejected distractors that introduced new subject matter: politics and religion were never mentioned, hybrid vigor was not discussed, and DNA complexity was not compared. An assumption that helped, and did not distort the result, was that “previous estimates” presuppose prior genome-based investigation. I should still note that the strongest support was not that all earlier genome analysis established the links, but that prior analysis had done so in some form.

What made the reasoning successful was staying close to textual entailment rather than background knowledge about evolution. In similar problems, I should continue distinguishing between what is explicitly stated, what is logically implied, and what is merely plausible. General rule: in inference questions, prefer the choice that is necessitated by the passage’s internal structure, especially by references to revision, comparison, or prior estimates.

item.context: A street comprehensive management committee has a total of 6 members: F, G, H, I, M and P. Each of these members shall serve as a member of at least one of the three sub-committees under the Comprehensive Management Committee. Each sub-committee consists of three different members. The known information is as follows: one of the six members serves as a member of three subcommittees. F is not a member of the same subcommittee as G. H is not a member of the same subcommittee as I.
item.question: If F is not a member of the same subcommittee as M, which of the following options must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: F and H are members of the same sub-committee.

choices.label: B
choices.text: F and I are members of the same sub-committee.

choices.label: C
choices.text: I and P are members of the same sub-committee.

choices.label: D
choices.text: M and G are members of the same sub-committee.

response:
Reasoning: Since F cannot be with G or M, any subcommittee containing F must be either {F,H,P} or {F,I,P}; so P is always with F. If it’s {F,I,P}, then C is true immediately. If it’s {F,H,P} and I were not with P, the other two groups couldn’t realize the required “one member serves on 3 subcommittees” condition. Hence I must be with P.
FINAL ANSWER: C
