For similar problems, I should continue identifying contrast words, temporal markers, and scope words like “at each stage.” A transferable rule is: when a passage presents two values as mutually opposed yet jointly necessary, prefer the option that preserves both under the stated timing or conditions, and reject answers that absolutize one side.

item.context: Conforming behavior refers to the phenomenon that an individual's behavior is consistent or similar to the behavior and will of others. Conforming behavior usually includes three situations: first, people abide by common social norms and produce similar behaviors to meet the needs of social living environment, so that social life can proceed normally; Second, similar cultural background and socialization process promote people to produce similar behavior. Third, the psychological interaction between the two sides in interpersonal communication also leads to consistent behavior
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following options does not belong to the consistent behavior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most college graduates are willing to work in large state-owned enterprises

choices.label: B
choices.text: Twins have been separated for many years, but they can still be recognized at a glance when they meet

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two cars scraped in the downtown area, and pedestrians stopped to watch

choices.label: D
choices.text: Works designed by architects of a design institute have similar styles

response:
Reasoning: Conforming behavior is about people showing similar actions/wills due to norms, shared background, or interpersonal influence. A, C, and D describe similar choices or behaviors. B describes twins looking alike, which is similarity in appearance, not behavior.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option against the three listed sources of conformity and checked whether the similarity described was actually behavioral. The key factor was distinguishing similarity in actions, preferences, or responses from mere similarity in physical traits or appearance. My success came from testing each choice against the core constraint that conformity must involve behavior shaped by norms, shared socialization, or interpersonal influence. For similar problems, isolate the defining element in the concept and eliminate choices that match only superficial similarity rather than the required type of similarity.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which option fails to match a definition built around behavioral similarity caused by one of three mechanisms: social norms, shared socialization, or interpersonal interaction. That interpretation was correct, and it was important to notice that the definition concerns behavior and will, not any kind of resemblance. My strategy was to map each option onto the three listed sources of conformity and eliminate any option that involved similarity without an underlying behavioral process. This was appropriate because the definition was structured as a set of necessary features, so the task was essentially a category-membership test.

The key evidence I used was that several options described people acting similarly, choosing similarly, gathering similarly, or creating in similar styles, all of which plausibly fit one of the listed mechanisms. The option I rejected described recognition based on physical similarity rather than conduct, intention, or socially shaped action. A critical assumption that helped was that “consistent behavior” should be interpreted narrowly as behavior, not broadly as any human similarity. I also implicitly checked whether the similarity arose from social influence or shared socialization rather than biology alone. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the causal structure in the definition, not just surface resemblance across people. For similar problems, I should continue separating essential attributes from incidental similarities and test each choice against every required element. A transferable rule is: when a definition specifies both a type of outcome and its causes, exclude options that match the outcome only superficially but fail the causal criterion.

item.context: Ms. Du: Newspapers and magazines rely on advertising revenue to reduce the unit price of each newspaper and magazine, that is to say, if there is no advertising, the unit price of newspapers and magazines is much higher. As a result, readers who buy newspapers and magazines benefit financially from advertisements in publications. Mr. Yang: Your statement is not valid. Who will pay for advertisements that seem to lead to price cuts in newspapers and magazines? In the end, they are not consumers, including those who buy newspapers and magazines. Because manufacturers spread the advertising expenses to consumers by raising the price of their products.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, can strongly weaken Mr. Yang's rebuttal to Ms. Du?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Due to the rise in prices, the prices of newspapers and magazines for the whole year have risen greatly compared with last year

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among the various forms of advertising, the effect of TV advertising is better than that of publication advertising

choices.label: C
choices.text: In recent years, more and more manufacturers have adopted newspapers and magazines for advertising, and advertising costs have also become higher and higher

choices.label: D
choices.text: Generally speaking, the advertising expenditure of various manufacturers is a constant, and they selectively take various forms such as radio, television, newspapers, magazines, street billboards, mail prints, and so on

response:
Reasoning: Mr. Yang argues publication ads make consumers pay more through higher product prices. If manufacturers’ total advertising budgets are generally fixed and only allocated among media, then using newspapers/magazines doesn’t necessarily raise product prices further, while it still helps lower publication prices. This weakens his rebuttal.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a weaken-the-rebuttal approach: first identified Mr. Yang’s core claim that publication advertising ultimately makes consumers pay through higher product prices, then looked for a choice that breaks that causal link. The key factor was whether advertising in newspapers and magazines adds extra manufacturer cost or merely reallocates an existing fixed advertising budget across different media. My success came from focusing on the hidden assumption in Mr. Yang’s argument—that choosing publication ads increases total advertising spending and therefore product prices. For similar problems, isolate the exact causal assumption behind the rebuttal and prefer choices that show the disputed cost or effect would exist anyway, even without the specific option being discussed.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a weakening task aimed specifically at Mr. Yang’s rebuttal, not at evaluating Ms. Du’s claim directly. The key dispute was whether advertisement-supported lower publication prices are offset because consumers ultimately pay higher prices for advertised products. My strategy was to identify the core causal link in Mr. Yang’s argument: manufacturers incur ad costs, then pass those costs on to consumers through product price increases. That was the right target because weakening that link undermines his claim that readers do not financially benefit.

The most important evidence I used was the idea that manufacturers’ total advertising budgets may already be fixed and merely redistributed across media channels. If that is true, choosing newspapers and magazines as one advertising outlet does not imply additional advertising expense that must be newly passed on to consumers. This directly attacks Mr. Yang’s assumption that publication advertising causes higher consumer prices, rather than simply reallocating existing ad spending. I also correctly ignored choices that discussed price trends, relative effectiveness, or rising ad spending without connecting them to the pass-through claim. A possible shortcut I used was treating “constant advertising expenditure” as sufficient without separately proving no price effect, but in context it strongly weakens the rebuttal because it removes the “extra cost” premise. The reasoning succeeded because it focused on the argument’s hidden assumption rather than surface details. In similar problems, I should explicitly isolate whether a rebuttal depends on added cost, causation, or total burden. General rule: to weaken an argument that claims costs are passed to consumers, look for evidence that the costs are fixed, reallocated, absorbed, or otherwise not incrementally caused by the disputed action.

item.context: From an analysis of broken pottery and statuary, archaeologists have estimated that an ancient settlement in southwestern Arabia was established around 1000 B. C. However, new evidence suggests that the settlement is considerably older: tests show that a piece of building timber recently uncovered at the site is substantially older than the pottery and statuary.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion drawn from the new evidence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The building timber bore marks suggesting that it had been salvaged from an earlier settlement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pieces of pottery and fragments of statues that were analyzed come from several parts of the site.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The type of pottery found at the site is similar to a type of pottery associated with civilizations that existed before 1000 B. C.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tests used to determine the age of the pottery and statuary had been devised more recently than those used to determine the age of the building timber.

response:
Reasoning: The new conclusion assumes the timber dates the settlement itself. If the timber was salvaged from an earlier settlement, then the wood could be much older than the construction at this site, so it would not show that this settlement is older than the pottery and statuary suggest.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a weakening-by-assumption approach: I identified the new argument’s core inference that the age of one timber piece reflects the age of the settlement itself. The key factor was the possibility of reuse, since reused materials can be older than the structure or site where they are later found. What made the reasoning succeed was focusing on the gap between “older artifact found there” and “the settlement is older.” For similar problems, isolate whether the evidence directly dates the target claim or could instead date a recycled, transported, or otherwise unrepresentative item.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as an argument-weaken task focused on the phrase “most seriously undermines the conclusion drawn from the new evidence.” The conclusion was not merely that the timber was old, but that the settlement itself must therefore be considerably older than previously estimated. My strategy was to identify the key assumption linking the evidence to the conclusion: that the timber’s age reflects the age of the settlement’s establishment. That was the appropriate strategy because weaken questions often turn on whether the evidence is genuinely representative of what the conclusion is about.

The crucial fact I used was the possibility that materials can predate the context in which they are found. If the timber had been reused or salvaged, its age would not date the founding of the settlement. I did not rely on side issues like how broad the pottery sample was or how recently different testing methods were developed, because those do not directly break the inference from old timber to old settlement. An important assumption in my reasoning was that construction materials can be transported and repurposed across sites and time periods. I should also have consciously checked whether any other option attacked the comparison between the timber and the pottery more directly, but none did so as powerfully.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the argument’s hidden bridge rather than on surface details about archaeology. In similar problems, I should continue to ask, “What must be true for this evidence to support this exact conclusion?” A general rule is: when an argument dates a whole event, site, or practice from one artifact, test whether that artifact could be unrepresentative, reused, or otherwise disconnected from the timing of the broader conclusion.

item.context: The bidding policy of the municipal government for post-earthquake recovery and reconstruction is that the lowest bidder can win the bid. Some people think that if this policy is implemented, some winning bidders will cut corners, resulting in poor quality of the project. This will not only lead to the consequences of additional construction investment, but also endanger people's lives. If we want to put an end to the tofu-dreg project, we must change this erroneous policy.
item.question: Which of the following statements is true can weaken the above argument most powerfully?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The need to rebuild damaged buildings can provide many employment opportunities for residents of the city

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city's construction contracts rarely specify the quality of construction materials and employment requirements

choices.label: C
choices.text: The policy also includes that only those construction companies that meet strict quality standards and have certain qualifications can bid

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the building design is flawed, even a building built with the best building materials and first-class engineering quality is also dangerous

response:
Reasoning: The argument assumes “lowest bidder wins” leads to poor quality because firms will cut corners. C most weakens this by showing bidding is restricted to qualified companies meeting strict quality standards, so low price does not necessarily mean low quality. A and B are irrelevant; D shifts blame but doesn’t address the policy directly.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-weaken approach: identify the conclusion, then look for the hidden link between “lowest bidder wins” and “poor-quality construction.” The key factor was that the argument depends on price being the main determinant of quality risk, so evidence that bidders are pre-screened for strict qualifications directly undercuts that causal link. My success came from targeting the premise-to-conclusion connection rather than choosing an option that was merely related to construction risks. For similar questions, first isolate the exact assumption that makes the argument work, then prefer the choice that most directly breaks that assumption rather than one that introduces an alternative concern.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a weakening problem: the task was to find the statement that most directly undermines the causal link between the bidding policy and low-quality construction. My strategy was to identify the argument’s core assumption, namely that awarding contracts to the lowest bidder necessarily creates an incentive to sacrifice quality. That was the right approach, because weakening questions are best handled by locating the hidden premise and testing which option attacks it most directly. I used the distinction between relevance and mechanism: a strong weakener had to address how the policy operates, not merely mention construction, danger, or rebuilding in general. I correctly recognized that options about employment benefits or contract details were not enough, because they did not challenge the claimed connection between low bids and “tofu-dreg” outcomes. I also noticed that an option about design flaws introduced an alternative source of danger, but it did not show that the policy itself was not problematic, so it was only a partial distraction. The successful part of my reasoning was focusing on eligibility constraints within the policy, since such constraints can block the inference from “cheap” to “unqualified” or “unsafe.” A key assumption I avoided was treating “lowest price” as equivalent to “lowest standards”; the best weakening answer showed why that equivalence may fail. In similar problems, I should keep separating background facts from premises that alter the argument’s causal chain. A general rule is: in causal-policy weakening questions, prefer the choice that directly breaks the policy-to-harm mechanism over choices that merely add side facts or alternate dangers.

item.context: Legal evil interest refers to the thing generated from the original thing according to a certain legal relationship. It is the legal income that the owner of the original thing should obtain from specific civil legal activities such as leasing and investment.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following is a legal evil interest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dividends from investing in treasury bonds

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fruit from an orchard contracted by a farmer

choices.label: C
choices.text: A puppy bred from a purebred dog in a pet store

choices.label: D
choices.text: With the money lent by a to B, B bought the lottery and won the grand prize of 100,000 yuan

response:
Reasoning: Legal fruits are income generated from the original property through a legal relationship like lease or investment. A fits because dividends/interest from treasury bond investment are civil legal income. B and C are natural fruits; D is lottery winnings, not legal fruit from the loan.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: separate “legal fruits” from other kinds of gains by checking whether the benefit arises from a civil legal relationship such as investment or leasing. The key factor was the source of the income—whether it is generated through a legally structured use of the original property, rather than through natural growth or accidental gain. My success came from classifying each option by type of yield: investment return versus natural offspring/produce versus unrelated windfall. For similar problems, first extract the defining mechanism in the rule, then test each option by asking how the benefit was produced, not just whether it came after the original asset.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for an example of a “legal fruit” or legal income derived from an original object through a recognized civil legal relationship, rather than a naturally produced increase. That interpretation was correct because the definition explicitly contrasted the source of the gain: it must arise from legal activity such as leasing or investment. My strategy was to classify each option by the mechanism that generated the benefit—legal transaction, natural production, biological reproduction, or accidental gain. That was the right approach because the key distinction in the definition is not merely “something valuable produced from something else,” but “produced through a legal relationship.”

The strongest evidence I used was the phrase “specific civil legal activities such as leasing and investment,” which directly matched the investment return in one option. I also used the legal distinction between natural fruits and legal fruits: crops and animal offspring are generated by nature or biology, not by a juridical arrangement. I correctly rejected the lottery prize because although the loaned money enabled the purchase, the winnings did not arise as a legal yield of the loan itself. One assumption that helped was treating treasury-bond returns as investment income recognized by law, which aligns with the definition. I should still note that I relied on category comparison rather than testing each option against every element of the definition in a formal way. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the causal relationship required by the definition, not just on superficial “profit.” A transferable rule is: when a definition distinguishes legal, natural, and accidental sources, classify each option by the source mechanism of the gain, not by the fact that gain occurred.

item.context: Legal and moral paradoxes: many people think that ethical behavior is not illegal, but in reality, some acts that conform to general moral principles are prohibited by law.
item.question: Which of the following does not belong to the phenomenon of Legal  and moral paradoxes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A nurse was charged with murder after helping a terminally ill cancer patient to die at his own request in order to relieve him of unbearable pain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A man paid 10,000 yuan to buy a boy from a human trafficker as his son. He treated him as his own child and showed great care. When the police came to rescue him two years later, the boy refused to leave his present parents.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In order to solve the difficulty of schooling for children of migrant workers, B established a low-fee elementary school. He was accused of illegally running the school and had to close it. As a result, many children dropped out of school again.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When a man returned home from prison, he threatened to take revenge on the Enemyand prepared a weapon. His father imprisoned him for three months  to prevent him from committing a murder. The act is suspected of unlawful detention.

response:
Reasoning: “Legal and moral paradoxes” are acts that seem morally justified yet are illegal. A, C, and D fit this: mercy killing, running a low-fee school, and detaining someone to prevent murder. B does not, because buying a trafficked child encourages trafficking and is not morally proper despite later care.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I identified the core pattern as conduct that aligns with a broadly accepted moral principle but is still prohibited by law, then tested each option against both parts. The key factor was separating sympathetic outcomes from genuine moral legitimacy; an act can look caring in context yet still violate an important moral norm. My success came from noticing that one option involved participating in child trafficking, which undermines the claim that the conduct conforms to general moral principles. For similar problems, I should explicitly check each choice for both necessary conditions of the definition, rather than excluding or including options based only on emotional appeal or consequences.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the prompt as asking for the option that fails to match a specific pattern: conduct that appears ethically defensible under ordinary moral intuitions yet is still prohibited by law. That interpretation was correct, because the key was the tension between legal illegality and moral approval, not merely any emotionally complicated case. My strategy was to test each option against both halves of the definition: first, whether the act violated law, and second, whether the act could plausibly be seen as conforming to a general moral principle such as compassion, protection, or public welfare. This was an appropriate classification strategy because the answer depended on membership in a defined category rather than on comparing degrees of wrongdoing.

The most important evidence I used was the moral valence of each act. Assisted death to relieve suffering, operating a school to educate disadvantaged children, and restraining someone to prevent a killing each have a recognizable moral rationale despite legal problems. By contrast, purchasing a trafficked child, even if followed by affectionate care, directly supports an exploitative criminal market, so the later kindness does not convert the initial act into something morally aligned. A shortcut that helped was separating motive from structural effect: good intentions are not enough if the act itself sustains serious harm. An alternative I needed to consider was whether sympathetic outcomes could blur moral judgment, but the category requires general moral legitimacy, not emotional complexity. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the definitional core rather than the pathos of the narratives. A transferable rule is: when classifying “moral-but-illegal” cases, evaluate the moral status of the act itself and its systemic consequences, not just the actor’s benevolent motive or the favorable result in one instance.

item.context: Researchers put two electrodes in a pool that a dolphin swam in. When the dolphin swam near the electrodes, the researchers would sometimes create a weak electric field by activating the electrodes. The dolphin would swim away if the electrodes were activated; otherwise it acted normally. The researchers then placed a plastic shield over small organs called vibrissal crypts located on the dolphin' s snout. With the crypts covered, the dolphin no longer swam away when the electrodes were activated.
item.question: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the wild, dolphins sometimes encounter strong electric fields.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Under normal circumstances, dolphins are unable to sense electric fields.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vibrissal crypts enable dolphins to sense electric fields.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electric fields interfere with the normal functioning of dolphins' vibrissal crypts.

response:
Reasoning: The dolphin reacted to the electric field by swimming away, showing it could detect the field. When the vibrissal crypts were covered, that reaction disappeared. This most strongly indicates those crypts are responsible for sensing electric fields, not that fields disrupt them or that wild dolphins encounter strong fields.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a causal-comparison approach: compare the dolphin’s behavior when the electric field was present with the crypts uncovered versus covered. The key factor was the change in response after the plastic shield was added; the field stayed the same, but blocking the crypts removed the avoidance behavior. That reasoning step correctly supported an inference about the function of the crypts rather than about wild conditions or interference effects. For similar problems, isolate the single changed condition in an experiment and infer only the role that change most directly supports.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the strongest supported causal inference from an experiment, not for a broader speculation about dolphin behavior in the wild. That was the correct framing, because the evidence compared the dolphin’s response before and after the vibrissal crypts were covered. My strategy was to track the behavioral change across the two conditions and identify what variable changed: the electric field remained available, but access to the crypts did not. This was appropriate because the experiment was designed like a functional test of a sensory organ.

The key evidence I used was the contrast: with uncovered crypts, activation of the electrodes produced avoidance; with covered crypts, the same activation no longer produced avoidance. That pattern supports an enabling role for the crypts in detection. I also correctly rejected choices that went beyond the data, such as claims about what dolphins encounter in the wild, because the experiment provided no ecological evidence. Another useful constraint was that the dolphin clearly could sense the field under normal conditions, so any answer denying that was directly contradicted.

An assumption in my reasoning was that the plastic shield blocked sensing rather than causing unrelated impairment, but that assumption is reasonable because the conclusion only needs strongest support, not proof. I also considered whether the field might disrupt the crypts, but that would not explain why covering them removed the behavioral response. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on experimental manipulation and eliminated answers that were unsupported or causally backward. General rule: when a structure is blocked and a specific response disappears while the stimulus remains constant, the best-supported inference is that the structure is necessary for detecting or mediating that stimulus.

item.context: Experts believe that once myopia occurs, it is irreversible. In particular, children with myopia at a low age are more likely to become highly myopic, resulting in visual impairment. Full exposure to sunlight can effectively protect eyesight. Outdoor activities of 2 hours a day and more than 10 hours a week can reduce the incidence of myopia in teenagers by more than 10%. This is mainly because the light intensity of the sun is hundreds of times higher than that of indoor light, the stronger the light is, the more dopamine is released, and dopamine can inhibit the occurrence and development of myopia. On the one hand, high-intensity light can reduce the pupil, deepen the depth of field and reduce blurring, on the other hand, it can also play a role in suppressing myopia.
item.question: Which of the following options is the most important part of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Myopia of the children at a low age is vision damage caused by weak light.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sunlight can effectively inhibit the occurrence and development of myopia.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The intensity of light is negatively correlated with the incidence of myopia.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Outdoor activities can effectively prevent the occurrence of myopia.

response:
Reasoning: The passage’s core claim is that sunlight/high-intensity light helps prevent and slow myopia, while outdoor activity is presented mainly as the way to get that sunlight. So the main idea is the inhibitory effect of sunlight on myopia, not just outdoor activity itself.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea summarization approach, trying to identify the central claim and treating the biological explanation about sunlight and dopamine as the core thesis. The key factor that misled me was overvaluing the mechanism of sunlight’s effect, while underweighting the passage’s more practical, repeatedly emphasized conclusion about daily outdoor activity reducing myopia incidence. My mistake was choosing the underlying cause instead of the passage’s primary takeaway for readers. For similar problems, I should distinguish between a supporting explanation and the author’s main actionable point, and prefer the broader conclusion that the evidence is organized to support.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s central claim, but I treated the explanatory mechanism as more central than the passage’s headline conclusion. My strategy was to identify the sentence that seemed to unify the rest of the details, and I chose the claim about sunlight because several later sentences explained why strong light affects myopia. That strategy was only partly appropriate: in main-idea questions, explanation density does not automatically determine the author’s main point. I used the causal chain about light intensity, dopamine release, pupil constriction, and reduced blur, but I underweighted the earlier practical claim about a specific preventive behavior and its measured effect. I also assumed that because outdoor activity was described as a means of receiving sunlight, it must be secondary, yet the passage framed that behavior with concrete duration thresholds and outcome data, which signals emphasis. Another missed clue was the wording “this is mainly because,” which often marks supporting evidence rather than the thesis itself. I should have compared each option against the passage’s overall structure: problem, intervention, evidence, mechanism. The error came from selecting the deepest cause instead of the broadest, most decision-relevant takeaway. In similar problems, I should distinguish between a recommendation, the evidence for it, and the biological explanation behind it. General rule: when identifying the “most important part” of a passage, prefer the highest-level claim that the other statements support, not the mechanism that merely justifies that claim.

item.context: The five senses have traditionally been viewed as distinct yet complementary. Each sense is thought to have its own range of stimuli that are incapable of stimulating the other senses. However, recent research has discovered that some people taste a banana and claim that they are tasting blue, or see a color and say that it has a specific smell. This shows that such people, called synesthesiacs, have senses that do not respect the usual boundaries between the five recognized senses.
item.question: Which one of the following statements, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recent evidence strongly suggests that there are other senses besides sight, touch, smell, hearing, and taste.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Synesthesiacs can be temporarily rid of their synesthetic experiences by the use of drugs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The particular ways in which sensory experiences overlap in synesthesiacs follow a definite pattern.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Synesthesiacs demonstrate a general, systematic impairment in their ability to use and understand words.

response:
Reasoning: The argument infers unusual sensory overlap from how synesthesiacs describe their experiences. If they have a systematic impairment in using and understanding words, then statements like “tasting blue” may reflect verbal confusion rather than actual boundary-crossing senses. That directly undermines the conclusion.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a weaken-the-evidence approach by identifying the argument’s main support: reports about how synesthesiacs describe their experiences. The key factor was that the conclusion depends on taking those descriptions literally as accurate evidence of cross-sensory perception. The successful step was noticing that if the speakers have a systematic language impairment, their statements may be unreliable descriptions rather than proof that sensory boundaries are crossed. For similar problems, test whether the evidence reflects the phenomenon itself or could instead be explained by a defect in reporting, measurement, or interpretation.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for a fact that attacks the link between the reported descriptions of experience and the conclusion about sensory boundaries. That was the right target, because the argument’s key evidence was not direct measurement of perception but what synesthesiacs “claim” or “say.” My strategy was to look for an answer choice that undermined the reliability or meaning of those reports rather than one that merely added background information about senses. That was appropriate for a weaken question, especially when the conclusion depends heavily on testimony. The crucial evidence I used was that the argument infers a perceptual phenomenon from language like “tasting blue” and “a color has a smell.” If those utterances could be explained by a language-processing problem, then the inference to cross-sensory perception becomes much weaker. I implicitly assumed the best weakening move would be to attack the evidential bridge rather than the broader theory of five senses, and that assumption was justified here. I also correctly rejected alternatives that were irrelevant or even potentially supportive, such as claims about patterned overlap or temporary suppression. The success came from identifying the argument’s vulnerability: it treated verbal reports as transparent evidence of underlying sensation. In similar problems, I should first ask whether the evidence is observational, behavioral, or linguistic, and then test whether an alternative explanation undercuts that evidential source. A useful general rule is: when a conclusion about mental states rests on what subjects say, a strong weakening answer often challenges whether their words reliably represent those states.

item.context: On the weekends, Eliza only reads romance novels. During the week, Eliza paints three days a week unless she has pressing family obligations or is substitute teaching at the local art school. Four days a week, Eliza practices her cello, and on Wednesdays, she gives cello lessons. Last week, Eliza had no pressing family obligations, nor did she substitute teach at the local art school. Ttherefore, she must have practiced her cello on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday.
item.question: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There was at least one day last week when Eliza read romance novels and painted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eliza does not practice her cello on the day that she gives cello lessons.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eliza does not give cello lessons on days that she substitute teaches at the local art school.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eliza never has pressing family obligations on the day she gives cello lessons.

response:
Reasoning: Since on weekends Eliza only reads romance novels, any cello practice must be on weekdays. She practices four days a week, and to conclude those days were Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday, the argument must rule out Wednesday. That requires assuming she does not practice cello on the day she gives lessons.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-analysis approach: identify what the conclusion needs in order to be guaranteed, then look for the unstated condition that eliminates alternative schedules. The key factor was that the conclusion names exactly four weekday practice days, so Wednesday had to be excluded somehow; the only given fact about Wednesday is that she gives lessons then. My success came from testing what would happen if she could still practice on Wednesday—then the stated conclusion would no longer be forced. For similar problems, I should explicitly search for remaining possibilities that would weaken the conclusion and select the assumption that blocks those possibilities.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as an LSAT-style assumption problem: identify a hidden premise required for the conclusion to follow, not merely a statement that is compatible with the facts. That interpretation was correct, and it mattered because the task was to test what the argument must presuppose in order to pin down the exact four practice days. My strategy was to compare the weekly scheduling rules with the conclusion and ask what gap remained between the premises and that specific schedule. The key evidence I used was that weekend reading excludes other weekend activities, and that painting must occupy three weekdays given the absence of family obligations and substitute teaching. I also used the fact that cello practice occurs four days per week and that Wednesday includes cello lessons.

The crucial inference was that the conclusion identifies every weekday except Wednesday as practice days, so the argument needs a reason Wednesday cannot also be a practice day. That was the right place to look for an assumption because the premises alone did not forbid practicing on lesson day. A shortcut that helped, and was justified here, was focusing on the excluded day rather than re-deriving the whole schedule from scratch. I should still note that other answer choices could have been tempting if treated as useful background rather than necessary support. The success came from distinguishing “helps explain the week” from “must be true for the conclusion to be forced.” A transferable rule is: when a conclusion specifies an exact set, test what premise is needed to eliminate every remaining alternative member of the set.

item.context: The raw materials of cement are very cheap, such as limestone and soil that can be found everywhere can be used as raw materials for cement. But the price of cement will be affected by the price of oil, because it consumes a lot of energy to change raw materials into cement in high-temperature furnaces.
item.question: Based on the above judgment, which of the following options is most likely to come to a conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Petroleum is one of the raw materials contained in cement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Petroleum is the energy source of some high temperature furnaces for making cement

choices.label: C
choices.text: The price of cement falls with the rise of oil prices

choices.label: D
choices.text: The higher the price of cement, the higher the price of limestone

response:
Reasoning: Cement’s raw materials are cheap, but cement price is affected by oil because making cement requires much energy in high-temperature furnaces. So the most likely conclusion is that oil is used as an energy source in some cement-producing furnaces, not as a raw material.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a causal inference approach: I linked the stated effect on cement prices to the described production process rather than to the composition of cement itself. The key clue was that oil affects price because cement production “consumes a lot of energy” in high-temperature furnaces, which supports an energy-source relationship. The successful step was distinguishing between something influencing manufacturing cost and something being a raw ingredient. For similar problems, map each statement to its role in the causal chain and choose the option that preserves that exact relationship instead of jumping to loosely related associations.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the conclusion most directly supported by the passage, not a merely related statement or a broader economic claim. That interpretation was correct, because the key premise was the causal link between oil prices and cement prices through energy consumption in high-temperature production. My strategy was to identify the bridge connecting “oil price affects cement price” with “cement requires a lot of energy to produce,” then select the option that made that bridge explicit. This was appropriate because the passage does not discuss all possible market effects; it points to one specific production-cost mechanism.

The crucial evidence I used was that raw materials are cheap and widespread, so oil’s relevance must come from processing rather than ingredients. I also correctly rejected the idea that oil is a raw material, since the passage contrasted raw materials with energy inputs. One assumption I implicitly used was that at least some furnaces rely on petroleum-derived fuel; that assumption was justified because otherwise oil prices would not be a natural explanation. The alternatives should be screened by direction and relevance: one option reversed the likely price relationship, and another claimed an unsupported correlation between cement and limestone prices. The reasoning succeeded because it distinguished between input categories—material inputs versus energy inputs—rather than focusing only on the word “oil.” In similar problems, I should map each answer choice to a specific sentence in the prompt and check whether it is a necessary or merely speculative extension. General rule: when a passage explains a price effect via production cost, infer the intermediate causal input named or implied, not an unrelated ingredient or secondary market consequence.

item.context: In a certain municipality, a judge overturned a suspect' s conviction for possession of an illegal weapon. The suspect had fled upon seeing police and subsequently discarded the illegal weapon after the police gave chase. The judge reasoned as follows: the only cause for the police giving chase was the suspect' s flight; by itself, flight from the police does not create a reasonable suspicion of a criminal act; evidence collected during an illegal chase is inadmissible; ttherefore, the evidence in this case was inadmissible.
item.question: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the judge's decision that the evidence was inadmissible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flight from the police should not itself be considered a criminal act.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People can legally flee from the police only when those people are not involved in a criminal act at the time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Police can legally give chase to a person only when the person's actions have created a reasonable suspicion of a criminal act.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Flight from the police could create a reasonable suspicion of a criminal act as long as other significant factors are involved.

response:
Reasoning: The missing link is that a chase is illegal unless the suspect’s actions created reasonable suspicion. Since the only basis for the chase was flight, and flight alone does not create reasonable suspicion, the chase was illegal; thus the discarded weapon was inadmissible.  
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a gap-filling approach: I identified the conclusion that the evidence was inadmissible and looked for the missing principle needed to connect “flight alone is not reasonable suspicion” to “the chase was illegal.” The key factor was the legal threshold for initiating a chase, because the judge’s argument already assumed that evidence from an illegal chase must be excluded. The successful step was noticing that the argument needed a rule about when police may chase, not a rule about whether flight is itself a crime. For similar problems, isolate the exact logical gap between the stated facts and the conclusion, and choose the principle that supplies that missing conditional link.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stimulus as asking for the missing normative bridge between the judge’s factual claims and the legal conclusion that the evidence had to be excluded. That was the right interpretation, because the argument already supplied most of the factual premises: the chase was triggered only by flight, and flight alone was said not to create reasonable suspicion. My strategy was to look for a principle that connected “no reasonable suspicion” to “the chase was illegal,” since the inadmissibility conclusion depended on that intermediate legal step. That was appropriate for a strengthen-by-principle question, especially one asking what “most helps to justify” a decision.

The key evidence I used was the argument’s structure: flight was the sole basis for pursuit; flight alone was insufficient; illegally obtained evidence is inadmissible. I correctly noticed that the missing premise had to govern when police may legally pursue someone, not merely describe flight in the abstract. I avoided choices that were too weak or tangential, such as statements about whether flight is itself criminal, because that does not determine whether pursuit is lawful. I also rejected principles that introduced extra conditions or exceptions, since the judge’s reasoning required a direct rule, not a possibility. The success came from matching the answer to the exact logical gap rather than to the general topic. In similar problems, I should continue mapping the argument into premises, missing bridge, and conclusion before evaluating answer choices. General rule: when a legal or causal conclusion depends on an unstated transition, prefer the option that explicitly authorizes that transition, not one that merely restates background facts or related concepts.

item.context: Market positioning is based on the position of competitors' existing products in the market, and according to the degree of importance consumers or users attach to certain characteristics or attributes of the product, it can strongly shape the company's products to be unique and give people a distinctive personality or image, and vividly convey this image to customers, so that the product can determine the appropriate position in the market. Market positioning is to shape the position of a product in the market, and this position depends on the consumer Or how users recognize this product.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following situations does not belong to market positioning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Coca-Cola Company's advertising campaign with the characteristics of being a leader in the world's beverage market

choices.label: B
choices.text: A certain store specializes in selling low-priced products in the marketing process

choices.label: C
choices.text: A clothing factory specializes in the production of clothing for the elderly

choices.label: D
choices.text: A restaurant has a prosperous business. The restaurant sells both breakfast, noon and evening meals, both low-priced bulk products and high-end meals

response:
Reasoning: Market positioning requires creating a clear, distinctive image or target attribute in consumers’ minds. A, B, and C each emphasize a specific position: leader brand, low-price strategy, and elderly clothing. D serves all times, all price levels, and broad needs, lacking a distinct market position.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: compare each option against the core elements of market positioning, especially whether it creates a distinctive image in consumers’ minds. The key factor was distinctiveness—A, B, and C each centered on a clear attribute or target segment, while one option described broad coverage rather than a specific perceived position. The successful step was focusing on the phrase about shaping a “unique” image recognized by consumers, instead of being distracted by business success or product variety. For similar problems, isolate the definition’s necessary conditions and eliminate any choice that is merely broad, operational, or descriptive without a clear differentiated consumer perception.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the definition as requiring a product or business to occupy a clear, distinctive place in consumers’ minds relative to competitors, based on salient attributes such as price, target user, or brand image. That interpretation was correct because the passage emphasized uniqueness, recognizability, and the formation of a specific consumer perception. My strategy was to test each option against the core criterion: does it present a focused attribute that meaningfully differentiates the offering? That was an appropriate approach for a definition-matching question, especially since several options described ordinary business behavior but only some reflected a deliberate positioning logic. I used the key facts that leadership claims, low-price emphasis, and serving a defined demographic each create a recognizable market image. I also noticed that one option described breadth and variety across time periods and price levels rather than a single differentiating identity, which was the decisive contrast. A possible shortcut I took was treating “distinctive image” as the dominant test and not separately analyzing competitor reference in every option, but here that shortcut aligned with the definition. I should still remember that positioning is not just any strategy; it must guide how customers categorize the offering. The transferable rule is: when applying a definition of positioning, distinguish focused differentiation from broad coverage, because serving many segments usually weakens rather than establishes a specific market position.

item.context: The senator has long held to the general principle that no true work of art is obscene, and thus that there is no conflict between the need to encourage free artistic expression and the need to protect the sensibilities of the public from obscenity. When well-known works generally viewed as obscene are cited as possible counterexamples, the senator justifies accepting the principle by saying that if these works really are obscene then they cannot be works of art.
item.question: The senator's reasoning contains which one of the following errors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It assumes what it seeks to establish.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It seeks to persuade by emotional rather than intellectual means.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contains an implicit contradiction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It relies on an assertion of the senator's authority.

response:
Reasoning: The senator’s “principle” is protected by redefining any apparent counterexample out of existence: if something is obscene, then it is not art. That simply assumes the disputed point—namely, that no work of art is obscene—rather than proving it. This is circular reasoning.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-identification approach by translating the senator’s claim into a conditional rule and then checking how the response to counterexamples functioned logically. The key factor was that the senator handled objections by defining any allegedly obscene artwork as “not art,” which simply restated the original principle instead of supporting it independently. My answer was correct because I recognized that the conclusion was being smuggled into the premise, making the reasoning circular. For similar problems, I should test whether a speaker answers counterexamples with an independent reason or merely reclassifies the example so the conclusion automatically remains true.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the flaw in the senator’s argument, not whether the senator’s principle might be defensible in some broader philosophical sense. The key task was to examine how the senator handled apparent counterexamples and determine whether that response provided independent support or merely restated the original claim. My strategy was to translate the argument into a conditional form: no true work of art is obscene, and if something is obscene, then it is not art. That was appropriate because LSAT flaw questions often turn on whether a speaker is using a definition neutrally or just building the conclusion into a premise. The decisive evidence was that the senator answered objections by saying that any cited obscene work must therefore not be art, which is just the original principle in reverse form. I correctly recognized that this does not supply a new reason; it simply protects the claim by excluding counterexamples through assertion. I did not get distracted by tempting but weaker alternatives such as emotional appeal or authority, because nothing in the stimulus depended on feelings or status. A possible pitfall would have been to mistake the move for mere redefinition, but the deeper issue is that the redefinition is being used to prove the very point at issue. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on whether the objection-response structure added support or only repeated the conclusion. In similar problems, I should test whether a premise could be accepted by someone who doubts the conclusion; if not, the reasoning is likely circular. General rule: when an argument dismisses every counterexample only by restating the disputed classification, it is assuming what it seeks to prove.

item.context: In a test of a brain health product, the first group took the product daily, and the second group did not. The first group did indeed have better cognitive abilities than the second group. Therefore, the experiment proves that this kind of health care product does have obvious health care effect on the brain.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, cannot support the above discussion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cognitive abilities of the two groups were comparable before the test

choices.label: B
choices.text: The brain product contains ingredients also found in some everyday foods

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two groups had equal numbers of people and similar family finances

choices.label: D
choices.text: This brain healthy product has been licensed to produce and sell, and has achieved a good market share

response:
Reasoning: The claim needs evidence that the product caused the better cognition. A and C help by showing the groups were comparable. D is weakly relevant at best. B does not support the causal claim; if the ingredients are common in ordinary foods, that does not show this product has a special brain-health effect.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a causal-support approach, asking which option would strengthen the claim that the product itself caused the later difference between groups. The key factor I focused on was group comparability, but I misapplied the timing: I treated “comparable before the test” as supportive, when the argument’s conclusion says the experiment already “proves” the effect, so that fact alone still does not rule out other confounders. My error was assuming a necessary experimental condition automatically provides support strong enough for the conclusion. In similar problems, I should distinguish between facts that are merely prerequisites for a valid experiment and facts that actually strengthen the specific causal inference being claimed.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task as asking which option failed to strengthen the causal conclusion that the product improved brain function, but I did not distinguish carefully enough between “does not strongly help” and “cannot support.” My strategy was to evaluate each choice for relevance to causal inference, focusing on whether it reduced confounding between the two groups. That framework was appropriate, but I applied it too loosely and treated the weakest-looking statement as the answer instead of checking whether any option actually undermined support. I correctly noticed that factors like equal group size and similar finances can help rule out alternative explanations, but I missed a key issue with the statement about pre-test comparability. In an experiment where one group is selected to take a product and the other is not, saying the groups started with similar cognitive ability does not by itself support the claim of an “obvious health care effect,” because it addresses only one baseline measure and does not establish valid experimental control, randomization, or exclusion of other differences. I also over-penalized the option about common ingredients, assuming that if ingredients appear in foods, the product becomes irrelevant; however, common ingredients can still support effectiveness if concentrated or combined differently. The main error was conflating “not sufficient proof” with “cannot support at all.” In similar problems, I should classify each option more precisely: does it strengthen, weaken, or merely fail to prove? A transferable rule is: when asked which statement cannot support a conclusion, test whether the statement provides any incremental evidential link, not whether it conclusively establishes the claim.

item.context: Agricultural resources: refers to the general term for all materials and energy that can be used in agriculture.
item.question: Which of the following is not agricultural resources?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There are more than 4,000 plant resources in Chongqing, including more than 2,000 vascular plants. The natural vegetation includes five main types of vegetation: broad-leaved forest, coniferous forest, bamboo forest, shrub, and sparse grass. Among them, subtropical green broad-leaved forest Is the main vegetation type

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tobacco is the second largest type of economic crop in Henan Province after cotton. The total output has always been the first in the country, and it is the country's largest tobacco production base

choices.label: C
choices.text: The famous specialty products in Xihu District of Hangzhou are the three traditional leading products of West Lake Longjing Tea, Jiuqu Hongmei, and West Lake Brasenia schreberi

choices.label: D
choices.text: Liuzhou, Guangxi, took advantage of local resources to develop a number of basic industries such as household chemicals, papermaking, sugar, cigarettes, textiles, and pharmaceuticals, as well as building materials, chemicals, and electrical equipment manufacturing

response:
Reasoning: Agricultural resources are materials/energy directly usable in agriculture, such as plants and crops. A, B, and C describe plant/crop or specialty agricultural products. D describes industrial development and manufacturing sectors, which are not agricultural resources.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a category-matching approach: compare each option to the definition and check whether it describes materials or energy usable in agriculture, rather than downstream economic activity. The key factor was the distinction between primary agricultural resources such as plants, crops, and specialty farm products versus secondary industrial processing and manufacturing. My success came from filtering out surface mentions of “resources” and focusing on the actual object being described. For similar problems, first classify each option by economic stage—resource, production, processing, or manufacturing—and eliminate choices that describe later-stage industry rather than the resource itself.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the option that does not describe materials or energy that serve as inputs or directly usable assets in agriculture. That interpretation was correct, because the definition focuses on resources themselves, not on downstream industries or economic outcomes. My strategy was to classify each option by whether it referred to biological resources, crop resources, or specialty agricultural products versus non-agricultural sectors. This was appropriate because three options clearly described vegetation, crops, or region-specific agricultural products, all of which fit the resource concept. The key evidence I used was the distinction between primary agricultural resources and secondary industrial processing or manufacturing activities. I implicitly relied on a category boundary: agricultural resources are things like land, water, plants, animals, and directly usable agricultural products, whereas industries such as chemicals, electrical equipment, and papermaking belong to industrial development. A possible trap was that some listed industries process agricultural outputs, which could make them seem agriculture-related, but “related to agriculture” is broader than “agricultural resources.” I succeeded because I focused on the noun being classified—resources—rather than on whether the activity had any connection to rural production. In similar problems, I should first identify the exact level of classification: resource, product, industry, process, or policy. A transferable rule is: when a definition names a category of underlying inputs, eliminate choices that describe downstream transformation, manufacturing, or sectoral development rather than the inputs themselves.

item.context: Curator: If our museum lends Venus to the Hart Institute for their show this spring, they will lend us their Rembrandt etchings for our print exhibition next fall. Having those etchings will increase attendance to the exhibition and hence increase revenue from our general admission fee. Museum Administrator: But Venus is our biggest attraction. Moreover the Hart' s show will run for twice as long as our exhibition. So on balance the number of patrons may decrease.
item.question: The point of the administrator's response to the curator is to question

choices.label: A
choices.text: whether getting the Rembrandt etchings from the Hart Institute is likely to increase attendance at the print exhibition

choices.label: B
choices.text: whether the number of patrons attracted by the Hart Institute's Rembrandt etchings will be larger than the number of patrons who do not come in the spring because Venus is on loan

choices.label: C
choices.text: whether the Hart Institute's Rembrandt etchings will be appreciated by those patrons of the curator's museum for whom the museum's biggest attraction is Venus

choices.label: D
choices.text: whether, if Venus is lent, the museum's revenue from general admission fees during the print exhibition will exceed its revenue from general admission fees during the Hart Institute's exhibition

response:
Reasoning: The curator argues the etchings will boost fall attendance and revenue. The administrator replies that lending out Venus, the museum’s top draw, for a longer spring period could reduce attendance enough to outweigh that gain. So the issue is which effect is larger overall.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a comparative-impact approach: I identified the curator’s claim as a net-benefit argument and then read the administrator’s reply as challenging that net calculation rather than denying either individual effect. The key factor was the administrator’s emphasis that Venus is the museum’s biggest draw and would be absent for a longer period, which makes the relevant issue a comparison between fall gains and spring losses in attendance. What helped was focusing on the phrase “on balance,” which signals an overall tradeoff. For similar problems, isolate the original conclusion, then ask whether the response attacks a premise, the causal link, or the comparison of competing effects.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the administrator’s argumentative purpose, not for the truth of any factual claim about attendance. That interpretation was correct because the response shifts the debate from “the etchings will help” to “the overall patron effect may still be negative.” My strategy was to compare the curator’s projected gain with the administrator’s proposed loss and identify the precise balance being challenged. That was appropriate because the phrase “So on balance” signals a net-effect comparison across two time periods. I used the key facts that Venus is the museum’s biggest attraction, that its absence could reduce spring attendance, and that the borrowing museum’s show lasts twice as long, potentially magnifying that loss. I also correctly noted that the administrator did not deny the etchings would attract visitors; instead, the administrator questioned whether that increase would outweigh the visitors lost while Venus was away. A possible trap was to focus only on fall revenue, but the administrator’s objection concerned total patrons, not appreciation, revenue at the other museum, or whether the etchings themselves had drawing power. The reasoning succeeded because I tracked which claim was being challenged rather than which claim was merely mentioned. In similar problems, I should isolate the conclusion of the first speaker and ask exactly which link or comparison the second speaker attacks. General rule: when a rebuttal introduces “but,” “however,” or “on balance,” look for a challenge to the net comparison, not necessarily to either component effect individually.

item.context: Manager: I recommend that our company reconsider the decision to completely abandon our allegedly difficult-to-use computer software and replace it companywide with a new software package advertised as more flexible and easier to use. Several other companies in our region officially replaced the software we currently use with the new package, and while their employees can all use the new software, unofficially many continue to use their former software as much as possible.
item.question: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the manager's statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The employees of the manager's company would find that the new software package lacks some of the capabilities of the present software.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The familiarity that employees have with a computer software package is a more important consideration in selecting software than flexibility or initial ease of use.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adopting the new software package would create two classes of employees, those who can use it and those who cannot.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many of the employees in the manager's company would not prefer the new software package to the software currently in use.

response:
Reasoning: The manager cites other companies where employees, though able to use the new software, still unofficially use the old one whenever possible. This most strongly suggests many users prefer the old software to the new one. It does not establish missing capabilities, a general rule about selection criteria, or inability to use the new software.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an inference-by-analogy approach: I looked at what the evidence about other companies most directly suggests about likely employee reactions at the manager’s company. The key clue was that employees elsewhere can use the new software but still choose the old one whenever possible, which supports a preference claim rather than a claim about inability or specific missing features. My success came from separating what is merely plausible from what is actually supported by the statements. For similar problems, infer only the weakest, most directly supported conclusion from the evidence and avoid stronger claims that add unstated causes or universal rules.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a “most strongly supported” inference task, not a flaw or strengthen question. That meant I needed to stay close to what the manager’s statements directly suggest and avoid stronger conclusions than the evidence warrants. My strategy was to identify the key evidence: at other companies, employees can use the new software, yet many still rely on the old software whenever possible. From that pattern, I inferred a comparative preference for the old software among many users, which fits the credited choice.

The reasoning was appropriate because it distinguished between what is observed and what would require extra assumptions. I correctly rejected the idea that the new software necessarily lacks capabilities, since continued use of the old software could reflect habit, efficiency, or preference rather than functional deficiency. I also rejected the broader claim about software-selection criteria because the manager’s evidence does not establish a general principle ranking familiarity over flexibility or ease of use. Likewise, I ruled out the option about two classes of employees because the passage explicitly says employees can use the new software.

What made the reasoning successful was respecting the phrase “most strongly supported” and choosing the answer that restated the evidence at the right level of caution. In similar problems, I should continue translating behavior evidence into the weakest justified attitude claim. General rule: on inference questions, prefer the answer that requires the fewest new assumptions and mirrors the scope and certainty of the stated evidence.

item.context: The maintenance of marriage is inseparable from the mutual trust between husband and wife. Trust is the basis for maintaining a stable and intimate relationship, but trust alone is not enough. They also need to have common interests and hobbies. Two people can spend time together and experience the fun of life. Therefore, trust and common interests and hobbies are the necessary factors for the stability of marriage.
item.question: According to the above words, which of the following can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Couples who trust each other and have common interests and hobbies will last for a long time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A marriage with only common interests is certainly unstable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A happy long-term marriage means that most of the two sides have common interests.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The relationship based on trust and common interests is the most ideal marriage relationship.

response:
Reasoning: The passage says trust and common interests/hobbies are necessary for marital stability. Necessary does not mean sufficient, so A is too strong. If a marriage has only common interests but lacks trust, it lacks a necessary condition for stability, so it is unstable. C and D add unsupported claims.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a necessary-vs.-sufficient condition analysis. The passage states that both trust and shared interests are necessary for marital stability, so I tested each option against that logical structure rather than against general beliefs about marriage. The key factor was that “trust alone is not enough” and the conclusion names both factors as necessary, which means lacking either one rules out stability. For similar problems, translate claims like “necessary,” “not enough,” and “basis” into condition logic, and reject any option that turns a necessary condition into a sufficient one.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the passage as making a claim about necessary conditions for marital stability: mutual trust is required, and shared interests are also required. That interpretation was correct because the key phrase was that these factors are “necessary,” which signals a one-way logical relationship rather than a guarantee. My strategy was to translate the verbal claims into conditional reasoning: if a marriage is stable, then it must include trust and common interests. That was the right strategy for this kind of inference question, because the main trap is confusing necessary conditions with sufficient ones.

The crucial evidence I used was the statement that trust alone is not enough and that both elements are necessary for stability. From that, I correctly rejected any choice claiming that the presence of both factors automatically ensures long duration or ideality, since the passage never said those factors are sufficient. I also noticed that some options introduced stronger ideas like “happy,” “most interests,” or “most ideal,” which were not supported by the text. One assumption that helped was treating “only common interests” as excluding trust; under the passage’s logic, that means a required condition is missing. I should still recognize that this depends on the ordinary meaning of “only,” so checking that language carefully matters.

What made the reasoning successful was preserving the exact direction of implication. In similar problems, I should always formalize claims about necessity before comparing answer choices. A general rule is: when a passage states that X is necessary for Y, you may infer “not X implies not Y,” but you may not infer “X implies Y.”

item.context: Twenty percent of the stores in Morganville' s downtown shopping district will fail within five years because they will be competing directly with the SaveMart discount department store newly opened in East Morganville. The downtown shopping district has lost business at this rate before and has always completely rebounded. Confidence that it will rebound again from the losses it is now about to suffer is ill founded, however, because __.
item.question: Which of the following most logically completes the argument below?

choices.label: A
choices.text: it is conceivable that the downtown shopping district could shrink substantially without collapsing altogether

choices.label: B
choices.text: the stores likely to be put out of business by direct competition from SaveMart are the downtown shopping district's anchor stores, on whose ability to draw shoppers many of the other downtown stores depend

choices.label: C
choices.text: the bus line that has long connected the downtown area of Morganville with East Morganville has a tradition of carrying shoppers who reside in East Morganville into downtown Morganville to shop

choices.label: D
choices.text: when the downtown shopping district has rebounded before, the business premises of a failed business were typically taken over by a business of the same kind as had been there before

response:
Reasoning: Past rebounds after losing 20% do not guarantee recovery now if the stores lost this time are uniquely important. If SaveMart drives out the downtown’s anchor stores, their loss would also hurt many dependent stores, making rebound much less likely than before.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a weaken-the-analogy approach: the argument relied on past rebounds, so I looked for a reason the current losses are importantly different from prior ones. The key factor was whether the 20 percent of stores threatened now play a structurally central role in sustaining the rest of the district. My success came from focusing on dependency within the shopping district rather than just the percentage of stores lost. For similar problems, test past-pattern arguments by asking whether the present case changes the role or importance of the things being lost, not just their number.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a weaken-the-analogy task: the argument said past losses were followed by recovery, and asked for the fact that would show the present case is importantly different. My strategy was to look for an answer choice that broke the inference from “this has happened before” to “it will rebound again.” That was the right strategy because the conclusion turned on whether the current 20 percent loss is relevantly similar to earlier losses. I focused on the causal structure of a shopping district, especially whether some stores matter more than others. The key evidence I used was that losing anchor stores can trigger secondary losses, since other businesses depend on the customer traffic those stores generate. That made the upcoming losses qualitatively different from a random or ordinary 20 percent decline, which is exactly what the argument needed.

I avoided being distracted by choices that merely described shopping patterns or occupancy history without explaining why rebound confidence is “ill founded.” One assumption underlying my reasoning was that not all store failures are equal in systemic impact; in this case that assumption was justified by the wording about dependence. I should still explicitly compare each option against the conclusion’s target: does it explain why past rebounds are not predictive now? The successful part of the reasoning was identifying a structural vulnerability rather than a surface similarity in percentage lost. A transferable rule is: when an argument relies on precedent, test whether the current case differs in a causally important way, not just in incidental details.

item.context: Four teachers of A, B, C and D speculate about the future of their graduating class before the college entrance examination. A said: If Li Ning can get into Peking University, Wang Lu can get into Peking University.  B said: I don't think anyone in this class can get into Peking University.  C said: Whether Wang Lu can get into Peking University, Li Ning couldn't get into Peking University. Dsaid: I think Wang Lu could not get into Peking University, but Li Ning could get into Peking University. The results of the college entrance examination showed that only one of the four teachers was right.
item.question: Based on the above, which of the following options can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Li Ning got into Peking University.

choices.label: B
