choices.text: Li Ning didn't get into Peking University.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wang Lu got into Peking University.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Wang Lu didn't get into Peking University.

response:
Reasoning: Let Li Ning = L, Wang Lu = W.  
A: L→W. B: ¬L∧¬W. C: ¬L. D: ¬W∧L.  
Checking cases, only (L,W)=(T,T) makes only A true, and (T,F) makes only D true. In both valid cases, L is true. So Li Ning definitely got into Peking University.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a case-analysis approach by translating each teacher’s statement into logical form and testing the possible truth values of the two outcomes. The key factor was the constraint that exactly one teacher was correct, which sharply limited which combinations of outcomes could work. The successful step was checking each possible \((L, W)\) scenario against all four statements instead of relying on intuition about implication or negation. For similar problems, systematically formalize each statement and exhaustively test the small set of possible cases under the “exactly one/at least one” condition before drawing a conclusion.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a logic consistency problem: translate each teacher’s statement into propositions about two students, then find which truth assignments make exactly one teacher correct. That interpretation was appropriate because the answer choices asked for what must be inferred, not merely what is possible. My strategy was to formalize the statements as \(L\) and \(W\), reducing ambiguity and making the “only one was right” condition testable. That was a good choice because the teachers’ claims include a conditional, conjunctions, and a statement independent of one variable, which are easy to mishandle in natural language.

A key fact I used correctly was that A’s statement \(L \to W\) is true whenever \(L\) is false, so it cannot be treated as asserting both students succeed. I also correctly recognized C’s statement as simply \(\neg L\), since “whether Wang Lu can get in, Li Ning couldn’t” means Wang Lu’s outcome is irrelevant. The exhaustive case check over the four \((L,W)\) possibilities was appropriate because there are only two binary variables, so completeness is easy to guarantee. One assumption that helped, and was justified, was that “only one teacher was right” means exactly one full statement is true, not “mostly right” or partially right.

The main alternative to consider would have been a direct contradiction analysis instead of a case table, but the case table is safer here because conditionals can interact subtly with negatives. What made the reasoning successful was not algebraic manipulation alone, but checking the global constraint after evaluating every individual statement. For similar problems, I should continue converting each sentence into precise logical form before testing answer choices. A transferable rule is: when a puzzle gives a small number of binary variables and an exact count of true statements, enumerate all truth assignments and enforce the count constraint only after evaluating each statement literally.

item.context: For one academic year all the students at a high school were observed. The aim was to test the hypothesis that studying more increased a student' s chances of earning a higher grade. It turned out that the students who spent the most time studying did not earn grades as high as did many students who studied less. Nonetheless, the researchers concluded that the results of the observation supported the initial hypothesis.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the researchers drew the conclusion described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In each course, the more a student studied, the better his or her grade was in that course.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The students who spent the least time studying tended to be students with no more than average involvement in extracurricular activities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students who spent more time studying understood the course material better than other students did.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The students who spent the most time studying earned higher grades than did some students who studied for less time than the average.

response:
Reasoning: The apparent contradiction can be explained if heavy studiers were taking harder courses. If, within each course, more studying led to a better grade, then studying still increased chances of higher grades even though top studiers overall didn’t have the highest grades.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a reconcile-the-paradox approach: the stimulus gave an overall pattern that seemed to conflict with the hypothesis, so I looked for an answer that could make both statements true at once. The key factor was the difference between aggregate results across all students and the relationship within smaller comparable groups, such as individual courses. My success came from noticing that an overall negative-looking pattern can coexist with a positive causal pattern inside each subgroup. For similar problems, I should explicitly test whether a seeming contradiction disappears when the data are partitioned into relevant comparison groups rather than treated as one undifferentiated whole.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for a fact that would reconcile an apparent conflict: overall, the heaviest studiers did not have the highest grades, yet the researchers still said the evidence supported the idea that more studying helps. That interpretation was correct because the task was not to find a direct restatement of the hypothesis, but an explanation for why the researchers could reasonably maintain it despite the aggregate pattern. My strategy was to look for a distinction between overall comparisons across all students and more controlled comparisons within relevant subgroups. That was appropriate because aggregate outcomes can hide positive relationships that appear when important background conditions are held constant.  

The key relationship I used was that course difficulty could confound the overall comparison: students who study the most may be concentrated in harder classes, depressing their raw grades relative to lighter studiers in easier classes. The strongest support, then, was the option showing that within each course, increased studying was associated with better grades. I correctly rejected choices that were merely consistent with studying more or with some weaker comparative claim, because they did not connect studying time to grade improvement in a way that explained the researchers’ inference. The success came from recognizing a Simpson’s-paradox-style structure: overall trends can differ from within-group trends. In similar problems, I should deliberately ask whether the evidence needs to be evaluated globally or conditional on a relevant subgroup. General rule: when a conclusion survives an apparent counterexample, look for a hidden variable that changes the proper unit of comparison.

item.context: Compared with the complexity of social life, the diet of primates may be better able to predict their brain capacity. Taking into account the evolutionary kinship and body size of each species, the authors found that primates that eat fruits have more brain tissue than primates that eat plant leaves. Although the authors' analysis does not explain why eating fruit brings a larger brain, they believe that this may be due to cognitive needs (related to memorizing fruit location and manual extraction of flesh) and caloric rewards (intake of calorie-rich fruits). Instead of heat-poor plant leaves) combined drive.
item.question: Which of the following matches the meaning of the above passage?

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea elimination approach: I compared each choice against what the passage explicitly claimed versus what it only suggested. The key factor was the cautious language in the passage—“may be better able to predict” and “does not explain why”—which signaled a correlation claim, not a definite causal conclusion or total rejection of other factors. My answer was correct because I matched that hedged wording to the option that preserved uncertainty and scope. For similar questions, I should track qualifiers closely and prefer the choice that restates the passage without strengthening, absolutizing, or oversimplifying it.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the passage as asking for the option that best paraphrased the main claim, not a detail or an exaggerated implication. That interpretation was correct because the stem asked which choice “matches the meaning,” so the task was to identify the broad takeaway of the passage. My strategy was to compare each option against the passage’s hedging and scope: the text said diet may be a better predictor, not that other factors are impossible or disproven. I used key qualifiers such as “may,” “better able to predict,” and “does not explain why,” which helped me reject choices that were absolute or stronger than the evidence. In particular, I noticed that one option overstated the criticism of existing hypotheses, another claimed causal clarity that the passage explicitly denied, and another turned a comparative statement into a total negation. Those eliminations were appropriate because reading-comprehension questions often test whether the reader preserves modality and degree. A hidden strength in my reasoning was that I distinguished correlation/prediction language from definitive causation. I should continue to test answer choices for exaggeration, especially when the passage includes uncertainty markers. A transferable rule is: when matching meaning, prefer the option that preserves the author’s qualifiers, comparison level, and evidential limits, and reject any option that adds certainty, universality, or stronger claims than the text supports.

item.context: In Country X' s last election, the Reform Party beat its main opponent, the Conservative Party, although pollsters, employing in-person interviews shortly before the vote, had projected a Conservative Party victory. Afterwards, the pollsters determined that, unlike Conservative Party supporters, Reform Party supporters were less likely to express their party preference during in-person interviews than they were during telephone interviews. Ttherefore, using only telephone interviews instead would likely result in more accurate projections for the next election.
item.question: Which of the following statements, if true, would most support the argument in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For each person interviewed in telephone polls before the next election, pollsters will be able to reasonably determine the likelihood of that person voting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the next election, pollsters will be able to conduct more in-person interviews than telephone interviews.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The number of voters in Country X's next election will be significantly larger than the number of voters in the last election.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Conservative Party will win the next election.

response:
Reasoning: The argument says telephone interviews would be more accurate because Reform supporters are more willing to reveal preferences by phone. This is strengthened if pollsters can also tell which phone respondents are actually likely to vote; otherwise phone data could still mislead. The other options are irrelevant or weaken support.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a strengthen-the-argument approach: I identified the conclusion that telephone-only polling would be more accurate and looked for a choice that removed an important remaining source of inaccuracy. The key factor was that even if people are more candid by telephone, projections still depend on whether the respondents are likely voters, so information about voter likelihood directly supports accuracy. My success came from testing whether each option affected the gap between more honest responses and better election predictions. For similar questions, first isolate the specific causal gap in the argument, then choose the option that makes that link more reliable rather than one that is merely related to the topic.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a strengthen-the-argument task: the passage offered a causal explanation for why one polling method failed and concluded that switching methods would improve future predictions. That interpretation was correct, because the key issue was not who would win the next election, but whether the proposed methodological change would actually make projections more accurate. My strategy was to identify the argument’s gap: even if telephone interviews elicit more honest partisan preferences from one group, accuracy still depends on whether the respondents represent actual voters. That was an appropriate strategy because strengthen questions are best handled by finding what assumption links the evidence to the conclusion.

The main evidence I used was the contrast between supporters’ willingness to disclose preferences in person versus by phone, and I recognized that turnout prediction is a separate requirement for forecast accuracy. I did not assume that improved disclosure alone guarantees better polling; instead, I looked for a choice that preserved representativeness and predictive usefulness. A shortcut that helped was eliminating choices that discussed election size, mode quantity, or eventual winner, since those do not directly validate the claimed accuracy improvement. I also correctly considered an alternative possibility: telephone interviews could still mislead if they included many nonvoters or otherwise unrepresentative respondents. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on what must be true for the conclusion to follow, rather than on superficially related election facts. In similar problems, I should explicitly test whether the proposed fix addresses all necessary conditions, not just the problem named in the stimulus. A general rule is: when an argument claims that changing a method will improve predictions, support must connect that method not only to better raw data, but also to the actual target outcome being predicted.

item.context: Consumers are not as susceptible as manufacturers think. They know what they need, although what they want may be far from what others think they want.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, can infer the above point of view is not rational?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most people buy products of the same brand year after year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When people shop with their peers, they usually rarely argue with their peers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If there are various brands of goods on the shelves of the store, consumers will be at a loss.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The company that advertises the most also has the largest sales.

response:
Reasoning: The view claims consumers are not easily influenced by manufacturers. If the firm that advertises the most also consistently sells the most, that suggests advertising strongly shapes consumer purchases, undermining the claim that consumers mainly act on their own independent judgment.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a weakening approach: I looked for the option that most directly contradicts the claim that consumers are not very susceptible to manufacturers’ influence. The key factor was the link between manufacturers’ advertising effort and consumer purchasing outcomes, because advertising is exactly the tool manufacturers use to shape wants. My answer was correct because I focused on evidence showing consumer behavior moves with manufacturer persuasion rather than on unrelated habits or peer effects. For similar problems, identify the core causal claim first, then choose the option that most directly shows the supposed “independent” behavior actually tracks the influence being denied.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the prompt as asking for a fact that would make the stated view irrational, not merely less persuasive. The claim in the stimulus is that consumers are relatively resistant to manufacturers’ influence and can distinguish their genuine needs from externally shaped wants. My strategy was to look for an option showing a strong causal link between manufacturer-controlled persuasion and consumer purchasing behavior. That was appropriate because the statement under attack is specifically about susceptibility to manufacturers, so the best counterevidence would connect manufacturer actions to market outcomes.

The key evidence I used was that advertising is a manufacturer-driven tool designed to influence consumers. If the firms that advertise most reliably achieve the highest sales, that pattern suggests consumer choices are significantly shaped by manufacturer messaging rather than by independent recognition of need. I correctly treated that as the most direct challenge to the passage’s central assumption. I also implicitly ruled out weaker alternatives: brand loyalty could reflect satisfaction or habit, peer conformity concerns influence from friends rather than manufacturers, and confusion from too many brands shows difficulty choosing rather than susceptibility to persuasion. One helpful assumption I made was that higher advertising and higher sales are meaningfully connected, not just coincidental. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the exact source of influence named in the claim. In similar problems, I should identify the claim’s core causal or psychological commitment and prefer answer choices that directly negate that commitment. General rule: when evaluating a statement about resistance to influence, the strongest underminer is evidence that the alleged influencer systematically changes behavior.

item.context: Over the last few decades, public outcries against pollution have brought about stricter regulations of emissions. The cities that had the most polluted air 30 years ago now have greatly improved air quality. This would not have happened without these stricter regulations.
item.question: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the statements above?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most of the public outcries against pollution came from people in the cities that had the most polluted air.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the city with the worst air pollution today, the air quality is better than it was 30 years ago.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The most polluted cities today are not the cities that were the most polluted 30 years ago.

response:
Reasoning: The passage says public outcries brought about stricter emissions regulations, and that the improved air quality in the formerly most polluted cities would not have happened without those regulations. So the outcries indirectly led to the improvement. The other choices add unsupported claims.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a causal-chain inference: public outcries led to stricter regulations, and those regulations were necessary for the later air-quality improvement, so the outcries indirectly contributed to that improvement. The key factor was linking the two stated causal steps without adding any new assumptions about which cities protested most or how cities rank today. My answer was correct because I distinguished an inference supported by the passage’s explicit causal structure from choices that required extra, unstated comparisons. For similar problems, map each stated cause-and-effect link and infer only what follows from combining those links, while rejecting options that introduce new groups, rankings, or quantities.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the statement that is logically supported by linking the causal claims in the stimulus, not for a merely plausible or strongest-sounding option. That interpretation was correct because the passage gave a causal chain: public outcries led to stricter regulations, and those regulations were necessary for the later improvement in air quality in the previously most polluted cities. My strategy was to combine those two stated relationships into an indirect causal inference, which is appropriate when a stimulus explicitly connects one event to another through an intermediate step. The key evidence I used was the phrase that the improvement “would not have happened without these stricter regulations,” which establishes the regulations as necessary to the improvement, and the earlier statement that public outcries brought about those regulations. I did not assume that outcries alone were sufficient; I only inferred that they played a causal role through the regulations. That distinction mattered, because unsupported strengthening of causation is a common trap in inference questions. I also correctly rejected alternatives that introduced new information about where the outcries came from, how today’s worst city compares, or whether the set of most polluted cities changed. Those options required comparisons or distributions the stimulus never stated. The reasoning succeeded because I tracked only explicit causal links and avoided importing unstated quantitative or ranking claims. In similar problems, I should continue separating what is directly supported from what is merely compatible with the passage. A transferable rule is: when a stimulus gives A caused B and B was required for C, you may infer that A contributed to C through B, but you may not infer additional facts about rankings, identities, or sufficiency unless they are explicitly provided.

item.context: The crime of producing and selling fake and inferior products refers to the act of producers or sellers intentionally adulterating, adulterating, passing off inferior products as good ones, passing off fake products as genuine ones or passing off substandard products as qualified ones with a sales amount of more than 50,000 yuan.

reflections.simple: I used a statutory-element matching approach: I broke the offense into required components—intentional adulteration or passing off, sale of the product, and a sales amount exceeding 50,000 yuan—and checked each option against those elements. reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the option that fits a very specific statutory definition, not just any dishonest sale. That interpretation was correct because the definition included both conduct elements—adulterating, passing off fake as genuine, or substandard as qualified—and a quantitative threshold of sales amount exceeding 50,000 yuan. My strategy was to treat the problem as an element-matching exercise: check each option against the required act and then against the monetary threshold. That was appropriate because criminal-law multiple choice questions often hinge on whether all statutory elements are satisfied, not whether the conduct seems generally wrongful.

The key evidence I used was the explicit sales threshold and the type of misconduct described in each option. I correctly recognized that one option involved adulteration plus a calculable contract amount above the threshold, while another involved only a much smaller total sale, and the remaining options pointed toward different offenses. An assumption that helped, and was justified here, was that “sales amount” could be inferred from the stated contract price multiplied by quantity. I also correctly resisted the shortcut of choosing based only on seriousness of harm, since the construction scenario involved poor materials but not necessarily this specific product-sale offense.

The successful part of my reasoning was distinguishing adjacent crimes such as fraud or construction-quality offenses from the named offense. In similar problems, I should continue to identify every statutory element, test each option systematically, and eliminate choices that satisfy only part of the definition. A general rule is: when a legal definition contains both conduct elements and numerical thresholds, require an option to satisfy every element explicitly before selecting it.

item.context: Due to the unique chemical characteristics of silk, it is difficult for embroidery to be preserved for a long time in the humid climate of Sichuan. Therefore, few embroidery products have been found in the archaeological research in Sichuan, so it is impossible to trace the origin of Shu embroidery by archaeological methods. However, Shu embroidery still has its glory in other forms. In 1986, a bronze statue about 4,800 years ago was unearthed at the Sanxingdui Site in Chengdu. The statue was dressed in a dragon costume with complicated dragon, beast and variant cloud and thunder patterns. With the level of textile technology at that time, these decorative patterns could not have been woven by a textile machine. Since the pattern of the embroidery is consistent with the embroidery residue of the Western Zhou Dynasty unearthed in Baoji, Shaanxi province in 1974, it is most likely that the embroidery was made with the lock embroidery method, which traces the history of Shu embroidery back to the Sanxingdui civilization in ancient Shu, which was contemporized with the Xia Civilization in the Central Plains.
item.question: Which of the following statements is true?

reflections.simple:
I used an inference-elimination approach: I matched each option against what the passage explicitly states and what it strongly implies. The key factor was the chain of evidence that the bronze statue wore a dragon costume with patterns unlikely to be woven, so they were most likely embroidered using lock embroidery. That made the statement about the bronze figure probably wearing embroidered ceremonial clothes the best-supported choice. 

What helped was distinguishing between “supported by the passage” and “goes beyond the passage,” which ruled out claims about origin, typical use, or limits of dating methods. For similar problems, I should keep tracing each answer choice back to a specific textual premise and reject any option that adds a new causal or historical claim not directly grounded in the passage.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which option is directly supported by the passage, not which one is historically plausible on its own. That framing was important because the passage contained several speculative-looking claims, but only one choice matched the author’s inference chain. My strategy was to trace the argument step by step: preservation limits archaeology in Sichuan, a bronze figure from Sanxingdui shows complex clothing patterns, those patterns were unlikely to be woven, and comparison with later embroidery residue suggests an embroidered technique. From there, I looked for the option that stayed closest to that evidence rather than extending it into a broader claim.

The key evidence I used successfully was the combination of “most likely” and the description of the figure’s dragon costume, which supports a probabilistic conclusion about what the figure was wearing. I also correctly rejected choices that reversed causation or made unsupported origin claims. One useful constraint was distinguishing between “lock embroidery” as a method and “Shu embroidery” as a regional tradition; the passage links them but does not establish the method’s origin. Another successful move was noticing that one option overgeneralized from a single artifact to “early period” usage overall, which the passage does not justify. My reasoning worked because I prioritized entailment over background knowledge. In similar problems, I should keep separating direct textual support from tempting historical extrapolation. A transferable rule is: in reading-comprehension inference questions, prefer the choice that preserves the passage’s level of certainty, scope, and direction of inference.

item.context: Stem cells are primordial cells with the potential of self-renewal and multi-directional differentiation, and they are also the origin cells that form various tissues and organs. When mature somatic cells die of aging or injury, stem cells produce their substitutes at any time to maintain a variety of cell renewal and tissue repair. Unfortunately, the ability of stem cell populations to proliferate and differentiate severely decreases with age. From this point of view, by intervening and restoring the vitality of stem cells in some way, it is expected to repair tissue function and achieve the effect of delaying aging.
item.question: Which of the following options is intended to describe this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The realization of the beautiful long-cherished wish of youth and immortality depends on the application of stem cell technology.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rejuvenated stem cells can replace all kinds of cells that die as a result of aging or injury.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stem cell technology will help to improve human health and quality of life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reason why the human body grows old is that senescent cells cannot be replaced by stem cells in time.

response:
Reasoning: The passage explains stem cells’ role in tissue renewal and suggests restoring stem cell vitality may repair function and delay aging. It broadly points to the health benefits of stem cell technology, not immortality, universal replacement, or the sole cause of aging.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea elimination approach: first identify the passage’s overall claim, then reject choices that were too absolute, too narrow, or more extreme than the text. The key clue was the cautious wording that restoring stem cell vitality is “expected” to repair tissue function and delay aging, which supports a broad benefit claim rather than certainty about immortality, total cell replacement, or a single cause of aging. My success came from matching the answer’s scope and tone to the passage. For similar problems, first paraphrase the author’s central claim in neutral terms, then choose the option that preserves that level of generality without adding stronger conclusions.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the passage as asking for the best overall summary or intended main idea, not a literal detail or a speculative extreme claim. That interpretation was correct because the passage moves from explaining what stem cells do, to noting age-related decline, to suggesting intervention as a way to repair tissue function and delay aging. My strategy was to identify the author’s central claim and then compare each option for scope and tone. This was appropriate because main-idea questions are usually solved by matching the option that preserves the passage’s level of certainty and generality.

The key evidence I used was that the passage says restoring stem cell vitality is “expected” to repair function and delay aging, which supports a beneficial medical application but not a guaranteed dramatic outcome. I also noticed that the passage discussed maintaining renewal and repair, which supports broad health improvement rather than a total explanation of aging. An important constraint was avoiding answer choices that overstate the text: immortality, replacement of all cell types, or a single-cause theory of aging. I correctly rejected those because they go beyond what the passage explicitly supports. One assumption I made, appropriately, was that “intended to describe this passage” calls for the most balanced paraphrase rather than the most eye-catching claim.

The reasoning succeeded because I tracked modality carefully: “expected to” is weaker than certainty. In similar problems, I should continue testing each option for exaggeration, exclusivity, or causal claims stronger than the passage. A transferable rule is: for main-idea questions, choose the option that preserves both the passage’s scope and degree of certainty, and eliminate choices that introduce stronger claims, broader universality, or narrower causation than the text provides.

item.context: Most people believe that the thinking of scientists is based on strict logical reasoning, rather than by analogy, intuition, epiphany and other visual means of thinking. But research shows that Nobel Prize winners use these visual thinking methods more than ordinary scientists, so visual thinking methods can help to achieve major scientific breakthroughs
item.question: Which of the following assumptions is the conclusion based on?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Methodical, step-by-step reasoning method is essential for general scientific research.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nobel Prize winners have the ability to think creatively through analogy, intuition, and epiphany.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nobel Prize winners have made major scientific breakthroughs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nobel Prize winners are smarter and harder-working than the general scientists.

response:
Reasoning: The argument infers that because Nobel Prize winners use visual thinking more often, such thinking helps produce major breakthroughs. This requires assuming Nobel Prize winners are people who have in fact achieved major scientific breakthroughs. Without that link, the comparison would not support the conclusion.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-bridge approach: I identified the evidence about Nobel Prize winners’ thinking style and the conclusion about achieving major scientific breakthroughs, then looked for the missing link connecting those two. The key factor was that the argument only works if the group being cited as evidence is actually representative of people who have achieved such breakthroughs. My success came from testing what would happen if that link were missing; without it, the evidence would not support the conclusion. For similar questions, explicitly map the gap between premise and conclusion and choose the option that must be true for the evidence to be relevant.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as an assumption problem asking for a necessary unstated link between the evidence and the conclusion. The argument’s structure was: Nobel Prize winners use visual thinking more than ordinary scientists; therefore, visual thinking can help produce major scientific breakthroughs. My strategy was to identify the gap between the group being described in the evidence and the outcome claimed in the conclusion. That was appropriate because assumption questions usually hinge on whether the evidence actually connects to the claimed result.

The key fact I used was that the conclusion is about achieving major breakthroughs, while the premise is specifically about Nobel Prize winners’ thinking styles. For the premise to support the conclusion, the argument must treat Nobel Prize winners as examples of people who have achieved such breakthroughs. Without that bridge, the evidence would only show a difference in thinking style between two groups, not anything about breakthrough-level success. I did not rely on whether visual thinking is the only cause, only on whether the example group is relevant to the outcome. That was an important restraint, since assumption questions require necessity, not a stronger causal claim than the argument needs.

I also correctly rejected distractions about creativity, intelligence, or general scientific method because those do not connect the premises to the conclusion in a necessary way. The success came from mapping premise terms to conclusion terms and checking for an omitted identity link. In similar problems, I should explicitly test each choice by asking: if this were false, would the argument lose its support? A general rule is: when an argument generalizes from a distinguished subgroup to a valued outcome, check whether it assumes that the subgroup actually possesses that outcome.

item.context: In April of this year, our country suffered the most powerful sandstorm disaster in recent years, with a loss of 6.5 billion U.S. dollars. The occurrence of sandstorm generally requires three conditions which are abundant sand and dust sources, strong winds and unstable atmospheric structure, namely, on sandy ground and bare ground without vegetation, the air is easily heated to blow up the dust. This shows that the grassland degradation and desertification caused by climate drought will inevitably cause a natural disaster such as sandstorms.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, can best refute the above statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: On the opposite side of Hulun Buir's degradation field, the grass height of Mongolian grassland is about 1 meter, and there are tens of thousands of yellow sheep moving there.

choices.label: B
choices.text: On the 10-kilometer-wide border between China and Mongolia, the grass still retains its previous height, but it is an uninhabited area.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Desertified land formed by overgrazing accounted for 29.4%.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Take the method of a large-scale recuperation to alleviate the pressure of human production on the ecological environment.

response:
Reasoning: The claim says climate drought inevitably causes grassland degradation/desertification, leading to sandstorms. Option B shows that in the same border area under similar natural conditions, uninhabited land still keeps tall grass. This indicates human activity, not drought alone, is key, so the “inevitably” claim is undermined.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a causal-refutation approach, looking for an option that would show the stated cause was not sufficient to produce the claimed effect. The key factor I focused on was the argument’s word “inevitably,” so I searched for a counterexample where similar drought-related natural conditions existed but degradation did not. My mistake was choosing a case that introduced a different variable—lack of human habitation—rather than a cleaner comparison showing grassland remained healthy even with grazing pressure, which more directly weakens the claim that climate drought necessarily leads to degradation and sandstorms. For similar problems, I should prefer the option that holds rival factors as constant and provides the strongest direct counterexample to the claimed necessity.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument as claiming a necessary causal chain: climate drought causes grassland degradation and desertification, and that in turn will inevitably produce sandstorms. My strategy was to attack the causal claim by finding evidence that separated human activity from natural conditions, which is generally appropriate for refuting an “inevitably caused by X” statement. However, I focused too narrowly on the contrast between inhabited and uninhabited land and treated that as decisive evidence against drought. The problem is that this only suggested a possible role for human activity; it did not directly show that drought-induced degradation is not sufficient or not inevitable. I missed that the strongest refutation would compare areas under broadly similar regional climate conditions while showing different outcomes despite a factor the argument would treat as aggravating. In other words, I should have looked for evidence that weakens the supposed link between desertification pressure and the predicted disaster, not merely evidence that another factor may matter.

My key mistaken assumption was that introducing an alternative cause automatically refutes a claim of inevitability. It does not, unless it shows the stated cause is not necessary or not sufficient. I also undervalued comparative evidence across adjacent regions, which is often stronger because it controls for background conditions better than a vague “uninhabited” description. A better reasoning method is to test each option against the exact logical target: necessity, sufficiency, or exclusivity. The transferable rule is: when an argument says “X will inevitably cause Y,” the best rebuttal is evidence of X without Y, or close comparison showing the claimed causal pathway fails under similar conditions.

item.context: There are red, blue, yellow, white and purple leather balls in five boxes. A, B, C, D, E. The five guessed the color of the ball in the box. A: the second box is purple and the third box is yellow. B: the second box is blue and the fourth box is red. C: the first box is red and the fifth box is white. D: The third box is blue and the fourth box is white. E: the second box is yellow and the fifth box is purple. When they were finished, they opened the box and found that each of them had only one correct guess.
item.question: Which of the following can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ball in the first box is blue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ball in the third box is not yellow.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ball in the fourth box is white.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ball in the fifth box is red.

response:
Reasoning: Since each person has exactly one correct guess, test box 2. If box 2 were purple or yellow, contradictions arise. So box 2 = blue. Then A forces box 3 = yellow, E forces box 5 = purple, D forces box 4 = white, and C forces box 1 = red. Thus only option C must be true.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a constraint-satisfaction approach: treating each person’s two statements as a pair with exactly one true statement, then checking shared boxes to see which color assignments were possible without violating that rule. The key factor was the overlap on the second box, because A, B, and E all make different claims about box 2, and resolving that sharply limited the rest of the arrangement. The successful step was propagating the “one true per person” condition after fixing a viable value, which forced consistent values in other boxes. For similar problems, convert each speaker’s claim into an exact-true-count constraint and use the most heavily cross-linked variable first to drive eliminations.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a constraint-satisfaction problem: each person made two color claims, and for each person exactly one of those two claims had to be true. My strategy was to treat each pair as an exclusive-or condition and use the fact that the five box colors are all distinct, which was appropriate for this kind of puzzle. The strongest move in my reasoning was to focus on the repeatedly mentioned positions, especially the second box, because several guesses overlapped there and that creates leverage. I used contradiction effectively: checking whether the second box could be purple or yellow led to conflicts with the “exactly one correct per person” condition and the one-color-per-box structure. After narrowing box 2, I propagated consequences through the remaining guesses, which is the right systematic approach for interconnected constraints. 

What made the reasoning successful was not just testing possibilities, but updating all speakers’ statements after each tentative placement rather than evaluating clues in isolation. A potential risk in my approach was assuming too quickly that a contradiction at one box assignment completely determined the rest; this only works if every downstream implication is checked against all clues. I also could have explicitly considered whether more than one full arrangement satisfied the clues, because the task asks what can be inferred, not necessarily for the complete arrangement. In similar problems, I should separate “deduced facts that must hold in every valid arrangement” from “one arrangement that happens to work.” A general transferable rule is: when each agent makes two statements and exactly one is true, encode each pair as an XOR constraint and propagate consequences globally, always checking uniqueness and consistency across all variables.

item.context: In early 1990, Queenston instituted a tax increase that gave its school system a larger operating budget. The school system used the larger budget to increase the total number of teachers in the system by 30 percent between 1990 and 1993. Nevertheless, there was no change in the average number of students per teacher between 1990 and 1993.
item.question: If the statements above are true, then on the basis of them which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The total number of students enrolled in Queenston's school system increased between 1990 and 1993.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No classes in Queenston's school system experienced an increase in enrollment between 1990 and 1993.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The quality of education in Queenston's school system improved between 1990 and 1993.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most teachers who worked for Queenston's school system in 1990 were still working for the system in 1993.

response:
Reasoning: If the average number of students per teacher stayed the same while the total number of teachers increased by 30%, then the total number of students must also have increased proportionally. The other choices are not logically required by the facts given.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a quantitative invariance approach: I focused on the relationship between total students, total teachers, and the average students per teacher. The key factor was that the average stayed unchanged while the number of teachers rose by 30%, which means total enrollment had to rise in the same proportion for the ratio to remain constant. My success came from translating the verbal statement into a ratio rather than getting distracted by unsupported claims about class sizes, quality, or staff retention. For similar problems, convert “average stayed the same” statements into an equation and test which option is forced by that fixed ratio.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a “must be true” inference problem, so the task was to identify what follows necessarily from the numerical relationship given, not what is merely plausible. My strategy was to translate the verbal statements into a proportional relationship: if the number of teachers rises while the average number of students per teacher stays unchanged, then total enrollment must move in the same direction. That was the right approach because the key fact is that total students equals teachers multiplied by students-per-teacher. I used the crucial constraint that the average stayed constant, which means the system did not offset the teacher increase by lowering class size overall. From that, an increase in the teacher count directly implies an increase in total students.

I also correctly rejected the other options because they introduced claims about individual classes, educational quality, or teacher retention, none of which is forced by the data. One assumption built into my reasoning was that “average number of students per teacher” refers to the system-wide ratio, and that is justified by the wording. A useful alternative I could have considered, even though unnecessary here, is testing the claim with simple numbers to verify the proportional logic. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on a definitional relationship rather than on causal speculation about budgets or schools. For similar problems, I should continue converting descriptive statements into equations or ratios before evaluating answer choices. General rule: when a ratio remains constant and one component increases, the corresponding total linked by multiplication must increase proportionally.

item.context: Information poverty alleviation: refers to the government as a social group to solve the economic and cultural poverty caused by information occlusion by means of information technology
item.question: Which of the following is Information poverty alleviation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A logistics company teamed up with an Internet giant to recruit a group of couriers from poor households in remote mountainous areas. After professional training, the couriers were hired to help them on the road to poverty alleviation and prosperity

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mobile phone manufacturer targeted at the rural market launched a low-cost, easy to operate, large screen, long battery life fashionable smart phone, villagers have replaced the original old mobile phone

choices.label: C
choices.text: A key middle school in the provincial capital has set up an online classroom, which is live-streamed remotely to a middle school in a poor county, so that teachers and students in the two places can share high-quality teaching resources. In recent years, the number of key universities in this county increased significantly

choices.label: D
choices.text: Returning home after graduation, Xiao Zhou opened an online shop with several classmates to sell home-grown dates on the Internet. The sales volume is gradually increasing, and the day is more and more prosperous

response:
Reasoning: Information poverty alleviation means using information technology to reduce poverty caused by lack of access to information/resources, especially in education or culture. Only C uses online live teaching to connect a poor county with high-quality educational resources, clearly fitting this definition.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I broke the concept into core elements—government-led or public-interest action, use of information technology, and reduction of poverty caused by information blockage, especially educational or cultural disadvantage. The key factor was that one option directly used remote online teaching to deliver high-quality information resources to a poor area and showed a poverty-alleviation outcome. My success came from filtering out options that involved ordinary employment, commercial product sales, or private e-commerce rather than alleviating information deprivation itself. For similar problems, extract every necessary condition from the definition and eliminate any choice that satisfies only the outcome of “poverty reduction” without matching the specific mechanism and actor.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for an example that matches a definition, so the key task was to map each option against the required elements of that definition. My strategy was to extract the core conditions: a government or socially oriented intervention, the use of information technology, and the alleviation of poverty specifically caused by information blockage or unequal access to knowledge. That strategy was appropriate because this is a definitional classification problem, not a general “which helps the poor” question. I focused on the fact that option C uses remote online classrooms to transmit educational resources from a stronger school to a poorer county, which directly addresses information and cultural disadvantage through technology. I also used the result described in the option—the increase in university admissions—as evidence that the intervention reduced a form of poverty linked to unequal access to educational information and resources.  

A useful assumption I made was that “government as a social group” need not mean only a formal government agency, but can include socially organized public-interest institutional action. I correctly rejected options centered on employment, consumer products, or private e-commerce because those reduce poverty mainly through jobs, market access, or product replacement rather than by overcoming information occlusion itself. One alternative I should still consciously test in similar problems is whether an option merely uses the Internet superficially versus using it as the mechanism that removes informational deprivation. The reasoning succeeded because I matched all parts of the definition rather than seizing on any option that involved technology and poverty. In similar problems, I should explicitly check every definitional component one by one and eliminate choices that satisfy only some of them. A transferable rule is: when classifying by definition, identify the necessary conditions, then accept only the option whose causal mechanism matches those conditions, not just its general positive outcome.

item.context: Food additives are chemically synthesized or natural substances added to food to improve the quality and color, aroma, taste, shape, and functions of antiseptic, freshness and processing technology. Food additives, as long as they are used in a reasonable way and in a reasonable dose, will not cause food safety issues.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings is a food additive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pigment, leavening agent, protein essence, preservative

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sweetener, moisture, emulsifier, sodium sulfide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monosodium glutamate, this sugar alcohol, vitamins, minerals

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coloring agent, poppy husk, flour treatment agent

response:
Reasoning: Food additives include sweeteners, flavor enhancers, nutrient fortifiers, colorants, preservatives, etc. Options B and D contain clearly inappropriate/illegal substances (“sodium sulfide,” “poppy husk”). A includes “protein essence,” which is not a standard legal food additive. C lists recognized additive types.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an elimination approach based on whether each listed substance seemed like a standard, legal food additive in practice. The key factor that drove my choice was my assumption that obviously suspicious items should disqualify an option, so I rejected any choice containing a substance I viewed as illegal or nonstandard. My error was relying on outside knowledge and regulatory judgment instead of matching the option to the definition and the test’s categorization scheme. For similar problems, I should evaluate choices by the definition and internal classification used in the question first, and avoid eliminating an option solely because one item seems unusual in real-world use.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the set made up entirely of standard, legally recognized examples of food additives, but the definition in the stem was broader than that. My strategy was elimination by spotting items that sounded “abnormal” or “illegal,” then choosing the option that looked most like a textbook list. That strategy was only partly appropriate because it relied too much on outside familiarity with regulatory categories and not enough on the wording actually provided. I used relevant facts such as sweeteners, emulsifiers, preservatives, and flavor enhancers being common additive classes, but I missed the key constraint that the definition focused on substances added to improve quality, preservation, processing, color, aroma, or taste. I also assumed that if one term in an option looked nonstandard, the whole option should be rejected, which was an unjustified shortcut. Another missed consideration was that some terms may be awkward translations or unconventional labels rather than true disqualifiers. I should have compared each option against the functional definition rather than against my mental list of familiar examples. The main cause of error was substituting “what is commonly regulated or familiar” for “what fits the stated definition.” In similar problems, I should first extract the exact necessary conditions from the prompt and test each item only against those conditions. A transferable rule is: when a definition question provides its own criteria, prioritize those criteria over external expectations about typicality, legality, or terminology.

item.context: One of the characteristics of spotted geese in flight is that they often fly in a certain formation, and the birds behind usually fly behind the side of the previous bird, so they have a common human formation. Some researchers believe that this formation can reduce air resistance and reduce flight energy consumption. However, opponents believe that if it is to reduce resistance, birds should choose a straight line formation, because one flight after another can minimize the air resistance that followers need to overcome.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, can best question the conclusion of the opponent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the flight, the leading geese will change positions with their rear companions from time to time, otherwise they will easily be exhausted

choices.label: B
choices.text: When flying, the spotted geese deviate from their companions in front of them, which can not minimize the air resistance, but can greatly reduce the physical energy consumption required for ascent

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spotted geese will have the need to determine the direction when flying, so they will not always fly in the shape of human

choices.label: D
choices.text: In speed skating competitions, athletes often advance in the shape of people. One athlete is in the front, followed by three others, and the last three players benefit from reduced resistance

response:
Reasoning: Opponents claim a straight line best reduces resistance. To weaken that, we need evidence the observed offset “human/V” formation provides another aerodynamic benefit. B says flying slightly off to the side may not minimize drag, but greatly reduces the energy needed for lift/ascent, undermining the opponent’s conclusion.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a weaken-the-argument approach: I identified the opponent’s core claim that minimizing air resistance is the only relevant criterion, then looked for an option showing the observed formation has a different energy-saving advantage. The key factor was the distinction between reducing drag and reducing total flight energy; those are related but not identical. My success came from spotting that an alternative aerodynamic benefit can undermine a “should choose straight line” conclusion even if straight-line drafting lowers resistance more. For similar problems, test whether the argument assumes a single optimization criterion, and look for choices introducing another relevant performance factor that changes what “best” means.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the option that most effectively weakens the opponents’ inference that, if the purpose were energy saving through reduced resistance, geese should fly in a straight line rather than in an offset formation. That interpretation was correct because the task was not to explain why geese fly as they do in general, but to challenge a specific conclusion about what formation would be optimal. My strategy was to identify the opponents’ core assumption: they equated total flight efficiency with only one factor, namely minimizing the drag on following birds. That was an appropriate weakening strategy, because the best rebuttal would show that flight efficiency can depend on something other than pure rearward drag reduction.

The key evidence I used was that an offset position might fail to minimize air resistance yet still reduce overall physical energy use by helping with lift or ascent. This directly attacks the hidden premise that the lowest-resistance arrangement must also be the lowest-energy arrangement. I did not rely on irrelevant facts such as position rotation or directional needs, because those explain behavior without undermining the opponents’ aerodynamic claim. I also recognized that an analogy like speed skating is weaker unless it directly addresses the same mechanism and formation geometry. The reasoning succeeded because it targeted the causal link in the argument, not just the surface behavior. In similar problems, I should keep isolating the exact premise that connects evidence to conclusion and look for answer choices that break that connection. A general rule is: when an argument claims one arrangement is best because it optimizes a single variable, weaken it by showing that the real objective depends on additional variables the argument ignored.

item.context: Theories generated by scientific research were used to develop several products that, although useful, damage the environment severely. The scientists who conducted the research, however, should not be held responsible for that damage, since they merely generated the theories and could neither foresee nor restrict the kinds of products that might be designed using those theories.
item.question: Which one of the following principles, if established, justifies the conclusion above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Individuals should be held responsible for the foreseeable undesirable consequences of the activities that they perform and receive credit for the foreseeable desirable consequences of those activities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Individuals who perform an activity should not be held responsible for any unforeseen undesirable consequences that arise from the use to which others put the results of that activity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Individuals are justified in performing an activity that has both desirable and undesirable foreseeable consequences only if they alone bear its undesirable consequences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Individuals who develop something that has desirable characteristics should not be held responsible for any undesirable characteristics that the thing has if improperly used.

response:
Reasoning: The argument says scientists only produced theories, and the harmful products were later uses by others that the scientists could not foresee or control. So the needed principle is that people are not responsible for unforeseen harmful consequences resulting from others’ use of their work.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a match-the-principle approach: I identified the conclusion and then looked for the answer choice that supplied a general rule connecting the premises to that conclusion. The key factor was the argument’s emphasis on two conditions at once: the harmful consequences were unforeseeable and they resulted from other people’s later use of the scientists’ work. My success came from tracking both constraints rather than focusing only on lack of control or only on usefulness. For similar questions, isolate the exact premise pair that drives the conclusion and choose the principle that explicitly includes all of those conditions, not just a broadly similar idea.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task correctly as a principle-justify question: the goal was not to find a merely compatible statement, but a rule that, if true, would make the conclusion follow. My strategy was to isolate the argument’s key premises: the scientists generated theories, others later used those theories to create damaging products, and the scientists could neither foresee nor control those uses. From there, I looked for an answer choice that linked lack of foreseeability and third-party use to absence of responsibility. That was the right strategy because principle questions usually hinge on matching the argument’s exact causal and moral structure, not on broad thematic similarity.

The crucial evidence I used was the pair of constraints in the stimulus: the consequences were not foreseeable, and the harmful outcomes arose through products designed by others. I did not rely on irrelevant details such as whether the research itself was beneficial or whether the products were useful, which helped keep the focus on responsibility. A possible trap would have been choosing a principle about all undesirable consequences of one’s actions, but the conclusion required the narrower condition involving others’ later use. Another trap would have been an answer about “improper use,” since the stimulus never says the products were misused. The reasoning succeeded because I matched both necessary elements of the argument rather than only one. In similar problems, I should continue translating the stimulus into a conditional rule before comparing choices. General rule: on justify-the-conclusion questions, select the principle that explicitly connects each stated premise to the conclusion with no extra shift in scope, actor, or type of consequence.

item.context: A middle school held two kinds of lectures on literature and science, and made statistics on the students' participation in the lectures. It was found that among the first grade students, some students participated in all literature lectures and some students participated in all science lectures.
item.question: If the above statement is true, which of the followings must be true??

choices.label: A
choices.text: First graders attended all the lectures

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each first grader attended at least one lecture

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every lecture was attended by first graders

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some first graders did not attend any lectures

response:
Reasoning: Since some first graders attended all literature lectures, every literature lecture had first-grade attendees. Since some first graders attended all science lectures, every science lecture also had first-grade attendees. Thus every lecture was attended by first graders. The other choices are not guaranteed.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a direct quantifier-based approach, separating the statement into two groups: first graders who attended all literature lectures and first graders who attended all science lectures. The key clue was the phrase “among the first grade students,” which I treated as identifying participants in each category, but I failed to consider the combined coverage implied by the two “some students” groups. My mistake was assuming the conclusion had to be about who attended each individual lecture, instead of noticing that together these first graders account for attendance at every lecture type. For similar problems, explicitly test whether separate existence claims over complementary categories jointly imply total coverage.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the statement as asserting two existential facts: there existed first graders who attended every literature lecture, and there existed first graders who attended every science lecture. From that, I concluded only that each lecture had at least one first-grade attendee, which led me to choose the option about every lecture being attended by first graders. That strategy was logically tidy, but it failed because I did not align my reading of the answer choices with the intended meaning of the prompt’s wording. In particular, I treated “First graders attended all the lectures” as if it meant “every first grader attended every lecture,” when it more naturally means “first graders, as a group, were present at all lectures.” Once that collective reading is used, the premises directly support that statement.

The key evidence I used was not wrong; I simply mapped it to the wrong option because of an overly strict interpretation of plural noun phrases. I also ignored the possibility that the test was distinguishing collective attendance from universal attendance. A better approach would be to test each option against both the logical structure and the ordinary-language reading intended in standardized verbal questions. The specific cause of error was quantifier confusion: I converted a collective claim into a universal one. In similar problems, I should explicitly distinguish “some members cover all events,” “all members cover all events,” and “the group covers all events.” General rule: when plural subjects appear in answer choices, check whether they are collective or distributive before applying formal logic.

item.context: Company manager: when we recruit talents, the most important thing is the comprehensive quality and ability, not the score. In talent recruitment, it is not uncommon for people with high scores and low abilities. Obviously, we do not want to recruit such talents. As can be seen from your report card, your academic score is very high, so we have some doubts about your ability and comprehensive quality.
item.question: Which of the following is most similar to the way managers draw conclusions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Company managers are not all smart people. Chen Ran is not a company manager, so Chen Ran may be smart people

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cats love to eat fish. No cat has myopia, so eating fish can prevent myopia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Health and happiness are the most important in one's life. Fame and wealth are floating clouds. Zhang Li receives both fame and wealth, so maybe Zhang Li is not happy

choices.label: D
choices.text: All glittering objects are not gold. The archaeological team dug up glittering objects, so what the archaeological team dug up may not be gold

response:
Reasoning: The manager reasons: “Some people with a certain visible trait may lack the desired essence; you have that trait, so you may lack the essence.” This matches “Not all glittering things are gold; this thing glitters, so it may not be gold.”
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an analogy-based structure match: I ignored the topic and compared the logical form of the manager’s argument to each option. The key factor was the pattern “a surface indicator does not reliably guarantee the underlying quality; this case has the indicator; therefore the underlying quality is doubtful or may be absent.” My success came from focusing on the weak inference from an observable trait to a possible lack of essence, rather than on the specific content about hiring or grades. For similar problems, first rewrite the argument in abstract form and choose the option with the same conditional/probabilistic reasoning pattern.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as an analogy task about matching the manager’s inference pattern, not about whether the manager’s conclusion was reasonable in real life. That interpretation was correct, because the key was the logical form: identifying a surface indicator, noting that some cases with that indicator lack the desired property, and then inferring that a particular case with the indicator may also lack that property. My strategy was to abstract the argument into a schema rather than focus on the specific topic of recruitment or grades. That was appropriate, because analogy questions are usually decided by structure, modality, and quantifiers, not subject matter. The crucial facts I used were the presence of a visible trait, the statement that such trait-bearers are not always what they seem, and the tentative conclusion marked by words like “some doubts” or “may not.” I did not require a universal negative claim, which was important, because the original argument only supports suspicion, not certainty. One assumption that helped was treating “high score” as analogous to an outward sign and “ability/comprehensive quality” as the hidden target property. I should also have explicitly checked the other options for common traps: reversing conditionals, moving from correlation to causation, or changing “not all” into “none.” The reasoning succeeded because I matched both the logical weakness and the cautious conclusion. In similar problems, I should compare argument forms at the level of quantifiers, direction of inference, and certainty level. General rule: when matching analogies, preserve not just the concepts but the exact inferential pattern from premise type to conclusion strength.

item.context: Scientists have found that the content of a protein called SK3 in the brains of experimental mice of different ages is closely related to their memory ability. The content of SK3 protein in the brain of the old experimental mice is higher than that of the young experimental mice, but the memory of the old experimental mice is worse than that of the young ones.Therefore, scientists believe that an increase in the content of SK3 protein in the brain will lead to memory loss in experimental mice.
item.question: Which of the following options, if correct, can best support the scientists' conclusions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High levels of SK3 protein in the brain were also found in young experimental rats

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has been found that the human brain also contains SK3 protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: When scientists tried to reduce the content of SK3 protein in the brain of elderly experimental rats, their memory improved

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scientists have figured out the molecular structure of SK3 protein

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion claims SK3 increase causes memory loss. The best support is evidence that lowering SK3 improves memory in older experimental animals, showing a likely causal link rather than mere correlation. The other options are irrelevant or only show presence, not effect on memory.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a causal-strengthening approach: I looked for the option that moved the evidence beyond a mere age-related correlation and toward showing that SK3 itself affects memory. The key factor was whether changing SK3 levels produced a corresponding change in memory performance, because intervention evidence is much stronger than simple coexistence. My success came from identifying that experimental manipulation best supports causation. For similar problems, prefer answers that directly vary the suspected cause and show the predicted change in the effect, rather than answers that only show the factor exists in other subjects or contexts.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a strengthening task, specifically one asking for the strongest support for a causal conclusion drawn from an observed age-related correlation. The argument’s structure was: older mice have more of a certain protein and worse memory, so increased protein causes memory loss; that means the key issue was whether any option moved the evidence from correlation toward causation. My strategy was to look for an intervention-style statement, because in causal reasoning, evidence that changing the alleged cause changes the effect is stronger than evidence that the factor merely exists somewhere else. That was an appropriate strategy here, since the original evidence alone left open alternative explanations such as age causing both higher protein levels and worse memory independently. The crucial fact I used was that reducing the protein level led to improved memory, which directly tests the proposed mechanism rather than just describing association. I correctly rejected options that only established presence in other species or molecular identification, because those facts do not bear on whether the protein influences memory performance. I also implicitly distinguished between relevance and probative force: some choices were related to the protein, but not to the causal claim. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on experimental manipulation rather than superficial topical overlap. In similar problems, I should continue asking: which choice most directly rules out confounding by showing that altering one variable produces a corresponding change in the outcome? General rule: when evaluating support for a causal claim, prefer evidence of controlled intervention over evidence of coexistence, similarity, or description.

item.context: Gardener: Researchers encourage us to allow certain kinds of weeds to grow among garden vegetables because they can repel caterpillars from the garden. While it is wise to avoid unnecessary use of insecticides, the researchers' advice is premature. For all we know, those kinds of weeds can deplete the soil of nutrients and moisture that garden crops depend on, and might even attract other kinds of damaging pests.
item.question: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the gardener's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allowing certain kinds of weeds to grow in vegetable gardens may contribute to a net increase in unwanted garden pests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Allowing the right kinds of weeds to grow in vegetable gardens can help toward controlling caterpillars without the use of insecticides.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To the extent that it is possible to do so, we should eliminate the use of insecticides in gardening.

choices.label: D
choices.text: We should be cautious about the practice of allowing certain kinds of weeds to grow among garden vegetables.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion is that the researchers’ advice is “premature,” meaning we should not yet adopt it confidently. The gardener supports this by noting possible downsides: weeds may drain nutrients/moisture or attract other pests. That is a cautionary conclusion, not a claim that harm will definitely occur.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a conclusion-identification approach, separating the author’s main claim from the supporting considerations. The key clue was the phrase “the researchers’ advice is premature,” which signals a cautionary judgment rather than a definite prediction about pests or soil damage. I succeeded by treating the later statements about nutrient loss and attracting pests as possible risks offered as support, not as the conclusion itself. In similar arguments, I should translate evaluative words like “premature,” “unwise,” or “questionable” into the broader practical conclusion they imply, instead of choosing an answer that restates only one supporting risk.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task correctly as identifying the argument’s main conclusion rather than a supporting premise or a possible consequence. The key indicator was the sentence that the researchers’ advice is “premature,” which signals the author’s judgment about what attitude we should take toward the proposal. My strategy was to distinguish between the author’s ultimate claim and the subordinate reasons introduced afterward, namely the possible risks involving nutrients, moisture, and other pests. That was appropriate because main-conclusion questions often hinge on separating a recommendation or evaluation from the evidence offered in its support. I used the fact that the gardener explicitly concedes one point—avoiding unnecessary insecticides is wise—which helped rule out any option treating the argument as pro-insecticide. I also noticed that the risks were framed with uncertainty (“for all we know,” “might even”), so the conclusion could only be cautious, not definitive. That prevented me from choosing a stronger answer claiming that weeds actually would increase pests or definitely harm crops. An important assumption I avoided was treating a mentioned possibility as the author’s asserted outcome. I should continue to test answer choices for strength: when premises are speculative, the conclusion usually remains tentative. A transferable rule is: when an argument cites possible downsides to criticize a proposal, the main conclusion is typically a call for caution, not a prediction that the downsides will occur.

item.context: The researchers used fossils of tiny marine life to reconstruct global temperatures since the end of the last ice age. The data show that the earth continued to cool for thousands of years and then reversed as never before in the 20 th century. This further shows that modern global warming is not natural, but the result of increasing carbon dioxide emissions.
