Carbon dioxide emissions have increased rapidly since the industrial revolution about 250 years ago, and marine fossil data show that the period from 1990 to 1910 was one of the coldest 10 years in the past 11,300 years, colder than 95% of the other years. However, the study points out that 100 years later, 2000 to 2010 is one of the warmest 10 years here. Global temperature records date back only to 1880, with the warmest decade from 2000 to 2010.
item.question: Which of the following options does not match the original text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbon dioxide emissions need to accumulate to a certain extent to cause greenhouse effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The time span of global temperature reconstructed from fossils far exceeds the existing temperature records.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For quite some time after the industrial revolution, carbon dioxide emissions increased and global temperatures continued to decline.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The temperature reconstructed by the researchers from 2000 to 2010 is different from the global temperature record.

response:
Reasoning: The fossil reconstruction and instrumental temperature records both identify 2000–2010 as among/the warmest decade, so they are not different. A, B, and C are consistent with the passage’s implications.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a consistency-checking approach, comparing each option against what the passage explicitly stated versus what it merely suggested. The key factor I relied on was the apparent agreement between fossil reconstruction and instrumental records for 2000–2010, which made me reject the option claiming they were different. My mistake was treating a causal mechanism not stated in the passage as a reasonable implication: the text says emissions increased and warming later accelerated, but it never says emissions must accumulate to some threshold before producing a greenhouse effect. For similar problems, I should reject choices that introduce unstated scientific mechanisms or necessary conditions unless the passage explicitly supports them.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task as asking for the statement least supported by the passage, which was correct, but I applied the wrong test for mismatch. My strategy was to look for a direct contradiction with an explicit sentence, and that led me to focus on the comparison between the reconstructed temperatures and the instrumental record. That approach was too narrow because “does not match” can also mean “adds a claim not warranted by the text,” not only “states the opposite.” I used the fact that both sources described the early 21st century as exceptionally warm, so I rejected the option about disagreement between them. That part of my reasoning was reasonable, but I failed to evaluate whether another option introduced a causal mechanism the passage never established. In particular, I treated an inference about emissions needing to build up over time as if it were supported by the mention of delayed warming after industrialization. That was an unjustified assumption: temporal sequence alone does not prove a threshold or accumulation requirement. I also should have separated descriptive claims in the passage from explanatory claims inserted by the choices. A better method is to classify each option as directly stated, validly implied, or speculative, and eliminate speculative additions first. The key lesson is: when a reading question asks what does not match, reject choices that require extra causal or mechanistic assumptions beyond the text, even if they sound plausible.

item.context: Last year a record number of new manufacturing jobs were created. Will this year bring another record? Well, any new manufacturing job is created either within an existing company or by the start-up of a new company. Within existing firms, new jobs have been created this year at well below last years record pace. At the same time, there is considerable evidence that the number of new companies starting up will be no higher this year than it was last year and there is no reason to think that the new companies starting up this year will create more jobs per company than did last year' s start-ups. So clearly, the number of new jobs created this year will fall short of last years record.
item.question: In the argument given, the two portions in boldface play which of the following ?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first is presented as an obvious truth on which the argument is based; the second is a claim that has been advanced In support of a position that the argument opposes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first is presented as an obvious truth on which the argument is based; the second is a judgment advanced in support of the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first is a generalization that the argument seeks to establish; the second is a conclusion that the argument draws in order to support that generalization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first provides evidence in support of the main conclusion of the argument; the second is a claim that the argument challenges.

response:
Reasoning: The first boldface statement is a basic, self-evident premise dividing all new jobs into two sources. The second boldface statement is also a supporting premise: if start-ups are not more numerous and won’t create more jobs per company, total new jobs will be lower. It supports, not opposes, the conclusion.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a structural argument-analysis approach: identify the main conclusion, then classify each boldface statement by its role relative to that conclusion. The key factor was seeing that the first boldface statement sets up the exhaustive division of all new manufacturing jobs into two sources, which the rest of the reasoning depends on, while the second is a predictive judgment used to limit one of those sources. My success came from distinguishing “background framework” from “supporting premise” and noticing that the second statement was endorsed by the author, not presented as an opposing view. For similar boldface problems, first map the conclusion and each premise’s function before matching any answer choice.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a boldface-role problem: the task was not to judge whether the conclusion was true, but to identify the function each boldfaced statement played within the argument’s structure. My strategy was to map the argument into premises and conclusion, then classify each boldface by whether it was background, evidence, an intermediate conclusion, or an opposing claim. That was the right method here because boldface questions depend more on argumentative role than on content. I correctly recognized the first boldface as a framework premise that partitions all new manufacturing jobs into two exhaustive sources, which the rest of the reasoning depends on. I also correctly treated the second boldface as support for the conclusion, since it limits one of those two sources by denying any basis for higher jobs-per-start-up. A key fact I used was that the author presents both boldfaced claims in his own voice, not as views held by opponents. That helped eliminate choices describing the second statement as something challenged or opposed. One assumption that worked well was reading “there is no reason to think” as a judgment offered by the author, not as neutral background. I should continue checking whether a statement is being established, assumed, or used as support before matching answer choices. A transferable rule is: in boldface questions, first identify the main conclusion, then ask for each boldfaced statement whether it is evidence, conclusion, background classification, or an attributed opposing view.

item.context: A study published in the British Medical Journal showed that people who ate the most white rice had a 55% higher risk of diabetes than those who ate the least. Some people concluded that eating more white rice is more likely to develop diabetes.
item.question: Which of the following situations, if it is true, can weaken the above conclusion the most?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genetics and many other factors can also increase the risk of diabetes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who do not eat or eat less staple food for a long time are also prone to diabetes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: White rice lacks nutrients such as dietary fiber that the human body needs every day.

choices.label: D
choices.text: People who eat much white rice have high intake of other types of food.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion assumes white rice itself causes higher diabetes risk. The strongest weakening is a confounder: if heavy white-rice eaters also consume more other foods that raise diabetes risk, the rice may not be the cause. A is too general, B doesn’t address comparison, C supports the conclusion.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a causal-weakening approach, looking for an alternative explanation that would break the link between high white-rice intake and diabetes risk. The key factor I focused on was confounding, so I chose the option about heavy rice eaters also consuming more other foods. My mistake was treating “other types of food” as necessarily risk-raising when the choice never says those foods increase diabetes; that makes it too speculative. In similar problems, I should prefer an option that directly shows the supposed harmful factor is not necessary for the outcome or that the comparison group can also face the same risk.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the strongest alternative explanation for the observed correlation, and that part was partly right, but I framed the conclusion too narrowly as “white rice itself causes diabetes.” The wording of the conclusion compared people who eat more white rice with those who eat less, so the key issue was not only confounding by other foods, but whether low intake itself might also be associated with higher risk. My strategy was to search for a classic third-variable explanation, which made me favor the option about heavy rice eaters consuming more of other foods. That strategy is often useful, but here I overlooked that a stronger weakening can come from showing the comparison group is not actually safer for the reason assumed. The important missed relationship was that if people who eat very little staple food are also prone to diabetes, then the simple “more rice, more diabetes” inference breaks down because both ends of intake may involve risk. I assumed the best weakener must identify another harmful factor among high-rice eaters, instead of considering whether low-rice eaters might also have elevated risk. I also underweighted how directly an answer challenges the comparison structure used in the conclusion. In similar problems, I should test each option against the exact causal claim: does it offer a competing cause, reverse the baseline, or show a non-linear relationship? A transferable rule is: when an argument infers causation from a high-group versus low-group comparison, the strongest weakener may be evidence that the low group is not an appropriate “safe” baseline, not just evidence of an extra risk factor in the high group.

item.context: The development and progress of human medicine not only benefit from the hard work of scientists, but also from the silent sacrifice of experimental animals. Before drug development into the clinical, we need to do a lot of animal experiments to explore the efficacy, toxicity, safe dose of drugs. However, there are many differences between human beings and rats, pigs, dogs, rabbits and other animals after all. Even if we have a correct understanding of the physiological structure of animals and the law of drug reaction, we can not easily and blindly transfer the result of our understanding to human beings.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, best supports this view?

choices.label: A
choices.text: According to the results of his anatomy of animals, Galen, an ancient Greek medical scientist, believed that whether in human veins or arteries, blood is an one-way movement, not a circular movement. Of course, this is not in line with the concept of modern science.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the Song Dynasty, Materia Medica Yan Yi recorded that some wild geese with broken wings were fed with natural copper, and then the wild geese flew away. In the eyes of modern people, it is unthinkable to eat natural copper to treat fractures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In 1882, German Robert Koch used guinea pigs to do experiments and concluded that tuberculosis is the causative bacterium of tuberculosis. Whether it comes from monkeys, cattle or humans, it has the same symptoms. For this discovery, he won the Nobel Prize.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In 1957, a pregnancy response drug called thalidomide was put on the market after being tested on rats. After a period of time, it was discovered that thalidomide can cause malformations in human fetuses, but it will not cause teratogenicity to rat fetuses.

response:
Reasoning: The claim is that animal results cannot be blindly applied to humans because species differ in drug responses. D directly shows this: thalidomide was safe in rats but caused human fetal malformations, proving animal findings may not predict human outcomes.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used direct support matching: I identified the conclusion as “animal experiment results cannot be blindly transferred to humans” and looked for the option that most clearly illustrated a human–animal difference in drug effects. The key factor was species-specific response to the same drug, because that directly strengthens the warning against generalizing from animals to humans. My success came from choosing the option with the strongest causal relevance, rather than one that was merely about animal experiments or medical history. For similar problems, first restate the exact claim in your own words, then select the choice that provides the most direct example of that precise relationship.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a strengthen task: I needed to find the option that most directly supports the claim that animal experiment results should not be transferred to humans uncritically. My strategy was to match the conclusion’s core causal idea—species differences can make drug effects differ—against the options and select the one that gave the most direct example. That was an appropriate strategy because support questions are usually strongest when an option mirrors the exact structure of the claim rather than merely discussing medicine or animals in general. I focused on the key evidential requirement: a case where an animal-based safety or efficacy result failed to predict the human outcome. Option D fit this requirement precisely by contrasting rat and human responses to the same drug. I also implicitly eliminated the other choices because they were weaker or off-target: some concerned outdated medical beliefs, some concerned folk medicine, and one showed successful cross-species inference rather than a failure of it. A helpful constraint I used was relevance to drug testing specifically, not just biological knowledge in general. One assumption behind my reasoning was that the best support should provide a concrete counterexample to blind extrapolation, and that assumption was sound here. The success came from tracking the exact logical gap in the passage: not whether animal experiments are useful, but whether their results can be directly generalized to humans. In similar problems, I should continue distinguishing between “about the topic” evidence and evidence that directly instantiates the claim’s mechanism. A general rule is: in strengthen questions, prefer the option that most closely reproduces the conclusion’s causal or comparative structure with a concrete, directly relevant case.

item.context: Differentiated market strategy refers to that enterprises design and produce different products, formulate and implement different marketing mix strategies (comprehensive application of various marketing means) based on the overall market segmentation and the demand characteristics of each segment market, and try to meet the differentiated market demand with differentiated products.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings belongs to differentiated market strategies:

choices.label: A
choices.text: An automobile manufacturing enterprise faces the working class and mainly produces economical cars. This kind of car has low price and low fuel consumption, and is deeply welcomed by the working class

choices.label: B
choices.text: A supermarket implements the membership system and gives gifts of different grades according to the number of member points

choices.label: C
choices.text: A computer produced by an enterprise sells well in the market. In order to broaden the market, it begin to develop mobile phones

choices.label: D
choices.text: A cosmetics manufacturer produces and sells different kinds of moisturizers for consumers of different ages

response:
Reasoning: Differentiated market strategy means segmenting the overall market and offering different products/marketing mixes to different segments. D matches this: the cosmetics maker targets consumers of different ages with different moisturizers. A is concentrated on one segment, B is loyalty promotion, and C is product expansion/diversification.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I broke the concept into required elements—market segmentation, different products for different segments, and distinct marketing efforts—and checked each option against all parts. The key factor was whether the company was serving multiple identified segments with tailored offerings rather than just one target group or a general business expansion tactic. My answer was correct because I distinguished true segmented targeting from look-alikes such as single-segment focus, membership rewards, and diversification into a new product line. For similar problems, I should explicitly list the definition’s necessary conditions and eliminate any option that satisfies only one feature but not the full structure.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for an example of a firm that both segments the market and tailors products plus marketing to the distinct needs of those segments. That interpretation was correct because the definition emphasized two linked elements: overall market segmentation and differentiated offerings aimed at each segment. My strategy was to test each option against the definition’s necessary conditions rather than rely on surface similarity to “marketing.” This was appropriate because several choices contained business tactics, but not all involved segmentation-based product differentiation.

The key evidence I used was the presence or absence of multiple target segments and corresponding product differences. I correctly recognized that one option focused on a single customer group, which fits concentrated targeting rather than differentiation across segments. I also distinguished a loyalty or reward mechanism from a true segmentation strategy, because incentives for existing members do not necessarily imply different products for different market segments. Likewise, I treated expansion into a new product category as diversification, not segmentation within one market.

A helpful assumption I made was that “different products for different needs” must be tied to identifiable customer subgroups, not just multiple products in general. What made the reasoning successful was matching each choice to the full definition, not just one phrase. In similar problems, I should continue identifying the defining criteria and then eliminate options that satisfy only part of them. General rule: when evaluating a definition-based multiple-choice question, require every core condition of the definition to be present before accepting an option.

item.context: Over the past three years, three canoes have been excavated successively on the beach of the Huaihe River in Xi County, Xinyang County, Henan Province. Among them, the first canoe was found under the beach of the Huaihe River of Zhangzhuang formation in Xuzhuang Village, suburban Township, Xixian County in 2010, which has been proved to be one of the earliest and largest canoes found in archaeology in China. The canoe is 9.3 meters long, 0.8 meters wide and 0.6 meters high. According to carbon-14 measurements, these canoes are made of the same materials as the wood produced in tropical Yunnan. This shows that in ancient times more than 3000 years ago, the climate of Henan was very similar to that of the tropics today. The climate on both sides of the middle and lower reaches of the Huaihe River is warm and humid, with tall and dense trees and a wide variety of animals and plants.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, can best support the above argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The raw materials of these canoes can not be transported from the remote primeval forests of Yunnan, but can only be used locally.

choices.label: B
choices.text: These canoes have been soaked in water for thousands of years and are very heavy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The story of carving a boat and seeking a sword took place in the land of Chu, including the south of Xuchang, Henan Province.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two ends of the canoe are pointed, chiseled from a complete log and well preserved.

response:
Reasoning: The argument infers ancient Henan’s climate from the canoe wood being the same as tropical Yunnan wood. This is best supported if the wood could not have been transported from Yunnan and had to be sourced locally; then such tropical-type wood must have grown in Henan then.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a strengthening approach: identify the argument’s main gap and choose the option that most directly closes it. The conclusion about ancient Henan’s climate depends on treating the canoe wood as evidence of local vegetation rather than imported material. The key supporting fact was that the wood could not realistically have been transported from distant Yunnan and therefore must have been sourced locally. For similar problems, first pinpoint the hidden assumption linking evidence to conclusion, then select the choice that makes that assumption much more credible.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a strengthening problem: the conclusion was not just that the canoes were old, but that ancient Henan had a tropical-like climate, and the support had to connect canoe material to local environmental conditions. That interpretation was correct because the argument depended on moving from “the wood matches tropical Yunnan wood” to “Henan once had similar climate and vegetation.” My strategy was to identify the argument’s hidden assumption and then choose the option that most directly reinforced it. Specifically, the missing link was whether the wood had to come from the excavation region rather than being imported from elsewhere. I used the fact that if the raw material could only be used locally, then matching tropical wood would imply that comparable trees once grew in Henan, which supports the climate claim.

I also correctly treated the other options as largely irrelevant details: weight, shape, preservation, and a historical anecdote do not strengthen the climate inference. One useful constraint I recognized was that the conclusion concerns ancient ecology, so the best support must address provenance of the wood, not merely properties of the canoe. A shortcut that worked here was asking, “What alternative explanation would weaken this argument?” The main alternative was long-distance transport from Yunnan, and the right answer blocked exactly that alternative. In similar problems, I should keep focusing on causal or inferential gaps between evidence and conclusion rather than on vivid descriptive facts. A general rule is: when an argument infers local historical conditions from an artifact’s material, the strongest support is evidence that the material was locally sourced rather than traded or transported.

item.context: Regarding Xiao Wang, Xiao Li and Xiao Zhang, we know that one of them is a lawyer, one is a doctor, and one is a teacher, and we also know that Xiao Zhang is older than the teacher; Xiao Wang and the doctor are different years old and the doctor is younger than Xiao Li.
item.question: Which of the followings can be concluded?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Xiao Wang is a lawyer. Xiao Li is a doctor. And Xiao Zhang is a teacher.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Xiao Wang is a doctor. Xiao Li is a teacher. And Xiao Zhang is a lawyer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Xiao Wang is a teacher. Xiao Li is a lawyer. And Xiao Zhang is a doctor.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Xiao Wang is a teacher. Xiao Li is a doctor. And Xiao Zhang is a lawyer.

response:
Reasoning: Since Xiao Wang is different in age from the doctor, Wang ≠ doctor. The doctor is younger than Xiao Li, so Li ≠ doctor. Therefore Zhang must be the doctor. Zhang is older than the teacher, so Zhang ≠ teacher. Li cannot be teacher, because then doctor Zhang would be younger than Li but also older than the teacher Li, impossible. So Wang = teacher, Li = lawyer, Zhang = doctor.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a process-of-elimination approach, translating each age statement into a restriction on who could hold each profession. The key step was noticing that “Xiao Wang and the doctor are different years old” implies Wang is not the doctor, and “the doctor is younger than Xiao Li” implies Li is not the doctor, forcing Zhang to be the doctor. From there, “Zhang is older than the teacher” ruled out Zhang as the teacher, and checking Li as teacher created an age contradiction. For similar problems, convert each statement into explicit “cannot be” constraints first, then test the remaining assignments against all relational conditions before choosing.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a constrained assignment problem: each person has a unique profession, and the age statements restrict which profession each person can hold. My strategy was to convert each age relation into an exclusion, then use the one-to-one matching among the three jobs to force the remaining assignments. That was appropriate because these problems are usually solved most reliably by eliminating impossibilities before making any positive claim.

The key facts I used were: Xiao Wang is not the doctor because “Xiao Wang and the doctor are different years old,” and Xiao Li is not the doctor because the doctor is younger than Xiao Li, so they cannot be the same person. From those two exclusions, it follows that Xiao Zhang must be the doctor. Then I used “Xiao Zhang is older than the teacher” to conclude Zhang cannot also be the teacher. At that point, teacher had to be either Wang or Li, and I tested Li as teacher against the earlier age relation. That check was important: if Li were the teacher, then Zhang as doctor would be younger than Li but Zhang is also older than the teacher, creating a contradiction.

What made the reasoning successful was linking role uniqueness with age inequalities, rather than treating each clue separately. A useful general rule is: in assignment problems with comparative constraints, first turn comparisons into identity exclusions, then use uniqueness to force candidates, and finally test any remaining alternatives for consistency across all clues.

item.context: Reflection refers to the regular response of animal body or human body to changes in internal and external environment with the participation of central nervous system.

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option against the requirement that a reflection must be a response in an animal or human involving the central nervous system. The key factor was the explicit scope of the definition, especially the central nervous system and the exclusion of plants. My success came from filtering the choices by biological category first, rather than getting distracted by whether each response was voluntary or learned. For similar problems, first extract every necessary condition from the definition and eliminate any option that fails even one required condition.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which option failed to meet the definition of a reflex-like response given in the stem, especially the requirement that the response occur with participation of a central nervous system. That interpretation was correct because the definition itself supplied the key criterion needed to classify the options. My strategy was to test each option against that criterion rather than rely on whether the behavior merely looked automatic or rapid. That was appropriate, since several animal behaviors in the list differ in type—withdrawal, conditioned salivation, prey-chasing—but all can still involve nervous-system activity.

The decisive evidence I used was the distinction between animal/human responses mediated by a nervous system and plant movements, which occur without any central nervous system. I did not need to determine whether the animal examples were innate or conditioned; the stem’s definition was broader than only unconditioned reflexes. A potential pitfall would have been assuming “reflection” meant only simple involuntary spinal reflexes, which might have led to over-questioning the learned salivation example or the cat’s predatory behavior. Another possible mistake would have been focusing on speed or automaticity alone, instead of the biological mechanism specified in the definition.

The reasoning succeeded because I anchored my choice in the explicit definitional constraint rather than superficial similarity among responses. item.context: Circular economy is essentially an ecological economy. It requires the use of ecological laws rather than mechanical laws to guide the economic activities of human society. Its characteristic is low exploitation, low emission and high utilization.
item.question: Which of the following is not a practice of the circular economy?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Returning farmland to Lake and farmland to forest.

response:
Reasoning: Circular economy emphasizes resource conservation, recycling, ecological restoration, and sustainable development. reflections.simple: I used definition-based elimination: I matched each option against the core features named in the prompt—low exploitation, low emission, and high utilization. My answer was correct because I anchored the comparison to the stated principles instead of relying on vague positive wording. reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which option conflicted with the defining principles of a circular economy: low exploitation, low emissions, and high resource utilization. That interpretation was correct, because the task was not to identify a generally good policy, but to test consistency with the stated ecological framework. My strategy was to compare each choice against the core features of circularity—recycling, recovery, reduced extraction, and ecological restoration. This was appropriate because the stem itself provided the decision criteria, so the best method was concept matching rather than outside factual recall.

The key evidence I used was that options about shifting to a circular model, building a recuperative or recovery-oriented economy, and restoring ecosystems all align with resource reuse and ecological balance. I also noticed that one option emphasized “growth,” which points toward expansion of output rather than closed-loop use of resources. A useful assumption I made was that terms like “recuperation” and ecological restoration are positively associated with circular systems, while pure growth language is not. That shortcut worked here, but it would be risky if a question used unfamiliar terms in a misleading way. The reasoning succeeded because I anchored my evaluation to the explicit definition in the prompt instead of relying on vague impressions. A transferable rule is: when a concept is defined in the stem, test each option directly against the defining constraints and reject the one whose core objective operates on a different principle.

item.context: Bigamy: refers to the fact that a married man and woman who have a spouse do not go through the divorce procedures and register their marriage with another person, or do not register a marriage but live with another person to form a de facto marriage relationship, and the behavior of unmarried men and women who know that others have a spouse and marry with them.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following is bigamy?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: A marries B without knowing that he is married.

response:
Reasoning: Bigamy requires a person who still has a spouse to marry another, or an unmarried person knowingly marrying someone who already has a spouse. In B, A is still in the divorce process, so the prior marriage is not yet ended, but A registers marriage with B anyway.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I broke the rule into its essential conditions and checked each option against them. The key factor was the legal status of the first marriage—being “during the divorce” means the prior marriage is still in force, so registering a new marriage meets the definition. My success came from focusing on the timing and legal validity of divorce rather than the broader relationship story. reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a definition-matching task: identify the option that satisfies every required element of bigamy, not just one that sounds morally similar. My strategy was to decompose the definition into two qualifying patterns: a person still legally married entering another marriage or de facto marital relationship, and an unmarried person knowingly marrying someone who is already married. That strategy was appropriate because the answer depended on legal status, knowledge, and timing rather than on general relationship facts. The key evidence I used was that being “during the divorce” means the prior marriage has not yet legally ended, so the person still has a spouse at the time of the later registration. I also correctly noted that the other person in that option was unmarried, which does not prevent the situation from qualifying under the first branch of the definition.

A useful part of my reasoning was distinguishing legal divorce completion from separation or intent to divorce; the definition turns on current marital status, not future status. I also implicitly rejected distractors that involved conduct after divorce, because once the prior marriage is dissolved, the central condition is gone. Another important filter was the knowledge requirement for the unmarried participant, which made the option involving ignorance inapplicable. What made the reasoning successful was mapping each option against the exact definitional clauses instead of relying on everyday intuition. In similar problems, I should continue translating definitions into necessary conditions and checking each answer clause by clause. General rule: in definition-based multiple choice, treat each listed element as a legal test, and eliminate any option that fails even one required condition.

item.context: Scientific outlook on development is to adhere to the people-oriented approach, establish a comprehensive, coordinated, and sustainable development concept, and promote the all-round development of the economy, society and people.

My strategy was to compare each option against the defining dimensions in the stem rather than judge them by whether they sound beneficial. The key evidence I used was that A and D clearly match sustainability and ecological balance, while C directly matches the people-oriented concern for livelihood. A useful distinction here was between a broad developmental concept and a specific policy instrument. One assumption I made was that an option can be positive or helpful yet still fail to represent the conceptual framework being asked about; that assumption was justified. item.context: Some people think that beauty is objective, for example, whether you see the beauty of Huangshan or not, it exists. Others think that beauty is subjective, some beautiful women in your eyes, in the eyes of others is not beautiful.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beauty is relative and exists in our subject's objective world

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beauty is subjective or objective, belongs to the radish cabbage each have some love

response:
Reasoning: The examples show both sides: beauty has an objective basis (e.g., Huangshan exists with qualities people can appreciate) but also varies with the subject’s feelings and standards. So beauty is neither purely subjective nor purely denied as objective; it is relative and tied to objective reality.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a synthesis approach: instead of choosing between the two positions, I looked for the option that reconciled both the objective example and the subjective example. The key factor was that the prompt presents beauty as having an objective basis while also varying across observers, so the best choice had to preserve both sides rather than reject one. My success came from matching that combined structure to the option that describes beauty as relative yet grounded in the objective world. For similar problems, identify whether the premises are contrasting alternatives or complementary clues, and prefer the answer that preserves all given conditions.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the prompt as asking for the most reasonable synthesis of two apparently competing claims about beauty, not for a defense of only one side. That interpretation was important, because the stem presented both objectivist and subjectivist examples without explicitly rejecting either. My strategy was to look for an option that preserved both constraints: beauty must have some basis in real features of things, yet judgments of beauty vary across observers. That was appropriate because multiple-choice philosophy-style questions often test whether you can reconcile partial truths rather than choose an extreme. 

The key evidence I used was the contrast between a natural landscape, which suggests beauty is not arbitrary, and differing opinions about people’s appearance, which suggests evaluation depends on the subject. I correctly rejected options that erased one side of the contrast, such as those denying any objectivity or reducing the issue to mere personal preference. One assumption that helped was treating the examples as complementary rather than contradictory. A possible trap would have been to overread the phrase “beautiful women in your eyes” as proving total subjectivity, but that would ignore the first example. Another alternative I should always consider in similar questions is whether the test is distinguishing “relative” from “purely subjective,” since those are not the same. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the relation between objective conditions and subjective appreciation. A transferable rule is: when a prompt presents evidence for two opposing views, first test whether the best answer integrates both under a higher-level distinction instead of choosing an absolute extreme.

item.context: The researchers found that over the past century and a half, there have been several periods of slowing earth's speed, each lasting about five years, and, crucially, that slowdown has been accompanied by an increase in powerful earthquakes. This led the researchers to conclude that the earth's slowing speed led to more powerful earthquakes.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, most questions the above conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During periods of slower earth rotation, about 25 to 30 strong earthquakes occur each year, and at other times, about 15 occur

choices.label: B
choices.text: There was no significant change in the number of volcanic eruptions during periods of slower earth rotation compared with other periods

choices.label: C
choices.text: As the Earth's rotation slows, the length of day and night changes, leading to more powerful earthquakes around the world

choices.label: D
choices.text: A slight shift in the core, which causes the earth to slow down, also leads to more powerful earthquakes around the world

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion assumes slowdown causes earthquakes because they occur together. The strongest challenge is an alternative cause explaining both events. Choice D gives a common cause—a core shift causes the slowdown and also causes more powerful earthquakes—so the slowdown itself may not be the cause.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a causal-weakening approach: the argument inferred causation from a recurring correlation, so I looked for information that would break that causal link. The key factor was whether any choice offered an alternative explanation for both the slowdown and the earthquakes rather than merely restating the correlation or supporting it. My success came from recognizing that a common-cause explanation most directly undermines “X led to Y.” For similar problems, when an argument moves from “these happen together” to “one caused the other,” first test whether a third factor could be producing both.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the argument as making a causal claim from a repeated correlation: periods of slower rotation were followed by more powerful earthquakes, so the slowdown was said to produce the earthquakes. That interpretation was correct, because the task was not to summarize the evidence but to identify what most undermines the causal inference. My strategy was to look for a classic weaken pattern: an alternative explanation that accounts for both correlated events without requiring one to cause the other. That was appropriate because causal arguments based on co-occurrence are especially vulnerable to common-cause explanations. I focused on the distinction between “associated with” and “led to,” which is the key logical gap in the researchers’ conclusion. The evidence I used correctly was that the premise only established accompaniment across several periods, not direct causation, mechanism, or experimental control. I also correctly rejected choices that merely restated the correlation or even strengthened the claimed mechanism rather than questioning it. A hidden assumption in the argument is that no third factor independently produced both the slowdown and the earthquakes. I should also have explicitly considered whether any option challenged timing, sample size, or the possibility of coincidence, though in this case the common-cause attack was strongest. The reasoning succeeded because it targeted the exact inferential leap rather than the topic details. General rule: when an argument infers causation from repeated correlation, test it by asking whether a third factor could generate both effects.

item.context: A city launched a monthly social welfare activities, the citizens registered enthusiastically. reflections.simple: I used a causal-explanation approach: identify the specific pattern causing suspicion, then look for the option that makes that pattern unsurprising without needing fraud. The key factor was that the concern centered on the repeated appearance of the same name, not necessarily the same person, so the strongest assuaging fact would show that this name is shared by many applicants. My success came from distinguishing between “same name” and “same individual,” which directly weakens the suspicious inference. reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as an argument-weakening task: the citizens infer cheating from the repeated appearance of the same name, and I needed the option that best explains that pattern innocently. My strategy was to identify the suspicious fact driving the doubt and then look for a choice that reduces the evidential force of that fact rather than merely offering reassurance. That was appropriate because the issue was not whether the lottery was generally monitored, but whether the repeated name actually indicates an unlikely event. The key relationship I used was that identical names do not necessarily identify the same person, so the probability judgment changes drastically if many registrants share that name. I also implicitly used the idea that a coincidence looks suspicious only when the underlying base rate is low or unknown. The strongest evidence was the option giving a large number of applicants with that name, because it directly attacks the assumption that “Li Xiang” refers to one recurring winner. I rejected the supervision option because procedural oversight is weaker than a concrete statistical explanation of the observed pattern. I also considered that another common-name example helps somewhat, but it is less directly tied to the four-month sequence in question. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the causal source of the suspicion and matching it with the answer that neutralizes it most specifically. In similar problems, I should first isolate the exact assumption behind the suspicion, then prefer answers that alter the probability model over answers that offer general credibility. A transferable rule is: when an argument treats repeated labels as repeated individuals, test whether shared identifiers create a misleading appearance of improbability.

item.context: A computer with signature recognition software installed - this software is limited to those who sign in the document to enter the computer - recognizes someone's signature not only by analyzing the shape of the signature, but also by analyzing features such as the pressure of the pen tip and the speed of the signature. reflections.simple: I used a direct entailment approach: I matched each option against what the passage explicitly guarantees and rejected choices that introduced new claims. The key factor was the statement that the system analyzes multiple signature features beyond shape, and that even the smartest forger cannot reproduce all of them. That made it valid to infer that forging skill alone would not be enough for access, which is why the choice about inability to enter by forgery was supported. reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the strongest conclusion that must follow strictly from the passage, not the most plausible real-world claim. That interpretation was correct, because the key task in deduction problems is to separate what is explicitly supported from what is merely suggestive. My strategy was to match the passage’s constraints to each answer choice and reject any option that introduced new information such as prevalence, value, or defects. This was appropriate because the passage gave a narrow factual claim about how the software verifies signatures and what a forger cannot reproduce. The crucial evidence was the combination of two statements: access depends on signature recognition, and the software evaluates features beyond visual shape that even an expert forger cannot fully mimic. From that, it follows that forging skill alone cannot be sufficient for access.

A useful assumption I made was that “cannot replicate all the features” means a forged signature would fail the software’s full recognition standard. That assumption was warranted by the setup describing the software as the gatekeeper for entry. I also correctly avoided being distracted by options that sounded realistic but were unsupported, such as claims about banks or institutional use. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on necessity rather than likelihood. In similar problems, I should continue testing each option by asking, “Is this forced by the text, or does it add outside information?” A general rule is: when a passage states a requirement depends on multiple conditions, and one proposed method cannot satisfy all of them, then that method alone cannot achieve the result.

item.context: Big-budget movies often gross two or three times the cost of their production and marketing. However, most of the movie industry' s total revenue comes from low-budget movies.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy above?

choices.text: Big-budget movies need to sell many more tickets than do low-budget movies, just to recoup their production costs.

reflections.simple: I used a reconcile-the-discrepancy approach: identify how both statements could be true at once rather than treating them as contradictory. The successful step was noticing that “most of the industry’s total revenue” depends on aggregate volume, not just how much a typical big-budget movie grosses. For similar problems, explicitly compare the unit of analysis in each statement and look for a quantity variable, such as number of cases, that can bridge the gap.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a “resolve the discrepancy” problem: one statement said big-budget films earn much more relative to their own costs, while the other said low-budget films generate most of the industry’s total revenue. The key was recognizing that the two claims operate at different levels of analysis—per movie versus aggregate across the whole industry. My strategy was to look for an answer choice that introduced a missing quantity capable of reconciling those levels, especially the number of films in each category. That was appropriate because totals depend not just on how much each item earns, but also on how many items there are.

The main evidence I used was the distinction between individual profitability or gross and total industry revenue. I correctly noticed that a small number of high-grossing films can still be outweighed by a much larger number of lower-grossing films. I did not rely on irrelevant details like insurance premiums or inflation, which do not connect the two claims. One assumption embedded in my reasoning was that “most of the industry’s total revenue” refers to the sum across many films, not average revenue per film; that assumption was justified by the wording. I should also note that I considered whether cost recovery mattered, but recouping costs is not what explains revenue share. The success came from identifying the missing variable that links individual performance to category-wide totals. In similar problems, I should explicitly test whether the apparent conflict comes from comparing averages, ratios, and totals. A transferable rule is: when two statements seem inconsistent, check whether they refer to different units of analysis and look for a quantity that converts one level into the other.

item.context: None of the initial causes of serious nuclear leakage accidents in nuclear power plants is equipment failure, which is caused by human error.
