reflections.complex:
I interpreted the prompt as an argument-completion task asking which conclusion is most strongly supported by an analogy about causes and long-run frequency, not which statement is merely plausible or rhetorically appealing. My strategy was to trace the causal chain in the stimulus: serious leakage accidents can originate in equipment failure; that equipment failure is attributed to human error; and that kind of human error is said to be no different in substance from errors behind other recurring accidents. From there, I used the final premise about long-run inevitability in the comparison cases to infer a parallel long-run tendency in the nuclear case. That was an appropriate strategy because the argument relies on analogical transfer plus a time-horizon claim, so the best-supported conclusion should preserve both of those features. The key evidence I used was the phrase “no substantive difference,” which licenses treating the nuclear case similarly to traffic jams and warehouse fires with respect to recurrence. I also correctly noticed that the conclusion had to be probabilistic or near-inevitable over time, not absolute or immediate.  

A potential pitfall would have been overreading the claim into an impossibility statement, a management-complexity comparison, or a broad attack on regulations, none of which the premises establish. Another possible mistake would have been ignoring the “initial causes” language and treating the passage as about all nuclear accidents rather than a specific route to serious leakage. What made the reasoning successful was matching the strength and scope of the conclusion to the strength and scope of the premises. In similar problems, I should explicitly map each premise to the conclusion and reject choices that introduce new domains, stronger modal language, or normative claims absent from the stimulus. General rule: when an argument says two causal mechanisms are substantively the same and one leads to near-inevitable outcomes over time, the supported conclusion is a parallel long-run risk claim, not a stronger, broader, or more policy-oriented statement.

item.context: In order to reduce traffic congestion, a city has taken measures such as the lower limit: On weekdays from Monday to Friday, non-commercial vehicles are restricted to one day in five groups according to their tail numbers 0, 5, 1, 6, 2, 7, 3, 8, 4 and 9, and not limited to weekends and legal holidays. Those who break the rules will be fined.
item.question: Which of the following descriptions about the travel of residents in the city may not violate the traffic restrictions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Zhao yi drives a commercial vehicle with a tail number of 1 and runs on the road every day.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Qian er has two private cars with different tail numbers and drives them every day.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zhang SAN and his neighbor have a total of three private cars, with different tail numbers. They cooperate and have two cars to drive every day.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Wang wu and three neighbors have six private cars with different ending numbers. They cooperate and drive five cars every day.

response:
Reasoning: Non-commercial vehicles are restricted one weekday by tail-number groups; commercial vehicles are not mentioned as restricted.  
B and C can still fail if the cars’ numbers fall in the same restricted group.  
D must fail: with 6 cars across 5 groups, some day 2 cars are restricted, so 5 cars can’t all run.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a combinatorial elimination approach: I checked how the weekday tail-number restriction applied to each scenario and tried to see whether daily driving was always possible. The key factor I noticed was that the restricted digits are paired into five weekday groups, but I made a faulty pigeonhole-style inference when evaluating the case with six cars and five cars driven per day. I assumed six different tail numbers across five groups guaranteed that some weekday would sideline two cars, but “different tail numbers” does not force coverage of all groups in that way. For similar problems, I should explicitly map or construct category assignments before using counting arguments, instead of jumping from “more items than groups” to an unsupported impossibility claim.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the rule mostly correctly: weekday restrictions apply only to non-commercial vehicles, grouped by paired tail numbers, with no restrictions on weekends or legal holidays. My strategy was to test each option against the grouping structure and look for a certainty claim such as “must violate” or “may not violate.” That was the right general approach, but I applied it inconsistently. For option D, I used a pigeonhole-style argument and assumed that six distinct tail numbers must occupy all five restriction groups in a way that forces two cars to be banned on some weekday. The flaw is that “different tail numbers” does not imply coverage of all five groups; two numbers can belong to the same group, leaving another group unused. If one group is unused, then on the day assigned to that unused group, none of the six cars is restricted, so five can be chosen legally. I correctly noticed that commercial vehicles are not explicitly restricted, but I treated that as sufficient without checking whether another option could also be feasible. I also should have represented the groups explicitly as pairs rather than reasoning only from counts of cars and groups. The specific error was substituting “six numbers across five groups” for the stronger claim “at least one car in every group,” which the problem never states. In similar problems, I should map each object to its constraint class before using counting arguments. General rule: when restrictions depend on equivalence classes, feasibility depends on the distribution across classes, not just the number of items.

item.context: Leclezio won the 2008 Nobel Prize for Literature, which is unexpected news in China. After all, although his works have only appeared sporadically in the domestic book market for nearly 20 years, although he is one of the first French contemporary writers to be translated and introduced in China, domestic readers' understanding of him is probably still at the name stage. Even the name is only heard of by a considerable class of French literature lovers. This shows neither the reader's ignorance nor the Nobel Prize's so-called unique taste, but only the long-standing gap between literature and popular culture.
item.question: Which of the following is the correct understanding of this text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most of the works that have won the Nobel Prize are unapproachable, and few people like them

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leclezio's works do not sell well in China

choices.label: C
choices.text: unique taste makes the Nobel Prize divorced from popular culture

choices.label: D
choices.text: Domestic readers know little about Nobel Prize-winning works

response:
Reasoning: The passage says Chinese readers know Leclezio only vaguely, despite some translations, showing a gap between literature and popular culture. It explicitly denies that this is due to readers’ ignorance or the Nobel’s “unique taste.” So A, B, and C are unsupported; D best matches.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an elimination-and-paraphrase approach, focusing closely on the sentence that says the situation shows “the long-standing gap between literature and popular culture.” The key factor that drove my choice was the explicit rejection of “readers’ ignorance” and the Nobel’s “unique taste,” which made me dismiss the option about domestic readers knowing little. My mistake was reading the passage too literally at the individual-author level and not inferring the broader claim about Nobel literature being relatively distant from mass readers. In similar problems, I should distinguish between a statement the passage explicitly denies as a cause and the broader phenomenon it still implies.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the passage too literally at the sentence level and not enough at the discourse level. The question was asking for the best overall understanding of the author’s point, not merely a statement that was directly paraphrased from one clause. My strategy was to match explicit wording: since the text says readers know Leclezio only at the level of his name, I chose the option about domestic readers knowing little. That approach was too shallow because it ignored that the passage uses Leclezio as an example to illustrate a broader claim about the relationship between serious literature and mass culture. I focused on what the passage denies—readers’ ignorance and the Nobel’s “unique taste”—without asking what positive inference the author is inviting instead.  

I also treated “Nobel Prize-winning works” and “Leclezio” as interchangeable, which was not justified by the passage’s structure. The author’s final sentence generalizes from one case to a wider pattern, so I should have evaluated which option captured that broader pattern rather than the most local fact. Another missed cue was the phrase about the “long-standing gap,” which signals a repeated, systemic phenomenon rather than a one-author knowledge gap. I should also have considered that an option can be inferentially stronger than a paraphrase if it better reflects the author’s main conclusion. The error came from privileging explicit mention over argumentative function. A better rule is: when a passage ends with a general explanatory claim, choose the option that matches that final generalization, not merely an earlier detail that prompted it.

item.context: The stems of trees and many plants usually contain a large amount of lignin which is difficult to be decomposed, so the efficiency of using them to extract biofuels is greatly reduced. At present, people have discovered a bacteria called Rhodococcus, which has the ability to decompose lignin in wood and other plants. Therefore, it is believed that Rhodococcus can be widely used in mostly discarded stalks, thereby greatly improving the utilization rate of biofuels.
item.question: Which one of the followings, if true, can best support the above conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rhodococcus can secrete an enzyme that has the ability to decompose lignin, but its secretion ability changes periodically.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some fungi also have the ability to decompose lignin. Studies have found that the growth of these fungi requires a specific temperature and humidity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rhodococcus is easy to cultivate. At present, the gene sequencing of Rhodococcus has been completed, so Rhodococcus can be used to produce enzymes that decompose lignin on a large scale.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lignin is a kind of oil-paper umbrella polymer material. So far, more than 95% of lignin is directly discharged into rivers or concentrated and burned, and few of them are used effectively.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion is about Rhodococcus being widely usable to improve biofuel utilization. The strongest support is evidence of practical large-scale application. C directly says Rhodococcus is easy to cultivate and can be mass-produced for lignin-degrading enzymes, making widespread use feasible.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a strengthen-the-conclusion approach, looking for the option that most directly bridges the gap between “can decompose lignin” and “can be widely used to improve biofuel utilization.” The key factor was feasibility at scale: the argument needed evidence that this bacterium or its enzymes could actually be produced and applied broadly, not just that lignin decomposition is possible in principle. My success came from identifying that one choice supplied the missing practical link of easy cultivation and large-scale enzyme production. For similar problems, I should explicitly ask what assumption connects the evidence to the conclusion, then choose the option that most directly makes that assumption true.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a strengthen-the-conclusion problem, not a mere fact-identification problem. The conclusion was not just that Rhodococcus can decompose lignin, because that premise was already given; it was the stronger claim that Rhodococcus can be widely used on discarded stalks to improve biofuel utilization. My strategy was to look for the option that most directly bridges the gap between laboratory capability and practical large-scale application. That was appropriate because strengthen questions often hinge on identifying the unstated feasibility condition behind the conclusion. I focused on the key constraint: for “widely used” to be credible, the organism or its lignin-degrading function must be scalable, cultivable, and deployable in quantity. Choice C supplied exactly that by indicating ease of cultivation and large-scale production of lignin-decomposing enzymes. I implicitly rejected options that were merely descriptive, comparative, or tangential, such as those discussing other organisms, periodic secretion, or the current waste of lignin. A useful alternative I did consider was whether evidence about competitors or lignin abundance might indirectly help, but those do not establish implementation feasibility. What made the reasoning successful was matching the answer to the argument’s weakest link rather than to the most familiar scientific fact. In similar problems, I should explicitly separate premise, conclusion, and missing operational assumption before evaluating choices. General rule: when a conclusion claims broad practical adoption, the strongest support is evidence that removes barriers to scalability and real-world use, not evidence that merely repeats the underlying mechanism.

item.context: If we do the three guarantees, that is, to ensure that highly pathogenic avian influenza does not spread through vehicles such as vehicles and ships. To ensure that traffic is smooth and that traffic is not blocked on the grounds of prevention and control. To ensure the prevention and control of avian influenza of all kinds of medical equipment, medicines, vaccines and other emergency supplies in a timely and rapid transport, then, highly pathogenic avian influenza can be prevented and treated.
item.question: Which of the following can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If highly pathogenic avian influenza can not be prevented and treated, then the prevention and control of avian influenza emergency supplies are not timely and rapid transport.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If highly pathogenic avian influenza cannot be prevented, it is spread by means of transport.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Either the highly pathogenic bird flu didn't spread, or we didn't do the three guarantees.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If highly pathogenic avian influenza cannot be prevented, then we are not ensuring smooth traffic.

response:
Reasoning: Let G = “do the three guarantees” and P = “avian influenza can be prevented and treated.” We have G → P. Also, by definition of G, G → “it didn’t spread through vehicles.” Option C is equivalent to that: “either it didn’t spread, or we didn’t do the three guarantees.”
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I translated the statement into conditional logic: doing the three guarantees implies successful prevention/treatment, and one component of those guarantees is stopping spread through transport. The key factor was recognizing that if “doing the three guarantees” includes “it does not spread through vehicles,” then by contraposition, if spread did occur, the three guarantees were not fully done; this matches the disjunctive form in the correct choice. The successful step was unpacking the bundled condition instead of treating it as a single opaque premise. For similar problems, break compound policies into their individual necessary components and test answer choices using valid conditional forms like contraposition, not converse or inverse.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stem as giving a sufficient condition: doing the “three guarantees” leads to successful prevention and treatment. That interpretation was correct, because the key logical form was conditional rather than causal proof of necessity. My strategy was to formalize the statement with symbols, treating the bundle of three guarantees as one antecedent and the prevention/treatment outcome as the consequent. That was appropriate, because symbolic translation makes it easier to test which option is entailed by the original statement.

The crucial evidence I used was that one of the three guarantees explicitly includes stopping spread through transportation, so “doing the three guarantees” implies “no spread through vehicles.” I also recognized that a choice phrased as “either not-X or not-Y” can be the contrapositive or material implication form of “Y implies X.” I avoided a common mistake by not inferring the converse: from “three guarantees imply prevention,” it does not follow that failure of prevention identifies which guarantee failed. That means options tying failure of prevention to one specific subcondition were too strong. I also did not assume that inability to prevent disease must be caused by transportation spread, which would have added unsupported causation.

What made the reasoning successful was separating sufficient conditions from necessary ones and checking entailment, not plausibility. In similar problems, I should continue translating compound policy statements into formal conditional structure before comparing options. General rule: when a statement gives a sufficient package of conditions, only infer consequences of that package or its valid contrapositives—not the converse, not a specific failed component, and not an unstated cause.

item.context: Boreal owls range over a much larger area than do other owls of similar size. Scientists have hypothesized that it is scarcity of prey that leads the owls to range so widely. This hypothesis would be hard to confirm directly, since it is not possible to produce a sufficiently accurate count of the populations of small mammals inhabiting the forests where boreal owls live. Careful study of owl behavior has, however, shown that boreal owls do range over larger areas when they live in regions where food of the sort eaten by small mammals is comparatively sparse. This indicates that the scientists' hypothesis is not sheer speculation.
item.question: In the argument given, the two boldfaced portions play which of the following roles?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first describes a position that the argument opposes; the second states the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first presents an explanatory hypothesis; the second presents evidence tending to support this hypothesis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first presents an explanatory hypothesis; the second presents evidence to support an alternative explanation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first describes a position that the argument opposes; the second presents evidence to undermine the support for the position being opposed.

response:
Reasoning: The first boldface is the scientists’ hypothesis explaining why boreal owls range widely: scarcity of prey. The second reports an observed correlation—owls range more widely where food for small mammals is sparse—which provides indirect evidence supporting that hypothesis, showing it is not mere speculation.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a role-identification approach: first classify each boldfaced statement by its function in the argument, then compare that structure to the answer choices. The key clue was that the first boldface is explicitly introduced as something “scientists have hypothesized,” while the second is introduced as a study result that “has shown” something, so it functions as supporting evidence. What helped was tracking the argument’s direction: the evidence is used to show the hypothesis is not mere speculation, not to oppose any position. For similar boldface questions, I should label each statement by source and function—hypothesis, evidence, conclusion, or opposing view—before reading the choices.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a boldface-role task, not as a test of whether the scientific hypothesis was true. The key was to identify the function each boldfaced statement played within the argument’s structure: one introduced a possible explanation, and the other supplied information used to assess that explanation. My strategy was to separate background, obstacle, evidence, and conclusion, which is the right approach for GMAT-style argument-role questions. I noticed that the first boldface was explicitly framed as something “scientists have hypothesized,” which signaled an explanatory hypothesis rather than a conclusion the author was asserting outright. I also used the fact that the second boldface came after “however” and after discussion of why direct confirmation was difficult, so it naturally functioned as indirect supporting evidence.  

An important part of the reasoning was recognizing that the evidence did not present a rival explanation; it linked food scarcity to wider ranging behavior in a way consistent with the hypothesis. I avoided the common shortcut of treating every later statement as the main conclusion. I also ruled out choices describing opposition, because nothing in the passage attacked the hypothesis; the final sentence actually defended it as more than “sheer speculation.” What made the reasoning successful was tracking how each statement related to the author’s final evaluative claim. In similar problems, I should keep identifying whether each boldface is a claim being argued for, evidence, background, concession, or an opposing view. General rule: determine boldface roles by their argumentative function relative to the conclusion, not by their subject matter alone.

item.context: There are three teachers, civil servants, and bank employees. Among them, A is not a bank employee, B is not a teacher, and C is not a civil servant. The teacher is older than B, and C is the youngest of the three.
item.question: Based on the above conditions, which of the following statements is wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A is a teacher

choices.label: B
choices.text: B is a civil servant

choices.label: C
choices.text: A is not a civil servant

choices.label: D
choices.text: C is not a bank employee

response:
Reasoning: C is youngest, so C cannot be the teacher because the teacher is older than B. Since C is also not a civil servant, C must be the bank employee. Then A, not being a bank employee, must be the teacher, and B must be the civil servant. So “C is not a bank employee” is wrong.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple:
I used a process-of-elimination approach, matching each person to the one job they could still hold after applying the “not” constraints and the age clue. The key factor was combining “the teacher is older than B” with “C is the youngest,” which ruled C out from being the teacher; then C’s remaining excluded role left only one possible occupation. From there, the rest of the assignments followed uniquely, which made it easy to test each statement. 

A useful general rule for similar problems is: translate each clue into explicit eliminations, identify the most restrictive clue first, and keep updating each person’s remaining possibilities until only one assignment remains for each.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the problem as a one-to-one assignment puzzle: each of the three people had a different job, and the task was to identify the statement that conflicts with all the constraints. That interpretation was correct, because the wording implies exactly one teacher, one civil servant, and one bank employee. My strategy was to combine the negative role constraints first, then use the age relation to eliminate the remaining ambiguity. That was appropriate because direct exclusions sharply reduce the possible assignments before checking the answer choices.

The key evidence I used was that the teacher is older than B, while C is the youngest, so C cannot be the teacher. I then combined that with the explicit statement that C is not a civil servant, which forces C into the only remaining occupation. From there, the remaining two roles were determined by A not being a bank employee and B not being a teacher. A useful feature of the reasoning was that each step was forced; I did not rely on guesswork or on testing options one by one.

The main assumption I used was exclusivity of occupations, and in this problem that assumption was justified. An alternative approach would have been to make a small grid of people versus jobs and mark impossibilities systematically. What made the reasoning successful was chaining constraints in the right order: age constraint first to eliminate one role, then explicit “not” conditions to finish the assignment. A transferable rule is: in matching problems, prioritize constraints that create impossibility by comparison or order, because they often convert partial exclusions into a uniquely forced placement.

item.context: Nowadays, film creations make a lot of repeated use of hot topics. There is a market for a theme, and many people flock on it, which is not a healthy film ecology. In contrast, the excavation of national culture is rare, such as the development of traditional festivals such as Dragon Boat Festival and Mid-Autumn Festival, and the use of national artistic elements such as Kunqu Opera and Huangmei Opera. Once the cultural wealth of the Chinese nation is excavated attentively, what is presented in front of the creators is a splendid treasure house of art, and domestic films will also usher in a spring of a hundred flowers blooming.
item.question: Which of the following is the most accurate summary of the main thrust of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Domestic movies need to try their best to get rid of the unhealthy ecology

choices.label: B
choices.text: Domestic movies will usher in a spring in which a hundred flowers blossom

choices.label: C
choices.text: Domestic films should not fall into the misunderstanding of theme reuse

choices.label: D
choices.text: Domestic movies should dig deep into the treasure of national culture

response:
Reasoning: The passage criticizes repeated use of hot topics, but its core emphasis is the positive solution: creators should excavate national culture and artistic traditions. That is presented as the way for domestic films to flourish.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea summarization approach: identify the problem mentioned, then distinguish it from the author’s real emphasis and proposed remedy. The key factor was that the passage spends more weight on the rarity and value of exploring national culture, and presents that as the path to future flourishing, so the positive recommendation is central. My answer was correct because I did not stop at the criticism of repetitive themes; I tracked what the passage ultimately advocates. For similar questions, first separate background criticism and predicted outcomes from the author’s core prescription, and choose the option that best captures that central recommendation.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the passage as asking for the central argument, not merely a detail or one side of a contrast. That was the key first step, because the paragraph contains both a criticism of current film trends and a proposed direction for improvement. My strategy was to identify the author’s evaluative structure: problem first, then remedy, then a positive forecast based on that remedy. This was appropriate because “main thrust” questions usually hinge on what the author is ultimately advocating, not on background complaints or predicted outcomes.

The evidence that mattered most was the contrast signaled by “in contrast” and the causal chain that followed: careful excavation of national culture leads to rich artistic resources and then to flourishing domestic film. I correctly treated the comments about repeated hot topics as context rather than the main point. I also avoided choosing the optimistic ending as the thesis, because it functions as a consequence of the recommendation rather than the recommendation itself. One assumption that helped was that the final value judgment in an argumentative passage often reveals the author’s main purpose. 

The main alternative I needed to guard against was selecting an option that captured only the criticism of “theme reuse.” What made the reasoning successful was distinguishing between diagnosis, prescription, and prediction. In similar problems, I should map each sentence to its role in the argument before matching choices. A transferable rule is: when a passage presents a problem, a solution, and an outcome, the main idea is usually the solution the author endorses, not the problem description or the promised result.

item.context: Last year, a town assigned three university student village officials, A, B and C, to work in Hefeng Village, Tuanjie Village and Yangmei Village respectively. At first, people did not know which of them was assigned to which village, but they just made the following three guesses: (1) A was assigned to work in Hefeng Village, and B was assigned to work in Tuanjie Village; (2) A was assigned to work in Tuanjie Village. C was assigned to work in Hefeng Village; (3) A was assigned to work in Yangmei Village, and B was assigned to work in Hefeng Village. It turned out that all three guesses were only half right.
item.question: It can be seen that which of the following is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A is assigned to work in Hefeng Village, B is assigned to Tuanjie Village, and C is assigned to Yangmei Village

choices.label: B
choices.text: A is assigned to Tuanjie Village, B is assigned  to Hefeng Village, and C is assigned  to Yangmei Village

choices.label: C
choices.text: An is assigned to work in Yangmei Village, B is assigned to Hefeng Village, and C is assigned to Tuanjie Village

choices.label: D
choices.text: A is assigned to work in Yangmei Village, B is assigned to Tuanjie Village, and C is assigned to Hefeng Village

response:
Reasoning: Each guess has two claims and is “half right,” so exactly one claim in each is true. If A=H or A=T, contradictions arise. Thus A=Y. Then guess (3) makes B≠H; guess (1) then forces B=T; hence C=H. This matches option D.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a constraint-satisfaction approach: each statement pair was treated as containing exactly one true claim because “half right” means one of two assertions is correct. The key factor was testing A’s possible assignments first, since A appears in all three guesses and quickly creates contradictions or forces the rest of the mapping. The successful step was converting the verbal condition into an exact logical rule and eliminating cases systematically rather than guessing from the options. For similar problems, translate each statement into a precise truth-count condition first, then start with the variable that appears most often to narrow the possibilities efficiently.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the problem correctly as a constraint-satisfaction question: each of the three guesses contained two specific assignment claims, and “only half right” meant exactly one of the two claims in each guess was true. That interpretation was crucial, because if “half right” were treated loosely as “partly right,” the deductions would not be rigorous. My strategy was to convert each statement into a pair of boolean conditions and use exclusivity of assignments to test possible placements for A first. That was appropriate because A appears in all three guesses, so fixing A sharply reduces the remaining possibilities.

The key evidence I used was the one-to-one matching between three people and three villages, plus the fact that every guess contributes exactly one true and one false claim. I considered A=H and A=T and recognized that each choice created conflicts with the truth pattern required across the three guesses. Once those were eliminated, A=Y followed, and the remaining two guesses constrained B and C uniquely. A useful shortcut I used was starting with the variable that appears most often, but this shortcut was valid only because I still checked consistency against all statements.

What made the reasoning successful was not trial-and-error alone, but systematically applying “exactly one true per pair” together with the permutation constraint. In similar problems, I should continue translating verbal conditions into exact logical forms before testing cases. A general rule is: when several two-part statements are each “half true,” represent each as an exclusive-or and combine that with any one-to-one assignment constraints to eliminate cases efficiently.

item.context: If you are a fan of books, you are bound to have many. Most book collectors also read books from their own collections; But some book collectors buy books because they like their value and their fine binding, and save reading for their leisure time, and once they think so, the new books are likely to go unread. However, as long as these cold books are borrowed by friends, collectors will be out of their wits and uneasy all day.
item.question: Based on the above information, which of the following can be concluded?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some collectors regard their books as friends.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some book collectors like to read their own books at leisure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some book collectors read through their collections.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some book collectors do not immediately read their new purchases.

response:
Reasoning: The passage explicitly says some collectors buy books for value/binding, postpone reading to leisure time, and thus new books are likely to go unread. This directly supports that some collectors do not read newly bought books right away. The other options add ideas not stated or are too strong.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a direct textual-inference approach: I looked for the option that restated the passage without adding assumptions. The key clue was the statement that some collectors buy books for their value and binding, save reading for leisure time, and therefore new books are likely to go unread. That supported an immediate conclusion about delayed reading, while the other choices required stronger or different claims than the passage gave. For similar problems, I should match answer choices to the weakest statement strictly guaranteed by the text and reject any option that paraphrases too aggressively or introduces new motives.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task as asking for the strongest conclusion that must follow from the passage, not merely something plausible. That interpretation was correct, because multiple-choice logic questions usually hinge on distinguishing direct entailment from attractive overreading. My strategy was to identify explicit quantifiers like “most,” “some,” and causal language like “once they think so, the new books are likely to go unread,” then map those onto the answer choices. That was an appropriate strategy because the passage gives a directly stated subgroup of collectors and a directly stated behavior.

The key evidence I used was that some collectors buy books for value and binding, postpone reading to leisure time, and therefore leave new books unread for at least some time. I correctly rejected options that introduced unsupported metaphors or stronger claims than the text warranted. For example, saying collectors regard books as “friends” confuses emotional distress over lending with literal personification, and saying someone “reads through their collections” overstates “most read books from their own collections.” One important assumption I handled correctly was that “likely to go unread” supports “do not immediately read,” which is weaker and therefore justified. I also considered whether “at leisure” meant they read their own books, but the passage does not guarantee that for the subgroup in question.

What made the reasoning successful was matching the exact logical strength of the passage to the exact logical strength of the option. In similar problems, I should continue translating text into minimal warranted claims instead of choosing answers that sound intuitively true. A transferable rule is: when evaluating conclusions, prefer the option that restates an explicitly supported claim at equal or weaker strength, and reject any option that adds motive, scope, or certainty not stated in the passage.

item.context: Paleontologists recently excavated two corresponding sets of dinosaur tracks, one left by a large grazing dinosaur and the other by a smaller predatory dinosaur. The two sets of tracks make abrupt turns repeatedly in tandem, suggesting that the predator was following the grazing dinosaur and had matched its stride. Modern predatory mammals, such as lions, usually match the stride of prey they are chasing immediately before they strike those prey. This suggests that the predatory dinosaur was chasing the grazing dinosaur and attacked immediately afterwards.
item.question: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the statement that the predatory dinosaur was following the grazing dinosaur and had matched its stride?

choices.label: A

reflections.simple: I used a close-reading, pronoun-resolution approach and focused mainly on identifying what “it/its” referred to in the passage. The key clue that drove my choice was the sentence about particles being captured by the earth’s magnetic field and then colliding with oxygen and nitrogen, which made me concentrate too narrowly on reference rather than checking whether each option was directly supported. My error was treating an unsupported inference about magnetic-field strength as if it were stated by the passage. reflections.complex: I interpreted the task as a search for the one statement that contradicted the passage, but I narrowed my attention too quickly to the obvious grammar issue involving the pronoun “it.” That interpretation was only partly correct, because the question was not asking which sentence had an unclear reference; it was asking which option was not supported by the passage’s stated content. My strategy was to test each option against explicit wording, but in practice I applied that test unevenly: I scrutinized the pronoun option closely and treated the others as broadly consistent without checking whether they added new causal claims. The passage says charged particles are captured by Earth’s magnetic field and guided toward the poles, but it does not compare stronger versus weaker magnetic fields or say that field strength changes aurora frequency. I missed that distinction between “is involved in the mechanism” and “affects the probability,” which is an inference beyond the text. I also assumed that because an option about pronoun reference looked flawed, it must be the intended wrong answer, even though the passage itself is grammatically awkward and such questions usually target meaning, not editorial errors. An alternative I should have considered was whether any option introduced an unstated variable or causal relationship. The specific cause of the error was prioritizing local grammatical ambiguity over global support from the passage. In similar problems, I should classify each choice as explicitly stated, reasonably paraphrased, or unsupported inference before deciding. A transferable rule is: when asked what is wrong “according to the passage,” eliminate choices that merely restate imperfect wording only after checking whether another choice adds information the passage never claims.

item.context: A company has developed an air conditioning management system that can automatically turn on and off the air conditioning by detecting the flow of people. item.question: Which of the following is the most reasonable explanation for the above phenomenon?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many employees have strong environmental awareness and have developed the habit of turning off the air conditioner when they go out

response:
Reasoning: The system’s value proposition is saving electricity in offices. If modern air conditioners already consume much less power, the extra savings from automatic on/off control may be too small to justify buying the system, explaining weak sales. Other options either support sales or are less central.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a cost-benefit reasoning approach, focusing on whether the product’s energy-saving advantage had become less valuable in the market. The key clue I prioritized was the claim that the system saves electricity, so I looked for an option that would weaken demand by reducing the importance of that benefit. My mistake was choosing an indirect market explanation instead of the more immediate adoption barrier: even a useful product can sell poorly if it is hard to use and requires specialized operators. For similar questions, I should first test whether an option directly explains why target customers would avoid purchasing, especially practical barriers like complexity, cost, or usability.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the strongest reason why a product with an apparently clear benefit still sold poorly, which was the right task. My strategy was to look for a factor that would weaken the product’s value proposition, and I focused almost entirely on whether the promised energy savings were still economically meaningful. That led me to prefer the market-background option about lower baseline air-conditioner energy use, because it seemed to reduce the incremental benefit of the system. The flaw is that I treated “reduced benefit” as automatically a better explanation than “adoption barrier,” without comparing which one more directly explains low purchasing behavior. In product-sales questions, a direct obstacle to use, installation, or operation often has more explanatory force than a general trend that merely shrinks the payoff. I also missed an important constraint in the stimulus: the system has already been on the market for years, so persistent weak sales suggest a practical impediment to implementation, not just a somewhat weaker need. My reasoning assumed buyers make decisions mainly on energy economics, but organizations also care about complexity, staffing, maintenance, and operational burden. I should have explicitly tested each option by asking: does this make customers less willing or less able to adopt the system? The overlooked alternative did that more directly than the one I chose. A better general rule is: when explaining weak adoption of a beneficial product, prioritize choices that create concrete friction in purchase or use over choices that only moderately reduce the product’s benefit.

item.context: Among the representatives of a public opinion forum on traffic regulation, one is from Heilongjiang, two are from the north, one is from Guangdong, two are only responsible for passenger transport, and three are only engaged in cargo transportation.
item.question: If the above introduction involves all the representatives of the symposium, which of the following is correct about the representatives participating in the symposium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It may be at least 3 people, and it may be at most 8 people

choices.label: B
choices.text: It may be at least 5 people, and it may be at most 8 people

choices.label: C
choices.text: It may be at least 5 people, and it may be at most 9people

choices.label: D
choices.text: It may be at least 3 people, and it may be at most 9 people

response:
Reasoning: “Only passenger” and “only cargo” are mutually exclusive, so at least \(2+3=5\) people. Geographic labels can overlap with these 5, so minimum is 5. For the maximum, make overlaps as small as possible: \(1\) Heilongjiang person overlaps with the \(2\) northerners, giving \(3\) geographic people total, plus \(2+3=5\) transport people, so \(3+5=8\).

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a set-overlap counting approach: treat each description as a group and minimize or maximize the total by allowing as much overlap as the wording permits or forcing as little overlap as possible. The key factor was that “only responsible for passenger transport” and “only engaged in cargo transportation” are mutually exclusive, so those two counts must contribute at least five distinct people. The successful step was recognizing that the geographic categories are not stated to be exclusive with the transport categories, and that the Heilongjiang representative can be one of the two northerners. For similar problems, first identify which categories must be disjoint and which may overlap, then compute bounds by explicitly maximizing and minimizing overlap.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as a set-overlap problem asking for the possible minimum and maximum total number of representatives, given several partially overlapping descriptions. That interpretation was correct, because the key is not to identify exact people, but to determine how much the listed categories can coincide or must remain distinct. My strategy was to separate the categories into those that are mutually exclusive and those that can overlap, then optimize overlap for the minimum and minimize overlap for the maximum. This was appropriate because “only responsible for passenger transport” and “only engaged in cargo transportation” define disjoint groups, so those counts impose a hard lower bound. I correctly used the fact that the geographic labels do not conflict with the transport-role labels, so they can be assigned to the same people when minimizing the total. For the maximum, I also correctly noticed that the person from Heilongjiang can be one of the two people from the north, so the geographic information contributes at most three distinct people rather than four. A shortcut that helped was treating each statement as a set count and asking whether intersections were required, forbidden, or optional. One alternative I needed to keep in mind was whether “from Heilongjiang” might force an additional person beyond “from the north,” but regional inclusion prevents that. The reasoning succeeded because I respected exclusivity constraints exactly and exploited overlap only where logically allowed. In similar problems, I should systematically classify every pair of categories as disjoint, subset-related, or freely overlapping before doing any arithmetic. A transferable rule is: when finding extrema from category counts, maximize overlap for minima and minimize overlap for maxima, but only within the logical compatibility structure of the categories.

item.context: To use the pool at City Gym, one must have a membership there. Sarah has a membership at City Gym. She must ttherefore use the pool there at least occasionally.
item.question: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: mistakes a policy that is strictly enforced for a policy to which exceptions are made

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that one or the other of two alternatives must be the case without establishing that no other alternative is possible

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a statement whose truth is required for the conclusion to be true as though it were a statement whose truth ensures that the conclusion is true

choices.label: D
choices.text: concludes that a person has a certain attribute simply because that person belongs to a group most of whose members have that attribute

response:
Reasoning: The argument says membership is necessary to use the pool, then assumes membership guarantees pool use. But a condition required for a conclusion can be true without ensuring that conclusion. Sarah can be a member and still never use the pool.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a conditional-reasoning approach, identifying the difference between a necessary condition and a sufficient condition. The key factor was that “having a membership” is required in order to use the pool, but that does not mean membership guarantees pool use. My success came from translating the argument into a one-way relationship and noticing that it was being reversed in effect. For similar problems, I should explicitly test whether a stated condition is merely required or actually enough to force the conclusion before accepting an inference.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument as testing whether the conclusion followed from a necessary-condition statement, and that was the right lens. The key structure was: using the pool requires membership, and from that the argument inferred that having membership implies pool use. My strategy was to translate the claim into a conditional relationship and check whether the conclusion reversed or overstated that relationship. That approach was appropriate because flaw questions often hinge on whether a condition is necessary, sufficient, or neither. The crucial fact I used was that a requirement for an activity does not by itself make the activity occur; it only limits who could do it. I also correctly noticed an unconsidered possibility: Sarah may satisfy the requirement and still never engage in the activity.  

What made the reasoning successful was resisting the tempting but invalid move from “must have X to do Y” to “has X, therefore does Y.” I did not rely on frequency, typical behavior, or exceptions, which helped eliminate the other choices. One assumption I correctly avoided was treating group membership as evidence of behavior. In similar problems, I should continue formalizing statements as “Y only if X” and then ask whether the conclusion illicitly turns a necessary condition into a sufficient one. General rule: if a statement says one condition is required for another, you may infer the first from the second, but not the second from the first.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a conditional-chain approach, translating each statement into a necessary-condition sequence and then linking the conditions transitively. The key factor was the repeated “cannot … without first …” structure, which signals that one step is required before another, allowing a clean A → B → C pattern. My success came from focusing on logical form rather than topic and noticing that only one choice preserved both the chained necessities and the conclusion about an unavoidable prior step. For similar problems, convert wording like “cannot without” or “unless” into conditional relationships first, then match the exact inference pattern rather than surface content.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stimulus as a pure conditional-reasoning question asking for the same logical form, not the same topic or plausibility. The key structure was a chain of necessary conditions: reaching the final destination required an intermediate stop, and that intermediate stop itself required an earlier stop, so the final destination also required the earlier stop. My strategy was to translate the language “cannot … without” and “must … before” into necessity relations and then look for transitivity across those relations. That was the right strategy because the argument does not depend on probabilities, quantities, or causal effects; it depends only on nested prerequisites. The crucial facts I used were that “Lhasa requires Chengdu” and “Chengdu requires Xian,” which combine into “Lhasa requires Xian.” I also correctly recognized that the conclusion states an unavoidable prerequisite rather than a sufficient path or one of several alternatives.

A possible trap would have been to confuse “requires” with “guarantees,” or to overlook that “unless” in an answer choice can also express a necessary condition. I also needed to avoid answer choices involving “some,” disjunctions, or probabilistic claims, because those introduce different inference patterns. The reasoning succeeded because I matched abstract form rather than surface wording. For similar problems, I should systematically symbolize prerequisite language and compare conclusion type: universal necessity, existential claim, or likelihood. A general rule is: when one condition is necessary for a second, and the second is necessary for a third, the first is necessary for the third.

item.context: Vicious boycott refers to uncivilized, irrational, and potentially serious boycott behaviors that the parties take when their legitimate rights have been damaged for a long time and cannot be resolved after repeated negotiations.
item.question: Which of the following is a vicious boycott?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The owner of a community could not tolerate the noise of the square dance. After many failed communications, he raised 260,000 yuan to purchase a loudspeaker system commonly known as the Tweeter and played car horns in the square every day

choices.label: B
choices.text: The orchard contracted by Lao Li has been visited by thieves many times. In order to avoid greater losses, he wrapped wire around several fruit trees and connected them to electricity. Since then, the orchard has never been stolen again

choices.label: C
choices.text: The community property found that the speed of the express delivery battery car was too fast and there was a safety hazard. They were repeatedly asked to slow down, but with little effect, so all express delivery battery cars were prohibited from entering the community

choices.label: D
choices.text: A certain community has been harassed by psoriasis advertisements for a long time, so I bought a call to death software and called the mobile phone numbers on the advertisements one by one, which quickly solved this old problem

response:
Reasoning: Vicious boycott is an irrational, uncivilized retaliatory act after rights are repeatedly infringed and negotiations fail. A fits best: after repeated failed communication about square-dance noise, the owner used loud horn noise to retaliate. B is dangerous anti-theft, C is management control, D lacks the negotiation element.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I broke the concept into elements like long-term rights infringement, repeated failed negotiation, and then an uncivilized or irrational retaliatory response. The key factor was that one option clearly included both prior communication attempts and a noisy retaliatory act that mirrored the original disturbance rather than solving it through lawful channels. My success came from separating retaliation from prevention or management: some choices involved deterrence or regulation, but not a boycott-style counterattack after failed negotiation. For similar problems, explicitly map each option against every required element of the definition and reject any choice missing even one core condition.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a definition-match problem: identify the option that fits all elements of “vicious boycott,” not just one dramatic or harmful feature. My strategy was to break the definition into components: a legitimate right has been harmed for a long time, repeated negotiation has failed, and the response is uncivilized, irrational, and potentially serious. That was the right approach because this kind of item is usually decided by checking necessary conditions one by one. In evaluating the choices, I correctly treated “repeated negotiations” as a key constraint rather than a background detail. I also distinguished retaliatory harassment from other kinds of conduct, such as self-protection or administrative restriction, which helped exclude the options that were harmful but not really “boycott” behavior in the defined sense.  

A useful part of the reasoning was noticing that the selected option involved reciprocal nuisance: the person responded to noise with intentionally amplified noise, which matches irrational and uncivilized retaliation after failed communication. I also correctly saw that one option was more like dangerous anti-theft prevention and another was a management rule, so they did not fit the conceptual category. My main shortcut was treating “vicious boycott” broadly as retaliatory obstruction rather than insisting on an economic boycott; in this question that was justified by the given definition. Still, I should always compare near-miss options more explicitly, especially when several involve escalation or harm. The success came from using the full definitional checklist instead of focusing only on severity. General rule: for definition-based multiple choice, map each option against every required element, and eliminate any choice missing even one core condition.

item.context: The enthusiastic acceptance of ascetic lifestyles evidenced in the surviving writings of monastic authors indicates that medieval societies were much less concerned with monetary gain than are contemporary Western cultures.

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-identification approach: I looked for the gap between the evidence cited and the broad conclusion drawn. The key factor was that the evidence came only from surviving writings of monastic authors, who are a narrow, self-selecting group with values that likely differ from the larger medieval population. My answer was correct because I focused on representativeness: the argument moved from a specialized subgroup to all of medieval society. For similar problems, I should explicitly test whether the source of evidence is representative of the population the conclusion is about before accepting any generalization.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the flaw in an argument that moves from evidence about one group’s writings to a conclusion about the values of an entire society. That interpretation was correct, because the core issue was not whether asceticism was defined precisely or whether modern standards were imposed, but whether the evidence base matched the scope of the conclusion. My strategy was to compare the population described in the premise with the population described in the conclusion. That is an appropriate flaw-identification method for arguments that infer broad social attitudes from a narrow body of evidence.

The key fact I used was that the surviving writings came from monastic authors, who are a specialized subgroup explicitly committed to religious renunciation. I correctly recognized that such people are especially likely to praise ascetic lifestyles, making them a poor proxy for all of medieval society. I also noticed that “surviving writings” introduces an additional filter, since what survives historically may be even less representative than what was originally written. A shortcut that helped was asking, “Who is speaking, and are they typical of the group the conclusion is about?” That shortcut worked well here.

I should also have briefly checked the other answer choices by matching each to the argument’s actual structure, rather than stopping once I found a plausible flaw. The reasoning succeeded because it focused on representativeness rather than on surface-level wording. A useful general rule is: when a conclusion describes a whole population, test whether the evidence comes from a subset that has a built-in bias on the very issue being inferred.

item.context: In some countries, national planners have attempted to address the problems resulting from increasing urbanization by reducing migration from rural areas. But some economists have suggested an alternative approach. These economists assert that planners could solve these problems effectively by trading goods or services produced by a predominantly urban population in order to obtain the agricultural products that were previously produced domestically.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, would provide the most support for the economists' assertion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Government subsidies to urban manufacturers can ease the problems caused by the migration of people from rural to urban areas.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Problems associated with migration to cities from rural areas are primarily due to trade imbalances between countries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A scarcity of agricultural products is a central element of many problems created by urbanization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All problems that have economic causes must have economic solutions.

response:
Reasoning: The economists’ plan is to replace domestic agriculture by importing agricultural products through trade. This would best solve urbanization problems if those problems stem largely from too little agriculture after rural-to-urban migration. Choice C directly supports that link; the others are irrelevant or too broad.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a support/strengthen approach: I identified the economists’ proposal as replacing lost domestic agriculture through trade, then looked for the choice that most directly connected that proposal to solving urbanization-related problems. The key factor was the causal link between rural-to-urban migration, reduced agricultural output, and the resulting urban problems. My reasoning succeeded because I focused on the answer that made imported agricultural goods directly address the core problem, rather than choices that were broader, off-topic, or merely tangential. For similar questions, first isolate the proposal’s mechanism, then choose the option that strengthens the exact causal step required for that mechanism to work.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a strengthen task: the goal was not to prove the economists’ policy works in every respect, but to find the fact that most directly increases the plausibility of their proposal. I recognized that the proposal depends on a causal link between urbanization and some problem that could be alleviated by obtaining agricultural goods through trade rather than producing them domestically. My strategy was to identify the mechanism embedded in the economists’ assertion and then look for the choice that most directly confirms that mechanism. That was appropriate because strengthen questions are best handled by mapping the claim’s assumptions and checking which option supports a necessary bridge.

The key evidence I used was that the economists want a predominantly urban population to trade for agricultural products, so their plan only addresses urbanization problems effectively if shortages of agricultural products are among those problems. I correctly dismissed the other choices because they were either off-mechanism, too broad, or introduced a different explanation. One useful constraint I implicitly applied was relevance: support must connect specifically to the proposed trade-for-agriculture solution, not merely to urbanization or economics in general. I did not rely on any risky shortcut like choosing the answer that restated the stimulus; instead I tested whether each option made the proposal more likely to succeed. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the proposal’s hidden assumption rather than surface wording. In similar problems, I should continue to ask, “What must be true for this plan to address the stated problem?” A transferable rule is: when evaluating a proposed solution, prefer the option that confirms the problem includes a factor the solution directly targets.

item.context: A, B, C, and D participated in the competition together, and their results were different.There are three people a, b, and c who guess the result. a said:A got the first, B got the second,b said:C got the second, D got the fourth,c said:A got the second, D got the fourth.In fact, all three of them were half right.
item.question: Which of the following is true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: D fourth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A first, C third.

choices.label: C
choices.text: B first, D third.

choices.label: D
choices.text: C first, D fourth.

response:
Reasoning: Since b and c both say “D got fourth” and each is half right, take D=4th. Then b’s “C=2nd” is false and c’s “A=2nd” is false. For a to be half right, “B=2nd” must be true and “A=1st” false. So remaining places give C=1st, A=3rd, B=2nd, D=4th.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a constraint-elimination approach: I treated each person’s two claims as a pair where exactly one must be true, then checked overlaps between the guesses. The key factor was that two different people made the same claim about D’s placement, which made that statement the most informative starting point because it affected two “half-right” conditions at once. The successful step was propagating the consequences of that shared claim and then forcing the remaining statements to balance to exactly one true per speaker. For similar problems, convert “half right” into an exact-count rule and test the statement that appears in multiple testimonies first, since shared claims usually create the strongest constraints.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a constraint-satisfaction problem: each of the three people made two claims, and “half right” means exactly one of each person’s two claims is true. My strategy was to look for overlap among the claims, because repeated statements often create strong constraints. In particular, two people made the same claim about one competitor’s finishing position, so testing that shared claim first was an efficient move. That was appropriate because if the shared claim were false, then both of those speakers would need their other claims to be true, which would force one competitor into two different positions and create a contradiction. Once the shared claim was fixed as true, I correctly propagated the consequences: each of those two speakers then had their remaining claim false. I then used the “exactly one true” condition on the first speaker to determine which of that speaker’s two claims had to hold. The remaining placements followed from uniqueness of ranks, which I implicitly used correctly.

A useful detail I handled well was that “results were different” means all four ranks are distinct, so no two people can share a place. I did assume that “half right” means one true and one false, but that is justified because each speaker made exactly two statements. An alternative approach would have been to formalize all six claims and test cases systematically, but the overlap-based shortcut was sound here because I checked consistency rather than guessing. The general rule is: in logic problems with paired claims and “exactly one true,” prioritize repeated statements and use contradiction to determine whether they must be true or false before assigning remaining positions.

item.context: Economist: The price of tap water in our region should be raised drastically. Supplies in local freshwater reservoirs have been declining for years because water is being used faster than it can be replenished. Since the price of tap water has been low, few users have bothered to adopt even easy conservation measures.
item.question: The two sections in boldface play which of the following roles in the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first is an observation for which the second provides an explanation; the second is the main conclusion but not the only conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first is the only conclusion; the second provides an explanation for the first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first is a conclusion for which support is provided, and which in turn supports the main conclusion; the second is the main conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first is a premise supporting the argument's main conclusion; so is the second.

response:
Reasoning: The main conclusion is “The price of tap water… should be raised drastically.” The first bold statement gives a reason: reservoir supplies are declining. The second also gives a reason: low prices have discouraged conservation. Both support the main conclusion directly.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I identified the argument’s main conclusion first by looking for the policy recommendation, then classified the boldfaced statements by how they supported that claim. The key factor was that both bold parts are presented as independent reasons for raising water prices: one establishes a scarcity problem, and the other shows why current pricing fails to encourage conservation. My success came from separating the conclusion from the background evidence instead of treating either boldface statement as an intermediate conclusion. For similar role-of-statement questions, first pinpoint the main conclusion, then test whether each highlighted statement is being supported or is instead supplying support.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as a boldface-role task: identify not whether the claims are true, but how each boldfaced statement functions within the structure of the argument. That interpretation was correct, because the key issue was locating the main conclusion and distinguishing it from supporting premises. My strategy was to first isolate the normative recommendation—raising the price drastically—as the main conclusion, since it is the only explicit “should” statement. Then I tested each boldfaced statement by asking whether it supported that recommendation, restated it, or was itself being supported by other claims. Both bold statements clearly supplied independent reasons for the recommendation: one described a scarcity problem, and the other described weak incentives for conservation under current pricing. I did not treat either bold statement as an intermediate conclusion because neither was presented as inferred from another claim in the passage. A possible trap was to see the second boldface as explaining the first, but that would confuse causal background with argumentative role. Another trap was to assume the first boldface was the main conclusion because it sounds important and policy-relevant, even though it is descriptive rather than prescriptive. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on conclusion markers and on support direction rather than on topic prominence. In similar problems, I should map each statement with arrows—what supports what—before matching answer choices. General rule: in argument-structure questions, identify the claim the author is trying to get the reader to accept, then classify every other statement only by its inferential relation to that claim.

item.context: Citizen: The primary factor determining a dog' s disposition is not its breed, but its home environment. A bad owner can undo generations of careful breeding. Legislation focusing on specific breeds of dogs would not address the effects of human behavior in raising and training animals. As a result, such breed-specific legislation could never effectively protect the public from vicious dogs. Moreover, in my view, the current laws are perfectly adequate.
item.question: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn by the citizen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The home environment of dogs would not be regulated by breed-specific legislation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Irresponsible dog owners are capable of producing dogs with bad dispositions regardless of generations of careful breeding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The vicious-dog laws that are currently in effect do not address the effects of human behavior in raising and training dogs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The public would not be effectively protected from violent dogs by breed-specific legislation.

response:
Reasoning: The citizen argues that breed-specific laws ignore the real cause of viciousness—how dogs are raised—so such laws “could never effectively protect the public from vicious dogs.” The remark about current laws is an additional opinion, not the main conclusion.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used conclusion-identification reasoning by separating premises from the author’s main claim and checking which choice matched the claim most directly. The key factor was the indicator phrase “As a result,” which signaled the conclusion that followed from the earlier premises about environment and owner behavior. My answer was correct because I treated the statements about breed and home environment as support, and the remark about current laws as an additional side opinion rather than the central point. For similar problems, I should locate conclusion indicators and then verify which answer restates the claim supported by the other statements, not a subsidiary premise or extra commentary.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task as a main-conclusion question: the goal was to identify the claim the citizen is trying to prove, not merely a premise or an additional opinion. That interpretation was correct because the argument contains supporting statements about dog disposition and owner behavior, then draws a policy consequence from them. My strategy was to track the argumentative structure by looking for conclusion indicators such as “as a result,” which signaled the central inference. That was appropriate here because the passage included both background claims and a final side comment about existing laws, making structure more important than topic matching.

The key evidence I used was the chain: disposition depends primarily on environment, breed-focused laws ignore environment, therefore those laws will fail at the public-safety goal. I also correctly treated the statement about current laws being “perfectly adequate” as a separate opinion rather than the main conclusion, since it is introduced with “moreover” and is not supported by the earlier reasoning. A tempting wrong path would have been to choose a premise that restated the environmental point or the claim about bad owners. Another tempting error would have been to select a statement about what the laws regulate rather than what follows from that fact. The reasoning succeeded because I distinguished intermediate support from the author’s ultimate policy judgment. In similar problems, I should map premise → intermediate claim → final evaluative or predictive claim before matching answer choices. General rule: in arguments with multiple assertions, the main conclusion is the claim most directly supported by the others and least likely to function as support for another statement.

item.context: According to a recent survey, 47% of Chinese said they only put some of the remaining cash at the end of the month into savings. Almost 1/3 of people say they don't save money at all. China's household savings rate will gradually decline in the future because of demographic factors (the aging of the previous generation of only children), increased affluence and improvements in the financial sector (such as the introduction of more insurance products). The savings rate of urban households is now lower than the national average.
item.question: Which of the following options is the main indication of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The consumption concept of careful calculation is being watered down.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Chinese broke the piggy bank.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The model of careful calculation and postponing consumption is becoming obsolete.

choices.label: D
choices.text: People's concept and mode of financial management have changed.

response:
Reasoning: The passage centers on declining savings behavior and its causes: demographics, higher affluence, and better financial products. This shows a broader shift in how people think about and manage money, not just weakened thrift or obsolete old habits alone.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea synthesis approach: I looked for the choice that best captured all the evidence in the passage rather than one striking detail. The key factor was that the passage gives multiple structural reasons for lower saving—demographics, rising affluence, and new financial products—so the conclusion had to be broader than simply “people save less.” My success came from distinguishing between narrow, emotionally worded options about thrift and the broader option about changing financial attitudes and methods. For similar problems, first group the passage’s supporting details by theme, then choose the option that covers all of them at the highest appropriate level of abstraction.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s central idea, not a detail, tone judgment, or catchy headline. That was the key framing choice, because the options ranged from narrow symptoms to a broader summary. My strategy was to distinguish between descriptive facts in the passage and the higher-level conclusion those facts supported. I used the evidence that the passage mentioned multiple causes of lower saving behavior—demographics, rising affluence, and financial-sector development—which pointed to a structural shift rather than a single attitude like reduced thrift. I also noticed that the passage compared urban households with the national average, which reinforced that it was describing an evolving pattern of household financial behavior. One useful assumption I made was that the best “main indication” should cover both changing ideas and changing practices, since the text discussed both saving habits and external conditions. I correctly rejected options that sounded vivid or ideological but captured only one facet, such as the decline of frugality or an outdated consumption model. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the breadth of the answer to the breadth of the passage. In similar problems, I should continue testing each option for scope: too narrow, too extreme, or appropriately comprehensive. A transferable rule is: when a passage gives several causes and several behavioral signs, the main idea should usually be the broad change they collectively illustrate, not any single symptom.

item.context: Astronomer: Earth was bombarded repeatedly by comets and asteroids early in its history. This bombardment probably sterilized the surface and prevented life from originating during this early period in Earth' s geological history. Meanwhile, Mars escaped severe bombardment, and so there could have been microbial life on Mars prior to there being such life on Earth. Because many meteorites originating from Mars have landed on Earth, life on Earth may have started when living microbes were carried here from Mars on a meteorite.
item.question: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the astronomer's argument by the statement that there could have been microbial life on Mars prior to there being such life on Earth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a claim for which justification is provided and that, if true, establishes the truth of the argument's main conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a claim for which some justification is provided and that is required in order to establish the argument's main conclusion.

choices.label: C
