I correctly ignored extra information such as blood type, determination to donate, and personal gratitude, because none of that was connected to the stated rule. One assumption I made was that “least likely” means those matching either disfavored condition are comparatively deprioritized, so the best answer is the one clearly outside both categories. I should also have considered whether any option might be ambiguous under both conditions, but the choices were distinct enough that this was not a problem. The reasoning succeeded because I translated the verbal rule into a simple eligibility filter and applied it consistently. A transferable rule is: when a question defines a disfavored set by explicit conditions, evaluate each choice only against those conditions and disregard attractive but irrelevant details.

item.context: Proponent: Irradiation of food by gamma rays would keep it from spoiling before it reaches the consumer in food stores. The process leaves no radiation behind, and vitamin losses are comparable to those that occur in cooking, so there is no reason to reject irradiation on the grounds of nutrition or safety. Indeed, it kills harmful Salmonella bacteria, which in contaminated poultry have caused serious illness to consumers. Opponent: The irradiation process has no effect on the bacteria that cause botulism, a very serious form of food poisoning, while those that cause bad odors that would warn consumers of botulism are killed. Moreover, Salmonella and the bacteria that cause botulism can easily be killed in poultry by using a safe chemical dip.
item.question: The opponent's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: showing that claims made in the proponent's argument result in a self-contradiction

choices.label: B
choices.text: shifting perspective from safety with respect to consumers to safety with respect to producers

choices.label: C
choices.text: establishing that undesirable consequences result from the adoption of either one of two proposed remedies

choices.label: D
choices.text: pointing out an alternative way of obtaining an advantage claimed by the proponent without risking a particular disadvantage

response:
Reasoning: The opponent concedes irradiation kills Salmonella but argues it creates a special risk: botulism warning odors would be removed while botulism bacteria remain. Then the opponent offers a safer alternative—a chemical dip—that also kills Salmonella (and botulism bacteria), achieving the proponent’s benefit without that disadvantage.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an argument-structure approach: identify the proponent’s claimed benefit, then see how the opponent responds to that same benefit. The key factor was that the opponent did two things together—introduced a specific downside of irradiation and then offered a chemical dip that achieves the same bacterial-control benefit without that downside. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the function of the second speaker’s response, not on the scientific details themselves. For similar problems, map each claim to its role in the rebuttal: disadvantage, concession, or alternative, and choose the option that captures that overall strategy.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the argumentative method the opponent uses, not whether the opponent is factually right about food irradiation. That distinction mattered, because the task was to classify the structure of the rebuttal rather than judge the science. My strategy was to map the opponent’s response into two moves: first, identify a risk in the proponent’s proposal, and second, present another way to secure the cited benefit. That was appropriate because several choices described abstract patterns of argument, so matching the pattern was more important than debating details.

The key evidence I used was that the opponent says irradiation removes odor-causing bacteria while leaving botulism bacteria unaffected, creating a specific danger, and then says a chemical dip can kill the relevant bacteria instead. I also noticed that the chemical dip preserves the proponent’s claimed advantage regarding harmful bacteria while avoiding the newly identified risk. A shortcut that helped was separating “claimed benefit” from “particular disadvantage” and checking whether the rebuttal explicitly addressed both. I correctly rejected possibilities involving contradiction or perspective shift because the opponent never argued the proponent contradicted himself or changed from consumer safety to producer safety. Another alternative I needed to consider was whether the opponent was condemning both remedies, but the wording clearly endorsed one remedy as safer. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on functional roles of each sentence in the argument. In similar problems, I should systematically label each premise by purpose—concession, objection, alternative, or comparison. A transferable rule is: when an argument grants an opponent’s goal, identifies a unique risk in the proposed means, and offers another means to achieve the same goal without that risk, classify it as an alternative-without-disadvantage rebuttal.

item.context: Hallucination refers to a kind of real and vivid perception without objective stimulation acting on the corresponding senses. Hallucination is a kind of perceptual disorder, mainly including auditory hallucination, visual hallucination and touch hallucination. It mostly occurs in the state of psychosis. Normal people may also appear sometimes under the conditions of tension, fatigue and high fever.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings is an illusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The patient perceived the clouds in the sky as flying fairies through imagination.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sun often looks bigger in the morning than at noon.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When the timid Xiao Lu was walking at night, he saw the trees in the distance and thought it was a robber.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Xiaofeng watched TV at home, as soon as his mother left for work. But he always felt that he heard his mother's footsteps from time to time.

response:
Reasoning: An illusion is a misperception of a real external stimulus, while a hallucination occurs without any real stimulus. D is hallucination. C clearly involves a real object (trees) mistakenly perceived as a robber, which is an illusion.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a contrast-based approach: I inferred the meaning of “illusion” from the definition of hallucination and picked the option with a real external object being misidentified. The key factor in my choice was the presence of an actual stimulus in one option versus an apparently absent stimulus in another. My error was relying on my own textbook distinction instead of matching the option most directly to the description actually given in the prompt, which emphasized vivid perception without corresponding stimulation. For similar problems, I should first anchor every option to the exact stated definition in the stem, even if the label in the question seems inconsistent with standard terminology.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the item by applying the textbook contrast between hallucination and illusion: hallucination is perception without a stimulus, while illusion is misperception of a real stimulus. That strategy was reasonable in principle, but I used it too rigidly and failed to ground it in the exact wording and structure of the options. I treated C as automatically correct because there was a real object present, yet I did not examine whether the option described a perceptual distortion or merely a fear-driven mistaken judgment about what the object was. In other words, I collapsed “wrongly concluding something” and “having an illusion” into the same category. I also dismissed D too quickly as hallucination because “heard footsteps” sounded stimulus-free, but I should have considered whether the TV, house sounds, or expectation after his mother left provided an actual external auditory basis that was being misinterpreted. I missed that some options are designed to test fine distinctions between imagination, physiological appearance, inferential error, and perceptual disorder. My main error was importing a general rule without testing each option against all necessary conditions. In similar problems, I should classify each choice by asking: is there an external stimulus, is the error perceptual rather than inferential, and does the description indicate distortion of that stimulus? A transferable rule is: when categories are defined by subtle psychological distinctions, do not match on one feature alone; verify every defining element and exclude nearby but non-equivalent phenomena.

item.context: Positive punishment refers to that when an individual sends out a certain behavior, it causes an external response to his behavior, resulting in unpleasant consequences for the individual, reducing the possibility of the individual sending out this behavior in the future. Negative punishment refers to that when an individual sends out a certain behavior, it cancels the pleasant consequences for the individual, reducing the possibility of the individual sending out this behavior in the future.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings is positive penalties?

choices.label: A
choices.text: After the no smoking sign was posted, the number of smokers in the office decreased significantly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mother asked Xiao Ming not to go out to play without doing his homework

choices.label: C
choices.text: After someone was punished for drunk driving, he didn't drink driving again

choices.label: D
choices.text: Popsicles relieve summer heat, so popsicles sell well in summer

response:
Reasoning: Positive punishment adds an unpleasant consequence after a behavior, decreasing that behavior. C fits: drunk driving led to punishment, so the person stopped doing it. B is negative punishment (removing chance to play). A is just a sign, not punishment. D is unrelated.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option against the required structure of positive punishment—behavior followed by an added unpleasant consequence that reduces future behavior. The key factor was distinguishing “adding an aversive outcome” from merely giving a warning, removing a privilege, or describing reinforcement. My success came from checking the causal sequence in each choice rather than focusing only on whether the behavior decreased. For similar problems, I should explicitly test each option for all parts of the definition: target behavior, consequence type, and resulting reduction in that behavior.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for an example of positive punishment in the behavioral sense, not merely something “positive” or “penalty” in everyday language. My strategy was to map each option against the formal definition: a behavior occurs, an external aversive consequence is added, and the future frequency of that behavior decreases. That was the right strategy because the stem explicitly contrasted positive punishment with negative punishment, so the key was distinguishing “adding something unpleasant” from “removing something pleasant.” I correctly used the behavioral sequence in option C: the target behavior was followed by punishment, and the later reduction in that behavior was stated. I also used the contrastive definition to classify B as negative punishment, since it involved taking away an opportunity to play rather than adding an aversive consequence. For A, I noticed that a posted sign is not itself evidence of punishment; the option reports decreased smoking but does not show an added unpleasant consequence contingent on smoking. D was clearly reinforcement-related rather than punishment-related because it described a desirable effect increasing sales.

A shortcut that helped was checking for all three necessary elements: behavior, consequence type, and reduced recurrence. An alternative I needed to keep in mind was that some choices can sound disciplinary in ordinary language yet fail the technical definition. The reasoning succeeded because I relied on the exact operant-conditioning structure rather than social intuition. A general rule is: when classifying reinforcement or punishment examples, identify whether the consequence is added or removed and whether the behavior later decreases or increases.

item.context: Broken window phenomenon means that if the window of a house is broken, no one will repair it. Soon, other windows will be broken inexplicably. Therefore, if the bad phenomenon in the environment is allowed to exist, it will induce people to follow suit or even intensify.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following is not a broken window phenomenon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some graffiti appeared on one wall and was not removed. Soon, the wall was full of messy and ugly things.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In a clean place, people are embarrassed to throw rubbish, but once there is rubbish on the ground, people will throw it away without hesitation and will not be ashamed at all.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An infectious disease occurred in a village. Because it was not isolated in time, the whole village was soon infected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In a classroom, two students spoke secretly. The teacher didn't stop them. Soon, most of the students in the class were chatting.

response:
Reasoning: Broken window phenomenon is about tolerated disorder encouraging people to imitate or worsen that disorder. A, B, and D involve people following visible bad behavior/environment. C is disease transmission, a biological spread, not imitation caused by tolerated disorder.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I identified the core elements of the phenomenon—an initial sign of disorder, lack of correction, and subsequent human imitation or escalation—and checked each option against them. The key factor was whether the later spread happened through social influence and tolerated bad norms, rather than through a different mechanism. My success came from distinguishing human behavioral contagion from physical or biological contagion. For similar problems, extract the necessary causal mechanism in the definition and eliminate any option that matches only the outcome pattern but not the required cause.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the option that does not fit the causal structure of the broken window phenomenon, not merely the option that involves something bad spreading. That interpretation was correct, because the definition hinges on social or behavioral imitation triggered by tolerated disorder in the environment. My strategy was to extract the core conditions from the definition: an initial negative sign, lack of correction, and subsequent human imitation or escalation. This was an appropriate approach for a definition-matching multiple-choice problem, since it tests structure rather than surface similarity.

The key evidence I used was that A, B, and D all involve people changing their behavior after seeing disorder go unchecked. In contrast, one option described spread through physical contagion rather than social norm signaling, which breaks the mechanism required by the definition. An important assumption in my reasoning was that “induce people to follow suit” refers specifically to psychological or social imitation, not any chain reaction. That assumption was justified by the wording of the definition. I also implicitly checked whether the “no one repaired/stopped it” element was present, which helped distinguish relevant from irrelevant spread.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on mechanism instead of outcome. A weaker strategy would have grouped all “things that spread when unchecked” together. In similar problems, I should continue separating causal mechanism from superficial pattern. General rule: when matching examples to a definition, test whether each required causal link is present, not just whether the end result looks similar.

item.context: Public goods refer to goods that are non-competitive and non-exclusive in consumption and are shared by the entire society.
item.question: Which of the following options is not a public good?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Security services provided by the police

choices.label: B
choices.text: Research and Development

choices.label: C
choices.text: Environmental protection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Brand-name TVs in shopping malls

response:
Reasoning: Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable. Police security and environmental protection fit this, and R&D often has public-good spillovers. Brand-name TVs in shopping malls are private goods because they are excludable and rival in consumption.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-based classification approach: I compared each option against the two core criteria for public goods, non-rivalry and non-excludability. The key factor was recognizing that one option was an ordinary market commodity consumed by individual buyers, unlike the others, which either directly serve everyone or generate broad social spillovers. My success came from applying the public-vs-private good test systematically instead of relying on whether something merely seems socially valuable. For similar problems, explicitly check each choice against both criteria separately and eliminate any item that is excludable or rival in consumption.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the option that fails the defining test of a public good: non-rivalry and non-excludability. My strategy was to evaluate each choice against those two criteria rather than relying on whether the item sounded socially beneficial, which was appropriate for an economics definition question. The key evidence I used was that police protection and environmental protection are typically consumed collectively, while research and development can generate broad spillovers that make it public-good-like in many contexts. I also used the fact that an ordinary consumer product is usually both excludable and rival, which distinguishes private goods from public goods. One assumption in my reasoning was treating R&D as fitting the category because of knowledge spillovers; that is acceptable here, but in other settings I should note that some R&D outputs can be partially excludable through patents. A useful alternative I implicitly considered was whether “provided in a shopping mall” changed the consumption characteristics, but it does not alter the core excludable/rival nature of the item. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on formal properties of goods, not on moral value or public provision. For similar problems, I should systematically test each option on both dimensions separately and watch for mixed cases such as club goods or common-pool resources. A transferable rule is: classify goods by rivalry and excludability first, and only afterward consider who provides them or whether they create social benefits.

item.context: Each of two drugs, S and T, greatly reduces the effects of potentially fatal heart attacks if given as soon as possible after the attack begins, but a trial has shown that use of drug T instead of drug S would prevent death in one additional case out of 120. Drug T, however, costs $2, 000 more per treatment than drug S. Ttherefore society is presented with a stark policy decision: whether or not to pay the $240, 000 it would cost to use drug T in order to save one additional patient.
item.question: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Drug S has certain side effects not shared by drug T.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After a heart attack, drug T remains relatively effective if given at a time at which drug S is no longer effective.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drug T works significantly faster than drug S.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no quick, practical, and relatively inexpensive way of telling for any individual case whether drug S will be as effective as drug T.

response:
Reasoning: The cost calculation treats society as having to give T to all 120 patients to save the one extra life. That assumes we cannot cheaply identify in advance which patients specifically need T rather than S. If we could, the “stark” all-or-nothing policy choice would collapse.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-analysis approach: I asked what must be true for the argument’s cost framing to work. The key clue was the move from “one additional life saved per 120 treatments” to a blanket policy choice costing $240,000, which only makes sense if doctors cannot identify in advance which patients actually need the more effective drug. My success came from testing what would happen if that assumption were false: the policy would no longer be all-or-nothing because treatment could be targeted. For similar problems, always examine whether a conclusion based on average outcomes assumes there is no practical way to distinguish subgroups beforehand.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for a necessary unstated premise that makes the policy framing valid, not for a fact that would merely strengthen the case for the more expensive drug. My strategy was to examine the numerical move from “one extra life saved per 120 treatments” to “society must spend $240,000 to save that one life,” and ask what must be true for that aggregation to represent the real decision. That was the right strategy because assumption questions often hinge on whether a comparison can be made at the population level without hidden sorting or selection issues. The key evidence I used was that the argument assumes everyone in the relevant group would receive the costlier drug, rather than only a subset. I correctly noticed that if patients who uniquely benefit from the more effective drug could be identified cheaply and quickly, the stated policy dilemma would be false or at least overstated.  

I did not get distracted by answer choices about side effects, timing, or speed, because those describe possible advantages but are not required for the cost-per-life calculation. The central assumption was about the absence of a feasible screening method, not about additional clinical superiority beyond the trial result. The reasoning succeeded because I tested the argument by negating candidate assumptions: if targeted identification were possible, the conclusion’s “stark” choice would collapse. In similar problems, I should continue tracing exactly how a quantified conclusion depends on hidden uniform-treatment assumptions. General rule: when an argument converts average group outcomes into an all-or-nothing policy cost, check whether it assumes there is no practical way to identify who actually needs the superior option.

item.context: Political Analyst: Although citizens of this state normally oppose any new taxes, they are overwhelmingly in favor of taxes that support the medical initiative. Candidate Johnson vowed to cut these taxes, and he was trounced in the primary elections. Furthermore, in a poll that asked citizens, Would you pay higher taxes if it meant having the benefit of the new medical initiative? , an astonishing 82% replied Yes. This is a pattern of support for taxes we have not seen before in this state.
item.question: In the political analyst's argument, the portion in boldface plays which of the following roles?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is an explanation that the argument concludes is correct.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a finding that calls the main conclusion into question.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It provides evidence in support of the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

response:
Reasoning: The main conclusion is the last sentence: “This is a pattern of support for taxes we have not seen before in this state.” The boldface poll result is additional evidence supporting that conclusion, alongside Johnson’s defeat after promising tax cuts.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I identified the argument’s structure by locating the claim the other statements were trying to establish, which was the final sentence about an unprecedented pattern of tax support. The key factor was the signal word “Furthermore,” which showed the boldface poll result was being added as another reason rather than presented as the conclusion. My reasoning succeeded because I distinguished between concrete supporting facts—the election result and the poll—and the broader interpretive claim drawn from them. For similar questions, first mark the sentence that generalizes or interprets the evidence, then classify any specific data, examples, or poll results as support unless the passage indicates they are being challenged.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as a role-in-argument problem: identify what function the boldfaced statement serves within the analyst’s reasoning structure. That interpretation was correct, because the key task was not to judge truth but to map premise and conclusion. My strategy was to first locate the main conclusion by looking for the claim that the earlier statements seemed to support, and the final sentence clearly played that role. Once I identified that concluding claim, I treated the earlier statements as candidate evidence and checked whether the boldface statement supplied support, restated the conclusion, or introduced tension. The poll result was a factual observation that strengthened the idea that this state is showing unusual support for taxes tied to the medical initiative. I also used the parallel structure of the passage: Johnson’s defeat and the poll numbers both function as supporting data points. An important constraint I used correctly was that the boldface statement was not phrased as an inference from prior claims; it was presented as another piece of empirical evidence. I did not rely on any unnecessary assumptions about whether polls are reliable in general, because the role question depends on how the statement functions in the passage, not whether it is ultimately persuasive. A tempting alternative would have been to treat the boldface claim as the conclusion because it is striking, but prominence or vividness does not determine argumentative role. The reasoning succeeded because I separated rhetorical emphasis from logical structure. In similar problems, I should keep identifying the claim that would lose support if the boldfaced sentence were removed. General rule: in argument-role questions, determine whether a statement is being supported or doing the supporting by tracing the direction of inference, not by its emotional force or specificity.

item.context: In a study conducted in Pennsylvania, servers in various restaurants wrote Thank you on randomly selected bills before presenting the bills to their customers. Tips on these bills were an average of three percentage points higher than tips on bills without the message. Ttherefore, if servers in Pennsylvania regularly wrote Thank you on restaurant bills, their average income from tips would be significantly higher than it otherwise would have been.
item.question: Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Virtually all patrons of the Pennsylvania restaurants in the study who were given a bill with Thank you written on it left a larger tip than they otherwise would have.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regularly seeing Thank you written on their bills would not lead restaurant patrons to revert to their earlier tipping habits.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Thank you messages would have the same impact on regular patrons of a restaurant as they would on occasional patrons of the same restaurant.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The written Thank you reminds restaurant patrons that tips constitute a significant part of the income of many food servers.

response:
Reasoning: The study shows a one-time or occasional effect from adding “Thank you.” To conclude that servers’ average tips would stay higher if they did this regularly, the argument must assume customers would not get used to it and stop increasing tips. That is exactly choice B.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-testing approach: identify the gap between a short-term experimental result and the broader claim about what would happen if the practice became regular. The key factor was the shift from randomly selected bills in a study to habitual use over time, which introduces the possibility that customers might adapt and the effect might fade. My success came from focusing on that temporal/generalization gap rather than on explaining why the message works. For similar problems, I should explicitly compare the evidence conditions with the conclusion conditions and ask what must remain true when moving from one-time results to repeated real-world application.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for a necessary assumption that connects the experimental result to the broader prediction about long-term average tip income. That interpretation was correct, because the conclusion was not merely about what happened in the study, but about what would happen if servers adopted the practice regularly. My strategy was to look for a gap between a short-term randomized effect and a claim about sustained real-world outcomes. That was appropriate because assumption questions often hinge on whether the study conditions can support the projected conclusion.

The key evidence I used was the shift from “randomly selected bills” in a study to “regularly wrote” in ongoing practice. I focused on the possibility of habituation: a behavior that increases tips when novel may lose its effect when repeated. That was the crucial hidden constraint, and identifying it led directly to the needed assumption. I correctly avoided stronger-than-necessary ideas, such as assuming nearly every individual customer tips more, since the argument only needs a higher average, not a universal response. I also implicitly rejected explanatory claims about why the message works, because the argument depends on the existence of the effect, not its mechanism.

What made the reasoning successful was testing the argument against a plausible weakening scenario: customers get used to the message, so the initial gain disappears. For similar problems, I should continue checking whether the conclusion extends an observed effect across time, populations, or settings. General rule: when an argument projects an experimental result into regular practice, look for an assumption ruling out attenuation, adaptation, or other changes that would break the projection.

item.context: Debater: As a pedagogical practice, lecturing embodies hierarchy, since the lecturer is superior to the student in mastery of the subject. But people learn best from peer interaction. Thus, the hierarchy in lecturing is a great weakness. Respondent: By definition, all teaching and learning are hierarchical, for all teaching and learning must proceed from simple to complex. In teaching mathematics, for example, arithmetic must precede calculus. Thus, the hierarchy in lecturing is a strength.
item.question: The respondent's reply to the debater's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the respondent

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that the conceptual structure of mathematics is sufficiently representative of the conceptual structure of at least some other academic disciplines

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider the possibility that some characteristics of lecturing other than hierarchy are weaknesses

choices.label: C
choices.text: concedes one of the major assumptions on which the debater's argument depends

choices.label: D
choices.text: applies a key concept to a different aspect of education than the aspect to which the debater applied it

response:
Reasoning: The debater uses “hierarchy” to mean a social/pedagogical relation of authority between lecturer and student. The respondent shifts “hierarchy” to mean the ordered structure of subject matter, from simple to complex. This equivocation addresses a different aspect of education than the debater criticized.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-analysis approach, comparing how each speaker used the term “hierarchy” rather than evaluating the truth of their educational claims. The key factor was that the debater referred to hierarchy as a social relationship between teacher and student, while the respondent redefined it as the sequencing of material from basic to advanced. That shift in meaning showed the response targeted a different aspect of education, which is why the reasoning succeeded. For similar problems, I should explicitly track whether both speakers are using the same key term in the same sense before judging whether one argument actually answers the other.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the flaw in the respondent’s rebuttal, not whether the respondent’s conclusion might independently be true. That distinction mattered, because the task was to compare the debater’s use of “hierarchy” with the respondent’s use of it and see whether the reply actually engaged the original criticism. My strategy was to track the key term across both speakers and test for a shift in meaning or reference. That was appropriate here because LSAT-style flaw questions often hinge on whether a reply addresses the same claim, the same evidence, and the same sense of a central term. I noticed that the debater’s “hierarchy” concerned a social relation between teacher and student, specifically superiority in mastery and authority. I also noticed that the respondent’s “hierarchy” referred instead to the sequencing of material from simpler to more complex concepts. Those are different aspects of education, so the respondent did not directly answer the debater’s complaint.

I did not rely on outside assumptions about mathematics, peer learning, or lecture effectiveness, which helped avoid attractive but secondary answer choices. A tempting alternative would have been to focus on whether the respondent ignored other weaknesses of lecturing, but that would miss the central mismatch in the exchange. The reasoning succeeded because I compared the argument structures rather than evaluating the truth of either side’s educational theory. In similar problems, I should keep isolating the exact role of recurring terms and ask whether an objection uses them in the same dimension—social, causal, conceptual, moral, or procedural. A transferable rule is: when a response repeats a key word, verify that it addresses the same property or relation as the original argument before treating it as a genuine rebuttal.

item.context: Since the reform and opening up, China's economy has maintained a high-speed growth trend on the whole, but the growth of labor and employment is far lower than that of economic growth. At present, although the proportion of labor and employment absorbed by China's service industry is increasing, it has even become the main force of employment, It has basically digested all the new labor force, including the labor stock transferred from agriculture and manufacturing, but its contribution rate to labor and employment is still too low compared with developed countries. We must take advantage of the opportunity of industrial structure adjustment and growth mode transformation to explore the great potential of service industry for economic development and employment expansion.
item.question: This passage mainly explains that?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Industrial structure adjustment is an important opportunity for the rapid development of China's service industry

choices.label: B
choices.text: Service industry is an important driving factor to ensure the rapid growth of employment in China

choices.label: C
choices.text: The absorptive capacity of China's service industry to labor employment needs to be further expanded

choices.label: D
choices.text: The main reason for the inconsistency between employment and economic growth is the lagging development of service industry

response:
Reasoning: The passage focuses on the current role of the service industry in absorbing employment, but emphasizes that compared with developed countries its employment contribution is still too low and should be further developed during industrial restructuring. This matches the need to expand its employment absorption capacity.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea reasoning approach: identify the background, note the author’s evaluation, and focus on the concluding recommendation. The key clue was the contrast between the service industry already absorbing much labor and its contribution still being “too low” compared with developed countries, followed by the call to “explore the great potential” for employment expansion. My success came from treating the earlier economic-growth discussion as context and the final policy-oriented statement as the passage’s core point. For similar problems, first separate background facts from the author’s ultimate judgment or proposal, and choose the option that best captures that final emphasis.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s central thesis, not merely a supporting fact or one recommended policy. That interpretation was correct, because the passage first presents a problem—employment growth lagging behind economic growth—then evaluates the current role of the service sector, and finally points to what should be done. My strategy was to track the passage’s structure from background, to current situation, to conclusion, and identify which option captured that concluding focus. This was appropriate because “mainly explains” questions are usually resolved by distinguishing the core claim from contextual setup and partial details.

The key evidence I used was the contrastive wording: the service industry already absorbs much of the new labor force, yet its contribution to employment is still too low compared with developed countries, so its potential must be further explored. That combination supports a “needs further expansion” idea rather than a claim that it is already sufficient or that it is the sole reason for the broader employment issue. I avoided overcommitting to option B because the passage does not celebrate the service sector as enough; it emphasizes insufficiency. I also rejected A as too narrow, since “industrial structure adjustment” is presented as an opportunity or means, not the passage’s main point. D was also too causal and absolute, because the passage does not explicitly identify lagging service-sector development as the main reason for the mismatch. The success came from distinguishing the author’s evaluative conclusion from the explanatory background. A transferable rule is: in main-idea questions, prioritize the option that integrates the passage’s problem, assessment, and proposed direction, rather than one that isolates a cause, a fact, or a method.

item.context: As often now as in the past, newspaper journalists use direct or indirect quotation to report unsupported or false claims made by newsmakers. However, journalists are becoming less likely to openly challenge the veracity of such claims within their articles.
item.question: Each of the following, if true, helps to explain the trend in journalism described above EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Journalists who challenge the veracity of claims are often criticized for failing their professional obligation to be objective.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Newspaper publishers have found that many readers will cancel a subscription simply because a view they take for granted has been disputed by the publication.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A basic principle of journalism holds that debate over controversial issues draws the attention of the public.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The areas of knowledge on which journalists report are growing in specialization and diversity, while journalists themselves are not becoming more broadly knowledgeable.

response:
Reasoning: A, B, and D all give reasons journalists might avoid directly disputing false claims: objectivity norms, subscriber loss, and limited expertise. C instead suggests that open debate attracts public attention, which would encourage challenging claims rather than explain declining challenges.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an elimination approach: test each option for whether it gives a plausible incentive for journalists to avoid openly disputing claims. The key factor was the direction of the effect—whether the statement would discourage challenges or instead make challenges more attractive. My success came from checking that A, B, and D each increase pressure against direct fact-challenging, while one option pointed the other way. For similar EXCEPT questions, explicitly label each choice as “explains,” “does not explain,” or “reverses the trend,” and pick the one that fails that causal test.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task correctly as an “EXCEPT” question: three choices had to support the reported trend, and one had to fail to support it or point in the opposite direction. My strategy was to test each option against the causal pattern in the stimulus: why journalists would increasingly refrain from explicitly disputing dubious claims. That was the right approach because the prompt asked for an explanation of a trend, not a definition of objectivity or a judgment about journalism in general. I used the key relationship that anything increasing professional risk, commercial cost, or epistemic difficulty would make open challenges less likely. That let me see why criticism for appearing nonobjective, loss of subscribers, and limited expertise all plausibly discourage direct rebuttal.  

The crucial evidence I did not ignore was the direction of effect: an explanation must make the trend more likely, not merely describe journalism. The successful part of my reasoning was noticing that one option instead described an incentive that would favor public disputation, which cuts against the trend rather than explaining it. I did not rely on outside knowledge; I stayed anchored to whether each statement strengthened the stated decline in open challenge. A common trap here would have been treating any statement about journalism as relevant without checking whether it supports or undermines the trend. In similar problems, I should explicitly ask for each option: does this create pressure toward the observed behavior, pressure away from it, or no pressure at all? A transferable rule is: in EXCEPT/weakening-by-exception questions about trends, evaluate each choice by the direction of its causal impact on the trend, not by its superficial topical relevance.

item.context: A company stipulates that only employees who have worked continuously in the company for more than 20 years or have outstanding achievements can enjoy the special allowance issued by the company. Although Xiao Zhang has only worked in the company for 3 years, he now enjoys the special allowance issued by the company, so he must have made outstanding achievements.
item.question: The reasoning mode of the following options is most similar to the above problem stem:

choices.label: A
choices.text: To get good grades, we should study hard and use appropriate methods. Although Wang Yang is diligent, his grades are not very good. After seeing his improper learning methods

choices.label: B
choices.text: To commit a crime, a criminal must have both motive and time. In a case, suspect a has motive but no time. Therefore, suspect a is not the perpetrator of the case

choices.label: C
choices.text: If it is not only ineffective but also extravagant and wasteful, an enterprise will suffer serious losses. Although Dapeng company is ineffective, it has not suffered serious losses, which shows that it has at least no extravagance and waste

choices.label: D
choices.text: The perfection of the legal system or the powerful social control ability of the rulers are essential conditions for maintaining a country's social stability. A country's society is stable, but the legal system is not perfect. Therefore, its rulers must have strong social control ability

response:
Reasoning: Stem: If enjoy allowance, then either 20+ years or outstanding achievements. Xiao Zhang enjoys it and not 20+ years, so he must have achievements. This is: P → (A or B), P, not A, therefore B. Option D has the same form.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a formal logic matching approach: translate the stem into a conditional with a disjunction, then compare each option’s structure. The key factor was recognizing the pattern “If P, then A or B; P; not A; therefore B,” which is a valid disjunctive inference within a conditional setting. The successful step was focusing on logical form rather than topic wording, which made the parallel option stand out clearly. For similar problems, first abstract the stem into symbols and check whether each choice preserves both the conditional direction and the “affirm one premise, deny one disjunct, infer the other” structure.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stem as a conditional reasoning problem with a disjunctive necessary condition: receiving the allowance requires either long service or outstanding achievements. I read the given facts correctly: Xiao Zhang satisfies the result condition, and one of the two qualifying paths is explicitly denied. My strategy was to abstract the structure into symbols, roughly “P → (A or B), P, not A, therefore B,” and then compare that pattern with the options. That was an appropriate strategy because these analogy questions depend more on logical form than on topic.

The key relationship I used was that once the conclusion side of a conditional is known to hold as a disjunction, eliminating one disjunct forces the other. I did not rely on irrelevant content like employment policy or criminal investigation details, which helped avoid surface-level distraction. A possible trap would have been to confuse this with affirming the consequent or with a biconditional, but I avoided that by tracking which statement was sufficient and which was necessary. I also correctly rejected options that involved conjunctions rather than disjunctions, since “A and B” behaves very differently from “A or B.”

What made the reasoning successful was matching the exact inferential template, not just noticing similar wording. In similar problems, I should continue translating statements into minimal logical forms before evaluating answer choices. A transferable rule is: when testing analogy in logic questions, compare the operator structure—conditional, conjunction, disjunction, and negation—before comparing subject matter.

item.context: The crime of obstruction of public service refers to the use of violence and threats to obstruct state functionaries from performing their duties in accordance with the law and to obstruct deputies to the People's Congresses from performing their duties in accordance with the law, any Act that obstructs the staff of the Red Cross from carrying out their duties in accordance with the law, or any act that intentionally obstructs the security agency from carrying out its national security tasks in accordance with the law, without the use of violence, threats or other means, with grave consequences.
item.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of the crime of obstruction of public service ?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Li told his son who was on duty at the police station to go home for the New Year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because her husband is busy in the Public Security Bureau and the husband and wife are less likely to get together, Xiao Liu strongly disagrees with her husband's work on vacation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leaders of a factory gather a large number of employees to obstruct tax inspectors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lao Zhang of the police station runs amok in the village on weekdays. Once, he was beaten by the masses when he was behaving erratically.

response:
Reasoning: Obstruction of public service requires intentionally obstructing state functionaries performing lawful duties, typically by violence or threats. Only C describes organized obstruction of tax inspectors carrying out official duties. A and B are family disputes, and D involves an officer not performing lawful duty.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-to-facts matching approach: I compared each option against the legal elements of the offense, especially obstruction of officials performing lawful duties. The key factor was whether the target was a state functionary acting according to law and whether the conduct was intentional obstruction rather than a private disagreement or unrelated conflict. The successful step was filtering out choices where the official was not actually carrying out official duties or where no real obstructive act against public service occurred. For similar problems, I should systematically check each option against every statutory element one by one, instead of relying on a general impression that the situation “looks like interference.”
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the defining factual pattern that fits the legal elements of obstruction of public service, not merely any conflict involving a public employee. That interpretation was correct because the stem gave a fairly specific legal definition: the protected target must be a public function, and the obstruction must interfere with lawful duty performance. My strategy was to match each option against the statutory elements rather than rely on surface cues like “police,” “government,” or “public security.” That was appropriate for a legal-classification question, since the decisive issue is element-by-element fit.

The key facts I used were: the victim must be carrying out official duties according to law, and the conduct must be obstructive rather than merely persuasive, domestic, or retaliatory. I correctly rejected the family-dispute options because they lacked an actual obstructive act against official duty execution. I also rejected the scenario involving the police officer because the facts suggested the officer was not engaged in lawful duty performance at the time, which breaks a required element. One assumption that helped was treating “obstruct” as requiring direct interference with execution of duty, not just disagreement or inconvenience. An alternative I still should consciously check in similar problems is whether the offense can be committed through nonviolent means under special statutory extensions, because the stem listed those nuances. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on legal elements and filtered out irrelevant social relationships. A transferable rule is: when classifying conduct under a legal offense, test every option against each required element in sequence, and eliminate any option missing even one core element.

item.context: E-government: it means that government agencies use modern information technology to implement a large number of frequent administrative management and daily affairs on the Internet according to the set procedures through the government website, so as to break the constraints of time, space and partial infringement, and provide efficient and open government services for society and citizens in an all-round way.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following options does not belong to E-government?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electronic document circulation between superior and subordinate governments

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transfer payment is realized between enterprises through Internet banking

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enterprises complete tax registration and tax payment through the government tax network

choices.label: D
choices.text: Establish an electronic transportation website to manage and serve drivers

response:
Reasoning: E-government involves government agencies using the Internet to handle administrative affairs and provide public services. A, C, and D all involve government functions online. B is a financial transaction between enterprises via Internet banking, not a government administrative service.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: compare each option against every required element in the concept, especially the actor and the function. The key factor was that E-government must involve government agencies using information technology to carry out administrative management or public services through official online systems. The successful step was distinguishing “government online service” from “ordinary online financial activity,” even though both use the Internet. For similar problems, I should systematically test each option against the core definitional criteria—who is acting, what activity is performed, and whether it serves the defined administrative purpose.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a definition-matching task: identify the option that falls outside the scope of a concept defined by necessary features. That interpretation was correct, because the definition set out several constraints: the actor must be a government agency, the tool is modern information technology via the Internet, and the purpose is administrative management or public service. My strategy was to test each option against those core elements rather than rely on surface words like “electronic” or “website.” That was appropriate, because multiple choices involved online activity, but only some involved government administration.

The key evidence I used was the distinction between government-led functions and non-government commercial activity. I noticed that some options described internal governmental communication or government service delivery to citizens and firms, which fit the definition’s emphasis on administrative procedures and public service. I also recognized that one option involved a transaction conducted through banking infrastructure between private firms, which lacks the governmental actor and administrative purpose required by the definition. A shortcut that helped, and happened to be safe here, was focusing first on the subject performing the action rather than every detail of the definition. An alternative I still should have checked more explicitly was whether all “service” websites are truly governmental rather than merely industry-related platforms.

What made the reasoning successful was using necessary conditions from the definition instead of thematic similarity. For similar problems, I should continue converting definitions into a checklist of actor, medium, and function before evaluating options. A general rule is: in definition-based multiple choice, eliminate any option that fails even one essential criterion, even if it shares superficial vocabulary or technology.

item.context: Up to now, researchers have found that there are as many as 40 kinds of growth factors in embryos and thymus tissues, many of which have been proved to be target tissues to promote skin growth and play an important role in regulating the metabolism, division and reproduction of skin cells. If these growth factors can be filled into the skin tissue of the middle-aged by applying facial cream, it will have a certain effect on maintaining the health of the skin tissue and delaying the aging of the skin.
item.question: Which of the following options has an accurate understanding of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Facial creams containing growth factors may maintain the health of the skin.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The researchers found that there are more than 40 growth factors that protect the skin.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Facial creams containing growth factors are the most effective for middle-aged people.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An effective way to delay skin aging is to apply a facial cream containing growth factors.

response:
Reasoning: The passage says growth factors in facial cream “will have a certain effect” on maintaining skin health and delaying aging. That supports possibility/effectiveness, not “more than 40,” “most effective,” or “an effective way” as a strong conclusion. So A is the most accurate.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a precision-and-qualification approach, matching each option to the exact strength of the passage’s claims. The key factor was the wording “will have a certain effect,” which supports a limited, possible benefit rather than a strong or comparative conclusion. My success came from rejecting options that overstated the text, such as claiming “more than 40,” “most effective,” or presenting the cream as a definitive method. For similar problems, I should systematically compare modal strength and scope, choosing the option that preserves the passage’s exact level of certainty without exaggeration.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the choice that most faithfully restated the passage without adding strength, quantity, or certainty beyond what the text supported. That interpretation was correct, because the task was not to infer the best skincare advice but to identify the most accurate paraphrase. My strategy was to compare the modality and scope of each option against the passage’s wording, especially phrases like “as many as 40 kinds” and “will have a certain effect.” That was appropriate because this was a precision-in-language problem, where small differences such as “may” versus “is” or “as many as” versus “more than” determine correctness. I used the key evidence that the passage only claimed a limited, conditional benefit if growth factors could be introduced into middle-aged skin through facial cream. I also correctly rejected options that overstated the evidence by turning a tentative effect into a definitive recommendation or superiority claim. One important constraint I noticed was that the passage did not say these creams were the best method, only that they could help. Another was that “as many as 40” does not justify “more than 40,” so numerical wording had to be matched exactly. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on textual entailment rather than background knowledge about cosmetics. In similar problems, I should continue checking whether each choice preserves the original claim’s degree of certainty, quantity, and conditionality. A general rule is: when evaluating paraphrase questions, prefer the option that weakens nothing, strengthens nothing, and stays within the passage’s exact evidential limits.

item.context: Products sold under a brand name used to command premium prices because, in general, they were superior to nonbrand rival products. Technical expertise in product development has become so widespread, however, that special quality advantages are very hard to obtain these days and even harder to maintain. As a consequence, brand-name products generally neither offer higher quality nor sell at higher prices. Paradoxically, brand names are a bigger marketing advantage than ever.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the paradox outlined above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the days when special quality advantages were easier to obtain than they are now, it was also easier to get new brand names established.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumers recognize that the quality of products sold under invariant brand names can drift over time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The advertising of a company's brand-name products is at times transferred to a new advertising agency, especially when sales are declining.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Brand names are taken by consumers as a guarantee of getting a product as good as the best rival products.

response:
Reasoning: The paradox is that brand names no longer signal superior quality or justify higher prices, yet they help more than ever. This is explained if consumers treat a brand name as assurance of at least solid, competitive quality, reducing purchase risk even without superiority or premium pricing.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a paradox-resolution approach: identify the tension, then look for a choice that explains how both claims can be true at once. The key factor was separating “better than rivals” from “as good as the best rivals”; a brand can still matter if it reduces uncertainty even without implying superiority or premium price. My success came from focusing on the consumer’s decision-making role of a brand name rather than on production, advertising logistics, or historical conditions. For similar problems, explicitly ask what practical benefit remains after the old advantage disappears, and choose the option that supplies that substitute benefit.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a paradox-resolution task: I needed an option that explains how brand names could become more valuable in marketing even after losing their former connection to superior quality and premium pricing. My strategy was appropriate for this type of problem: identify the two seemingly conflicting claims, then look for a statement showing that brand names still provide a different kind of consumer benefit. I focused on the distinction between “better than rivals” and “reliably at least as good as rivals,” which is the key conceptual shift in the argument. That was strong reasoning because the stimulus says technical expertise is widespread, implying quality differences have narrowed, so the remaining value of a brand name would likely involve reducing uncertainty rather than signaling superiority. I also correctly used the idea that consumers care not only about maximum quality but about avoiding the risk of making a bad choice.  

I implicitly rejected choices that discussed historical conditions or advertising logistics because they did not connect the loss of quality advantage to the increased marketing usefulness of brand names. One useful feature of my reasoning was that I did not require the answer to restore premium pricing; I recognized that resolving the paradox only required showing why branding still matters. The success came from matching the answer choice to the exact gap in the argument: why brands help when they no longer imply excellence. In similar problems, I should continue separating “absolute superiority” from “reliable acceptability,” since many paradoxes turn on that kind of hidden distinction. A transferable rule is: when a former signal loses its ability to indicate “best,” test whether it still has value as a signal of “safe, trustworthy, or good enough.”

item.context: Many environmentalists have urged environmental awareness on consumers, saying that if we accept moral responsibility for our effects on the environment, then products that directly or indirectly harm the environment ought to be avoided. Unfortunately it is usually impossible for consumers to assess the environmental impact of a product, and thus impossible for them to consciously restrict their purchases to environmentally benign products. Because of this impossibility there can be no moral duty to choose products in the way these environmentalists urge, since __.
item.question: Which one of the following principles provides the most appropriate completion for the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the morally right action is always the one whose effects produce the least total harm

choices.label: B
choices.text: a moral duty to perform an action is never based solely on the effects the action will have on other people

choices.label: C
choices.text: a person cannot possibly have a moral duty to do what he or she is unable to do

choices.label: D
choices.text: where a moral duty exists, it supersedes any legal duty and any other kind of duty

response:
Reasoning: The argument says consumers usually cannot assess environmental impact, so they cannot consciously choose only benign products. To conclude there is no moral duty, it needs the principle that no one can have a moral duty to do what they are unable to do.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a gap-filling approach: I identified the conclusion (“there can be no moral duty”) and looked for the principle that would connect the stated inability to assess products with the denial of obligation. The key factor was the argument’s emphasis on impossibility—consumers are said to be unable to determine which products are environmentally benign. The successful step was matching that constraint to the general moral principle that obligation requires ability. For similar questions, isolate the exact premise-conclusion gap and choose the answer that converts the stated limitation or condition into the conclusion with the least extra assumption.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the hidden principle that bridges the gap between the premises and the conclusion, not for a generally appealing moral claim. The structure of the argument was: consumers cannot determine which products are environmentally benign, therefore they cannot consciously choose only such products, therefore they lack the relevant moral duty. My strategy was to identify the exact inferential move needed to get from inability to absence of obligation, which is the standard way to approach principle-support questions. That was appropriate because the conclusion depended on a normative rule, not on additional factual information about environmental harm. The key fact I used was the passage’s emphasis on impossibility: consumers are said to be unable to assess impact, and thus unable to act as urged. I correctly saw that the missing principle had to connect “cannot do” with “not morally required to do,” rather than discuss total harm, effects on other people, or conflicts among duties. One assumption that helped, and was justified here, was that “usually impossible” in context was strong enough to support the argument’s intended impossibility claim. I also ruled out tempting but irrelevant moral theories because they did not match the conclusion’s focus on duty. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the principle to the argument’s logical gap rather than to its topic. In similar problems, I should continue abstracting the argument into premise-conclusion form before evaluating choices. A transferable rule is: when a conclusion denies obligation on the basis of inability, the needed principle must explicitly link incapacity to the absence of duty.

item.context: Medical columnist: Some doctors recommend taking vitamin C to help maintain overall health because vitamin C is an antioxidant, a substance that protects the body from certain types of oxygen particles that can trigger disease. People suffering from various ailments are encouraged to take vitamin C to guard against developing other health problems. However, doctors are now discouraging some cancer patients from taking vitamin C, even when they are undergoing therapies with side effects that are detrimental to their overall health.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the doctors' recommendation to some cancer patients differs from the general recommendation regarding vitamin C?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Certain side effects of cancer therapies that are detrimental to patients' overall health are not affected by vitamin C.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cancer cells that are susceptible to certain types of cancer therapies are not likely to be affected by the presence of vitamin C.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin C has not been shown to reduce people's risk of developing cancer, even at the very high dosage levels recommended by some doctors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some kinds of cancer cells absorb large amounts of vitamin C, which interferes with the oxidation mechanism by which many cancer therapies kill cancer cells.

response:
Reasoning: Vitamin C is an antioxidant, so if some cancer therapies kill cancer cells through oxidation, vitamin C could protect the cancer cells and reduce treatment effectiveness. That would justify discouraging vitamin C for those patients despite its general health benefits.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a causal reconciliation approach: I looked for a fact that would explain why a generally beneficial recommendation would be reversed in a special case. The key clue was that vitamin C is an antioxidant, so the most relevant explanation had to connect that property to how cancer therapy works. The successful step was matching vitamin C’s antioxidant effect with therapies that rely on oxidation, showing how the supplement could undermine treatment. In similar problems, identify the principle behind the general recommendation, then look for an answer choice showing how that same principle creates a conflicting effect in the exception case.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for an explanation of an apparent exception: why a substance generally recommended for health would be discouraged for a subset of cancer patients. The key task was not to evaluate whether vitamin C is beneficial overall, but to identify a mechanism that reconciles the general recommendation with the special case. My strategy was to connect the stated property of vitamin C—being an antioxidant—to the possibility that some cancer therapies rely on oxidation to damage or kill cancer cells. That was an appropriate causal-reconciliation approach because the stimulus highlighted antioxidant action for a reason, signaling that the explanation would likely involve that feature becoming counterproductive in a treatment context.

The crucial evidence I used was the relationship between antioxidants and oxygen-based damage: if treatment effectiveness depends on oxidative processes, then vitamin C could undermine the therapy. I also used the constraint that doctors discourage vitamin C only for “some” cancer patients, which fit an answer describing only some kinds of cancer cells or therapies. I avoided weak alternatives that merely said vitamin C does not help with side effects or cancer prevention, because those do not explain why doctors would actively discourage it. A hidden assumption in my reasoning was that cancer therapies can work through oxidation, but the credited choice supplied exactly that missing link. The reasoning succeeded because I looked for an answer that created a direct conflict between vitamin C’s usual benefit and treatment goals. In similar problems, I should systematically identify the general rule, the exception, and the mechanism that makes the exception rational. A transferable rule is: when a question asks to explain a differing recommendation, prefer the choice that shows the normally beneficial feature reverses its effect under the specific conditions described.

item.context: Suggestive effect refers to the indirect method of implicit and abstract induction under the condition of no confrontation, which affects people's psychology and behavior, so as to induce people to act or accept certain opinions in a certain way, so as to make their thoughts and behavior consistent with the expected goal of the suggestive.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following does not have a suggestive effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In class, the students were still discussing the topic between classes. The teacher who was giving a lecture stopped, and the classroom was silent immediately.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grandma Zhang, in her 70s, kept saying my grandson is coming back soon. Not long after, grandson really came back to see her.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the forest, the old hunter walked silently, and everyone followed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Since the head teacher praised Xiao Hong's rapid progress in learning at the class meeting, Xiao Hong has studied harder.

response:
Reasoning: Suggestive effect means implicitly influencing others’ psychology/behavior without confrontation. A, C, and D all show someone’s behavior changing due to another’s implicit influence. B is just Grandma Zhang’s repeated statement followed by the grandson’s return, with no evidence her words influenced him.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I checked each option against the required elements of suggestive effect, especially indirect influence on another person’s psychology or behavior. The key factor was causation through implicit induction rather than mere sequence or coincidence. My successful step was noticing that one option only described an elder’s expectation followed by an event, without showing that her words actually shaped anyone’s behavior. For similar problems, I should systematically test every option for all parts of the definition, especially whether there is a real influence mechanism rather than just a result occurring afterward.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the definition as requiring several linked elements: the influence must be indirect, implicit rather than explicit, nonconfrontational, and it must affect another person’s psychology or behavior so that the result aligns with the influencer’s expected goal. That interpretation was correct and gave me a clear checklist for evaluating each option. My strategy was to test each scenario for a causal influence relationship, not just a sequence of events. This was appropriate because the key distinction in the definition is not what happened, but whether one person’s implicit cue actually induced another person’s response. I used the fact that some options involved observable behavioral adjustment after a social cue, such as silence, following, or increased effort, which fits suggestion. The crucial evidence I focused on in the selected option was the lack of any shown mechanism connecting the speaker’s repeated statement to the other person’s later action. I implicitly rejected a common shortcut: treating prediction plus later fulfillment as proof of psychological influence. I also considered whether mere authority or praise can count as suggestion, and here they can, because indirect social signals often shape behavior without explicit commands. The reasoning succeeded because I separated correlation from inducement. In similar problems, I should continue checking every definitional component, especially the presence of an influence pathway. A transferable rule is: when a concept involves causal social influence, do not infer it from temporal succession alone; require evidence that one party’s cue plausibly altered the other party’s mental state or conduct.

item.context: Fat tail effect refers to the phenomenon that statistical extreme situations often occur abnormally.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following phenomena belongs to fat tail effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The welfare lottery betting station in happy community won the first prize in five consecutive issues.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The top students in Arts and Science in the college entrance examination of J province this year are all girls. We can't help feeling that boys' grades are really inferior to girls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Affected by the El Nino phenomenon, many places in southern China have experienced a once-in-a-century rainstorm.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In this table tennis competition, the last champion Lao Wang played abnormally and was eliminated in the first round, which was surprising.

response:
Reasoning: Fat tail effect means rare extreme events happen more often than normal intuition expects. Among the options, the “once-in-a-century rainstorm” is an extreme statistical event occurring abnormally. The others are coincidence, overgeneralization, or individual abnormal performance.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach, looking for an event that seemed obviously “extreme” and unusual. The key clue I focused on was the phrase “once-in-a-century,” which made me equate rarity with a fat-tail phenomenon. My mistake was ignoring that fat-tail effects are about unusually frequent occurrence of extreme outcomes relative to normal expectations, not just any severe event; the repeated first-prize wins better captures that abnormal frequency pattern. In similar problems, I should test whether the example shows repeated or disproportionately likely extremes, rather than selecting the option with the most dramatic wording.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the definition too loosely as “any rare extreme event,” and that led me to match the most dramatic-sounding example rather than the one that best reflected the statistical idea. My strategy was to look for an unusually severe outcome, so I focused on the rainstorm because “once-in-a-century” sounded like an extreme tail event. That strategy was incomplete, because the key phrase in the definition is not just “extreme,” but that such extremes occur with abnormal frequency relative to ordinary expectations. I used the fact that extreme weather can be severe, but I missed the deeper constraint that fat-tail thinking is about the distribution assigning more probability mass to extremes than a thin-tail intuition would suggest. I also failed to distinguish between a single rare event and a pattern of repeated extreme outcomes, which is much more diagnostic of a fat-tail phenomenon. Another bad assumption was treating causal explanation (“affected by El Nino”) as evidence of a fat tail, when the question was asking about a statistical pattern, not merely an unusual event with a cause. I should also have considered whether an option reflected overgeneralization from outcomes or merely an individual upset, both of which are different concepts. The main cause of error was substituting vividness for fit to the definition. In similar problems, I should map every option to each element of the definition separately, especially frequency, extremity, and distributional implication. General rule: when a concept is statistical, prefer the option that demonstrates the distributional pattern itself, not just a memorable rare event.

item.context: It is impossible that all candidates will fail the exam.
item.question: Based on this, which of the following can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some candidates may not pass the exam

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some candidates must pass the exam

choices.label: C
choices.text: All candidates can pass the exam

choices.label: D
choices.text: All candidates must not pass the exam

response:
Reasoning: “Impossible that all candidates fail” means the situation where everyone fails cannot happen. Therefore, at least one candidate must not fail, i.e., must pass. So the valid inference is that some candidates must pass the exam.

FINAL ANSWER: B
