reflections.simple: I used a direct logical translation approach, converting “it is impossible that all candidates fail” into the negation of a universal claim. The key factor was recognizing that “not all fail” guarantees at least one exception, which in this context means at least one candidate passes. My success came from handling the quantifiers correctly: negating “all fail” becomes “some do not fail,” not merely “some may not fail.” For similar problems, rewrite statements with words like all, some, impossible, and must into formal quantifier logic before comparing answer choices.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the statement as a modal logic claim about what outcomes are ruled out: the world in which every candidate fails is not possible. That interpretation was correct because the key phrase is “it is impossible that,” which expresses necessity about the negation of a scenario. My strategy was to translate the sentence into its logical equivalent: not(all fail), which implies at least one candidate does not fail. From there, given the exam context, “does not fail” supports the conclusion that at least one candidate must pass, so the inference matched the strongest warranted option.

The reasoning succeeded because I focused on quantifiers and modality rather than on everyday phrasing. The crucial constraint I used was the equivalence between denying a universal failure outcome and asserting the existence of at least one non-failure case. I did not rely on weaker possibilities such as “may not pass,” which would not capture the necessity in the premise. I also avoided being distracted by overly broad alternatives like “all can pass,” which introduces a possibility not guaranteed by the statement.

One assumption embedded in the reasoning is that “pass” is the relevant complement of “fail” in this testing context; that assumption is standard here and consistent with the answer set. A useful improvement for similar problems is to explicitly classify answer choices by strength: must, may, all, some. General rule: when a statement says a universal condition is impossible, infer the necessary existence of at least one counterexample, and prefer the strongest option that exactly matches that logical form.

item.context: There are differences in the way of understanding, the logic of thinking and even the overall cultural concept between China and the West. For example, Western-style persistence may lead to gradual understanding, emphasizing the relationship between subject and object and the accuracy of object description, while Chinese-style persistence leads to harmony and understanding, and there is often some vagueness in describing the object. However, there is no superiority or inferiority between the two, only the dialogue and enlightenment, complementarity and harmony arising from the differences. Through differences to achieve neutralization, such harmony but differences can achieve a harmonious, rich and colorful world.
item.question: Which of the following does not have a correct understanding of this paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The West pays attention to the accuracy of object description, while China tends to coexist clarity and fuzziness

choices.label: B
choices.text: The differences between China and the West are opposing and unreconciled, both of them are difficult to sustain

choices.label: C
choices.text: There are differences in cultural concepts, but there is no difference between the advantages and disadvantages of right and wrong

choices.label: D
choices.text: The realization of a rich and colorful world is the purpose of inspiring the dialogue between the two cultures

response:
Reasoning: The paragraph stresses complementarity, dialogue, and “harmony with differences,” not irreconcilable opposition. A, C, and D align with the text’s meaning, while B directly contradicts it.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a contrast-and-elimination approach, matching each option against the paragraph’s core claims about difference, complementarity, and harmony. The key factor was the author’s explicit statement that the two traditions are neither superior nor inferior and can reach “harmony with differences” through dialogue and mutual enlightenment. My success came from prioritizing that central thesis over isolated details, which made the contradictory option stand out clearly. For similar problems, I should first identify the passage’s main evaluative stance, then reject any choice that reverses or exaggerates that stance.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the option that misrepresented the paragraph, not the one that best summarized it. My strategy was to identify the passage’s core claims and then test each choice against those claims for consistency. The key textual evidence was the repeated emphasis on “no superiority or inferiority,” “dialogue and enlightenment,” “complementarity,” and “harmony but differences,” which clearly frame cultural difference as productive rather than antagonistic. I also used the contrast in thinking styles—precision in object description versus harmony and some vagueness—to verify that the paragraph acknowledged differences without ranking them. That made it reasonable to accept choices that preserved difference, equality, and mutual enrichment.  

A useful part of my reasoning was noticing that one option introduced a much stronger claim than the passage supported: it turned difference into unreconciled opposition and instability. That was not just unsupported; it directly contradicted the passage’s conclusion about neutralization and harmonious coexistence. I did assume that “purpose” language in one choice was acceptable because the paragraph presents a rich, colorful world as the outcome and implicit aim of dialogue; that assumption was defensible here. An alternative risk would have been over-reading the sentence about vagueness and precision and treating it as a value judgment, but the passage explicitly blocks that reading. The reason the reasoning succeeded is that I prioritized the author’s evaluative stance, not just the descriptive comparison. A transferable rule is: when a passage contrasts two approaches but explicitly denies superiority and emphasizes complementarity, eliminate any option that reframes the contrast as conflict, incompatibility, or mutual invalidation.

item.context: According to the traditional theory of memory, memory is like a videotape, each recall is to find a certain video within the corresponding time in the brain to play back. The theory of scene construction gives another explanation for memory: the human brain only records fragments when it encodes memory; when needed, the human brain connects and complements these fragments in a logical way consistent with the state of the subject's current beliefs to form memories.
item.question: Which of the following options can not be explained by the theory of scene construction but not by the traditional theory of memory?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some people with Alzheimer's lose the ability to remember.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People's memories of the same past many times, the content will change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: According to one statistic, eyewitnesses identify people whom the police know to be incorrect in 20% to 25% of cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: British psychologist Kimberly Weber succeeded in implanting false memories of childhood by showing subjects some synthetic fake photos.

response:
Reasoning: Scene construction explains reconstructive changes and false memories, so B, C, and D fit it better than the “videotape” view. But A, memory loss in Alzheimer’s, can be explained by traditional memory theory as damage to storage/retrieval, so it is not distinctive evidence for scene construction.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a contrast-of-explanatory-power approach: I checked which option is specifically better explained by reconstructive memory than by a storage-and-playback model. The key factor was whether the phenomenon involved distortion, updating, or fabrication during recall, since those are hallmark predictions of scene construction. My success came from separating “can be explained at all” from “can be explained by one theory but not the other”; memory loss itself does not uniquely favor reconstruction. For similar problems, explicitly test each option against both theories and eliminate any choice that is compatible with both, even if it is broadly related to memory.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the option that is **not uniquely supported** by scene construction over the traditional “videotape” theory. That distinction mattered: the task was not to find something scene construction explains, but something that does **not create an advantage** for scene construction relative to the older view. My strategy was to test each option for whether it depends on memory being reconstructive rather than simply stored and replayed. That was an appropriate strategy because the stem explicitly contrasts fixed playback with fragment-based reconstruction shaped by current beliefs.

The key evidence I used was that repeated retellings changing memory content, mistaken eyewitness identification, and experimentally implanted false memories all point to reconstruction, distortion, and supplementation. Those are difficult for a literal playback model to explain, but natural for scene construction. By contrast, simple loss of remembering ability only indicates a failure somewhere in memory functioning, which both theories could accommodate. An important assumption I made was that the traditional theory still allows memory failure due to damage, even if it treats intact memories as stored records. That assumption was justified because storage-and-retrieval models do not imply perfect preservation under disease.

I also correctly considered the alternative reading that some options merely describe memory phenomena, while others specifically discriminate between theories. The success of the reasoning came from focusing on **comparative explanatory power**, not on whether an option was generally memory-related. For similar problems, I should explicitly ask: “Which option distinguishes the theories, rather than merely fitting one of them?” A transferable rule is: when a question asks what one theory explains **but another does not**, eliminate any option that is compatible with both theories, even if it is strongly associated with the topic.

item.context: Meerkat sentinels,  so-called because they watch for predators while other meerkat group members forage, almost never fall victim to those predators, yet the foragers often do. This advantage accruing to the sentinel does not mean that its watchful behavior is entirely self-interested. On the contrary, the sentinel' s behavior is an example of animal behavior motivated at least in part by altruism. The loud bark emitted by the sentinel as it dashes for the cover of the nearest hole alerts other group members to the presence of danger.
item.question: Which one of the following is a questionable reasoning technique employed in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: concluding that a claim is false on the grounds that insufficient evidence has been offered to support it

choices.label: B
choices.text: appealing to evidence that tends to undermine rather than support the argument's conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: appealing to evidence that presupposes the truth of the argument's conclusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring solely from an effect produced by an action that a purpose of the action is to produce that effect

response:
Reasoning: The argument treats the bark’s beneficial effect on other meerkats as evidence that producing that benefit is part of the sentinel’s motivation. But an action’s effect does not by itself show its purpose. The bark could simply be a self-protective response that incidentally alerts others.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-identification approach: I separated the evidence from the conclusion and asked whether the evidence established motivation or only described outcomes. The key factor was the jump from “the bark alerts others” to “the behavior is motivated at least in part by altruism,” which treats a beneficial effect as proof of purpose. My answer was correct because I focused on that effect-versus-intent gap rather than getting distracted by the discussion of predator risk. For similar problems, explicitly test whether the argument is moving from what an action causes to why the agent did it, and reject that move unless independent evidence of motive is provided.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the flaw in the argument’s reasoning, not whether the conclusion about altruism was actually true. My strategy was to identify the conclusion, isolate the evidence offered for it, and then ask whether that evidence logically established the claimed motivation. That was the right approach for a flaw question, because the conclusion concerned purpose or motive, while the evidence described an observable consequence of the behavior. The key fact I used was that the bark alerts other group members, but the argument moved from that effect to the claim that the behavior is motivated at least partly by altruism. I recognized that this is a classic mismatch between outcome and intention: an action can benefit others without being performed for their benefit. I did not rely on outside biological knowledge; instead, I focused on the structure of the inference, which made the reasoning strong. A shortcut that helped was asking, “Could the same behavior occur for a self-interested reason while still producing this effect?” Since yes, the inference was unsupported. I also implicitly ruled out other flaw types by checking whether the argument attacked a claim for lack of evidence, used self-undermining evidence, or assumed its conclusion. What made the reasoning successful was precise attention to the difference between causal effects and motivating purposes. In similar problems, I should continue testing whether the evidence shows what happened, why it happened, or merely what resulted. General rule: never infer an agent’s intention solely from the beneficial or harmful consequences of the agent’s action.

item.context: Art critic: Abstract paintings are nonrepresentational, and so the only measure of their worth is their interplay of color, texture, and form. But for a painting to spur the viewer to political action, instances of social injustice must be not only represented, but also clearly comprehensible as such. Ttherefore, abstract painting can never be a politically significant art form.
item.question: Which one of the following is an assumption that is required by the art critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Paintings that fail to move a viewer to political action cannot be politically significant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The interplay of color, texture, and form is not a measure of the worth of representational paintings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Unless people view representations of social injustice, their political activity is insignificant.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Abstract painting cannot stimulate people to act.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion says abstract painting can never be politically significant because it cannot represent injustice clearly enough to spur political action. This requires assuming that if a painting does not move viewers to political action, then it is not politically significant. That is exactly choice A.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-negation approach: I linked the premise about what is needed to spur political action with the conclusion that abstract painting can never be politically significant, then looked for the bridge between those ideas. The key factor was that the argument moves from “cannot produce political action in this way” to “therefore not politically significant,” which requires equating political significance with the capacity to move viewers to action. My success came from identifying that missing bridge rather than getting distracted by side claims about representation or artistic worth. For similar problems, I should test whether the conclusion introduces a stronger standard than the premises and then look for the assumption that makes that standard necessary.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument correctly as an assumption question asking for a statement the conclusion depends on, not merely one that would strengthen it. The structure was: abstract paintings are nonrepresentational; only representational and clearly comprehensible depictions of injustice can spur political action; therefore abstract painting can never be politically significant. My strategy was to identify the gap between the intermediate claim about spurring political action and the final claim about political significance. That was appropriate because the conclusion introduced a stronger evaluative category than the premises explicitly supported. I focused on the missing bridge: the argument needs political significance to depend on the capacity to move viewers to political action. Without that bridge, the premises would show at most that abstract painting cannot produce one particular political effect, not that it lacks all political significance.  

I correctly rejected the temptation to choose an answer that merely restated a premise in stronger language, such as saying abstract painting cannot stimulate people to act. That option would not connect action-stimulation to political significance. I also did not get distracted by irrelevant claims about representational painting generally, which helped avoid answer choice B. The successful part of the reasoning was noticing that the conclusion used a necessary condition for significance that had not yet been established. In similar problems, I should continue testing each option with a negation check: if negating the choice allows the conclusion to survive, it is not required. The transferable rule is: when a conclusion applies a broad evaluative label based on failure to meet one specific standard, look for the hidden assumption that treats that standard as necessary for the label.

item.context: A certain naval force has 7 ships of A, B, C, D, E, H, and G. It is planned to form two fleets to sail. There are 3 ships in the first formation and 4 ships in the second formation. The formation must meet the following conditions: (1) The aircraft carrier must be listed in the second formation; (2) E and C have at most one formation in the first formation; 3) A and C are not in the same formation; (4) If B is arranged in the first formation, D must also be arranged in the first formation.
item.question: If A is in the second formation, which of the following ships must also be in the second formation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B

choices.label: B
choices.text: C

choices.label: C
choices.text: D

choices.label: D
choices.text: E

response:
Reasoning: If A is in the second formation, then by condition (3), C cannot be in the second, so C must be in the first. By condition (2), E and C can have at most one ship in the first formation. Since C is already in the first, E cannot be there, so E must be in the second.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a constraint-chaining approach: I assumed the given condition, then applied each rule in sequence to force placements across the two formations. The key factor was combining the rule that A and C cannot be together with the rule limiting E and C to at most one ship in the first formation; once C was forced into the first, E was forced out of it. The success came from translating “at most one of E and C in the first formation” correctly and using it immediately after placing C. For similar problems, first place any item fixed by the question stem, then propagate every conditional and counting restriction before considering answer choices.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a conditional “must be true” problem: assuming one ship is fixed in the second formation, determine which option is forced into that same formation under all valid arrangements. My strategy was to chain the rules deductively rather than test all answer choices by brute force, which was appropriate because the constraints were strong and interacted directly. The key inference was to apply the separation rule first: once that ship was placed in the second formation, its incompatible partner had to be in the first. Then I used the rule limiting how many of two named ships could be in the first formation; with one already forced there, the other could not also be there, so it had to be in the second. That was a clean use of necessity rather than possibility.

A strength of the reasoning was that it tracked exact implications from the premises instead of relying on informal intuition about ship placement. I also correctly ignored irrelevant rules once the needed conclusion was already forced; the aircraft-carrier condition and the conditional about two other ships did not affect this chain. One assumption embedded in the reasoning was that “at most one in the first formation” means zero or one, which is essential and was interpreted properly. An alternative approach would have been to test each option for whether it could be placed in the first formation without contradiction, but the direct rule-combination was more efficient. The success came from recognizing which rules were immediately activated by the given condition and which were not. In similar problems, I should first identify any rule that turns the given assumption into a forced placement, then propagate that consequence through counting or exclusivity constraints. A general rule is: in constrained-grouping problems, combine a binary exclusion rule with a capacity limit to derive necessity, and distinguish sharply between what is merely allowed and what is logically forced.

item.context: Insufficient rain can cause crops to falter and agricultural prices to rise. Records indicate that during a certain nation' s recent crisis, faltering crops and rising agricultural prices prompted the government to take over food distribution in an effort to prevent starvation. Thus, the weather must have played an important role in bringing about the crisis.
item.question: The argument's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers, merely from the fact that one event could have caused a second event, that the first event in fact caused the second

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses the term crisis equivocally in the reasoning, referring to both a political crisis and an economic crisis

choices.label: C
choices.text: concludes, merely from the fact that the period of insufficient rain occurred before the nation's crisis, that insufficient rain caused the nation's crisis

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to take into account the possibility that the scarcity was not severe enough to justify the government's taking over food distribution

response:
Reasoning: The argument moves from “insufficient rain can cause crop failure and high prices” plus “crop failure and high prices occurred during the crisis” to “weather played an important role.” That assumes a possible cause was the actual cause, without evidence ruling out other causes.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a causal-flaw approach: I mapped the premises as “X can cause Y” and “Y happened,” then checked whether the conclusion improperly treated X as the actual cause. The key clue was that the argument never established insufficient rain actually occurred or that weather, rather than some other factor, produced the crop problems and price increases. My success came from recognizing the classic possibility-to-actuality fallacy in causal reasoning. For similar problems, I should explicitly test whether the evidence shows only that a cause is possible, versus showing that it actually operated in the case described.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the flaw in a causal argument, not for an assessment of whether the conclusion was plausible in real life. That interpretation was correct because the passage moved from a general causal possibility about insufficient rain to a specific historical conclusion about what contributed to a crisis. My strategy was to map the argument’s structure: general claim about what weather can cause, observation that those effects occurred, then conclusion that weather therefore played an important causal role. That was the right strategy because flaw questions are best handled by abstracting the reasoning pattern before comparing answer choices.

The key evidence I used was that the premises established only a possible causal pathway, not that this pathway actually operated in the case described. I also correctly noticed that the argument did not eliminate alternative causes of crop failure or price increases, such as war, policy errors, or distribution breakdowns. An assumption built into the argument was that because weather is one possible explanation of those effects, it was the real explanation here. I correctly rejected the temptation to treat this as a mere post hoc flaw, since the argument was not relying only on temporal order. I also rejected equivocation because the term “crisis” was not doing the argumentative work.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the gap between “can cause” and “did cause.” In similar problems, I should explicitly test whether the premises show necessity, sufficiency, or only possibility. General rule: when an argument infers actual causation from the mere existence of a possible causal mechanism plus matching effects, it commits a possibility-to-actuality causal fallacy.

item.context: NorthAir charges low fares for its economy class seats, but it provides very cramped seating and few amenities. Market research shows that economy passengers would willingly pay more for wider seating and better service, and additional revenue provided by these higher ticket prices would more than cover the additional cost of providing these amenities. Even though NorthAir is searching for ways to improve its profitability, it has decided not to make these improvements.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, would most help to explain NorthAir ' s decision in light of its objectives?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The number of people who would be willing to pay the high fares NorthAir charges for its business-class seats would decrease if its economy-class seating were more acceptable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A few of NorthAir' s economy-class passengers are satisfied with the service they receive, given the low price they pay.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Very few people avoid flying on NorthAir because of the cramped seating and poor service offered in economy class.

choices.label: D
choices.text: None of NorthAir' s competitors offers significantly better seating and service to economy-class passengers than NorthAir does.

response:
Reasoning: If improving economy would cause some passengers to stop buying NorthAir’s higher-profit business-class seats, the airline could lose more revenue than it gains from upgraded economy fares. That directly explains why a profitability-focused airline would reject the change despite economy passengers’ stated willingness to pay more.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a profit-maximization approach, looking for a hidden tradeoff that could make an apparently profitable economy upgrade reduce overall profits. The key factor was cannibalization: improving economy could pull customers away from a more profitable business-class product, offsetting the gains from higher economy fares. My success came from checking total-system effects rather than evaluating the economy cabin in isolation. For similar problems, always test whether a proposed improvement in one segment could reduce profits elsewhere through substitution, lost premium sales, or other indirect effects.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking for a fact that reconciles an apparent tension: the airline could profit on the economy product itself by upgrading it, yet still rationally decline to do so because of some broader profitability effect. My strategy was to look for an explanation that operated at the company level rather than only within the economy segment. That was appropriate because the stimulus already said the higher economy fares would cover the added amenity costs, so any good explanation had to come from an indirect consequence the original analysis left out. The key evidence I used was the distinction between segment profitability and total profitability. I focused on the possibility of cannibalization: improving a lower-tier product can reduce demand for a higher-margin premium product. That is exactly the kind of hidden tradeoff that can make a seemingly profitable improvement unattractive overall. I implicitly assumed that business-class seats are sufficiently profitable that even a modest loss there could outweigh gains in economy, and that assumption fit the “in light of its objectives” wording. I should still note that alternatives about customer satisfaction, current avoidance rates, or competitors’ offerings do not address the missing financial mechanism as directly. The reasoning succeeded because I searched for a choice that supplied the omitted constraint in the profit calculation. A transferable rule is: when a plan appears profitable on its own terms, the best explanation for rejecting it usually identifies a second-order effect on another revenue stream, cost center, or strategic objective that the initial argument ignored.

item.context: Start-up companies financed by venture capitalists have a much lower failure rate than companies financed by other means. Source of financing, ttherefore, must be a more important causative factor in the success of a start-up company than are such factors as the personal characteristics of the entrepreneur, the quality of strategic planning, or the management structure of the company.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The management structures of start-up companies are generally less formal than the management structures of ongoing businesses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: More than half of all new companies fail within five years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Venture capitalists base their decisions to fund start. up companies on such factors as the characteristics of the entrepreneur and quality of strategic planning of the company.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The strategic planning of a start-up company is a less important factor in the long-term success of the company than are the personal characteristics of the entrepreneur.

response:
Reasoning: The argument treats financing source as the cause of success. But if venture capitalists choose companies based on entrepreneur quality and strategic planning, then those underlying factors may explain the lower failure rate instead. That undermines the causal claim about financing itself.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a causal-weakening approach: I looked for an alternative explanation for the correlation between venture-capital financing and lower failure rates. The key factor was selection bias—if venture capitalists choose firms based on strong entrepreneurs and solid planning, then those traits, not the financing source itself, could be driving success. My success came from identifying that the argument confuses “companies funded by X do better” with “X causes them to do better.” For similar problems, test any causal claim by asking whether the alleged cause might simply be selecting cases that already possess the real success-producing features.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a causal-weaken problem: the stimulus observed a correlation between venture-capital funding and lower failure rates, then concluded that financing source is a more important cause of success than other business factors. My strategy was to look for an alternative explanation that would preserve the correlation while undercutting the causal inference. That is the right strategy here, because the key logical gap is the move from “companies with X have better outcomes” to “X is the main cause of the better outcomes.” The crucial fact I used was that venture capitalists may select companies partly because of the entrepreneur’s characteristics and the quality of the company’s planning. If that is true, then the funded group is not comparable to the non-funded group, and the lower failure rate may reflect preexisting strengths rather than the effect of funding itself. I did not rely on irrelevant background facts such as general business failure rates or broad differences in management structure, which would not directly address the comparison the argument makes. An assumption I correctly challenged was that funding source is independent of the other success-related variables. I also implicitly considered whether any answer merely described one factor’s importance without connecting it to the funding decision, and rejected that as too weak. The reasoning succeeded because it targeted selection bias, which is the main vulnerability in arguments based on outcome differences between selected and unselected groups. In similar problems, I should explicitly test whether the groups differ before the alleged cause occurs. A transferable rule is: when an argument infers causation from superior outcomes in a screened or chosen group, first ask whether the selector used preexisting success predictors, because that can explain the outcome without crediting the alleged cause.

item.context: For a certain type of ulcer, traditional therapy can completely heal 44% of patients' ulcers within 6 months. A new therapy for this type of ulcer has achieved obvious improves in 80% of the ulcers treated in a 6-month trial. 61% of ulcers were healed. Since the trial only treated those ulcers very severe, this new treatment is obviously more effective than traditional treatments.
item.question: In order to better compare the effects of the two therapies, is there any additional evidence that needs to be added?

choices.label: A
choices.text: What is the difference between the methods used in the two therapies?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Is there a big difference in the cost of the two therapies?

choices.label: C
choices.text: What is the proportion of patients with this type of ulcer, treated under traditional therapies in 6 months, who have achieved significant improvement?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Among the patients who participated in the 6-month trial of the new therapy, what percentage of the people were dissatisfied with the recovery rate?

response:
Reasoning: The comparison is flawed because the new therapy reports both “improvement” and “healed,” while the traditional therapy gives only “healed.” To compare effectiveness fairly, we need the traditional therapy’s rate of significant improvement, especially since the new trial involved very severe ulcers.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a comparability-based reasoning approach: I checked whether the evidence for the two treatments measured the same outcome. The key factor was that one therapy was described using both “obvious improvement” and “healed,” while the other was described only by “completely healed,” so the comparison was not on matched criteria. My success came from noticing that to evaluate “more effective,” we need the same benchmark for both groups, not extra details like cost or patient satisfaction. For similar problems, first align the outcome measure, time frame, and population before comparing two treatments or interventions.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking what missing piece of evidence would make the comparison between the two therapies valid, not which therapy is actually better. That was the right framing, because the argument compares outcomes reported in different ways: traditional therapy is described by complete healing, while the new therapy is described by both improvement and healing. My strategy was to look for a mismatch in the metrics being compared and then identify which answer choice would supply the missing comparable measure. That was appropriate because arguments about comparative effectiveness depend on holding the outcome standard constant across groups. The key fact I used was that “80% improved” under the new therapy cannot be meaningfully compared with “44% healed” under the traditional therapy, since improvement is a broader and weaker outcome than healing. I also noticed that the new trial involved very severe ulcers, but I treated that as background rather than the central flaw, which was sensible because none of the choices directly addressed severity matching. One assumption behind my reasoning was that “obvious improvement” and “complete healing” are distinct endpoints that should not be conflated. I should also have explicitly checked each alternative by asking whether it affects effectiveness comparison or merely practical considerations like cost or satisfaction. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on comparability of outcome measures rather than being distracted by the stronger-looking percentages. A transferable rule is: when evaluating comparative claims, first verify that the groups are measured on the same outcome, over the same time frame, and under sufficiently similar conditions before drawing conclusions from the numbers.

item.context: Modern Western Aesthetics, instead of applying the traditional philosophical methods in the past, it moves towards psychological aesthetics and scientific aesthetics. Psychological aesthetics uses scientific methods to study human aesthetic psychology, focusing on the subject; scientific aesthetics uses scientific methods to analyze the structure and function of aesthetic objects, focusing on the object. But no matter which method is adopted, they think that endless philosophical and speculative discussions on the essence of beauty (the definition of beauty) are meaningless.
item.question: It can be seen from this.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Modern Western aesthetics believes that the philosophical thinking of traditional aesthetics is meaningless and the methods are not scientific

choices.label: B
choices.text: Psychological aesthetics studies the aesthetic psychology of people, focusing on the study of the subject and content of aesthetic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scientific aesthetics focuses on the study of aesthetic objects, that is, scientific analysis of the structure and function of aesthetic objects

choices.label: D
choices.text: The philosophical discussion on the essence of beauty should be discarded

response:
Reasoning: The passage directly states that scientific aesthetics focuses on the object and uses scientific methods to analyze the structure and function of aesthetic objects. A and D are too absolute, and B adds unsupported “content of aesthetic.”
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a direct textual inference approach: compare each option against the passage and eliminate any that add claims stronger than what is stated. The key factor was the passage’s explicit contrast between psychological aesthetics and scientific aesthetics, especially the clear statement that scientific aesthetics analyzes the structure and function of aesthetic objects and focuses on the object. The successful step was noticing that A and D overgeneralize from “endless discussions are meaningless” to rejecting all traditional philosophy, while B introduces extra wording not supported by the text. For similar problems, I should choose the option that most closely restates the passage and reject choices that contain stronger, broader, or added claims.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the statement most directly supported by the passage, not for a broader evaluation of modern Western aesthetics. That interpretation was correct, because the prompt ended with “It can be seen from this,” which signals an inference grounded closely in the text. My strategy was to compare each option against the passage and eliminate choices that overstated, distorted, or added content. That was appropriate here because the passage provided explicit contrasts between psychological aesthetics and scientific aesthetics, along with a limited claim about discussions of beauty’s essence. The key evidence I used was the sentence saying scientific aesthetics analyzes the structure and function of aesthetic objects and focuses on the object. I also noticed that one distractor added an extra element not stated in the passage, and two others converted a limited description into sweeping normative or evaluative conclusions. Those were exactly the kinds of unsupported extensions this type of reading question often tests.

The reasoning succeeded because I distinguished between “the passage says X thinkers regard something as meaningless” and “therefore all traditional philosophy is meaningless” or “therefore it should be discarded.” I avoided assuming that criticism of one issue implies rejection of an entire tradition. One alternative I needed to check carefully was whether a partially correct option contained even a small addition that made it invalid. In similar problems, I should continue using a strict textual-support standard: prefer the option that restates a specific claim, and reject any choice that adds value judgments, universal language, or extra categories not explicitly given. A transferable rule is: in inference questions, the best answer is usually the one with the least interpretive expansion beyond the passage’s exact scope.

item.context: Does watching someone else eat fill one' s own stomach? In which one of the following does the reasoning most closely parallel that employed in the passage?
item.question: Some people believe that witnessing violence in movies will discharge aggressive energy.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some people think nationalism is defensible. Hasn't nationalism been the excuse for committing abominable crimes?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some people think workaholics are compensating for a lack of interpersonal skills. However, aren't most doctors workaholics?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some people think that economists can control inflation. Can meteorologists make the sun shine?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some people think appropriating supplies at work for their own personal use is morally wrong. Isn't shoplifting morally wrong?

response:
Reasoning: The passage rejects a claim by analogy: merely witnessing something doesn’t produce the corresponding effect in oneself. Choice C similarly rejects a claimed power by comparing it to an obviously impossible one, using a rhetorical analogy to undermine the original belief.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used analogical reasoning: I looked for an answer that attacks a claim by comparing it to a different case where the same underlying assumption is clearly absurd. The key factor was the passage’s structure—challenging whether merely observing or predicting something gives one causal control over it. My success came from matching that exact pattern of reasoning, not just the topic or tone. For similar problems, identify the abstract logic first and choose the option that preserves the same causal relationship, not merely one that sounds skeptical or rhetorical.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the answer choice that matched the passage’s argument form, not its topic. That was the right interpretation, because the key task was to identify a parallel pattern of reasoning rather than to judge whether the conclusion was true. My strategy was to abstract the passage into a structure: it challenges a causal belief by using a rhetorical comparison to an obviously absurd case. That was appropriate because LSAT parallel-reasoning questions are usually best handled by stripping away subject matter and comparing logical form.

The crucial feature I noticed was that the passage does not provide empirical evidence; instead, it uses an analogy framed as a rhetorical question to suggest that merely observing or witnessing something does not generate the corresponding physical or psychological outcome. I also implicitly recognized that the argument is dismissive rather than evidentiary: it undermines a claim by comparing it to another claim that seems plainly false. A possible shortcut I used was focusing on “rhetorical analogy attacking a supposed causal power,” which worked here because one option shared that exact style. I correctly rejected choices that relied on different moves, such as citing bad consequences, offering a counterexample, or appealing to consistency in moral judgment.

What made the reasoning successful was matching both the method and the argumentative posture, not just the superficial presence of a question. In similar problems, I should continue identifying whether the original argument uses analogy, counterexample, principle application, or causal critique before reading the choices. A transferable rule is: when solving parallel-reasoning questions, map the argument’s functional structure—claim type, support type, and inference move—before comparing answer choices.

item.context: By examining the fossilized leaves of any prehistoric plant it is possible to determine the climate in which that specimen grew because the size and shape of a leaf are unique to a given climate. Since the climate at a given location depends on the altitude at that location, it follows that the size and shape of a fossilized leaf also indicates the altitude at which the plant grew.
item.question: The reasoning in the argument is vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the size and shape of a leaf as if they were the only physical characteristics of a leaf that depend on climate

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on a weak analogy between a leaf and the fossil of a leaf as evidence for the claims advanced

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to demonstrate that no species of plant can long survive a violent change in its environment

choices.label: D
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that locations at different altitudes can have the same climate

response:
Reasoning: The argument assumes climate uniquely determines altitude at a location. But different altitudes can share the same climate, so knowing leaf shape may indicate climate without uniquely indicating altitude. Thus the conclusion about altitude does not follow from the premises.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a conditional/uniqueness analysis: the argument moved from leaf traits identifying climate to climate identifying altitude, so I checked whether that second link was one-to-one. The key factor was that “altitude affects climate” does not mean “climate uniquely determines altitude”; the same climate can occur at multiple altitudes. My success came from spotting this reversal error in the causal/inferential chain. For similar problems, test each step in a chain of reasoning for whether the relationship is sufficient, necessary, or unique before accepting a conclusion that identifies one variable from another.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the stimulus as an argument about whether one indicator can be used to infer another through an intermediate variable. The key structure was: leaf traits identify climate, climate depends on altitude, therefore leaf traits identify altitude. My strategy was to test whether the relationship from climate to altitude was one-to-one, because a valid inference through a middle term requires enough uniqueness to preserve identification. That was the right strategy here: even if leaf shape reliably tracks climate, the conclusion fails if the same climate can occur at multiple altitudes. The crucial fact I used was that dependence does not imply uniqueness; saying climate depends on altitude does not mean each climate corresponds to exactly one altitude. I did not get distracted by irrelevant issues such as whether fossils perfectly preserve leaves or whether other leaf characteristics also vary with climate, because those points do not attack the logical bridge to the conclusion. The successful part of the reasoning was noticing an equivocation between “is influenced by” and “uniquely determines.” An alternative I appropriately rejected was reading the premise as if altitude fully fixes climate in a reversible way. In similar problems, I should explicitly check whether each step in a chain supports reverse inference or only forward dependence. A general rule is: when an argument infers X from Y because both relate to Z, verify that the Y–Z and Z–X links are sufficiently exclusive rather than merely causal or correlational.

item.context: Government procurement refers to the behavior that governments at all levels use national financial funds and government loans to purchase goods, projects and services in order to engage in daily government activities or meet the purpose of public services. Government procurement not only refers to the specific procurement process, but also the general name of procurement policy, procurement procedure, procurement process and procurement management, It is a system to manage public procurement
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the  followings is not government procurement:

choices.label: A
choices.text: A municipal government stipulates that office supplies exceeding a certain amount must be reported to relevant departments for centralized procurement

choices.label: B
choices.text: In order to facilitate citizens' travel, a municipal government rented a short message platform of a telecom company to send free short messages to citizens

choices.label: C
choices.text: In order to improve the local educational conditions, a county government allocated special funds to a primary school to renovate the school buildings, and stipulated that it must be carried out in strict accordance with the bidding procedures

choices.label: D
choices.text: A municipal government selects a hotel as the designated reception hotel through public bidding

response:
Reasoning: Government procurement requires the government itself to use fiscal funds to purchase goods, projects, or services. In C, the county government only allocates special funds to a school; it is funding construction, not directly making the procurement itself. The others are direct government purchases or procurement arrangements.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I checked whether each option involved a government body using public funds to purchase goods, projects, or services for government activity or public service. The key factor I focused on was “direct purchase by the government,” which led me to reject the case where funds were allocated to a school. My mistake was treating “allocation of special funds plus required bidding for renovation” as not procurement, while overlooking that merely designating a provider through bidding is not itself necessarily a purchase. For similar problems, I should distinguish between a completed or intended funded transaction and a regulatory/preferential qualification arrangement that does not itself establish procurement.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the definition too narrowly, focusing on whether the government was itself the immediate buyer in a single transaction rather than on the broader idea of a public procurement system. My strategy was to test each option against the phrase “use financial funds to purchase goods, projects, and services,” but I underused the part of the definition that says procurement also includes procurement policy, procedures, process, and management. That omission was decisive. In the school-renovation option, I treated the allocation of special funds as mere funding and concluded there was no procurement, but the description also included mandatory bidding procedures for a public project, which fits the broader institutional meaning of procurement. I made an implicit assumption that procurement must be executed directly by a government office, instead of recognizing that governments can organize or require procurement for publicly funded projects. At the same time, I failed to scrutinize the “designated hotel” arrangement as a potentially regulatory or qualification-setting act rather than an actual purchase of services. I should have compared all options on the distinction between purchasing behavior and vendor designation/administrative arrangement. The specific cause of error was over-weighting “direct payment by government” and under-weighting “procurement management” versus “non-purchase designation.” In similar problems, I should extract every definitional component and check each option against all of them, not just the most concrete element. General rule: when a definition includes both substantive acts and institutional processes, classify cases by the full scope of the definition and distinguish actual acquisition from mere approval, designation, or regulation.

item.context: There are few places where people can listen more easily than moving planes, ships and trains. There is a wonderful connection between the landscape in front of us and the ideas that may arise in our minds; broad thinking often requires broad landscapes, while new ideas come from strange places.
item.question: Which of the following options is intended to explain of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Travel broadens one's horizons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The scenery on a trip often leads to thinking.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The role of a traveler can increase one's life experience.

choices.label: D
choices.text: People's thinking point of view is easily affected by the environment.

response:
Reasoning: The passage emphasizes a link between the changing scenery during travel and the ideas that arise in our minds. It specifically says landscapes can inspire broad thinking and strange places can spark new ideas, so the focus is on scenery prompting thought during a trip.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea matching approach: I compared each option to the passage’s central relationship rather than to isolated words. The key factor was the repeated causal link between external scenery and internal thought—landscape and strange places were presented as triggers for ideas. The successful step was focusing on the passage’s specific mechanism, not broader travel benefits like experience or worldview. For similar problems, identify the exact cause-and-effect claim in the text and choose the option that preserves that relationship most precisely, avoiding answers that are merely related but more general.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the best paraphrase of the passage’s main explanatory point, not just a loosely related theme about travel. That was the right framing, because the passage is focused on a specific causal link: movement through landscapes stimulates thought. My strategy was to identify the passage’s repeated idea and then match it to the option that preserved both elements of that idea—travel context and mental activity. This was appropriate because the wording gives direct textual evidence: “landscape in front of us” is tied to “ideas that may arise in our minds,” and “broad landscapes” and “strange places” are both presented as triggers for thinking. I correctly used those explicit relationships rather than choosing a broader, more attractive slogan about travel generally improving people.

A key success was rejecting answers that were too general or shifted the emphasis from thought-generation to life experience or worldview. The passage is not mainly about personal growth, accumulated experience, or environmental influence in the abstract; it is about scenery during travel prompting reflection and ideas. One assumption that helped was treating “intended to explain” as “best summary of the author’s point,” which fit this item type. An alternative I needed to keep in mind was the broad environment-based choice, but it lacked the travel-scenery specificity central to the text. The main lesson is: when a passage states a concrete cause-and-effect relation, choose the option that preserves that relation with the same level of specificity, and avoid broader statements that are only indirectly implied.

item.context: Scientists have recently discovered that, in doses massive enough to kill cells, almost any chemical is carcinogenic because cell death causes rapid division among surviving cells, promoting cancer-causing mutations. A few chemicals are also carcinogenic without causing cell death. Until now studies of the carcinogenicity of food additives have always involved administering to test animals doses of additives larger than the largest possible human exposure levels and massive enough to kill large numbers of cells in the animals, and then observing the animals' cancer rates.
item.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following conclusions is most strongly supported by them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carcinogenic chemicals are usually absorbed in small doses in the natural environment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most of the food additives that are now banned because of carcinogenicity could safely be used in human foods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the doses heretofore used in carcinogenicity studies of food additives, cell death often does not occur in test animals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Until now results of carcinogenicity studies encouraged overestimation of the degree to which some food additives are carcinogenic.

response:
Reasoning: Studies used extremely high doses that kill cells. Since almost any chemical can appear carcinogenic at such doses due to cell death–induced cell division, those studies could make some additives seem more carcinogenic than they really are at realistic human exposure levels. This most strongly supports overestimation.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a causal-reasoning approach: I linked the testing method to a possible distortion in the observed outcome. The key factor was the statement that massive, cell-killing doses can make almost any chemical appear carcinogenic, while the food-additive studies always used such unrealistically high doses. The successful step was comparing test conditions with real human exposure and noticing that the studies could inflate apparent risk for additives that are only carcinogenic under extreme dosing. For similar problems, map how experimental conditions differ from real-world conditions and ask whether that mismatch could systematically bias the conclusion upward or downward.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the strongest inference from the premises, not for a claim that was guaranteed in every case or a broader policy recommendation. My strategy was to trace the causal chain in the stimulus: very high doses kill cells; cell death triggers rapid division in surviving cells; rapid division can promote mutations; therefore many chemicals can look carcinogenic under those testing conditions. That was an appropriate inference strategy because the answer had to connect the testing method to a likely distortion in study results. The key evidence I used was the contrast between the doses used in animal studies and the “largest possible human exposure levels,” which implied that the studies were not measuring ordinary real-world risk directly. I also used the important qualifier that only a few chemicals are carcinogenic even without cell death, which supports the idea that some positive findings may be artifacts of extreme dosing. I avoided assuming that all banned additives are safe, which would have gone beyond the evidence. I also rejected choices that contradicted explicit premises, such as denying that cell death occurred at those doses. What made the reasoning successful was distinguishing “could exaggerate carcinogenicity in some cases” from stronger, unjustified conclusions about all additives. In similar problems, I should keep tracking scope words like “some,” “most strongly supported,” and “until now.” A good general rule is: when experimental conditions systematically differ from real exposure conditions, the strongest supported conclusion is often about possible bias in the results, not about absolute safety or danger.

item.context: A parent believes that only imagination can carry out creative work, but imagination and knowledge are natural enemies. People's imagination disappears in the process of acquiring knowledge. Because knowledge is logical, and imagination has no rules to follow. In other words, the essence of knowledge is science, and the characteristic of imagination is absurdity. The human brain cannot tolerate two tigers in one mountain; in preschool, imagination dominates, and the brain is occupied by imagination; after school, most people's imagination is expelled by knowledge, and they become knowledgeable but unimaginative and can only repeat the discoveries of their predecessors all their lives.
item.question: Which of the following contradicts the parent's above point of view?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If you want your children to do creative work, don't send them to school

choices.label: B
choices.text: If enough knowledge is obtained, creative work cannot be carried out

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who discover knowledge have a certain imagination

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some people have no imagination, but can carry out creative work

response:
Reasoning: The parent claims only imagination enables creative work, and knowledge destroys imagination. Option D directly denies the core claim by saying creative work can be done without imagination. C only suggests discoverers may have imagination, which is less directly contradictory.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple:
I used a contradiction test: I identified the parent’s core claims, then checked which option most directly denied a necessary link in that argument. The key factor was the statement that only imagination can produce creative work, combined with the claim that knowledge suppresses imagination. Because of that, the strongest contradiction would be any option showing creative work can occur without imagination.  

My success came from targeting the argument’s central necessary condition rather than getting distracted by side claims about school or knowledge. For similar problems, first reduce the argument to its core causal or necessary-condition statements, then choose the option that directly negates one of those core statements rather than one that merely weakens a supporting detail.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the option that most directly negates the parent’s argument, not merely one that is unrelated or weaker. The parent’s position had two linked claims: creative work requires imagination, and acquiring knowledge eliminates imagination. My strategy was to identify the core necessary condition in the argument and then look for an option that denies that condition. That was appropriate because to “contradict” the viewpoint, the strongest move is to show that creative work can occur even when the alleged requirement is absent.

The key evidence I used was the statement “only imagination can carry out creative work,” which means imagination is presented as necessary for creativity. From that, any case of creative work without imagination would be a direct contradiction. I correctly recognized that one option merely fit the parent’s view, while another was only partially related and did not challenge the main inference. A possible shortcut I used was prioritizing formal logical contradiction over broader thematic tension, but here that was exactly the right approach. I also implicitly distinguished between “supports,” “is consistent with,” and “contradicts,” which is essential in argument questions.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the parent’s strongest universal claim rather than the rhetoric about school, science, or absurdity. In similar problems, I should first extract the argument into simple conditional structure and test each choice against that structure. General rule: when a statement says “only X can produce Y,” the cleanest contradiction is “Y occurs without X.”

item.context: Even if social efforts provide an equal opportunity system, people will still form an income gap in the initial distribution. Since capital is also rewarded in a market economy, people who own capital can also get paid by owning capital,It widens the income gap in the initial distribution. Therefore, when the market economic system is adopted, in order to narrow the income distribution gap, we must narrow the gap formed in the initial distribution through the state-led redistribution process; otherwise, it will be due to the excessive income distribution gap, the formation of excessive differentiation and conflict of social strata, leading to the contradiction of excess public property.
item.question: Which of the following is the main content of this text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Income balance is difficult to achieve

choices.label: B
choices.text: The redistribution process is essential

choices.label: C
choices.text: The distribution gap originates from the system

choices.label: D
choices.text: The income distribution system must be reformed

response:
Reasoning: The passage argues that market economies naturally create initial income gaps, especially through capital ownership, so the state must reduce these gaps through redistribution to prevent social conflict. The core message is the necessity of redistribution, not merely that balance is hard or reform is needed.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach: identify the problem described, then focus on the author’s conclusion signaled by “therefore.” The key factor was that the passage does not stop at explaining why income gaps arise; it argues that the state must reduce those gaps through redistribution to avoid social conflict. My success came from separating supporting premises about market inequality and capital income from the central claim about what must be done. For similar questions, first locate the author’s final prescription or judgment, then choose the option that captures that conclusion rather than a background cause or partial detail.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s central claim, not a supporting detail or a broader background theme. That was the right framing, because the paragraph builds toward a policy conclusion rather than merely describing inequality in market economies. My strategy was to identify the argumentative structure: first, the text explains why gaps arise in initial distribution, then it argues that state action is needed to reduce those gaps. This was appropriate because “main content” questions are usually answered by tracking the conclusion signaled by words like “therefore” and “otherwise.”

The key evidence I used was the causal chain: market rewards labor and capital, capital ownership enlarges initial inequality, and unchecked inequality leads to social conflict. I correctly treated the discussion of capital and initial distribution as reasons supporting a larger claim, not as the main point themselves. A possible trap was to focus on the descriptive claim that income gaps naturally emerge, but that would have ignored the passage’s normative emphasis on what must be done. Another tempting alternative was the reform-oriented choice, but the passage did not broadly discuss redesigning the entire income distribution system; it specifically stressed the role of state redistribution.

What made the reasoning successful was distinguishing between premise and conclusion. In similar problems, I should continue mapping signal words and asking which statement would still capture the passage if supporting examples were removed. A transferable rule is: when a passage presents causes and then uses a conclusion marker to recommend an action, the main idea is usually the recommended action, not the background causes.

item.context: Philosopher: Some of the most ardent philosophical opponents of democracy have rightly noted that both the inherently best and the inherently worst possible forms of government are those that concentrate political power in the hands of a few. Thus, since democracy is a consistently mediocre form of government, it is a better choice than rule by the few.
item.question: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the philosopher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The best form of government is the one that is most likely to produce an outcome that is on the whole good.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A society should adopt a democratic form of government if and only if most members of the society prefer a democratic form of government.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In choosing a form of government, it is better for a society to avoid the inherently worst than to seek to attain the best.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Democratic governments are not truly equitable unless they are designed to prevent interest groups from exerting undue influence on the political process.

response:
Reasoning: The argument prefers democracy because rule by the few, while possibly best, can also be worst. To justify choosing the “mediocre” option, we need a principle saying avoiding the worst outcome is more important than pursuing the best. That is exactly option C.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a gap-filling approach: I identified the conclusion favoring democracy and looked for the missing normative bridge from the premises to that choice. The key factor was the contrast that rule by the few can yield either the best or the worst government, while democracy is described as reliably mediocre; that setup requires a principle prioritizing risk avoidance over reaching the highest possible outcome. The success came from spotting that the argument needs a decision rule about how to choose under extreme upside and downside possibilities. For similar questions, explicitly compare what the premises establish with what the conclusion needs, then choose the answer that supplies that exact decision principle.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for a missing normative principle that would bridge the philosopher’s descriptive claims about types of government to the conclusion that democracy should be chosen. That interpretation was correct, because the stimulus did not merely compare governments; it argued from the possibility of extreme outcomes to a recommendation. My strategy was to identify the gap between the premises and conclusion: if rule by the few can yield either the best or the worst government, while democracy is “consistently mediocre,” then some value judgment is needed to prefer stable mediocrity over risky extremes. That made a principle about prioritizing avoidance of the worst outcome the natural candidate. The key evidence I used was the contrast between “inherently best and inherently worst” for concentrated power and “consistently mediocre” for democracy. I also noticed that the argument was comparative, not about popular preference, procedural fairness, or expected overall goodness, which helped eliminate the other choices. One assumption built into my reasoning was that the philosopher treats the risk of the worst outcome as more important than the chance of the best outcome. I should still have considered whether an expected-value principle could also support the conclusion, but the stimulus gave no likelihood information, so that approach was weaker. The reasoning succeeded because I looked for the exact bridge principle rather than a generally attractive political idea. In similar problems, I should explicitly ask what evaluative rule must be true for the conclusion to follow from the stated comparison. General rule: when an argument chooses a safer middle option over a risky option with higher upside and lower downside, the needed principle usually ranks avoiding catastrophic outcomes above pursuing optimal ones.

item.context: The core of government reform is to simplify administration and delegate power and change functions. The central government has repeatedly ordered and implemented the list system, but the results are difficult to satisfy the people. In many places and departments, it is difficult to put the power that should be delegated in place. The management environment is difficult to manage well. So many mass entrepreneurship and innovation behaviors are subject to the suspension of policies, and so many enterprises are not killed in battle, but fall in the last mile of administrative examination and approval.
item.question: Which of the following is mainly explained in the above text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The deeper the reform, the greater the resistance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reform is unavoidable, and labor pains are inevitable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The deepening of reform cannot be delayed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The great potential of innovation and development lies in reform.

response:
Reasoning: The passage focuses on current problems in administrative approval and insufficient delegation of power, which are blocking entrepreneurship and enterprises. This highlights the urgency of pushing reform deeper and faster, not just resistance or inevitability of pain.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach: identify the passage’s problem statement, then infer the author’s intended conclusion from the consequences described. The key factor was the chain of reasoning that incomplete delegation and poor administrative streamlining are directly harming entrepreneurship and causing firms to fail at the “last mile” of approval. What helped was focusing on the passage’s emphasis on urgency and obstruction, rather than getting distracted by broader themes like resistance, pain, or reform’s long-term benefits. For similar questions, trace the author’s concrete problems to the implied call to action and choose the option that matches that urgency most directly.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the passage as asking for the main point, not a detail or a side observation. The key task was to identify the author’s central emphasis from a problem-description paragraph: repeated orders to streamline administration have not been effectively implemented, and this failure is obstructing entrepreneurship and business activity. My strategy was to trace the causal chain in the text—insufficient delegation of power leads to poor administrative conditions, which then create bottlenecks for innovation and firms—and then ask what conclusion that chain supports. That was an appropriate strategy because the passage is argumentative: it lists consequences in order to justify a broader reform stance.

The strongest evidence I used was the repeated focus on current blockage, especially the “last mile” of administrative approval, which signals urgency rather than abstract commentary. I correctly avoided over-weighting emotionally plausible options about “resistance” or “labor pains,” because the passage did not emphasize conflict or inevitability; it emphasized delay and unfinished implementation. One assumption that helped was treating the listed problems as support for a policy conclusion, not as independent complaints. I should still note that another tempting possibility was the option about reform enabling innovation, since the passage mentions entrepreneurship and enterprise, but that was secondary evidence rather than the author’s main thesis. The reasoning succeeded because I distinguished between consequences cited as examples and the underlying claim they were meant to support. In similar problems, I should explicitly separate diagnosis, consequence, and conclusion before matching an answer choice. General rule: when a passage lists failures and harms after describing an incomplete policy effort, the main idea is usually the necessity or urgency of carrying that effort further, not merely the existence of harm or resistance.

item.context: Last night, Ma Hui either went to the gym to play ball, or went to visit his teacher Qin Nan. If Ma Hui drove last night, then he did not gymnasium to play ball. Only if Ma Hui and his teacher Qin Nan agreed in advance, he would Go to visit his teacher. In fact, Ma Hui and his teacher Qin Nan didn't make an agreement in advance.
item.question: Based on the above statement, which of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Last Night Ma Hui and his teacher Qin Nan went to the gymnasium to play ball

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ma Hui visited his teacher Qin Nan last night

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ma Hui didn't drive last night

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ma Hui didn't go to the gymnasium to play ball

response:
Reasoning: Visiting teacher requires prior agreement: V → A. But there was no prior agreement, so not A, hence not V. Since Ma Hui either went to the gym or visited his teacher, he must have gone to the gym. Also, if he drove then he didn’t go to the gym: D → not G. Since G is true, D must be false.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple:
I used a chain of conditional reasoning with contraposition and elimination. The key factor was translating “only if” correctly: visiting the teacher requires prior agreement, so when the agreement is explicitly denied, visiting is ruled out. From the either-or statement, that forces the gym option, and combining that with “if he drove, then he did not go to the gym” lets me contrapose to conclude he did not drive.  

The successful step was linking the forced gym conclusion to the driving condition, rather than stopping after ruling out the visit. For similar problems, I should systematically convert “only if” into a necessary-condition statement, use contraposition when the necessary condition is false, and then combine the result with any exclusive alternatives to force what must be true.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which option is logically forced by the premises, not which option is merely plausible. My strategy was to translate each statement into conditional form and then chain the implications: visiting the teacher requires prior agreement, and there was no prior agreement. That made the key step a contrapositive inference: from “visit only if agreed in advance” and “no agreement,” conclude “no visit.” This was appropriate because the problem is purely propositional and depends on necessary-condition reasoning rather than common-sense storytelling.
