choices.text: When answering difficult questions, the prefrontal cortex is more active than simple questions

response:
Reasoning: The passage says sleep deprivation suppresses some brain functional areas to different degrees. Simple tasks suffer because affected areas are needed, while difficult tasks can be compensated by extra activation of the prefrontal cortex. So the underlying cause is the differing suppression effects, not just strategy or activation itself.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a causal-summary approach: I tried to identify the deepest explanation in the passage and chose the option that sounded most like an underlying mechanism. The key clue I focused on was that sleep deprivation suppresses some brain areas to varying degrees, but I underweighted the passage’s more specific comparison between simple and difficult questions. My mistake was preferring a broad background condition over the direct differentiating cause the text explicitly tied to difficult-question performance. For similar problems, I should choose the option that most directly explains the contrast asked about, especially when the passage names a specific compensatory mechanism for one case but not the other.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the deepest physiological explanation behind the performance gap between simple and difficult questions under sleep deprivation, and that framing led me to search for a broad upstream cause. That strategy was partly reasonable, but I overemphasized a general statement in the passage instead of identifying the most direct causal mechanism tied to the contrast the question asked about. I relied on the sentence saying some brain areas are suppressed to varying degrees and treated that as the “root cause,” but I did not notice that this fact explains impairment in general, not specifically why difficult questions are preserved while simple ones are not. The key evidence I underused was the contrastive explanation: in difficult problems there is additional activation and compensatory involvement of the prefrontal cortex. That is a more targeted account of the difference between the two types of questions than the broader statement about suppression. My main assumption was that “root cause” must refer to the earliest or most general biological cause, when in multiple-choice reading questions it often refers to the passage’s most direct stated explanation for the observed difference. I also failed to compare answer choices by scope: one option matched the precise contrast, while my choice described a background condition affecting many tasks. A better approach is to ask, “Which option most directly explains the difference named in the question, not just the overall phenomenon?” The transferable rule is: when a passage gives both a general condition and a specific compensatory mechanism, choose the mechanism if the question asks why two outcomes differ.

item.context: At the entrance to Aristotle's College, there was a sign that said, No admission for those who do not understand logic. One day, a group of people came, they are logical people.
item.question: If the words on the label are accurately understood and strictly enforced, only one of the following assertions will be true.  Which of the following options is the true assertion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They may not be allowed in

choices.label: B
choices.text: They will not be allowed to enter

choices.label: C
choices.text: They will be allowed to enter

choices.label: D
choices.text: They cannot be allowed in

response:
Reasoning: The sign excludes only people who do not understand logic. Since the group are logical people, they are taken to understand logic, so the prohibition does not apply to them. Thus they are allowed in; the stronger negative options are false, and “may not” is not the strict consequence.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a direct conditional-logic approach: translate the sign into a rule that excludes exactly those lacking understanding of logic, then test whether the group falls into that excluded category. The key factor was treating “they are logical people” as evidence that they do understand logic, so the condition for exclusion was not met. What helped was distinguishing between a rule that bans one class of people and a rule that permits everyone else by strict enforcement in this context. For similar problems, first rewrite the statement as an if-then rule and check whether the subject matches the forbidden set before judging stronger or weaker modal claims like “may,” “will,” or “cannot.”
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the statement as a conditional rule about admission: anyone lacking understanding of logic is excluded. The key task was not to infer anything broad about the college, but to determine what follows strictly from that admission rule when applied to a group described as “logical people.” My strategy was to translate the sign into a set relation: the barred set is “those who do not understand logic,” so anyone outside that set is not prohibited by the sign. That was appropriate because the question emphasized accurate understanding and strict enforcement, which favors formal logical interpretation over conversational ambiguity.

The central fact I used was that “logical people” reasonably entails people who understand logic. Given that, the sign’s only exclusion condition does not apply to them. I also used the wording of the options: “will be allowed” matches the direct consequence of not being in the forbidden class, while “may not” is weaker and does not fit the claim that only one option is true. A possible trap was to treat the sign as giving only a necessary condition for entry, leaving open other reasons for exclusion, but the question’s framing pushes us to evaluate admission solely under the stated rule. Another trap would have been confusing “logical” with “uses sound reasoning” rather than “understands logic,” but here that connection was justified by context. The reasoning succeeded because I mapped the natural-language rule into a precise conditional and checked each option against that structure. For similar problems, I should explicitly distinguish between “forbidden if not P” and “allowed iff P,” then use the question’s enforcement language to decide whether stronger conclusions are licensed. General rule: when a problem gives a single exclusion condition and asks what follows under strict enforcement, first identify the excluded class, then test whether the subject belongs to that class before evaluating modal wording like “may,” “will,” or “cannot.”

item.context: Tanya would refrain from littering if everyone else refrained from littering. None of her friends litter, and ttherefore she does not litter either.
item.question: Which one of the following uses flawed reasoning most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All residents of the same neighborhood have some goals in common. One group of neighborhood residents wants improvements made to a local park, so some other residents of that neighborhood must share this goal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If all of a restaurant's customers like its food, it must be an exceptional restaurant. Everyone whom Sherryl consulted liked the food at Chez Louis, so it must be an exceptional restaurant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a talented artist is willing to starve for her career, then her friends should take her choice of profession seriously. Donna's friends take her choice of profession seriously, and she is willing to starve for her career, so she must be a talented artist.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Herbert will stop selling office supplies in his store if none of his regular customers complains. Some of his regular customers never knew that Herbert sold office supplies, so those customers will not complain.

response:
Reasoning: The flaw is treating a condition about all relevant people as satisfied by only a subset. Original: “everyone else” becomes just “her friends.” Similarly, B replaces “all customers” with only “everyone Sherryl consulted,” then draws the same conclusion.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-matching approach: I abstracted the argument’s structure and looked for an option with the same quantifier error. The key factor was the shift from a universal condition about all relevant people (“everyone else”) to evidence about only a limited subset (“her friends”), then treating that subset as if it satisfied the full condition. My answer was correct because I focused on that scope mismatch rather than the topic. In similar problems, first translate the argument into a bare logical pattern—especially noting words like all, everyone, some, and only—then match the same mistaken quantifier shift.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stimulus as an argument that moves from a conditional requiring a universal condition to a conclusion based on evidence about only a limited subgroup. That interpretation was correct: the key issue was not the social topic, but the shift from “everyone else” to “none of her friends.” My strategy was to abstract the form first: “If all members of a broad class have property X, then subject has property Y; some narrower subclass has property X; therefore subject has property Y.” That was the right strategy for a parallel flaw question, because the task is to match defective structure rather than surface wording.

The crucial fact I used was the mismatch between the scope of the condition and the scope of the evidence. I correctly noticed that “friends” is only a subset of “everyone else,” just as “people consulted” is only a subset of “all customers.” I avoided being distracted by whether the premises seemed plausible in real life, which often derails LSAT flaw comparisons. One assumption underlying my reasoning was that the flaw was insufficient evidence for a universal antecedent, rather than, say, affirming the consequent or causal reasoning. That assumption was appropriate because the conclusion depended on treating a partial sample as if it established a universal claim.

I should still have checked the other choices more explicitly for competing formal similarities, especially ones involving conditional misuse. What made the reasoning successful was identifying the exact quantifier error: substituting “some” or “a subset” for “all.” In similar problems, I should translate quantifiers carefully and compare class size relationships before comparing subject matter. General rule: when an argument requires a condition about an entire group, evidence about only a selected subset does not establish that condition unless the subset is shown to be exhaustive or representative in the needed way.

item.context: Global warming has had a lot of effects on human beings, but also on other life on Earth. The increase of precipitation can improve vegetation, which is beneficial to the growth of rodents. The study shows that the increase in precipitation has enriched the vegetation in the already arid Inner Mongolia region. The food of rats was also increased, and the number of long-clawed sand rats increased.
item.question: Which of the following options best weakens the above conclusions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: According to statistics, the vegetation coverage in some areas has not increased

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is estimated that the global desertification area has increased in recent years

choices.label: C
choices.text: The increase of vegetation in Inner Mongolia is closely related to ecological protection in recent years

choices.label: D
choices.text: The increase of vegetation has increased the natural enemies of various animals, including rats

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion links increased precipitation to more vegetation and then more rats. The strongest weakening option provides an alternative cause for the vegetation increase. If vegetation rose mainly because of ecological protection measures, the claimed causal chain from precipitation is undermined.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a causal-chain approach, looking for an answer that attacked the link from increased precipitation to more vegetation and then to more rats. The key clue I focused on was the possibility of an alternative cause for vegetation growth, so I chose the option that challenged the precipitation-to-vegetation step. My mistake was weakening an intermediate cause instead of the conclusion itself: I overlooked the stronger choice that accepts more vegetation but shows why rat numbers would not necessarily rise because another part of the system changes too. In similar causal questions, I should prefer an option that directly blocks the final predicted outcome over one that only offers a competing cause for an earlier step.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument as making a single causal chain: more precipitation led to more vegetation, which led to more rodents. That interpretation was only partly correct, because I focused too narrowly on attacking the first link while neglecting the full conclusion about rat population growth. My strategy was to look for an alternative cause, and that is often a strong weakening method in causal arguments. However, in this case I treated “vegetation increase” as the central claim to weaken, even though the passage’s ultimate conclusion concerned the increase in the number of rats. I used one relevant fact—that showing another cause for vegetation can weaken the precipitation-to-vegetation link—but I missed the more direct issue of whether more vegetation necessarily produces more rats overall.

The key constraint I overlooked is that an argument about population growth must consider both positive and negative effects on that population. I implicitly assumed that more food is sufficient to increase rat numbers, which ignored offsetting mechanisms such as predation. I also failed to compare the answer choices by asking which one most directly undercuts the conclusion rather than merely one premise. A better alternative to consider would have been any option showing that increased vegetation could simultaneously harm rodents or prevent population growth. The specific cause of my error was prioritizing an indirect causal rebuttal over a direct challenge to the claimed outcome. In similar problems, I should map the full causal structure and test whether an option attacks the conclusion itself, not just an upstream link. General rule: when weakening a causal chain, prefer evidence that introduces a countervailing factor affecting the final result over evidence that only offers an alternative explanation for an intermediate step.

item.context: The number of North American children who are obese -- that is, who have more body fat than do 85 percent of North American children their age -- is steadily increasing, according to four major studies conducted over the past 15 years.
item.question: If the finding reported above is correct, it can be properly concluded that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the incidence of obesity in North American children tends to increase as the children grow older

choices.label: B
choices.text: when four major studies all produce similar results, those studies must be accurate

choices.label: C
choices.text: the number of North American children who are not obese increased over the past 15 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: over the past 15 years, the number of North American children who are underweight has declined

response:
Reasoning: “Obese” here means the top 15% in body fat for each age group. So if the number of obese children increased, the total number of children must also have increased. Since 85% are not obese, their number would have increased too. The other choices are unsupported.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a proportional-definition approach: since “obese” is defined as children above the 85th percentile of body fat for their age, that category always represents a fixed fraction of the child population. The key clue was that an increase in the number of children in that fixed-fraction group implies an increase in the total number of children, which in turn implies an increase in the much larger complementary group. The successful step was translating the percentile definition into a constant percentage rather than treating “obese” as an independent medical count. For similar problems, convert comparative or percentile-based definitions into numerical relationships before testing what must follow.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the statement correctly by focusing on the definition of “obese” as a relative category: children with more body fat than 85 percent of peers their age. That means, within any age group, “obese” represents about the top 15 percent, so the conclusion had to come from proportions and total population size rather than from absolute body-fat thresholds. My strategy was to translate the verbal definition into a fixed fraction and then infer what an increase in the number in that fraction implies about the whole group. That was appropriate because the prompt asked what “can be properly concluded,” so I needed a logically necessary consequence, not a likely causal explanation.

The key fact I used was that if a fixed percentage group gets larger in number, then the underlying total group must also be larger. From that, it follows that the complementary group—the other 85 percent—would also be larger in number. I did not rely on any unsupported assumptions about changes in body composition, aging, or study reliability, which helped avoid the traps in the other choices. A possible hidden assumption was treating the percentile-based definition as stable across the relevant comparisons, but that assumption is built into the wording of the stimulus itself. I also properly rejected alternatives that tried to infer trends by age, study accuracy, or underweight rates, since none of those follows from the given information.

What made the reasoning successful was converting the definition into a mathematical structure: fixed subset versus whole set. For similar problems, I should keep separating absolute numbers from percentages and ask which quantities are actually constrained by the wording. General rule: when a category is defined as a constant proportion of a population, any increase in the number in that category entails an increase in the total population and in the complementary category’s number as well.

item.context: Custom-made tourism refers to a travel method in which tourists and travel service providers jointly negotiate a travel plan to fully meet the personalized requirements of travel.
item.question: Which of the following is not a custom-made tourism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A travel agency recently searched out 10-day tour of Europe, a week tour of five coastal cities and other products. If the tourists feel the price is appropriate, they can buy a trip.

choices.label: B
choices.text: According to the tourist's individual budget and travel goals, an online travel website makes a itinerary plan. After repeated communication with the customer, a customer satisfaction plan is finally formed and a special person is arranged to accompany the supervision.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A travel agency organized a food tourism project. At the request of tourists, it carefully selected a few distinctive food shops and booked local individual houses to accompany the tour. After returning, the tourists were very satisfied.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Xiao Li and some friends who are keen on photography have made an activity plan to photograph the desert scenery. After much bargaining with the travel agent, the plan was finally completed and the participants had an interesting vacation.

response:
Reasoning: Custom-made tourism requires joint negotiation and a personalized itinerary tailored to the tourist’s needs. B, C, and D all involve requests, communication, and adjustment. A only offers pre-designed standard products for tourists to choose from, so it is not custom-made tourism.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option against the essential elements of custom-made tourism, especially joint negotiation and personalization. The key factor was whether the travel plan was created or adjusted through back-and-forth communication to meet a specific traveler’s needs, rather than simply selecting a prepackaged product. My success came from isolating the defining criteria and checking each choice for those features instead of being distracted by travel details like destination or duration. For similar problems, first extract the minimum necessary conditions from the definition, then eliminate any option that only shows a general service or standard offering without those required conditions.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as a definition-matching task: identify the option that fails to satisfy the defining features of custom-made tourism, rather than the one that merely seems less personalized. My strategy was to extract the core conditions from the definition—joint negotiation and a travel plan designed to fully meet individualized requirements—and test each option against those conditions. That was appropriate because the key to these problems is not overall plausibility but whether each example contains every necessary element of the definition. I used the right evidence by distinguishing between a pre-existing package offered for purchase and a plan created through back-and-forth discussion with a traveler. I also noticed that several choices included signals such as “repeated communication,” “at the request of tourists,” or “after bargaining,” which directly support the negotiation requirement. A helpful implicit assumption was that customization must happen before purchase and must shape the itinerary itself, not just involve selecting among fixed products. I should still note that one tempting alternative was the food-tour example, because it was organized by an agency first, but the later modifications requested by tourists preserved the custom-made character. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on necessary conditions rather than surface-level travel themes or quality of service. In similar problems, I should explicitly separate “choice among standard options” from “co-creation of the option.” General rule: when evaluating category definitions, test each example for all required criteria, and reject any case that replaces individualized construction with selection from ready-made alternatives.

item.context: The population of City A has maintained negative growth for a long time. According to this, education experts believe that due to the declining number of school-age children, the number of primary and junior high school students in City A will continue decreasing.
item.question: Which of the followings, if correct, will most effectively point out that the inferences of the education expert are flawed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Due to various reasons, there are a few cases of unmarried births or illegal births of second child that have not been effectively counted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: With the rapid increase of migrant workers, their children will go to elementary and junior high schools in City A

choices.label: C
choices.text: Due to the implementation of the relocation of schools and the uneven distribution of educational resources, the number of students in many elementary and junior high schools in City A has increased significantly in recent years

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reduction in the number of students in school will enable small-class teaching to be truly realized, thereby contributing to the improvement of the quality of education

response:
Reasoning: The expert infers fewer school-age children from long-term negative population growth, then concludes student numbers will keep falling. This ignores inflow effects. If many migrant workers move in and their children attend local schools, student numbers may rise despite negative population growth.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a weakening-the-argument approach: identify the expert’s chain of reasoning and look for an option that breaks the link between overall population decline and local student enrollment. The key factor was that school enrollment depends not only on births or resident population trends, but also on migration into the city by families with school-age children. My answer was correct because I focused on an alternative source of students that directly undermines the prediction of continued decline. For similar problems, I should test whether the conclusion relies on an assumed one-to-one relationship and then look for outside variables—like migration, policy, or reclassification—that can disrupt that relationship.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for a weakening option: not whether the city’s population is shrinking, but whether that fact really justifies predicting a continued decline in local primary and junior high enrollment. That interpretation was correct because the target was the expert’s inference, not the truth of negative population growth itself. My strategy was to identify the hidden assumption linking total population trend to student enrollment trend, namely that fewer residents overall means fewer school-age children attending schools in that city. That was an appropriate approach because flaw questions often depend on exposing a missing causal or demographic link.

The key evidence I used was that school enrollment depends on who actually attends local schools, not just on registered population totals or long-run citywide growth rates. I focused on a possible offsetting factor: inward migration of families with children. That directly attacks the prediction because it introduces a source of students independent of the city’s native birth trend. I avoided being distracted by options that merely described undercounting, school consolidation, or educational benefits, since those do not squarely show the inference from population decline to enrollment decline is unreliable. One assumption in my reasoning was that migrant workers’ children would be numerous enough to matter, but that is acceptable in a “if correct” weaken question.

What made the reasoning successful was matching the answer choice to the exact inferential gap rather than to a superficially related education fact. In similar problems, I should explicitly map the argument as premise → hidden assumption → conclusion, then look for an option that breaks that bridge. General rule: when a prediction moves from a broad population trend to a narrower subgroup outcome, test whether migration, composition changes, or institutional factors sever the connection.

item.context: Psychologists observing a shopping mall parking lot found that, on average, drivers spent 39 seconds leaving a parking space when another car was quietly waiting to enter it, 51 seconds if the driver of the waiting car honked impatiently, but only 32 seconds leaving a space when no one was waiting. This suggests that drivers feel possessive of their parking spaces even when leaving them, and that this possessiveness increases in reaction to indications that another driver wants the space.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The amount of time drivers spend entering a parking space is not noticeably affected by whether other drivers are waiting for them to do so, nor by whether those other drivers are honking impatiently.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parking spaces in shopping mall parking lots are unrepresentative of parking spaces in general with respect to the likelihood that other cars will be waiting to enter them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Almost any driver leaving a parking space will feel angry at another driver who honks impatiently, and this anger will influence the amount of time spent leaving the space.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The more pressure most drivers feel because others are waiting for them to perform maneuvers with their cars, the less quickly they are able to perform them.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion attributes slower leaving to possessiveness. Choice D gives a simpler alternative: drivers under pressure from someone waiting, especially honking, perform parking maneuvers more slowly. That explains all the timing differences without assuming possessiveness.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a causal-weaken approach: identify the author’s explanation for the timing differences and look for an alternative cause that would produce the same pattern. The key factor was that the evidence was purely behavioral timing, so a different psychological mechanism could undercut the claim that possessiveness was responsible. My success came from noticing that pressure from being watched or honked at explains both why drivers take longer when someone waits and why they take even longer when the waiting driver honks. For similar problems, test causal conclusions by asking whether another factor could account for the observed effect just as well as the proposed explanation.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a weaken-the-argument task: the goal was not to explain the data directly, but to identify a fact that most undermines the inference from the observed timing differences to a psychological claim about possessiveness. My strategy was to look for an alternative causal explanation that would account for the same pattern of behavior without relying on the author’s proposed motive. That was appropriate because the argument moved from correlation-like observations to a specific mental-state explanation, which is vulnerable to competing causes. The key evidence in the stimulus was the ordered pattern of times: fastest when no one waited, slower when someone waited, and slowest when the person waiting honked. I focused on the fact that this pattern could arise from social pressure or stress rather than territoriality, especially because honking plausibly increases pressure.

A useful assumption I avoided was that a delay necessarily reflects a desire to “hold onto” the space. Instead, I treated delay as behavior that can result from multiple mechanisms. I also correctly gave less weight to options about representativeness or entering spaces, since those do not directly attack the causal interpretation of the observed leaving times. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the answer choice to the exact explanatory gap in the argument: behavior was observed, motive was inferred. For similar problems, I should continue asking, “What nonconclusion mechanism could produce the same data pattern?” A general rule is: when an argument infers a specific attitude or intention from behavior, the strongest weakening move is often an alternative causal process that predicts the same behavior under the same conditions.

item.context: In a certain wildlife park, park rangers are able to track the movements of many rhinoceroses because those animals wear radio collars. When, as often happens, a collar slips off, it is put back on. Putting a collar on a rhinoceros involves immobilizing the animal by shooting it with a tranquilizer dart. Female rhinoceroses that have been frequently recollared have significantly lower fertility rates than uncollared females. Probably, ttherefore, some substance in the tranquilizer inhibits fertility.
item.question: In evaluating the argument, it would be most useful to determine which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether male rhinoceroses in the wildlife park lose their collars any more often than the park's female rhinoceroses do

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether radio collars are the only practical means that park rangers have for tracking the movements of rhinoceroses in the park

choices.label: C
choices.text: How often park rangers need to use tranquilizer darts to immobilize rhinoceroses for reasons other than attaching radio collars

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether there are more collared female rhinoceroses than uncollared female rhinoceroses in the park

response:
Reasoning: The argument infers causation from correlation. To evaluate it, we should check whether tranquilizer darts are used in other situations, since lowered fertility might be linked to tranquilization itself rather than specifically to recollaring. That is exactly what C addresses.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a causal-evaluation approach: the conclusion blamed reduced fertility on a substance in the tranquilizer, so I looked for information that would test whether tranquilizer exposure tracks the fertility effect. The key factor was the alternative explanation that females who are frequently recollared may also be tranquilized for other reasons, which would weaken the link between recollaring and the alleged cause. My success came from focusing on whether the proposed cause is uniquely associated with the observed outcome, rather than getting distracted by background facts about collars or population counts. For similar problems, I should ask what additional source could produce the same suspected cause or effect and prefer the choice that measures that confounding exposure directly.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as an argument-evaluation task: not “which answer explains the conclusion,” but “what fact would be most useful in judging whether the causal inference is sound.” The argument’s structure was a classic correlation-to-causation move: frequently recollared females have lower fertility, so the author blames a substance in the tranquilizer. My strategy was to look for an alternative causal pathway or a missing comparison that would test whether tranquilization, rather than some other feature of recollaring, is actually responsible. That was appropriate because evaluation questions often turn on identifying what competing explanation would weaken or strengthen the inference. I focused on the fact that recollaring requires immobilization by dart, and therefore repeated exposure to tranquilizer may be confounded with any other reason rangers dart the same animals. The key evidence I used was the mismatch between the observed group difference and the specific causal claim about “some substance in the tranquilizer.” I did not assume the conclusion was wrong; instead, I asked what information would discriminate between “tranquilizer causes reduced fertility” and “some other aspect of handling or selection causes it.” Other options were less relevant because they addressed logistics, population counts, or males, none of which bears directly on the causal mechanism affecting female fertility. The reasoning succeeded because it targeted a hidden variable: tranquilizer exposure outside the recollaring context could reveal whether the proposed cause is over-specific. In similar problems, I should explicitly map the observed correlation, the proposed cause, and at least one rival explanation before checking the choices. A general rule is: when an argument infers a specific cause from an associated procedure, the best evaluative question tests whether the same suspected cause occurs independently of the procedure or whether the effect could arise from another linked factor.

item.context: With the development of computer technology to a trillion times or higher, the processor speed has exceeded the transmission speed, which creates a technical bottleneck in the application field and hinders the further development of the application. Anyone who has tried to dial-up the Internet to watch streaming videos will know that no matter how fast the processor is, it can't improve the file loading speed. In today's big data and cloud computing, there is a large amount of information interacting between servers. A kind of laser device, vertical cavity surface emitting laser, can be used to transmit data at high speed in optical fiber network. Compared with the traditional cable system, it can transmit a larger amount of data at a faster speed.
item.question: Which of the following statements is inconsistent with the original text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The computer processor is not proportional to the data transmission speed

choices.label: B
choices.text: The speed of computer processors can no longer meet the requirements of applications

choices.label: C
choices.text: The technology of high-speed data transmission has not made a substantial breakthrough for a long time

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scientists have made important progress in laser communication technology

response:
Reasoning: The text says processor speed has already exceeded transmission speed; the bottleneck is data transmission, not processor speed. So saying processor speed can no longer meet application requirements contradicts the passage. A and D match the text; C is less direct but not the clearest contradiction.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a contrast-based reading approach: identify the passage’s main bottleneck, then test each option against that core claim. The decisive clue was the statement that processor speed has already exceeded transmission speed, so the limitation lies in data transfer rather than computing power. My answer was correct because I tracked the causal structure of the passage instead of focusing on isolated phrases like “hinders development.” For similar problems, first locate what the text says is the limiting factor, then eliminate any option that reverses that relationship.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the option that contradicted the passage, not merely one that was unsupported or weaker than the others. That distinction mattered, because some choices were only indirectly addressed, while one directly reversed the passage’s causal structure. My strategy was to identify the passage’s core claim: processor speed has advanced so much that transmission speed has become the bottleneck. From that, I checked each option against the stated relationship between computing speed and data-transfer speed.

The key evidence I used was the example about streaming video: faster processors do not improve loading speed when transmission is limiting. I also used the final sentence about a laser device enabling faster, higher-capacity transmission, which supported the idea of progress in communication technology. I avoided assuming that every answer had to be explicitly stated; instead, I looked for what was logically entailed or contradicted by the text. That was appropriate here, because one option inverted the passage by claiming processor speed was the limiting factor.

An alternative I still had to consider was the statement about lack of substantial breakthrough in high-speed transmission. That option was not clearly established by the passage, but it was not as directly inconsistent as the processor-speed claim. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the passage’s bottleneck analysis rather than isolated phrases. In similar problems, I should separate “not mentioned,” “supported,” and “contradicted” more explicitly. General rule: when a passage identifies X as exceeding Y and Y as the bottleneck, any option claiming X is insufficient is the strongest contradiction.

item.context: Critic: Although some people claim it is inconsistent to support freedom of speech and also support legislation limiting the amount of violence in TV programs, it is not. We can limit TV program content because the damage done by violent programs is more harmful than the decrease in freedom of speech that would result from the limitations envisioned by the legislation.
item.question: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the critic's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One can support freedom of speech while at the same time recognizing that it can sometimes be overridden by other interests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When facing a choice between restricting freedom of speech or not, we must decide based on what would make the greatest number of people the happiest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the exercise of a basic freedom leads to some harm, then the exercise of that freedom should be restricted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In evaluating legislation that would impinge on a basic freedom, we should consider the consequences of not passing the legislation.

response:
Reasoning: The critic argues free speech is important but not absolute: it can be limited when competing harms are greater than the loss of freedom. That is exactly the principle in A. D is too weak because merely considering consequences does not justify overriding the freedom.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a principle-matching approach: I identified the critic’s core reasoning as balancing a basic freedom against competing harms, then looked for the answer choice that explicitly authorizes that kind of override. The key factor was the claim that limiting violent content is justified because the harm prevented outweighs the loss of freedom, which requires a principle saying free speech is not absolute. My success came from distinguishing a principle that justifies overriding a right from one that merely says consequences should be considered. For similar problems, first isolate the exact inferential gap—here, from “harm is greater” to “restriction is consistent”—and choose the principle that directly licenses that move.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for a principle that bridges the critic’s premise to the conclusion that supporting speech limits in this case is not inconsistent with supporting freedom of speech in general. My strategy was to identify the core logical move: the critic treats freedom of speech as an important value that can nevertheless be outweighed by competing harms. That was the right approach because principle questions are usually solved by matching the abstract structure of the argument rather than by debating the policy itself. I focused on the explicit comparison in the stimulus between the harm caused by violent programming and the reduction in freedom caused by regulation. The key fact I used was that the critic was not denying the value of free speech, but arguing that another interest can override it in certain circumstances. That directly supports a principle allowing support for a basic freedom while recognizing exceptions.

I also correctly rejected a tempting alternative by noticing that a principle about merely considering consequences would be too weak to justify the stronger conclusion about consistency. I did not rely on any unnecessary assumptions such as utilitarianism or a rule that any harm justifies restriction. That mattered because one wrong turn on these questions is to choose an answer that is broader or harsher than the argument requires. The reasoning succeeded because I matched degree and scope: the argument needed a conditional override principle, not a blanket restriction rule. In similar problems, I should continue isolating the exact inferential gap and ask whether the answer authorizes the move actually made, rather than one that is stronger, weaker, or differently framed. A transferable rule is: when an argument reconciles commitment to a value with an exception, the supporting principle must show how that value can remain genuine while being defeasible in some cases.

item.context: Last year a global disturbance of weather patterns disrupted harvests in many of the world's important agricultural areas. Worldwide production of soybeans, an important source of protein for people and livestock alike, was not adversely affected, however. Indeed, last year's soybean crop was actually slightly larger than average. Nevertheless, the weather phenomenon is probably responsible for a recent increase in the world price of soybeans.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, provides the strongest justification for the attribution of the increase in soybean prices to the weather phenomenon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Last year's harvest of anchovies, which provide an important protein source for livestock, was disrupted by the effects of the weather phenomenon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The world price of soybeans also rose several years ago, immediately after an earlier occurrence of a similar global weather disturbance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most countries that produce soybeans for export had above-average harvests of a number of food crops other than soybeans last year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heavy rains attributable to the weather phenomenon improved grazing pastures last year, allowing farmers in many parts of the world to reduce their dependence on supplemental feed.

response:
Reasoning: Since soybean output was normal, the price rise is best explained by increased demand. If anchovies—another important protein source for livestock—had a poor harvest because of the same weather phenomenon, buyers would switch to soybeans, pushing soybean prices up even without a soybean shortage.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a causal-explanation approach: since soybean supply was not reduced, I looked for a way the weather phenomenon could still raise soybean prices indirectly. The key clue was that soybeans are a protein source for both people and livestock, so a weather-caused disruption to another major protein source could shift demand toward soybeans and increase price. My success came from checking both sides of price formation and not assuming only reduced soybean supply could explain higher prices. For similar problems, explicitly test whether the proposed cause could affect price through substitutes or demand shifts, not just through the product’s own production.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as an argument-strengthening task: the issue was not whether soybean prices rose, but how the weather phenomenon could plausibly explain that rise despite soybean production being normal or slightly above average. My strategy was to look for an indirect causal pathway, since the passage explicitly removed the most obvious explanation of reduced soybean supply. That was the right approach because when a direct supply effect is blocked, the strongest justification usually comes from a linked change in demand or in substitute goods. I used the key economic relationship that prices can increase either because supply falls or because demand rises, and the stimulus strongly suggested that any valid answer would have to work through demand. I also relied on the fact that soybeans are a protein source for both people and livestock, which made substitute protein sources especially relevant. The successful step was recognizing that disruption in another feed protein could shift buyers toward soybeans, connecting the weather event to soybean prices without contradicting the production data. I implicitly rejected choices that were merely correlational, irrelevant to soybean demand, or that would reduce need for soybeans. One improvement for similar problems is to map the causal gap explicitly: identify what fact seems to weaken the stated cause, then search for a mechanism that bypasses that weakness. A general rule is: when an argument claims a cause despite unchanged supply, evaluate whether the proposed evidence shows a weather-driven shift in demand, especially through substitutes or complements.

item.context: The son does not dislike his mother's ugliness, and the family dog does not dislike the family's poverty. People who love their hometown will not speak ill of their hometown, and Zhang San will never speak ill of his hometown. It can be seen that how much he loves his hometown!
item.question: Which of the following options is most similar to the above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The wick of an oil lamp must be picked up in order to shine brighter, and sometimes it is the same to be a man and do things. You have to make the truth clear when you speak, or others will pretend that they do not know and convince others with reason, so that others have nothing to say. If I hadn't heard Director Zhang's words, I was still wondering whether I should sign up for the industry competition or not. Everything is clear now. It seems that Director Zhang's words are too important

choices.label: B
choices.text: If you don't go into a tiger's den, you can't get a tiger's son. Great success is often accompanied by great risks. Li Si's investment in stocks has achieved high returns. It can be seen how much risk he has taken

choices.label: C
choices.text: If jade is not carved, it will not become an artifact; if one does not study hard, he will not know how to deal with the world. People who pursue progress will not dislike learning. Professor Wang has been doing nothing and disliking learning since his retirement. It can be seen that Professor Wang is no longer a pursuer of progress

choices.label: D
choices.text: A person cannot be judged by his appearance or appearance, just as the sea water cannot be measured by a bucket. A talented man will not show his talent, and Mr. Li has never shown his talent. It can be seen what a talented man he is

response:
Reasoning: The argument uses the fallacy “If P then Q; Q, therefore P.”  
Original: Love hometown → not speak ill; Zhang San doesn’t speak ill → therefore he loves it.  
D has the same pattern: Talented person → won’t show talent; Mr. Li doesn’t show talent → therefore he is talented.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a structural analogy approach, focusing on the conditional form of the argument rather than its subject matter. The key clue was the inference pattern: “If someone has trait P, then they won’t do Q; this person doesn’t do Q; therefore they have trait P,” which is affirming the consequent in disguise. My success came from isolating that exact logical structure in the choices and ignoring extra decorative statements. For similar problems, first translate each argument into a simple if-then form and match the inference pattern, not the wording or topic.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as an analogy task about argument structure, not about whether the conclusion was actually true. That was the right framing, because the key was to match the logical form of the original passage rather than its topic or rhetoric. My strategy was to isolate the inference pattern: a conditional statement was given, then its consequent was observed in a specific case, and from that the antecedent was inferred. That is the classic form of affirming the consequent, so identifying the fallacy gave me a precise template to compare against the choices.

The most important evidence I used was the relationship “love hometown → do not speak ill of hometown,” followed by “does not speak ill,” then “therefore loves hometown.” I also correctly recognized that the earlier remarks about the son, mother, and dog were decorative and not part of the core inference. A possible trap would have been to match on surface similarity, such as emotional language or praise, instead of formal structure. Another risk would have been to choose an option using a different invalid pattern, such as reversing a necessary condition or drawing a causal conclusion from correlation.

The reasoning succeeded because I abstracted the argument before comparing answer choices. In similar problems, I should continue translating each passage into conditional or logical form first, then test whether the answer preserves both the premise type and the inference move. General rule: in argument-analogy questions, match the exact inferential structure, especially whether the argument affirms the consequent, denies the antecedent, or uses a valid rule like modus ponens.

item.context: Professor Yan will give a lecture only when Professor Tian and Professor Li give lectures. Professor Yan did not give a lecture, so Professor Tian must not have given a lecture, and Professor Li did not give a lecture either.
item.question: Which of the following options is most similar to the logical structure of the stem of the question?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only when you study well and maintain a good relationship with your classmates can you be awarded a scholarship. Xiao Zhang studies well and has a good relationship with his classmates, so he is sure to be awarded a scholarship

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only when you study well and maintain a good relationship with your classmates can you be awarded a scholarship. Xiao Zhang didn't get a scholarship, so he must not study well

choices.label: C
choices.text: As long as you study well and maintain a good relationship with your classmates, you can be awarded a scholarship. Xiao Zhang didn't get a scholarship, so he must not study well and have a bad relationship with his classmates

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only when you study well and maintain a good relationship with your classmates can you be awarded a scholarship. Xiao Zhang didn't get the scholarship, so he must not study well and have a tense relationship with his classmates

response:
Reasoning: Stem: “Y only if T and L” means Y → (T ∧ L). Then it concludes from ¬Y that ¬T and ¬L, which is the same invalid form as “C only if A and B; ¬C, so ¬A and ¬B.” This matches D.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I translated the stem into conditional form: “only when” becomes a necessary-condition statement, so the structure was \(Y \rightarrow (T \land L)\). The key factor was noticing that the argument then moved from denying the result to denying both necessary conditions, an invalid pattern that still had to be matched structurally. My success came from focusing on the exact logical form, including the conjunction in the necessary conditions and the conclusion denying both parts. For similar problems, first symbolize the statement and then compare whether the option preserves both the conditional direction and the same mistaken inference pattern.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stem as a conditional statement with a compound necessary condition: “Professor Yan will give a lecture only when Professor Tian and Professor Li give lectures” translates to Yan → (Tian ∧ Li). That interpretation was correct, and it was essential because the argument’s flaw depends on distinguishing a necessary condition from a sufficient one. My strategy was to formalize the structure and then compare answer choices by logical form rather than by surface wording. That was appropriate here because analogy questions are about matching inference patterns, including invalid ones.

The key evidence I used was that the conclusion moves from ¬Yan to ¬Tian and ¬Li, which is an invalid inference from denying the antecedent. I also noticed that the conclusion negates both conjuncts, not just one, so the matching option needed both the same conditional setup and the same mistaken move from “did not get X” to “not A and not B.” A shortcut that helped was abstracting the stem to “P only if (Q ∧ R); not P; therefore not Q and not R.” I correctly rejected options that reversed the conditional or concluded the consequent from the presence of the necessary conditions.

One alternative I needed to consider carefully was whether any option merely matched the topic but not the exact inferential error. The reasoning succeeded because I tracked both the connective “only when” and the conjunction in the necessary condition. For similar problems, I should always map statements into symbolic form before comparing options. A transferable rule is: when matching logical structure, preserve not just the conditional direction but also the exact error pattern, including whether the conclusion negates one condition, both conditions, or their conjunction.

item.context: In recent years, all kinds of funny and frivolous network languages have invaded the territory of traditional Chinese on a large scale. Although there are many different voices in the academic and social circles, it is certain that if there is no timely and reasonable identification and guidance and let it flow, it will undoubtedly dispel the poetry and charm of traditional Chinese. it will not only separate the cultural heritage of Chinese, but also challenge the seriousness and standardization of the national language and make it fall into the danger of game and random rewriting.
item.question: Which of the following options is intended to be explained in this paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The network languages should be identified and guided in a timely and reasonable manner

choices.label: B
choices.text: The position of traditional Chinese is in jeopardy

choices.label: C
choices.text: The poetry and charm of network languages are far inferior to traditional language

choices.label: D
choices.text: Internet languages have had a certain impact on traditional Chinese

response:
Reasoning: The paragraph’s core claim is not just that internet language impacts traditional Chinese, but that without timely and reasonable regulation/guidance, it will harm traditional Chinese’s heritage and norms. So the author mainly wants to stress the need for guidance.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea/author-intent approach: identify the thesis by looking for the sentence that expresses the author’s purpose rather than supporting consequences. The key clue was the conditional structure “if there is no timely and reasonable identification and guidance,” which signals that the warning about harm serves to justify a recommendation. My success came from distinguishing the central claim from the negative effects listed afterward, which are supporting reasons rather than the paragraph’s main point. For similar problems, first separate the author’s recommendation or judgment from the evidence used to support it, and choose the option that captures that governing purpose.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the author’s main intended point, not merely a detail that appears in the passage. That was the right framing, because the paragraph contains both a background fact and a normative conclusion, and the task is to identify which one the author is using the passage to emphasize. My strategy was to separate the setup from the thesis: first, the spread of internet language is described; then, the sentence beginning with the conditional warning introduces the author’s real argumentative focus. That strategy was appropriate because “if… then…” structures often signal the writer’s main concern and policy recommendation rather than a neutral observation. I used the key constraint that the paragraph warns against “letting it flow” without “timely and reasonable identification and guidance,” which points to advocated action. I also correctly noticed that claims about harm to cultural inheritance and linguistic seriousness function as supporting reasons, not the central point themselves. A shortcut that helped was distinguishing descriptive options from prescriptive ones; the passage moves beyond description into recommendation. I should still be careful in similar questions to test whether the strongest statement is the author’s thesis or only an effect used to justify it. One alternative I needed to rule out was the broader-impact option, since it is true but less complete and less purpose-revealing. The transferable rule is: when a passage presents a phenomenon and then warns what will happen unless some action is taken, the main idea is usually the advocated response, with the harms serving as evidence.

item.context: Although many areas of today's international affairs are still subject to the number one superpower, the United States, on the issue of United Nations reform, only one country, one vote and 2/3 majority can get the reform plan and pass the voting rules.Objectively speaking, although it is in a weak position, Africa, which has 1/4 seats in the United comrades-in-arms International, expresses its will and provides an once-in-a-lifetime historical opportunity to deal with great powers.
item.question: Which of the following can express the meaning of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Africa holds nearly a quarter of the seats in the United Nations

choices.label: B
choices.text: Today, many areas of international affairs are still subject to the number one superpower, the United States

choices.label: C
choices.text: The UN reform plan needs to be approved by two - thirds of the member states

choices.label: D
choices.text: The voting rules of the United Nations provide an opportunity for Africa to strive for decision-making power on the reform of the United Nations

response:
Reasoning: The passage’s focus is not just facts about U.S. power, Africa’s seats, or the 2/3 rule alone, but the implication: because UN reform follows one-country-one-vote and a 2/3 majority, Africa’s voting weight gives it a rare chance to influence reform decisions.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea synthesis approach: instead of picking an option that repeated one detail, I combined the passage’s key premises about UN voting rules and Africa’s seat share to identify the broader implication. The decisive clue was the passage’s emphasis that “one country, one vote” plus a two-thirds threshold creates a rare opportunity for Africa despite its otherwise weak position. What helped was tracking the author’s conclusion-oriented language about “historical opportunity,” not getting distracted by background statements. For similar problems, first separate supporting facts from the author’s takeaway, then choose the option that captures the inference those facts are used to support.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the main idea of the passage, not merely a detail that was mentioned in it. That was the key to the correct reasoning, because the passage lists several facts but uses them to support one larger conclusion about Africa’s strategic opportunity in UN reform. My strategy was to distinguish between background premises and the author’s central claim. Specifically, I treated the references to U.S. dominance, Africa’s share of seats, and the two-thirds voting rule as supporting conditions rather than as standalone answers. The crucial relationship I used was causal: because UN reform is decided by one-country-one-vote and a supermajority, Africa’s voting bloc gains leverage despite its otherwise weak position. I did not get distracted by answer choices that simply repeated isolated facts from the passage. That was appropriate because summary questions usually reward the option that integrates multiple details into the passage’s purpose.

A shortcut that helped was asking, “Why are these facts being mentioned together?” rather than “Which fact is true?” I also implicitly checked tone: the phrase about a “once-in-a-lifetime historical opportunity” signaled that the author was emphasizing possibility and agency, not just describing institutional rules. An alternative I needed to consider was whether the passage’s focus might simply be the UN rule itself, but that would have ignored the explicit emphasis on Africa’s opportunity. The reasoning succeeded because I looked for the author’s conclusion rather than the most concrete sentence fragment. A transferable rule is: when a passage presents several facts and then highlights an implication, choose the option that captures the implication those facts jointly support, not an option that restates only one premise.

item.context: It is virtually certain that the government contract for building the new highway will be awarded to either Phoenix Contracting or Cartwright Company. I have just learned that the government has decided not to award the contract to Cartwright Company. It is ttherefore almost inevitable that Phoenix Contracting will be awarded the contract.
item.question: The argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: concluding that it is extremely likely that an event will occur by ruling out the only probable alternative

choices.label: B
choices.text: refuting a claim that a particular event is inevitable by establishing the possibility of an alternative event

choices.label: C
choices.text: predicting a future event on the basis of an established pattern of past events

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring, from a claim that one of two possible events will occur, that the other event will not occur

response:
Reasoning: The argument says the contract will almost certainly go to either Phoenix or Cartwright. Once Cartwright is ruled out, it concludes Phoenix is almost certain to get it. That is concluding an event is extremely likely by eliminating the only probable alternative.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an argument-structure approach: identify the initial probability claim, then see how the conclusion follows after one option is eliminated. The key factor was the phrase indicating that only two contenders were virtually certain, which made ruling out one of them strongly support the other. My success came from matching the conclusion pattern to the answer choice rather than getting distracted by the specific contract details. For similar problems, first translate the stimulus into a simple logical form—“likely A or B; not B; therefore likely A”—and then choose the option that mirrors that form.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the argument’s method of reasoning, not whether the conclusion was true in the real world. That distinction mattered, because the task was to match the structure: an initial claim that only two outcomes are seriously in play, followed by elimination of one, then a strong prediction of the other. My strategy was to abstract the content into a simple form: “either X or Y is virtually certain; not Y; therefore X is almost inevitable.” That was the right strategy for a flaw/method question because these are best solved by identifying logical form rather than focusing on the highway-contract details. The key evidence I used was the phrase “either Phoenix or Cartwright” combined with “not Cartwright,” which makes Phoenix the only remaining probable option. I also noticed the qualifiers “virtually certain” and “almost inevitable,” which supported an answer choice about extreme likelihood rather than strict deductive certainty.

A shortcut that helped was recognizing that the argument did not claim a history, causal pattern, or contradiction, which ruled out several alternatives quickly. I should still have consciously checked whether “either of two possible events” meant absolutely only two possibilities or only two probable possibilities, because that distinction affects whether the answer should mention certainty or likelihood. The successful part of the reasoning was matching the answer choice’s wording to the argument’s modal strength. On similar problems, I should continue translating the argument into a bare logical template and compare that template to each option’s structure and level of certainty. General rule: when a method-of-reasoning question includes probability language, track not just which options remain but also whether the conclusion preserves the argument’s degree of confidence.

item.context: In the past, the railroads in Ostronia were run as regional monopolies and operated with little regard for what customers wanted. In recent years, with improvements to the Ostronian national highway network, the railroad companies have faced heavy competition from long-distance trucking companies. But because of government subsidies that have permitted Ostronain railroad companies to operate even while incurring substantial losses, the companies continue to disregard customers' needs and desires.
item.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true on the basis of them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Without government subsidies, railroad companies in Ostronia would have to increase the prices they charge their customers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In recent years, some companies in Ostronia that have had little regard for the desires of their customers have nonetheless survived.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the government of Ostronia ceases to subsidize railroad companies, few of those companies will continue to operate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The transportation system in Ostronia is no more efficient today than in was in the past.

response:
Reasoning: The passage says railroad companies have continued to disregard customers’ needs, and government subsidies have allowed them to keep operating despite substantial losses. So at least some companies with little regard for customer desires have nonetheless survived in recent years. The other options add unsupported predictions or comparisons.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a direct entailment approach: I matched each answer choice against only what the stimulus explicitly guarantees, rejecting anything that required prediction or extra economic assumptions. The key clue was the statement that subsidies allowed railroad companies to keep operating despite substantial losses while they continued to disregard customers’ needs, which directly supports that some such companies survived in recent years. The successful step was translating “continue to operate” into the weaker, safer conclusion “have nonetheless survived.” For similar must-be-true questions, convert strong causal language in the stimulus into the narrowest conclusion it undeniably supports, and eliminate choices that speculate about what would happen under changed conditions.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a “must be true” inference problem, which means the right answer had to follow directly from the stated facts rather than from plausible speculation. My strategy was to identify the concrete entities mentioned, track what was said about them over time, and then test each choice for whether it merely seemed reasonable or was logically compelled. That was appropriate here because the stimulus gave a causal explanation for why the railroad companies continue operating despite losses and despite ignoring customer preferences. The key evidence I used was that the railroads had little regard for customers, faced competition, incurred substantial losses, and nevertheless continue to operate because subsidies permit it. From those facts, it follows that at least some companies in Ostronia that disregard customer desires have survived in recent years.  

What made the reasoning successful was resisting stronger claims than the text warranted. I correctly rejected choices that predicted what would happen without subsidies or made broad claims about national transportation efficiency, because those go beyond the information given. A hidden assumption to avoid in this kind of problem is treating “continues to operate” as support for any specific future business response, such as raising prices or shutting down. Another important alternative I considered was whether the competition or losses implied inefficiency, but the stimulus never established that comparison. The precise transferable rule is: in must-be-true questions, prefer the answer that restates a combination of explicit premises, and reject any answer that introduces forecasts, counterfactuals, or comparative judgments not directly stated.

item.context: Among the doctors in a tertiary hospital, the number of doctors graduated from specialized hospitals is greater than the number of doctors graduated from non-specialized hospitals, and the number of female doctors is greater than the number of male doctors.
item.question: If the above statement is true, then which of the following statements about the doctor in this hospital must also be true? (1) The number of female doctors graduating from non-specialized hospitals is greater than the number of male doctors graduating from specialized hospitals. (2) The number of male doctors graduated from specialized hospitals is greater than the number of male doctors graduated from non-specialized hospitals. (3) The number of female doctors graduated from specialized hospitals is greater than the number of male doctors graduated from non-specialized hospitals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: only (2)

choices.label: C
choices.text: only (3)

response:
Reasoning: Let specialized/non-specialized and female/male counts be FS, FN, MS, MN. Given: FS+MS > FN+MN and FS+FN > MS+MN. Adding them gives 2FS > 2MN, so FS > MN, which is statement (3). Statements (1) and (2) need not hold; counterexamples exist.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an algebraic partitioning approach, defining four groups by gender and hospital type, then translating the two “greater than” conditions into inequalities. The key clue was that adding the two inequalities isolates one cell against its diagonal opposite, which correctly established one required statement. My mistake was stopping too early and assuming another statement “need not hold” without testing whether subtracting or rearranging the original inequalities would force it; in fact, comparing the specialized and total gender counts also constrains the male subgroup split. For similar problems, systematically derive all implied inequalities from the same variables before relying on counterexamples.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the problem as a 2×2 counting setup, which was the right overall structure, but my notation was too ambiguous and that weakened the analysis. By writing symbols like FS, FN, MS, and MN without keeping the two dimensions completely explicit, I made it easier to slide into comparing the wrong cells. My strategy was to translate the two given majority statements into inequalities and combine them algebraically; that method was appropriate, and it successfully established one required relationship. The problem is that I stopped after finding one consequence and then dismissed the remaining statements too quickly instead of systematically testing whether they were forced by the same constraints. In particular, I used addition of inequalities but did not check what subtraction or rearrangement might imply, so I missed another necessary comparison. I also treated my informal sense that statement (2) “need not hold” as enough, without constructing a valid counterexample that satisfied all original conditions and matched the exact wording of the categories. That is the specific failure: I relied on a shortcut judgment rather than a full constraint check. A better approach is to keep a strict table of the four cells, derive all independent inequalities obtainable from the premises, and only reject an option after an explicit model verifies its negation is possible. The transferable rule is: in 2×2 count problems, use unambiguous variables and exhaust the algebraic consequences of the totals before drawing conclusions about individual cells.

item.context: The average life expectancy of the population is an important indicator reflecting the health level of the people in a country and region. The sixth national census shows that the average life expectancy of the Chinese population reached 74.83 years in 2010, while the average life expectancy of the population in the early days of the founding of the People's Republic of China was only about 35 years. Therefore, the elderly people that people thought more than sixty years ago now seem to be just middle-aged people.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, would most weaken the above point of view?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Since the founding of the People's Republic of China, the decrease in the number of newborn infant deaths is the most important reason for the increase in the average life expectancy of the population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the early days of the founding of the People's Republic of China, the country was shifting from war to peace. The situation in the country was still unstable and the population was much lower than it is now.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the early days of the founding of the People's Republic of China, the living environment was more difficult, and people's nutritional level was much worse than it is now.

choices.label: D
choices.text: With the development of medicine, the level of medical care has been greatly improved compared with the early days of the founding of the People's Republic of China.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion wrongly uses higher average life expectancy to infer that people once considered elderly would now be only middle-aged. If the increase mainly came from fewer infant deaths, average life expectancy rises without showing that older adults age much later.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a causal-logic weakening approach: I checked whether the evidence about rising average life expectancy actually supported the claim about who counts as elderly versus middle-aged. The key factor was that “average life expectancy” can increase for reasons unrelated to slower aging or better survival at older ages, especially if infant mortality drops sharply. My answer was correct because I focused on the gap between a population average and the specific conclusion about age categories for older adults. For similar problems, test whether a statistic reflects the same subgroup or mechanism as the conclusion before treating it as direct support.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the argument as moving from a change in a population-level statistic, average life expectancy, to a claim about how the meaning of “elderly” for an individual person should shift. That interpretation was correct, because the key issue was whether the cited statistic actually supports the conclusion about people in their sixties now seeming only middle-aged. My strategy was to test whether the premise and conclusion were linked by the same concept: average lifespan versus the age at which a person becomes old. This was appropriate, because weakening the argument required showing that the rise in the average could occur without implying slower aging or a later onset of old age. The crucial fact I used was that average life expectancy can be raised substantially by reducing deaths at the very beginning of life, not just by extending later-life survival. That exposes a hidden assumption in the argument: it assumes that a higher national average means people who already reached adulthood are aging into old age later than before. I correctly rejected choices that merely explained why life expectancy improved, since causal support for the premise does not attack the inference to the conclusion. The main reason the reasoning succeeded was that I focused on the mismatch between demographic averages and individual aging categories. In similar problems, I should explicitly ask whether the evidence measures the same dimension as the conclusion. A general rule is: when an argument shifts from a group average to a claim about individual cases, test whether changes in the average could be driven by a different subgroup or mechanism.
