General rule: when a passage states that success depends on two jointly necessary traits, the best paraphrase must retain both traits and their joint necessity.

item.context: The effectiveness of national governance is an important indicator to reflect the advantages of the system. The institutional advantages of socialism with Chinese characteristics need to be transformed into the effectiveness of national governance, which needs to be realized and demonstrated through the effectiveness of governance. We should be good at using systems and laws to govern the country and turn all aspects of institutional advantages into the effectiveness of managing the country. Promoting the modernization of the national governance system and governance capacity is the only way to give full play to the superiority of the socialist system.
item.question: Which of the following options is emphasized in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The advantage of our country's system needs to be reflected by the effectiveness of good governance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rely on the law to promote the modernization of China's governance system and governance capacity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The socialist system has a great impact on the modernization of governance in our country.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To govern the country, we must give full play to the superiority of our socialist system.

response:
Reasoning: The passage stresses that the institutional advantages of socialism with Chinese characteristics must be transformed into “governance effectiveness” and reflected through good governance outcomes. Other options are partial or reversed emphases.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea matching approach: I identified the repeated concepts in the passage and looked for the option that summarized them most completely. The key factor was the passage’s emphasis on transforming “institutional advantages” into “governance effectiveness” and showing those advantages through actual governance results. My answer was correct because I distinguished the central claim from supporting means, such as using laws and promoting modernization, which were mentioned but not presented as the main emphasis. For similar questions, first separate the core conclusion from the methods or conditions that support it, then choose the option that captures the broadest repeated idea.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the central emphasis of the entire passage, not just a detail mentioned within it. That was the right frame, because the paragraph presents a main claim and then supports it with explanation about systems, laws, and modernization. My strategy was to identify the repeated conceptual chain: institutional advantage → governance effectiveness → modernization of governance. This was appropriate because “emphasized” questions usually require tracking the dominant idea across multiple sentences rather than selecting a supporting means or consequence.

The key evidence I used was the passage’s repeated insistence that institutional advantages must be “transformed into” and “demonstrated through” governance effectiveness. I correctly treated the reference to using systems and laws as an instrument, not the central thesis. I also noticed that modernization of the governance system and capacity was framed as a way to fully realize the system’s superiority, which makes it subordinate to the broader point. A possible trap was to over-focus on the phrase about law, since it is concrete and policy-like, but that would have confused a method with the main emphasis.

What made the reasoning successful was distinguishing between primary claim, means, and implication. In similar problems, I should keep mapping each sentence’s role before matching options. General rule: when a passage contains a thesis plus mechanisms for achieving it, choose the option that captures the thesis, not one that isolates a mechanism or downstream effect.

item.context: The bystander effect, also known as the responsibility dispersion effect, refers to the inhibitory effect on rescue behavior caused by the presence of others in an emergency.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following situations is in line with the bystander effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There was a truck rollover on the highway, everyone helped the truck driver Xiao Yang to protect the goods from looting

choices.label: B
choices.text: When a pedestrian fell down on the road, Xiao Li saw no one around to witness it and was afraid to take responsibility and dare not help

choices.label: C
choices.text: A fire broke out near the supermarket, Xiao Zhang urged his wife to call the police, and his wife answered that someone must have called the police

choices.label: D
choices.text: Someone fell into the water at the beach, and the lifeguard Xiao Wang yelled while running to remind the onlookers not to go into the water at will

response:
Reasoning: The bystander effect means people are less likely to help because others are present, assuming someone else will act. In C, Xiao Zhang’s wife thinks “someone must have called the police,” showing responsibility dispersion. A shows active help, B is fear of responsibility without others present, D is safety instruction.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I extracted the core mechanism of the bystander effect—reduced helping because responsibility is diffused among other people—and compared each option against that mechanism. The key factor was whether the person failed to act specifically because others were present and presumed someone else would intervene. My answer was correct because I focused on the causal reason for inaction, not just whether an emergency occurred. For similar questions, isolate the defining trigger and outcome in the concept, then eliminate choices that show helping behavior or inaction caused by a different motive.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for a situation that matches a very specific definition: reduced helping behavior in an emergency because other people are present. My strategy was to map each option against the key elements of the definition rather than relying on surface similarity to emergencies or helping. The crucial elements I used were: an emergency exists, other people are present or assumed to be present, and that presence inhibits direct action through diffusion of responsibility. That was an appropriate strategy because several distractors involved emergencies but failed on the inhibition-by-others condition.

I correctly rejected the option where people actively coordinated to help, because that is the opposite of inhibited rescue behavior. I also correctly rejected the case involving fear of personal liability when no one else was present, because that reflects self-protection, not dispersed responsibility. Likewise, I excluded the lifeguard scenario because it involved professional intervention and crowd control rather than hesitation caused by others’ presence. The successful step was focusing on the causal mechanism, not merely whether an emergency occurred.

One assumption that helped was treating “someone must have already acted” as equivalent to diffusion of responsibility, which fits the concept well. In similar problems, I should continue identifying the exact mechanism named in the definition and test each option for all required conditions. A transferable rule is: when matching a scenario to a concept definition, verify the full causal chain, not just one shared feature.

item.context: In the 1940s, more than 7000 books were published in the United States, of which only more than 10 became the best-selling books. A publisher in New York found that the best-selling books of the year were related to three subjects, one related to President Lincoln, one related to doctors, and the other related to dogs.He thought that if these three kinds of content were combined, they would be the best-selling books.So he planned to publish the Pet Dog of the President of the United States and Physicians, which turned out to be a particularly poor seller.
item.question: Which of the following options best indicates the flaw in the above reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is considered that the attribute of the whole is also possessed by the part.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is considered that the attributes that the part has also belong to the whole.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ignoring other possible reasons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The result of a phenomenon is regarded as the cause of this phenomenon.

response:
Reasoning: The publisher assumes that because some best-sellers involved Lincoln, doctors, or dogs, those topics caused the success. He then combines them, mistaking a feature of successful books for the reason they succeeded. This is a causal fallacy.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a causal-flaw approach, focusing on the publisher’s assumption that certain subjects explained why those books sold well. The key clue, though, was not just that those topics appeared in successful books, but that he treated properties found in separate instances or parts as if combining them would produce the same property in a new whole. My mistake was classifying the argument as confusing cause and effect instead of spotting the composition-style error. In similar problems, I should ask whether the argument transfers a trait from individual cases or components to a combined object or total category without justification.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the logical flaw in the publisher’s inference from patterns among best-sellers to a prediction about a new book. That part was correct, but I classified the flaw too narrowly as causal reasoning. My strategy was to look for an argument that treated a correlated feature as the cause of success, because the publisher noticed recurring subjects and then inferred marketability from them. That strategy fit part of the surface structure, but it missed the more specific structural error in how he combined those features. The crucial evidence I underused was that the three subjects appeared separately across different successful books, and the publisher assumed that merging them into one book would preserve the same desirable property. This is not merely “feature mistaken for cause”; it is a composition-type mistake, where what is true of parts or instances is projected onto a combined whole.

I also overlooked that the argument does not actually claim those subjects caused success in a rigorous explanatory sense; it mainly assumes their presence is transferable when aggregated. An alternative I should have considered was whether the flaw concerns moving from “successful books each had one of these traits” to “a book with all these traits will therefore be successful.” The error came from focusing on content words like “related to” and “best-selling” and jumping to causation, instead of mapping the inferential form. In similar problems, I should first abstract the argument: identify whether it moves from parts to whole, whole to parts, correlation to cause, or ignores alternatives. A useful general rule is: when an argument combines several individually successful elements and assumes the combination inherits the same success, test for an invalid transfer from properties of parts or cases to the composite whole.

item.context: To succeed in a particular career, a person must have both talent and tenacity. Hans did not succeed in his career. Ttherefore, he must not have had both talent and tenacity.
item.question: Which one of the following contains the same logical flaw as that in the passage above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some plants grow fast when given fertilizer or a lot of light. Ttherefore, this fast-growing plant received either fertilizer or a lot of light.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It does not always snow when it is cold and cloudy. Ttherefore, it need not be either cold or cloudy for it to snow.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a person does not have both strong muscles and efficient oxygen transfer, that person cannot run far. Ttherefore, if Erica can run far, either she has strong muscles or else she has efficient oxygen transfer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To make good coffee, you need clear water and fresh coffee beans. Whoever made this bad coffee must not have used both clear water and fresh coffee beans.

response:
Reasoning: The passage commits the inverse error: from “If success, then both talent and tenacity” it concludes “If not success, then not both.” Choice D has the same form: “If good coffee, then clear water and fresh beans”; “bad coffee, so not both.”
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-matching approach by translating the argument into conditional form and comparing answer choices for the same invalid inference pattern. The key factor was recognizing the structure “both conditions are necessary for success/good outcome,” followed by “the outcome did not occur, so the person must have lacked at least one condition,” which is a mistaken reversal from a necessary condition. My success came from focusing on the logical form rather than the topic and spotting the same move in the matching choice. For similar problems, first identify whether a condition is necessary or sufficient, then test whether the conclusion improperly infers from the absence of the result to the absence of the required conditions.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument as giving a necessary condition for success: succeeding requires having both talent and tenacity. From there, the conclusion denied the necessary condition merely because the outcome did not occur, so I correctly identified the flaw as moving from “if success, then both traits” to “not success, therefore not both traits.” My strategy was to translate the statement into a conditional form and then compare answer choices for the same invalid pattern. That was appropriate because flaw questions often hinge on structural equivalence rather than topic similarity.

The key relationship I used was that a necessary condition cannot be negated from the absence of the result. In other words, failure could arise from many other causes, so the argument improperly treated one requirement as if it were a sufficient explanation. I did not rely on surface wording like “must” or “need”; instead, I tracked the logical roles of outcome and prerequisite. That helped me avoid being distracted by answer choices involving disjunctions or different subject matter.

Choice D matched because it also stated a requirement for a positive outcome and then inferred from a negative outcome that the requirement was absent. The success of my reasoning came from distinguishing necessary-condition reasoning from valid contraposition. A transferable rule is: when an argument has the form “Outcome requires condition,” you may infer “if outcome, then condition,” but you may not infer “if no outcome, then no condition.”

item.context: After investigating and analyzing the five friends of a victim, the four police officers made the following assumptions: A said: these five people are suspected. B said: Lao Chen can't escape the relationship, he is suspected. C said: these five people are not all suspected. D said: there must be someone committing a crime among the five people.
item.question: If only one of the four guesses is correct, which of the followings is true??

choices.label: A
choices.text: A's conjecture is correct. Lao Chen is the most suspect

choices.label: B
choices.text: C's conjecture is correct. Lao Chen is not suspected

choices.label: C
choices.text: C's conjecture is correct, but Lao Chen may commit a crime

choices.label: D
choices.text: D's conjecture is correct. Lao Chen is suspected

response:
Reasoning: A and C are exact opposites: “all five are suspected” vs “not all five are suspected,” so exactly one of them must be true. Since only one of the four statements is true, B and D must both be false. Thus Lao Chen is not suspected, and C is the only correct statement.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a logical-consistency approach, comparing the statements for contradiction and checking which truth assignments fit the condition that exactly one statement is true. The key factor was that A and C are direct opposites, so one of them must be true and they cannot both share the same truth value. That forced B and D to be false, and the crucial successful step was recognizing that this immediately determines Lao Chen’s status from B’s falsity. For similar problems, first identify mutually exclusive or complementary statements, then use the “exactly one true” constraint to eliminate the remaining options systematically.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the problem as a logic-consistency question: four statements were made about suspicion and guilt, and exactly one statement could be true. That interpretation was correct, because the key was not to identify the criminal directly but to test which combination of truth values was possible. My strategy was to look first for statements that were logical complements, since those create strong constraints under an “exactly one true” condition. In particular, “all five are suspected” and “not all five are suspected” are direct opposites, so one of them must be true and both cannot share the same truth value. That immediately implied that the only true statement had to be one of those two, which forced the other two statements to be false.

The evidence I used correctly was the opposition between universal and negated-universal claims, plus the consequence of falsity for the statement about Lao Chen being suspected. I also correctly treated B and D as separate claims rather than assuming that “suspected” and “committed a crime” were interchangeable. A possible trap would have been to overread D as somehow supporting B, but guilt and suspicion are not the same proposition. The reasoning succeeded because it reduced the problem structurally before considering any narrative meaning. In similar problems, I should first identify contradiction pairs, equivalences, and implication links before evaluating answer choices. A transferable rule is: when exactly one statement is true, first locate any pair that must contain one truth; that pair often determines the truth values of all remaining statements.

item.context: Generally, bacteria grow and multiply at room temperature, and the low temperature environment stops growing and can only maintain life. But Yersinia is just the opposite. Not only is it not afraid of low temperature and cold, but it only multiplies at about 0 degree. Food stored in the refrigerator, Make Yersinia in its best growth state.
item.question: Which of the following can be derived from this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yersinia cannot survive at room temperature

choices.label: B
choices.text: The environment for the growth of general bacteria  is also suitable for the growth of Yersinia

choices.label: C
choices.text: The optimal growth temperature of Yersinia is not suitable for general bacteria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only Yersinia bacteria exist in the refrigerator at 0 degree

response:
Reasoning: The passage says most bacteria grow at room temperature and low temperature only preserves them, while Yersinia grows best around 0°C in the refrigerator. So Yersinia’s optimal growth temperature differs from and is unsuitable for general bacteria’s growth.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a contrast-based reasoning approach: I compared the stated growth conditions for general bacteria with the opposite pattern described for Yersinia, then looked for the option that captured that incompatibility. The key factor was the sentence that low temperature stops the growth of general bacteria but is the best growth state for Yersinia, which directly supports a difference in suitable growth temperatures. My success came from distinguishing what was explicitly contrasted from stronger unsupported claims like “cannot survive” or “only Yersinia exists.” For similar problems, translate each statement into a precise condition comparison and choose only the conclusion that is fully guaranteed by those conditions.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the statement that must follow from the contrast drawn in the passage, not merely one that sounds plausible. My strategy was to compare the growth conditions of “generally, bacteria” with those of Yersinia and look for the option that preserved that contrast without adding new claims. That was appropriate because the passage explicitly sets up an opposition: ordinary bacteria multiply at room temperature, while low temperature inhibits their growth; Yersinia, by contrast, multiplies around 0°C and even thrives in refrigerated food. The key evidence I used was the phrase “just the opposite,” which signals that Yersinia’s favorable growth condition is unfavorable for ordinary bacteria. From that, I inferred that Yersinia’s optimal temperature would not be a suitable growth temperature for general bacteria.

I also correctly avoided stronger claims that the passage did not justify. For example, nothing stated that Yersinia cannot survive at room temperature, only that it multiplies at about 0°C. Likewise, the passage did not say refrigerators contain only Yersinia, so exclusivity would be an unjustified leap. A risky assumption would have been to equate “not best” with “cannot survive,” but I did not make that move. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on necessary implication rather than possibility or exaggeration. In similar problems, I should continue testing each option against the exact strength of the text. General rule: when a passage contrasts two categories, the safest inference preserves only the stated contrast and avoids converting comparative claims into absolute ones.

item.context: The development of a country should be committed to making the cake of economic development bigger, on this basis, pay attention to fair distribution. For regional economic development, the concept of comparative advantage should be firmly established. There are great differences in physical and geographical conditions in different places. Even if the two natural conditions are exactly the same, geographically adjacent provinces or cities, the best mode of development is not for everyone to develop the same production structure, but should have their own division of labor.
item.question: Which of the following options is emphasized by the author through this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The model of regional development should be different in different geographical conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The two geographically adjacent cities should also have their own different characteristics.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The economic development of different regions should be consistent with the local comparative advantages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The best model of the development  is not suitable for all geographical conditions.

response:
Reasoning: The passage’s core point is to “firmly establish the concept of comparative advantage” in regional development. Differences in geography matter, but even similar neighboring regions should divide labor rather than copy each other. So the emphasis is that regional development should match each area’s comparative advantages.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea reasoning approach: identify the thesis statement, then treat the later sentences as support and examples. The key factor was the explicit claim that regional development should “firmly establish the concept of comparative advantage,” while the discussion of neighboring areas and differing conditions illustrated that principle rather than replacing it. My success came from distinguishing the author’s central conclusion from narrower supporting details. For similar questions, first locate the broad guiding principle in the passage, then test each option by asking whether it summarizes that principle or only restates one example.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the author’s central emphasis, not merely a detail mentioned in the passage. That distinction mattered because several options echoed part of the text, but only one captured the governing principle tying the examples together. My strategy was to identify the thesis sentence first—“the concept of comparative advantage should be firmly established”—and then treat the later remarks about geography and neighboring regions as supporting illustrations. That was appropriate because the passage moves from a general claim to examples, so the main idea should be broader than any single example.

The key evidence I used was the contrast between “same production structure for everyone” and “their own division of labor,” which signals a principle of differentiated development based on local strengths. I also correctly recognized that geographic difference was not the ultimate point; it was evidence for why comparative advantage matters. A shortcut that worked here was checking whether an option described a universal rule or just one scenario. I should still note that alternatives focusing on adjacent cities or differing conditions were tempting because they repeated vivid parts of the passage. Those options were narrower than the author’s argument and therefore secondary. The reasoning succeeded because I prioritized the author’s explicit normative claim over descriptive examples. In similar problems, I should map which sentences state the thesis and which merely justify it. A transferable rule is: when a passage presents a principle followed by examples, choose the option that preserves the principle’s scope rather than one that copies an illustrative detail.

item.context: After hearing the words money is like dung and friends are worth a thousand dollars, some people feel that there is a logical problem, because they can come to the absurd conclusion that friends are like dung.
item.question: Since the conclusion that friends are like dung cannot be established, which of the following can be logically deduced?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The statement that money is like dung is false.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If friends are really  worth a thousand dollars, then money is not like dung.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The statement that friends are worth a thousand dollars is true.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Money is like dung and friends are worth  a thousand dollars are either true or false.

response:
Reasoning: The failed inference shows only that these expressions are figurative/non-transitive; it does not prove either statement true or false individually, nor that one excludes the other. So A, B, and C do not follow. The only logically safe choice is the tautological one.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an elimination approach, treating both premises as loose figurative claims and concluding that only a tautology could be deduced. The key overlooked factor was the problem’s conditional setup: if combining the two statements would yield an absurd conclusion, and that conclusion cannot be established, then at least one of the original statements must fail whenever the other is assumed true. My mistake was dismissing the relation between the two statements instead of translating the failed chain into a conditional incompatibility. For similar problems, when a pair of premises would imply an impossible result, infer a conditional denying one premise given the other, rather than defaulting to a trivial tautology.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the problem as asking what can be deduced from the fact that combining the two sayings appears to support an absurd conclusion, but I treated the sayings too loosely as figurative expressions rather than as premises in a logical relation. My strategy was to dismiss the comparison term “like” as non-transitive and then choose the option that looked like a harmless tautology. That strategy was inappropriate because the question explicitly asked what follows given that the absurd conclusion cannot be established; it was probing the implications of that failure, not asking for a comment about figurative language in general. I used the fact that the conclusion does not follow, but I missed the stronger relationship: if one premise would make the bad inference possible together with the other, then accepting one constrains the other. In particular, I failed to test whether the impossibility of the conclusion rules out the simultaneous acceptance of the two statements under the condition stated in one choice. I assumed that because neither original statement could be individually verified or falsified, no informative deduction was possible. That shortcut ignored conditional reasoning, where you may not know whether a premise is true, yet still know what would have to be false if another premise were true. I also should have compared the answer choices by logical strength rather than by rhetorical plausibility. The specific error was treating “cannot establish the conclusion” as merely “the inference pattern is invalid,” instead of asking what incompatibility the problem intended me to infer. In similar problems, I should translate the setup into conditional form and ask which option captures the exact consequence of avoiding the absurd result. General rule: when a question says an unacceptable conclusion cannot follow from two claims, check whether that forces a conditional exclusion between those claims, not just whether each claim is independently uncertain.

item.context: In the information age, the existence form of information is different from the previous information form. It is sound, light and electricity,magnetism, code and other forms exist. This makes it easy to transfer, that is, it is easy to be modified, stolen or illegally spread and used. coupled with the increasingly wide application of information technology, various social effects brought about by information technology products are also unexpected. In the information meeting, the direct communication between people is greatly reduced, replaced by indirect, non-face-to-face, non-direct contact. There are various forms of communication, and the behavior of people related to information is difficult to be restricted by traditional ethical norms.
item.question: As an introduction to an article, which of the following is most likely to be discussed later in this article?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Update of the form of information

choices.label: B
choices.text: Information society and information ethics

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diversification of forms of interpersonal communication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Information technology products and lifestyle

response:
Reasoning: The passage highlights how new information forms and technologies make information easy to alter, steal, and spread, while weakening traditional face-to-face interaction and ethical constraints. This sets up a discussion about ethical issues arising in the information society, not just technology or communication forms alone.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea and forward-prediction approach: I identified the passage’s central concern and inferred what topic an introduction like this would lead into. The key factor was that the passage did not just describe new information forms or communication methods; it emphasized problems such as easy modification, theft, illegal dissemination, and the weakening of traditional ethical restraints. My success came from tracking the author’s evaluative focus rather than getting distracted by concrete examples. For similar questions, first separate background examples from the passage’s real issue, then choose the option that captures that broader issue.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the prompt as asking for the most likely continuation topic of an introductory paragraph, not for a detail already stated in the paragraph. That distinction mattered, because the best answer needed to capture the paragraph’s central problem and likely article theme rather than a single example mentioned in passing. My strategy was to identify the dominant idea running through the passage: new information forms and technologies make information easier to manipulate and circulate, while traditional ethical restraints on behavior become weaker in mediated communication. That was an appropriate strategy because introductory paragraphs usually move from background conditions to the core issue the article will analyze.

The evidence I used was the repeated emphasis on modification, theft, illegal dissemination, unexpected social effects, reduced direct communication, and the difficulty of regulating behavior by traditional ethical norms. These clues point beyond mere technological change toward moral and social questions created by that change. I correctly rejected narrower options because they captured only one surface feature, such as communication forms or product impacts, rather than the unifying concern. An assumption that helped was that article introductions often culminate in a conceptual discussion, especially when the paragraph ends with a normative problem. I should still remember to test whether an option names the broad issue tying all examples together rather than just repeating one example. The key lesson is: when asked what an introduction will discuss next, identify the passage’s final tension or problem statement and choose the option that abstracts that tension at the right level of generality.

item.context: Zoologist: It is true that over the past 15 years, there has been a fourfold increase in government funding to preserve endangered species, while the number of endangered species needing such preservation has increased by only 70% (there were, however, a large number of endangered species to begin with 15 years ago). Taking into account inflation, the amount of funding is at least double what it was 15 years ago. Nevertheless, the current amount of funding from the government for species preservation is inadequate and must be enhanced.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to reconcile the zoologist's conclusion with the above evidence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The two government agencies responsible for species preservation are typically under budget and are known for an utter lack of cooperation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Unlike today, funding for the preservation of species was essentially nonexistent 15 years ago.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Over the past 15 years, the salaries of conservationists employed by the government to work on species preservation solutions have increased at a rate twice that of inflation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Within the past 15 years, there have been breakthroughs in species demography that allow scientists to identify those species most in need of protection far before they face any real risk of extinction.

response:
Reasoning: Funding more than doubled in real terms and endangered species rose only 70%, so adequacy seems improved. This is reconciled if preservation costs also rose substantially beyond inflation. If conservationists’ salaries increased faster than inflation, much of the extra funding is absorbed by higher costs, leaving funding still inadequate.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a quantitative reconciliation approach: I compared the real increase in funding with the smaller increase in the number of endangered species and looked for a choice that would explain why adequacy still had not improved enough. The key clue I underweighted was the statement that there were already many endangered species 15 years ago, which means a percentage increase in species does not capture the size of the total need. My mistake was assuming the best reconciliation had to involve rising preservation costs, rather than considering that the earlier funding base may have been so low that even a large increase still leaves funding inadequate. In similar problems, first test whether the argument depends on baseline levels, not just percentage changes.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for a fact that explains why funding can be much higher than before and still be inadequate now, which was the right task. My strategy was to look for a new cost pressure that would consume the added money, so I focused on the answer about salaries rising faster than inflation. That approach was plausible in form, but I used it too loosely: I treated any increase in costs as sufficient without checking whether it actually reconciled the scale of the evidence. The argument emphasized that there were already many endangered species 15 years ago, so the key issue was not just changing costs per worker but the possibility that the earlier funding level was extremely low relative to the need. I missed that a comparison like “double the old amount” does not show adequacy if the starting point was near zero; percentage growth from a tiny base can still leave funding far too small. By contrast, the salary option affects only one component of spending and gives no reason to think the original baseline was inadequate or that salaries dominate the budget. I also failed to test the choices against the conclusion’s exact tension: why improved funding figures do not undermine the claim of inadequacy. In similar problems, I should ask whether the answer attacks the denominator, the baseline, or the relevance of the comparison, not just whether it introduces a new burden. A transferable rule is: when an argument relies on growth rates or percentage increases, always examine the starting level before inferring anything about sufficiency.

item.context: Recent unexpectedly heavy rainfalls in the metropolitan area have filled the reservoirs and streams; water rationing, ttherefore, will not be necessary this summer.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the author's prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Water rationing was imposed in the city in three of the last five years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In most years the city receives less total precipitation in the summer than it receives in any other season.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The water company's capacity to pump water to customers has not kept up with the increased demand created by population growth in the metropolitan area.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The long-range weather forecast predicts lower-than-average temperatures for this summer.

response:
Reasoning: The argument assumes full reservoirs and streams mean no rationing. But if rationing could still be needed because the system cannot pump enough water to meet demand, then the prediction is undermined even with abundant water supply. That is exactly what option C says.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a weaken-the-argument approach by identifying the conclusion’s assumption: that abundant recent rainfall guarantees enough usable water for the summer. The key factor was distinguishing total water supply from the ability to deliver that water to customers; the prediction fails if distribution capacity is insufficient. My success came from spotting that the argument treated “full reservoirs” as equivalent to “no rationing needed,” overlooking an infrastructure bottleneck. For similar problems, I should test whether the stated evidence supports the conclusion only under hidden assumptions, especially by separating resource availability from access, delivery, or operational constraints.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the fact that most weakens the prediction that water rationing will not be necessary, not merely a fact related to water supply. That interpretation was important because the conclusion concerned rationing, which can result from distribution limits as well as lack of water. My strategy was to identify the argument’s core assumption: that full reservoirs and streams are sufficient to guarantee adequate water service throughout the summer. That was an appropriate weakening approach because it tested whether the stated evidence actually ensured the conclusion.

The key relationship I used was the distinction between total water availability and the system’s ability to deliver that water to customers. I recognized that an infrastructure bottleneck could cause rationing even when raw water supplies are abundant. I also correctly treated historical frequency and seasonal precipitation patterns as less direct, since they do not by themselves show that this summer’s prediction fails. One assumption I avoided was equating “more water in storage” with “no practical shortage,” which is exactly the gap the argument leaves open.

I should still note that other choices might look tempting if one focuses too narrowly on drought conditions rather than operational constraints. The reasoning succeeded because it targeted the necessary link between evidence and conclusion rather than the topic in general. In similar problems, I should explicitly ask what hidden condition must hold for the conclusion to follow. General rule: when an argument predicts no shortage, test both supply sufficiency and delivery capacity, because either can independently determine the outcome.

item.context: The job motivation method means that if there is a cultivable talent who has both ability and political integrity, can manage, make good use of people, and can open up a new situation in a department, then you should grasp the actual needs, maximize the strengths and avoid weaknesses, and promptly promote and reuse them, so as not to hit the Maximum positivity.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following belong to the job motivation method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the enterprise research stage, the upper-level leaders take the lead, lead by example, and lead a group of technical backbones to overcome difficulties

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leader A has a good impression of his unit's employee B, so he promotes him as the unit supervisor

choices.label: C
choices.text: The leader of a certain unit is very dissatisfied with the work habits of C, who is high-powered, so he transferred him to other departments to do work outside of his profession

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ding worked in the network department of a certain unit, and showed superhuman management skills in an ordinary job, and was immediately promoted to office director

response:
Reasoning: The method requires promptly promoting and reusing a capable, politically sound, managerial talent based on actual needs and strengths. D matches this: Ding showed strong management ability and was immediately promoted appropriately. A is leading by example, B is favoritism, C misuses talent.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I broke the concept into core criteria and checked each option against them. The key factor was whether the person demonstrated strong, cultivable management talent and was then promptly promoted in a way that used that strength to open a new situation. My success came from filtering out choices that only showed leadership style, personal favoritism, or misassignment of talent rather than recognition and reuse of ability. For similar problems, I should convert the definition into a checklist of necessary elements and eliminate any option missing even one essential condition.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the definition as a classification task: identify the option that fits a specific talent-management method rather than just a generally good leadership behavior. My strategy was to extract the key necessary conditions from the definition: the person must be demonstrably capable, have integrity or at least no contrary evidence, show managerial or talent-using ability, be able to open a new situation, and then be promptly promoted in a way that uses strengths rather than wasting them. That was an appropriate strategy because definition questions are usually solved by matching explicit criteria, not by choosing the most admirable scenario. The crucial evidence I used was the contrast between “promptly promote and reuse talent” and the wrong patterns of favoritism, role mismatch, or simple personal leadership. I also correctly noticed that one option described leading a team through difficulties, which is effective leadership but not a personnel promotion mechanism. Another option depended on a leader’s favorable impression rather than demonstrated ability, so it failed the evidence-based selection requirement. A third option actually violated the “maximize strengths and avoid weaknesses” clause by moving a strong performer outside his specialty. The reasoning succeeded because I treated the definition as conjunctive: several traits had to appear together, not just one. In similar problems, I should explicitly separate core conditions from background detail and eliminate choices that satisfy only a superficial fragment. General rule: when judging whether an example fits a formal definition, map each option against every necessary element and reject any option that lacks even one essential criterion.

item.context: Political scientist: One of the most interesting dilemmas in contemporary democratic politics concerns the regulation of political campaign spending. People certainly should be free, within broad limits, to spend their money as they choose. On the other hand, candidates who can vastly outspend all rivals have an unfair advantage in publicizing their platforms. Democratic governments have a strong obligation to ensure that all voices have an equal chance to be heard, but governments should not subsidize expensive campaigns for each candidate. The resolution of the dilemma, ttherefore, is clear: __.
item.question: Which one of the following most logically completes the political scientist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: all wealthy persons should be prohibited from spending their own money on political campaigns

choices.label: B
choices.text: only candidates with significant campaign resources should be permitted to run for public office

choices.label: C
choices.text: an upper limit on the political campaign spending of each candidate is warranted

choices.label: D
choices.text: government subsidization of all political campaigns at a low percentage of their total cost is warranted

response:
Reasoning: The argument balances freedom to spend money with fairness in elections and rejects government subsidizing expensive campaigns. A spending cap best preserves broad spending freedom while preventing candidates from gaining an unfair publicity advantage through vastly greater resources.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple:
I used a balancing approach: I identified the competing principles in the stimulus and looked for the option that reconciled both rather than maximizing only one. The key clue was the combination of two constraints: large spending disparities are unfair, yet governments should not fund costly campaigns. That pushed the reasoning toward a rule that reduces inequality in campaign visibility without requiring public subsidy.

The successful step was treating the conclusion as a policy compromise implied by the premises, not as an extreme extension of any single premise. For similar problems, I should explicitly list each premise-imposed constraint and choose the answer that satisfies all of them with the least additional assumption.
reflections.complex:

item.context: Recently, a health hospital conducted a six-week weight-loss test. Participants lost an average of 9 kg. Male participants lost an average of 13 kg, and female participants lost an average of 7 kg. The doctor attributed the difference in weight loss between men and women to the weight of male participants are heavy than females before the test.
item.question: Which of the following conclusions can be drawn from the above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Female participants weighed less than the male participants before the test

choices.label: B
choices.text: All participants lost weight

choices.label: C
choices.text: There are more female participants than male participants

choices.label: D
choices.text: Male participants weighed less than the female participants after losing weight

response:
Reasoning: Let male participants be \(m\) and female participants be \(f\). Using the averages: \(\frac{13m+7f}{m+f}=9\). So \(13m+7f=9m+9f\), giving \(4m=2f\), hence \(f=2m\). Therefore, there were more female participants than male participants. Other options are not guaranteed.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an algebraic weighted-average approach: I treated the overall average loss as a mixture of the male and female average losses and set up an equation linking the group sizes. The key factor was that the overall average of 9 kg lies between 13 kg and 7 kg, so the counts must balance those two subgroup averages in a precise ratio. The successful step was converting that intuition into \((13m + 7f)/(m+f)=9\), which revealed the relative number of men and women. For similar problems, translate averages of subgroups into a weighted-average equation before judging which conclusion must follow.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which statement must follow from the three averages, not which statement seems plausible from the doctor’s explanation. That distinction mattered, because the doctor’s causal claim about men being heavier beforehand is not itself enough to justify several of the choices. My strategy was to treat the overall average as a weighted average of the male and female subgroup averages, using the unknown numbers of men and women as weights. That was the right method because weighted-average problems are determined by both subgroup means and subgroup sizes.

The key relationship I used was that an overall mean of 9 lies between subgroup means of 13 and 7, so the subgroup farther above the overall mean must be smaller in size than the subgroup below it. Writing the equation made that exact: the distances from the overall mean are 4 and 2, so the counts must be in the inverse ratio 1:2. I correctly ignored the tempting but unsupported claims about everyone losing weight or post-test weights, because averages do not imply anything about every individual or final ordering. I also recognized that “men were heavier before the test” was extra narrative, not needed for the logical deduction.

What made the reasoning successful was translating words into a weighted-average equation instead of relying on intuition alone. In similar problems, I should explicitly test each option against what averages can and cannot guarantee. A transferable rule is: when an overall average and subgroup averages are given, infer subgroup proportions by balancing deviations from the total mean, and avoid drawing individual-level conclusions from group averages.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a causal-weaken approach: I identified the economist’s chain as “insurance reduces depositor monitoring, which increases bank failures,” then looked for a fact showing an alternative effect of insurance on failures. The key factor was evidence about what happened without insurance—depositors’ fear itself could trigger failures, which undercuts the claim that more depositor selectivity would make the system safer. The successful step was testing the argument at the policy comparison point: insured versus uninsured systems. For similar problems, I should check whether the proposed cause also prevents the same outcome through another mechanism, because that directly weakens a simple causal story.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a weaken-the-argument task: the goal was not to find a statement merely related to deposit insurance, but one that most directly undermined the economist’s causal claim that insurance increases bank failures by removing depositor incentives to screen banks. My strategy was to identify the argument’s mechanism and then look for an option showing either that the mechanism does not operate as claimed or that insurance could reduce failures through a stronger opposing mechanism. That was appropriate because causal weakening questions are best handled by testing the link between cause and effect rather than focusing on surface plausibility. The key evidence I used was that, in the absence of insurance, depositors’ fear itself led to frequent bank failures, which suggests depositor behavior can destabilize banks rather than simply discipline them. This directly challenges the economist’s assumption that more selective or anxious depositors would make banks safer overall. I also implicitly recognized that the argument ignored bank runs as an alternative causal pathway. I considered the relevant contrast class correctly: not just whether depositors have incentives, but whether those incentives improve system stability. One strength in my reasoning was that I evaluated the option in terms of net effect on bank failures, which is exactly what the conclusion concerns. To improve further on similar questions, I should systematically ask whether the proposed remedy may introduce a worse countervailing effect. A general rule is: when an argument claims that removing a constraint causes harm by reducing caution, a strong weakening answer often shows that restoring that caution creates panic, inefficiency, or some other destabilizing force that outweighs the alleged benefit.

item.context: The authority of the law comes from the inner support and sincere belief of the people. If a good law is not strictly enforced, it will form a broken window effect, damage the dignity of the law and shake the foundation of the law. However, when emphasizing the legal system, many people intentionally or unintentionally exclude the people and like to say that the rule of law is not governing the people, but governing officials. Indeed, when we talk about governing the country according to law, being in power according to law, and administering according to law, we are mainly aimed at those who exercise power, and we need to earnestly grasp the key minority of leading cadres. However, no matter running the country, being in power or administrating, all need the cooperation of citizens. Citizens not only need to be the result of relative obedience to the exercise of relevant powers, but also need to participate in managing state affairs, managing economic and cultural undertakings, and managing social affairs through various ways and forms according to legal regulations. On the one hand, it is necessary to emphasize that party members and cadres, especially leading cadres, should play an exemplary and leading role, on the other hand, we should adhere to the mass line of the rule of law and cultivate citizens' awareness of abiding by the law in a down-to-earth manner. It is necessary to make people truly realize and bear in mind that citizens' failure to perform their legal obligations, like administrative subjects' failure to perform their legal duties, is an infringement of public interests and the legitimate rights and interests of others; illegal or improper private acts should be punished and corrected in accordance with the law.
item.question: Which of the following options is intended to be explained in this paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Establish and improve the government's decision-making mechanism according to law on the basis of abiding by existing laws

choices.label: B
choices.text: The timeliness of law enforcement depends on citizen participation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The law is the consistency of the overall expression of the will of all the people

choices.label: D
choices.text: Illegal or improper exercise of power should be sanctioned and correcte

response:
Reasoning: The paragraph argues rule of law is not only about restraining officials; it also requires citizens’ support, participation, and law-abiding consciousness. It stresses that effective legal implementation depends on the public, not just the “key minority” of cadres. Thus B best matches the main idea.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea matching approach: I compared each option against the paragraph’s repeated emphasis rather than focusing on isolated details. The key factor was the contrast the passage draws between regulating officials and requiring citizens’ cooperation, participation, and law-abiding awareness for the legal system to function effectively. My answer was correct because I tracked the author’s central shift from “rule of law targets power holders” to “it also depends on the public.” For similar problems, first identify the passage’s contrast or correction structure, then choose the option that captures that broader relationship rather than a narrower supporting point.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task as asking for the paragraph’s central explanatory point, not just a detail mentioned in passing. That was the right framing, because the passage contrasts two incomplete views of rule of law: focusing only on officials versus recognizing the indispensable role of ordinary citizens. My strategy was to trace the paragraph’s structure—opening with the source of legal authority in public belief, then warning against excluding the people, and finally arguing that governance according to law requires citizens’ cooperation and participation. This was appropriate because the best answer had to capture the paragraph’s main argumentative thread rather than a narrower legal principle. The key evidence I used was the repeated emphasis on “cooperation of citizens,” public participation in state and social affairs, and cultivating citizens’ law-abiding awareness. I also noticed the parallelism between officials’ legal duties and citizens’ legal obligations, which reinforced that enforcement effectiveness is social, not merely top-down. A potential trap was choosing an option about sanctioning misuse of power, since that appears in the passage, but only as one side of a broader comparison. Another trap was confusing a background principle with the author’s intended emphasis. What made the reasoning successful was prioritizing the passage’s contrast-and-conclusion structure over isolated phrases. In similar problems, I should first identify who or what the author says is being wrongly excluded, because that often reveals the true thesis. A transferable rule is: when a passage rejects a common framing and then adds a neglected factor, the correct main idea usually centers on that newly emphasized factor.

item.context: Many elementary schools have recently offered computer-assisted educational programs. Students' reactions after several years have been decidedly mixed. Whereas students have found computers very useful in studying arithmetic, they have found them of little help in studying science, and of no help at all with their reading and writing skills.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the students' mixed reactions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Of the disciplines and skills mentioned, the exactness of arithmetic makes it most suitable to computer-assisted education.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Young students are more likely to maintain interest in training programs that use the newest computers and video graphics than in those that do not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students in these schools began reading and doing arithmetic before learning to use computers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many elementary school teachers are reluctant to use computer technology in their classrooms.

response:
Reasoning: The pattern is: computers help most in arithmetic, less in science, not in reading/writing. This is best explained if arithmetic’s exact, rule-based nature makes it especially suited to computer-assisted instruction, unlike the others. The other choices do not explain the difference among subjects.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a comparative explanation approach: I matched the differing student reactions across subjects to the choice that best accounted for why one subject would benefit more than others from the same tool. The key factor was the contrast between arithmetic and the less computer-suited areas, so I looked for a property that distinguished arithmetic in a way relevant to computer-assisted instruction. The successful step was focusing on an answer that explained the pattern of differences, not just a general fact about computers or schools. For similar questions, identify the exact pattern in the evidence first, then choose the option that explains that pattern across all cases rather than one that is merely plausible in isolation.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for a causal explanation of the pattern across subjects, not merely a statement about computers or schools in general. That interpretation was correct because the key phrase was “most helps to explain the students’ mixed reactions,” which requires accounting for the differences among arithmetic, science, and reading/writing. My strategy was to compare the answer choices by asking which one mapped directly onto the observed variation in usefulness. That was an appropriate strategy for an LSAT-style explain-the-discrepancy question, because the best answer should connect a relevant property of one subject area to why computer assistance would work better there than elsewhere.

The crucial evidence I used was the ranking built into the stimulus: very useful for arithmetic, little help for science, and no help for reading and writing. I focused on the idea that a more exact, rule-governed subject would fit computer-based instruction better than less exact or more language-dependent skills. I also correctly rejected choices that were too general, such as those about student interest, prior learning sequence, or teacher reluctance, because they did not explain the subject-by-subject differences. One assumption in my reasoning was that “computer-assisted education” is more effective in areas where tasks can be formalized and checked precisely; here, that assumption was directly supported rather than speculative. An alternative I still should systematically consider in similar problems is whether any wrong choice could explain the pattern indirectly, but none did so here. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the structure of the answer to the structure of the evidence. A useful general rule is: when a question asks for an explanation of mixed outcomes, prefer the choice that identifies a relevant feature varying across the cases, not one that merely affects all cases uniformly.

item.context: There is strong evidence that the cause of migraines (severe recurrent headaches) is not psychological but instead is purely physiological. Yet several studies have found that people being professionally treated for migraines rate higher on a standard psychological scale of anxiety than do people not being professionally treated for migraines.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most people who have migraines and who seek professional treatment remain in treatment until they stop having migraines, whether their doctors consider the cause to be physiological or psychological.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who have migraine headaches tend to have relatives who also have migraine headaches.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who have migraine headaches often suffer these headaches when under emotional stress.

choices.label: D
choices.text: People who rate higher on the standard psychological scale of anxiety are more likely to seek professional treatment than are people who rate lower on the scale.

response:
Reasoning: The studies compare treated migraine sufferers with people not being professionally treated. If more anxious people are simply more likely to seek professional treatment, the higher anxiety scores among treated patients do not show migraines are psychological. This explains the mismatch without contradicting a physiological cause.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a discrepancy-resolution approach: I looked for a difference between the two groups being compared that could explain the anxiety result without changing the claim that migraines are physiological. The key factor was that the studies measured people in treatment versus people not in treatment, not all migraine sufferers versus non-sufferers. The successful step was recognizing a selection effect: if more anxious people are more likely to seek treatment, the treated group will score higher on anxiety regardless of what causes migraines. For similar problems, explicitly test whether the compared groups differ because of self-selection or sampling before inferring anything about causation.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for a fact that reconciles two claims rather than supports one against the other. The apparent conflict was between a physiological account of migraines and the observation that treated migraine patients score higher on anxiety measures. My strategy was to look for a selection-effect explanation: perhaps the people in treatment are not representative of all migraine sufferers. That was an appropriate approach because the study compared those being professionally treated with those not being treated, not migraine sufferers with non-sufferers in general. The key evidence I used was the wording of the comparison group, which made it natural to ask what predicts entering treatment. I also recognized that higher anxiety among treated patients would not imply a psychological cause if anxiety instead affects help-seeking behavior.

A shortcut that helped was distinguishing correlation from causation: anxiety scores in a subgroup do not establish the origin of the underlying condition. I should still note that alternative explanations could have involved stress as a trigger or treatment duration, but those would not directly explain why the treated group differs from the untreated group. The reasoning succeeded because it targeted the exact source of the discrepancy: sampling bias in who appears in treatment. In similar problems, I should first identify whether the groups being compared differ in ways other than the variable of interest. General rule: when a conclusion treats a subgroup’s trait as evidence about a condition’s cause, test whether the subgroup was selected in a way that independently correlates with that trait.

item.context: Gerrit: While browsing in a record store I noticed that one copy of a recording I wanted had mistakenly been priced at a quarter of the list price. When I finally reached the cashier I was told that the price had been mismarked and I would have to pay the full list price. Since I had wasted an hour standing in line, the retailer was morally obligated to sell me the recording at the lower price. Saskia: I disagree. You knew that a mistake had been made, and you were simply trying to take advantage of that mistake.
item.question: Which one of the following principles, if established, would most help to justify Saskia's position?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Customers of retail stores are morally entitled to profit from any mistakes that the retailers make in marking prices.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Retailers are morally entitled to update marked prices periodically in order to reflect changes in manufacturers' suggested prices.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Retailers are morally obligated to sell an item to a customer at a mismarked price only if that customer was genuinely misled about the intended price by the mismarking.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The price displayed on an item in a retail store morally constitutes an irrevocable offer to sell the item at that price.

response:
Reasoning: Saskia says Gerrit knew the lower price was a mistake, so he wasn’t genuinely misled. A principle saying retailers must honor a mismarked price only when the customer was actually misled directly supports her objection. A and D support Gerrit; B is irrelevant.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a principle-matching approach: I identified Saskia’s core objection and looked for the answer choice that turned that objection into a general rule. The key factor was Gerrit’s awareness that the price was a mistake, because Saskia’s argument depends on the idea that he was not actually misled and was instead exploiting an error. My success came from separating choices that support the retailer’s obligation only conditionally from choices that broadly favor customers or treat posted prices as automatically binding. For similar problems, first restate the speaker’s exact reasoning as an if-then principle, then choose the option that most directly supplies that condition.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking for a general principle that would justify Saskia’s moral objection, not Gerrit’s complaint. The key task was to bridge Saskia’s claim—Gerrit knew the price was a mistake and was exploiting it—to a rule about when a retailer is or is not morally required to honor a mismarked price. My strategy was appropriate for a principle-strengthen question: identify the conclusion, isolate the factual premise emphasized by the speaker, and look for an answer choice that converts that premise into a normative rule. I focused on the crucial fact that Gerrit was aware of the error, which means he was not deceived or relying in good faith on the marked price. That made the relevant distinction whether moral obligation depends on the customer being genuinely misled. I also used elimination well: one option supported customers exploiting mistakes, another supported irrevocable offers, and another concerned routine price updates rather than mistaken pricing. An assumption in my reasoning was that Saskia’s objection is about fairness and reliance rather than legal contract formation, which fit the wording “morally obligated.” I should still note that in similar questions, tempting answers often echo retail policy or legal doctrine without addressing the exact moral condition in dispute. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the answer’s conditional structure to Saskia’s explicit rationale. A transferable rule is: when evaluating principle questions, choose the option that turns the argument’s decisive fact into a necessary or sufficient condition for the stated judgment.

item.context: China's grain problem still depends on itself, which is determined by China's national conditions as a country with a large population. Grain price is the objective result of the process of market creation. Instead of racking our brains on price intervention, we should take a long-term view, earnestly make great efforts in agricultural infrastructure and agricultural technological progress, cherish every inch of land, and make good use of every factor input to maintain the steady growth of grain output and the appropriate level of grain self-sufficiency. On this basis, it is possible to have the courage to regardless of the wind and waves, it is better to take a stroll.
item.question: Which of the following options is represented by the underlined this basis in the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Introduce foreign advanced agricultural technology to change the structure of agricultural production

choices.label: B
choices.text: Raise the selling price of grain and mobilize farmers' enthusiasm for growing grain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Improve agricultural production factors to ensure adequate and appropriate food production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intensify macro-control to prevent the grain market from falling into a blind misunderstanding

response:
Reasoning: “On this basis” refers to the immediately previous measures: strengthening agricultural infrastructure and technology, protecting land, using production factors well, and maintaining stable grain output and proper self-sufficiency. This matches improving agricultural production factors to ensure adequate and appropriate food production.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a referential reading approach: I traced the phrase “on this basis” back to the concrete measures named just before it and looked for the option that summarized those measures. The key factor was the cluster of ideas about infrastructure, technology, land protection, factor input, stable output, and appropriate self-sufficiency, which together point to improving production conditions rather than price or macro-market intervention. My success came from matching the pronoun-like phrase to its nearest substantive antecedent in the passage instead of choosing an option based on a broader policy theme. For similar problems, first identify exactly which prior sentence or clause a phrase like “this basis” refers to, then select the option that best paraphrases that specific content.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking what concrete content the phrase “on this basis” referred back to in the passage, so the key task was identifying the antecedent of a discourse marker rather than evaluating policy merits. That interpretation was correct, because the phrase clearly pointed to the cluster of measures named immediately before it. My strategy was to trace the referential chain in the paragraph: first reject price intervention as the focus, then collect the positive actions the author endorsed, and finally match those actions to the choice that summarized them. This was an appropriate strategy because the question tested cohesion and paraphrase recognition, not outside knowledge about agriculture or economics. The evidence I used was the explicit list: agricultural infrastructure, technological progress, land protection, factor input, stable output, and self-sufficiency. I also noticed the contrast structure “instead of… we should…,” which helped rule out choices centered on price manipulation or macro-control. One useful assumption was that “this basis” would summarize the immediately preceding program, not the broader opening claim about national conditions. I should still remember that summary options may compress several ideas, so I must compare all components, not just one phrase like “technology.” The reasoning succeeded because I followed local textual reference and authorial contrast rather than being distracted by plausible policy language. In similar problems, I should first identify discourse signals such as “this,” “therefore,” and “instead,” then map each answer to the exact span of text it paraphrases. General rule: when a question asks what a pronoun or summarizing phrase refers to, anchor it to the nearest coherent proposition set that the author affirms, especially after contrast markers.

item.context: In the United States, all academicians of X Research Institute are opposed to human consumption of genetically modified food, while all the leaders of Y company, which specializes in producing genetically modified corn, believe that genetically modified food is safe and advocate people to eat it at ease. Some university professors also serve as the leaders of Y company.
item.question: Assuming that the above statement is true, which of the followings must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some university professors are academicians of the American X Research Institute

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some academicians support human consumption of genetically modified food

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some university professors support people to eat genetically modified food

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some university professors do not support people eating genetically modified food

response:
Reasoning: All leaders of Y support people eating genetically modified food. Since some university professors are also leaders of Y, those professors support eating genetically modified food. Nothing links university professors to X, so A and D need not be true. B contradicts X’s stance and is unsupported.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a direct set-relationship approach: translate each group claim into subset statements, then trace what must follow for the overlapping group. The key factor was the existential overlap: some university professors are leaders of Y, and all Y leaders advocate eating genetically modified food, so that overlap guarantees at least some professors hold that view. The successful step was separating universal claims from existential ones and only concluding what is forced by their combination. For similar problems, map each statement as “all A are B” or “some C are A,” then chain only those links that preserve necessity and avoid inventing connections between unrelated groups.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as a “must be true” inference problem built from set relationships and quantified statements, and that interpretation was correct. My strategy was to translate each sentence into category links: one group uniformly opposes consumption, another group uniformly supports and advocates it, and there is a stated overlap between university professors and the second group. That was the appropriate method because “must be true” questions are best handled by tracking what is guaranteed by universal claims plus existence claims. The key evidence I used correctly was the combination of “all leaders of Y support eating genetically modified food” with “some university professors are leaders of Y,” which yields an existential conclusion about at least one professor’s stance. I also correctly noticed that there was no stated overlap between university professors and the research institute, so any claim connecting those groups was unsupported. Another useful part of the reasoning was recognizing that a universal claim about all academicians of one institute does not imply anything about all academicians everywhere. I avoided a common assumption trap: treating “some professors are leaders of Y” as if it implied anything about professors outside that overlap. The successful part of the reasoning was distinguishing guaranteed overlap from merely possible overlap. In similar problems, I should continue converting statements into explicit set-inclusion and intersection forms before evaluating choices. A transferable rule is: when a problem combines “all A are B” with “some C are A,” the valid conclusion is “some C are B,” but no stronger or cross-category claim follows without an explicit link.

item.context: A warehouse has six warehouses and is arranged in order from 1 to 6. There are six kinds of goods, namely F, G, L, M, P and T. Each warehouse stores exactly one of the six kinds of goods, and different kinds of goods cannot be stored in the same warehouse. The following conditions need to be met when storing goods: (1) the warehouse number for storing goods G is larger than that for storing L. (2) the warehouse number for storing goods L is larger than that for storing T.
