item.context: Insurers and doctors are well aware that the incidence of lower-back injuries among office workers who spend long hours sitting is higher than that among people who regularly do physical work of a type known to place heavy stresses on the lower back. This shows that office equipment and furniture are not properly designed to promote workers' health.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consistent physical exercise is one of the most effective ways to prevent or recover from lower-back injuries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most of the lower-back injuries that office workers suffer occur while they are on the job.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When they are at home, laborers and office workers tend to spend similar amounts of time sitting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insurance companies tend to dislike selling policies to companies whose workers often claim to have back pain.

response:
Reasoning: The argument assumes office furniture design causes the higher injury rate. A provides a strong alternative explanation: physical workers may be protected because regular physical activity helps prevent lower-back injuries, so the comparison does not show furniture is the problem.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a weaken-the-argument approach by identifying the conclusion, then looking for an answer that offered an alternative cause for the difference in injury rates. The key factor was that the argument moved from a correlation between job type and injury incidence to a claim specifically about office furniture design, so any explanation that broke that causal link would undermine it. My success came from noticing that one choice explained why physically demanding workers might have fewer injuries without implying office furniture is defective. For similar problems, explicitly test whether the evidence rules out competing explanations before accepting a causal conclusion.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a weaken-the-argument task: the issue was not which statement was true in isolation, but which one most damaged the inference from a statistical comparison to a design conclusion. My strategy was to identify the argument’s causal leap. The premise compared injury rates between sedentary office workers and people doing physically demanding labor, and the conclusion blamed office equipment and furniture. I focused on whether there was an alternative explanation for the difference in injury rates, which is the right strategy for weakening causal reasoning based on comparative data.

The key fact I used was that regular physical activity could itself reduce lower-back injuries, making the lower injury rate among laborers compatible with a protective effect of exercise rather than a harmful effect of furniture. That directly attacked the comparison the argument relied on. I also implicitly recognized a missing control: the two groups differed in more than office furniture exposure. My successful shortcut was to ask, “What else systematically differs between these groups that could explain the outcome?” That was appropriate here because the conclusion singled out one cause without ruling out competitors.

I should also note why the other options were weaker: some merely described where injuries happen or offered irrelevant insurer preferences rather than challenging the causal inference. The general rule is: when an argument infers a cause from a difference between groups, look for an answer that identifies a confounding variable that could produce the same difference.

item.context: Differentiated competition: refers to the operation mode in which multiple enterprises in the same industry adopt flexible and changeable personalized means to establish a good corporate image and win the market in a short period of fierce competition.
item.question: Which of the following is Differentiated competition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the Spring Festival, several online short video platforms launched campaigns to grab red envelopes, with 500 million yuan for one and 800 million yuan for another. The competition has become white-hot

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the case of other real estate developers have reduced prices to promote sales, a real estate to improve the quality of real estate, the introduction of famous university resources, sales far ahead of other real estate at the same time

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every year and festivals, several large electrical shopping malls in the city will launch a gift of small household appliances, extended warranty period and other preferential activities, citizens often wait until then to focus on purchasing

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the general depression of physical bookstores in the environment, located in the bustling block of a bookstore has maintained its market positioning, committed to selling high-quality professional books, for the local cultural landmark

response:
Reasoning: Differentiated competition means using personalized, non-price methods to stand out from rivals and quickly win market share. B fits: while others cut prices, the developer improves quality and adds education resources, creating differentiation. A and C are mainly promotional price wars; D is long-term positioning, not short-term fierce competition.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I broke the concept into its key elements—same industry, personalized/flexible means, building image, and winning in a short period under fierce competition—and checked each option against those criteria. The decisive factor was distinguishing true differentiation from simple price or promotion battles; only one option relied on improving product quality and adding distinctive resources instead of just discounting. A helpful reasoning step was noticing that another option described long-term niche positioning rather than short-term competitive tactics. For similar problems, explicitly convert the definition into a checklist and eliminate choices that match only part of it, especially when they substitute promotion, price cuts, or long-term strategy for differentiation.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for an example of competition through differentiation rather than through uniform price-cutting or routine promotion, and that interpretation was correct. The definition had three key elements: multiple firms in the same industry, flexible or personalized means, and the goal of building a favorable image and winning in intense competition. My strategy was to map each option against those elements and eliminate choices that relied mainly on price incentives or did not show competitive differentiation. That was appropriate because this is a definition-matching problem, so the best method is feature comparison rather than intuition about which business tactic seems “smart.”

The most important evidence I used was the contrast between price competition and non-price differentiation. In the selected option, one firm responded to rivals’ price cuts by improving product quality and adding distinctive educational resources, which clearly created a unique offering and stronger brand image. I also correctly recognized that options centered on red-envelope giveaways, gifts, and similar promotions are closer to sales promotions or price wars than differentiated competition. For the bookstore option, I noticed it reflected stable long-term niche positioning, but it lacked the short-term, head-to-head competitive context emphasized in the definition.

A shortcut that helped was treating “personalized means” as requiring substantive uniqueness, not just larger promotional spending. A possibility I still needed to consider carefully was whether long-term specialization could count as differentiation; the tie-breaker was the definition’s emphasis on fierce short-period competition. The reasoning succeeded because I anchored on all parts of the definition rather than only one attractive phrase like “good corporate image.” A transferable rule is: when matching a scenario to a business concept, identify the concept’s necessary conditions and reject options that satisfy only a general business-success theme without matching the defining mechanism.

item.context: The survey results released by a scientific research institution show that while the book reading rate continues to decline, the online reading rate has increased year by year, from 3.7% in 1999 to 47.8% in 2008. In the face of the irresistible information technology revolution, it is not easy for traditional libraries to maintain their position or even expand.
item.question: According to this passage, which of the following options is incorrect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Traditional libraries need to come in with the times to attract readers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People don't like reading more and more.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The information technology revolution is changing people's reading behavior and reading style.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The revolution of information technology has brought some pressure to the traditional library.

response:
Reasoning: The passage shows a shift from traditional/book reading to online reading, not a general dislike of reading. A, C, and D are supported by the trend and its impact on libraries. So the incorrect option is B.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a support-versus-overreach approach: I matched each option against what the passage directly stated or reasonably implied. The key clue was the contrast between declining book reading and rising online reading, which shows a change in medium rather than a decline in reading itself. My success came from separating “less traditional reading” from “less reading overall,” avoiding a common scope shift. For similar problems, explicitly test whether an option changes the category being discussed—for example, from one form of behavior to the whole behavior—and reject choices that generalize beyond the evidence.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task correctly as a “find the unsupported statement” question, not a “find the true statement” question, which is important because the passage mixed direct facts with implications. My strategy was to separate what the passage explicitly said from what each option inferred, then test whether each inference was warranted. That was appropriate here because the key contrast in the passage is not between reading and not reading, but between traditional book reading and online reading. The most important evidence was the numerical rise in online reading alongside the decline in book reading, which shows a shift in medium rather than a collapse of reading itself. I also used the final sentence about traditional libraries struggling under the information technology revolution to support the options about pressure on libraries and the need to adapt. A crucial assumption I avoided was equating “book reading declines” with “people increasingly dislike reading,” which would have ignored the compensating rise in online reading. Another possibility I correctly considered was that some options were paraphrases rather than direct quotations, so they could still be valid if they matched the passage’s logic. The reasoning succeeded because I tracked the exact variable being measured: reading format, not reading motivation overall. In similar problems, I should explicitly identify whether the data show substitution, reduction, or growth before judging broader claims. A general rule is: when evidence shows movement from one category to another, do not infer an overall decline in the larger activity unless total participation is actually addressed.

item.context: There are three achievements in life: knowledge, achievement and morality. In terms of achievements, the most successful person in history was Emperor Taixiang Gao of all the dynasties. Liu Bang succeeded because Xiang Yu was bad. If Xiang Yu were better, he would never have succeeded. Learning is a personal matter, success is related to others, morality can become great philosophers, not because there are no great philosophers in Germany. It was British connivance and French negligence that allowed Hitler to run amok. In history, some people really deserve to be called heroes, but they failed in the face of someone better than them. Some people were bad at first, but they succeeded in the face of someone worse. As the saying goes, The Times have no heroes, make nobody become a hero
item.question: Which of the following is the main point of text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first emperors of all dynasties were successful people

choices.label: B
choices.text: Success depends on fate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kant was more successful than Hitler

choices.label: D
choices.text: Achievement in learning depends largely on individual effort

response:
Reasoning: The passage argues that worldly success/achievement is heavily shaped by external conditions and rivals—people may win because opponents are worse, or fail because opponents are better. This matches the idea that success depends more on circumstance/fate than purely on personal merit.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea synthesis approach: I looked for the repeated contrast across the examples rather than focusing on any single historical reference. The key factor was the passage’s claim that success is shaped by external circumstances—especially the quality of opponents and the broader times—rather than solely by personal ability or virtue. What helped was recognizing that the closing proverb restated the author’s thesis in general form, which is often where the main point appears. For similar problems, trace the repeated causal pattern across all examples and choose the option that captures that shared principle most broadly.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the passage as contrasting three domains—learning, achievement, and morality—and then focusing mainly on why worldly achievement does not track personal merit as closely as the other two. That interpretation was appropriate because most of the examples centered on military and political success being contingent on opponents, timing, and surrounding conditions rather than intrinsic excellence. My strategy was to look for the recurring causal pattern across the examples instead of getting distracted by the historical names. That was effective because the passage repeatedly says people can succeed against weaker rivals and fail against stronger ones, which points to external circumstance as the governing idea.

The key evidence I used was the comparison between personal study being “one’s own matter” and success being “related to others,” plus the proverb about an age without heroes elevating ordinary people. I correctly treated those as general claims, not isolated anecdotes. A shortcut that helped was rejecting options that captured only a detail, such as one historical figure or one subtopic like study. I also implicitly assumed the author’s target was the broad thesis behind the examples rather than the examples themselves, and here that assumption was justified. The main alternative I needed to consider was whether the passage was really about comparative morality or scholarship, but the text used those mostly as contrasts. The success of the reasoning came from tracking the author’s abstraction level. General rule: when a passage gives multiple anecdotes, infer the principle that explains all of them, and choose the option at that same level of generality.

item.context: Lao Zhang, Lao Zhang's sister, Lao Zhang's son and Lao Zhang's daughter have a table tennis match. After the competition, it was found that the age of the first place was the same as that of the fourth place, but the sex of the first twin (one of the above four) was different from that of the fourth place.
item.question: Based on the above information, which of the following is No. 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lao Zhang.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lao Zhang's daughter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lao Zhang's sister.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lao Zhang's son.

response:
Reasoning: First and fourth are the same age but different sexes, so they must be the son and daughter (the only plausible opposite-sex same-age pair). Thus No. 1 is one of the twins; among the options, the intended choice is Lao Zhang’s son.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a pattern-matching approach: I looked for the only obvious opposite-sex same-age pair and assumed the tied ages had to be the children. The key clue was the combination of “same age” and “different sex,” which strongly suggests twins, but I treated that as enough to identify the winner. My mistake was stopping too early: from that clue, I could infer the first and fourth places were the twin pair, but not which twin was first. In similar problems, I should separate what the clues determine exactly from what remains undetermined, and avoid choosing between symmetric options unless an extra constraint breaks the symmetry.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the key condition correctly at a surface level: first and fourth had the same age but different sexes, so they had to be the twin pair among the four people. That part of the strategy was appropriate, because no other pair in the set is naturally licensed to share an age. The failure came after that deduction, when I stopped too early and treated “first place is one of the twins” as enough to select an option. I did not examine whether the wording imposed any directional clue about which twin could be first rather than merely identifying the first–fourth pair. In effect, I jumped from a valid set-level conclusion to an unjustified individual-level conclusion.

The main shortcut I took was assuming the male twin was the intended answer because the pair “son and daughter” had been identified, without testing symmetry between them. I also ignored that if the evidence leaves two twins equally possible, then my reasoning has not yet distinguished the answer choices. A better approach would be to check whether the language, translation, or familial role descriptions introduce asymmetries I had overlooked, instead of forcing a choice from partial information. I should also explicitly ask: “Does this evidence determine a unique person, or only a subset?” The specific cause of error was overcommitting after an incomplete deduction. General rule: when a condition identifies a class of candidates but not a single candidate, do not infer uniqueness unless an additional constraint breaks the symmetry.

item.context: In recent years, falling objects occur frequently, which is widely concerned by the society. It is undeniable that the legal provisions avoid the difficulty of claim after falling objects and ensure that the legitimate rights and interests of the infringed are effectively protected. However, the provisions of tort liability law obviously lag, that is to say, only after the infringement occurs, the law will intervene. Then, when the tort occurs, the tragedy of injury or death has occurred, and it is impossible to achieve the effect of mending after the sheep has been lost. Therefore, how to strengthen the pre-function of the law and make the law a safety net for falling objects is the key to solve the problem.
item.question: Which of the following has nothing to do with the gist of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Strengthen the legislative source design to effectively avoid falling objects from height

choices.label: B
choices.text: The regulations on legal liability for infringement of objects falling from height are not perfect

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is an obvious lag in the law on falling objects

choices.label: D
choices.text: Build a solid safety net and let the law become Zhuge in advance

response:
Reasoning: The passage focuses on the law’s lagging, post-event intervention and argues for stronger preventive legal design. A, C, and D match this theme. B talks generally about imperfect liability regulations, which is not the main point.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea matching approach: I compared each option to the passage’s central contrast between after-the-fact liability and preventive legal design. The key clue was the author’s emphasis that current law intervenes only after harm occurs, so the real focus is on strengthening the law’s prior, preventive function. My success came from separating a broad criticism of “imperfect liability rules” from the more specific argument about legal lag and prevention. For similar questions, first identify the passage’s precise thesis and preferred solution, then eliminate choices that are merely related background complaints but not the author’s core point.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the option least related to the passage’s central idea, not the option that was simply false or unsupported in isolation. That distinction mattered because the passage did mention existing legal provisions, but only as background before shifting to its main concern: the law acts too late and should function preventively. My strategy was to identify the passage’s thesis by tracking the contrast structure: first, current law helps with claims after harm; then, this is inadequate because intervention occurs only after tragedy; therefore, the key is strengthening the law’s preemptive role. That was an appropriate strategy because “gist” questions are usually resolved by following the author’s argumentative pivot and conclusion. I used the facts that the passage explicitly emphasizes legal lag, post-infringement intervention, and the need for a preventive “safety net,” which aligned with choices about prevention and advance protection. I also noticed that one option reframed the issue as “not perfect” liability rules, which is broader and less precise than the passage’s complaint of temporal lag. A possible trap was to equate “lagging” with “imperfect,” but that would blur a specific criticism into a generic one. I should also have considered whether any option merely paraphrased rhetoric rather than substance, but here those preventive options still matched the core conclusion. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the author’s main claim rather than every statement mentioned. In similar problems, I should distinguish between background concessions and the actual argumentative endpoint. A transferable rule is: when asked for the option unrelated to the gist, identify the passage’s conclusion and preferred remedy, then eliminate choices that only restate a weaker, more general, or merely introductory point.

item.context: Health officials now recommend that people reduce their intake of foods that are high in cholesterol, such as red meat. The recent decline in the total consumption of beef indicates that many people are following this recommendation. But restaurants specializing in steak are flourishing despite an overall decline in the restaurant industry. So clearly there still are a lot of people completely ignoring the health recommendation.
item.question: The argument is vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It presupposes that the popularity of restaurants that specialize in steaks is a result of a decrease in the price of beef.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It assumes without warrant that people who eat steak at steak restaurants do not need to reduce their intake of foods that are high in cholesterol.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It neglects to consider whether restaurants that specialize in steak try to attract customers by offering steak dinners at low prices.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It fails to consider whether the people who patronize steak restaurants have heeded the health officials by reducing their cholesterol intake in their at-home diets.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion says flourishing steak restaurants show many people are completely ignoring the recommendation. But that overlooks the possibility that these people may eat less cholesterol-rich food at home and only occasionally eat steak out. So restaurant success does not prove complete noncompliance.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-analysis approach: I identified the conclusion (“many people are completely ignoring the recommendation”) and tested whether the evidence really established that strong claim. The key factor was the gap between eating at steak restaurants and completely failing to reduce cholesterol intake overall, since people could still cut back in other parts of their diet. My success came from noticing the argument overgeneralized from one behavior to a total pattern of behavior. For similar problems, I should compare the strength of the conclusion to the scope of the evidence and look for plausible alternative ways both could be true.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the specific flaw in the argument’s move from one observation to a stronger conclusion. The key distinction was between evidence that some people still eat steak and the conclusion that many people are completely ignoring the recommendation. My strategy was to test whether the evidence could be true even if the conclusion were false, which is appropriate for flaw questions. I focused on the gap between “steak restaurants are flourishing” and “their customers have not reduced cholesterol intake overall.” That was the decisive relationship, because the recommendation concerns reducing intake, not eliminating all consumption of steak or red meat.

The reasoning succeeded because it used a counterpossibility directly tied to the recommendation: people could cut back at home yet still occasionally dine at steak restaurants. This undermines the claim of complete noncompliance without denying the restaurant trend. I did not get distracted by causal side issues such as beef prices or restaurant marketing, because those do not address the argument’s central inferential leap. I also avoided assuming that restaurant patrons are a separate group from health-conscious consumers. The important constraint was the word “completely,” which made the conclusion stronger than the evidence supported. In similar problems, I should identify whether the conclusion is about total behavior while the evidence concerns only one context or subset of behavior. General rule: when an argument infers overall noncompliance from behavior in a limited setting, test whether compliance could still exist in other settings.

item.context: Although the technology of self-driving is updated so fast that the public is dizzying. But so far, no company has launched a complete and mature product and most companies are still stuck in self-driving testing. For a new technology, the closer the test is to the real environment, the more accurate the results will be. However, cars are different from other products, once an accident occurs, it will endanger public safety. As a result, driverless towns were born based on this demand. At present, Shanghai, Zhejiang, Beijing and other places are scrambling to build self-driving towns and the enthusiasm of local governments has greatly promoted the further research of self-driving. Technology is important, but it is clearly not the only decisive link in the future self-driving field.
item.question: Which of the following options is intended to describe the self-driving industry?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Technology is not the only determinant of its development.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It faces many unresolved technical barriers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is favored by more and more local governments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no way for it to leave the intervention and support of the government.

response:
Reasoning: The passage’s main point is that while self-driving technology matters, real-world testing requires government-supported driverless towns, showing development depends on more than technology alone. B and C are partial details; D is too absolute.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea summarization approach, focusing on the author’s concluding sentence that technology is not the only decisive factor. The key clue I underweighted was the passage’s stronger causal chain: because real-road testing is risky, dedicated testing towns emerged, and local governments are actively building them, which makes government involvement central rather than incidental. My mistake was choosing the broader, less committal summary instead of the option that captured the passage’s concrete dependence relationship. For similar questions, I should prefer the choice that reflects the passage’s specific mechanism or dependency, not just its most general concluding remark.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question too much as asking for the passage’s broad thesis, and I selected the sentence that looked like a direct paraphrase of the concluding line. That strategy is often useful in main-idea questions, but here I failed to distinguish between a general summary statement and the option “intended to describe the industry” more specifically. I focused on the explicit sentence that technology is “not the only decisive link,” and treated it as the author’s final claim, without asking what the non-technical factor actually was in the passage. The key evidence I underused was the repeated emphasis on driverless towns, local governments “scrambling to build” them, and the statement that this enthusiasm has “greatly promoted” further research. Those details point to a dependence relationship, not just a vague claim that multiple factors matter. I also dismissed the government-related option as “too absolute” without testing whether the passage’s structure was building toward precisely that stronger implication. A better alternative analysis would compare which option best captures the passage’s concrete causal chain: safety risks → need for special testing environments → government-built towns → industry progress. My error came from matching surface wording rather than tracing the argument’s logic. In similar problems, I should identify the passage’s central mechanism, not just its concluding phrase. A transferable rule is: when one option restates a general sentence and another captures the author’s developed causal dependency, prefer the option supported by the full argument structure.

item.context: England has a large area of wetlands rich in natural gas. Environmentalists have long opposed the exploitation of natural gas in wetlands, arguing that it would upset the ecological balance of England's wetlands, with a direct and serious consequence of polluting water sources. However, this worry is untenable. According to the relevant statistics in the past 50 years, it has never been reported that the water source has been polluted by the exploitation of natural gas.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, would best strengthen the above argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The wetlands in England have been exploiting natural gas for more than 100 years and have never caused water pollution

choices.label: B
choices.text: England has sufficient capacity to control any pollution caused by the exploitation of natural gas

choices.label: C
choices.text: In England, there is no substantial difference between wetlands that exploit natural gas and wetlands that do not exploit natural gas

choices.label: D
choices.text: In England, there is no real difference between wetlands where natural gas is exploited and before it is exploited

response:
Reasoning: The argument claims natural gas exploitation in England’s wetlands does not pollute water, based on no reported cases in 50 years. A most directly strengthens this by extending the same evidence over an even longer period and confirming no water pollution occurred.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a direct-evidence approach, looking for the choice that most strongly reinforced the claim that gas exploitation does not harm wetlands or pollute water. The key factor I focused on was the argument’s reliance on historical nonreporting of water pollution, which led me to prefer an option that extended that same pattern over a longer time. My mistake was treating “more of the same evidence” as strongest, instead of asking which option most directly addressed the environmentalists’ core causal concern about ecological change from exploitation. For similar problems, I should match the support to the argument’s exact disputed link and prefer evidence that rules out the alleged harmful effect, not just evidence that repeats past observations.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question too narrowly as asking for the choice that most supports the claim “natural gas exploitation has not polluted water,” when the argument actually tries to dismiss a broader environmentalist concern about upsetting the ecological balance and thereby causing water pollution. My strategy was to favor the option that most directly reinforced the cited historical evidence, so I chose the answer that simply extended the “no pollution reported” timeline. That was a plausible strengthening move, but it mostly duplicated the argument’s existing evidence instead of addressing its vulnerability. The key missing relationship was that the objection was not only about reported pollution incidents; it was about whether exploitation changes the wetlands in a way that could plausibly lead to pollution. I overlooked that a stronger support would connect exploitation to no meaningful environmental change in the wetlands themselves. I also assumed that “more years without reports” is automatically stronger, but repeated absence-of-report evidence is often weaker than evidence about unchanged conditions or mechanisms. I should have compared the answer choices by asking which one most directly blocks the environmentalists’ causal story, not which one merely adds more of the same kind of observation. I also underweighted choices about similarity or no difference, even though those directly bear on whether ecological balance is disrupted. The specific error was relying on evidential quantity instead of causal relevance. A transferable rule is: when an argument rejects a predicted harmful effect, the strongest support usually attacks the causal pathway behind the prediction, rather than merely extending past non-occurrence data.

item.context: A car manufacturer launched two models, which are the standard model and the luxury model. The safety performance of the luxury model was much better than that of the standard model. After the two models were launched at the same time, the sales volume of the luxury model has not exceeded the standard model. Therefore, the manufacturer believed that the safe performance was not the primary factor that customers focused on.
item.question: If the following options are right, which one can best weaken the manufacturer's view?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most customers have higher confidence in the standard model.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The price of the luxury model is not much different from that of the standard model.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most customers believe that the safety performance of the standard model is sufficient to meet the needs of daily life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of the buyers of the standard model are collective customers, so the sales volume of it has always been high.

response:
Reasoning: The manufacturer infers from lower luxury sales that safety isn’t primary. But if standard-model sales are inflated because many are bulk/collective purchases, sales volume doesn’t reflect ordinary customers’ true priorities. This directly weakens the conclusion drawn from sales comparison.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a causal-weaken approach, looking for an alternative explanation for why the better-performing model did not outsell the standard model. The key clue I focused on was the sales-volume comparison, so I chose an option that explained those sales through bulk purchasing rather than customer preferences. The mistake was targeting a side factor that distorts sales totals without addressing the core link between safety performance and customer choice; the stronger weakening point is whether customers see the standard model’s safety as already good enough. In similar problems, I should test whether an option directly challenges the argument’s assumed decision criterion, not just the observed outcome.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking which option most undermines the manufacturer’s inference from sales data to customer priorities, and that general interpretation was correct. My strategy was to attack the link between sales volume and true consumer preference by looking for a confounding factor that made the comparison between the two models misleading. That is why I chose the option about collective buyers inflating standard-model sales. This was a plausible weakening move, but it was not the strongest one because it focused on who bought the cars rather than on whether safety could still matter to customers. I missed the more direct point that customers may care about safety a great deal while still not choosing the safer model if the standard model already clears their safety threshold. That fact undermines the manufacturer’s reasoning more precisely, because it shows the evidence is compatible with safety being important, just not in a “more is always better” way. My error came from assuming that any distortion in sales counts was the best rebuttal, instead of asking what assumption the conclusion truly required. The key hidden assumption was: if safety were a primary concern, customers would prefer the model with better safety performance. I should have tested that assumption directly and looked for an option showing diminishing returns or sufficiency. In similar problems, I should distinguish between rebutting the evidence and attacking the specific causal or inferential bridge. General rule: when a claim infers “X is not important because people did not choose the option with more X,” first ask whether decision-makers may value X only up to an adequate threshold.

item.context: When a caterpillar emerges from the egg on a tree branch, it immediately climbs upward until it finds a leaf bud to eat. Biologists thought that this behavior displayed an innate tendency to move in the direction opposite to the pull of gravity. In a recent experiment, a strong light source was placed at the bottom of a tree, and caterpillars, after hatching, climbed downward.
item.question: Which of the following hypotheses is best supported by the statements given?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Newly hatched caterpillars move toward the leaf bud nearest to them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Caterpillars have an innate tendency to move in the direction of gravity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Newly hatched caterpillars move towards the strongest light source in the environment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Newly hatched caterpillars are unable to see in the dark.

response:
Reasoning: Caterpillars normally climb upward, but when a strong light was placed below, they climbed downward instead. This shows their movement is better explained by attraction to light rather than by an innate tendency to move opposite gravity. The experiment directly supports movement toward the strongest light source.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a compare-the-hypotheses approach, checking which choice best explained both the normal upward movement and the reversal under altered conditions. The key factor was that changing the light location changed the caterpillars’ direction, which isolates light as the likely driver rather than gravity. The successful step was treating the experiment as evidence against the original gravity explanation and in favor of the variable that was manipulated. For similar problems, identify the experimental change first and prefer the hypothesis that directly predicts the observed behavioral shift when that variable is altered.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which hypothesis is most strongly supported by the experimental result, not which statement merely sounds plausible. My strategy was to compare the original explanation for the caterpillars’ upward movement with the new evidence from the light manipulation and ask which hypothesis best accounts for both observations. That was appropriate because the experiment was designed to distinguish between two possible directional cues: gravity and light. The key evidence I used was that the caterpillars reversed direction when a strong light source was placed below them, which undermines the idea that they rigidly move opposite gravity. I also used the fact that the behavior changed systematically with the environment, which is exactly what would be expected if an external cue rather than a fixed gravitational program were guiding movement.  

I avoided being distracted by unsupported alternatives such as movement toward the nearest bud, since the experiment said nothing about bud location. I also correctly rejected the option about inability to see in the dark because the setup demonstrated responsiveness to light, not a limitation specific to darkness. A possible shortcut I used, appropriately, was treating the experiment as a test of causal control: whichever variable, when manipulated, changes behavior is likely the governing cue. The success came from focusing on what the new result disconfirmed as well as what it positively supported. For similar problems, I should explicitly ask which answer explains both the baseline behavior and the experimental reversal. A transferable rule is: when an experiment changes one cue and behavior changes accordingly, prefer the hypothesis that tracks the manipulated cue over one that predicts no change.

item.context: Different from ordinary villages, the ancient village in Huizhou has developed to a higher form in the aspects of site layout, human settlement concept, ploughing and reading culture, clan inheritance, Confucian businessman spirit and so on. It has a profound accumulation of Chinese traditional culture. Experiencing the ancient villages in Huizhou is like going through a long time and space. We can not only feel the natural scenery like ink painting, but also appreciate the survival wisdom of the ancients from the rural history and culture.
item.question: According to the context, which of the following options makes Huizhou ancient villages different from ordinary villages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Architectural aesthetics

choices.label: B
choices.text: Historical accumulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cultural form

choices.label: D
choices.text: Survival wisdom

response:
Reasoning: The passage says Huizhou ancient villages differ from ordinary villages because they developed to a higher form in layout, settlement ideas, farming-and-reading culture, clan inheritance, and Confucian merchant spirit. These are mainly features of a distinctive cultural form, not just architecture, history, or wisdom alone.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a summarizing-and-matching approach: I identified the passage’s listed distinguishing features, then looked for the option that best captured them at the highest level. The key factor was that the text emphasized multiple organized aspects—layout, settlement ideas, farming-and-reading culture, clan inheritance, and merchant spirit—which together describe an overall cultural pattern rather than a single trait. My success came from grouping the examples into one broader category instead of choosing a detail mentioned later in the passage. For similar problems, first classify the evidence into the most inclusive concept, then choose the option that covers all listed features rather than one partial example.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the broadest category that explains how Huizhou ancient villages differ from ordinary villages according to the passage, not just for a detail mentioned in the description. That interpretation was correct because the stem asked what “makes” them different, which points to an underlying defining feature rather than a single effect or example. My strategy was to compare the answer choices against the list in the passage—site layout, human settlement concept, ploughing-and-reading culture, clan inheritance, and Confucian businessman spirit—and then identify the option that best subsumed all of them. This was an appropriate abstraction strategy because the text presented multiple dimensions, so the correct choice needed to be a category broad enough to cover them together. I used the fact that these dimensions include values, social organization, ways of living, and intellectual traditions, which are better captured by a cultural characterization than by a purely physical or historical one. I also noticed that “survival wisdom” appears as something visitors can appreciate from the villages, which makes it more of an outcome of the culture than the main distinguishing category. One useful assumption I made was that the test was looking for the most inclusive paraphrase of the passage, and in this case that assumption fit the evidence. I still should have explicitly tested each distractor: architecture is too narrow, historical accumulation is background, and survival wisdom is derivative. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the scope of the option to the scope of the textual evidence. For similar problems, I should classify listed details by level—example, feature, theme, or essence—and choose the option at the same conceptual level as the question. General rule: when a passage lists several heterogeneous traits, prefer the answer that unifies them at the correct level of abstraction rather than one that repeats only one prominent detail.

item.context: Mayor: Our city faces a difficult environmental problem caused by the enormous amount of garbage that we must dispose of. Although new recycling projects could greatly reduce this amount, these projects would actually be counterproductive to the goal of minimizing the overall amount of environmental damage.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to resolve the apparent inconsistency in the mayor's claims about new recycling projects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: More recycling would give industries in the mayor's city a greater incentive to use recycled materials in their manufacturing processes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The vehicles that pick up materials for recycling create less pollution than would be caused by incinerating those materials.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The great costs of new recycling projects would prevent other pollution-reducing projects from being undertaken.

choices.label: D
choices.text: People who recycle feel less justified in consuming more than they need than do people who do not recycle.

response:
Reasoning: The inconsistency is resolved if recycling reduces garbage disposal but still increases total environmental harm indirectly. If recycling projects are so costly that they prevent more effective pollution-reducing projects, then they could be counterproductive to minimizing overall environmental damage.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a paradox-resolution approach: I looked for a choice that would make both claims true at once, namely that recycling reduces garbage yet can still worsen total environmental outcomes. The key factor was the mayor’s shift from the narrow problem of garbage disposal to the broader standard of overall environmental damage. The successful step was recognizing that an indirect tradeoff, especially one involving limited resources, can make an apparently beneficial project counterproductive overall. In similar problems, explicitly identify the two competing measures in the stimulus and prefer answers that connect them through a broader-cost or opportunity-cost mechanism.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a paradox-resolution task: the mayor says recycling would reduce garbage, yet still worsen the broader environmental objective. That means the right approach was not to challenge either claim directly, but to find a fact that makes both simultaneously true. My strategy was to look for a distinction between a local benefit and a global cost, which is exactly the kind of contrast that often resolves these LSAT-style inconsistencies. The key evidence pattern I used was that reducing garbage volume is not identical to reducing total environmental damage; those are different metrics. I focused on an indirect effect, namely that implementing recycling could consume resources that would otherwise go to measures with larger environmental benefits. That was an appropriate assumption structure because it preserves the stated benefit of recycling while explaining why it could still be counterproductive overall.

I did not need to compare every answer in equal depth once I saw an option that created a clear tradeoff between competing environmental priorities. Still, the alternatives should be screened systematically: some merely strengthen recycling as beneficial, while others address side effects that do not explain why it would undermine the overall goal. What made the reasoning successful was recognizing the phrase “overall environmental damage” as inviting a broader cost-benefit frame rather than a narrow waste-reduction frame. In similar problems, I should explicitly identify the two apparently conflicting claims and ask what hidden variable could make them compatible. A transferable rule is: when a proposal helps on one dimension but is said to hurt the overall objective, look for an indirect cost, opportunity cost, or broader metric that distinguishes the two evaluations.

item.context: Most disposable plastic containers are now labeled with a code number (from 1 to 9) indicating the type or quality of the plastic. Plastics with the lowest code numbers are the easiest for recycling plants to recycle and are thus the most likely to be recycled after use rather than dumped in landfills. Plastics labeled with the highest numbers are only rarely recycled. Consumers can make a significant long-term reduction in the amount of waste that goes unrecycled, ttherefore, by refusing to purchase those products packaged in plastic containers labeled with the highest code numbers.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Communities that collect all discarded plastic containers for potential recycling later dump in landfills plastics with higher-numbered codes only when it is clear that no recycler will take them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A plastic container almost always has a higher code number after it is recycled than it had before recycling because the recycling process causes a degradation of the quality of the plastic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cost of collecting, sorting, and recycling discarded plastics is currently higher than the cost of manufacturing new plastics from virgin materials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many consumers are unaware of the codes that are stamped on the plastic containers.

response:
Reasoning: The argument assumes avoiding high-number plastics reduces unrecycled waste. But if recycling itself turns lower-code plastics into higher-code plastics, then buying high-code containers may support use of already recycled material. Refusing them could reduce demand for recycled plastic and weaken the claimed long-term waste reduction.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-weaken approach: I identified the conclusion that refusing high-code plastics will reduce unrecycled waste, then looked for a choice showing that high-code plastics might actually play a useful role in the recycling cycle. The key factor was the long-term claim, which made it relevant that recycled plastic can become higher-code plastic after processing. That relationship supports the idea that buying some high-code containers may sustain demand for products made from recycled material, undermining the recommendation. For similar problems, test a policy conclusion by asking whether the discouraged behavior might indirectly support the very goal the argument is trying to achieve.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stimulus as a causal policy argument: if consumers avoid products in certain plastic containers, the total amount of plastic waste that remains unrecycled will decrease over time. That interpretation was correct, because the key task was not to identify a fact about recycling in general, but to find information that weakens the claimed link between consumer refusal and long-term waste reduction. My strategy was to look for a hidden assumption in that causal chain, specifically the assumption that high-code plastics are simply “bad” endpoints rather than part of a recycling process. That was appropriate because weaken questions are often best handled by identifying what the conclusion must presuppose.

The crucial fact I used was that a product with a high code number could result from prior recycling, meaning the label may reflect recycled history rather than mere recyclability. This matters because it challenges the argument’s simple equation: high code number = should be avoided. I also correctly focused on the phrase “long-term reduction,” which opens the door to effects on market demand and recycling cycles, not just immediate disposal outcomes. A shortcut that helped was asking whether the recommendation could backfire by discouraging use of recycled material.

I should still note alternatives more systematically, especially options about consumer awareness or costs, since those can seem relevant but may not attack the logic directly. The reasoning succeeded because I distinguished between facts about current recycling difficulty and facts about how consumer choices affect the recycling system over time. A transferable rule is: when an argument recommends avoiding outputs with undesirable properties, test whether those outputs may actually be byproducts or indicators of the very process the argument wants to promote.

item.context: A unit needs to send one or two people to help the poor in the countryside. After the publicity call, all the people have to sign up. After some consideration, the leadership will finally send candidates to focus on Xiao Wang, Xiao Zhang and Xiao Li, and reached the following consensus: (1) if Wang is selected, then Xiao Zhang will be selected; (2) if Xiao Li is selected, Xiao Wang will not be selected; (3) if Xiao Zhang is selected, Xiao Li will be selected; (4) it is impossible for both Xiao Wang and Xiao Li to be selected.
item.question: Which of the following can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Xiao Wang will be selected, but Xiao Li will not be selected.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Xiao Zhang will be selected, but Xiao Wang will not be selected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Xiao Li will be selected, but Xiao Zhang will not be selected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Xiao Li will be selected, but Xiao Wang will not be selected.

response:
Reasoning: From (1) and (3), if Wang is selected, then Zhang and Li are also selected. But (2)/(4) say if Li is selected, Wang cannot be selected. So Wang cannot be selected. Since they must send one or two people, Li must be selected; Zhang may or may not be selected.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a conditional-logic approach, chaining the implications together and checking them against the limit that only one or two people can be sent. The key factor was that selecting Wang forces Zhang, and Zhang forces Li, which creates a chain that clashes with the rule that Wang and Li cannot both be selected; that contradiction eliminates Wang. The successful step was reducing the problem by ruling out one candidate first, then using the “must send one or two people” constraint to determine what still had to happen. For similar problems, translate each statement into if-then form, combine the chains, and test each candidate for contradiction before considering the remaining possibilities.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for a statement that must be true under all the given selection rules, not merely one that could be true in some scenario. That interpretation was correct, so the right strategy was to translate each sentence into conditional constraints and then look for forced consequences. I used a chaining approach: one rule implied a second person, and that implication triggered another rule, which then conflicted with a separate prohibition. This was appropriate because the problem is essentially about logical dependency rather than probability or preference.

The key evidence I used was the chain from one candidate to another to a third candidate, combined with the rule that one pair cannot be selected together. That let me eliminate one candidate entirely, which is stronger than just checking answer options one by one. I also correctly used the “send one or two people” condition to infer that at least one remaining feasible person had to be chosen; without that condition, non-selection of everyone would remain possible. One subtle assumption in my reasoning was treating rule (2) and rule (4) as reinforcing the same incompatibility; that was fine, but I needed to keep clear which contradiction came from implication and which came from direct exclusion. I should also have explicitly considered whether the second candidate in the final pair was forced or optional, since some answer choices depended on that distinction. The reasoning succeeded because I derived an impossibility first, then used the minimum-selection requirement to force what remained. A general rule for similar problems is: when conditionals form a chain, test each starting assumption to see whether it leads to a contradiction with any exclusivity rule, then use any “at least one” or “exactly one/two” constraint to convert eliminations into necessities.

item.context: Gift contract is a contract in which the donor gives his property to the donee free of charge, and the donee expresses to accept the gift.
item.question: Which of the following situation is not a gift contract?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In order to encourage his nephew Wang Jun to study hard, Wang promised to give Wang Jun a computer and a camera, but the computer would be given first, and the camera would be given when the final grades were good.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At a large-scale disaster relief performance hosted by the civil affairs department, a company publicly announced a donation of 1 million yuan to the disaster relief foundation established by the civil affairs department.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A sees that B is in financial difficulties and gives 500 yuan to B. B doesn't want it. A puts the money in B's drawer while B is not there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Company A decided to donate two computers to a Hope Elementary School before the company's legal representative was replaced, then the company was unwilling to honor its promise.

response:
Reasoning: A, B, and D all involve a donation promise/offer that can form a gift contract if accepted by the donee or relevant organization. In C, B explicitly refuses the money, so there is no acceptance. Without acceptance, no gift contract is formed.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a rule-based contract analysis: check each scenario for the core elements of a gift contract, especially the donor’s intent and the donee’s acceptance. The key factor was that a gift contract is not unilateral in effect here; the donee must express or at least manifest acceptance, so an explicit refusal blocks formation. My answer was correct because I focused on the acceptance requirement rather than being distracted by whether the property was physically delivered. For similar problems, first map every option to the legal elements one by one and eliminate any case where a required element is expressly missing.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking which scenario fails to satisfy the legal elements of a gift contract, not which gift promise is revocable or enforceable. That interpretation was correct because the definition in the stem explicitly required both a gratuitous transfer intention by the donor and acceptance by the donee. My strategy was to test each option against those two elements, especially the acceptance requirement, rather than getting distracted by delivery timing, conditions, or later refusal to perform. That was appropriate because several options were designed to look problematic for other reasons, such as conditional gifting, public donation, or change of mind after a promise. The key evidence I used was that one scenario contained an express refusal by the recipient, which directly negated acceptance. I correctly treated that refusal as more important than the donor’s later unilateral act of placing the money somewhere accessible to the recipient. A shortcut that helped was focusing first on whether assent existed on both sides before analyzing enforceability issues. The main alternative possibilities I should still consciously screen in similar problems are invalidity due to lack of capacity, illegality, or failure of required formalities, if those elements are implicated. What made the reasoning successful was separating contract formation from performance and revocation. A transferable rule is: when a question gives a legal definition, evaluate each option strictly element by element, and eliminate any choice that clearly fails one required element before considering secondary complications.

item.context: In 2009, an Air France plane crashed. If France and other countries do not take active search and rescue action, the wreckage will not be found as soon as possible. The investigation report on the crash would have been more objective if the plane design company had provided technical support and sent experts to participate in the cause analysis.
item.question: If the above statement is true, which of the following can not be false?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Or France and many other countries to take active search and rescue operations, or will not find the wreckage of the plane as soon as possible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Unless the crashed aircraft design company provides technical support, the wreckage of the crashed plane will be found as soon as possible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If France and other countries take active search and rescue operations, the wreckage of the crashed plane will be found as soon as possible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The investigation report on the crash would have been more objective if the plane design company had provided technical support.

response:
Reasoning: Let F = active search/rescue, W = wreckage found ASAP. The statement gives ¬F → ¬W, which is exactly equivalent to “F or not W” (Option A).  
B and C are not implied.  
D weakens a conjunction antecedent into a single condition, so it need not follow.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used formal conditional-logic translation: I converted the statement about search and rescue into a conditional and then checked which option was logically equivalent or necessarily implied. The key factor was recognizing that “if not active search and rescue, then not found as soon as possible” has the equivalent disjunctive form “either active search and rescue, or not found as soon as possible.” My success came from applying the material implication rule correctly instead of relying on surface wording. For similar problems, always translate each statement into symbols and test answer choices using valid equivalences like \(P \to Q \equiv \neg P \lor Q\), rather than guessing from everyday language.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking which option must be true, since “cannot be false” is the same as “logically guaranteed by the premises.” My strategy was to translate the first sentence into propositional form: if no active search and rescue occurs, then the wreckage is not found as soon as possible. From there, I used a standard logical equivalence: a conditional of the form ¬F → ¬W is equivalent to F ∨ ¬W, which matched one option exactly. That was an appropriate strategy because this is a validity question, not a plausibility or commonsense question. I also correctly recognized that the second sentence about the investigation report was independent of the wreckage-search claim, so it could not support answer choices about search timing.

A key fact I used was that “if P then Q” can be rewritten as “not P or Q”; applying that carefully avoided relying on informal intuition. I also correctly rejected the tempting converse in the option that said active search would guarantee timely discovery, because the original statement did not assert sufficiency. For the option about the design company, I noticed it improperly altered the condition structure by dropping part of the antecedent or changing the topic altogether. One assumption I handled well was not treating real-world likelihood as logical necessity. In similar problems, I should continue converting each sentence into symbolic form and then test each option for equivalence, converse, inverse, or strengthening. General rule: when a question asks what “must be true,” prefer exact logical consequences of the premises and reject choices that add strength, reverse direction, or mix independent statements.

item.context: A good writer, like a famous tea, is the cohesion of the aura of years, mountains and rivers. In addition to acquired skill training, talent and growth environment are inseparable. The backbone of Chinese contemporary literary world, such as Mo Yan, Jia Pingwa, Alai, Chi Zijian and so on, clearly reflects the profound shaping of his writing by the regional environment. Most of these writers were born in remote villages, and their works are mainly local themes, and many of them take their hometown as a literary base. This reflects a phenomenon of contemporary Chinese literature, that is, works with local themes account for the vast majority. Even if most of the writing and reading groups live in the city, the intersection between them is still rural: writers who live in the city, write novels about the country, and read to readers who live in the city but have local memories.
item.question: Which of the followings is most likely to be described next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The influence of Writers' growing Environment on Literary creation

choices.label: B
choices.text: The representative works of famous local writers in the contemporary literary world

choices.label: C
choices.text: Why Contemporary Literature is keen on the creation of local themes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The changing trend of narrative theme in contemporary Chinese literature

response:
Reasoning: The passage first notes environment shapes writers, then identifies a broader phenomenon: contemporary Chinese literature is dominated by local/rural themes, even for urban writers/readers. The most likely next part would explain the cause of this phenomenon rather than list works or discuss changing trends.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a forward-structure approach: I tracked how the passage moved from examples of writers shaped by place to a broader claim about the dominance of local themes. The key clue was the final sentence, which reframed the issue as a general literary phenomenon involving both writers and readers, signaling a likely shift into explanation. What helped was distinguishing between background evidence and the main topic being set up for expansion. For similar questions, identify the passage’s final broad claim and choose the option that most naturally explains or develops that claim, rather than one that merely repeats earlier examples.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the most natural continuation of the passage, not merely the main idea of what had already been stated. That distinction mattered, because continuation questions depend on discourse flow: what claim has just been introduced, and what kind of support usually follows it. My strategy was to track the passage’s progression from individual writers shaped by regional environments to a broader literary pattern in which local themes dominate contemporary writing. That was appropriate because the final sentences clearly elevated the discussion from examples to a general phenomenon. I used the key signal phrase “This reflects a phenomenon of contemporary Chinese literature” as evidence that the author was about to explain that phenomenon in more depth. I also noticed that the passage had already given examples of writers, so a next paragraph listing representative works would likely repeat rather than advance the argument. I rejected the “changing trend” option because the passage did not discuss time-based change, only current prevalence. I also rejected the broader “influence of writers’ growing environment” option because that idea had already been used as setup and was narrower than the concluding focus. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the answer choice to the passage’s final rhetorical move rather than to its opening topic. In similar problems, I should identify the last unresolved claim and ask what kind of paragraph would most logically develop it: explanation, illustration, contrast, or consequence. A transferable rule is: in “what comes next” questions, prioritize the option that extends the passage’s most recent generalization, not the one that merely restates earlier background.

item.context: A compound sentence refers to a sentence composed of two or more single sentences that are related in meaning and do not contain each other in structure.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings is a compound sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The final result proves that you can't rely solely on ingenuity, you also need to work hard to succeed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The distant verdant mountains and the sunset are the most beautiful scenery here.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Xiao Zhang used to be a worker, and because of the guidance of a master, he was engaged in technology development.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the woods, young pioneers in twos and threes are collecting mushrooms separately.

response:
Reasoning: A contains two coordinate clauses: “you can't rely solely on ingenuity” and “you also need to work hard to succeed,” which are related in meaning. B and D are simple sentences; C has a causal phrase, not two independent clauses.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a clause-structure approach, looking for two independent propositions joined in coordination and rejecting options that seemed like simple sentences with modifiers. The key factor that misled me was treating punctuation and semantic parallelism as enough, while overlooking the formal requirement that each part be a complete single sentence and that one not merely be attached without a proper structural link. My error was accepting a run-on/comma-splice type construction as compound while dismissing a sentence that actually contains two full predications linked by coordination, even though one clause includes an internal causal adverbial. In similar problems, I should test each side explicitly: isolate the segments around the linker and verify that both can stand alone as full clauses before judging the sentence type.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task too narrowly: I treated “compound sentence” as requiring two fully independent clauses joined in a clearly coordinate way, but the definition only required two or more single sentences that are semantically related and not structurally embedded in one another. My strategy was to scan for an obvious pair of clauses separated by punctuation and then eliminate choices with modifiers or causal phrases. That strategy was only partly appropriate because it relied on surface grammar markers rather than testing each option against the exact definition. In particular, I assumed that a causal connector inside one part automatically prevented the sentence from being compound, even though the two parts could still be separate clause-level statements. I also failed to distinguish between a run-on-style juxtaposition and a standard compound structure; I accepted one option because it had two propositions, but I did not adequately consider whether it was presented as a proper compound sentence under the intended grammar standard. The key evidence I missed was that one candidate contained two clause-level assertions linked by coordination, while the causal material functioned internally within one clause rather than subordinating the whole sentence. I should also have considered whether punctuation and conjunction use affected grammatical classification, not just semantic duality. The specific cause of error was substituting my own simplified rule—“two propositions equals compound”—for the stricter textbook classification being tested. In similar problems, I should parse clause boundaries first, then determine whether any clause is embedded inside another, and only afterward judge the sentence type. A transferable rule is: classify sentence structure by syntactic relations among clauses, not merely by how many ideas the sentence expresses.

item.context: Recently, there is a view circulating on the Internet that the profiteering glasses industry has created 99% of myopia. Some netizens say that businesses can only sell glasses blindly, but their eyesight can still be restored after myopia, but they can't be taken off if they are worn, so they can try not to wear them without glasses. This triggered a rebuke from many people for being mercenary and making huge profits, which led to a discussion about the more you wear glasses, the more nearsighted you are. However, clinical studies have shown that when myopia is induced in adolescence, the degree of myopia increases with or without glasses. This is because the eyeballs of growing teenagers are also developing, so the degree of myopia is not stable. However, as long as the degree of myopia is accurately detected, glasses will not be the culprit of deepening degree.
item.question: Which of the following is the main content of this text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eyesight can still be restored after wearing myopic glasses

choices.label: B
choices.text: Wearing glasses has nothing to do with the deepening of myopia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deepening of myopia is not necessarily related to wearing glasses

choices.label: D

The most important evidence was the final conditional statement: pulsars can be used for interstellar navigation if their signals can be received and their positions are known. reflections.complex:

My strategy was to abstract the argument into a formal pattern—if P then Q; Q; therefore P—and then look for an answer choice with the same invalid reversal. item.context: All bridges built from 1950 to 1960 are in serious need of rehabilitation. Some bridges constructed in this period, however, were built according to faulty engineering design. That is the bad news. The good news is that at least some bridges in serious need of rehabilitation are not suspension bridges, since no suspension bridges are among the bridges that were built according to faulty engineering design.
item.question: If the statements above are true, then, on the basis of those statements, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some bridges that were built according to faulty engineering design are not bridges other than suspension bridges.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some bridges that were built according to faulty engineering design are in serious need of rehabilitation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some suspension bridges are in serious need of rehabilitation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some bridges built from 1950 to 1960 are not in serious need of rehabilitation.

response:
Reasoning: From “All bridges built from 1950 to 1960 need rehabilitation” and “Some bridges built in this period were built according to faulty design,” those some faulty-design bridges must also need rehabilitation. So at least some faulty-design bridges are in serious need of rehabilitation.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a direct set-logic approach, linking the universal statement about all bridges from 1950–1960 to the existential statement that some bridges from that period had faulty design. The key factor was recognizing that the “some” faulty-design bridges are a subset of the 1950–1960 bridges, so they automatically inherit the property of being in serious need of rehabilitation. The success came from combining an “all” statement with a “some” statement without getting distracted by the extra information about suspension bridges. For similar problems, first map each statement into subset/existence relationships, then test which conclusion follows by chaining only the statements that actually overlap.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a “must be true” inference problem, so the task was to identify what follows with certainty from the stated quantifiers and category relationships. My strategy was to translate the key statements into set relations: all bridges built from 1950–1960 are in serious need of rehabilitation, and some bridges built in that period were built according to faulty engineering design. That was the right approach because “all” and “some” statements can be combined directly when one group is contained within another. The crucial evidence I used was that the “some” faulty-design bridges are explicitly a subset of the 1950–1960 bridges, and the entire 1950–1960 set is contained within the rehabilitation-needed set. Therefore those same “some” bridges must also be in serious need of rehabilitation. I did not need to rely on the suspension-bridge statement to establish the correct answer, which was a sign that the inference came from the stronger, simpler premises. That was appropriate because extra premises in LSAT-style arguments often distract rather than support the necessary conclusion. One assumption I avoided was treating “some” as “all,” which would have overextended the claim. I also correctly rejected answer choices that required unsupported existential claims about suspension bridges or contradicted the universal premise. The reasoning succeeded because I tracked subset inheritance carefully across two linked premises. A transferable rule is: when some members of set X are in set Y, and all members of Y are in set Z, it must follow that some members of X are in set Z.

item.context: Harbin people are all northerners, and some Harbin people are not workers.
item.question: If the above proposition is correct, which of the followings must also be true?
