The error came from choosing the most alarming consequence instead of the option that most directly weakens the proposal’s underlying effectiveness. A better general rule is: in strengthen/weaken questions, prefer the choice that most directly affects the causal or functional basis of the claim, not the one that merely adds a potentially solvable practical obstacle.

item.context: Sophistical Refutations of Aristotle tells such a sophistry: You have a dog, it has children, because it is a father; it is yours, so it is your father; you beat it is to beat your own father.
item.question: Which of the following has the same logical fallacy as the above sophistry?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dog has four legs and a sheep has four legs, so a dog can be a sheep

choices.label: B
choices.text: Get up, Czech, the rooster has already crowed. What does it matter to me? I'm not a hen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When someone said that Oudi Demo lied, he quibbled: Whoever lied says something that didn't exist; things that didn't exist could not be said, so no one lied.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Your point of view has been proved to be wrong, then my criticism of your point of view is correct. Since my point of view is correct, then your point of view is definitely wrong.

response:
Reasoning: The dog sophism equivocates on ownership/relationship terms: “yours” means “belonging to you,” then is shifted to “your father.” Option C uses the same kind of equivocation, shifting the meaning of “lying” into “saying what does not exist,” then exploiting that ambiguity.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an analogy-based approach, looking for an option with the same surface feature of equivocation on a word or phrase. The key clue I focused on was the shift from “your dog” to “your father,” which made me overcommit to ambiguity in meaning rather than the argument’s structure. My mistake was ignoring that the sophism works by illegitimately converting a relation and then treating the converse as established, which is closer to the flawed back-and-forth inference in the credited option. For similar problems, I should compare the formal pattern of inference first, and only use wording ambiguity as a secondary check.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question too narrowly as a hunt for equivocation on a single word, and that led me to force the original sophism into a semantic-ambiguity pattern. The crucial structure, however, is not just wordplay about “your” or “father,” but an illicit shift from a qualified relation to an unqualified conclusion. In the dog argument, “it is yours” and “it is a father” are improperly fused into “it is your father,” which treats two separate predicates as though they formed a genuine relational predicate. My strategy focused on lexical ambiguity, so I chose the option that also seemed to redefine a term, but that missed the deeper formal pattern. I used one real feature of the argument—surface ambiguity—but ignored the stronger evidence in the inference step itself. I assumed that any sophism from Aristotle here would most likely be an equivocation case, which was an overgeneralization. I should have compared the answer choices by mapping premise-to-conclusion structure, not by matching isolated words or rhetorical flavor. One alternative I should have tested was whether any option similarly turns “a correct criticism of your view” into “my view is correct,” which parallels the original’s relational slide. The error was caused by classifying the fallacy too early, before checking whether the inferential form matched. In similar problems, I should identify exactly what role each predicate plays and ask whether the conclusion preserves that role. General rule: when an argument moves from “X has property P about Y” to “X has property Q” or “Y stands in relation R to X,” verify that no hidden shift in grammatical or relational structure has occurred.

item.context: Theorist: Hatred and anger, grief and despair, love and joy are pairs of emotions that consist of the same core feeling and are distinguishable from each other only in terms of the social conditions that cause them and the behavior they in turn cause. So even if the meaning of a given piece of music is the emotion it elicits, this can mean only that music produces the core of a given emotion, for music is merely sound and, ttherefore, by itself creates neither social conditions nor human behavior.
item.question: The claim that music is merely sound plays which one of the following roles in the theorist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a generalization a particular instance of which is cited by the argument in order to undermine the viewpoint that the argument is attacking.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a claim that is offered as partial support for the argument's conclusion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a portion of the conclusion drawn in the argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a hypothesis that must be rejected, according to the argument, because it is inconsistent with certain evidence.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion is that music can elicit only the core of an emotion, not the socially conditioned/full emotion. “Music is merely sound” is used as support for that conclusion, because from it the theorist infers music cannot itself create social conditions or behavior.  
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used an argument-structure approach: identify the main conclusion, then determine whether the cited claim functions as evidence, a sub-conclusion, or part of the conclusion itself. The key factor was the inferential chain: from “music is merely sound,” the theorist derives that music cannot create social conditions or behavior, which then supports the claim about eliciting only the core of an emotion. My success came from tracing that claim as a supporting premise rather than confusing it with the conclusion. For similar problems, first map the conclusion and intermediate inferences, then classify each statement by what it is used to support.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the argumentative function of one specific claim, not whether that claim was true or whether the overall argument was persuasive. My strategy was to identify the conclusion first and then see how the targeted sentence connected to it in the chain of support. That was appropriate here because role questions depend on structure: a statement can be evidence, an intermediate conclusion, background, or the main conclusion depending on how it is used. I recognized that the conclusion was that music can produce only the core of an emotion, and I saw that the claim about music being merely sound was used to justify the follow-up statement that music cannot create social conditions or human behavior. Those facts matter because the theorist had defined differences among paired emotions in terms of social causes and resulting behavior. I did not assume the “merely sound” claim was itself the conclusion, because the argument goes on to derive something further from it. I also implicitly ruled out answer choices that described attacking another viewpoint, citing evidence against a hypothesis, or including part of the conclusion, because none matched the local structure. What made the reasoning successful was tracing the inferential sequence instead of matching words loosely. In similar problems, I should continue distinguishing between direct support and derived implications within multi-step arguments. General rule: when asked for a statement’s role, map the argument as premise → sub-conclusion → conclusion and classify the statement by its actual inferential job, not by its rhetorical emphasis.

item.context: Professor: A person who can select a beverage from among 50 varieties of cola is less free than one who has only these 5 choices: wine, coffee, apple juice, milk, and water. It is clear, then, that meaningful freedom cannot be measured simply by the number of alternatives available; the extent of the differences among the alternatives is also a relevant factor.
item.question: The professor's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: inferring one general principle from another, more general, principle

choices.label: B
choices.text: supporting its conclusion by means of an analogy

choices.label: C
choices.text: supporting a general principle by means of an example

choices.label: D
choices.text: claiming that whatever holds for each member of a group must hold for the whole group

response:
Reasoning: The professor gives a specific comparison—50 cola options versus 5 very different beverages—to illustrate and support the broader claim that freedom is not measured only by number of choices, but also by how different the choices are. That is using an example to support a general principle.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an argument-structure approach, identifying the broad conclusion and then asking what role the cola-versus-beverage comparison played. The key clue was that the comparison was a single concrete case offered to justify a more general claim about how freedom should be assessed. My success came from focusing on function rather than topic: I asked whether the comparison was being treated as a parallel analogy or as an instance illustrating a rule. For similar problems, first separate the conclusion from the evidence, then classify the evidence by its role—example, analogy, principle, or whole-part inference.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the argument’s method of reasoning, not whether the professor’s conclusion about freedom was true. That was the right frame, because LSAT-style prompts of this form usually test argumentative structure rather than content. My strategy was to identify the conclusion first—the claim about how meaningful freedom should be measured—and then determine how the earlier cola-versus-beverage comparison functioned relative to that conclusion. I recognized that the comparison was a concrete case offered in support of a broader claim, which matches the pattern of example-to-principle reasoning. The key evidence was the shift from one specific scenario to a general statement about what factors are relevant in measuring freedom. I did not treat the cola/beverage comparison as an analogy, and that was important, because the argument was not drawing a parallel between two separate domains; it was using one illustrative case from the same domain. A possible trap was to confuse “comparison” with “analogy,” but comparisons can serve simply as examples. Another trap would have been to overread the wording “it is clear, then” and assume a formal deduction from a prior principle, which the passage does not contain. What made the reasoning successful was tracking the role each sentence played instead of focusing on topic words alone. In similar problems, I should keep asking: is the author applying a rule, inferring a rule, or illustrating a rule? General lesson: when a passage moves from a single concrete instance to a broad evaluative claim, the argument is typically supporting a general principle by example.

item.context: The researchers mixed a certain plant lactic acid bacteria into the feed of the experimental rats. After the experimental rats ate the feed for 4 weeks, they continued to exert mental pressure sufficient to cause sleep disorders for two weeks, and then let the experimental rats pedal the wheel during the nocturnal activity period to test their activity. The results showed that the downward trend of the activity of the experimental rats extracted with the lactic acid bacteria was curbed, However, the rats in the control group who did not eat the feed containing the lactic acid bacteria had difficulty falling asleep during the day and lack of sleep, resulting in a significant decrease in their activity at night. Therefore, the researchers believe that the intake of lactic acid bacteria can improve the sleep disorder caused by mental stress.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, questions the above conclusion most?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The experimental rats usually sleep during the day and come out at night

choices.label: B
choices.text: The expression of a gene related to sleep disorder was inhibited in the experimental mice extracted with lactic acid bacteria

choices.label: C
choices.text: The composition of the plant lactic acid bacteria is inconsistent with that of most lactic acid bacteria

choices.label: D
choices.text: In addition to pedaling the wheel, the experimental rats had no other activities at night

response:
Reasoning: The experiment tested one specific plant lactic acid bacterium, but the conclusion generalizes to “lactic acid bacteria” overall. If this strain is compositionally unlike most lactic acid bacteria, the conclusion is overgeneralized and weakened most.  
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a scope-matching weakening approach: compare the evidence actually tested with the breadth of the conclusion drawn. The key factor was that the study examined one specific plant-derived lactic acid bacterium, while the conclusion generalized to lactic acid bacteria as a whole. My answer was correct because I focused on that representativeness gap rather than on details that merely supported the experiment or were irrelevant to causation. For similar problems, I should always check whether a conclusion extends from a special case, subgroup, or single sample to a broader class without justification.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the statement that most seriously weakens the researchers’ causal conclusion, not the statement that merely adds detail about the rats’ behavior or supports the result. My strategy was to look for a mismatch between what the experiment actually established and what the conclusion claimed. The key evidence I used was that the study tested one particular plant-derived bacterial strain in one experimental setup, while the conclusion spoke broadly about “the intake of lactic acid bacteria” improving stress-related sleep disorder. That creates a scope problem: evidence about a special case does not automatically justify a claim about the whole category. I also recognized that some options were either irrelevant background conditions or direct strengthening evidence, so they could not be the best challenge. A shortcut that helped was classifying answers by role: support, irrelevant description, methodological limitation, or overgeneralization. The successful part of my reasoning was prioritizing external validity over side details about rats’ day-night cycle or limited nighttime activities. An alternative I should always still check is whether any option attacks the measurement itself, because flawed measurement can weaken causation even more strongly than overgeneralization. In similar problems, I should explicitly compare the population, treatment, and outcome tested with the population, treatment, and outcome claimed. General rule: when an argument infers a broad causal claim from evidence about a narrow or atypical instance, the strongest weakening move is often to show that the tested instance is not representative of the broader category.

item.context: Leisure sports refers to various forms of sports activities that people voluntarily choose and engage in under the relatively free social living environment and conditions. It is not only a social phenomenon of sports, but also an existing form of sports. It is one of the main ways of social leisure activities.
item.question: According to the above definition, the following belong to leisure sports?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Marathon runner Xiao Li plays with his friends during the holidays

choices.label: B
choices.text: As a private bodyguard, Xiao Wang receives four hours of catching and fighting training every day

choices.label: C
choices.text: All the students of a high school finish half an hour of long-distance running every afternoon according to the requirements of the school

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mr. Zhao, who has been injured in his leg and is recovering, is guided by a nurse to take a 15 minute walk outdoors every day at the request of the doctor

response:
Reasoning: Leisure sports are voluntarily chosen activities done in free time for leisure. A fits: playing with friends during holidays is voluntary and recreational. B is job training, C is compulsory school exercise, and D is medical rehabilitation, not leisure sport.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I broke the concept into key conditions such as voluntary participation, relatively free time, and leisure-oriented activity, then checked each option against those conditions. The decisive factor was whether the activity was chosen freely for recreation rather than required by work, school, or medical treatment. My success came from filtering out choices that involved obligation or instrumental purposes, even though they were still physical activities. For similar problems, I should explicitly convert the definition into a short checklist and reject any option that fails even one essential condition.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the definition as requiring two core conditions: the activity must be voluntarily chosen, and it must occur in a relatively free living context as a form of leisure rather than obligation. That interpretation was correct because the key task was not merely to identify “physical activity,” but to distinguish leisure sport from work, school, or medical activity. My strategy was to test each option against the necessary elements in the definition, especially voluntariness and social-leisure context. This was appropriate because the answer choices were designed around near-misses: all involved movement or exercise, but only one matched the full definition.

The evidence I used effectively was the contrast between optional recreation and externally imposed activity. I correctly recognized that professional training connected to employment, mandatory school running, and doctor-directed rehabilitation each fail the leisure criterion even if they involve bodily exercise. One useful assumption I made was that “plays with friends during the holidays” indicates free time and self-directed participation; that assumption fit the wording. I also avoided a common shortcut error: equating any sport-related activity with leisure sport. An alternative possibility I should always consider in similar questions is whether a competitive athlete’s informal activity could still count as leisure if detached from training or duty; here, the context supported that distinction. The reasoning succeeded because I applied the definition conjunctively rather than focusing on only one feature. A general rule is: when a concept is defined by multiple conditions, evaluate each option by checking every required condition, and reject choices that satisfy only part of the definition.

item.context: People like officials solve problems that have answers from morning to night, and their minds have been trained to be like this, so they are not the material of being a politician. The task of a politician is to deal with unanswered questions and to deal with problems that are likely to be unsolvable. However, the more a person is trained to be an excellent official, the more he thinks that all the problems have answers and that they can be solved, so when they encounter problems that may be unsolvable, they will be helpless and even pat their buttocks and walk away. , The more a person is trained as an official, the more he will become an incompetent political figure.
item.question: Which of the following is the most accurate summary of the main idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An excellent official always thinks that there are answers to questions

choices.label: B
choices.text: The task of a politician is to deal with unanswered questions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Not all officials can become political figures

choices.label: D
choices.text: The best official is the worst politician

response:
Reasoning: The passage contrasts officials and politicians: officials are trained to solve answerable problems, while politicians face unanswered or unsolvable ones. It concludes that the more excellent one is as an official, the more incompetent one may be as a political figure. This is best captured by D.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a contrast-and-conclusion approach: I identified the two roles the passage opposes and then looked for the option that captured the author’s final evaluative claim rather than just one supporting point. The key factor was the progression “the more excellent as an official, the more incompetent as a political figure,” which states a strong inverse relationship. My success came from prioritizing the passage’s concluding synthesis over partial statements about only officials or only politicians. For similar problems, first separate background/supporting contrasts from the author’s ultimate judgment, and choose the option that expresses that full relationship most completely.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the passage’s overall thesis, not just a true detail mentioned in the middle. My strategy was to track the contrast structure: the author first describes how officials are trained, then explains what politicians must handle, and finally draws a comparative conclusion about what happens when someone excels in the first role. That was an appropriate method because “main idea” questions are usually resolved by following the passage’s argumentative progression and identifying the final, most general claim. The key evidence I used was the repeated “the more … the more …” pattern, which showed that the author was not merely describing officials or politicians separately, but arguing an inverse relationship between excellence in one and competence in the other. I also correctly noticed that some choices captured only supporting points, such as the idea that politicians face unanswered questions or that officials assume all problems are solvable.  

A useful assumption I made was that the strongest summary would combine both sides of the contrast rather than isolate one side. The alternatives I needed to screen out were those that were too narrow or too weak, especially ones that stated only a premise or a partial consequence. What made the reasoning successful was prioritizing the author’s conclusion over earlier descriptive statements. In similar problems, I should keep distinguishing between background claims, supporting contrasts, and the sentence that synthesizes them into the main point. A transferable rule is: when asked for a passage’s main idea, prefer the choice that captures the author’s full comparative conclusion, not a statement that is merely true within the passage.

item.context: Hazel: Faster and more accurate order processing would help our business. To increase profits, we should process orders electronically rather than manually, because customers' orders will then go directly to all relevant parties. Max: We would lose money if we started processing orders electronically. Most people prefer to interact with human beings when placing orders. If we switch to electronic order processing, our business will appear cold and inhuman, and we will attract fewer customers.
item.question: Hazel and Max disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: faster and more accurate order processing would be financially beneficial to their business

choices.label: B
choices.text: electronic order processing is faster and more accurate than is manual order processing

choices.label: C
choices.text: their business has an obligation to be as profitable as possible

choices.label: D
choices.text: switching to electronic order processing would be financially beneficial to their business

response:
Reasoning: Hazel argues that switching to electronic order processing would increase profits; Max argues it would lose money by driving customers away. So they disagree about the financial effect of switching. They do not clearly disagree about speed/accuracy itself.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a compare-the-conclusions approach: I identified each speaker’s main claim and checked which answer choice captured the exact point of conflict. The key factor was that Hazel tied electronic processing to increased profits, while Max tied the same switch to lost money, so their disagreement was about the net financial effect of adopting the system. The successful step was separating supporting reasons like speed, accuracy, and customer preference from the ultimate conclusion each person defended. In similar problems, first restate each speaker’s bottom-line conclusion in simple terms, then choose the option that reflects that direct contradiction rather than one of the premises.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the precise point of disagreement between Hazel and Max, not which speaker had the stronger argument. That interpretation was correct, because disagreement questions hinge on comparing each speaker’s commitments and finding the claim one affirms while the other denies. My strategy was to translate each statement into a simple conclusion: Hazel says switching to electronic processing would increase profits, while Max says it would cause losses. That was an appropriate approach because both speakers gave different reasons, but the answer had to capture their conflicting bottom-line judgment.

The key evidence I used was that Hazel explicitly links electronic processing to higher profits, and Max explicitly links the same switch to losing money. I also correctly noticed that Max never directly denies that electronic processing is faster or more accurate; instead, he argues that customer preference for human interaction would outweigh any efficiency gain. That distinction ruled out the tempting choice about speed and accuracy. A shortcut that helped was separating premises from conclusions, so I did not confuse Hazel’s reason about efficiency with the actual issue in dispute. I should also note that another wrong path would have been inferring disagreement about business obligations, since neither speaker discusses moral duty at all.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on explicit claims rather than implied attitudes. In similar problems, I should systematically test each answer by asking whether one speaker commits to it and the other rejects it. General rule: in dialogue disagreement questions, identify each speaker’s conclusion and choose the option that captures a direct contradiction, not merely different supporting considerations.

item.context: Commodity is the product of labor produced for exchange.
item.question: Which of the following is not a commodity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gold jewelry in a department store

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pigs fed by professional pig farmers

choices.label: C
choices.text: The vegetables that Zhao grows in front of the house for his own consumption

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medical oxygen

response:
Reasoning: A commodity is produced for exchange. Gold jewelry, professionally raised pigs, and medical oxygen are made to be sold. Vegetables Zhao grows for his own family’s consumption are for self-use, not exchange, so they are not commodities.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option against the criterion “produced by labor for exchange.” The key factor was the intended use of the product, especially whether it enters the market or is kept for direct personal consumption. My success came from identifying that one option involved self-use rather than sale, which breaks the “for exchange” condition even though labor was involved. For similar problems, explicitly test every option against each part of the definition, and eliminate any choice that fails even one required condition.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as testing the defining condition in the given statement: a commodity must be both a product of labor and produced for exchange. That interpretation was correct because the problem supplied a precise conceptual criterion rather than asking about market value, usefulness, or physical form. My strategy was to compare each option against that definition and identify the one that failed the “for exchange” requirement. This was appropriate because the answer turned entirely on classification by definition, not on economic complexity.

The key evidence I used was the contrast between items clearly intended for sale and the one produced for direct personal use. I correctly recognized that goods sold in stores, raised by professional producers, or supplied in commercial settings satisfy exchange-oriented production. The crucial relationship was that self-consumption breaks commodity status even if labor was involved in producing the good. A possible shortcut I used was assuming that “department store,” “professional farmers,” and “medical oxygen” imply market exchange, which is reasonable here because the wording strongly signals commercial circulation.

I did not need to explore many alternatives, but one subtle possibility would have been distinguishing a useful good from a commodity; usefulness alone is insufficient. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the exact definitional constraint rather than surface features like tangibility or necessity. In similar problems, I should continue translating the prompt into a checklist of necessary conditions and test each option against every condition. General rule: when a concept is defined by multiple criteria, eliminate any option that fails even one necessary criterion, especially if the question asks for an exception.

item.context: S: People who are old enough to fight for their country are old enough to vote for the people who make decisions about war and peace. This government clearly regards 17 year olds as old enough to fight, so it should acknowledge their right to vote. T: Your argument is a good one only to the extent that fighting and voting are the same kind of activity. Fighting well requires strength, muscular coordination, and in a modern army instant and automatic response to orders. Performed responsibly, voting, unlike fighting, is essentially a deliberative activity requiring reasoning power and knowledge of both history and human nature.
item.question: T responds to S's argument by

choices.label: A
choices.text: calling into question S's understanding of the concept of rights

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing for a conclusion opposite to the one drawn by S

choices.label: C
choices.text: challenging the truth of a claim on which S's conclusion is based

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that S has ignored the distinction between having a right to do something and having an obligation to do that thing

response:
Reasoning: T does not discuss rights vs obligations, nor directly claim the opposite conclusion. Instead, T attacks S’s key premise that readiness to fight implies readiness to vote, by arguing the two activities require very different abilities.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an argument-structure approach: I identified S’s conclusion and then looked for whether T attacked the conclusion directly or undermined a supporting premise. The key factor was T’s claim that the abilities needed for fighting and for voting are importantly different, which weakens S’s link from being fit to fight to being fit to vote. My success came from focusing on the dependency in S’s reasoning rather than getting distracted by the language of rights. For similar problems, first isolate the conclusion, then test whether the response disputes a premise, the inference, or the conclusion itself.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the argumentative role of T’s response, not whether T’s position was substantively persuasive. That distinction mattered, because the task was to classify how T attacks S’s reasoning structure. My strategy was to identify S’s conclusion and the premise linking military eligibility to voting eligibility, then ask which answer choice best described T’s criticism of that link. That was appropriate because argument-role questions are usually resolved by mapping premise, conclusion, and objection type rather than debating the policy issue itself.

The key evidence I used was that T focuses on differences between fighting and voting: one depends on obedience and physical capacities, while the other depends on deliberation and judgment. From that, I inferred that T is not mainly discussing rights, obligations, or a reverse political conclusion, but instead disputing the premise that qualification for one activity supports qualification for the other. An assumption underlying my reasoning was that S’s argument depends on an analogy between fighting and voting, and T’s response works by denying that the analogy holds strongly enough. I also correctly considered and rejected the distractor about rights versus obligations because T never introduces duty language. Likewise, I rejected the “opposite conclusion” option because T critiques the support for S’s conclusion rather than explicitly proving the contrary. The success came from distinguishing between attacking a premise and attacking a concept. General rule: when a response emphasizes relevant differences between two compared activities, it is usually challenging the truth or applicability of the analogy-based premise, not merely disagreeing with the conclusion.

item.context: In an experiment, biologists repeatedly shone a bright light into a tank containing a sea snail and simultaneously shook the tank. The snail invariably responded by tensing its muscular foot,  a typical reaction in sea snails to ocean turbulence. After several repetitions of this procedure, the snail tensed its foot whenever the biologists shone the light into its tank, even when the tank was not simultaneously shaken. Ttherefore, the snail must have learned to associate the shining of the bright light with the shaking of the tank.
item.question: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sea snail used in the experiment did not differ significantly from other members of its species in its reaction to external stimuli.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tensing of the muscular foot in sea snails is an instinctual rather than a learned response to ocean turbulence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All sea snails react to ocean turbulence in the same way as the sea snail in the experiment did.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The appearance of a bright light alone would ordinarily not result in the sea snail's tensing its foot.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion says the snail learned an association because it later reacted to light alone. That requires assuming the light by itself would not normally cause foot-tensing; otherwise the later response need not be due to learned association. A and C generalize beyond this snail; B is irrelevant.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a necessary-assumption approach: I asked what must be true for the observed later response to support the claim of learned association rather than some alternative explanation. The key factor was ruling out the possibility that the light itself naturally triggers the foot-tensing response, because if it did, the conclusion about learning would not follow. My success came from testing the argument against competing explanations and identifying the one the argument had to exclude. For similar problems, explicitly negate each candidate assumption and see whether the conclusion could still stand; if it could, that choice is not required.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for a necessary assumption, not merely a helpful premise or a strongly supported statement. My strategy was to test what the conclusion depends on: the argument infers learned association from the fact that, after repeated pairings, the snail reacted to the light alone. That kind of causal-learning inference requires ruling out an alternative explanation, namely that the light itself already triggered the response independently of any conditioning. I focused on whether the later behavior genuinely indicated a new association, which is the right approach for assumption questions involving experiments.  

The key evidence I used was the contrast between the original response to shaking and the later response to light alone after repeated pairings. I correctly recognized that choices about other sea snails or species-wide uniformity were outside the argument’s scope because the conclusion concerned this particular snail. I also noted that whether the turbulence response is instinctive or learned does not affect whether a new association was formed in the experiment. The crucial assumption was about the baseline effect of light alone before conditioning. Without that, the observed post-experiment behavior would not uniquely support the conclusion.  

What made the reasoning successful was checking for an alternative cause and seeing which option blocks it. In similar problems, I should continue asking: “If this choice were false, could the conclusion still stand?” General rule: for required-assumption questions, identify the gap between evidence and conclusion, then look for the premise that eliminates the most relevant competing explanation without adding unnecessary generalizations.

item.context: A certain tropical island received food donations in the form of powdered milk for distribution to its poorest residents, who were thought to be malnourished. Subsequently, the rate of liver cancers among those islanders increased sharply. The donated milk was probably to blame: recent laboratory research on rats has shown that rats briefly exposed to the substances aflatoxin tend to develop liver cancer when fed casein, a milk protein. This result is relevant because __.
item.question: Which of the following most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: powdered milk is the most appropriate form in which to send milk to a tropical destination

choices.label: B
choices.text: the people who were given the donated milk had been screened for their ability to digest milk

choices.label: C
choices.text: casein is not the only protein contained in milk

choices.label: D
choices.text: in the tropics, peanuts, a staple of these island residents, support a mold growth that produces aflatoxin

response:
Reasoning: The rat study matters only if the islanders were likely exposed to aflatoxin and then consumed milk protein (casein). If their staple food in the tropics—peanuts—commonly carries mold that produces aflatoxin, the donated powdered milk could plausibly have triggered increased liver cancer.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a relevance/bridge approach: I looked for the missing fact that would connect the rat experiment to the islanders’ real-world situation. The key factor was that the study only matters if the islanders were likely exposed to aflatoxin before consuming milk protein, so I focused on finding an answer choice that established a local source of aflatoxin exposure. My success came from identifying the causal chain required by the argument rather than getting distracted by general facts about milk. For similar problems, explicitly map each link needed to transfer a lab finding to the target population and choose the option that supplies the missing link.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the missing premise that makes the rat study applicable to the island case, not merely a fact about milk or nutrition. The key task was relevance matching: identify what conditions in the laboratory finding had to be mirrored in the real-world situation for the evidence to support the claim about the donated food. I used a conditional-transfer strategy, looking for two linked elements from the study—exposure to a particular carcinogenic substance and later consumption of a milk protein—and then asking which option connected those elements to the islanders. That strategy was appropriate because strengthen/completion questions often hinge on whether an experimental result can be generalized to the target population.

The decisive evidence was that the study did not show milk alone causes cancer; it showed increased risk under a specific interaction. So I needed an answer that supplied a plausible source of the other required factor among the island residents. I correctly rejected choices that were irrelevant to that causal bridge, such as logistical claims about powdered milk or digestive screening. One assumption I handled well was that “relevant because” signals a need for contextual applicability, not a broader fact about milk composition. I also implicitly considered alternatives by checking whether any option established the necessary background exposure rather than merely commenting on milk. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on causal structure instead of surface topic overlap. A transferable rule is: when evidence comes from a study with multiple necessary conditions, the best supporting completion is the one that shows those conditions also hold in the case at issue.

item.context: Property income refers to the income derived from movable property (such as bank deposits, securities, etc.) and real property (such as houses, vehicles, land, collectibles, etc.) owned by the family.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings is not classified as property income?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dividends from property operations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patent income from the transfer of property use rights.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Non-property appreciation income.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interest and rent from the transfer of the right to use the property.

response:
Reasoning: Property income comes from owning property and earning returns like dividends, interest, rent, or fees from transferring use rights. Options A, B, and D fit this. Non-property appreciation income is not income derived from property ownership/use under the definition.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: compare each option against the stated requirement that the income must be derived from owned movable or real property. The key factor was distinguishing ongoing returns generated by ownership or use-right transfers—such as dividends, interest, rent, or similar rights-based income—from gains that do not arise directly from property as defined. My success came from checking whether each option fit the mechanism in the definition, rather than relying on familiar financial terms alone. For similar problems, explicitly test each choice against every part of the definition and eliminate any option that fails the source-of-income condition.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a definition-matching task: identify which option does **not** fall under income generated from owning movable or immovable property. That interpretation was correct, because the key issue was classification by source of income rather than whether the income sounded profitable or legal. My strategy was to compare each option against the definition’s core mechanism: income must come from property ownership or from allowing others to use that property. That was appropriate because the definition explicitly included examples like bank deposits, securities, houses, and land, which point to returns such as dividends, interest, rent, and use-right transfers.

The evidence I relied on was that dividends, patent licensing-type returns, and interest or rent all involve an identifiable asset producing income. I also noticed that the phrase “transfer of the right to use” strongly signals property income, since the owner retains ownership while monetizing use. The crucial distinction was with appreciation income: a rise in value is not necessarily the same as income derived from operating, renting, licensing, or investing property. One assumption I made was that “property income” here refers to current returns from property, not every gain associated with property; in this context, that assumption was justified.

An alternative I should still consciously test in similar problems is whether “appreciation” might be treated as capital gains under a broader definition, but the wording here excluded that. What made the reasoning successful was isolating the **source mechanism** of the income rather than relying on surface familiarity with financial terms. A transferable rule is: **when classifying economic categories, identify the exact causal pathway named in the definition and reject options that involve value change without the specified source relationship.**

item.context: Beginning in the 1950s, popular music was revolutionized by the electrification of musical instruments, which has enabled musicians to play with increased volume. Because individual musicians can play with increased volume, the average number of musicians per band has decreased. Nevertheless, electrification has increased rather than decreased the overall number of musicians who play popular music professionally.
item.question: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the statements above, if those statements are true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The number of amateur musicians who play popular music has decreased.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many professional musicians play in more than one band.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The number of professional musicians in some bands has increased.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The total number of professional bands has increased as a result of electrification.

response:
Reasoning: If the average number of musicians per band decreased, but the overall number of professional musicians increased, then there must be more bands than before. Otherwise total musicians would not rise. This is the strongest conclusion supported by the statements.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a quantitative relationship: total professional musicians depends on the average number of musicians per band multiplied by the number of bands. The key clue was that average band size went down while the overall number of professional musicians went up; for both statements to be true, the number of bands had to rise enough to offset the smaller average size. My success came from translating the verbal claims into a simple product relationship instead of getting distracted by unsupported possibilities about amateurs or multi-band membership. For similar problems, convert comparative statements into variables or equations and test what must change when one factor decreases but the total increases.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the conclusion most directly implied by the relationship between three quantities: volume capability, average band size, and total number of professional musicians. That interpretation was correct, because the argument is fundamentally about how changes in averages and totals constrain the number of groups. My strategy was to translate the verbal statements into a simple multiplicative relationship: total professional musicians is roughly the number of bands times the average musicians per band. That was an appropriate strategy because the answer choices concern structural consequences of those quantities, not causal details about style or amateur participation.

The key evidence I used was that average musicians per band went down while the total number of professional musicians went up. If one factor in a product decreases and the overall product increases, the other factor must increase sufficiently; here, that other factor is the number of bands. I also correctly ignored distractors that introduced unsupported topics, such as amateurs or musicians playing in multiple bands, because nothing in the stimulus addressed those issues. One assumption I effectively relied on was that “overall number of musicians who play professionally” tracks band membership counts in the ordinary way; that assumption is built into the wording and is reasonable. An alternative I should still consciously test in similar problems is whether a hidden variable could explain the change without forcing the target conclusion. Here, none of the alternatives undermined the numerical implication.

What made the reasoning successful was recognizing a quantitative constraint rather than looking for a merely plausible sociological story. In similar problems, I should continue formalizing comparative statements into relationships among totals, averages, and counts. General rule: when a total increases despite a decrease in average units per group, infer an increase in the number of groups, unless the stimulus explicitly provides another offsetting variable.

item.context: Marianna: The problem of drunk driving has been somewhat ameliorated by public education and stricter laws. Additional measures are nevertheless needed. People still drive after drinking, and when they do the probability is greatly increased that they will cause an accident involving death or serious injury. David: I think you exaggerate the dangers of driving while drunk. Actually, a driver who is in an automobile accident is slightly less likely to be seriously injured if drunk than if sober.
item.question: In responding to Marianna's argument, David makes which one of the following errors of reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He argues against a point that is not one that Marianna was making.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He contradicts Marianna's conclusion without giving any evidence for his point of view.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He directs his criticism against the person making the argument rather than directing it against the argument itself.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He contradicts himself.

response:
Reasoning: Marianna’s claim is that drunk driving raises the probability of causing an accident with death or serious injury. David replies about whether a drunk driver is less likely to be injured once an accident occurs. That addresses a different issue, so he attacks a point she was not making.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a relevance/mismatch approach: I compared Marianna’s actual claim with the claim David answered and checked whether they were about the same issue. The key factor was the difference between causing an accident that results in death or serious injury and being injured oneself once an accident has already happened. My answer was correct because I tracked the shift in subject matter rather than getting distracted by the surface similarity that both statements mention injury and drunk driving. For similar problems, explicitly identify the conclusion and evidence of the first speaker, then test whether the reply addresses that exact conclusion or subtly switches to a different question.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the flaw in David’s reply relative to Marianna’s actual claim, not whether either speaker’s factual statements were true. That was the right frame, because flaw questions often turn on whether the response is relevant to the original argument. My strategy was to compare the logical content of each statement: Marianna focused on the increased likelihood that drinking leads to causing an accident involving death or serious injury, while David focused on the likelihood of the drunk driver being seriously injured after an accident occurs. Those are different conditional relationships, so his response did not engage her point. The key evidence I used was the distinction between causing a harmful accident and being harmed in an accident. I also implicitly noticed that Marianna’s concern was public safety overall, whereas David narrowed the discussion to the drunk driver’s own injury risk. A possible shortcut I used was pattern recognition for “irrelevant rebuttal,” but here that shortcut was appropriate because the subject shift was explicit. I correctly rejected the alternatives because David did offer evidence of a sort, did not attack Marianna personally, and did not contradict himself. What made the reasoning successful was isolating the exact claim under dispute instead of reacting to the shared topic of drunk driving in general. In similar problems, I should systematically map each speaker’s claim into premise-conclusion form and check whether the reply matches the same variable, event, and outcome. General rule: when evaluating a response, compare not just the topic but the precise proposition, since arguments often go wrong by answering a different question from the one actually asked.

item.context: Human height is one of the biological traits. For a long time, people believe that height is mainly determined by genetic, dietary and environmental factors. However, after recognizing the role of genes, people began to think that genes play a major role in determining height. Therefore, after the completion of the human genome project, they began to look for genes related to height and obtain their relationship with health, disease and other related information and knowledge.
item.question: Which of the following is most likely to be described in the above paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: People with large height gap also have great differences in appearance and health.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diet, environment and personal health status have an impact on genes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Look for data related to height genes and make empirical analysis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The genes that determine height also affect health, disease and so on.

response:
Reasoning: The paragraph says researchers, after the Human Genome Project, started searching for height-related genes and studying their links to health and disease. This most naturally leads to collecting relevant gene data and analyzing it empirically, rather than already asserting a firm conclusion.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a forward-inference approach: I identified the paragraph’s setup as background leading into the next likely topic, then chose the option that best matched a natural continuation. The key clue was the final sentence, which emphasizes that after the Human Genome Project, researchers “began to look for genes related to height” and obtain related information, which points to a research process rather than a settled finding. My success came from distinguishing between a description of ongoing investigation and a conclusion about what those genes already do. For similar questions, first decide whether the passage is introducing a research direction, reporting a result, or making a claim, and then pick the option that matches that discourse role.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking what topic would most naturally come next in the paragraph, not which statement was generally true about height. That interpretation was correct because the passage describes a shift in scientific attention: from broad beliefs about height to post-genome-project efforts to investigate height-related genes. My strategy was to track the paragraph’s sequence of ideas and infer the likely next step in that research process. That was appropriate because the wording “they began to look for genes related to height and obtain their relationship with health, disease and other related information” points to an ongoing investigative activity rather than a final biological conclusion.

The key evidence I used was the action-oriented language: “began to look for” and “obtain information and knowledge.” Those phrases imply data collection and analysis, which supports a research-method continuation. I correctly avoided overcommitting to a stronger claim that the genes already were known to affect health and disease in a definite way. One assumption that helped was treating the passage as a description of scientific workflow: identify candidate genes, gather data, then analyze associations. I should also note that alternative choices were weaker because they either introduced unsupported causal claims or shifted away from the paragraph’s focus on research activity.

What made the reasoning successful was matching the answer choice to the paragraph’s level of certainty and stage of inquiry. For similar problems, I should explicitly distinguish between “research aims” and “research findings.” A transferable rule is: when a passage describes investigators beginning to search for relationships, prefer an answer about collecting or analyzing evidence over one that states a definitive causal conclusion.

item.context: Mr. Zhang: smoking all year round may be harmful to health. Ms. Li: your conclusion reflects a misunderstanding of the public. My grandfather lived to be 96, but he has been smoking since he was young.
item.question: Which of the followings best points out the loopholes in Ms. Li's Refutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Try to rely on a counterexample to overturn a general conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Try to resort to individual cases to establish causal links between unrelated phenomena.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Try to use a counterexample to refute a possible conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Challenge popular opinions based on personal experience improperly

response:
Reasoning: Mr. Zhang only says smoking may be harmful, a probabilistic/general claim. Ms. Li uses one exceptional case to deny that possibility. A single counterexample cannot overturn a “may” claim. So the flaw is using a counterexample to refute a possible conclusion.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-identification approach by comparing the logical strength of the original claim with the kind of evidence used in the rebuttal. The key factor was that the original statement was only a possibility claim (“may be harmful”), while the response relied on one elderly smoker as if a single exception could defeat that weaker, probabilistic conclusion. What helped was noticing the mismatch between a general possible-risk statement and an anecdotal counterexample. For similar problems, I should first classify the claim type—universal, probabilistic, or possible—then test whether the rebuttal’s evidence is strong enough for that exact claim type.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the flaw in Ms. Li’s rebuttal, not whether smoking is in fact harmful. That interpretation was correct, because the task was about logical structure: Mr. Zhang made a weak modal claim, and Ms. Li tried to defeat it. My strategy was to compare the strength of the original claim with the kind of evidence offered against it. This was appropriate because flaw questions often turn on mismatches between a conclusion’s logical form and the rebuttal’s evidential form.

The key fact I used was that “may be harmful” is a possibility claim, not a universal claim like “everyone who smokes is harmed.” I also noticed that Ms. Li relied on one anecdotal case of a long-lived smoker. The crucial relationship is that a single favorable instance does not negate a statement that only asserts possible harm. An assumption that helped was treating “my grandfather” as a counterexample attempt rather than as causal evidence, which fit the wording of the rebuttal. I did briefly need to distinguish this from the more common flaw of using one exception against a general rule; here the original statement was weaker than a general rule. A tempting alternative was the option about causal links, but Ms. Li was not trying to prove causation, only to dismiss a possibility claim. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the answer choice to the exact modality of the claim. General lesson: when evaluating rebuttals, first classify the original statement as universal, typical, or merely possible, then test whether the opposing evidence could logically defeat that specific strength of claim.

item.context: We have witnessed that the future technologies in science fiction that only existed in the imagination were realized one by one and changed the real world. Perhaps one day, science fiction will no longer think about and simulate the actual role of technology, but will focus all on the theme of the narrator, the fate of mankind and even the fate of the universe. We still have to thank them for helping us imagine the future world. But, I hope someone can always ask sincerely like Jules Verne more than a hundred years ago: Is it really impossible for people to travel around the earth in a shorter time?
item.question: According to this text, we can know that the author wants science fiction works?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Imagine the impact of technological development on mankind as much as possible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pay more attention to the development of the science fiction storyline itself.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Can continue to inspire and inspire future technological innovation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Efforts should be made to explore the specific performance of future technology applications.

response:
Reasoning: The author appreciates science fiction for imagining future technology and hopes it will keep asking bold, practical questions like Jules Verne did, which can inspire real inventions. So the author wants sci-fi to continue stimulating technological innovation.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an author-intent approach, focusing on the passage’s evaluative language about what science fiction has done and what the author hopes it will keep doing. The key clue was the closing wish that writers continue asking forward-looking technological questions “like Jules Verne,” after noting that imagined technologies later became reality. My answer was correct because I prioritized the author’s concluding emphasis over the speculative middle sentence about possible future themes. For similar questions, I should weigh the author’s final explicit hope or recommendation most heavily when it clarifies the main attitude or desired direction.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the author’s normative preference for what science fiction should continue doing, not merely a summary of what science fiction has done in the past. That interpretation was important because the passage contrasts two tendencies: future science fiction might shift away from technological simulation, yet the author expresses hope that it will keep asking the kind of forward-looking questions that once preceded real inventions. My strategy was to track the evaluative language in the passage, especially phrases such as “we still have to thank them” and the concluding “I hope,” since those phrases usually reveal the author’s desired direction. That was an appropriate strategy because the answer depended more on attitude and emphasis than on factual detail. The key evidence I used was the reference to imagined technologies being realized “one by one” and the praise of Jules Verne for posing seemingly impossible technological possibilities. Those details support the idea that the author values science fiction as a stimulus to real-world innovation, rather than as pure storytelling or only speculative description. I did not rely on unsupported assumptions about literary quality or plot, which helped avoid distractors focused on narrative development. The main alternative I needed to distinguish from my choice was the option about depicting specific future applications, which is close but narrower than the broader function of inspiring innovation. The reasoning succeeded because I followed the passage’s final rhetorical question as the strongest clue to authorial intention. In similar problems, I should identify contrast structures and then privilege the author’s concluding hope or judgment over earlier descriptive background. A useful general rule is: when a passage contrasts what a field may become with what the author hopes it remains, infer the answer from the author’s explicit value statement, not from the neutral description of existing trends.

item.context: Phobia refers to the patient's strong fear of a certain object or situation or when interacting with people, and take the initiative to avoid to relieve the anxiety.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following options is phobia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Xiaohong has been afraid of bugs since she was a child, and she hid behind her parents when she saw them. Now Xiaohong is 20 years old, she is still afraid of bugs, and she screams and jumps when she sees them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The construction worker Xiao Zhang fell off the high fence at one time and caused a fracture. After his recovery, he was afraid of reaching the high place and changed his job. He moved his house to the first floor, and he dared not even watch TV about the high altitude.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yu Yanyan is particularly afraid of the dark, and when it is almost dark, she has to go home as soon as possible, unless she goes to a night market with more lights. If she needs to be in a dark place, she dares to go unless someone must be with her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Liu Yan is a very introverted person. She blushes at the sight of strangers. When meeting members of the opposite sex, things get wrose that she can't even speak, soshe is particularly afraid of social occasions. She is very nervous every time when the company organizes activities.

response:
Reasoning: Phobia involves excessive, persistent fear plus active avoidance that disrupts life. B best fits: after the accident, Xiao Zhang avoids heights broadly, changes jobs, moves to the first floor, and even avoids TV about high places. The others are fear, shyness, or less clearly pathological.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I checked each option against all required elements—strong fear of a specific object/situation, anxiety relief through active avoidance, and behavior serious enough to shape daily life. The key factor was the breadth of avoidance behavior, especially life changes made to escape the feared stimulus, which most clearly signaled more than ordinary fear. My success came from comparing the options by completeness rather than picking the one with the strongest emotion alone. For similar problems, I should systematically turn the definition into a checklist and eliminate any choice that does not satisfy every condition explicitly.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the definition as requiring three elements: a strong fear tied to a specific object, situation, or interpersonal context; anxiety produced by that trigger; and主动 avoidance used to reduce that anxiety. My strategy was to compare each option against those components rather than asking only whether the person seemed “very afraid.” That was appropriate because several choices describe ordinary fear or personality traits, but the definition is narrower and behavior-based. The key evidence I used was the presence of broad, deliberate avoidance that reshaped daily life, since avoidance is explicitly part of the definition and often distinguishes phobia from simple dislike or nervousness. I also noticed that one option described fear generalizing beyond the original trigger, which strengthened the inference that the condition was persistent and impairing rather than momentary. A useful assumption I made was that the best answer would show both intensity and life adjustment, not just emotional reaction. However, I should recognize that I somewhat relied on clinical intuition (“pathological” vs. “normal”) instead of strictly mapping every clause of the definition to each choice. I also could have more explicitly tested the social-fear option against the definition, since fear of people can qualify if avoidance is central. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the definitional constraint of active avoidance rather than on vivid fear language like screaming or blushing. In similar problems, I should build a checklist from the definition and evaluate each option feature by feature. General rule: when a concept is defined by multiple necessary conditions, select the option that satisfies all stated conditions, especially the least obvious one that distinguishes it from close distractors.

item.context: With the rapid development of the Internet, it has become a reality to buy your favorite goods without leaving home. Even in countries and regions with a low level of economic development, people can meet their pursuit of material life through online shopping.
item.question: Which of the followings best questions the above point of view?

choices.label: A
choices.text: With the growth of online shopping sales, related taxes and fees will also increase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even in the era when there is no Internet, people can still buy the goods they want through brick-and-mortar stores

choices.label: C
choices.text: The display of goods on the Internet can not fully reflect the real situation

choices.label: D
choices.text: People's satisfaction with the pursuit of material life only depends on the level of economic development of the region

response:
Reasoning: The claim says online shopping lets people satisfy material needs even in less developed areas. The strongest challenge is that online displays may not match the actual goods, so buying online may not truly meet people’s needs or expectations. Other options are irrelevant or do not directly weaken the claim.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a direct-weaken approach, looking for an option that attacked online shopping itself, so I focused on whether Internet product displays are reliable. The key clue I overweighted was the phrase about “meeting their pursuit of material life,” which I interpreted as successful purchasing satisfaction rather than a claim about what determines that satisfaction. My mistake was treating the conclusion as a practical claim about shopping quality instead of identifying the deeper causal assumption about economic development and material satisfaction. In similar problems, I should first restate the core claim in causal or dependency terms, then choose the option that challenges that underlying relationship rather than a side issue.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument as making a practical claim about whether online shopping is a reliable way for people in less developed regions to obtain desired goods. Based on that reading, I used a direct-weaken strategy: I looked for an option showing that online purchasing may fail to deliver what consumers expect. That is why I chose the option about inaccurate online display, since it attacks the effectiveness of online shopping as a purchasing channel. However, I missed that the conclusion was framed less as a logistics claim and more as a claim about what determines people’s ability to satisfy material pursuits. The key issue was not whether online shopping is imperfect, but whether the argument wrongly treats Internet access as sufficient despite another factor possibly being decisive.

I focused on a concrete objection to one premise mechanism and ignored the deeper causal structure of the statement. In particular, I did not test whether any choice challenged the assumption that online shopping can overcome limits created by low economic development. I also underrated answers that introduce a stronger determinant of the outcome, because they looked too absolute at first glance. In problems asking which choice “best questions” a viewpoint, I should compare answers by how directly they attack the viewpoint’s core dependency, not by how plausibly they criticize a side feature. A transferable rule is: when an argument claims factor X enables outcome Y even under condition Z, the strongest challenge is often a choice asserting that Z still controls Y regardless of X.

item.context: In a certain factory, the union membership was higher in 2010 than in 2008. For the period from 2007 to 2011, the percentage of factory workers that were members of the union remained constant.
item.question: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Throughout this entire manufacturing sector, factory worker unions saw growth from 2008 to 2010

choices.label: B
choices.text: The union membership in 2009 was higher than it was in 2008

choices.label: C
choices.text: The factory had more employees in 2010 than in 2008

choices.label: D
choices.text: In 2010, there were fewer non-union employees in this factory than there were in 2008

response:
Reasoning: If the percentage of workers in the union stayed constant, then the number of union members could only rise if the total number of employees rose. Since union membership was higher in 2010 than in 2008, the factory must have had more employees in 2010 than in 2008.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple:
I used a proportional-reasoning approach: treating union membership as a constant percentage of total employees across the years. The key factor was that if a percentage stays fixed, any increase in the part implies an increase in the whole. That step made the inference to total factory employment valid, while the other choices added claims about other years, other factories, or non-union counts that were not forced by the premises.  

Lesson: In percentage problems, translate the statement into a part–whole relationship and ask which quantity must change when one quantity changes while the ratio stays constant.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the prompt as a proportional reasoning question: it asked what must follow from two facts about union membership counts and a constant membership percentage over several years. That interpretation was correct, because the key distinction was between an absolute number of union members and the percentage of workers who were union members. My strategy was to translate the verbal statements into a relationship like “union members = constant fraction × total employees,” then reason about how a higher count with the same fraction implies a larger total. That was an appropriate strategy because it focused on what is logically forced, not what merely sounds plausible.

The crucial evidence I used was the combination of “higher in 2010 than in 2008” and “percentage remained constant,” which together constrain total workforce size. I correctly ignored irrelevant temptations about the whole manufacturing sector and about non-union workers, since those are not directly entailed. One assumption I made, appropriately, was that the percentage refers to the same factory’s workforce in each year, so the base population could vary while the rate stayed fixed. I could also have checked alternatives more explicitly by asking whether each one had to be true or only could be true. What made the reasoning successful was preserving the distinction between rate and quantity. For similar problems, I should systematically express statements as equations or ratios before comparing years. General rule: when a subgroup’s proportion remains constant, any increase in the subgroup’s count requires a proportional increase in the whole group’s count.

item.context: For years scientists have been scanning the skies in the hope of finding life on other planets. But in spite of the ever-increasing sophistication of the equipment they employ, some of it costing hundreds of millions of dollars, not the first shred of evidence of such life has been forthcoming. And there is no reason to think that these scientists will be anymore successful in the future, no matter how much money is invested in the search. The dream of finding extraterrestrial life is destined to remain a dream, as science' s experience up to this point should indicate.
item.question: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only if scientists had already found evidence of life on other planets would continued search be justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Scientists searching for extraterrestrial life will not find it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is no reason to believe that life exists on other planets.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The equipment that scientists employ is not as sophisticated as it should be.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion is that the search will remain unsuccessful: despite years of effort and better equipment, no evidence has been found, and the author says there is no reason to think future searches will succeed. That matches a claim about scientists not finding extraterrestrial life, not about whether such life exists.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a conclusion-focused approach: I separated the evidence about years of unsuccessful searches and improved equipment from the author’s final claim about future results. The key factor was the shift from past failure to the prediction that the search “is destined to remain a dream,” which targets the success of the search rather than the actual existence of extraterrestrial life. My success came from distinguishing a claim about what scientists will find from a stronger, different claim about what exists. For similar main-point questions, identify the sentence that makes the author’s ultimate prediction or judgment, and choose the option that matches that claim without strengthening it or changing its subject.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the argument’s main conclusion, not for an assumption, implication, or background premise. That was the key first step, because the stimulus contains both descriptive evidence about past failed searches and a predictive claim about future failure. My strategy was to separate premises from conclusion by looking for the author’s strongest asserted claim, especially the sentence about scientists not being successful in the future and the dream remaining a dream. That was appropriate because “main point” questions usually hinge on identifying which statement the other statements are supporting.

The evidence I used correctly was the contrast between repeated searches with increasingly sophisticated equipment and the explicit claim that this lack of results indicates future searches will also fail. I also noticed an important distinction: the argument is about the success of scientists’ search, not directly about whether extraterrestrial life exists. That distinction ruled out an answer that overstates the conclusion from “we won’t find it” to “it doesn’t exist.” I did not assume the argument was sound; I only tracked what it concluded. That helped me avoid being distracted by whether the reasoning commits a hasty generalization from past failures.

The alternatives should be tested for scope and wording: some choices introduced conditions or claims about equipment that the argument never makes. What made the reasoning successful was matching the conclusion’s exact level of commitment and subject matter.
