The mayor replies with the same statistic and a comparison to predecessors, which does not answer the objection that the new jobs were filled by relocated outsiders.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a relevance-based flaw analysis: I identified the challenger’s core objection, then checked whether the mayor’s reply actually answered that objection or merely repeated favorable facts. The key factor was the distinction between an increase in the number of jobs in the city and an increase in job opportunities for existing city residents. My success came from tracking that shift carefully and noticing that the mayor responded to the statistic, not to the causal issue raised by the challenger. For similar problems, isolate the exact criticism first, then test whether the response addresses that precise point rather than a nearby but easier claim.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the flaw in the mayor’s reply specifically as a response to the challenger, not as a general criticism of the mayor’s record. My strategy was to isolate the challenger’s core objection, then test whether the mayor’s answer actually engaged that objection. The key distinction I used was between an increase in the number of jobs located in the city and an increase in job opportunities available to existing city residents. That distinction was central because the challenger did not deny the statistics; instead, the challenger argued that the added jobs were taken by relocated outsiders and therefore did not vindicate the mayor’s supporters. The mayor’s response simply repeated the job-growth figure and added a comparison with predecessors, which leaves the causal objection untouched.

This was an appropriate reasoning strategy because flaw questions often turn on whether a reply addresses the issue raised or shifts to a different claim. I did not rely on irrelevant numerical assumptions, such as how many unemployed voters existed or whether employment was a top issue, because those points were not necessary to assess the exchange. I also avoided being distracted by the mayor’s statement that the challenger “does not dispute the employment statistics,” since agreement on the numbers is compatible with disagreement about their significance. A possible alternative I should always check in such questions is whether the response misstates the opponent’s view, but here the larger defect was more direct: nonresponse to the substantive objection. The success of the reasoning came from tracking the exact target of the criticism rather than the surface topic. General rule: when evaluating a rebuttal, identify the opponent’s precise claim and ask whether the answer addresses that claim’s substance, not merely a related fact or metric.

item.context: On the first day of trout season a team of biologists went with local trout anglers to the Macawber River. Each angler who caught at least 2 trout chose exactly 2 of these trout for the biologists to weigh. A total of 90 fish were weighed. The measurements show that at the beginning of this season the average trout in the Macawber River weighed approximately 1. 6 kilograms.
item.question: The reasoning above is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: does not consider whether any fish other than trout were caught

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to take into account measurements from the same time in previous seasons

choices.label: C
choices.text: makes a generalization from a sample that is unlikely to be representative

choices.label: D
choices.text: relies on evidence that is anecdotal rather than scientific

response:
Reasoning: The sample is likely biased: only trout caught on opening day by anglers, and only from anglers who caught at least 2 trout, with those anglers choosing which 2 fish to submit. That makes the weighed fish unlikely to represent the average trout in the whole river.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-analysis approach, asking whether the evidence sample matched the broader population named in the conclusion. The key clue was the strong selection bias: only fish caught by anglers on one day were eligible, only anglers with at least two catches contributed, and those anglers themselves selected which two fish to be weighed. That chain of filtering made the sample unlikely to represent all trout in the river, which directly supported the criticism. For similar problems, I should test whether the sampling process systematically excludes or overrepresents parts of the target group before accepting any average or generalization.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the main flaw in the argument’s inference from a limited set of weighed fish to a claim about the average trout in the entire river at the start of the season. That interpretation was correct because the conclusion was a population-level claim, so the key task was to test whether the sample supported that generalization. My strategy was to look for selection bias in how the evidence was gathered rather than getting distracted by side issues about biology or seasonality. That was appropriate because the setup described several filters on which fish ended up being weighed: only fish caught by anglers, only on opening day, only from anglers who caught at least two trout, and only two fish chosen by those anglers. Those facts strongly suggest the measured fish were not randomly or neutrally selected from the river’s trout population.

The most important evidence was the anglers’ ability to choose which two fish to submit, since that creates a direct opportunity for nonrepresentative selection. I also correctly noticed that excluding anglers who caught fewer than two trout could systematically omit certain fish or locations from the sample. A bad shortcut would have been to treat “90 fish” as automatically sufficient, ignoring how they were selected; sample size does not cure sampling bias. I also properly rejected alternatives like needing prior seasons’ data, since the claim was about the current season, not change over time. The reasoning succeeded because it focused on representativeness, which is the central requirement when inferring a population average from a sample. A general rule is: when an argument estimates a population characteristic, first examine the sampling process for selection mechanisms that could systematically skew the sample away from the target population.

item.context: After a trial, the case A member said to B: I believe the suspect must be true, but he may not have said the truth.
item.question: Does A mean excluding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The suspect did not tell him what he knew.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The suspect said everything he knew.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The suspect concealed the truth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The suspect distorted the truth.

response:
Reasoning: “He must be true” suggests the suspect didn’t lie, but “may not have said the truth” means he may not have told all he knew. So A implies omission/concealment, not fabrication. The excluded meaning is “distorted the truth,” which would mean lying.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a contrast-based interpretation: I separated “must be true” from “may not have said the truth” and treated them as distinguishing honesty from completeness. The key factor was recognizing that someone can speak truthfully yet still omit relevant information, so the statement points toward concealment rather than fabrication. My success came from mapping each answer choice to that distinction and eliminating the one that required actual falsification. For similar problems, explicitly test whether the language contrasts partial truth, omission, and outright lying before matching choices.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the statement as contrasting two different dimensions of testimony: whether the suspect’s statements were false versus whether they were complete. That was the right reading, because the phrase about being “true” points to sincerity or factual correctness, while the phrase about “may not have said the truth” suggests withholding rather than inventing. My strategy was to separate kinds of dishonesty into omission and commission, then compare each choice against that distinction. That approach was appropriate because the options were semantically close, so the key was identifying which meanings remain compatible with the statement and which one is ruled out.

The main evidence I used was the tension between “must be true” and “may not have said the truth.” I treated this as allowing concealment or incomplete disclosure, but not active falsification. A crucial assumption was that “not saying the truth” in context could mean “not telling the whole truth,” not necessarily “uttering falsehoods.” That assumption was justified by the first clause, which already limited the suspect to being truthful. I should also have explicitly checked each option one by one rather than relying only on an intuitive contrast. The successful part of the reasoning was recognizing that “concealed” and “did not say everything known” are compatible with truthful but incomplete testimony. The excluded option was the one that required direct falsification, which contradicted the first clause. A transferable rule is: when a statement combines apparent opposites, first distinguish different senses of the key term, then eliminate any choice that violates one clause instead of reconciling both.

item.context: The results showed that after heating sweet corn for 10 minutes, 25 minutes and 50 minutes at 115  degree, its anti free radical activity increased by 22%, 44% and 53% respectively. Therefore, the longer the heating time, the better the anti-aging effect of corn.
item.question: Which of the following items, if true,  cannotweaken the above conclusion:

choices.label: A
choices.text: After heating for 65 minutes, the anti free radical activity of maize decreased

choices.label: B
choices.text: Compared with sweet corn, the increase of anti free radical activity of waxy corn after heating for the same time is very small

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sweet corn is a rare kind of corn, which is not representative

choices.label: D
choices.text: For maize, it is not that the higher the activity of anti free radical, the better its anti-aging effect

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion links longer heating time to better anti-aging effect for corn generally. A weakens it by showing decline at 65 min; C weakens representativeness; D weakens the assumed link between anti-free-radical activity and anti-aging. B only says waxy corn improves less than sweet corn, not that longer heating is worse.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a weakening-test approach: check which option fails to attack the conclusion’s logic, evidence, or scope. The key factor was separating the claim about “longer heating time” from side issues like differences across corn varieties; an option only weakens if it undermines the time→effect relationship or the proxy from anti-free-radical activity to anti-aging. My success came from noticing that one choice merely compared another type of corn with sweet corn, without showing that increasing heating time stops helping within the studied case. For similar problems, map the conclusion into its exact variables and scope, then eliminate choices that introduce a different comparison instead of challenging that specific link.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the option that does **not** undercut the argument’s conclusion, so the task was to identify the statement least damaging to the inference rather than the one most supported by the data. My strategy was to separate the argument into its evidence and conclusion: the evidence concerned increased anti-free-radical activity in sweet corn at several heating times, while the conclusion generalized from that to a broader claim about longer heating and anti-aging effects of corn. That was an appropriate strategy because weakening questions usually turn on whether a choice attacks the data pattern, the scope of the generalization, or the link between indicator and claimed outcome. I correctly noticed three vulnerable points: the time trend could fail at longer durations, the sample might not represent corn generally, and anti-free-radical activity might not justify claims about anti-aging. I also used a useful contrast test on the remaining option: if another corn type improves less than sweet corn for the same heating time, that does not show that increasing heating time is ineffective within the studied case. An assumption in my reasoning was that “cannot weaken” means even if true, the option leaves the core inference intact, not merely weakens it only slightly. I should also have explicitly distinguished between attacking **magnitude across varieties** and attacking the **direction of effect over time**. The reasoning succeeded because I tracked relevance precisely: a statement about cross-variety differences does not by itself refute a time-based trend. In similar problems, I should map each choice to a specific premise-conclusion link and ask, “Does this challenge trend, scope, or causal bridge?” A transferable rule is: when evaluating weaken-except questions, eliminate choices that attack any necessary inferential step, and keep the one that introduces a difference irrelevant to that step.

item.context: Faced with a financial crisis, Upland University' s board of trustees reduced the budget for the university' s computer center from last year' s $4 million to $1. 5 million for the coming year. However, the center cannot operate on less than $2. 5 million. Since the board cannot divert funds from other programs to the computer center, there is no way that the center can be kept operating for the coming year.
item.question: The conclusion of the argument is properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The computer center has no source of funds other than those budgeted to it for the coming year by the university's board of trustees.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The budgets of other programs at the university were also reduced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The computer center did not use all of the $4 million that was budgeted to it last year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The board of trustees at the university value other programs at the university more highly than they do the computer center.

response:
Reasoning: To conclude the center cannot be kept operating, we must assume it has no other possible funding besides the board’s allocation. We already know the board cannot divert other university funds, and $1.5 million is below the $2.5 million needed. Without assuming no outside/other funds, the conclusion would not follow.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a necessary-assumption approach: identify the gap between the premises and the conclusion, then ask what unstated condition must hold for the conclusion to be guaranteed. The key factor was that the argument rules out only one funding option—transfers from other programs—while the conclusion says there is “no way” to keep the center operating, which requires eliminating any other possible source of money. The successful step was noticing that without an assumption excluding alternative funding, the conclusion is too strong. For similar problems, test strong conclusions by checking whether all plausible alternatives have been ruled out; if not, the needed assumption is the one that closes that exact loophole.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a necessary-assumption problem: the issue was not which statement sounded helpful, but which unstated premise had to be true for the conclusion to follow. My strategy was to identify the gap between the premises and the conclusion. The premises established only that the board’s allocation was below the center’s minimum operating requirement and that funds could not be shifted from other university programs. The conclusion, however, was stronger: that there was no way to keep the center operating. That stronger claim required ruling out every other possible funding source, and I correctly focused on that missing link.

The key evidence I used was the mismatch between the $1.5 million budget and the $2.5 million minimum, combined with the explicit restriction on internal reallocation. I did not assume that a budget shortfall alone proves shutdown; instead, I tested what alternative means of operating might still exist. The crucial assumption was that the center lacked any independent or external source of funds, including carryover money, donations, grants, or fees. I appropriately rejected answer choices that were merely plausible background facts but not logically required. What made the reasoning successful was treating the conclusion as universal (“no way”) and asking what possibility would weaken it. In similar problems, I should continue using the rule: for necessary-assumption questions, identify the exact logical gap and ask what alternative scenario must be excluded for the conclusion to stand.

item.context: Commentator: A political constitution that provides the framework for the laws of a nation must be interpreted to apply to new situations not envisioned by its authors. Although these interpretations express the moral and political beliefs of the interpreters, they are usually portrayed as embodying the intentions of the authors. This fiction is vital because without it the illusion, so necessary for political stability, that laws are the bequest of a long tradition rather than the preferences of contemporary politicians would vanish.
item.question: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the commentator's statements, if they are true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The perceived lack of a long legal tradition in a nation makes the political stability of that nation dependent upon the fiction that its present political leaders share the intentions of the authors of the constitution of that nation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Political instability will ensue if people come to believe there is a divergence between the beliefs of the authors of their constitution and those of their present political leaders.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A written constitution preserves the illusion that laws are the bequest of a long tradition rather than the creations of modern politicians.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Political instability will increase if the people of a nation cease to believe that their constitution is being interpreted consistently with the intentions of its authors.

response:
Reasoning: The commentator says portraying interpretations as authorial intent is a vital fiction because otherwise the illusion necessary for political stability would vanish. So if people stop believing interpretations match the authors’ intentions, political instability would increase. A adds unsupported claims; B is too broad; C overstates what a written constitution itself does.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a direct support approach: identify the causal chain in the stimulus and match it to the choice that restates it with minimal distortion. The key factor was the claim that the “fiction” of fidelity to the authors’ intentions is “vital” because without it the illusion necessary for political stability would disappear. My success came from translating that into a conditional idea: if that belief goes away, stability is undermined, and then rejecting choices that added new elements like present leaders or written constitutions themselves. For similar problems, isolate the author’s explicit causal claim and prefer the option that weakly paraphrases it rather than one that extends it with extra assumptions.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the claim most directly supported by the commentator’s premises, not the claim that sounded most plausible politically. My strategy was to identify the causal chain in the stimulus: constitutional interpretations are presented as authorial intent; that presentation sustains an illusion of continuity with tradition; and that illusion is said to be necessary for political stability. That was the right strategy because “most strongly supported” questions usually turn on tracing explicit dependencies rather than importing outside assumptions. The key evidence I used was the commentator’s statement that the fiction is “vital” because without it the necessary illusion would vanish. From that, it is reasonable to infer that if the fiction collapses, stability is threatened or reduced.

I also correctly rejected choices that added new conditions, such as claims about nations lacking a long tradition or about “present political leaders” specifically, because the stimulus did not mention those elements. Another good move was noticing that one option attributed too much power to the mere existence of a written constitution, whereas the stimulus focused on how interpretations are portrayed. The strongest support depended on public belief about interpretation, not on constitutional form alone. My reasoning succeeded because I distinguished between what is necessary in the argument and what is merely associated with it. In similar problems, I should continue mapping necessity claims carefully: if X is vital because without X, Y disappears, and Y is necessary for Z, then losing X supports predicting reduced Z. General rule: on inference questions, prefer the answer that preserves the exact causal and conceptual structure of the stimulus with the fewest added assumptions.

item.context: If one wants to succeed, then one should act as though one were genuinely confident about one' s abilities, even if one actually distrusts one' s skills. Success is much more easily obtained by those who genuinely believe themselves capable of succeeding than by those filled with self-doubts.
item.question: Which one of the following statements, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Success is usually more a matter of luck or determination than of skill.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Self-doubt can hamper as well as aid the development of the skills necessary for success.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genuine confidence is often a by-product of pretended self-confidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Those who convince others that they are capable of succeeding usually have few self-doubts.

response:
Reasoning: The argument recommends acting confident despite self-doubt because genuine confidence helps success. The strongest support is that pretending confidence often produces genuine confidence, linking the recommended behavior to the stated advantage. The other choices are less directly supportive or irrelevant.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a strengthen-the-argument approach by identifying the conclusion, the stated premise, and the gap between them. The key factor was that the argument moves from “genuine confidence helps success” to “therefore, act confident even if you are not,” so it needed a bridge connecting pretended confidence to real confidence. My success came from spotting that one choice directly linked the recommended action to the beneficial condition cited in the premise. For similar problems, explicitly ask: “What missing causal or logical link would make the conclusion follow from the evidence?”
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a strengthen-the-argument task: the stimulus gives a recommendation, and I needed the answer choice that most directly supports the move from premise to advice. The key structure was that the author claims genuine confidence helps produce success, then concludes that even people who lack confidence should act confident. My strategy was to look for the missing bridge between “genuine confidence is useful” and “pretending confidence is advisable.” That was the right strategy because strengthen questions often turn on identifying the argument’s gap rather than just finding a generally favorable statement.

The crucial relationship I used was that acting confident is not the same as being genuinely confident, so the argument needed some connection between the two. The credited choice supplied exactly that connection by indicating that pretended confidence can lead to real confidence. I correctly rejected answers that were merely adjacent to the topic, such as those about skill development or how others perceive confidence, because they did not directly justify the recommendation. One assumption I implicitly tested was that the advice only makes sense if the recommended behavior has some tendency to produce the condition the author says is beneficial. I also properly noticed that a statement weakening the importance of confidence for success would not strengthen the argument. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the argument’s internal gap instead of on surface-level relevance. In similar problems, I should continue mapping premise-to-conclusion links and asking what unstated premise would make the conclusion more reasonable. A transferable rule is: when an argument recommends a behavior because of the value of some state, the best strengthening evidence often shows that the behavior tends to create that state.

item.context: Advertisement: My five-year-old identical twins wear matching clothing. I washed two of their soiled matching shirts, one in my regular laundry detergent, and one in new WAVE laundry detergent. The shirt washed in WAVE came out cleaner than the other shirt, so WAVE cleans better than my regular laundry detergent.
item.question: Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument in the advertisement above depends?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most pairs of young identical twins tend to wear matching clothing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The shirt laundered in the regular laundry detergent was not significantly less clean than the other shirt before being laundered.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clothes washed in WAVE laundry detergent will come out cleaner than clothes washed in any other brand of laundry detergent

choices.label: D
choices.text: A soiled shirt laundered on a regular basis in the same laundry detergent will come out equally clean each time it is laundered.

response:
Reasoning: The argument compares two shirts after washing and concludes WAVE is better. This requires assuming the shirts were similarly dirty beforehand; otherwise, the cleaner result could just be because that shirt started out less soiled. Choice B states that needed assumption.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-analysis approach: identify the conclusion, then ask what must be true for the evidence to support it. The key factor was the comparison between two washed shirts—this comparison only supports the detergent claim if the shirts started at roughly the same level of dirtiness. My success came from spotting that a difference in initial conditions would create an alternative explanation for the outcome. For similar problems, test causal or comparative claims by checking whether the items being compared were equivalent before the treatment, and eliminate choices that are stronger than necessary.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking for a necessary assumption behind the advertisement’s inference, not for a fact that would strengthen it most or a conclusion that follows from it. The core argument moved from a single comparison of two washed shirts to a claim that one detergent cleans better than the other. My strategy was to test what must be true for that comparison to support the conclusion, which is the right approach for assumption questions. I focused on whether the shirts were comparable before washing, because if they were not, the observed difference after washing would not isolate the effect of the detergents. The key evidence was the causal structure: to attribute the cleaner outcome to the detergent, other relevant variables must not differ in a way that explains the result. I correctly identified initial dirtiness as one such variable and recognized that the argument depends on ruling out the possibility that the shirt washed in the regular detergent started out dirtier. I did not get distracted by broader or stronger claims, such as whether the detergent works better than every other brand or whether identical twins usually wear matching clothes. That was important because assumption questions often tempt test-takers with irrelevant context or overly strong statements. What made the reasoning successful was matching the assumption to the exact gap between evidence and conclusion rather than to the topic generally. In similar problems, I should continue asking: “What alternative explanation would break the argument, and what must be true to block it?” A general rule is that when an argument infers causation or superiority from a comparison, it usually assumes the items compared were relevantly similar before the tested factor was introduced.

item.context: Counselor: Many people assume that personal conflicts are inevitable, but that assumption is just not so. Personal conflicts arise primarily because people are being irrational. For instance, people often find it easier to ascribe bad qualities to a person than good ones -- even when there is more evidence of the latter. If someone suspects that a friend is unreliable, for example, a single instance may turn this suspicion into a feeling of certainty, whereas a belief that someone is reliable is normally built up only after many years of personal interaction.
item.question: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion drawn in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Personal conflicts are not inevitable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is irrational to allow a single instance to turn one's suspicion that a friend is unreliable into a feeling of certainty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Even when there is more evidence of good qualities than of bad ones, people find it easier to ascribe bad qualities than good ones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unlike a suspicion that a friend is unreliable, a belief that someone is reliable is normally built up only after many years of personal interaction.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion is the claim the counselor is arguing for: the assumption that personal conflicts are inevitable is false. The rest explains why—conflicts arise from irrationality—and gives an example of irrational negative judgment. So the main conclusion is that personal conflicts are not inevitable.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a conclusion-identification approach: I separated the author’s main point from the supporting explanation and example. The key clue was the contrast between the common assumption and the counselor’s rebuttal, followed by “for instance,” which signaled that the later claims were evidence rather than the thesis. My success came from treating the irrationality discussion and the friend example as support for the broader claim, not as competing conclusions. For similar problems, first locate the statement that the rest of the passage is trying to justify, and treat examples or psychological explanations as premises unless the argument explicitly builds toward them.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the stimulus as asking for the argument’s top-level claim, not a supported subclaim or illustrative example. That was the right framing, because the passage begins with a common assumption and immediately rejects it, which is a classic indicator of the main conclusion. My strategy was to separate the claims by role: thesis, supporting reason, and example. Specifically, I treated the statement about conflicts arising from irrationality as support for the broader point, and I treated the discussion of how people judge unreliability as evidence for that support. That structure fit the passage well because the “for instance” phrase clearly marks what follows as illustrative rather than central. The key evidence I used was the hierarchy of support: example about negative attributions → claim about irrationality → rejection of inevitability. I did not assume that the most psychologically detailed statement was the conclusion; instead, I looked for what the other statements were trying to establish. An alternative mistake would have been to choose the vivid example about judging friends, since test writers often place appealing detail in answer choices. The reasoning succeeded because I tracked argument indicators and distinguished between a claim being explained and a claim being defended. For similar problems, I should keep mapping each sentence’s function before comparing choices. A transferable rule is: in main-conclusion questions, prefer the claim that the other statements collectively support, and treat “for example,” “for instance,” and similar markers as evidence that a statement is not the primary conclusion.

item.context: Anthropologist: It has been claimed that religious prohibitions against eating certain types of food are evidence against the belief that all cultural phenomena have a purely economic explanation. After all, the reasoning goes, only a moral or spiritual motive could persuade people to forgo readily available sources of nutrients. But the species whose consumption is prohibited are usually essential elements of ecosystems containing other species that are used as food. The preservation of the prohibited species thus tends to help preserve the other species. Ttherefore, such prohibitions do indeed have an economic motivation.
item.question: The reasoning in the anthropologist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that people could have a reason for adopting a certain policy and nevertheless not realize what that reason is

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses the key term prohibition in two different senses

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers, merely from the claim that a practice has a certain desirable consequence, that this consequence must provide a motivation for the practice

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers, merely from the claim that a certain cultural phenomenon has no economic explanation, that the explanation of this phenomenon must be spiritual or moral

response:
Reasoning: The anthropologist argues that because food taboos help preserve ecosystems and thus food supplies, they therefore have an economic motivation. That wrongly infers motive from beneficial effect: a practice’s desirable consequence does not show that consequence motivated the practice.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-identification approach: I separated the argument’s evidence from its conclusion and checked whether the conclusion about motivation was actually supported. The key clue was the shift from “this prohibition helps preserve food resources” to “therefore it was economically motivated,” which moves from consequence to cause. My success came from recognizing that beneficial effects do not by themselves establish the reason a practice was adopted. For similar problems, test whether an argument is illegitimately inferring intention, motive, or origin from the fact that something produces a useful outcome.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the flaw in the anthropologist’s reasoning, not whether the conclusion itself might be true. The key issue was the move from “this prohibition has an economically beneficial effect” to “therefore it was economically motivated.” My strategy was to track the argument’s structure: objection, rebuttal, evidence, conclusion, and then test whether the conclusion was stronger than the evidence. That was appropriate here because LSAT flaw questions often hinge on a gap between observed consequences and inferred intentions. The crucial fact I used was that preserving a species can help preserve food sources, but I also noticed that this only establishes a possible benefit, not an actual motive. I avoided being distracted by the mention of “moral or spiritual motive,” since the flaw was not mainly about excluding those motives but about illegitimately proving an economic one. One assumption embedded in the argument is that beneficial outcomes reveal the reason a practice arose or was maintained. I should also have considered whether the argument confused explanation at the social level with motivation at the individual level, though that would still support the same flaw pattern. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the difference between consequence and cause. In similar problems, I should explicitly ask whether the evidence shows origin, purpose, or merely effect. A good general rule is: never infer a practice’s motivating reason solely from the fact that the practice produces a useful result.

item.context: In terms of high-level determination and public awareness, the pace of air pollution control is accelerating. Adjusting energy structure, industrial transformation and upgrading, the need for the government to do more, this is an indisputable priority. At the same time, as every citizen can do less complaining, do more from their own, such as no firecrackers, take more public transport and so on.
item.question: Which of the following is the main point of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every citizen should bear his due responsibility in air pollution control

choices.label: B
choices.text: Air pollution control needs the joint efforts of the government and every citizen

choices.label: C
choices.text: The government should assume the primary responsibility in air pollution control

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both the government and citizens have begun to take an active part in air pollution control

response:
Reasoning: The text says government action is an “indisputable priority” for structural changes, while citizens should also act in daily life. So the central idea is that both sides must contribute, not just one or merely that they already have.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea synthesis approach: I identified the two groups mentioned and compared their roles instead of focusing on a single sentence. The key factor was the passage’s contrast structure—first stressing government action as a priority, then adding that citizens should also change everyday behavior—showing complementary responsibilities. The successful step was not letting the stronger wording about the government overshadow the second half of the passage. For similar problems, combine all major claims in the passage and choose the option that captures their relationship, not just the most emphatic detail.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s central claim, not a supporting detail or a description of current events. That was the right framing, because the text contrasts two levels of action: government-led structural measures and citizen-led everyday behavior. My strategy was to identify the passage’s structure and ask what idea unified both parts, rather than focusing on the strongest individual phrase. That approach was appropriate because main-point questions usually require synthesis across sentences, especially when the passage presents multiple actors or responsibilities.

The key evidence I used was that the government is described as having a priority role in major policy areas, while citizens are also urged to change personal habits. I correctly noticed that the passage was normative—about what should be done—rather than simply reporting that people are already participating, which ruled out the option about activity already having begun. I also avoided the common shortcut of treating the sentence with the strongest wording (“indisputable priority”) as automatically the main point. Instead, I recognized that this phrase only specified one side of a broader shared-responsibility argument.

An alternative I needed to keep in mind was that some answer choices can capture only one paragraph component, making them too narrow. What made the reasoning successful was matching the answer to the full scope of the passage. In similar problems, I should continue separating “main idea” from “emphasized detail.” A transferable rule is: when a passage assigns complementary roles to multiple parties, the main point is usually the combined responsibility unless the text explicitly excludes one side.

item.context: If a person's behavior has a harmful impact on others and society, others or society can certainly blame and interfere with him. But what if this is not the case? For example, if a person smokes in the house where he lives alone, a person yells in the wilderness, and a person surfs the Internet in the middle of the night, should we care? In my opinion, whether or not to interfere with an act depends on whether such interference is conducive to the improvement of the public interest, whether it infringes upon the legitimate rights of the parties, and so on.
item.question: Which of the followings is what the speaker in the subject is most willing to say?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Social interests always take precedence over personal interests

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interference with individual behavior does not improve the interests of society as a whole.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acts that do not harm the interests of others should not be criticized and interfered by society.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When one person's behavior is beneficial to others, the overall interests of a society can be improved.

response:
Reasoning: The speaker says interference should depend on public interest and rights. For acts like smoking alone, yelling in wilderness, surfing at night—if they don’t harm others, society need not interfere. This matches the idea that harmless private acts should not be criticized or interfered with.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a principle-matching approach: I compared the speaker’s stated criterion for interference—public interest and legitimate rights—with the choices to find the one that best restated that standard. The key clue was the contrast between behaviors that harm others and private acts that do not, which showed the speaker rejects automatic interference in harmless personal conduct. My success came from focusing on the conditional structure of the argument rather than extreme wording in the options. For similar problems, first extract the author’s decision rule, then choose the option that matches its scope and conditions without exaggerating it into an absolute claim.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the option that best captures the speaker’s governing principle, not merely one example from the passage. My strategy was to extract the decision rule stated at the end: interference is justified only when it serves public interest and does not violate legitimate rights. That was an appropriate approach because the examples were illustrative, while the final sentence gave the actual standard for judgment. I used the key contrast in the passage between behaviors that harm others and behaviors that appear private and non-harmful. From that contrast, I inferred that society’s blame or intervention is not warranted for conduct that does not affect others’ interests. I also implicitly rejected stronger claims, such as the idea that social interests always override personal interests, because the speaker includes protection of legitimate rights as a constraint. One assumption in my reasoning was that the listed private acts were meant as paradigms of non-harmful conduct; that assumption fit the author’s wording and examples. I should still have explicitly checked whether any option overstated the conclusion, since multiple choices often turn on words like “always” or broad causal claims. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the answer choice to the speaker’s conditional principle rather than to a peripheral detail. In similar problems, I should identify the author’s criterion, then test each option for scope, strength, and consistency with all stated conditions. A transferable rule is: when a passage presents examples and then states a standard, choose the option that paraphrases the standard with the least distortion, not the one that merely echoes a topic word.

item.context: Henry: Some scientists explain the dance of honeybees as the means by which honeybees communicate the location of whatever food source they have just visited to other members of the hive. But honeybees do not need so complicated a mechanism to communicate that information. Forager honeybees returning to their hive simply leave a scent trail from the food source they have just visited. There must ttherefore be some other explanation for the honeybees' dance. Winifred: Not necessarily. Most animals have several ways of accomplishing critical tasks. Bees of some species can navigate using either the position of the Sun or the memory of landmarks. Similarly, for honeybees, scent trails are a supplementary not an exclusive means of communicating.
item.question: The point at issue between Henry and Winifred is whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: there is more than one valid explanation for the dance of the honeybees

choices.label: B
choices.text: the honeybee is the only species of bee that is capable of communicating navigational information to other hive members

choices.label: C
choices.text: honeybees communicate the location of food sources through their dance

choices.label: D
choices.text: theories of animal behavior can be established on the basis of evidence about only one species of animal

response:
Reasoning: Henry denies that the dance explains how honeybees communicate food location, since he thinks scent trails do that instead. Winifred argues scent trails could be only supplementary, so the dance could still communicate location. Thus they disagree about whether honeybees use dance to communicate food-source location.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a disagreement-identification approach: I paraphrased each speaker’s conclusion and looked for the exact claim one rejects and the other allows. The key factor was Henry’s inference that because scent trails can convey food location, the dance must have some different function, while Winifred directly challenges that inference by saying scent trails can be merely supplementary. The successful step was focusing on their competing views about the dance’s role rather than on the side example about other species. For similar problems, isolate each speaker’s bottom-line claim and test answer choices against the precise proposition on which their conclusions diverge.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the exact proposition on which Henry and Winifred disagree, not for a summary of their broader views about bees. That interpretation was correct because “the point at issue” in dialogue questions usually means the claim one speaker accepts and the other rejects. My strategy was to identify Henry’s conclusion, then test whether Winifred directly challenged that conclusion or only one premise. Henry’s reasoning was: if scent trails already communicate food location, then the dance is unnecessary for that purpose, so its explanation must lie elsewhere. Winifred attacked the necessity assumption by arguing that animals can use multiple mechanisms for the same important function. The key evidence I used was her statement that scent trails are “supplementary not exclusive,” which preserves a communicative role for the dance rather than replacing it. I did not get distracted by examples about other bee species or scientific method, which were not central to the disagreement. A possible trap was to think they were debating whether there are multiple explanations for the dance, but Winifred was really defending coexistence of multiple communication methods, not multiple explanations of the dance’s purpose. The reasoning succeeded because I translated each speaker’s statements into a clear yes/no stance on a single claim. For similar problems, I should map each speaker’s commitments separately and ask whether one denies the other’s conclusion or merely qualifies a premise. General rule: in “point at issue” questions, isolate a proposition such that one speaker must agree with it and the other must reject it, rather than choosing a statement that is merely discussed.

item.context: In nature, microscopic objects generally refer to particles with a spatial scale of less than 10-6 cm and a mass of less than 10-15 grams, including molecules, atoms, atomic nuclei, elementary particles and other material levels. Microscopic particles and various phenomena in extremely small spaces. , Generally referred to as microscopic phenomena. Microscopic particles and microscopic phenomena are collectively referred to as the microscopic world. The motion of the microscopic world obeys the laws reflected by quantum mechanics and quantum electrodynamics.
item.question: Which of the following is the most accurate retelling of the main meaning of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: What is a micro object

choices.label: B
choices.text: What are the components of micro-objects

choices.label: C
choices.text: What is a micro phenomenon

choices.label: D
choices.text: What is the micro world

response:
Reasoning: The passage defines microscopic objects and microscopic phenomena, then states these together are called the microscopic world, which is the overall focus. So the most accurate summary is the definition of the microscopic world.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a synthesis approach: instead of stopping at the first definition, I tracked how the passage builds from smaller concepts to a broader category. The key factor was the sentence saying microscopic particles and microscopic phenomena are collectively called the microscopic world, which showed the passage’s central idea is the umbrella concept rather than any single component. My success came from recognizing the text’s structure—definitions of parts followed by a final inclusive definition. For similar problems, identify whether a passage lists subparts in order to explain a larger whole, and choose the option that captures that highest-level concept.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s overall main idea, not for a detail that appeared in only one sentence. That interpretation was correct because the prompt asked for the “most accurate retelling of the main meaning,” which requires identifying the broadest concept that organizes all the definitions. My strategy was to track the structure of the passage: first it defines microscopic objects, then microscopic phenomena, and finally unifies them under a larger category. That was an appropriate summarization strategy because main-idea questions often hinge on the relationship between listed parts and the final umbrella concept.

The key evidence I used was the passage’s explicit progression from parts to whole. I recognized that the text was not merely listing examples or focusing only on one subtopic, but building toward a comprehensive definition. An assumption that helped, and happened to be justified, was that the final sentence naming the collective category signaled the author’s central point. I also correctly rejected narrower alternatives that captured only one component, such as the object definition or phenomenon definition alone.

What made the reasoning successful was matching answer scope to passage scope. For similar problems, I should keep testing each option by asking: does it cover everything in the passage, or only one section of it? A transferable rule is: when a passage defines multiple subcategories and then combines them into a larger labeled whole, the main idea is usually that larger unifying concept.

item.context: Using broad-spectrum weed killers on weeds that are competing with crops for sunlight, water, and nutrients presents a difficulty: how to keep the crop from being killed along with the weeds. For at least some food crops, specially treated seed that produces plants resistant to weed killers is under development. This resistance wears off as the plants mature. Ttherefore, the special seed treatment will be especially useful for plants that __.
item.question: Which of the following most logically completes the argument below?

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide, as they approach maturity, shade dense enough to keep weeds from growing

choices.label: B
choices.text: produce large seeds that are easy to treat individually, as corn and beans do

choices.label: C
choices.text: are cultivated specifically for the seed they produce rather than for their leaves or roots

choices.label: D
choices.text: produce their crop over an extended period of time, as summer squash does

response:
Reasoning: The resistance disappears as plants mature, so it helps most if mature crop plants can suppress weeds without herbicide afterward. Plants that develop dense shade near maturity would prevent weed growth once resistance wears off. Other options don’t solve the timing problem.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a conditional/timing-based approach: identify the problem the seed treatment solves early on, then ask what must happen after the resistance fades. The key clue was that the protection “wears off as the plants mature,” so the best crops are those that no longer need chemical weed control at that stage. The successful step was connecting the loss of resistance to a natural late-stage weed-suppression mechanism. For similar problems, map each answer choice to the argument’s timeline and pick the one that directly closes the gap created when a stated benefit ends.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which crop characteristic would make temporary herbicide resistance most valuable, given that the resistance ends at maturity. That interpretation was correct because the key issue was not simply “which crops can be treated,” but “which crops remain protected after the treatment’s benefit disappears.” My strategy was to trace the time sequence in the stimulus: early growth requires protection from weeds, and later growth requires some other mechanism once resistance fades. That was an appropriate strategy because the argument hinges on the transition from immature to mature plants.

The central fact I used was that weed competition matters early, while the crop’s own mature traits may later reduce or eliminate that problem. I correctly focused on a choice that supplied a later-stage, non-herbicide way to suppress weeds. I also correctly rejected options that were relevant to seed handling, harvesting goals, or croping duration but did not address the timing problem created by temporary resistance. One assumption that helped was that the best answer must directly resolve the specific “difficulty” stated in the prompt, not just describe a crop that could in some general way benefit from treatment. An alternative I needed to consider, and did consider, was whether long production periods would make temporary resistance more useful, but that actually worsens the mismatch between fading resistance and continuing vulnerability.

What made the reasoning successful was identifying the missing condition: a crop must become self-protective as it matures. For similar problems, I should continue mapping each answer choice against the causal chain and timing constraints in the stimulus. A transferable rule is: when a benefit is temporary, the best completion usually names a feature that takes over the needed function after the benefit ends.

item.context: In the past 20 years, the relative position of BRICS and developed countries in Europe and America has changed rapidly and greatly. What needs to be emphasized is not only rapid and huge, but also coincidental, because the rise of the BRICS countries follow very different development strategies and different growth models. Apart from the synchronization of time, the BRICS economic miracle has little in common. If the BRICS miracle does mean anything, perhaps the most accurate conclusion is that these countries have tested the ancient truth that all roads lead to Rome with their own success. it proves that emerging economies can rise on their own and catch up with and surpass the Western world.
item.question: Which of the following is the main content of this text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fixed consultation mechanism should be established among BRICS countries

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every country has the right to choose its own path of development

choices.label: C
choices.text: Emerging economies show strength that impresses the world

choices.label: D
choices.text: There are great differences in development models among BRICS countries

response:
Reasoning: The passage stresses that BRICS succeeded through very different strategies, showing there is no single Western path to modernization. The key idea is that countries can choose development roads suited to themselves. D is only a supporting point, not the main message.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach: identify the author’s conclusion and separate it from supporting details. The key clue was the sentence comparing the BRICS experience to “all roads lead to Rome,” which generalizes from their different models to a broader principle about development paths. My answer was correct because I treated the differences among BRICS countries as evidence, not the central claim. For similar questions, first locate the broad takeaway or author’s judgment, then reject options that merely restate examples, background, or supporting facts.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s central thesis rather than a detail that was merely emphasized along the way, and that was the key to arriving at the right choice. My strategy was to separate supporting observations from the author’s concluding claim: the text first notes the rapid rise of BRICS, then stresses their differing models, and finally draws a broader implication from that contrast. That structure matters because “different development strategies” is presented as evidence for a larger point, not as the endpoint of the passage. I used the cue phrase “if the BRICS miracle does mean anything, perhaps the most accurate conclusion is…” to identify where the main idea was explicitly stated. I also recognized that the passage contrasts diverse paths with a common outcome, which supports a principle about development autonomy rather than a claim limited to BRICS alone. One assumption that helped, appropriately, was that authorial conclusions often appear near the end in summary language. I still needed to consider alternatives carefully, especially the option about differences among BRICS, because it was strongly represented in the text and could have been mistaken for the main idea. What made the reasoning successful was distinguishing between a premise and the inference drawn from it. For similar problems, I should keep asking: which option restates evidence, and which option captures the author’s final abstraction from that evidence? A transferable rule is: when a passage presents examples or contrasts and then states what they “prove” or “mean,” the main idea is usually that concluding principle, not the examples themselves.

item.context: Mimicry refers to that some organisms have a similar form with another organism or surrounding natural objects in the process of evolution. This similarity is very high and almost difficult to distinguish. It can protect one species or two species.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following belongs to mimicry?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Although dolphins, penguins and hairtail belong to cetaceans, birds and fish respectively, they have evolved streamlined bodies to adapt to marine life.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Polar bears live in the snowy Arctic. In order to protect themselves from being discovered by prey, their fur gradually turns white similar to the surrounding environment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Giant salamander, commonly known as giant salamander, has lived on the earth for hundreds of millions of years. When stimulated, its cry is similar to the cry of human babies, which makes people can't bear to hurt. It also has a deterrent effect on some predators.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cuckoos will lay eggs similar to their host eggs in the host nest, and their chicks will squeeze the host chicks out of the nest soon after hatching, and enjoy the feeding of their host parents who are only half their size.

response:
Reasoning: Mimicry is close resemblance to another organism/object to deceive or gain protection. A is convergent adaptation, B is protective coloration, and C is sound imitation. D describes cuckoo eggs mimicking host eggs, a classic case of mimicry.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a category-matching approach, looking for the option that best fit the idea of one organism resembling another organism to gain protection or advantage. The key factor that misled me was overemphasizing resemblance to another organism, so I chose the egg example and underweighted that the definition also explicitly includes resemblance to surrounding natural objects. My mistake was applying a narrower, textbook-style notion of mimicry instead of using the broader definition given in the prompt. In similar problems, I should anchor my reasoning to the exact wording of the provided definition and test every option against all parts of that definition before choosing the most familiar example.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the definition too narrowly by treating mimicry as only resemblance to another organism used to deceive a perceiver. The wording, however, explicitly included resemblance to “surrounding natural objects,” so the concept in this question was broader than the biological subtype I focused on. My strategy was to classify each option by standard textbook categories—convergent evolution, camouflage, acoustic imitation, and brood-parasitic egg mimicry—and then pick the one that matched my preferred technical definition. That strategy was inappropriate because the task required matching the option to the definition as given in the prompt, not importing a stricter external definition. I used one valid fact—that brood parasites can mimic host eggs—but I missed the stronger clue that environmental resemblance for protection was directly named in the definition. I also assumed “protect one species or two species” pointed toward interspecies resemblance, which biased me away from camouflage-like resemblance to background objects. I should have considered that exam definitions in verbal reasoning often merge categories that biology may separate. The main error was replacing the problem’s operational definition with my own disciplinary schema. In similar problems, I should first extract the exact necessary conditions from the stated definition and test each option only against those conditions. A transferable rule is: when a question supplies a definition, prioritize that local definition over outside taxonomy, especially if answer choices include borderline cases.

item.context: Over 90 percent of the human brain currently serves no purpose, as is evident from the fact that many people with significant brain damage show no discernible adverse effects. So once humans begin to tap into this tremendous source of creativity and innovation, many problems that today seem insurmountable will be within our ability to solve.
item.question: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The argument infers that certain parts of the brain do nothing merely on the basis of the assertion that we do not know what they do.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The argument presumes, without providing justification, that the only reason that any problem remains unsolved is a lack of creativity and innovation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The argument infers that problems will be solved merely on the basis of the claim that they will be within our ability to solve.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The argument presumes, without providing justification, that the currently unused parts of the brain are a potential source of tremendous creativity and innovation.

response:
Reasoning: The argument moves from “90% of the brain serves no purpose” and “some brain damage has no visible effects” to the claim that these unused parts could provide “tremendous creativity and innovation.” That crucial link is unsupported. It is not merely ignorance (A), nor about all unsolved problems (B), nor a modal confusion (C).

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a gap-finding approach: identify the evidence, identify the conclusion, then test what hidden assumption is needed to get from one to the other. The key factor was that the argument didn’t just claim most of the brain is unused; it went further and treated that supposed unused portion as a reservoir of creativity and innovation. My success came from noticing that this is the unsupported bridge in the reasoning, rather than getting distracted by weaker issues in the wording. For similar flaw questions, isolate the exact new concept introduced in the conclusion and check whether the premises give any reason to attribute that property.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the argument’s logical flaw, not whether its factual claims about the brain are true. My strategy was to identify the conclusion, then look for the missing link between the premises and that conclusion. The key conclusion was not just that much of the brain is unused, but that using it would yield major gains in creativity and innovation that would help solve difficult problems. I noticed that the premises gave, at most, a claim about lack of present function, supported by anecdotal brain-damage observations, but they did not establish anything about positive untapped capacity. That made D the best match, because it targets the unsupported move from “unused” to “valuable source of creativity.”

I also compared the alternatives by checking whether they described the actual inferential gap. A was too strong because the argument did not rest simply on ignorance about brain function; it offered supposed evidence from brain damage. B overstated the conclusion, since the argument did not claim that lack of creativity is the only reason problems remain unsolved. C focused on a weaker verbal issue about “within our ability” versus “will be solved,” which was not the central flaw. The reasoning succeeded because I distinguished between absence of known function and presence of latent beneficial function. In similar problems, I should keep isolating the exact bridge assumption required for the conclusion. General rule: when an argument moves from “currently unused or nonessential” to “therefore a powerful untapped resource,” test whether it has justified that positive potential rather than merely the absence of an observed role.

item.context: Consumer advocate: Businesses are typically motivated primarily by the desire to make as great a profit as possible, and advertising helps businesses to achieve this goal. But it is clear that the motive of maximizing profits does not impel businesses to present accurate information in their advertisements. It follows that consumers should be skeptical of the claims made in advertisements.
item.question: Each of the following, if true, would strengthen the consumer advocate's argument EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many consumers have a cynical attitude toward advertising.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Those who create advertisements are less concerned with the accuracy than with the creativity of advertisements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The laws regulating truth in advertising are not applicable to many of the most common forms of inaccurate advertising.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Businesses know that they can usually maximize their profits by using inaccurate information in their advertisements.

response:
Reasoning: A does not show that ads are actually less accurate or that skepticism is warranted; it only reports consumers’ attitudes. B, C, and D all support the idea that advertising is not strongly constrained toward truth and may favor inaccuracy.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a relevance test: I checked which option most directly affected the argument’s link between profit motive, ad accuracy, and the recommendation that consumers be skeptical. The key factor was whether a choice provided evidence that businesses or advertisers have incentives or opportunities to present inaccurate information. My answer was correct because I separated support for the conclusion from mere description of consumers’ existing attitudes; one choice only reported an attitude and did not make the advocate’s reasoning stronger. In similar strengthen-EXCEPT questions, map the core causal chain first and eliminate any option that does not add evidence to a premise or the inference.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task correctly as an “EXCEPT” strengthen question: identify the option that does not add support to the conclusion that consumers should distrust advertising claims. My strategy was to map the argument’s structure first—profit motive supports advertising, but profit motive does not ensure accuracy, therefore skepticism is warranted—and then test each option for whether it strengthens that chain. That was an appropriate method because EXCEPT questions are best handled by asking how each answer affects the conclusion rather than by looking for a generally plausible statement. I used the key distinction between evidence about advertisers’ incentives and evidence about consumers’ attitudes. The successful part of my reasoning was recognizing that statements about reduced concern for accuracy, weak legal constraints, or profit from inaccuracy all reinforce the claim that advertisements are not reliably truthful. I also correctly noticed that one option merely described what consumers already think, which does not show that skepticism is justified. A hidden assumption I avoided was treating widespread belief as evidence of truth; the argument needed support about ad reliability, not about public opinion. An alternative trap would have been to think that if many consumers are cynical, then skepticism must be reasonable, but that confuses prevalence with evidential support. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on relevance to the conclusion’s justification, not surface topic match. In similar problems, I should explicitly separate answers that bear on motives, incentives, or truth conditions from answers that only report reactions or perceptions. General rule: in strengthen-EXCEPT questions, eliminate choices that provide causal or evidential support for the conclusion, and look for the choice that is merely descriptive, tangential, or about beliefs rather than the fact to be established.

item.context: In an ancient painting appraisal meeting, regarding the work No. 008, only technically analyzed, the conclusion is as follows: if the work is from the Tang Dynasty or the Five Dynasties period, then it is not a work of the Later Tang Dynasty and the Later Zhou Dynasty. After further experts The appraisal learned that it is not a work of the Tang Dynasty.
item.question: Which of the following options can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is not a work of the Five Dynasties period

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a work of the Five Dynasties period

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a work from the post-Tang period

choices.label: D
choices.text: It may be the work of the later Zhou period

response:
Reasoning: The premise is conditional: if it is Tang or Five Dynasties, then it is not Later Tang or Later Zhou. We only know it is not Tang. That does not prove it is or is not Five Dynasties. So A, B, and C cannot be concluded; the only remaining possible statement is D.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used conditional-logic elimination: translate the statement into an implication and test what follows after adding the new fact that it is not Tang. The key factor was that the premise only restricts cases where the work is Tang or Five Dynasties; it does not say that being not Tang determines any dynasty by itself. The successful step was avoiding the invalid move from “if P then not Q” plus “not P” to any conclusion about Q, which ruled out stronger claims and left only the possibility statement. For similar problems, first mark which statements are sufficient conditions and never infer a definite conclusion from denying the antecedent; instead, check which options remain logically possible.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a propositional-logic inference task rather than a history question, which was the right starting point. The key structure was a conditional statement with a disjunctive antecedent: “if Tang or Five Dynasties, then not Later Tang and not Later Zhou,” plus the added fact “not Tang.” My strategy was to test what follows strictly from the conditional and the new negative fact, instead of using background knowledge about dynastic relationships. That was appropriate because the problem depends on formal entailment, not real-world chronology.

The main evidence I used correctly was that denying one part of the antecedent does not trigger the conditional, and it also does not deny the other disjunct. In other words, from “not Tang,” I could not infer either “not Five Dynasties” or “Five Dynasties.” I also correctly noticed that the conditional only restricts certain cases; it does not rule out possibilities outside the antecedent, so a modal conclusion like “may be” remained viable. An important assumption I avoided was treating “Later Tang” as automatically included under “Tang” in the logical wording; the labels had to be handled exactly as stated. I should still be explicit in future problems about checking each option against models that satisfy the premises. The reasoning succeeded because I distinguished between what is impossible, what is necessary, and what is merely consistent. General rule: when given a conditional and a negation of only one disjunct in its antecedent, do not infer the status of the other disjunct; instead, evaluate options by consistency versus entailment.

item.context: Nostalgia is a lingering feeling of people. The reason why nostalgia lasts forever after being washed over the years is not because it has much charm in itself, but because it can provide people with material for reflection, so that people can trigger the perception of life or draw power from it in the process of some kind of drastic or broken change that people have experienced or are experiencing.
item.question: Which of the following options matches the content of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nostalgia is a kind of emotion, which has certain psychological effect

choices.label: B
choices.text: The recollection of past events is the most basic emotion of human beings

choices.label: C
choices.text: The object of nostalgia is something that causes dramatic changes in life

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reason for nostalgia is that old things have a specific positive effect on people

response:
Reasoning: The passage explains nostalgia endures not due to its own charm, but because old memories/things help people reflect, gain life insight, and draw strength during change. This matches the idea that old things have a positive effect on people.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a paraphrase-and-elimination approach: I identified the passage’s main claim about why nostalgia endures, then matched that claim to the option that preserved the cause-and-effect structure. The key factor was the sentence saying nostalgia lasts not because of its own charm, but because it gives people material for reflection and strength during life changes. My success came from focusing on the passage’s explanation of function rather than getting distracted by broader statements about emotion. For similar problems, first isolate the author’s stated reason and choose the option that captures that exact explanatory relationship, not just a related theme.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the passage as explaining the durability of nostalgia, not defining nostalgia in general or identifying its object. That was the key reading move: the sentence contrasts two possible explanations, rejecting “its own charm” and endorsing its reflective and empowering function. My strategy was to map each option against that contrast structure and look for the one that preserved the author’s causal claim. This was appropriate because the question asked which option “matches the content,” so the task was paraphrase validation rather than inference beyond the text.

The decisive evidence was the phrase that nostalgia provides “material for reflection” and allows people to “trigger the perception of life or draw power” during major change. I used that to conclude the passage focuses on the beneficial effect nostalgia has on people, rather than on nostalgia as a universal basic emotion or on the type of object remembered. An assumption that helped, and happened to be safe here, was treating “old things” or past experiences as the practical source of nostalgia, even though the passage emphasizes function more than object. I also correctly rejected alternatives that overgeneralized (“most basic emotion”) or shifted the focus from effect to object (“something that causes dramatic changes”). The main reason the reasoning succeeded was attention to the passage’s explicit cause-effect language. In similar problems, I should keep testing options against the passage’s logical structure—especially contrasts, negations, and stated reasons. A transferable rule is: when a passage says “not because X, but because Y,” the correct paraphrase must center on Y and avoid answers that merely restate X or switch categories.

item.context: Deposit is a sum of money paid by one party to the other in writing as security for a claim. If the party who pays the deposit does not fulfill the agreement, he has no right to ask the other party to return the deposit; if the party who accepts the deposit does not fulfill the agreement, he must return the deposit twice to the other party.
item.question: Which of the following is the deposit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A is in urgent need of cash and wants to sell his property. B is a friend of A. When he learned of this, he first lent A 10,000 yuan to meet the emergency. A made a written promise that he would sell the house to B at a below market price.

choices.label: B
choices.text: B is interested in buying A's house.
