choices.text: The installation cost of the alarm system with built-in sound sensor is much higher than that of the traditional smoke alarm system

response:
Reasoning: The claim is that sound-detecting alarms can replace smoke alarms by warning earlier. If many deadly indoor fires begin in mattresses/sofas and generate heavy smoke without distinctive sounds, the new alarms could miss exactly the dangerous fires smoke alarms detect, undermining the replacement claim.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a weaken-the-argument approach by focusing on the gap between the product’s feature and the conclusion that it can replace traditional smoke alarms. The key factor was whether the new alarm would reliably detect the kinds of fires that most threaten residents, not just whether it works in some cases. My success came from identifying a choice showing that common dangerous fires can produce smoke without the precursor sounds the device depends on, which directly attacks the replacement claim. In similar problems, test whether the proposed substitute covers all critical cases handled by the current solution; if it misses an important class of cases, that strongly weakens the argument.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking not which option merely criticizes the new alarm, but which one most directly undermines the claim that it can better replace traditional smoke alarms. That distinction mattered because the salesman’s conclusion was comparative and practical: the device is valuable only if it reliably protects people in the kinds of fires that actually kill them. My strategy was to identify the argument’s core assumption, namely that dangerous indoor fires are typically preceded by detectable heat-induced sounds from building materials. Once that assumption was clear, I looked for an option showing a class of important fires where the proposed detection mechanism would fail.

The reasoning succeeded because I focused on mechanism mismatch rather than on side issues like cost or the general usefulness of existing smoke alarms. I used the fact that smoke poisoning is the main fatal factor, so any strong weakening answer should connect to smoke-producing fires that the new system might miss. I also recognized that an answer about materials making sounds after ignition would not seriously challenge the claim of earlier detection, and that evidence smoke alarms save lives does not show the new system would perform worse. A possible shortcut I avoided was treating any criticism of the product as sufficient. The key alternative to consider was whether an option attacked timing, coverage, or practicality; only coverage of common deadly fires truly targeted the conclusion. The general lesson is: when evaluating a replacement claim, test whether the proposed substitute handles the most important cases the original handles, especially the high-risk cases driving the argument.

item.context: Measurements of the motion of the planet Uranus seem to show Uranus being tugged by a force pulling it away from the Sun and the inner planets. Neptune and Pluto, the two known planets whose orbits are farther from the Sun than is the orbit of Uranus, do not have enough mass to exert the force that the measurements indicate. Ttherefore, in addition to the known planets, there must be at least one planet in our solar system that we have yet to discover.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is a belt of comets beyond the orbit of Pluto with powerful gravitational pull.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The force the Sun exerts on Uranus is weaker than the force it exerts on the inner planets.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither Neptune nor Pluto is as massive as Uranus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pluto was not discovered until 1930.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion requires that only an undiscovered planet could cause Uranus’s observed pull. If a belt of comets beyond Pluto has enough gravitational pull, then the effect could be explained without positing another planet. That directly undermines the argument’s main inference.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a weaken-the-conclusion approach by identifying the argument’s core assumption: that only an undiscovered planet could explain Uranus’s anomalous motion. The key factor was whether there could be another source of gravitational pull beyond Uranus that fits the observations without requiring a new planet. My success came from looking for an alternative cause that explains the same evidence and directly blocks the jump from “known planets are insufficient” to “there must be another planet.” For similar problems, test causal or explanatory conclusions by asking whether a different mechanism could produce the same observed effect.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a weaken-the-argument task: the issue was not whether Uranus is affected by some force, but whether that force justifies concluding that there must be an undiscovered planet. My strategy was to identify the argument’s core assumption, namely that only a planet-sized body beyond Uranus could explain the observed tug. That was the right strategy for this kind of causal/explanatory inference, because weakening requires introducing a plausible alternative explanation or showing the inference is too strong. I focused on whether any choice supplied another source of gravitational influence located beyond Uranus, and that directly targeted the gap between evidence and conclusion. The key fact I used was that the argument ruled out only the two known outer planets as insufficiently massive; it did not rule out all nonplanetary sources of gravity. I also correctly ignored choices that were merely background facts or comparisons that did not affect the existence of an alternative explanation. A potential shortcut I used, but appropriately, was treating “must be at least one planet” as vulnerable to any option that explains the data without requiring a planet. Other possibilities to consider in similar problems include flawed measurements, mistaken assumptions about forces, or other celestial bodies besides planets. What made the reasoning successful was matching the answer choice to the exact logical vulnerability rather than to surface astronomy content. In similar questions, I should continue isolating the conclusion’s necessary assumption and ask, “What else could explain the same evidence?” General rule: when an argument infers a specific hidden cause from observed effects, the strongest weakener often presents a credible alternative cause that fits the observations equally well.

item.context: Global warming has contributed to a rise in global sea level not only because it causes glaciers and ice sheets to melt, but also simply because when water is heated its volume increases. But this rise in global sea level is less than it otherwise would be, since over the years artificial reservoirs have been built all around the world that collectively contain a great deal of water that would otherwise reach the sea.
item.question: Which one of the following can most reasonably be concluded on the basis of the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Little is known about the contribution of global warming to the rise in global sea level.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The amount of water that results from the melting of glaciers and ice sheets cannot be determined by looking at the rise in global sea level alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rises in global sea level that occurred before the world's reservoirs were built are difficult to explain.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The exact magnitude of the rise in global sea level is in dispute.

response:
Reasoning: Sea level rise reflects several factors: melting ice, thermal expansion, and reduction due to water trapped in reservoirs. So you cannot infer the amount from melting alone just by observing total sea level rise. Nothing suggests ignorance, dispute, or unexplained earlier rises.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a causal decomposition approach: I broke the observed sea-level rise into multiple contributing and offsetting factors, then asked what could and could not be inferred from the total effect alone. The key factor was that sea level reflects not just meltwater, but also thermal expansion and a counteracting reduction from water retained in reservoirs. The successful step was recognizing that when several causes jointly determine one observed outcome, that outcome cannot isolate the size of just one cause. For similar problems, explicitly list all stated contributors and offsets before drawing any conclusion from a net result.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the conclusion that must follow from the passage, not merely a plausible background claim. That was the right framing, because the stimulus described multiple causes affecting observed sea level and asked what can be concluded from that setup. My strategy was to track the net effect on sea level: some factors raise it, while reservoir storage reduces how much rise would otherwise be observed. This was appropriate because the key logical structure was that the measured outcome reflects several interacting contributors, not a single source.

The crucial evidence I used was that sea level rise comes from both melting land ice and thermal expansion, and that reservoir construction offsets part of the rise by retaining water on land. From that, it follows that observed sea level change alone cannot isolate one contributor. I correctly rejected choices about uncertainty, dispute, or unexplained historical rises because the passage never mentioned lack of knowledge, disagreement, or past anomalies. An assumption that helped was treating “cannot be determined by looking at … alone” as a standard inference when multiple variables jointly produce one observable result. I should still note that this depends on distinguishing “insufficient by itself” from “impossible in principle with additional data.”

One alternative to consider was whether the passage supported any broader skepticism about climate science, but that would have gone beyond the text. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on causal composition rather than on the topic’s general controversy. In similar problems, I should explicitly map each cause and offset before testing answer choices. General rule: when an observed quantity is the net result of multiple causal factors, that quantity alone cannot determine the magnitude of any one factor.

item.context: The number of Chinese cultural relics lost overseas is huge and the situation is very complicated. If one spends a lot of money to buy them regardless of the circumstances, it is tantamount to acknowledging the legitimacy of these cultural relics lost overseas, which is difficult to accept. Chinese cultural relics, no matter where they are -- whether in China or any other country in the world, whether they are in the hands of the state or in the hands of individuals, are important to the public display, it represents The Chinese culture, which needs to be publicized and displayed. Conservation is not an end in itself, the end is to use it, to use it to promote our culture.
item.question: Which of the following is the meaning of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: China's loss of cultural relics abroad is complicated

choices.label: B
choices.text: The purpose of conservation is to use cultural relics to promote culture

choices.label: C
choices.text: To return cultural relics, we should think calmly and act rationally

choices.label: D
choices.text: The loss of Chinese cultural relics overseas is not recognized as legitimate

response:
Reasoning: The passage says overseas relic issues are complex, and blindly paying high prices is inappropriate because it may legitimize their loss. It stresses rational handling and that relic protection should ultimately serve cultural promotion. So the overall meaning is to stay calm and rational in seeking their return.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach: I compared the passage’s supporting points and inferred the broader stance they were building toward. The key factor was the warning that paying high prices “regardless of the circumstances” would effectively legitimize the overseas loss, which signaled the author was arguing against impulsive recovery methods rather than just describing relics or conservation. My success came from separating supporting details, like cultural promotion, from the author’s overall recommendation about how to handle repatriation. For similar problems, first identify the author’s final practical position, then treat examples and explanations as support rather than the main point.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s main intended message, not merely a detail repeated in one sentence. My strategy was to distinguish between supporting points and the author’s overall conclusion, which was appropriate for a “meaning of the text” question. I used three linked facts from the passage: the overseas-relics situation is complex, indiscriminate spending can imply acceptance of that situation, and cultural relics ultimately matter because they serve public cultural display. From those points, I inferred that the author was arguing for a measured approach rather than making a purely factual statement about relics. That was the key success: I treated the first and last ideas as reasons supporting a broader stance, rather than as independent answer targets. I also avoided choosing an option that was merely textually true but too narrow, which is a common trap in main-idea questions. One assumption I made was that the mention of “buy them regardless of circumstances” implied criticism of impulsive repatriation efforts; here that assumption fit the author’s intent. The alternatives I needed to screen out were options that captured only background complexity or only the instrumental value of conservation. What made the reasoning successful was mapping each sentence to its role: problem, caution, principle, then implied recommendation. In similar problems, I should continue asking, “Which option best subsumes the others as supporting evidence?” A transferable rule is: for main-idea questions, prefer the choice that explains why the author included multiple supporting claims, not the choice that repeats the most obvious sentence.

item.context: Hidden curriculum refers to the school learning experience that is not clearly specified in the school curriculum plan, is not a formal examination without awareness.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following options is not hidden curriculum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colleges and universities organize students to participate in two days of military training to cultivate and exercise their willpower.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When children are learning mathematics courses, they develop an attitude that likes to learn mathematics.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A university set up a campus culture festival to let students know the school motto and style of study.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Teachers and students participate in extracurricular activities together to establish an equal and harmonious relationship between teachers and students.

response:
Reasoning: Hidden curriculum is implicit, unintended, and not formally specified. B, C, and D involve attitudes, culture, and relationships formed indirectly. A is a deliberate, organized activity with an explicit educational goal—cultivating willpower—so it is part of the formal/explicit curriculum, not hidden.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach, separating explicit, planned school activities from implicit learning outcomes. The key factor should have been whether the item described an actual school-provided experience outside the formal curriculum, versus a learner’s personal byproduct that arises during formal subject study. My error was treating “deliberate and organized” as automatically non-hidden, while overlooking that hidden curriculum can also be conveyed through organized school culture and activities; the real mismatch was the option describing an attitude formed within ordinary formal instruction rather than a distinct hidden-curriculum experience. For similar problems, first identify the core category boundary, then eliminate choices that are merely outcomes of formal teaching rather than informal curricular influences themselves.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task as asking which option was outside the definition of hidden curriculum, but I narrowed the definition too quickly to “unintended and implicit,” which was only part of what needed to be checked. My strategy was to contrast explicit, organized activities with indirect outcomes, so I treated any planned educational activity as non-hidden. That was too coarse, because the question was about the learning experience described in each option, not whether the surrounding event was institutionally organized. I used one valid feature—formal specification—but I failed to weigh the other key feature in the stem: experiences that are not clearly included in the curriculum plan and are not directly examined. I also overlooked that school culture, teacher-student relations, and extracurricular participation can still function as hidden curriculum even when schools intentionally arrange them. My main mistaken assumption was that “deliberately organized by the school” automatically means “formal curriculum,” which is not a reliable equivalence. I should have considered whether each option described a byproduct of subject learning versus a broader socializing experience embedded in school life. The error came from classifying by the school’s intention rather than by the curricular status of the learning outcome itself. In similar problems, I should test each option against every clause of the definition, not just the most salient one. General rule: when a concept is defined by multiple conditions, classify examples by the status of the outcome within the system described, not merely by whether an activity was planned.

item.context: In the late 1980' s, the population of sea otters in the North Pacific Ocean began to decline. Of the two plausible explanations for the decline-increased predation by killer whales or disease-disease is the more likely. After all, a concurrent sharp decline in the populations of seals and sea lions was almost certainly caused by a pollution-related disease, which could have spread to sea otters, whereas the population of killer whales did not change noticeably.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is no indication that substantial numbers of sea otters migrated to other locations from the North Pacific in the 1980's.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Along the Pacific coast of North America in the 1980's, sea otters were absent from many locations where they had been relatively common in former times.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The North Pacific populations of seals and sea lions cover a wider geographic area than does the population of sea otters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Killer whales in the North Pacific usually prey on seals and sea lions but will, when this food source is scarce, seek out other prey.

response:
Reasoning: The argument favors disease because killer whale numbers stayed stable. But if killer whales normally eat seals/sea lions and switch to sea otters when those prey decline, then otter decline could be due to increased predation without any increase in whale population. This directly weakens the reasoning.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a causal-argument weakening approach: identify the author’s main support for preferring one explanation over the other, then look for a choice that breaks that support. The key factor was the assumption that increased predation would require an increase in the killer whale population. The successful step was noticing that predation pressure can rise even when predator numbers stay constant if predators switch prey after seals and sea lions decline. For similar problems, test whether the argument wrongly equates a stable population level with a stable causal impact, and look for changes in behavior or interactions that could alter effects without changing counts.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a weaken-the-argument task: the goal was not to find the best explanation overall, but to identify a fact that most undermines the argument’s preference for one explanation over the other. My strategy was to isolate the argument’s core inference: because killer whale numbers stayed roughly constant, increased predation was treated as less likely than disease. That was the right target, because weakening questions often hinge on exposing a gap between the evidence cited and the conclusion drawn. I focused on whether predation could increase even without an increase in predator population, which is exactly the hidden assumption in the argument. The crucial relationship was behavioral rather than numerical: predators can shift prey when their usual food declines, so constant predator numbers do not imply constant predation pressure on a particular species. I did not need to challenge the disease story directly; it was enough to show that the alternative explanation remained plausible. That made the prey-switching option especially strong, because it connected the seal and sea lion decline to a mechanism for otter decline. Other options were weaker because they discussed migration, historical absence, or geographic range without directly attacking the inference. The reasoning succeeded because it identified the argument’s dependence on population counts as a proxy for predation intensity. In similar problems, I should explicitly ask what assumption links the stated evidence to the conclusion. General rule: when an argument rules out causation based on unchanged agent numbers, test whether each agent’s behavior or target could have changed instead.

item.context: From 1996 to 2004, the average family income in a certain country decreased by 10 percent, after adjustments for inflation. Opponents of the political party that ruled during this time claim that this was due to mismanagement of the economy by that party.
item.question: Each of the following rejoinders, if true, directly counters the opponents' explanation of the decrease in average family income EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: There had been a rise in family income in 1996, after adjustments for inflation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Younger wage earners usually earn less than older ones, and the average age of household wage earners fell during most years in the past several decades.

choices.label: C
choices.text: During the period, international events beyond the control of the country's government had a negative effect on family incomes in the country.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The biggest decreases in family income resulted from policies enacted before the ruling party came to power in 1996.

response:
Reasoning: To counter “the ruling party mismanaged the economy,” a rejoinder should offer another cause of the income drop. B, C, and D each provide alternative explanations. A only says income had risen in 1996, which does not explain the later decline or rebut mismanagement.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an elimination approach: identify which options provide an alternative causal explanation for the income decline and thus directly weaken the claim of mismanagement. The key factor was the word “directly counters,” which means the rejoinder must explain the decrease by pointing to some other cause or constraint outside the ruling party’s responsibility. My success came from distinguishing evidence about a different time point from evidence about the cause of the decline itself; one choice mentioned a rise in 1996 but did not account for why income fell over the full period. For similar problems, I should test each option by asking: “Does this specifically offer a competing explanation for the stated effect, or is it merely background information?”
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task correctly as an “EXCEPT” weaken question: identify the one statement that does **not** directly undermine the opponents’ causal claim about why income fell. My strategy was to test each option for whether it supplied a plausible alternative cause, shifted responsibility away from the ruling party, or otherwise broke the link between the party’s management and the observed decline. That was the right framework because the opponents’ claim was causal, so the strongest rejoinders would be competing causes or evidence of lack of control. I used the key distinction between a fact that is merely consistent with the decline and a fact that actually explains it away. In evaluating the options, I noticed that some pointed to demographic composition, external shocks, or earlier policies, all of which directly challenge the attribution of blame. By contrast, the option I selected referred to an earlier increase in income, which says little about the cause of the subsequent multiyear decrease.

A useful assumption I made was that “directly counters” requires relevance to the alleged cause, not just any fact about income trends. One alternative I still needed to guard against was whether a prior increase might indirectly suggest competent management, but that would be too weak and not a direct rebuttal of the later decline. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on causal structure rather than on whether a statement sounded politically favorable. For similar problems, I should explicitly map the claim as “effect + alleged cause” and ask whether each choice attacks the cause, offers another cause, or is merely background. General rule: in causal-argument questions, prefer answers that change the explanation of the effect, not answers that only describe nearby facts without explanatory force.

item.context: It is common to respond to a person who is exhorting us to change our behavior by drawing attention to that person' s own behavior. This response, however, is irrational. Whether or not someone in fact heeds his or her own advice is irrelevant to whether that person' s advice should be heeded.
item.question: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Other countries argue that if we are serious about disarming we should go ahead and disarm to show our good intentions, but this is irrational, for we could make the same argument about them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: We should not be too severe in our condemnation of the salesperson; we have all lied at one point or another. It is irrational to condemn a person for wrongs committed by everybody.

choices.label: C
choices.text: One should not dismiss the philosopher's argument that matter does not exist by pointing out that the philosopher acts as though matter exists. People's actions have no effect on the strength of their arguments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When one country accuses another country of violating human rights standards, the accused country can reduce the damage to its reputation by drawing attention to the human rights record of its accuser because this tactic distracts critical attention.

response:
Reasoning: The original rejects the “you do it too” response: a person’s hypocrisy is irrelevant to whether their advice is good. Choice C matches this exactly, saying we should not reject a philosopher’s claim because the philosopher behaves inconsistently; behavior does not affect argument strength.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an argument-structure matching approach: I identified the original as rejecting a tu quoque move, where a speaker’s inconsistent behavior is treated as relevant to the truth or worth of the claim. The key factor was the relevance principle: the source’s behavior does not bear on whether the advice or argument itself should be accepted. My success came from focusing on that abstract pattern rather than the surface topic, which made the parallel easy to spot. For similar problems, first restate the stimulus in general logical form and then choose the option that preserves the same relevance/irrelevance relationship.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the stimulus as identifying a tu quoque pattern: replying to advice by pointing out that the adviser does not follow it, and then rejecting that reply as irrational because the adviser’s conduct is irrelevant to the advice’s merit. That interpretation was correct, and it led me to look for an argument with the same structure: an attempted rebuttal based on inconsistency between a person’s claims and actions, followed by the principle that such inconsistency does not bear on the truth or force of the claim. My strategy was to abstract the argument to its logical form rather than focus on its topic, which is the right approach for a parallel-reasoning question. The key relationship I used was “speaker behavior is irrelevant to evaluative status of speaker’s claim/advice.” I also correctly distinguished this from choices about reciprocity, shared guilt, or rhetorical effectiveness, which may involve criticism or hypocrisy but not the same relevance principle. A hidden assumption in the stimulus is that advice should be assessed independently of whether the adviser personally complies with it, and the matching answer had the same assumption about arguments. I should still note that similar choices can tempt by mentioning accusations or inconsistent behavior, so it is important to ask whether the conclusion concerns logical relevance or merely strategy. What made the reasoning successful was matching both the objection and the reason it fails, not just noticing the word “irrational.” In similar problems, I should continue translating each option into a compact schema before comparing content. General rule: when testing analogy in argumentation, match the role that a fact plays in the reasoning, especially whether it is treated as relevant or irrelevant to the conclusion.

item.context: The government has no right to tax earnings from labor. Taxation of this kind requires the laborer to devote a certain percentage of hours worked to earning money for the government. Thus, such taxation forces the laborer to work, in part, for another' s purpose. Since involuntary servitude can be defined as forced work for another' s purpose, just as involuntary servitude is pernicious, so is taxing earnings from labor.
item.question: The argument uses which one of the following argumentative techniques?

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing the authority of an economic theory in order to justify a moral principle

choices.label: B
choices.text: inferring that since two institutions are similar in one respect, they are similar in another respect

choices.label: C
choices.text: deriving a general principle about the rights of individuals from a judgment concerning the obligations of governments

choices.label: D
choices.text: presupposing the inevitability of a hierarchical class system in order to oppose a given economic practice

response:
Reasoning: The argument says taxation of labor earnings is like involuntary servitude in one key respect: both force someone to work for another’s purpose. It then concludes taxation is also pernicious, transferring a judgment from one institution to another based on that similarity.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used an analogy-identification approach: I looked for whether the argument was transferring an evaluative judgment from one practice to another based on a shared feature. The key factor was that the reasoning moved from “both involve forced work for another’s purpose” to “both are pernicious,” which is the hallmark of arguing from similarity in one respect to similarity in another. My success came from focusing on the structure of the inference rather than the political content of the claim. For similar problems, strip the argument to premise-conclusion form and ask whether it extends a judgment through an asserted resemblance.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the argument’s form, not whether its conclusion about taxation was morally or politically defensible. That was the correct framing, because the task was to identify the argumentative technique used. My strategy was to abstract the passage into structure: institution X shares a feature with institution Y, and because Y has a negative status, X is assigned a similar negative status. That structural translation was appropriate for an argument-technique question, where the key is the inference pattern rather than the topic.

The crucial evidence I used was the explicit comparison between taxation of labor income and involuntary servitude. I noticed that the argument first established one similarity—both allegedly involve being made to work for another’s purpose—and then transferred a further evaluative property—being pernicious. That is exactly the kind of analogical move these questions often test. I did not get distracted by the definitional language about involuntary servitude, because the conclusion still depended on extending a judgment across the comparison.

A possible trap would have been to confuse the argument with one deriving rights from government duties or one appealing to economic theory, but neither was actually present in the text. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the conclusion-generating step, not just isolated phrases. In similar problems, I should identify the premise-to-conclusion bridge and ask whether the author is classifying, analogizing, defining, or appealing to authority. General rule: when an argument transfers an evaluation from one case to another on the basis of a shared feature, treat it as analogical reasoning.

item.context: The competition between electric vehicles and internal combustion vehicles has a history of more than one hundred years. For a long time, the development of internal combustion vehicles has been outstanding and has made great progress. In recent years, with the development of battery technology, electric vehicles have occupied many fields, such as bicycles, motorcycles, small transport vehicles, large urban buses, airport and port ferries and so on. As a result, it has been proposed that the time for electric vehicles to completely replace internal combustion vehicles is coming, and even some countries and places have proposed a timetable for banning the sale of fuel cars. But some opponents say that internal combustion vehicles and electric vehicles will continue to move in the opposite direction for quite a long time in the future.
item.question: Which of the following options, if true, can best support the opponents of the above point of view?

choices.label: A
choices.text: After more than one hundred years of development, internal combustion vehicles have become very mature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The disposal of waste batteries and the application of special materials in batteries may bring some social problems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some experts pointed out that from the life cycle of pure electric vehicles, emissions of the carbon dioxide  may not be less than gasoline vehicles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The three major anxieties in the development of electric vehicles are mileage anxiety, charging anxiety and battery anxiety, which shows that the technology of power battery is far from mature and there is still a long way to go.

response:
Reasoning: The opponents claim EVs and internal combustion vehicles will coexist for a long time. D most directly supports this by showing EV core technology is still immature: range, charging, and battery concerns remain significant, so full replacement is not imminent.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a strengthen-the-argument approach, looking for the option that most directly supports long-term coexistence rather than merely praising one side or criticizing the other in a limited way. The key factor was whether the choice showed a continuing structural obstacle to full replacement, and the persistent battery-related anxieties did that best because they imply EV adoption will remain constrained for a long time. The successful step was prioritizing evidence about future feasibility over general background facts like current maturity. For similar problems, I should choose the option that most directly reinforces the conclusion’s timeline or causal claim, not just any statement that sounds favorable.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task correctly as a strengthening question: the goal was not to show that electric vehicles have problems in general, but to identify the fact that most directly supports the claim that the two vehicle types will continue to coexist for a long time. My strategy was to look for the option that most clearly blocks the prediction of complete replacement in the near or medium term. That was an appropriate approach because the opponents’ conclusion is about duration and continued competition, so the strongest support should concern a persistent barrier to full substitution. I focused on evidence about technological immaturity and practical adoption obstacles, since these create ongoing limits on market replacement. That reasoning used an important constraint: to support long-term coexistence, the evidence should concern broad, structural limitations rather than a minor drawback or a backward-looking fact.  

I implicitly rejected choices that were weaker because they were either descriptive of the current success of internal combustion vehicles, raised external social concerns, or questioned one environmental advantage without proving slow replacement. A key assumption in my reasoning was that unresolved battery, charging, and range issues materially affect consumer adoption and infrastructure development over time. That assumption was justified because these are core usage constraints, not peripheral criticisms. The reasoning succeeded because I prioritized direct relevance to the conclusion over plausibility in isolation. In similar problems, I should continue asking: which option most directly strengthens the exact claim, especially its time horizon and mechanism? A transferable rule is: in strengthening questions, prefer evidence that establishes a durable causal obstacle to the predicted outcome, not merely a fact that is true or somewhat related.

item.context: The State has proposed a plan requiring all young people to perform community service as a requirement for graduation from high school. The goal is to use the young people to provide services to correct social ills, especially those in housing and crime. Young people, however, should only be required to participate in educational activities to graduate from high school. For that reason, the proposed program should not be implemented.
item.question: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Community service does not provide any educational benefit to young people.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some of the social ills that could be helped are being ignored by this program.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Young people do not cause the social ills mentioned.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Community service is not beneficial to young people.

response:
Reasoning: The argument says graduation requirements should include only educational activities. To conclude mandatory community service should not be required, it must assume community service is not educational. If it did provide educational benefit, the conclusion would not follow.  
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a necessary-assumption approach: I identified the conclusion, then asked what unstated premise must be true for that conclusion to follow from the principle that graduation requirements should include only educational activities. The key factor was the link between “only educational activities should be required” and “therefore this community service requirement should not be implemented”; that link works only if the service is not educational. The successful step was testing whether the conclusion would weaken or collapse if community service had educational value. For similar problems, explicitly connect the stated rule to the disputed policy and identify the missing condition that makes the policy violate the rule.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument as drawing a boundary around legitimate graduation requirements: only educational activities may be required, therefore the proposed service program must be excluded. That interpretation was correct because the conclusion depended on classifying the proposed activity as outside the permitted category, not on weighing its social value. My strategy was to identify the argument’s principle (“only educational activities”) and then ask what unstated link was needed to move from that principle to rejection of the program. That was the right approach for an assumption question, especially one built around a category rule.

The key evidence I used was the logical structure: if all required activities must be educational, then the argument needs the service program to lack educational status. I appropriately ignored side issues like whether the program helps society, whether youth caused the problems, or whether other problems are neglected, because those facts do not connect the premise to the conclusion. The crucial assumption was stronger than “not mainly educational” or “not beneficial”; it had to exclude educational benefit in a way that blocks the program from fitting the rule. One shortcut that worked here was translating the argument into a conditional form and testing what must be true for the conclusion to follow. I should still remember, in similar problems, to compare close answer choices for scope: “educational benefit” is narrower and more relevant than “beneficial” in general. The transferable lesson is: when an argument applies a rule to reject a case, look for the hidden premise that says the case fails the rule’s qualifying condition.

item.context: Advertisement refers to the use of certain media or forms, such as newspapers, television, street signs, shop windows, etc. , at the expense of commodity operators and service providers for commercial purposes, a public  promo, directly or indirectly, to promote goods or service.
item.question: Which of the following is an advertising campaign?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In order to sell the cement better, the factory director gave one million gifts to the contractor in the neighboring county.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Obama spent a lot of money on television and in the press to become president.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By sponsoring the Chinese sports delegation to the Olympic Games, Li Ning brand clothing has achieved good social and economic benefits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The teacher made it a rule that the students must use ball-point pens in the examination.

response:
Reasoning: Advertising is a public commercial promotion by a business, directly or indirectly, to promote goods/services. A is private gifting, not public promotion. B is political, not commercial goods/services. D is a classroom rule. C uses Olympic sponsorship to publicly promote Li Ning clothing.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option against the required elements of advertising—public promotion, use of media/forms, commercial purpose, and promotion of goods or services. The key factor was distinguishing commercial publicity from private transactions, political campaigning, or non-commercial rules. My success came from checking all parts of the definition rather than focusing on only one surface feature like “spending money” or “promotion.” For similar problems, I should explicitly list the necessary criteria from the definition and test each option against every criterion before choosing.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which option matched a definition-based category: a public, commercial promotion conducted through some medium or form by a business or service provider. That interpretation was correct, because the key task was not to find any persuasive activity, but to match all parts of the definition. My strategy was elimination by testing each option against the definition’s necessary conditions: commercial purpose, public-facing promotion, and connection to goods or services. That was appropriate because several choices contained persuasion or spending, but only one fit the full structure of advertising rather than just influence.

The most important evidence I used was the distinction between private inducement and public promotion, and between commercial promotion and noncommercial or unrelated behavior. I correctly rejected the gifting example because it was targeted bribery or relationship-building, not a public promotional act. I also correctly ruled out the political spending example because campaigning for office is not promotion of goods or services. Another useful constraint was that a mere rule or requirement, without promotional intent or media exposure, does not become advertising.

One assumption that helped was treating sponsorship as an indirect promotional medium, which aligns with the definition’s “directly or indirectly” language. An alternative I needed to consider was whether “certain media or forms” could include sponsorship rather than only traditional ads; recognizing the broader wording prevented an overly narrow reading. The reasoning succeeded because I matched each option against every definitional element instead of focusing on surface similarity like “spent money” or “influenced people.” In similar problems, I should explicitly turn the definition into a checklist of required features and reject any option missing even one. General rule: in definition-matching questions, classify by necessary conditions, not by general association or vibe.

item.context: China's special climatic environment has led to the formation of the custom of hot food in China. Hot food can not be touched directly by hand. Cutlery is needed to help you eat. During the warring States period, lacquer ware entered into the food utensils and gradually replaced the bronze ware. When using lacquer ware to carry food, if you use a knife and fork to eat, it will cause a lot of scratches and damage on the surface of the lacquer ware, affecting the beauty of the lacquer ware. Taking advantage of the good elasticity of bamboo, the ancestors of ancient China first made bamboo clips, accumulated experience in using them, and finally evolved chopsticks.
item.question: Which of the followings is not mentioned?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chinese chopsticks evolved from bamboo clips.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The use of chopsticks in the ancients was related to the use of food utensils.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The custom of eating hot food contributed to the emergence of chopsticks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: During the warring States period, people gave up knives and forks to use bamboo chopsticks.

response:
Reasoning: The passage mentions hot food, lacquer ware replacing bronze ware, and bamboo clips evolving into chopsticks. It links chopsticks to hot food and utensils, but it does not state that during the Warring States period people explicitly gave up knives and forks to use bamboo chopsticks.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a passage-elimination approach: I checked each option against whether it was explicitly supported by the text rather than whether it seemed historically plausible. The key clue was the passage’s chain of causation—hot food required utensils, lacquer ware was easily scratched by knives and forks, and bamboo clips gradually evolved into chopsticks. My success came from noticing that one choice added an unstated step about people “giving up” knives and forks specifically during the Warring States period, which the passage never directly says. For similar questions, I should test each option for exact textual support and reject choices that introduce extra timing, causation, or actions beyond the passage.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as a reading-comprehension task asking which statement was absent from the passage, not which statement was false in general. That distinction mattered, because the right strategy was to compare each choice against explicit statements and reasonable inferences from the text. I used an elimination approach: one option was directly stated about the origin from bamboo clips, another was supported by the link between chopsticks and lacquer ware, and another was supported by the connection between hot food and the need for utensils. The remaining option introduced a stronger historical claim about a specific period and a complete replacement of one eating method by another. The passage mentioned lacquer ware entering food utensils during that period, but it did not say people “gave up” knives and forks then. My reasoning succeeded because I noticed the difference between a causal chain in the passage and a dated transition claim added by the option. A key assumption I handled correctly was that “not mentioned” includes claims that go beyond the text, even if they sound plausible. An alternative I still needed to consider was whether the passage only implied, rather than explicitly stated, the connection between utensils and chopsticks. In similar problems, I should separate direct textual support, valid inference, and unsupported embellishment. General rule: when asked for what is “not mentioned,” reject choices that add extra time, degree, or certainty not warranted by the passage.

item.context: Societies cannot dedicate themselves to the study of fine arts unless they have spare time, and people only have spare time when food, shelter, and water are abundant. Although some archeologists believe that the first paintings were actually made to illustrate the plight of starving prehistoric man during the dry season, these early painters must have first discovered the ability to mix minerals to make paint colors. These complex experimentations were the result of a dedication to the study of fine arts.
item.question: The argument leads to the conclusion that

choices.label: A
choices.text: prehistoric man could have accidentally discovered how to mix minerals to make paint colors

choices.label: B
choices.text: the study of fine art began in societies that at some time had abundant food, shelter, and water

choices.label: C
choices.text: whenever people have food, shelter, and water, they will dedicate themselves to the study of fine arts

choices.label: D
choices.text: the study of fine art cannot be done unless one has the ability to mix minerals to make paint colors

response:
Reasoning: The argument says dedication to fine arts requires spare time, which requires abundant food, shelter, and water. Since making paint colors came from dedication to fine arts, early fine art must have arisen in a society that at some point had those abundances. Other choices add claims not supported.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a conditional-chain approach, linking each premise into a sequence: dedication to fine arts requires spare time, and spare time requires abundant basic resources. The key factor was the statement that discovering paint-mixing resulted from a dedication to fine arts, which lets the resource-abundance condition be carried back to the earliest painters. My success came from following only what the premises guaranteed and rejecting choices that reversed conditions or added stronger claims than stated. For similar problems, explicitly map each “only if” and “unless” statement into a one-way conditional chain, then choose the conclusion that matches that direction without converting it into a converse.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the conclusion forced by chaining together the premises, not for a tempting background claim about prehistoric painting. That interpretation was correct, because the dry-season example was a distraction and the real structure was conditional: dedication to fine arts requires spare time, and spare time requires abundant basic resources. My strategy was to translate the statements into a dependency chain and then ask what must be true if early painters engaged in the experimentation described. That was appropriate because the argument’s force came from necessary conditions, not from probabilities or causal speculation. The key evidence I used was that the paint-mixing experiments were described as resulting from dedication to fine arts, which triggers the earlier conditions about spare time and abundance. I also correctly avoided reversing the conditional relationships: abundance may be necessary for artistic study, but it is not said to be sufficient. That helped eliminate the choice claiming that whenever basic needs are met, people will study fine arts. Another good move was rejecting claims that introduced unsupported absolutes about paint mixing being required for all fine art. The reasoning succeeded because I preserved the direction of implication and kept track of what was necessary versus what was merely associated. In similar problems, I should continue formalizing each premise and testing answer choices for illegal reversals, overgeneralizations, and added assumptions. A transferable rule is: when an argument gives a chain of necessary conditions, the valid conclusion must also preserve that direction and cannot strengthen a necessary condition into a sufficient one.

item.context: Complementary pricing strategy means that enterprises set lower prices for main products (products with high value) and higher prices for ancillary products (products with low value), which is conducive to increasing overall sales and increasing enterprise profits
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings uses complementary pricing strategies :

choices.label: A
choices.text: An online game launched by enterprise A is deeply loved by consumers, driving the hot sales of game peripheral products

choices.label: B
choices.text: For the twelve zodiac series teacups sold in Dshopping mall, the price of complete sets will be more favorable than that of single purchase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Company C has launched three new smart phones with 16g, 64g and 128G memory, with large price differences

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inkjet printer produced by manufacturer B has good quality and low price, but the price of ink cartridge has been high

response:
Reasoning: Complementary pricing is selling the main product cheaply and the necessary complementary product expensively to increase total profit. Only D fits: the printer is low-priced, while the complementary ink cartridges are high-priced. A is incidental demand, B is bundle pricing, C is versioned pricing.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used definition matching by breaking the concept into two required parts: a low-priced main product and a high-priced complementary product that consumers need afterward. The key factor was the pricing relationship between the core item and its ancillary item, not just whether one product helped sell another. My success came from ruling out distractors by identifying other pricing strategies such as bundling, product versioning, or simple spillover demand. For similar problems, convert the definition into a checklist of necessary conditions and verify that each option satisfies all of them, not just part of the pattern.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the definition correctly: the key structure was a low-priced core product paired with a high-priced complementary or ancillary product, with profit shifting from the main item to the follow-on item. My strategy was to map each option to a known pricing pattern and test whether it matched that structure exactly. That was appropriate because the answer choices represented different commercial mechanisms that can look superficially similar unless the definition is applied component by component. I used the crucial constraints in the definition: there must be a main product, an ancillary product, and an intentional price contrast between them. In option A, I recognized a spillover effect in demand rather than a pricing strategy; popularity of one product causing sales of another is not the same as pricing the first low and the second high. In option B, I identified bundle discounting, which changes the price of a package rather than shifting profit from a core item to its complement. In option C, I treated the differences as product versioning or price discrimination across configurations, not complementary pricing, because the items are substitutes within a line rather than complements. My reasoning succeeded because I focused on the relational structure between products, not merely on whether two products were both sold by the same firm. A transferable rule is: when a definition specifies a strategy, verify the exact economic relationship among the items—complements, substitutes, bundles, or sequential purchases—before matching an example. In similar problems, I should continue classifying distractors by their underlying mechanism, since many wrong choices mimic one surface feature while violating the core structural condition.

item.context: According to the science of enterprise management, the human resources management department plays a very important role in the process of modern enterprise management, but it is found that the department is not fully involved in the decision-making of the company's development planning, and the senior managers hired by the company are all decided by CEO. Therefore, the human resources management department more often only plays a supporting and supporting role.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, will most weaken the above argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The human resources management department has the right to hire middle managers

choices.label: B
choices.text: For individual large companies, the manager of the human resources management department has the right to attend the company's top decision-making meeting

choices.label: C
choices.text: Talent is the core element of the company's development, and the human resources management department can attract and retain talents for the company

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the world's top 500 enterprises, human resources management departments select and transfer personnel from employees with front-line work experience

response:
Reasoning: The claim says HR is “only supporting” because it isn’t fully involved in development planning and CEOs decide senior hires. If HR still has authority to hire middle managers, it directly participates in important managerial staffing, showing it is not merely auxiliary.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a direct counterexample approach: I looked for an option showing HR still has some meaningful management authority, so I chose the one about hiring middle managers. The key clue I underweighted was that the argument’s conclusion rests specifically on HR not being fully involved in development planning and top-level decision-making, not just on whether it has any staffing power. My mistake was attacking the conclusion too indirectly: authority over mid-level hiring does not refute the claim that HR mainly plays a supporting role in strategic decisions. For similar questions, target the exact premise-conclusion link and prefer options that challenge the stated decision-making level or scope, not just show general importance.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument as claiming that HR is merely auxiliary because it lacks meaningful participation in the company’s most important decisions. That interpretation was broadly correct, but my mistake was in treating any nontrivial authority as enough to weaken the conclusion. My strategy was to look for an option showing HR had real power, and I chose evidence that HR can hire middle managers. That does show influence, but it does not directly address the argument’s core basis: exclusion from development planning and top-level executive selection. The argument is specifically about whether HR is involved in strategic decision-making, not whether it performs important operational personnel functions.

I therefore used a too-shallow weakening test: “Does this make HR seem important?” instead of the stronger test, “Does this undermine the exact evidence supporting the conclusion?” I also overlooked the hierarchy in the stimulus: development planning and senior hiring are top-level decisions, so evidence about middle-management hiring is weaker because it sits at a lower level. A better alternative was to prioritize any option linking HR to top decision forums or strategic planning processes. The specific error was matching on “personnel authority” rather than “strategic participation.” In similar problems, I should identify the conclusion’s causal bridge and attack that bridge directly. General rule: when weakening an argument, prefer evidence that contradicts the argument’s stated criterion over evidence that merely offers a different positive fact.

item.context: Wu Xu, Zheng Jie and Shen Yao plan to revisit Nanjing. They choose one of aircraft, train, car and ship, but their travel modes are different. If Zheng Jie chooses car, Wu Xu does not choose ship; If Wu Xu chooses to travel by train, Shen Yao does not choose to fly; Shen Yao chooses   plane or train to travel
item.question: According to the above statement, which of the followings must be wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shen Yao chooses plane, while Zheng Jie chosses  car

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shen Yao chooses plane, while Zheng Jie chooses ship

choices.label: C
choices.text: Shen Yao chooses train, while Zheng Jie chosses  car

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shen Yao chooses train, while Zheng Jie chosses  plane

response:
Reasoning: Since Shen Yao must choose plane or train:  
- In A, if S=plane and Z=car, then Z=car implies W≠ship, so W must=train. But W=train implies S≠plane, contradiction.  
- B, C, and D can all be arranged without contradiction.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a constraint-satisfaction approach: I translated each statement into conditional restrictions, then tested each option by assigning the named modes and checking whether the remaining traveler could still take a distinct valid mode. The key factor was chaining two rules together: when Zheng Jie takes car, Wu Xu cannot take ship, so with Shen Yao fixed to plane or train and all modes different, Wu Xu is forced into train; that then triggers the rule forbidding Shen Yao from flying. The success came from following the forced assignment step-by-step instead of checking conditions in isolation. For similar problems, I should systematically combine conditionals after each temporary assignment and look for forced choices created by “all different” constraints.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task correctly as a “must be wrong” constraint-satisfaction question: test each option against the given conditions and see whether any assignment of the remaining person and mode can make it consistent. My strategy was to start from the strongest fixed condition, namely that Shen Yao is limited to two possible modes, and then combine that with the conditional rules and the requirement that all three people use different modes. That was an appropriate method because these problems are best handled by chaining implications rather than trying to imagine all assignments at once. The key evidence I used successfully was the interaction between “if Zheng Jie uses car, Wu Xu does not use ship” and “if Wu Xu uses train, Shen Yao does not fly.” In the incompatible option, once two travelers’ modes were fixed, the “all different” rule forced Wu Xu into a single remaining mode, which then triggered a contradiction with Shen Yao’s assigned mode. That was the decisive step.

A useful feature of my reasoning was that I did not just look at one rule in isolation; I checked how uniqueness plus conditionals can create hidden forced assignments. I also correctly recognized that the other options only need one consistent completion, not proof that all completions work. One assumption that helped, and was justified, was treating the four modes as a pool from which only three distinct ones are chosen. An alternative approach I could also have used is a compact table of cases for Shen Yao’s two possibilities, which would make the forced contradictions even clearer. The main reason the reasoning succeeded is that I converted verbal conditions into a short implication chain instead of relying on intuition. A transferable rule is: in “must be false” multiple-choice logic problems, combine fixed option statements with exclusivity constraints first, because they often force the remaining variable and expose contradictions immediately.

item.context: The proposed law banning the sale of cigarettes to minors is justified because minors should not smoke. But the proposed ban on cigarette vending machines would be like setting up roadblocks to catch one in 500 people driving without a license. Roadblocks stop everyone, not just those who break the law.
item.question: According to the passage above, which of the following is the author's idea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A law banning the sale of cigarettes to minors would have no practical effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The enforcement of the ban on cigarette vending machines has done nothing to stop minors from smoking.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The police should step up investigation and prosecution of unlicensed drivers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A ban on automatic cigarette vending machines would be an inconvenience for many adults who want to buy cigarettes.

response:
Reasoning: The author supports banning sales to minors but opposes banning vending machines because such a ban burdens everyone, including lawful adult buyers, just as roadblocks inconvenience all drivers to catch a few violators. So the main idea is inconvenience to many adults.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an analogy-based reasoning approach, mapping the “roadblocks” example onto the vending-machine ban to infer the author’s principle. The key factor was the statement that roadblocks “stop everyone, not just those who break the law,” which signals objection to a policy because it burdens many lawful people to catch a relatively small number of violators. My success came from identifying that the author was criticizing the broad inconvenience imposed on compliant adults, not denying the problem of minors smoking. For similar problems, translate the analogy into its underlying principle and match the answer choice that preserves that same burden-or-fairness relationship.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the author’s underlying point, not merely a fact mentioned in the passage. That was the key move, because the roadblock analogy signaled that the author’s concern was about a policy imposing costs on many compliant people in order to catch a small number of violators. My strategy was to identify the structure of the argument: first, concession that restricting minors is justified, then objection to a broader enforcement method because it affects everyone. That strategy was appropriate because analogy questions usually depend on matching the relationship between the example and the conclusion, not on literal details about cigarettes or driving. The crucial evidence was the sentence “Roadblocks stop everyone, not just those who break the law,” which directly points to inconvenience or burden on lawful individuals. I did not get distracted by answer choices that shifted the topic to effectiveness, law enforcement policy, or claims unsupported by the passage. A tempting mistake would have been to infer that the ban fails to reduce smoking, but the passage never argues ineffectiveness; it argues overbreadth. The reasoning succeeded because I separated the author’s approval of the goal from disapproval of the method. In similar problems, I should explicitly map analogy elements to the principle they illustrate. General rule: when an argument uses an analogy, identify the shared principle being transferred and choose the option that preserves that principle without adding new claims.

item.context: Administrative license refers to the act of an administrative organ granting a citizen, legal person or other organization permission to engage in certain activities upon examination in accordance with law.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following is an administrative license?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The A provincial government approved the land expropriation declaration submitted by a municipal government.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Company B appointed Sun Qiang as the Plenipotentiary, making him responsible for business negotiations with foreign parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The C Trade and Industry Bureau issued a business license to a school canteen on the application of it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The D Public Security Bureau agreed to grant a criminal suspect bail pending trial on the application of him.

response:
Reasoning: An administrative license is permission granted by an administrative organ to a citizen/legal person/organization to engage in certain activities after legal review. A is inter-government approval, B is internal company authorization, and D is a criminal procedural measure, not a license. C fits exactly.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used definition matching by breaking the concept into elements: an administrative organ, a citizen/legal person/organization applicant, legal examination, and permission to engage in a specific activity. The key factor was distinguishing “permission to conduct business” from other government acts like inter-agency approval, internal corporate delegation, or criminal procedure decisions. The successful step was checking each option against every part of the definition rather than relying on surface wording like “approved” or “agreed.” In similar problems, I should convert the definition into a checklist and eliminate options that fail even one required element.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as a definition-matching task: identify which option fits all elements of “administrative license,” not just the idea of “approval” in a broad sense. That interpretation was correct because the definition contains several necessary conditions: the actor must be an administrative organ, the recipient must be a citizen/legal person/organization, the act must follow examination according to law, and the result must be permission to engage in certain activities. My strategy was to test each option against those elements one by one, which was appropriate for a legal-concept multiple-choice question. The key evidence I used was the distinction between public administrative permission and other kinds of authorization, such as internal delegation, hierarchical governmental approval, or procedural decisions in criminal justice. I correctly recognized that one option involved approval between government organs rather than permission granted to a regulated outside entity. I also correctly excluded the company appointment because private organizational authorization is not an administrative act. Another useful distinction was that a coercive or procedural judicial/public security measure is not the same as a market-entry or activity-permission license. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the legal nature of the act rather than superficial words like “approved” or “agreed.” A possible risk would have been assuming any official approval counts as a license, but I avoided that by checking the recipient and function of the act. In similar problems, I should continue decomposing statutory definitions into mandatory elements and eliminate choices that fail even one element. A general rule is: when applying a formal definition, classify each option by necessary conditions and reject any option that matches the wording only superficially but not in legal function.

item.context: New technology is a great changer. However, will the speed of life and death of new technology connive at the superficiality of WYSIWYG and bring about the phenomenon of both flowers and wild? Some people have been saddened by the thinning of cultural air and think that China is entering a cultural mini-era. Libraries are getting better and better, but there are fewer and fewer good books and readers; physical bookstores and newsstands are withering and cities are losing their cultural lungs. No wonder some people cry to save reading from computers and mobile phones. It is even said that only by unplugging the Internet cable and turning off the mobile phone can we return to the real cultural life.
item.question: Which of the following options is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The development of new technology is the direct cause of the mini era of Chinese culture.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cultural anxiety caused by the upgrading and development of technological means.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To return to real cultural life, we must properly reject new technologies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Computers and mobile phones can save reading.

response:
Reasoning: The passage presents worries and sadness about how new technology may affect culture and reading, describing a kind of cultural anxiety. It does not say technology is the direct cause, nor that rejecting technology is necessary, nor that phones/computers save reading.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea elimination approach: I identified the passage’s overall stance as describing worry and unease about cultural decline in the context of new technology, then rejected options that overstated causation or turned reported opinions into the author’s conclusion. The key factor was the passage’s rhetorical framing—phrases about people being saddened, crying out, and fearing decline signal cultural anxiety rather than a firm claim that technology directly causes the problem. My success came from distinguishing description of social sentiment from endorsement of extreme solutions. For similar problems, first decide whether the passage is asserting a fact, reporting attitudes, or presenting debate, and choose the option that matches that level exactly.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the passage as a description of attitudes toward technological change rather than a factual claim that technology had already destroyed culture. That was the key interpretive move, because the question asked which option best captured the passage’s meaning, not which option repeated one alarming detail. My strategy was to identify the author’s overall tone and then test each choice against that tone. This was appropriate because the passage is argumentative and rhetorical, filled with worries, examples, and quoted sentiments rather than hard causal proof.

The evidence I used correctly was that the passage lists concerns: thinning cultural atmosphere, fewer good books and readers, decline of bookstores, and calls to “save reading” from screens. These details support the existence of cultural anxiety linked to new technological developments. I also correctly rejected stronger claims that the passage did not justify, especially direct causation and prescriptive necessity. A major assumption I avoided was treating rhetorical complaints as the author’s endorsed conclusion. I also considered alternatives by checking whether any option overstated, reversed, or narrowed the passage’s meaning.

What made the reasoning successful was distinguishing between “people fear X” and “the text proves X.” In similar problems, I should continue separating description of social reactions from endorsement of those reactions. A transferable rule is: when a passage presents concern, debate, or lament, prefer the option that captures the stance or discourse-level theme, not an option that upgrades suggestion into established cause or mandatory solution.

item.context: In countries where automobile insurance includes compensation for whiplash injuries sustained in automobile accidents, reports of having suffered such injuries are twice as frequent as they are in countries where whiplash is not covered. Some commentators have argued, correctly, that since there is presently no objective test for whiplash, spurious reports of whiplash injuries cannot be readily identified . These commentators are, however, wrong to draw the further conclusion that in the countries with the higher rates of reported whiplash injuries, half of the reported cases are spurious: clearly, in countries where automobile insurance does not include compensation for whiplash, people often have little incentive to report whiplash injuries that they actually have suffered.
item.question: In the argument given, the two boldfaced portions play which of the following roles?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first is a claim that has been used to support a conclusion that the argument accepts; the second is that conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first is a finding whose accuracy is evaluated in the argument; the second is an intermediate conclusion drawn to support the judgment reached by the argument on the accuracy of that finding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first is a claim that the argument disputes; the second is a narrower claim that the argument accepts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first is a finding whose implications are at issue in the argument; the second is an intermediate conclusion that has been used to support a conclusion that the argument criticizes.

response:
Reasoning: The first boldface is the reported cross-country difference in whiplash reports, a finding everyone accepts but whose implications are disputed. The second boldface is a premise the commentators use to support their further conclusion that half the reports are spurious—a conclusion the argument rejects.  
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a role-analysis approach: I identified the author’s conclusion, then mapped how the commentators’ reasoning fit around it. The key factor was separating an accepted observation from the disputed inference drawn from it: the cross-country reporting difference is not challenged, but what it implies is. The successful step was noticing that the second boldface is not the main conclusion of the passage; it is a supporting claim in the commentators’ argument that leads to the conclusion the author rejects.
