The successful part of my reasoning was recognizing a substitution-versus-displacement issue: reduced use in one category may be offset by increased use elsewhere. A tempting shortcut would have been to equate “cotton is cleaner in this application” with “the net environment is better,” but I avoided that. In similar problems, I should keep testing whether a local substitution actually changes the total amount of the harmful activity. General rule: when an argument claims that replacing X with Y will reduce harm, check whether demand for X is merely shifted rather than eliminated.

item.context: To suit the needs of corporate clients, advertising agencies have successfully modified a strategy originally developed for political campaigns. This strategy aims to provide clients with free publicity and air time by designing an advertising campaign that is controversial, thus drawing prime-time media coverage and evoking public comment by officials.
item.question: The statements above, if true, most seriously undermine which one of the following assertions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Campaign managers have transformed political campaigns by making increasing use of strategies borrowed from corporate advertising campaigns.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only a small percentage of eligible voters admit to being influenced by advertising campaigns in deciding how to vote.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Advertising agencies that specialize in campaigns for corporate clients are not usually chosen for political campaigns.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The usefulness of an advertising campaign is based solely on the degree to which the campaign's advertisements persuade their audiences.

response:
Reasoning: The passage says agencies use controversial ads to generate free publicity, media coverage, and official comment. That means a campaign can be useful for reasons other than directly persuading its audience through the ads themselves, which most strongly contradicts the claim that usefulness is based solely on persuasive effect.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a contradiction/undermine approach: I identified what the stimulus positively supports, then looked for the choice that its truth would directly weaken. The key factor was the passage’s claim that controversial campaigns are valuable because they generate free publicity, media coverage, and official reactions, which are benefits independent of the ads’ direct persuasive power. My answer was correct because I focused on the word “solely” and recognized that the stimulus presents an additional source of usefulness. For similar problems, test strong claims by asking whether the stimulus gives even one alternative mechanism or exception; if it does, that claim is the best target.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking which assertion is most weakened by the passage, not which one is merely unrelated or unsupported. The key task was to identify the passage’s central mechanism of effectiveness: the campaign works by generating controversy, which then attracts unpaid media exposure and public commentary. My strategy was to compare that mechanism against each answer choice and ask which claim it directly conflicts with. That was appropriate because “most seriously undermine” requires finding a statement that the passage makes less plausible through a clear competing account.

The crucial evidence was that the strategy provides “free publicity and air time” by provoking media coverage, not necessarily by making the ad itself more persuasive to its immediate audience. I used the distinction between direct persuasion and indirect campaign value, and that distinction is exactly what the passage supports. An important assumption behind my reasoning was that media attention can itself be beneficial even if the advertisement’s intrinsic persuasive force is limited; that assumption is licensed by the passage. I also correctly avoided overreading the claim about political origins into answers about who borrows from whom or who is hired most often. The main alternative to consider was whether any option about political versus corporate campaign practices was contradicted, but the passage only established one direction of borrowing and did not rule out others. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on what the passage explicitly presents as useful, rather than on broader background claims. A transferable rule is: when a passage gives one concrete causal source of effectiveness, it strongly undermines any answer claiming that effectiveness depends solely on some different source.

item.context: A certain experimental fungicide causes no harm to garden plants, though only if it is diluted at least to ten parts water to one part fungicide. Moreover, this fungicide is known to be so effective against powdery mildew that it has the capacity to eliminate it completely from rose plants. Thus this fungicide, as long as it is sufficiently diluted, provides a means of eliminating powdery mildew from rose plants that involves no risk of harming the plants.
item.question: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The effectiveness of the fungicide does not depend on its being more concentrated than one part in ten parts of water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When the fungicide is sufficiently diluted, it does not present any risk of harm to people, animals, or beneficial insects.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a fungicide is to be effective against powdery mildew on rose plants, it must eliminate the powdery mildew completely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Powdery mildew is the only fungal infection that affects rose plants.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion says the fungicide can eliminate mildew with no risk to plants, provided it is sufficiently diluted. For that to work, it must still be effective when diluted to the safe level. So the argument assumes effectiveness does not require a stronger concentration than 1:10.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-analysis approach: I identified the conclusion’s two required conditions—safe for plants when diluted enough, and effective against mildew—and checked what unstated link was needed to combine them. The key factor was that the evidence established safety only at a certain dilution, while effectiveness was stated more generally, so the argument needed effectiveness to still hold at that safe dilution. My success came from spotting that gap between “safe concentration” and “effective concentration.” For similar questions, explicitly test whether the conclusion combines two separate claims and then look for the missing assumption that makes both true under the same conditions.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as an assumption question asking for a necessary unstated link between the premises and the conclusion, not merely a statement that would strengthen the argument. That interpretation was correct, because the argument moved from two separate facts—safe when sufficiently diluted, and highly effective against powdery mildew—to a combined conclusion about a safe-and-effective treatment. My strategy was to identify the gap created by combining those two properties and ask what must be true for both to hold at the same time. That was the right method here, since the conclusion depended on the fungicide being effective specifically at the dilution level that makes it harmless to plants. The key evidence I used was the conditional statement about safety at a minimum dilution and the separate statement about efficacy, which did not explicitly say efficacy persisted under that dilution. I correctly noticed that the argument would fail if the fungicide only worked at a stronger, unsafe concentration. I did not rely on irrelevant side issues such as harm to insects or whether mildew is the only fungal problem, which helped avoid attractive but unnecessary choices. The success came from testing necessity: if the chosen statement were false, the conclusion could not stand. In similar problems, I should keep asking whether each answer is required for the argument’s inference rather than merely consistent with the topic. General rule: when an argument combines “safe under condition X” with “effective in general,” check whether it assumes effectiveness still holds under condition X.

item.context: An American scholar did an experiment in which the children were shown three-spoke pictures: chicken, cow and grass, and then asked to divide them into two categories. As a result, most Chinese children put cattle and grass in one category, chickens in another category, and most American children put cattle and chicken in one category and grass in another category. As a result, American scholars have come to the conclusion that Chinese children are used to classifying things according to the relationship between things, while American children are used to classifying things according to the category of entity to which they belong.
item.question: Which of the following must be assumed by the scholar to draw a conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Horses and grasses are classified into one category according to the relationship between things

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ducks and eggs are grouped into one category according to the entity category to which they belong

choices.label: C
choices.text: As long as American children put cattle and chickens into the same category, they are used to classifying them according to their respective entity categories

choices.label: D
choices.text: American children are not accustomed to classifying things according to the relationship between things as long as they classify cattle and chickens into the same category

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion about American children requires assuming that grouping cow and chicken together really reflects classification by shared entity type, not some other basis. Without that, the experiment wouldn’t support the scholar’s claim. A and B are irrelevant; D is stronger than needed.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a necessary-assumption approach: identify the gap between the observed grouping behavior and the broader claim about the children’s habitual classification style. The key factor was that the scholar inferred a mental rule from one pairing, so the argument needed a link showing that putting cattle and chickens together indicates grouping by entity category rather than some other reason. My success came from testing which option directly bridges that inference without adding extra claims. For similar problems, isolate the exact observational evidence and ask what hidden premise is required to make that evidence support the stated interpretation.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as an assumption question: not which option is true or plausible, but which unstated premise is necessary for the scholar’s conclusion to follow from the observed sorting behavior. That interpretation was correct, because the evidence was only about how children grouped three items, while the conclusion generalized about their habitual classification style. My strategy was to test which answer bridges the gap between the observed grouping and the claimed cognitive principle. Specifically, I focused on the American children, since the conclusion says that when they grouped cattle with chicken, this supports classification by entity category rather than by some other basis. That made option C attractive because it links the specific observed act of grouping those two items to the inferred reason for grouping them.

The key evidence I used was that cattle and chicken can be seen as belonging to the same broad class, while cattle and grass can be linked by an ecological or functional relationship. I correctly rejected A and B because they discuss other examples rather than a necessary premise connecting the experiment to the conclusion. I also rejected D because it adds an unnecessary exclusivity claim: the scholar need not assume American children never use relational classification. The main success in my reasoning was distinguishing a sufficient bridge from an overstrong claim. For similar problems, I should keep asking: “What exact inference from observation to explanation requires support?” General rule: in assumption questions, prefer the option that is required to interpret the evidence in the way the conclusion needs, not one that merely strengthens it or overstates it.

item.context: The 1980s have been characterized as a period of selfish individualism that threatens the cohesion of society. But this characterization is true of any time. Throughout history all human actions have been motivated by selfishness. When the deeper implications are considered, even the simplest unselfish acts prove to be instances of selfish concern for the human species.
item.question: Which one of the following is a flaw in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The argument relies on two different uses of the term selfish.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim that selfishness has been present throughout history is not actually relevant to the argument.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The argument mentions only humans and does not consider the behavior of other species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No statistical evidence is provided to show that humans act selfishly more often than they act unselfishly.

response:
Reasoning: The argument shifts from “selfish” meaning concern for one’s own interests to a broader meaning that includes concern for humanity as a whole. Calling unselfish acts “selfish concern for the human species” changes the meaning of the key term, creating an equivocation.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-identification approach, tracking how the key term functioned across the argument rather than evaluating whether the conclusion was true. The decisive clue was that “selfish” first referred to ordinary self-interest by an individual, but later was stretched to include concern for the human species, which is a different concept. That shift in meaning supported the conclusion only by equivocating on the same word. For similar problems, I should explicitly test whether a repeated key term keeps the same definition from premise to conclusion.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the argument’s logical flaw, not whether its conclusion was psychologically plausible. That was the right framing, because LSAT-style flaw questions usually turn on how the reasoning connects premises to conclusion. My strategy was to track the key term “selfish” across the argument and test whether it kept the same meaning. That was appropriate here because the conclusion depends almost entirely on extending the label “selfish” to every action, including apparently unselfish ones.

The crucial evidence was the movement from ordinary selfishness, meaning pursuit of one’s own interests, to “selfish concern for the human species,” which is much broader and not equivalent. I correctly noticed that the argument tries to preserve its universal claim by redefining the central term rather than proving it. I did not get distracted by irrelevant issues such as statistical support or comparative claims about other species, which the stimulus did not need. One shortcut that helped, rather than hurt, was asking whether an “unselfish act” could still count as selfish only by changing definitions; that exposed the equivocation quickly.

The main reason the reasoning succeeded is that I focused on semantic consistency instead of debating the truth of the premises. In similar problems, I should continue checking whether a conclusion is sustained only by stretching a key word. A precise transferable rule is: when an argument reaches a sweeping conclusion by reclassifying apparent counterexamples, test whether the key term has shifted in meaning between premise and conclusion.

item.context: In recent years, the total amount of river runoff and water resources in the South has increased, with an increase of nearly 5%, while the amount of water resources in the North has decreased significantly, especially in the Yellow River, Huaihe River, Haihe River and Liaohe River. The total amount of resources has decreased by 12%. According to the current normal needs, if the groundwater is not over exploited, the country will be short of nearly 40 billion cubic meters in normal years.
item.question: Which of the following is this passage intended to emphasize?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In recent years, the national water shortage is still very serious.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The total amount of water resources in North China is significantly lower than that in South China.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The distribution of water resources in the South and north of China is uneven.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The total amount of water resources in China showed a downward trend as a whole.

response:
Reasoning: The passage gives regional changes in water resources, then concludes that without overusing groundwater, China would still face a shortage of nearly 40 billion cubic meters in normal years. This overall conclusion emphasizes the seriousness of the national water shortage, not just regional imbalance.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach: I compared the supporting details about regional changes with the passage’s concluding statement to identify what point the author was driving toward. The key factor was the final sentence saying that even under normal conditions, and without overexploiting groundwater, the country would still face a large shortfall; that turns the earlier data into evidence for a broader national problem. The successful step was prioritizing the author’s conclusion over intermediate descriptive facts like north-south differences. For similar problems, treat statistics and contrasts as support, then choose the option that best matches the passage’s ultimate claim or takeaway.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s main emphasis, not just a fact that appears in the middle. That distinction mattered because the paragraph first presents regional trends in water resources, then ends with a nationwide consequence: even under normal demand, there remains a large shortfall if groundwater is not overexploited. My strategy was to identify the statement that functions as the author’s conclusion, giving more weight to the final sentence than to the supporting statistics before it. That was appropriate here because the earlier contrasts between South and North serve as evidence for a broader national problem rather than as the central point themselves.

The key evidence I used was the explicit statement about a shortage of nearly 40 billion cubic meters in normal years. I correctly recognized that this is stronger and more comprehensive than observations about uneven distribution or regional decline alone. One assumption behind my reasoning was that the passage is structured as “data first, conclusion last,” which is a reliable but not universal pattern; here it fit well. I also implicitly ruled out choices that merely restated partial details, such as north-south imbalance or overall decline, because they did not capture the passage’s final emphasis.

The reasoning succeeded because I distinguished supporting facts from the author’s intended takeaway. In similar problems, I should keep asking which sentence answers “So what?” rather than choosing the most noticeable statistic. A transferable rule is: when identifying a passage’s emphasis, prefer the option that integrates the supporting details into the author’s stated overall conclusion, rather than an option that repeats only one subsidiary fact.

item.context: Administrative punishment refers to administrative sanctions imposed by administrative agencies on citizens, legal persons or other organizations that constitute administrative violations.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following is an administrative penalty?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The school severely punishes students who cheat on exams.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The judge sentenced the thief to 10 years in prison.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The health department imposes a penalty of suspension of business on restaurants that fail the sanitation inspection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A supermarket imposes a penalty of one penalty ten on the thief.

response:
Reasoning: An administrative penalty must be imposed by an administrative agency for an administrative violation. A is a school’s internal discipline, B is a criminal punishment by a court, and D is a private supermarket’s measure. Only C is a sanction by the health department.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I broke the concept into required elements—an administrative agency, a target such as a citizen or organization, and a sanction for an administrative violation—and checked each option against those criteria. The key factor was identifying the actor imposing the punishment, because only a government administrative department qualifies, not a school, court, or private business. The answer was correct because I filtered out options by legal nature of the punishing body before considering the punishment itself. For similar problems, first translate the definition into a short checklist of necessary conditions and eliminate any option that fails even one condition.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as a definition-matching task: identify which option fits all required elements of an administrative punishment, not just any kind of punishment. That interpretation was correct because the definition contained multiple necessary conditions: the actor must be an administrative agency, the target must be a citizen/legal person/organization, and the conduct must be an administrative violation. My strategy was to test each option against those elements one by one, which is the right method for classification questions built on formal definitions. The key evidence I used was the identity of the punishing body: a school is not acting as an administrative enforcement agency in student discipline, a judge imposing imprisonment is exercising criminal judicial power, and a supermarket is a private actor rather than a public authority. I also used the nature of the sanction to distinguish internal discipline, criminal punishment, and private retaliation from administrative sanctions. A useful implicit assumption I made was that “administrative penalty” depends more on legal authority and procedural role than on the everyday meaning of “punish.” I could also have checked more explicitly whether the punished conduct in each option was an “administrative violation,” but the source of authority already ruled most options out. The reasoning succeeded because I matched every option against the full definition instead of reacting to surface words like “penalty” or “punish.” In similar problems, I should continue decomposing definitions into necessary criteria and eliminate choices that fail even one criterion. General rule: when a concept is defined by institutional role, legal relationship, and triggering conduct, classify cases by those structural features rather than by the ordinary-language label attached to the action.

item.context: Political theorist: The chief foundations of all governments are the legal system and the police force; and as there cannot be a good legal system where the police are not well paid, it follows that where the police are well paid there will be a good legal system.
item.question: The reasoning in the argument is not sound because it fails to establish that

choices.label: A
choices.text: many governments with bad legal systems have poorly paid police forces

choices.label: B
choices.text: a well-paid police force is sufficient to guarantee a good legal system

choices.label: C
choices.text: some bad governments have good legal systems

choices.label: D
choices.text: a well-paid police force cannot be effective without a good legal system

response:
Reasoning: The premise gives only a necessary condition: if a legal system is good, then the police are well paid. The conclusion wrongly treats that as sufficient, inferring that well-paid police guarantee a good legal system. That has not been established.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a conditional-reasoning approach, translating the claim into an if-then relationship and checking whether the conclusion reversed that relationship. The key factor was that the premise established police being well paid as a necessary condition for a good legal system, while the conclusion treated it as a sufficient condition. My answer was correct because I identified this as a mistaken reversal of the conditional. For similar problems, explicitly label each condition as necessary or sufficient and test whether the argument illegitimately switches or reverses them.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument as testing whether the conclusion validly followed from the stated conditional relationship between a good legal system and well-paid police. That interpretation was correct because the flaw hinged on the direction of implication, not on empirical claims about governments in general. My strategy was to translate the key premise into a conditional form: a good legal system requires well-paid police. From there, I checked whether the conclusion preserved that direction or reversed it. This was an appropriate strategy because flaw questions often depend on distinguishing necessary conditions from sufficient conditions.

The crucial evidence was the structure “cannot be a good legal system where the police are not well paid,” which supports only one-way dependence. I correctly noticed that the conclusion treated the presence of the necessary condition as if it guaranteed the outcome. I did not rely on irrelevant content about governments, legal systems, or policing quality beyond their logical roles, which helped avoid distraction from the answer choices involving broader political claims. A shortcut that worked here was abstracting the argument into form rather than evaluating it substantively. I also implicitly ruled out alternatives that introduced comparisons, examples, or additional causal assumptions not required to diagnose the flaw. The reasoning succeeded because I identified the exact missing link: the argument never showed that the cited condition was enough by itself. A transferable rule is: when an argument goes from “X requires Y” to “Y ensures X,” test for illicit reversal of a conditional before considering content-based objections.

item.context: Despite the efforts of a small minority of graduate students at one university to unionize, the majority of graduate students there remain unaware of the attempt. Most of those who are aware believe that a union would not represent their interests or that, if it did, it would not effectively pursue them. Thus, the graduate students at the university should not unionize, since the majority of them obviously disapprove of the attempt.
item.question: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: blurs the distinction between active disapproval and mere lack of approval

choices.label: B
choices.text: tries to establish a conclusion simply on the premise that the conclusion agrees with a long-standing practice

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes that simply because a majority of a population is unaware of something, it must not be a good idea

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to exclude alternative explanations for why some graduate students disapprove of unionizing

response:
Reasoning: The argument treats unawareness and skepticism as “obvious disapproval.” But many students are merely unaware, not opposed. So it conflates not approving or not knowing with actively disapproving, making the majority’s supposed opposition unsupported.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-identification approach by separating the premises into groups: students who were unaware and students who were aware but skeptical, then comparing that evidence to the conclusion about majority disapproval. The key factor was that “unaware” does not equal “disapprove,” so the argument treated absence of support or knowledge as active opposition. My reasoning succeeded because I focused on whether the evidence actually established the claimed attitude of the majority. For similar questions, explicitly test each category in the premises against the exact conclusion term and reject arguments that shift from non-support, ignorance, or inaction to affirmative opposition.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the precise logical flaw in the argument, not whether unionization is desirable. My strategy was to track how the conclusion about what the graduate students “obviously” think was inferred from the premises about awareness and attitudes. That was appropriate because flaw questions usually turn on whether the conclusion overstates what the evidence establishes. The key evidence I used was that many students were said to be unaware of the effort, while only “most of those who are aware” held negative views; those are different categories and cannot simply be added together as if both showed opposition. I correctly noticed that the argument moved from “not aware” or “not persuaded” to “disapprove,” which is a stronger claim. A shortcut that helped, and in this case did not mislead me, was checking whether any answer choice captured a confusion between absence of support and presence of opposition. I also implicitly ruled out alternatives involving tradition, causal explanation, or a general principle about majority unawareness because the argument’s language did not depend on those structures. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the quantifiers and attitude labels rather than on the political content. In similar problems, I should systematically compare each premise category with the conclusion category and ask whether any mental state has been strengthened without justification. General rule: when an argument infers opposition from silence, ignorance, or nonendorsement, test whether it illegitimately converts “not in favor” into “against.”

item.context: The giant-toothed shark, which became extinct 2.6 million years ago, is more than 15 meters long and has a powerful bite force, and its 3-meter-wide jaw can crush a car. However, a recent study shows that giant-toothed sharks prefer minke whales less than 5 meters long rather than larger baleen whales. However, due to climate change, the population of minke whales has plummeted. Based on this, the researchers believe that giant-toothed sharks became extinct due to lack of food.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, weakens the above conclusion most?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sharp decline in the population of minke whales 2.6 million years ago was due to lack of food

choices.label: B
choices.text: Baleen whales are the fastest of all whales and are difficult to be preyed on by giant tooth sharks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Giant tooth sharks also like to prey on smaller seals and now extinct dwarf sperm whales

choices.label: D
choices.text: Large whales such as humpback whales and blue whales that lived at the same time as giant-toothed sharks have evolved

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion assumes giant-toothed sharks depended mainly on minke whales. If they also commonly preyed on other animals, then the decline of minke whales would not necessarily cause food shortage severe enough to drive extinction. Choice C directly provides alternative food sources, so it weakens the conclusion most.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a causal-weaken approach: identify the argument’s core claim that a drop in one prey species caused the predator’s extinction, then look for evidence that breaks that dependency. The key factor was whether giant-toothed sharks relied mainly on minke whales or had other substantial food sources available. My success came from targeting the assumption of exclusivity: if the sharks also preyed on other animals, the alleged food shortage becomes much less compelling. For similar problems, explicitly test causal arguments by asking what hidden assumption links the cause to the effect, then choose the option that provides an alternative explanation or an alternative resource/path.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument as a causal explanation: researchers infer that one prey population’s decline led to the predator’s extinction through food scarcity. That interpretation was correct, because the key task was not to identify a related fact, but to find information that most undermines the causal link between prey decline and extinction. My strategy was to test the argument’s hidden assumption, namely that the sharks depended heavily enough on that prey that losing it would create a fatal shortage. That was an appropriate weakening approach, because causal claims are often vulnerable when they ignore alternative causes or overlooked alternatives that break necessity.

The crucial evidence I used was the distinction between “preferred” prey and “exclusive” or “indispensable” prey. I correctly recognized that preferring one food source does not imply inability to survive on others. The strongest weakening information therefore would show the sharks had additional viable prey, reducing the force of the food-shortage explanation. I also implicitly compared the other options by asking whether they attacked the conclusion directly or merely added background facts. That comparison mattered because some choices were consistent with the conclusion or too indirect to weaken it much.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on dependency rather than size, speed, or contemporaneous species facts. In similar problems, I should continue identifying the exact assumption that must hold for a causal explanation to work. A general rule: when an argument claims that loss of one factor caused failure or extinction, test whether that factor was truly necessary by looking for substitutes, alternative resources, or resilience mechanisms.

item.context: A study of adults who suffer from migraine headaches revealed that a significant proportion of the study participants suffer from a complex syndrome characterized by a set of three symptoms. Those who suffer from the syndrome experienced excessive anxiety during early childhood. As adolescents, these people began experiencing migraine headaches. As these people approached the age of 20, they also began to experience recurring bouts of depression. Since this pattern is invariant, always with excessive anxiety at its beginning, it follows that excessive anxiety in childhood is one of the causes of migraine headaches and depression in later life.
item.question: The reasoning in the argument is vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It fails to rule out the possibility that all of the characteristic symptoms of the syndrome have a common cause.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It does not specify the proportion of those in the general population who suffer from the syndrome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It does not establish why the study of migraine sufferers was restricted to adult participants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It makes a generalization that is inconsistent with the evidence.

response:
Reasoning: The argument infers causation from a fixed sequence of symptoms. But an invariant order does not show that childhood anxiety causes the later conditions; all three symptoms could result from some underlying common cause. That alternative is not ruled out.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a causal-flaw approach: I looked for whether the argument moved from correlation or sequence to causation without enough support. The key clue was the claim that because the pattern is “invariant,” the earliest symptom must be a cause of the later ones. My success came from noticing that a fixed temporal order does not eliminate the possibility of a single underlying factor producing all three symptoms at different times. For similar problems, when an argument infers causation from timing or regular succession, explicitly test whether a common cause could explain the whole pattern.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the flaw in the argument’s move from an observed temporal pattern to a causal conclusion. My strategy was to identify the conclusion first, then test whether the premises actually ruled out standard causal alternatives. That was appropriate here because the argument relies on the sequence “first anxiety, then migraines, then depression” and treats that order as proof that the first event causes the later ones. The key evidence I used was that temporal priority and invariance of order do not by themselves establish causation. I also noticed that the study described a syndrome, which strongly suggests the possibility that the symptoms are linked through some underlying condition rather than through a simple chain of cause and effect.  

A crucial assumption in the argument is “if X always comes first, X causes what follows,” which is not a valid causal principle. The main alternative that had to be considered was a shared underlying factor producing all three symptoms at different developmental stages. I did not get distracted by irrelevant issues such as sample proportion or why adults were studied, which helped keep the analysis focused on the actual inferential gap. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the flaw to a classic pattern: confusing sequence with causation while ignoring common-cause explanations. In similar problems, I should systematically ask whether the evidence shows causation, correlation, sequence, or merely co-occurrence. General rule: whenever an argument infers causation from a consistent order of events, test whether a third factor could explain all the observed events without any one of them causing the others.

item.context: Psychologists today recognize childhood as a separate stage of life which can only be understood in its own terms, and they wonder why the Western world took so long to see the folly of regarding children simply as small, inadequately socialized adults. Most psychologists, however, persist in regarding people 70 to 90 years old as though they were 35 year olds who just happen to have white hair and extra leisure time. But old age is as fundamentally different from young adulthood and middle age as childhood is -- a fact attested to by the organization of modern social and economic life. Surely it is time, ttherefore, to acknowledge that serious research into the unique psychology of advanced age has become indispensable.
item.question: Which one of the following principles, if established, would provide the strongest backing for the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whenever most practitioners of a given discipline approach a particular problem in the same way, that uniformity is good evidence that all similar problems should also be approached in that way.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whenever psychologists agree that a single psychology is inadequate for two distinct age groups, they should be prepared to show that there are greater differences between the two age groups than there are between individuals in the same age group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whenever two groups of people are so related to each other that any member of the second group must previously have been a member of the first, people in the first group should not be regarded simply as deviant members of the second group.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whenever a society's economic life is so organized that two distinct times of life are treated as being fundamentally different from one another, each time of life can be understood only in terms of its own distinct psychology.

response:
Reasoning: The argument moves from: childhood is recognized as distinct; old age is also fundamentally different, as shown by modern social/economic organization; therefore old age needs its own psychology. The strongest supporting principle is that when society organizes two life stages as fundamentally different, each must be understood through a distinct psychology.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a principle-matching approach: I identified the argument’s premises and conclusion, then looked for a rule that would directly connect them. The key clue was the author’s appeal to “the organization of modern social and economic life” as evidence that old age is fundamentally different, which needed a principle linking social/economic differentiation to distinct psychology. My success came from choosing the option that validated exactly that inferential step rather than one discussing psychologists’ agreement or general uniformity. For similar problems, first isolate the gap between evidence and conclusion, then select the principle that most directly licenses that specific move.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for a principle that would justify the argument’s key inferential move, not merely restate one of its premises. The conclusion was that research into the psychology of advanced age is indispensable, so I looked for a rule connecting the cited evidence to that conclusion. My strategy was to identify the argument’s central bridge: the passage treats social and economic recognition of two life stages as evidence that those stages require distinct psychological understanding. That was the right strategy for a principle-strengthen question, because the best answer had to validate the transition from “society treats them as fundamentally different” to “they must be understood through a distinct psychology.”

The evidence I used well was the analogy between childhood and old age and the explicit mention of modern social and economic organization. I correctly noticed that the passage relies on that organization as support, so the strongest principle would elevate that support into a general rule. I avoided being distracted by answer choices about consensus among psychologists or comparisons between individuals within age groups, because those issues were not necessary to the author’s reasoning. One assumption built into my reasoning was that the argument depends more on societal structure than on developmental continuity or practitioner agreement, and that assumption fit the text. I should still have considered whether a tempting alternative might capture the childhood analogy more directly, but I saw that such alternatives failed to connect the premises to the conclusion as tightly. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the exact logical gap rather than on surface themes like age differences in general. A transferable rule is: in principle questions, identify the premise-to-conclusion jump and prefer the option that turns the argument’s specific cited evidence into a sufficient general warrant.

item.context: The incubation effect refers to the phenomenon that after a period of time, a problem that has not been solved is unexpectedly answered.
item.question: Which of the following is not the incubation effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mountain is followed by a stream of water. When in doubt there was no way out, a village appeared.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inadvertently a turn around, the man was standing in the light of the scattered place.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Something that took a lot of effort not to find, but people got by accident.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It took three years to come up with two verses. People cry when they chant it.

response:
Reasoning: Incubation means a solution appears unexpectedly after being stuck for a while. A, B, and C all describe sudden insight or accidental discovery after difficulty. D describes deliberate, prolonged effort over three years, not an unexpected answer after incubation.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option to the core features of incubation, namely being stuck on a problem and then reaching a solution unexpectedly after a break or delay. The key factor was whether the answer emerged suddenly and indirectly rather than through continuous, effortful work. My success came from identifying that one option emphasized long-term deliberate composition instead of an unplanned breakthrough. For similar problems, I should explicitly test each choice against every defining condition of the concept, not just whether it vaguely involves time or difficulty.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the option that does not match the defining structure of incubation: being stuck on a problem, stepping away or letting time pass, and then arriving at an answer unexpectedly. That interpretation was correct, because the key distinction is not merely “taking a long time,” but the combination of prior impasse and later unplanned insight. My strategy was to extract the core features of the definition and compare each option against those features rather than focusing on literary style or familiarity of the expressions. This was appropriate because several choices were metaphorical, so surface wording could be distracting. I used the contrast between “unexpectedly answered” and “effortful, deliberate production” as the main diagnostic criterion. In particular, I recognized that accidental discovery or sudden illumination can fit incubation, while sustained conscious crafting without a break in approach does not. One assumption I made was that the poetic wording in some choices still intended to represent sudden insight, and that assumption was reasonable in context. I also implicitly considered whether “after a period of time” alone was sufficient, and correctly rejected that shortcut. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on necessary conditions, not just loosely related ideas like difficulty or elapsed time. In similar problems, I should continue to identify the minimal defining traits of the target concept and test each option against all of them. A transferable rule is: when classifying examples of a concept, distinguish essential features from merely associated features, and eliminate options that match the latter but not the former.

item.context: The researchers arranged an experiment in which 100 subjects were divided into two groups: the experimental group who drank a small glass of red wine and the control group that did not drink alcohol, and then asked the two groups to count the number of times basketball players passed the ball to each other in a video. The results showed that all the subjects in the control group were accurate, while only 18% of the subjects in the experimental group were accurate. After testing, the blood alcohol concentration of the subjects in the experimental group was only half that of the drunk driving law, and experts pointed out that the results of the study may allow lawmakers to redefine the legal value of drunk driving.
item.question: Which of the following, if true,can best support the opinions of the above-mentioned experts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If the fixed value of drunk driving law is set too low, many non-drinkers may be defined as drunk driving

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even if the blood alcohol concentration is only half of the legal value for drunk driving, it will affect vision and reaction speed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drinking too much alcohol not only harms your health, but also affects your driving safety

choices.label: D
choices.text: As long as the alcohol concentration in the blood does not exceed the limit of drunk driving, you can drive on the road

response:
Reasoning: Experts suggest lowering the legal drunk-driving threshold because impairment appeared even at half the current legal limit. The best support is that such a low blood alcohol concentration still harms abilities crucial for driving, like vision and reaction speed. That directly connects the experiment to traffic law.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a relevance-and-bridge approach: I looked for the option that most directly connected the experiment’s finding at a sub-legal alcohol level to the policy conclusion about changing drunk-driving standards. The key factor was that subjects showed major impairment even when their blood alcohol concentration was only half the legal limit, so the strongest support had to show that this level also affects abilities tied to driving. The successful step was focusing on the missing link between lab performance and road safety, rather than on general statements about alcohol. For similar problems, identify the conclusion’s weakest link and choose the option that directly supplies that specific connection.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a strengthening task: the experiment showed impairment at a blood alcohol level below the current legal threshold, and the experts concluded this could justify changing the law. The key reasoning step was to identify what gap needed support between the study’s finding and the policy implication. I recognized that the experiment itself measured attention to a visual task, not driving directly, so the strongest support would be an answer linking low-level alcohol consumption to abilities relevant to safe driving. That made my strategy appropriate: look for the choice that connects sub-legal blood alcohol concentration to actual driving-related impairment rather than to general facts about alcohol.

The evidence I relied on was the contrast between the control group’s accuracy and the experimental group’s low accuracy, plus the fact that the experimental group’s blood alcohol concentration was only half the legal limit. I correctly treated that as evidence of meaningful impairment below the current standard. I did not make the mistake of choosing a statement that was merely true about alcohol in general, because general harm does not specifically support redefining a legal threshold. I also rejected choices that weakened or contradicted the experts’ conclusion. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the missing bridge from laboratory performance impairment to road-safety relevance. In similar problems, I should explicitly ask: “What new fact would make the conclusion follow more directly from the study?” A general rule is: in strengthen questions, prefer the option that connects the exact experimental finding to the exact practical conclusion, rather than one that only restates background knowledge.

item.context: According to the Cultural relics Protection Law, even if the ownership of a building or other facility protected as a cultural relic belongs to an individual, the owner has no right to repair, decorate or even rebuild it. This provision is not appropriate because sometimes owners propose to modify the appearance and internal structure of cultural relics because they are convinced that doing so will enhance their value by strengthening and beautifying them.
item.question: Which of the following options, if true, most weakens the above argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The transformation of cultural relic buildings may not necessarily play the role of reinforcement and beautification, but sometimes become irrelevant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some cultural relic buildings are in disrepair. If they are not rebuilt in time, their value will be seriously damaged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The real value of cultural relic architecture is that it is a historical relic and any change to its original appearance is reducing its value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An owner cannot dispose of his property, which is a violation of his basic rights.

response:
Reasoning: The argument says owners should be allowed to modify relics because changes may “enhance value.” The strongest weakening is that a relic’s value lies in its original historical authenticity, so altering appearance or structure actually reduces value. That directly undercuts the argument’s core assumption.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-weaken approach: I identified the argument’s core premise that owner-made repairs or alterations can increase a cultural relic’s value. The key factor was the meaning of “value” for cultural relics—if their value comes from historical authenticity, then strengthening or beautifying them is not necessarily beneficial. My success came from targeting that central assumption directly rather than choosing an option that only discussed practical exceptions or owner rights. For similar questions, first identify the argument’s hidden definition or standard, then choose the option that attacks that standard most directly.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the prompt as asking for the option that most undermines the objection to the law, not the law itself. The objection’s core claim was that owners may want to alter protected buildings because such alterations can increase their value through reinforcement and beautification. My strategy was to identify the argument’s central assumption about “value” and then look for a choice that attacked that assumption directly. That was appropriate because weakening questions are usually best handled by finding the premise that links the evidence to the conclusion.

The key relationship I used was that the argument treats value as something that can be increased by making a structure stronger or more attractive. I noticed that if the relevant kind of value is instead historical authenticity, then improvement in appearance or durability would not support the conclusion. I correctly prioritized a conceptual attack on the meaning of value over choices that merely discussed practical outcomes in some cases. For example, a statement that modifications sometimes fail would only show uncertainty, not defeat the argument’s principle. I also avoided being distracted by choices about property rights, because the argument was about appropriateness based on preservation value, not legal entitlement in general.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the argument’s hidden definition of value. In similar problems, I should keep asking: what must the author mean by a key term for the conclusion to work? A transferable rule is: when an argument depends on improving something’s “value,” test whether the relevant value standard is the one the argument assumes.

item.context: The Chinese government's investment in biotechnology research and development is second only to the United States, ranking second in the world. Some experts believe that if we hesitate to promote the production of genetically modified crops that are confirmed to be safe, it will not only make us miss the opportunity in international competition, but also It will cause a huge waste of huge public R&D funds.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, cannot challenge the expert's statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Of the Chinese government's biotechnology R&D investment, only a very small amount is used for genetically modified crop research

choices.label: B
choices.text: International competition mainly depends on theoretical innovation, not technical promotion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hurrying to promote imperfect R&D results may cause greater waste of public R&D funds

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many countries that oppose the promotion of the production of genetically modified crops have invested little in the field of biotechnology research and development

response:
Reasoning: The expert says delaying safe GM crop commercialization risks losing competitive advantage and wasting large public R&D funds. A, B, and C each weaken that link. D only says some anti-GM countries invested little in biotech; this neither undermines the expert’s causal claim nor the China-specific argument.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a weakening-test approach: I identified the expert’s core claim as a causal chain linking hesitation in promotion to lost international competitiveness and wasted public R&D spending, then checked which option failed to undercut that chain. The key factor was whether an option directly challenged either the size/relevance of the investment, the basis of competition, or the risk of waste from promotion decisions. The success came from separating China-specific causal reasoning from mere background facts about other countries. For similar problems, first restate the exact claim structure, then eliminate choices that are only loosely related or comparative but do not attack the claim’s causal link or assumptions.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as an exception-type weakening problem: identify the option that does not undermine the expert’s claim. The expert’s statement had two linked predictions about hesitation in promoting safe genetically modified crops: losing international competitive opportunity and wasting public R&D investment. My strategy was to test each option against those two links and ask whether it attacked the scale of investment, the source of competition, or the risk of waste. That was an appropriate strategy because exception questions are best handled by evaluating each choice’s relevance to the exact conclusion rather than looking for what sounds generally negative.

The key evidence I used was the structure of the argument: “if we hesitate, then bad consequence 1 and bad consequence 2.” Options that reduce the importance of GM-specific investment, deny that promotion matters for competition, or suggest promotion itself could waste more funds all directly target that structure. I correctly noticed that one option was only a loose comparison about other countries’ attitudes and investment levels, without bearing on whether hesitation in China would produce the predicted harms. A potential shortcut I avoided was treating any anti-promotion fact as a challenge; instead, I checked whether it actually weakened the causal or evaluative claims. The success came from distinguishing relevance from mere topic overlap. In similar problems, I should continue mapping each answer to a specific premise-conclusion connection. A transferable rule is: in “cannot weaken” questions, eliminate choices that directly attack assumptions, and keep the choice that is merely adjacent in subject matter but does not affect the argument’s logic.

item.context: Subway lines 1, 2, 3 and 4 have been put into operation in a city, and the time required for each station to run and stop is the same. Xiao Zhang, Xiao Wang and Xiao Li are employees of the same unit, which is near beikou subway station. One morning, 3 people all take line 1 to go to work in Evergreen station at the same time, but 3 people have different ideas about the bus route. It is known that :(1) if line 1 is crowded, xiao zhang will take line 2, then transfer to line 3, and then take 3 stops to beikou station; If line 1 is not crowded, Xiao Zhang can take line 2 after three stops, and then four stops to Beikou Station. (2) Only when Line 1 was crowded, xiao Wang took 2 stops, then transferred to Line 3, and took 3 stops to Beikou Station. (3) If line 1 is not crowded, Xiao Li can take line 4 after four stops, then transfer to Line 4 after three stops, then transfer to Line 3 after three stops, and take line 1 to Beikou Station. The Subway line 1 was not crowded this morning.
item.question: Which of the following is most likely to be inconsistent with the above information, given the same total transfer and walking time among three people?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Xiao Wang and Xiao Li arrived at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Xiao Zhang and Xiao Wang arrived at the same time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Xiao Wang arrived at work before Xiao Li.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Xiao Li got to work before Xiao Zhang.

response:
Reasoning: Since Line 1 was not crowded: Zhang’s route is 3 + 4 = 7 stops. Li’s route needs at least 4 + 3 + 3 plus another Line 1 segment, so definitely more than 7 stops. With equal transfer/walking time, Li cannot arrive before Zhang. Thus D is inconsistent.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a route-length comparison approach: first fix the condition that Line 1 was not crowded, then translate each person’s stated plan into the number of stops traveled, treating transfer and walking time as equal across all three. The key factor was that Xiao Zhang’s non-crowded route is fully specified and relatively short, while Xiao Li’s non-crowded route already includes several segments before even returning to Line 1, so his total must be longer. The successful step was comparing minimum guaranteed travel lengths rather than trying to reconstruct the whole network. For similar problems, convert each conditional statement into concrete lower/upper bounds and eliminate choices by comparing unavoidable totals under the given condition.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a comparative travel-time problem under a fixed condition: line 1 was not crowded, and transfer plus walking time was assumed equal across all three people, so the only relevant difference was in-train travel time. That interpretation was correct, because the statements were conditional and the question asked which timing relation was incompatible with those conditions. My strategy was to translate each person’s allowed route, under the actual condition, into a count of stops and compare those counts. This was appropriate because the problem explicitly states that the running-and-stopping time per station is the same, which makes stop count a valid proxy for rail travel time.

The key evidence I used successfully was that Xiao Zhang’s non-crowded route totaled a fixed number of stops, while Xiao Li’s non-crowded route included several specified segments plus an additional final segment, guaranteeing a strictly longer trip. I also correctly ignored Xiao Wang’s crowded-only route, since the condition for using it was not met, and the prompt did not force a unique route for him under the actual condition. A useful shortcut I took was not needing the exact last segment for Xiao Li; it was enough to prove it was positive. That shortcut was justified because the task was to eliminate an impossible ordering, not compute exact arrival times.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on inequalities rather than overcommitting to unspecified network details. In similar problems, I should continue isolating which conditional branches are active and compare only quantities that are invariant under the problem’s assumptions. A general rule is: when a problem equalizes all non-core costs, reduce each option to the remaining measurable quantity and look for strict dominance, since any strict lower bound can rule out an ordering without full reconstruction.

item.context: A leading critic of space exploration contends that it would be wrong, given current technology, to send a group of explorers to Mars, since the explorers would be unlikely to survive the trip. But that exaggerates the risk. There would be a well-engineered backup system at every stage of the long and complicated journey. A fatal catastrophe is quite unlikely at any given stage if such a backup system is in place.
item.question: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers that something cannot occur merely from the fact that it is unlikely to occur

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejects a view merely on the grounds that an inadequate argument has been made for it

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about what must be the case based on evidence about what is probably the case

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers that something is true of a whole merely from the fact that it is true of each of the parts

response:
Reasoning: The argument assumes that because a fatal catastrophe is unlikely at each individual stage, the entire journey is therefore unlikely to be fatal. But many low risks across multiple stages can add up to a significant overall risk. That is a parts-to-whole flaw.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used flaw-identification by comparing the structure of the evidence to the conclusion. The key clue was the shift from “unlikely at any given stage” to a claim about the safety of the entire journey, which treats stage-by-stage risk as if it automatically determines overall risk. My answer was correct because I recognized this as a part-to-whole inference: what is true of each segment need not be true of the total process. For similar problems, I should explicitly test whether a conclusion about an aggregate is being supported only by claims about individual components.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the specific logical flaw in the rebuttal to the critic, not for an assessment of whether Mars travel is actually safe. The key was to separate the conclusion about the entire expedition from the evidence given about each stage of the expedition. My strategy was to map the argument structurally: each stage has a low probability of fatal catastrophe, therefore the whole journey’s risk is being treated as low. That was an appropriate strategy because flaw questions are best handled by abstracting away from the topic and comparing premise scope with conclusion scope. The decisive relationship I used was that a property of each part does not automatically transfer to the whole when probabilities can accumulate across parts. I did not need outside knowledge about space travel; the flaw was visible purely from the argument’s form. A shortcut that helped was recognizing the classic composition pattern: “true of each component, so true of the entire system.” I should also have actively ruled out the other options by checking whether the argument denied possibility, rejected a claim because of weak support, or shifted from probable to certain; it did none of those. The reasoning succeeded because it focused on how risk combines over a sequence, which is exactly what the argument ignored. In similar problems, I should explicitly test whether local claims aggregate cleanly to global claims or whether interaction and accumulation matter. General rule: when an argument moves from statements about individual parts, stages, or members to a conclusion about the whole, always check whether the inferred property is one that legitimately composes.

item.context: Robert: True appreciation of Haydn' s music demands that you hear it exactly as he intended it to be heard; that is, exactly as he heard it. Since he heard it on eighteenth-century instruments, it follows that so should we. Kari: But what makes you so sure that Haydn ever heard his music played as he had intended it to be played? After all, Haydn was writing at a time when the performer was expected, as a matter of course, not just to interpret but to modify the written score.
item.question: Kari adopts which of the following strategies in criticizing Robert's position?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She offers a reason to believe that one of the premises of his argument is false.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She defends a competing view of musical authenticity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She attacks his judgment by suggesting that he does not recognize the importance of the performer's creativity to the audience's appreciation of a musical composition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She appeals to an academic authority in order to challenge the factual basis of his conclusion.

response:
Reasoning: Kari challenges Robert’s key premise that Haydn heard his music “exactly as he intended it.” By noting performers commonly altered scores, she gives a reason to think that premise is false, rather than proposing her own theory or citing authority.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an argument-structure approach: I identified Robert’s conclusion and the premises supporting it, then checked whether Kari challenged the conclusion directly or undermined a premise. The key clue was Kari’s question about whether Haydn ever actually heard his music played as he intended, plus her supporting point that performers routinely modified scores. That showed she was targeting the factual assumption linking Haydn’s intentions to what he actually heard. A good rule for similar questions is to map each speaker’s claim and ask whether the response attacks a premise, attacks the inference, or offers an alternative view.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the argumentative method Kari uses, not whether her criticism is ultimately true or whether historical instruments are best. That was the right framing, because the answer choices describe types of criticism rather than substantive positions about music. My strategy was to isolate Robert’s conclusion and then identify the premise Kari targets. Robert’s reasoning depends on the assumption that hearing Haydn as Haydn heard it is equivalent to hearing Haydn as Haydn intended it, and Kari directly questions that equivalence. The key evidence was her point that performers in Haydn’s era routinely modified the score, which gives a concrete reason to doubt that Haydn actually heard performances matching his own intentions. I correctly distinguished that move from presenting an alternative theory of authenticity, since Kari does not offer a rival standard for appreciation. I also avoided being distracted by tempting language about performer creativity, because she mentions performers only to undermine a factual premise, not to argue that creativity is aesthetically superior. A bad shortcut would have been to choose the option mentioning creativity just because her example involves performers changing the score. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on argument structure: conclusion, supporting premise, and where the criticism lands. In similar problems, I should first map the original argument, then ask whether the response attacks a premise, the inference, or the conclusion. General rule: when a speaker questions whether a stated supporting condition actually obtained, that is an attack on a premise, even if the example used introduces broader thematic issues.

item.context: Carl: Researchers who perform operations on animals for experimental purposes are legally required to complete detailed pain protocols indicating whether the animals will be at risk of pain and, if so, what steps will be taken to minimize or alleviate it. Yet when human beings undergo operations, such protocols are never required. If lawmakers were as concerned about human beings as they seem to be about animals, there would be pain protocols for human beings too. Debbie: But consider this: a person for whom a doctor wants to schedule surgery can simply be told what pain to expect and can then decide whether or not to undergo the operation. So you see, pain protocols are unnecessary for human beings.
item.question: Debbie attempts to counter Carl' s argument by

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy that illustrates a major flaw in Carl's argument

choices.label: B
choices.text: claiming that Carl's argument should be rejected because it is based on an appeal to sentimentality rather than on reasoned principles

choices.label: C
choices.text: pointing out a relevant difference to undermine an analogy on which Carl bases his conclusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: offering a specific example to demonstrate that Carl's argument is based on a claim that can be neither confirmed nor disproved

response:
Reasoning: Carl’s conclusion relies on comparing animals and humans as if they are relevantly similar regarding pain protocols. Debbie counters by identifying a key difference: humans can be informed and consent to surgery, whereas animals cannot. This undermines the comparison Carl depends on.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used an argument-structure approach: I identified Carl’s reasoning as resting on a comparison between animals and humans, then looked for how Debbie attacked that comparison. The key factor was Debbie’s emphasis on informed consent—humans can be told the risks and choose, which creates a relevant difference from animals. The successful step was recognizing that this was not a new analogy or an attack on Carl’s motives, but a distinction that weakens the comparison underlying his conclusion. For similar problems, first ask whether the response challenges a premise directly or instead shows that the two compared cases differ in a way that matters to the conclusion.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking about Debbie’s argumentative move, not whether her conclusion about pain protocols is true. The key task was to identify the logical relationship between Carl’s argument and Debbie’s response. My strategy was to look for the structure of Carl’s reasoning: he compares animal research subjects with human surgical patients and infers that similar concern should produce similar procedural requirements. That revealed an analogy at the core of Carl’s argument, even though it was not presented in explicit “just as” language. I then examined Debbie’s reply for whether it attacked the analogy itself or introduced some other kind of objection. Her point about humans being able to receive information and choose whether to proceed identifies a relevant difference in decision-making capacity and consent. That difference matters directly to whether the same protocol is needed in both cases, so it weakens the comparison rather than merely criticizing Carl’s tone or giving an example. I did not rely on outside facts; I used only the roles described in the prompt: animals are protected through formal protocols, while humans can be informed and decide. A possible trap was to miss the implicit analogy because Carl framed it as a fairness complaint rather than a direct comparison. Another trap was to confuse Debbie’s response with a policy defense instead of a logical rebuttal. What made the reasoning successful was matching argument form to answer choice language. A transferable rule is: when one speaker argues that two cases should be treated alike, and the reply cites a difference that affects the conclusion, the reply is undermining the original analogy by pointing to a relevant disanalogy.

item.context: Environmental scientist: It is true that over the past ten years, there has been a sixfold increase in government funding for the preservation of wetlands, while the total area of wetlands needing such preservation has increased only twofold (although this area was already large ten years ago). Even when inflation is taken into account, the amount of funding now is at least three times what it was ten years ago. Nevertheless, the current amount of government funding for the preservation of wetlands is inadequate and should be augmented.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to reconcile the environmental scientist's conclusion with the evidence cited above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Over the past ten years, the salaries of scientists employed by the government to work on the preservation of wetlands have increased at a rate higher than the inflation rate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The governmental agency responsible for administering wetland-preservation funds has been consistently mismanaged and run inefficiently over the past ten years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Unlike today, funding for the preservation of wetlands was almost nonexistent ten years ago.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Research over the past ten years has enabled scientists today to identify wetlands in need of preservation well before the areas are at serious risk of destruction.

response:
Reasoning: The evidence says funding rose much faster than the area needing preservation, but that does not show the current level is sufficient. If funding was almost nonexistent ten years ago, then even a large multiple increase could still leave it far too low now.  
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a reconcile-the-paradox approach: I looked for a choice that explains how funding could rise much faster than need yet still remain inadequate. The key clue was that all the evidence was comparative over time, so the conclusion could still hold if the starting baseline was extremely low. My successful step was focusing on absolute sufficiency rather than being distracted by growth rates alone. For similar problems, translate percentage or multiple increases back into baseline terms and ask whether a large relative increase could still leave the total inadequate.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a reconcile-the-discrepancy problem: the stimulus gave facts that made funding seem much more generous than before, yet the conclusion said it was still inadequate. My strategy was to look for an answer choice showing that the comparison to ten years ago was misleading as evidence of current sufficiency. That was appropriate because the apparent tension came from relative growth rates, not from any direct claim about the absolute amount needed now. The key fact I used was that a large multiple increase can still leave funding inadequate if the starting level was extremely low. I also noticed the parenthetical remark that the area needing preservation was already large ten years ago, which suggested baseline conditions mattered. My reasoning avoided the trap of treating “increased more than inflation” or “increased faster than need” as proof of adequacy. I implicitly rejected choices that explained higher costs or inefficiency, because those would weaken confidence in current funding administration but did less to reconcile the conclusion with the speaker’s own cited evidence. I should also note that I correctly focused on whether an option connected the evidence to the conclusion, rather than merely providing a new complaint. The success came from distinguishing absolute sufficiency from percentage growth. In similar problems, I should ask whether the evidence is comparative while the conclusion is absolute. General rule: when a conclusion about adequacy seems inconsistent with large increases, test whether the baseline was so low that even substantial growth still fails to meet the relevant need.

item.context: When the old art, such as novel and drama, gradually deviates from the attention of the world and gives way to the upstart of film and television, a kind of cultural poverty is shrouded in all kinds of criticism. In the face of strong industrial culture, cultural criticism has almost become promotional advertising.
item.question: Which of the following options is the correct answer to the meaning of a cultural poverty is shrouded in all kinds of criticism mentioned in this paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cultural poverty makes criticism impossible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The taste of all kinds of cultural criticism is declining.

choices.label: C
