So the reasoning pattern matched the flaw described in choice B.  

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on necessity versus sufficiency rather than getting distracted by the archaeological setting or by the contrast between ceremonial structure and city. I did not assume that urban populations always generate specialized farms; I kept track of the weaker claim that they are only a precondition. An alternative I needed to check was whether the flaw involved ambiguity in “markets” or overgeneralization from one class member, but neither matched the structure. The correct diagnosis is that the argument infers too much from a missing effect. A useful general rule is: when a statement says one condition is necessary for another, you may infer “not necessary condition, therefore not dependent phenomenon,” but not the converse “not phenomenon, therefore not necessary condition.”

item.context: Emotional incentive method is a management incentive method to stimulate the enthusiasm of the managed through good emotional relationship, so as to improve work efficiency.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following belongs to emotional incentive effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An employee felt helpless because he was satirized, attacked and retaliated for accusing the manager at the meeting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An employee was asked to wait for work and reflect on himself because he was suspected of collecting customer benefits without permission. He was very sad.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The thought and action of the employees were praised by the leaders, resulting in the mood of continuing to adhere to it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The manager decided not to allow employees to talk about family affairs in the company in the future.

response:
Reasoning: Emotional incentive means motivating people through positive emotional relationships to improve enthusiasm and efficiency. Only C describes leaders praising an employee, creating positive feelings and encouraging continued good behavior. A and B are negative emotions, and D is a restrictive rule, not emotional motivation.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I broke the concept into core elements—good emotional relationship, stimulation of enthusiasm, and improved work motivation—and checked each option against those requirements. The key factor was distinguishing positive emotional encouragement from punishment, distress, or simple rule-setting. My success came from noticing that praise creates a supportive emotional bond that reinforces continued effort, while the other choices do not motivate through positive emotion. For similar problems, extract the necessary conditions from the definition and verify that the option satisfies all of them, not just one related feature.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a definition-matching task: identify the option that fits a management method based on emotional connection used to increase enthusiasm and thereby improve work efficiency. That interpretation was correct, because the key elements were not just “emotion” in general, but specifically a managerial incentive effect grounded in a good emotional relationship. My strategy was to extract the definition into necessary conditions: there must be a manager-to-employee action, it must generate a positive emotional response, and that response must motivate continued or improved work behavior. This was an appropriate approach because several options mentioned emotions, but only one could satisfy the full structure of the definition.

The most important evidence I used was the contrast between positive encouragement and negative emotional consequences. I correctly rejected options describing punishment, distress, or restrictive rules, because those may affect emotion but do not constitute incentive through a good emotional relationship. A useful assumption I made was that “incentive” in management usually implies reinforcement rather than mere control or discipline. I also considered the possibility that any emotional reaction might qualify, but the definition’s phrase about “good emotional relationship” ruled that out. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on all components of the definition rather than matching a single keyword like “sad” or “emotion.” For similar problems, I should continue converting definitions into a checklist of required features and test each option against every feature. A transferable rule is: in definition-based multiple choice, distinguish between examples that share surface vocabulary and those that satisfy the definition’s causal mechanism and evaluative direction.

item.context: Energy-saving lamps require less electricity and are more power-saving. Therefore, if people only use energy-saving lamps and do not use ordinary incandescent lamps that consume a lot of electricity, it will save a lot of electricity bills.
item.question: Which of the following options is the hypothesis on which the above argument depends?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The brightness of energy-saving lamps is at least as bright as that of ordinary incandescent lamps.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People can reduce environmental pollution by using less electricity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People always want to reduce electricity bills, water rate and so on.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Energy-saving lamps are no cheaper than ordinary incandescent lamps.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion assumes energy-saving lamps can provide the needed lighting without requiring extra lamps or reduced brightness. If they were dimmer, people might need more of them, weakening the claim that switching would save much on electricity bills. Other options are irrelevant to the argument’s logic.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-testing approach: identify what must be true for the conclusion about lower electricity bills to hold after replacing one type of lamp with another. The key factor was comparability of lighting output, because lower electricity use only supports lower bills if the replacement still provides the needed brightness without requiring additional lamps. My success came from checking whether the argument was holding other relevant conditions constant and spotting that the hidden premise was “same lighting service.” For similar problems, translate the conclusion into a like-for-like comparison and ask what unstated condition must hold for that comparison to be valid.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for a necessary assumption, not merely a helpful fact or a desirable consequence. That distinction mattered because the conclusion was not just “energy-saving lamps use less electricity,” but that replacing ordinary bulbs with them would save people substantial electricity costs. My strategy was to test what condition must hold for the replacement to preserve the same practical lighting function; that is an appropriate method for assumption questions because the conclusion depends on a fair comparison. I focused on functional equivalence: if the new lamp type does not deliver comparable illumination, then people might need more lamps or accept reduced lighting, and the cost-saving claim becomes unstable.  

The key evidence I used was the gap between lower electricity consumption per lamp and lower total electricity spending in actual use. I correctly ignored choices about environmental benefits and consumer preferences because they do not connect the premises to the conclusion. I also recognized that purchase price is outside the stated claim, which concerns electricity bills rather than total lifetime cost. A subtle assumption in my reasoning was that “using only” the new lamps implies substitution for the same lighting purpose, so performance comparability matters. What made the reasoning successful was identifying the hidden comparability requirement rather than being distracted by broader but irrelevant considerations. In similar problems, I should continue asking: “What must be true for the stated advantage to transfer from unit-level performance to outcome-level benefit?” A general rule is: when an argument infers savings from a substitute, test whether the substitute must provide equivalent function under comparable conditions.

item.context: When any theoretical science could not be foreseen, and its practical application might not be foreseen at all. Marx was pleased. But his joy was extraordinary when he made a discovery that would have an immediate revolutionary effect on industry, and on the development of history in general.
item.question: Which of the following best restates the above statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Marx was deeply interested in scientific discoveries that were closely related to practice and could have a significant impact on it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Marx attached great importance to every new discovery in the theoretical discipline, and therefore felt sincere joy at any new discovery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marx attached great importance to the revolutionary impact of his discoveries on the development of industry and history in general.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marx was remarkably prescient and therefore sensitive to new discoveries in theoretical science.

response:
Reasoning: The statement contrasts Marx’s pleasure in theoretical discoveries with his even greater joy when a discovery had immediate practical, revolutionary effects on industry and history. So the best restatement is that he especially valued science closely connected to practice and major impact.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a contrast-based paraphrase approach: first identify the baseline idea, then compare it with the stronger condition signaled by “extraordinary” joy. The key factor was the passage’s distinction between general pleasure in theoretical science and greater enthusiasm when a discovery had immediate practical and revolutionary effects. My success came from tracking that comparative structure instead of focusing on only one clause or exaggerating it into “every” discovery. For similar problems, I should isolate contrast words and degree markers, then choose the option that preserves both the comparison and the scope without adding absolutes.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the sentence as making a comparison between two kinds of discoveries: purely theoretical ones, whose practical effects might be distant or unforeseeable, and discoveries with immediate practical and historical consequences. That interpretation was correct because the key structure is contrastive: Marx was pleased in one case, but especially pleased in the other. My strategy was to identify the main contrast and then match it to the option that preserved both the practical orientation and the greater significance attached to real-world impact. This was appropriate because restatement questions usually hinge on preserving emphasis, not just paraphrasing isolated phrases. I used the evidence that the passage explicitly mentions “immediate revolutionary effect on industry” and “development of history in general,” which signals practical relevance plus large-scale consequence. I also noticed that the statement is not about all discoveries equally, so I avoided options that overgeneralized his reaction. A shortcut that helped was treating “But his joy was extraordinary when…” as the author’s real point of emphasis. I should still have considered more carefully whether an option captured the contrast or only the second half, since some distractors often narrow the statement too much. The successful part of the reasoning was distinguishing “valued especially” from “valued exclusively” and from “valued everything equally.” In similar problems, I should systematically test each option for scope, emphasis, and whether it preserves comparative structure. A transferable rule is: when a sentence contrasts two cases, the best paraphrase must preserve both the baseline case and the stronger emphasis, rather than flattening or exaggerating one side.

item.context: Technological innovation refers to the economic development, only new technology and new inventions in the production of the first application, is in the production system to establish a new production function or supply function. The new combination economics, which causes a kind of factor of production and production conditions, emphasizes that planned innovation is not exclusive. Uncertainty, marketability and systemic characteristics.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following behaviors belongs to technological innovation in the field of economics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The space technology of the United States is extremely developed and advanced. The space shuttle can fly freely in space

choices.label: B
choices.text: A Japanese food factory introduced foreign advanced production technology to improve product quality

choices.label: C
choices.text: After continuous exploration, Haier Group has produced household appliances suitable for the needs of all kinds of people and achieved great market returns

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microsoft's technology can find the content of any computer using Microsoft

response:
Reasoning: Technological innovation in economics means applying new combinations in production that create marketable economic value, not just possessing advanced technology or importing it. C shows developing products to meet market needs and achieving returns, fitting economic technological innovation best.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used definition matching: I broke the concept into economic application, creation of a new production/supply function, and marketability, then checked which option showed those features rather than just advanced technology. The key factor was that the definition emphasizes innovation as commercially applied and embedded in production, not merely invention, technical strength, or technology importation. My success came from filtering out choices that described capability or adoption alone and focusing on the one with market-oriented product development and economic return. For similar problems, convert the definition into 2–3 required criteria and test each option against all of them, not just the most obvious keyword.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the option that fits an economic definition of technological innovation, not merely a scientific or engineering achievement. The key distinction in my reasoning was that the definition emphasized first application in production, creation of a new production or supply function, and marketability within an economic system. My strategy was therefore to screen out choices that described technological capability in the abstract, or simple adoption of existing technology, and focus on whether the behavior reflected a new market-oriented production combination. That was appropriate because the definition did not treat any advanced technology as innovation; it required economic implementation and commercial relevance. The main evidence I used correctly was the contrast between “having advanced technology” and “transforming production to meet demand and generate returns.” I also correctly treated importing foreign technology as insufficient, because introduction alone does not necessarily establish a new production function from the firm’s own innovation activity. One assumption that helped was reading “new combination” broadly enough to include adapting production toward differentiated consumer needs, rather than narrowly restricting innovation to inventions. I should still note that this kind of item depends heavily on excluding distractors that are only technologically impressive, so careful alignment with each definitional clause matters. The reason the reasoning succeeded is that I matched the answer choice to the economic criteria of commercialization, production application, and market outcome, instead of being distracted by technical sophistication. A transferable rule is: when a concept is defined by both technical change and economic function, evaluate options by whether they operationalize the change in production and market activity, not by whether they merely describe advanced technology.

item.context: In August 2014, more than 200 Russian trucks carrying relief supplies entered eastern Ukraine, and if the Ukrainian government's military operations in the east directly or indirectly attacked the Russian convoy, it may trigger strong measures by the Russian side; if Ukrainian government forces temporarily suspend military operations in the east to ensure the safety of the Russian convoy, it will give the civilian armed forces at a disadvantage a chance to catch their breath.
item.question: If the above statement is true, which of the following options must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If Ukrainian government forces attack Russian convoys, the civilian armed forces at a disadvantage will not have a chance to catch their breath.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the Ukrainian government forces do not give the civilian armed forces a chance to catch their breath, it may trigger the Russian side to take strong measures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the civilian armed forces in eastern Ukraine have a chance to catch their breath, Russia will not take strong measures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Russian convoy entered Ukraine to help civilian armed forces in eastern Ukraine.

response:
Reasoning: The statement gives two outcomes: attacking the convoy may provoke strong Russian measures; suspending operations gives the disadvantaged armed forces breathing space. So if Ukraine does not give them breathing space, it means it does not suspend operations, leaving the convoy exposed to attack and thus possibly triggering strong Russian measures.  
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a conditional-reasoning approach, mapping the two stated possibilities: attacking the convoy could lead to strong Russian measures, while suspending operations would give the disadvantaged armed forces breathing room. The key factor was treating “not giving them a chance to catch their breath” as the practical alternative to suspension, which keeps military pressure on and preserves the risk described in the first condition. What helped was linking the options to the structure of the original statement rather than importing outside facts about motives. For similar problems, translate each clause into if-then form and test choices by checking whether they follow from those exact conditions or add unsupported assumptions.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a “must be true” inference task based on two conditional statements embedded in a political scenario. The key was to translate the prose into logical structure rather than rely on the real-world context of Russia and Ukraine. My strategy was to identify the two given links: attacking the convoy could lead to strong Russian measures, and suspending operations would give the disadvantaged armed forces time to recover. That approach was appropriate because “must be true” questions usually depend on valid conditional reasoning, not plausibility or background assumptions.

The successful part of my reasoning was noticing that the absence of breathing space implies the absence of suspension, which in this setting leaves open continued operations against the convoy and therefore the possibility of strong measures. I also correctly rejected choices that introduced stronger claims than the passage supported, such as definite intentions or negations that were never established. One assumption I used was that continued military operations create the relevant risk to the convoy; that worked here because the original statement framed the dilemma as attack versus suspension. I should still note that this inference depends on reading the two clauses as exhaustive practical alternatives in the scenario.

I should have explicitly tested each option for necessity rather than moving quickly to the one that sounded best. In similar problems, I should formalize statements, check contrapositives carefully, and avoid treating “may” as “will.” A transferable rule is: in must-be-true questions, only infer what follows from the exact logical relationships stated, especially when modal words like “may,” “if,” and “will” limit the strength of valid conclusions.

item.context: Between 1977 and 1987, the country of Ravonia lost about 12, 000 jobs in logging and wood processing, representing a 15 percent decrease in employment in the country' s timber industry. Paradoxically, this loss of jobs occurred even as the amount of wood taken from the forests of Ravoinia increased by 10 percent.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In 1977, overall unemployment in Ravonia was approximately 10 percent; in 1987, Ravonia's unemployment rate was 15 percent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Between 1977 and 1987, the total number of acres of timberland in Ravonia fell, while the demand for wood products increased.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Since 1 977, a growing proportion of the timber that has been cut in Ravonia has been exported as raw, unprocessed wood.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Since 1977, domestic sales of wood and wood products have increased by more than export sales have increased.

response:
Reasoning: The paradox is more wood harvested but fewer logging/wood-processing jobs. This is best explained if more timber was exported as raw, unprocessed wood, reducing domestic wood-processing employment even while total wood cut increased.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a paradox-resolution approach: identify the two facts that seem to conflict, then look for a choice that changes the link between them rather than merely adding background information. The key factor was that the jobs lost were specifically in logging and wood processing, while the amount of wood taken from forests increased, so the best explanation had to show how output could rise without supporting as many domestic industry jobs. My success came from focusing on the “wood processing” part and recognizing that exporting more raw timber would reduce processing employment even if harvesting increased. For similar problems, isolate exactly which stage of an industry the employment statistic covers and prefer answers that shift activity out of that stage while leaving total output intact.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a paradox-resolution task: explain how timber output could rise while employment in logging and wood processing fell. My strategy was to look for an answer that separated volume of wood removed from the amount of labor required in the domestic timber industry. That was appropriate because paradox questions usually turn on identifying a distinction between two quantities that were initially treated as if they moved together. I focused on the fact that the employment decline was specifically in logging and wood processing, not in all sectors related to wood sales or demand. The key evidence I used was that if more harvested timber left the country before being processed, then wood extraction could increase without supporting as many domestic processing jobs. I did not need to assume a decline in demand; instead, I looked for a structural change in where value-added processing occurred.  

I also implicitly rejected choices that discussed broader unemployment, total timberland, or relative sales growth, because those facts do not directly explain why jobs in this industry fell despite higher harvest levels. A possible alternative explanation could have involved mechanization, but since that was not offered, I correctly chose the option that most directly linked output and labor. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the explanation to the exact scope of the employment category mentioned. For similar problems, I should explicitly identify each variable in the paradox and ask what hidden distinction could let them move in opposite directions. General rule: when two trends seem inconsistent, look for an answer that changes the connection between them rather than one that merely adds unrelated background facts.

item.context: Recently, the sales of a certain brand of washing powder have increased significantly. At the same time, the advertising costs of the brand have also increased significantly. Industry participants believe that the growth of the sales of this brand of washing powder is due to the promotional role of advertising.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, can weaken the above conclusion the most?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Few people who noticed the ads for this brand of washing powder bought it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among the buyers of this brand of washing powder, few people pay attention to the brand's advertisement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The advertising cost of this brand of washing powder is not more than that of other brands.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Consumers Association has received more complaints about this brand of washing powder than other brands.

response:
Reasoning: The claim is that advertising caused the sales increase. The strongest weakening shows buyers were generally not influenced by the ads. If few actual buyers even paid attention to the advertisement, the sales growth is unlikely due to advertising. A is weaker because some non-buyers seeing ads doesn’t rule out ad effectiveness.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a causal-weakening approach: identify the claimed cause of increased sales and look for evidence that disconnects the sales increase from that cause. The key factor was whether the people whose behavior changed—the buyers—were actually exposed to or influenced by the ads. My answer was correct because I focused on the relevant population rather than on general ad visibility or side facts about competitors and complaints. For similar problems, test a causal claim by checking whether the alleged cause is present among the specific cases where the effect occurred.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a causal-weakening problem: the stimulus did not merely report a correlation between higher ad spending and higher sales, but endorsed the conclusion that advertising caused the sales increase. My strategy was to look for an answer that most directly broke the causal link by showing that the supposed cause did not meaningfully affect the people whose behavior changed. That was an appropriate strategy because, in causal arguments, the strongest weakening often comes from evidence that the effect occurred largely among cases untouched by the alleged cause. I focused on the relationship between ad exposure and actual purchasers, which is the key evidentiary point. The crucial fact in my reasoning was that if few buyers even noticed the ads, then advertising is less plausible as the driver of increased sales. I also distinguished this from evidence about people who noticed ads but did not buy, because that does not tell us enough about the composition of the buying group. A hidden assumption in the original argument is that increased advertising expenditure translated into consumer attention and then into purchases. I implicitly tested that assumption, which is why the reasoning succeeded. An alternative I needed to consider was whether a choice only attacked ad spending relative to competitors or brand reputation; those are more peripheral unless they undermine the causal pathway itself. The transferable lesson is: when weakening a causal claim, prefer evidence showing that the alleged cause was absent or irrelevant among the cases exhibiting the alleged effect.

item.context: The unfair competition refers to the acts of business operators that violate the provisions of the unfair competition law, harm the legitimate rights and interests of other business operators and disrupt the social and economic order. Operators are legal persons, other economic organizations and individuals engaged in commodity business or profit-making services.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following is not a unfair competition act?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some underground factory will be produced from the poor quality wine affixed to the brand name of the wine for sale.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A factory adopts advanced technology to occupy a favorable market position by reducing cost and then selling price.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The distributor is required by the local government to sell only locally produced plum beer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The use of the name, packaging, decoration similar to a well-known goods, causing confusion with other people's well-known goods, so that the buyer mistaken for the well-known goods.

response:
Reasoning: Unfair competition requires violating the law and harming others’ legitimate rights/interests. A is counterfeiting, D is passing off, and C is administrative restriction disrupting fair competition. B is lawful competition through better technology, lower costs, and lower prices.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used definitional elimination: I matched each option against the elements of unfair competition—illegal conduct, harm to other operators’ legitimate interests, and disruption of market order. The key factor was distinguishing lawful competitive advantage from deceptive or coercive market interference. My success came from recognizing that improving technology, lowering costs, and cutting prices is normal market competition rather than a prohibited act. In similar problems, I should test each option against every required element of the definition and separate legitimate competition from conduct that relies on fraud, confusion, or improper restriction.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as a classification task: identify which scenario falls outside the legal definition of unfair competition. That interpretation was correct because the definition included three elements that had to be checked together: violation of the unfair competition law, harm to other operators’ legitimate interests, and disruption of market order. My strategy was to test each option against the definition rather than rely on whether the conduct merely seemed aggressive or disadvantageous to rivals. That was appropriate here because some business behavior harms competitors in a market sense without being unlawful or “unfair” in the legal sense. I used the key distinction between deceptive/coercive conduct and legitimate efficiency-based competition. In particular, I recognized that counterfeiting, confusing imitation, and government-imposed exclusivity all distort market choice through means other than normal competition. A helpful assumption I made was that improving technology, lowering costs, and cutting prices are ordinarily lawful unless accompanied by predatory pricing or other prohibited conduct; that assumption fit the facts presented. An alternative I still should consciously check in similar problems is whether any “low price” scenario hints at below-cost exclusionary conduct, because not all price reductions are automatically fair. The reasoning succeeded because I anchored the analysis in the legal elements instead of the surface outcome that one firm gains market share. The transferable rule is: when a definition-based question asks for an exception, separate lawful competitive advantage from competition obtained through deception, coercion, or misuse of power.

item.context: Those influenced by modern Western science take it for granted that a genuine belief in astrology is proof of a credulous and unscientific mind. Yet, in the past, people of indisputable intellectual and scientific brilliance accepted astrology as a fact. Ttherefore, there is no scientific basis for rejecting astrology.
item.question: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Although the conclusion is intended to hold in all cultures, the evidence advanced in its support is drawn only from those cultures strongly influenced by modern Western science.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The implicit assumption that all practitioners of Western science believe in astrology is false.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A belief can be consistent with the available evidence and accepted scientific theories at one time but not with the accepted evidence and theories of a later time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Since it is controversial whether astrology has a scientific basis, any argument that attempts to prove that it has will be specious.

response:
Reasoning: The argument treats past acceptance by brilliant thinkers as evidence that astrology cannot be scientifically rejected now. But scientific standards and available evidence change over time; a view once compatible with science may later be undermined. So the argument ignores historical change in evidence and theory.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-analysis approach, looking for the gap between the premise about past belief and the conclusion about present scientific legitimacy. The key factor was the time shift: the argument moves from what brilliant people accepted in the past to what can be scientifically rejected now. My success came from noticing that acceptance by intelligent people is only relevant relative to the evidence and theories available at their time, which may differ from current science. For similar problems, explicitly test whether an argument improperly transfers support across different time periods, contexts, or standards without showing that the relevant conditions stayed the same.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the flaw in an argument, not whether astrology is true or false. The key structure was: brilliant people in the past believed astrology, so there is no scientific basis for rejecting it. My strategy was to test whether the evidence actually supported the conclusion under standard flaw categories, especially appeals to authority and historical evidence. That was appropriate because the argument moved from past acceptance by intelligent people to a present claim about scientific legitimacy. The crucial fact I used was that scientific evidence and accepted theories are time-dependent; what seems reasonable under one body of evidence may become unreasonable under another. I also noticed that the argument relied on the prestige of past thinkers without showing that their belief remained supported by current standards of inquiry. A shortcut that helped was translating the argument into a temporal mismatch: past belief does not settle present scientific status. I should also have checked alternatives more explicitly, especially whether any choice attacked a weaker or irrelevant feature of the argument. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the gap between historical acceptance and current scientific justification, which is exactly where the argument is vulnerable. In similar problems, I should identify shifts in time, standards, or context between premises and conclusion before evaluating authority-based support. General rule: when an argument infers present scientific validity from past expert acceptance, test whether the evidential framework may have changed.

item.context: Siphonage refers to the use of the effect of the height difference of the liquid level, the liquid is filled with an inverted U-shaped tube structure, the high end of the opening is placed in a container filled with liquid, the liquid in the container will continue to flow out through the siphon from the lower position of the opening.
item.question: According to the above definition, the following are not part of the siphon principle:

choices.label: A
choices.text: The driver used a rubber hose to suck petrol or diesel out of the tank

choices.label: B
choices.text: In China, the water surface of the Middle and lower Reaches of the Yellow River is mostly higher than the ground outside the dike

choices.label: C
choices.text: When Xiao Wang is changing water in his family's aquarium, he squeezes the air out of the tube and then inserts the tube into the water, which keeps the water flowing out

choices.label: D
choices.text: Xiao Liu lives in a residential area on the 30th floor, the tap water in the home comes from the secondary water supply

response:
Reasoning: A and C both use a tube with a height difference to keep liquid flowing, which matches siphonage. D is water supplied by pumps/pressure in a secondary water-supply system, not by a siphon.  
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used definitional matching: I compared each option against the required elements of a siphon—an inverted U-shaped tube, liquid priming, and sustained flow caused by a height difference. The key factor was identifying the mechanism, not just whether liquid moves through a tube; A and C fit the siphon setup, while the residential water-supply case depends on external pressure/pumping. The successful step was separating “flow through pipes” from “flow driven by siphon conditions.” For similar problems, map each choice to every defining condition and reject any option that uses a different causal mechanism, even if the surface result looks similar.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a definition-matching task: identify the option that does not rely on siphonage as defined by a filled inverted-U tube and a liquid-level height difference that sustains outflow. That interpretation was correct, because the key was not merely “moving liquid through a tube,” but matching the mechanism in the definition. My strategy was to compare each option against the defining structural and causal features: a tube, prior filling or priming, and continued flow driven by a higher source level than the outlet. This was appropriate because definition questions are best handled by checking necessary conditions rather than by loose similarity.

The strongest evidence I used was that two options clearly involved tube-based transfer after priming, while one option described a general water-level fact rather than an application mechanism, and another described pressure-based building water delivery. I implicitly treated the river example as still connected to siphon-related reasoning because it referenced height difference, but I did not need to fully resolve that ambiguity once I recognized the distinctly different mechanism in the building-supply option. A useful assumption I made was that municipal or secondary water supply operates through pumps and pressure systems, not a self-sustaining siphon. The main reason the reasoning succeeded is that I focused on the physical cause of flow, not the superficial appearance of water moving from one place to another.

In similar problems, I should explicitly separate “similar outcome” from “same mechanism.” A transferable rule is: when classifying by definition, test each option against the definition’s necessary mechanism, not just against a general resemblance in effect.

item.context: Reviewer: Many historians claim, in their own treatment of subject matter, to be as little affected as any natural scientist by moral or aesthetic preconceptions. But we clearly cannot accept these proclamations of objectivity, for it is easy to find instances of false historical explanations embodying the ideological and other prejudices of their authors.
item.question: The reviewer's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that the model of objectivity offered by the natural sciences should apply in other fields

choices.label: B
choices.text: takes for granted that some historical work that embodies prejudices is written by historians who purport to be objective

choices.label: C
choices.text: offers evidence that undermines rather than supports the conclusion it reaches

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to recognize that not all historical explanations embodying ideologies are false

response:
Reasoning: The reviewer rejects historians’ claims of objectivity by citing biased, false historical explanations, but never shows those examples come from the very historians making the claims. So the argument assumes that some historians who purport to be objective are the ones producing the prejudiced work.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-analysis approach: I matched the conclusion being attacked with the evidence offered and checked whether the evidence actually targeted the same group. The key factor was the gap between “many historians claim objectivity” and “it is easy to find biased historical explanations”; that only works if the biased examples were produced by those same self-described objective historians. My success came from spotting that unstated link. For similar problems, explicitly test whether the evidence concerns the exact people, cases, or category named in the conclusion before accepting the inference.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the specific logical flaw in the reviewer’s attack on historians’ claims of objectivity, not whether the reviewer’s conclusion might be true in some broader sense. My strategy was to identify the gap between the evidence cited and the group being criticized. The reviewer moves from “some false historical explanations reflect prejudice” to “we cannot accept historians’ proclamations of objectivity,” which only works if the biased works were produced by the same historians making those proclamations. I focused on that missing link, which was the key evidentiary weakness.

The crucial fact I used was that the argument targets historians who claim to be objective, while the support mentions only the existence of prejudiced historical explanations. I correctly noticed that the argument never established overlap between those two sets. A shortcut that helped was translating the argument into categories: claimants of objectivity, authors of biased work, and false explanations. That made the unsupported assumption visible.

I should also note why rival flaw choices were weaker: some addressed issues the argument did not depend on, while others criticized positions the reviewer never explicitly took. The reasoning succeeded because I tested whether the evidence, if true, actually refuted the specific claim under attack. For similar problems, I should systematically ask whether the evidence concerns the same people, cases, or class named in the conclusion. General rule: when an argument attacks a group’s claim using examples of a defect, verify that the examples are shown to come from members of that group.

item.context: People see that others are in an emergency situation and do not go to rescue, not because of the loss of humanity, but because the presence of other people reduces their sense of responsibility, thereby inhibiting people's motivation to rescue. This kind of responsibility distraction, also known as onlooker effect of the individual. The responsibility of the individual becomes unclear, thus the sense of responsibility is diluted, and things eventually happen in a way that no one thinks will happen. Because of the proliferation of responsibility, the crimes caused by not doing justice and failing to save,   the feelings of guilt will also spread to other people. The risk of a person's moral evaluation is greatly reduced, and the moral condemnation he feels is also greatly reduced, so that it is entirely possible to adopt the same attitude and behavior in the next similar situation.
item.question: Which of the following options is mainly introduced?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Measures to avoid moral indifference.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Causes of moral indifference.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The psychological mechanism of the onlooker effect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The background environment where theonlooker effect is beginning to appear.

response:
Reasoning: The passage explains how the presence of others diffuses personal responsibility, weakens guilt and moral condemnation, and leads people not to help. This focuses on how the bystander/onlooker effect works psychologically, not on solutions or background.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea classification approach: I identified the passage’s central focus by tracking what most sentences were explaining. The key factor was that the text repeatedly described a causal chain—others’ presence diffuses responsibility, lowers guilt and moral pressure, and inhibits helping behavior—which is a mechanism, not a remedy or background setting. My success came from distinguishing “what causes a phenomenon” in general from “how the phenomenon operates psychologically” in detail. For similar questions, I should map the passage’s repeated cause-and-effect steps and choose the option that best captures that explanatory level, rather than a broader but less precise theme.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s main explanatory focus, not merely its topic label. That was the right framing, because the passage did more than mention the onlooker effect; it described how it operates through diluted responsibility, reduced guilt, and weaker moral self-judgment. My strategy was to identify the passage’s dominant function: whether it defined causes, proposed remedies, gave background, or explained an internal process. That was appropriate here because the answer choices were organized by rhetorical role rather than by isolated keywords.

The key evidence I used was the chain of explanation: other people are present, responsibility becomes unclear, motivation to help decreases, guilt is spread out, and moral condemnation is reduced. Those details point to a mechanism, not just a general cause. A possible trap would have been choosing the option about causes of moral indifference, since the passage does discuss why people fail to act. However, that choice would be too broad, because the text specifically analyzes the psychological process underlying one named phenomenon.

I did not rely on any unsupported assumptions; instead, I matched the passage structure to the most precise option. The successful part of the reasoning was distinguishing between “cause” as a broad category and “psychological mechanism” as a more exact description. In similar problems, I should keep prioritizing the answer that captures the passage’s level of specificity. A transferable rule is: when several choices are partially true, select the one that best matches the text’s explanatory depth and rhetorical purpose, not just its surface subject.

item.context: Researchers in one country have reported that they have found meteorites from about 200 million years ago in strata in a certain area, and they are likely to be traces of flying debris when a giant meteorite hit what is now Quebec, Canada. The clay layer, which is about 5 centimeters thick, also contains high concentrations of elements such as iridium and platinum, which are 50 to 2000 times higher than those normally found on the earth's surface. In addition, this rock also contains special minerals in the strata at the end of the Baikui period. Since the strata also contain marine plankton fossils, it can be determined that the impact period was about 215 million years ago.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, can best support the above findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The rocks in this area were formed after the accumulation layer of the deep sea floor was exposed to the surface in ancient times

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mass extinction of ammonites and other species in the late Paleozoic Triassic (about 200 to 237 million years ago)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elements such as iridium and platinum are unique to meteorites and are usually present in trace amounts on the surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: In ancient times, there were a number of meteorites hitting the earth

response:
Reasoning: The finding relies on unusual enrichment of iridium/platinum in a thin clay layer to infer meteorite debris. If these elements are characteristic of meteorites and rare on Earth’s surface, that strongly supports the conclusion that the layer records fallout from a major impact event. Other options are weaker or irrelevant.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a support-strengthening approach: identify the claim that needs backing and choose the option that most directly links the observed evidence to the conclusion. The key factor was the abnormal concentration of iridium and platinum in the clay layer, since the argument depends on those elements being a reliable indicator of extraterrestrial material. My success came from matching the evidence to the needed bridge assumption: if those elements are characteristic of meteorites and rare on Earth’s surface, the inference becomes much stronger. For similar problems, first isolate the conclusion’s weakest evidentiary link, then prefer the choice that directly validates that link over choices that are merely related background facts.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which additional fact would most strengthen the researchers’ inference that the unusual clay layer records debris from a meteor impact rather than some ordinary geological process. That interpretation was correct because the passage already listed observations—thin clay layer, anomalously high iridium and platinum, special minerals, and marine plankton fossils—and the task was to identify the strongest supporting link. My strategy was to look for the answer choice that connected the cited evidence to the claimed cause with the fewest extra assumptions. That was appropriate, because strengthening questions are usually best answered by a statement that makes the observed evidence much more diagnostic of the proposed explanation.

The key evidence I used was the abnormal concentration of iridium and platinum relative to normal surface levels. I treated those elements as a potential signature of extraterrestrial material, and the strongest support would be a premise confirming that signature. I also correctly judged that the other choices were weaker because they were either background facts, broad historical claims, or only loosely related to this specific layer. One assumption I relied on was that “best support” means causal discrimination, not merely contextual plausibility. I should still explicitly compare whether any alternative choice explains the dating evidence or stratigraphic setting more directly. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on evidential relevance: the best support is the statement that turns an anomaly into a marker. A transferable rule is: in strengthen questions, prefer the option that directly links the cited evidence to the conclusion and rules out ordinary alternative sources.

item.context: A.I has been used in medical services for a long time. The performance of the robot doctor looks magical, but in the eyes of A.I experts, these medical applications belong to the category of image recognition in computer vision and the image recognition technology supported by big data has surpassed the performance of human beings in many aspects. It is normal to show strength in the field of medical imaging.
item.question: Which of the following options is intended to be explained in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Progress of A.I in the field of medical image recognition

choices.label: B
choices.text: A.I has become mature in medical image recognition

choices.label: C
choices.text: AI 's medical performance has surpassed that of human beings

choices.label: D
choices.text: A.I will enter the field of medical services in an all-round way

response:
Reasoning: The passage explains that “robot doctor” abilities in medicine mainly come from image recognition, where AI supported by big data is already very strong and often exceeds humans. So it is emphasizing the maturity/strength of AI in medical image recognition, not all medical services.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach: identify the passage’s central explanatory point rather than latch onto one impressive detail. The key factor was that the text narrows “robot doctor” performance to image recognition in computer vision and frames its strong results in medical imaging as “normal,” which signals a mature, established capability rather than a broad claim about all medical services. The successful step was distinguishing the scope of the passage from stronger or wider answer choices. For similar questions, first map the passage’s subject boundaries and choose the option that matches both the topic and the degree of claim.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the passage as an explanatory contrast: what seems “magical” in medical AI is being reframed by experts as a narrower and more familiar capability, namely computer-vision-based image recognition. That interpretation was correct because the key task was not to identify every claim in the passage, but to infer the author’s main explanatory intent. My strategy was to track the rhetorical structure of the paragraph: first, an appearance (“robot doctor looks magical”), then an expert reinterpretation, then a supporting reason (“image recognition supported by big data has surpassed humans in many aspects”), and finally a conclusion about why strong performance in medical imaging is unsurprising. This was an appropriate strategy because “intended to be explained” asks for the central takeaway, not an isolated detail.

The main evidence I used was the narrowing move from broad “medical services” to the specific domain of “medical imaging,” plus the claim that this technology is already highly advanced. I correctly avoided overextending the statement that AI surpasses humans “in many aspects” into a blanket claim about all medical performance. I also rejected the option about full-scale entry into all medical services because the passage never made a future-looking expansion argument. A hidden assumption in my reasoning was that “normal to show strength” implies technological maturity rather than just temporary success; here that assumption fit the passage well. An alternative I needed to keep checking was whether the paragraph was mainly about progress rather than maturity, since both are close concepts. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on scope: the author limited the claim to one subfield and explained current capability there. A general rule to transfer is: when several choices differ by breadth, prefer the one whose scope exactly matches the passage’s explicit narrowing and rhetorical conclusion.

item.context: Targeted sales refers to the marketing method in which merchants sell goods to specific customers for a specific purpose at a lower price than the same kind of goods in the market.
item.question: Which of the following options belongs to targeted sales?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In order to gain popularity and attract car buyers, a car city decided to give doctors and teachers a discount of 20000 yuan on the day of opening, which is much cheaper than many 4S stores

choices.label: B
choices.text: In order to celebrate the 10th anniversary of the company, the board of directors of a company decided to distribute souvenirs to employees. After negotiation with a leather goods manufacturer, it bought a batch of fashionable and high-grade real leather bags at a preferential price

choices.label: C
choices.text: In order to avoid waste, a fresh food store stipulates that after 8 p.m. every day, all non frozen fresh fish and fresh meat products will be sold at a 50% discount

choices.label: D
choices.text: In order to achieve a good start in the first quarter, a food production enterprise carried out promotional activities online and offline at the low price line of the industry and the sales volume increased significantly

response:
Reasoning: Targeted sales means selling to a specific customer group for a specific purpose at a lower-than-market price. A targets doctors and teachers specifically with a special discount. B is bulk procurement, C is time-based clearance, and D is general promotion.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I broke the concept into required elements—specific customers, specific purpose, and lower-than-market price—and checked each option against all three. The key factor was that one choice limited the discount to a clearly identified customer group, while the others were based on bulk purchasing, time-based clearance, or broad promotion rather than customer targeting. My success came from testing every condition in the definition instead of focusing on “low price” alone. For similar problems, I should translate the definition into a short checklist and reject any option that misses even one required element.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the definition as requiring three elements simultaneously: a specific customer group, a specific selling purpose, and a price lower than the market price for the same kind of goods. That interpretation was correct and gave me a clean checklist rather than relying on surface impressions like “discount” or “promotion.” My strategy was to test each option against the full definition, which was appropriate because this is a concept-matching question with multiple necessary conditions. The key evidence I used was that one option singled out doctors and teachers, stated a concrete business objective, and described a price advantage relative to comparable sellers. I also correctly noticed that the other choices each missed at least one required feature: one was procurement rather than retail marketing, one was time-based clearance to reduce waste, and one was a broad promotional campaign not aimed at a distinct customer segment.

A useful assumption I made was that “specific customers” means a deliberately selected subgroup, not just whoever shops at a certain time or channel. That assumption helped distinguish targeted sales from ordinary discounting. I should still remain alert in similar questions to whether “specific purpose” refers to the seller’s motive or the buyer’s use, since ambiguous wording can matter. Another possibility worth checking in such problems is whether bulk institutional purchasing can count as “specific customers,” but here the overall scenario clearly did not fit retail targeted marketing. The reasoning succeeded because I matched all necessary components of the definition rather than choosing the option with the largest discount. General rule: when evaluating definitional multiple-choice questions, convert the definition into mandatory criteria and eliminate any option that fails even one criterion.

item.context: Symbol is a sign that refers to a certain object, which is agreed by people. It can include all phenomena that show meaning through feeling in any form. In these phenomena, something that can be felt is the embodiment of the meaning of the object.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings is a symbol?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tongue coating observed in TCM diagnosis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A compass used by people traveling in the wild.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Traffic lights used for intersection indication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The smell of human body when search and rescue dogs save people.

response:
Reasoning: A symbol is a conventional sign whose meaning is socially agreed upon. Traffic lights convey “stop,” “go,” etc. by public convention. Tongue coating and body smell are natural signs, not agreed symbols; a compass is a tool, not primarily a symbolic sign.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: identify the key condition in the prompt and test each option against it. The decisive factor was the phrase “agreed by people,” which points to a conventional, socially assigned meaning rather than a natural indicator or a practical instrument. My answer was correct because I separated conventional signs from natural signs: tongue coating and body odor indicate conditions naturally, while a compass functions as a tool, not a socially assigned sign. For similar problems, first extract the necessary criterion in the definition, then eliminate options that fit only part of it even if they seem meaning-related.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the option that fits a semiotic definition of a symbol: a sign whose meaning depends on social agreement rather than a natural causal link. That interpretation was correct because the key phrase was “agreed by people,” which distinguishes conventional signs from symptoms, traces, or instruments. My strategy was to classify each option by the source of its meaning: convention, natural indication, or practical function. This was appropriate because the definition itself gives a criterion about how the sign refers to its object, not about usefulness or perceptibility alone. I used the fact that some signs mean what they do because communities assign and learn that meaning, while others indicate something through physical correlation. I correctly recognized that bodily odor and tongue coating function as natural indicators, since their significance comes from empirical association rather than human stipulation. I also noted that a compass is mainly an orienting device, and although it provides information, its relation to direction is not primarily an arbitrary social convention in the same way a symbolic code is. One assumption that helped was treating “symbol” narrowly as a conventional sign, which matched the wording here. An alternative I needed to guard against was confusing any object that conveys information with a symbol. The reasoning succeeded because I separated “sign by agreement” from “sign by nature” and from “tool.” General rule: when a definition includes a criterion about the basis of meaning, classify options by that basis first, not by their practical use or familiarity.

item.context: People cannot be morally responsible for things over which they have no control. Ttherefore, they should not be held morally responsible for any inevitable consequences of such things, either. Determining whether adults have any control over the treatment they are receiving can be difficult. Hence in some cases it can be difficult to know whether adults bear any moral responsibility for the way they are treated. Everyone, however, sometimes acts in ways that are an inevitable consequence of treatment received as an infant, and infants clearly cannot control, and so are not morally responsible for, the treatment they receive.
item.question: Anyone making the claims above would be logically committed to which one of the following further claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a given action is within a certain person's control that person should be held morally responsible for the consequences of that action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An infant should never be held morally responsible for an action that infant has performed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There are certain commonly performed actions for which no one performing those actions should ever be held morally responsible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No adult should be held morally responsible for every action he or she performs.

response:
Reasoning: If an action is an inevitable consequence of treatment received as an infant, then the person is not morally responsible for it, since infants had no control over that treatment. Because everyone sometimes acts in such ways, every adult has at least some actions for which they are not morally responsible.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a chain-of-commitment approach: translate each premise into a conditional, then link them to the claim that everyone sometimes acts in ways that stem inevitably from infant treatment. The key factor was combining “infants have no control over their treatment” with “people are not morally responsible for inevitable consequences of things beyond their control,” and then applying the universal statement about everyone sometimes acting that way. My success came from tracking that “everyone sometimes” includes adults, which guarantees at least one exception to total responsibility. For similar problems, map universal claims and conditional links explicitly, then test which option must follow for every member of the relevant group.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the argument as linking lack of control over an originating condition to lack of moral responsibility for inevitable consequences of that condition. That was the right framing, because the conclusion had to be something the speaker was forced to accept from those stated principles, not something merely plausible. My strategy was to chain the premises: infants lack control over their treatment, inevitable consequences of uncontrollable things are not morally attributable, and everyone sometimes acts in ways that are inevitable consequences of infant treatment. From that, I inferred that each person has at least some actions for which moral responsibility is excluded. That use of universal language—especially “everyone sometimes”—was the key evidence, because it guarantees at least one exempt action for every adult. I also correctly avoided stronger answer patterns that would require a converse principle, such as “if within control, then morally responsible,” since the passage never states that control is sufficient for responsibility. Another important constraint was distinguishing “some actions” from “all actions” or “no actions”; the premises only support a partial limitation on responsibility. The reasoning succeeded because it respected quantifiers and did not import unstated moral assumptions. In similar problems, I should continue mapping each premise into conditional or quantified form before testing choices. General rule: when an argument gives only a necessary condition for responsibility, do not infer a sufficient condition, and track universal/existential claims exactly.

item.context: Philosopher: It is absurd to argue that people are morally obligated to act in a certain way simply because not acting in that way would be unnatural. An unnatural action is either a violation of the laws of nature or a statistical anomaly. There is no possibility of acting as one cannot, nor does the mere fact that something is not usually done provide any good reason not to do it.
item.question: Which one of the following most accurately describes a technique used in the philosopher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: stating the definition of a key term of the argument

choices.label: B
choices.text: using statistical findings to dispute a claim

choices.label: C
choices.text: using empirical evidence to support one definition of a key term of the argument over another

choices.label: D
choices.text: undermining a claim by showing that the claim is self-contradictory

response:
Reasoning: The philosopher defines “unnatural” in two possible senses: violating laws of nature or being statistically unusual. He then argues that neither sense supports a moral obligation. This is primarily a definitional move about a key term, not use of evidence, statistics, or contradiction.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a definitional-analysis approach: I identified the philosopher’s target term, “unnatural,” and tracked how the argument split that term into two meanings before evaluating each one. The key factor was that the argument depends on clarifying the possible senses of a word, not on presenting data or exposing a contradiction. My success came from matching the argument’s structure—definition first, then showing that neither definition supports the moral conclusion—to the answer choice. For similar problems, first isolate any ambiguous key term and ask whether the author is resolving the argument by defining or disambiguating that term.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking about the argumentative method the philosopher used, not about whether the philosopher’s conclusion was sound. That was the right framing, because the answer choices focused on techniques such as definition, empirical support, and contradiction. My strategy was to identify what the philosopher actually does in the passage: he takes the word “unnatural” and breaks it into two possible meanings. That is a classic sign of a definitional move, so choosing the option about defining a key term was appropriate.

The key evidence I used was the sentence explaining that an unnatural action is either a violation of natural law or a statistical anomaly. I also noticed that the rest of the argument tests each definition and shows why neither yields the moral conclusion. An important assumption I made was that “stating the definition” can include giving alternative definitions and then reasoning from them; in this context, that assumption was justified. I correctly rejected the statistical-evidence option because the passage mentions statistical anomaly conceptually, not through data or findings. I also rejected the contradiction option because the philosopher does not show the opposing view is self-contradictory; he shows it lacks support under either definition. A possible alternative would have been to overemphasize the dilemma structure, but none of the choices described that better than a definitional technique. The general lesson is: when a stimulus clarifies an ambiguous term and then evaluates the argument under each meaning, classify the method primarily as definition-based unless the answer choices point to a more specific named structure.

item.context: Secret passwords are often used to control access to computers. When employees are allowed to make up their own passwords, they are likely to setup as passwords their initials or birth dates. To improve security, employers should assign randomly generated passwords to employees rather than allowing employees to make up their own
item.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion drawn above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Randomly generated passwords are so difficult for employees to recall that they often record the passwords in places where the passwords could be easily seen by others.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Control of physical access to computers by the use of locked doors and guards should be used in addition to passwords in order to maintain security

choices.label: C
choices.text: If passwords are generated randomly, it is theoretically possible that employees will be assigned passwords that they might have selected on their own.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Computer systems protected by passwords are designed to ignore commands that are entered by employees or others who use invalid passwords.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion says random passwords improve security. But if random passwords are hard to remember, employees may write them down where others can see them, creating a major security weakness that can outweigh the benefit of unpredictability. That directly undermines the conclusion most strongly.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a weaken-the-conclusion approach: identify the claim being supported, then look for the option that introduces a stronger security drawback to the proposed policy than the argument acknowledges. The key factor was that the conclusion depends on random passwords increasing security overall, so an answer showing they create a new vulnerability directly attacks that core assumption. My success came from comparing choices for relevance to the exact recommendation rather than to password security in general. For similar problems, test each option by asking whether it directly reduces the net benefit of the proposed action, not whether it merely adds background information or a minor exception.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a weaken-the-argument task: the claim was not merely that employee-chosen passwords can be weak, but that assigning random passwords would therefore improve security overall. My strategy was to identify the conclusion and then look for an answer choice that introduced a countervailing effect strong enough to reduce or reverse the claimed security gain. That was the right approach because weaken questions often hinge on whether a proposed solution creates a new problem. I focused on the practical comparison between predictability and usability, which is the key relationship in the argument. The important evidence I used was that employee-created passwords may be guessable, but randomly assigned ones may be hard to remember; if that memory burden leads to visible written records, security can be compromised in a different way. I did not get distracted by options that were merely compatible with the conclusion, irrelevant, or only theoretically possible. A crucial assumption in the original argument is that increased randomness translates directly into increased real-world security; I correctly tested that assumption rather than accepting it. I should also note that the strongest weakener in these problems is usually the one that affects the policy’s net effect, not one that just adds background information. What made the reasoning successful was comparing the proposed fix against actual human behavior, not just abstract password strength. In similar problems, I should explicitly ask: does the recommendation improve the target outcome once implementation effects are included? General rule: when evaluating a proposed solution, test whether behavioral or practical consequences offset the intended benefit.

item.context: Feedforward control means to eliminate the possible deviation in the bud by observing the situation, sorting out the information, mastering the law, predicting the trend, correctly predicting the possible problems in the future, and taking measures in advance.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following belongs to feedforward control?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stock investors predict the possible risks of stock investment this year according to the stock market in previous years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An enterprise formulates its strategy according to its scale, core competitiveness and development plan.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An e-commerce network has formulated several schemes to deal with possible market changes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A factory adjusted its production mode because of the rising prices of raw materials, fuels and other materials.

response:
Reasoning: Feedforward control is proactive: anticipate future changes/problems and prepare measures beforehand. C fits best because it creates plans in advance for possible market changes. A is only prediction, B is general strategic planning, and D is a reaction after prices have risen.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definitional matching approach: I broke the concept into core elements—predicting future problems and taking preventive measures in advance—and compared each option against both parts. The key factor was that feedforward control requires not just forecasting but also prearranged action before the problem occurs. My success came from ruling out choices that had only prediction, broad planning, or reactive adjustment, and selecting the one that explicitly prepared response schemes for possible future changes. For similar problems, I should convert the definition into a checklist of necessary conditions and reject any option that satisfies only part of that checklist.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for an example that matched all parts of the definition, not just one fragment of it. The key elements were prediction of possible future problems and taking preventive measures in advance, so I treated it as a two-step criterion: foresee and pre-act. That strategy was appropriate because several options contained partial matches, and the task depended on distinguishing a full definition match from a near miss. I used the contrast between proactive control and reactive adjustment to eliminate the choice that responded after conditions had already changed. I also noticed that merely analyzing risk or making a broad strategy is not enough unless there is a concrete advance-response mechanism aimed at anticipated deviations. 

One useful fact I relied on was that the definition emphasizes “taking measures in advance,” which excludes cases limited to forecasting or general planning. I implicitly assumed that strategic planning and feedforward control are not identical, and that assumption was justified because the definition is narrower and more operational. The main alternative I needed to consider carefully was the option about investors, since it involved prediction, but it lacked explicit preventive control action. The reasoning succeeded because I evaluated each choice against every component of the definition rather than matching on a single keyword like “predict.” In similar problems, I should continue decomposing definitions into necessary conditions and test each option against all of them. General rule: when applying a formal definition in multiple choice, reject any option that satisfies only a subset of the defining conditions, even if it sounds thematically related.

item.context: A technology company plans to develop a prototype laptop that uses iris scanners that can distinguish one user from another. The inventor of this laptop claims that it will reduce insurance and security costs at offices, as only authorized users will be able to turn on the laptop, making it a less appealing target for thieves.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, most supports the company's implementing its plan to develop the prototype?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colored contacts allow people to change their eye color, without altering any of the other characteristics of their iris.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insurance and security companies provide other services to companies in addition to protecting laptops.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is considerable variation in the color and patterns present in most people's irises.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In-person security services will not suffer from technological glitches when allowing access to laptops.

response:
Reasoning: The plan depends on iris scanners reliably distinguishing authorized users from others. Choice C directly supports that by stating people’s irises vary considerably in color and patterns, making identification feasible. A weakens, B is irrelevant, and D compares unrelated security services.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a support-the-plan approach: identify the inventor’s core assumption and choose the option that makes that assumption more plausible.
