B had intended to sell the fruits to C, so it suspended the negotiation with C. As a result, A reneged before signing the contract, resulting in the decay of B's fruits due to the failure to sell them in time.

response:
Reasoning: Contracting fault liability requires bad faith in negotiations causing the other party’s reliance loss. In A, A stopped cooperation because it discovered defects in B’s own technology, so A’s withdrawal was justified and not a bad-faith breach of pre-contractual duties. The others involve deception or malicious negotiation.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I checked each option for the elements of pre-contractual liability, especially bad faith or a breach of the duty of good faith during negotiations, plus reliance loss suffered by the other party. The key factor was whether the party’s withdrawal was unjustified and trust-damaging, or instead based on a legitimate problem discovered in the other side’s ability to perform. My success came from separating justified termination due to the counterparty’s defect from deceptive or retaliatory conduct that induces reliance. For similar problems, first test each scenario against every required element of the definition, and eliminate any option where one core element—especially wrongful bad-faith conduct—is missing.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the one scenario in which pre-contractual liability would not attach, meaning I needed to test each option against the definition’s core elements: a duty arising during negotiations, a breach of good faith, and reliance loss suffered by the other side. My strategy was to identify whether the withdrawing party acted in bad faith or instead had a legitimate reason to stop negotiations. That was an appropriate approach because the definition focuses on trust-interest damages, not on any loss that happens to occur before a contract is formed. In the option I chose, I relied on the fact that the withdrawal followed the discovery of a real problem in the counterparty’s technology, which broke the chain from reliance loss to wrongful conduct. I treated that fact as evidence of justified termination rather than deceptive inducement. By contrast, the other scenarios involved stronger indicators of bad faith, misrepresentation, or intentional manipulation of the other party’s reliance. One assumption that helped, and happened to be sound, was that good-faith withdrawal for a substantive defect is different from inducing reliance without honest intent to contract. A possible pitfall would have been to focus only on who suffered economic loss, because loss alone does not establish pre-contractual fault. The success of the reasoning came from matching facts to each legal element instead of reacting to the size of the damages. A general rule for similar problems is: when a definition includes both reliance and fault, always separate “did the other party rely?” from “was that reliance wrongfully induced or wrongfully frustrated?”

item.context: If we only look at the value of cultural relics, the paper version of ancient literature is indeed not suitable to be opened to readers on a large scale, otherwise, frequent reading and the resulting bacterial invasion will certainly affect their preservation to a great extent. However, from the perspective of the value of historical materials, it should have been open to the society, because only in this way can the literature value of ancient books be fully realized and great progress can be made in academic research.
item.question: Which of the following options is the passage that focuses on the description of ancient literature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Need the public to participate in the research

choices.label: B
choices.text: Protection technology needs to be improved

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether it is open or not is a difficult problem

choices.label: D
choices.text: More attention should be paid to the attributes of cultural relics

response:
Reasoning: The passage presents two opposing viewpoints: protecting ancient literature as cultural relics versus opening them for historical/material research value. Its main focus is the difficulty of deciding whether to open them to the public.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a contrast-and-main-idea approach: I identified the passage’s two competing perspectives and then asked what overarching issue the author was emphasizing. The key clue was the “however” structure, which set up a tension between preservation value and research value rather than arguing only one side. My answer was correct because I focused on the relationship between the two claims and recognized that the passage centered on the conflict itself. For similar problems, I should first map each side of a contrastive passage, then choose the option that captures the higher-level dispute rather than a single supporting point.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the main focus of the passage, not a detail that merely appears in one part of it. That was the correct framing, because the passage contrasts two legitimate values of ancient literature: preservation as cultural relics and access as historical materials. My strategy was to identify the argumentative structure first, especially the signal words showing concession and opposition, and then infer the central issue that connects both sides. This was appropriate because the options were not asking for a factual detail but for the passage’s descriptive emphasis.

The key evidence I used was that the passage gives one reason against broad access and one reason in favor of it, with neither side dismissed outright. That balance matters: it indicates a tension or dilemma rather than advocacy for only one position. I avoided the common shortcut of selecting an option that matches the final clause, which would have overemphasized the research value. I also ruled out options focused on public participation, technology, or stronger relic protection because those are not developed as the passage’s central theme.

What made the reasoning successful was attention to scope: I chose the option that summarized the whole passage rather than one side of the contrast. In similar problems, I should continue mapping the passage’s structure before evaluating answer choices. A transferable rule is: when a passage presents competing considerations with parallel support, the main idea is often the conflict or decision problem itself, not either consideration in isolation.

item.context: A 24-year study of 1, 500 adults showed that those subjects with a high intake of foods rich in betacarotene were much less likely to die from cancer or heart disease than were those with a low intake of such foods. On the other hand, taking beta-carotene supplements for 12 years had no positive or negative effect on the health of subjects in a separate study of 20, 000 adults.
item.question: Each of the following, if true, would help to resolve the apparent discrepancy between the results of the two studies EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: The human body processes the beta-carotene present in foods much more efficiently than it does beta-carotene supplements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the 24-year study, the percentage of the subjects who had a high intake of betacarotene-rich foods who smoked cigarettes was much smaller than the percentage of the subjects with a low intake of beta-carotene-rich foods who smoked.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-carotene must be taken for longer than 12 years to have any cancer-preventive effects.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the 12-year study, half of the subjects were given beta-carotene supplements and half were given a placebo.

response:
Reasoning: A explains why foods help but supplements do not. B explains the food-study result as a smoking confound. C explains no effect in 12 years if benefits require longer. D merely describes the design of the supplement study and does not explain the differing outcomes.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an “explain the discrepancy” approach: test each option by asking whether it could make both study results simultaneously plausible. The key factor was whether a choice identified a meaningful difference between the studies, such as absorption, duration, or a confounding variable. My success came from rejecting the tempting-but-irrelevant detail that only described the supplement study’s setup without connecting it to why the outcomes differed. For similar problems, explicitly check whether each option provides a causal or comparative bridge between the conflicting results, rather than merely restating one study’s methodology.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task correctly as an “EXCEPT” question: identify the option that does **not** help explain why food-based beta-carotene was associated with better outcomes while supplement-based beta-carotene was not. My strategy was to test each choice for explanatory relevance to the discrepancy rather than for whether it was merely true or methodologically respectable. That was the right approach because the issue was not which study was better, but which fact could reconcile the two findings. I used the key relationship that a resolution must connect the difference in outcomes to some meaningful difference between food intake and supplement intake, or to some confounding factor in one study.  

Option A fit because it proposed a mechanism distinguishing foods from supplements. Option B fit because it introduced smoking as a confounder, which could make the food group look healthier for reasons unrelated to beta-carotene itself. Option C fit because it explained why a 12-year supplement trial might fail to show an effect seen in a 24-year observational study. I correctly saw that D only described the internal design of the supplement study and did not address the mismatch between the studies’ results. The successful part of my reasoning was separating “good study design detail” from “fact that resolves the discrepancy.” In similar problems, I should explicitly ask of each option: does this create a causal bridge, reveal a confound, or explain a time/mechanism difference? A transferable rule is: in discrepancy questions, eliminate choices that are merely procedural or descriptive unless they directly account for why the results differ.

item.context: A civilized city competition was held in a certain province. Four judges analyzed and predicted the possibility of three cities, such as A and B, C, which were generally favored, to win the title of civilized city. Judge A said: either City A can get it, or City C can get it. Judge B said: if cities An and C can get it, then City B can also get it. Judge C said: only when City B can't get it or City C can get it, City A can't get it. Judge Ding said: I think the possibility of city B getting it is zero, while cities An and C are sure to get it. After the end of the evaluation, it was found that only one of the four judges predicted the validity of the prediction.
item.question: Based on this, it can be concluded which city can be awarded the title of civilized city?

choices.label: A
choices.text: City A

choices.label: B
choices.text: City B

choices.label: C
choices.text: City C

choices.label: D
choices.text: City A ,B,C

response:
Reasoning: Let A, B, C mean the cities win.  
Statements:  
A: A∨C  
B: (A∧C)→B  
C: ¬A→(¬B∨C)  
D: ¬B∧A∧C  

Checking possibilities, only A=0, B=1, C=0 makes exactly one judge correct: only Judge B’s statement is true.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I translated each judge’s claim into propositional logic and then tested winner combinations against the condition that exactly one judge’s prediction is true. The key factor was expressing the conditional statements precisely, especially Judge B’s implication and Judge C’s “only when” structure, so each case could be evaluated consistently. The successful step was checking the truth values globally against the “only one valid prediction” constraint rather than judging statements in isolation. For similar problems, formalize every statement first, then use the exclusivity condition to eliminate cases systematically.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task correctly as a propositional-logic consistency problem: determine which city-status assignment makes exactly one judge’s statement true. My strategy was to translate each judge’s prediction into formal logical expressions and then test candidate truth assignments against the “only one valid prediction” constraint. That was an appropriate method because the problem hinges on implication, disjunction, and conjunction, and informal reading can easily hide logical structure. The key evidence I used was the formalization of the four statements, especially the stronger content of Judge Ding’s claim, which fixed three variables at once and sharply constrained the possibilities. I also correctly treated Judge B’s statement as an implication, which can be true even when its antecedent is false; that matters because many options survive or fail on vacuous truth. One subtle point was Judge C’s “only when” phrasing, which I rendered as a conditional with “City A cannot get it” as the consequent; getting that direction wrong would have changed the whole result.  

A shortcut I used was to search directly for assignments that satisfy the “exactly one true statement” condition rather than evaluating answer choices first, and that was efficient here. I should note, however, that this method works only if each natural-language statement has been translated precisely; otherwise exhaustive checking just propagates an early mistake. An alternative I could also have considered was deriving contradictions from assuming each city combination, which might be faster in some cases than brute-force checking. The reasoning succeeded because I preserved the semantics of implication and did not confuse “if,” “only when,” and “or.” A transferable rule is: in logic-word problems, first convert every statement into formal notation with careful attention to directionality, then enforce global constraints like “exactly one true” systematically rather than relying on intuitive plausibility.

item.context: Commodity price difference refers to the price difference of the same commodity due to different circulation links, purchase and sales, purchase and sales seasons and quality.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following is not a commodity price difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vegetables in the supermarket cost 1.5 yuan a catty in the morning and 2 yuan a catty in the afternoon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The price of Volkswagen car is different from that of Fukang car.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The beef in land a is 2 yuan cheaper than that in land B, because land a is a pastoral area.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The price of the same book when it was first published was different from that two years later.

response:
Reasoning: Commodity price difference means the same commodity has different prices due to circulation, season, region, or quality. A, C, and D all describe the same commodity with changing prices. B compares two different car brands, so it is not a commodity price difference.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option against the requirement that the price difference must involve the same commodity, with variation caused by circulation stage, time/season, place, or quality. The key factor was the phrase “the same commodity,” which immediately excludes comparisons between distinct products rather than different prices of one product. My success came from checking that A, C, and D each kept the item essentially the same while changing context, while B changed the commodity itself. For similar problems, first isolate the core necessary condition in the definition, then eliminate any option that violates that condition even if other details seem superficially related.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the definition as requiring two elements at once: it must involve the same commodity, and the price variation must come from one of the listed factors such as circulation links, buying/selling conditions, season, or quality. That was the right reading of the question, because the task was not simply to find any price difference, but to test whether each option matched the definition exactly. My strategy was a definition-to-option matching approach: check each choice against the “same commodity” requirement first, then test the stated reason for the difference. That strategy was appropriate because one violated the definition at the most basic category level, while the others still described one commodity under changing conditions. The key evidence I used correctly was that brand-different cars are different goods, not the same good priced differently. I also correctly noticed that time of day, place of sale or production conditions, and publication timing can function as circulation or temporal conditions affecting price. A possible shortcut I used was grouping several listed causes together rather than mapping each option to a single named phrase in the definition, but in this case that shortcut was safe. An alternative I should still consciously consider in similar problems is whether an option seems close because of a price comparison but actually fails a hidden definitional requirement. What made the reasoning successful was prioritizing the necessary condition “same commodity” before evaluating the cause of the price gap. In future definition questions, I should systematically separate identity conditions from causal conditions. General rule: when testing examples against a definition, first eliminate any option that fails the core identity criterion, even if the surface pattern looks similar.

item.context: One is likely to feel comfortable approaching a stranger if the stranger is of one' s approximate age. Ttherefore, long-term friends are probably of the same approximate age as each other since most long-term friendships begin because someone felt comfortable approaching a stranger.
item.question: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes, without warrant, that one is likely to feel uncomfortable approaching a person only if that person is a stranger

choices.label: B
choices.text: infers that a characteristic is present in a situation from the fact that that characteristic is present in most similar situations

choices.label: C
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that one is less likely to feel comfortable approaching someone who is one's approximate age if that person is a stranger than if that person is not a stranger

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to address whether one is likely to feel comfortable approaching a stranger who is not one's approximate age

response:
Reasoning: The argument treats being of approximate age as if it were required for feeling comfortable approaching a stranger, when it was only given as a factor that makes such comfort likely. It ignores whether people may also feel comfortable approaching strangers not of their age.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-analysis approach: I tracked the conditional movement from “people are likely to feel comfortable approaching strangers of similar age” to the conclusion that long-term friends are therefore probably similar in age. The key factor was noticing that the premise gives one sufficient condition for comfort, not the only condition. My success came from spotting that the argument treated similar age as if it were necessary for approaching a stranger, without considering other strangers one might also feel comfortable approaching. For similar problems, test whether the argument illegitimately converts “can make X likely” into “must be present for X.”
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the specific logical gap between the premise about when people feel comfortable approaching strangers and the conclusion about the age similarity of long-term friends. That interpretation was correct, because the task was not to evaluate whether the conclusion is plausible in real life, but to identify what the argument failed to establish. My strategy was to compare the strength and direction of the premise with the strength and direction of the conclusion. The key relationship I used was that “if someone is of approximate age, comfort is likely” does not imply “if comfort occurs, approximate age was present” or “if a friendship began through comfort, same age is probable.” I focused on the missing case: the argument never considered whether people also often feel comfortable approaching strangers outside their age group. That was the right evidentiary test, because if comfort extends beyond same-age strangers, the conclusion about friends’ ages loses support. I did not assume the premise stated a necessary condition; instead, I checked whether the conclusion improperly treated it like one. The main alternative I had to rule out was whether the flaw involved stranger versus non-stranger status, but that was irrelevant to the conclusion’s age claim. What made the reasoning successful was distinguishing a sufficient-condition tendency from a necessary-condition inference. In similar problems, I should systematically ask: does the argument move from “X can make Y likely” to “when Y occurs, X was probably present”? A general rule is that evidence showing one factor increases an outcome does not by itself show that the factor explains most instances of that outcome.

item.context: Critic: Historians purport to discover the patterns inherent in the course of events. But historians actually impose, rather than find, such patterns by choosing what to include in and exclude from their historical narratives. Thus, properly understood, histories reveal more about the presuppositions underlying different historians' attempts to understand what happened than about what actually happened.
item.question: The critic's argument depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Which pattern a historian imposes upon events is affected by that historian's presuppositions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Historians have many presuppositions in common with one another.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most historians cannot become aware of the presuppositions that they bring to their narratives.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no way to determine with certainty whether a pattern described by a historian is actually present in and not merely imposed upon the events.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion says histories reveal historians’ presuppositions more than actual events. That only follows if the patterns historians impose through selection are shaped by those presuppositions. Without that link, selective narration wouldn’t show presuppositions. B, C, and D are unnecessary.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a necessary-assumption approach: identify the conclusion, then ask what unstated link must connect the premise about historians selecting material to the conclusion about histories revealing historians’ presuppositions. The key factor was the gap between “historians impose patterns by inclusion/exclusion” and “therefore histories reveal the historians’ presuppositions”; that gap is filled only if the imposed pattern is shaped by those presuppositions. My success came from testing whether the conclusion could still follow without that link and seeing that it could not. For similar problems, explicitly map premise-to-conclusion gaps and look for the assumption that provides the missing causal or explanatory bridge.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as an assumption question asking for a necessary bridge between the premises and the conclusion. The argument’s structure was: historians select and omit facts, that selection imposes patterns, and therefore histories reveal historians’ presuppositions more than the events themselves. My strategy was to identify the gap between “patterns are imposed” and “those histories reveal presuppositions,” then look for the answer that explicitly connected those two ideas. That was appropriate because assumption questions often turn on the missing causal or explanatory link needed for the conclusion to follow.

The key evidence I used was that the conclusion was specifically about presuppositions, not merely about subjectivity or uncertainty. I correctly noticed that if imposed patterns were unrelated to a historian’s presuppositions, then the premises would not support the claim that histories reveal those presuppositions. I also correctly rejected the distractors because they introduced stronger or different claims: common presuppositions across historians, lack of self-awareness, or impossibility of certainty. Those might be relevant to broader debates about history, but they were not required by this argument.

A potential shortcut I used—successfully here—was focusing on repeated terms and conceptual links in the stimulus. The main transferable lesson is: in necessary-assumption questions, isolate the exact new concept in the conclusion and ask what unstated link must connect it to the premises. More precisely, when an argument moves from a process being selective or constructed to a claim about what that process reveals, the needed assumption usually ties the nature of the construction to the alleged revealed feature.

item.context: Under the conditions of a market economy, if a company wants to achieve its own profit, it must first produce or provide something that is valuable to others. If the company disregards the interests of others and uses deceptive means to conduct improper exchanges, not only is it not tolerated by the society and it must be punished by law. The market economy inherently requires companies to follow the exchange rules of honesty, fairness, and responsibility. These exchange rules contain the moral power to maintain and promote the development of the enterprise. In other words, companies that do not have moral power are not against others. Or socially responsible companies will eventually be eliminated.
item.question: Which of the following options is meant to illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhancing corporate morality is an inherent requirement for the healthy development of the market economy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enhancing corporate moralityis to enhance corporate responsibility and mission.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enhancing corporate morality is a necessary condition for the sustainable development of modern enterprises.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enhancing corporate morality is a means for companies to avoid legal punishment.

response:
Reasoning: The passage emphasizes that moral conduct and social responsibility are essential for a company’s survival and long-term development in a market economy; otherwise, it will be eliminated. This goes beyond just legality or mission and points to sustainability.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea matching approach: identify the passage’s conclusion and compare each option to see which one captures both the core claim and its scope. The key factor was the statement that firms lacking moral power or social responsibility “will eventually be eliminated,” which directly links morality to long-term survival rather than merely legality or general market health. My success came from focusing on the passage’s strongest consequence—sustainable development of the enterprise itself. For similar questions, isolate the author’s final claim and choose the option that preserves both the subject and the exact level of conclusion, not a broader, narrower, or merely related idea.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the main idea illustrated by the passage, not just a detail mentioned within it. That interpretation was correct, because the passage built an argument from market exchange, to moral rules, to long-term enterprise survival. My strategy was to identify the conclusion signaled by the final restatement: firms lacking moral force or social responsibility will eventually be eliminated. That was an appropriate strategy because the answer needed to match the passage’s overall claim rather than a partial supporting point.

The key evidence I used was the chain of necessity in the passage: profit depends on creating value for others, improper exchanges provoke social and legal consequences, and honesty, fairness, and responsibility sustain enterprise development. I correctly noticed that this supports a condition for survival and development, not merely compliance with law. I also distinguished the strongest claim from weaker or narrower options: legal punishment appeared only as one consequence, while sustainability was the broader endpoint. A possible shortcut I used was equating “eventually be eliminated” with “necessary condition for sustainable development,” and in this case that inference was justified by the wording. I should still check, in similar questions, whether “necessary condition” is too strong unless the text clearly excludes survival without the stated factor. I also should compare whether an option describes the market economy in general or enterprises specifically, since both appeared in the passage. The reasoning succeeded because I mapped each answer choice to its scope and role in the argument. A transferable rule is: when a passage presents causes, constraints, and an ultimate consequence, choose the option that captures the final necessity relation, not a subsidiary example or side effect.

item.context: Organizational control means that the organization uses various rules and regulations and reward and punishment means to restrict the behavior of members in the organization, so as to ensure that the organization's decisions and instructions can be effectively implemented and maintain the order of the organization.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following best reflects organizational control?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A university has continuously strengthened its foreign exchanges, and the number of visiting scholars has increased year by year

choices.label: B
choices.text: A company holds an induction meeting every year to familiarize new team members with the environment as soon as possible

choices.label: C
choices.text: In order to improve the production enthusiasm of employees, a salary calculation of a manufacturer is changed from time performance to piece performance

choices.label: D
choices.text: A foreign enterprise implements the clock in system. If employees go to see customers, they can not clock in, but they must report to their superiors the day before

response:
Reasoning: Organizational control focuses on using rules/regulations or rewards/punishments to constrain members’ behavior and maintain organizational order. D clearly shows a formal attendance rule plus reporting requirement to regulate employee behavior. A and B are not control, and C is mainly incentive adjustment, not order-maintaining control.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: compare each option against the full set of elements in the definition, especially rules/regulations that restrict behavior to ensure implementation and maintain order. The key factor was whether the organization imposed a concrete behavioral constraint or procedure, not merely encouragement, training, or general management improvement. My success came from separating true control mechanisms from incentives and orientation activities, which may influence behavior but do not directly function as formal restrictive control. For similar problems, I should test each option against every required part of the definition and prefer the one showing explicit enforceable rules governing member behavior.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the option that most directly matches a definitional pattern: the organization restricts member behavior through rules, regulations, rewards, or punishments in order to secure compliance and preserve order. That interpretation was correct, because this was a classic definition-matching problem rather than a general management question about any organizational practice. My strategy was to identify the key components of the definition—behavioral restriction, formal mechanism, and implementation of organizational instructions—and then test each option against all of those elements. This was appropriate because the best answer needed to satisfy the full definition, not just sound related to management or human resources. The strongest evidence I used was the presence of an explicit procedural rule governing employee conduct and reporting obligations, which directly reflects formal control over behavior. I also correctly rejected options that described growth, orientation, or motivation because those involve development or incentives without necessarily imposing operational constraints to maintain order. One subtle point I handled well was distinguishing incentive systems from control systems: a pay change can influence effort, but influence alone is not the same as regulating compliance through explicit rules. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the option to the mechanism specified in the definition, not to the broad theme of organizational management. In similar problems, I should continue decomposing definitions into necessary conditions and verify that the chosen option contains the defining mechanism rather than merely a plausible organizational effect. A transferable rule is: when a question gives a formal definition, select the option that instantiates the definition’s core mechanism and purpose together, not one that is only loosely associated by topic.

item.context: Psychologist: Identical twins are virtually the same genetically. Moreover, according to some studies, identical twins separated at birth and brought up in vastly different environments show a strong tendency to report similar ethical beliefs, dress in the same way, and have similar careers. Thus, many of our inclinations must be genetic in origin, and not subject to environmental influences.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the psychologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Scientists are far from being able to link any specific genes to specific inclinations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many people, including identical twins, undergo radical changes in their lifestyles at some point in their lives.

choices.label: C
choices.text: While some studies of identical twins separated at birth reveal a high percentage of similar personality traits, they also show a few differences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Identical twins who grow up together tend to develop different beliefs, tastes, and careers in order to differentiate themselves from each other.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion is too strong: it says many inclinations are genetic and not subject to environmental influence. Choice D shows environment can significantly shape identical twins’ beliefs, tastes, and careers, since twins raised together may deliberately become different. That directly weakens the claim that such inclinations are not environmentally influenced.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a weakening approach by targeting the conclusion’s strongest claim: that many inclinations are genetic and not shaped by environment. The key factor was the argument’s leap from similarity among separated identical twins to the broad claim that environment does not matter. My successful step was noticing that evidence about twins raised together becoming different shows social context can actively shape beliefs, tastes, and careers, undercutting the conclusion. For similar problems, isolate the exact causal or generalizing leap in the conclusion and prefer the choice that introduces an alternative influence on the same traits.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a weaken-the-argument task aimed at the psychologist’s inference from twin studies to a broad claim about genetic determination. The key issue was not whether genes matter at all, but whether the cited evidence justified the stronger conclusion that many inclinations are genetic and not subject to environmental influences. My strategy was to look for an answer choice that introduced an environmental mechanism capable of producing or altering the very inclinations the psychologist treated as genetically fixed. That was appropriate because the argument depended on treating similarities among separated twins as evidence against environmental causation.

The crucial relationship I used was that if identical twins raised together often become different in beliefs, tastes, and careers in response to their shared social situation, then environment can clearly shape those outcomes. This directly undercuts the conclusion’s “not subject to environmental influences” language, which is much stronger than merely saying genetics plays a role. I avoided being distracted by choices that were only mildly weakening, such as evidence of a few differences or uncertainty about specific gene links, because those do not challenge the underlying inference as strongly. One assumption in my reasoning was that deliberate differentiation counts as an environmental influence, which is justified because it arises from social context and interaction. I also correctly considered that the strongest weakener would attack the conclusion, not merely the studies’ precision. What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the gap between correlation in separated twins and a claim of genetic immunity from environment. A transferable rule is: when an argument moves from evidence of one cause to the exclusion of another, the best weakener often shows that the allegedly excluded cause can still produce substantial variation in the same outcome.

item.context: The researchers sequenced the DNA of parents and their children and found that the father's age was associated with mutations in the children's DNA, while the children's DNA of older fathers had mutations linked to autism and schizophrenia. As a result, the researchers concluded, men are more likely to have children as they age.The older a man is, the higher his child's risk of disease.
item.question: If the following argument is true, which of the following questions  the conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The older a man gets, the poorer the quality of his sperm and the more genetic mutations it contains.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The incidence of autism and schizophrenia was significantly higher in males than in females.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many of the couples were of the same age and the children were more likely to have mutations from older mothers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The best reproductive age of male is later than that of female, but the whole reproductive age of male is significantly longer than that of female.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion blames fathers’ age for higher disease risk in children. Choice C suggests the mutations may instead be associated with older mothers, especially if many couples were the same age. That provides an alternative explanation and weakens the conclusion most directly.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a weakening-by-alternative-cause approach: I looked for a choice that would undermine the claimed link between paternal age and children’s disease risk. The key factor was causation versus correlation—if parents were often the same age, then maternal age could be a confounding variable rather than the father’s age being the true driver. My answer was correct because I identified the option that introduced a competing explanation for the observed mutations. In similar problems, I should test causal conclusions by checking whether another correlated factor could account for the evidence just as well or better.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a weakening task: identify which option, if true, would most undermine the causal conclusion that increasing paternal age raises a child’s disease risk. That interpretation was correct because the stimulus moved from an observed association to a broader claim about fathers’ age causing harmful outcomes in children. My strategy was to look for an alternative explanation or a confounding variable that could account for the observed mutations without assigning primary responsibility to paternal age. That is the right strategy for causal arguments, especially when the evidence is correlational.

The key fact I used was that parents’ ages are often related, so if many couples were similar in age, maternal age could track paternal age. I correctly noticed that an answer introducing older mothers as a more likely source of mutations attacks the attribution of cause, not just a side detail. I avoided weaker options that merely supported the original mechanism or discussed facts irrelevant to the conclusion’s logic. One assumption that helped was treating the researchers’ evidence as vulnerable to confounding unless the study controlled for both parents’ ages. An alternative I also implicitly considered was whether any option challenged disease relevance or mutation quality directly, but those did not undermine the causal inference as strongly.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the gap between correlation and causation rather than on biological plausibility alone. In similar problems, I should continue asking: “What hidden variable could produce the same pattern?” A transferable rule is: when an argument infers causation from an observed association, the strongest weakening evidence is often a plausible confounder that covaries with the alleged cause and better explains the effect.

item.context: Academician He Zuoxiu, an anti-counterfeiting fighter, said: Dolly is dead, but many cloned cattle and sheep are not dead. Why should we doubt the cloning technology? -- there are still premature deaths of bisexual children!
item.question: What does this passage mean that

choices.label: A
choices.text: Academician He Zuoxiu is an anti-counterfeiting fighter

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dolly the cloned sheep is dead

choices.label: C
choices.text: Academician He Zuoxiu is full of confidence in cloning technology

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bisexual children have the risk of premature death

response:
Reasoning: The passage argues that one should not reject cloning just because Dolly died, since many cloned animals survive. It compares this to “bisexual children” still having premature deaths, implying such children can face that risk. So the implied meaning is about the risk, not confidence or identity.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a local inference approach, focusing on the comparison about premature deaths and treating the last clause as the main implied meaning. The key clue I underweighted was the speaker’s rhetorical question: after noting Dolly died but many cloned cattle and sheep did not, he is challenging the idea that cloning should be doubted. My mistake was latching onto a literal side example instead of identifying the author’s overall attitude and argumentative purpose. For similar questions, I should first determine the speaker’s stance from the full sentence structure and rhetoric, then treat examples or analogies as support rather than the main point.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question too narrowly as asking for the literal implication of the comparison in the quotation, rather than the speaker’s overall stance conveyed by the rhetoric. My strategy was to extract the most concrete factual statement from the sentence, so I focused on the phrase about premature deaths and selected the option that restated that detail. That approach was inappropriate for an “What does this passage mean” question, which often tests the author’s attitude, intention, or conclusion rather than a local paraphrase. I used one visible fact from the passage, but I missed the stronger discourse cue: the speaker is arguing against doubting cloning technology despite one famous failure. The key relationship I underused was contrast—“Dolly is dead, but many cloned cattle and sheep are not dead”—which supports confidence in the technology’s viability. I also overlooked the rhetorical question, which functions as a defense of cloning rather than a warning about biological risk. My main assumption was that the analogy’s content was the target meaning, when in fact the analogy served only as supporting evidence for the speaker’s position. I should also have considered whether each option described a background fact, a detail, or the speaker’s viewpoint, and prioritized the viewpoint option. The specific cause of error was confusing a subordinate example with the main claim of the passage. In similar problems, I should first identify the thesis sentence and the function of each supporting clause before matching answer choices. A general rule: when a passage contains contrast plus a rhetorical question, infer the speaker’s overall evaluative stance first, and treat factual details as evidence unless the question explicitly asks for a detail.

item.context: Material evidence refers to material traces and objects that can prove the true circumstances of a case.  Physical evidence is characterized by its appearance, quality, characteristics and location, reflecting some facts of the case, which can be used to prove the truth of the case.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following options belongs to material evidence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There was a traffic accident on the expressway, the scene photo taken by the traffic police when surveying the scene

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the trial of a vicious murder case, the witness was worried about retaliation and refused to appear in court to testify, and provided a tape recording the testimony

choices.label: C
choices.text: A stolen vehicle recovered by the police in a certain area during an operation against motor vehicle theft

choices.label: D
choices.text: According to the fingerprints taken by the police at the theft scene, the fingerprint identification report made by the appraisal staff

response:
Reasoning: Material evidence means the physical object itself that directly exists in the case. A is photographic/documentary evidence, B is audiovisual/testimonial evidence, and D is expert opinion. The recovered stolen vehicle is the actual object involved in the crime, so it is material evidence.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: compare each option against the category “physical traces and objects” and eliminate items that are records, statements, or reports rather than the object itself. The key factor was distinguishing direct physical objects involved in the case from evidence that only documents, describes, or analyzes those objects. My answer was correct because I classified each option by evidence type before choosing, instead of focusing only on how useful it seemed for proving facts. For similar problems, first map every option to its evidentiary form—object, document, testimony, audiovisual material, or expert conclusion—and select only the one that matches the definition’s core attributes.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which option is the physical object or trace itself, rather than a representation, statement, or analysis derived from it. That interpretation was correct because the definition emphasized material traces and objects with observable properties and location that directly reflect facts of the case. My strategy was to classify each option by evidence type: object evidence versus documentary, audiovisual, testimonial, or expert evidence. This was appropriate because the answer depended less on the factual scenario and more on legal categorization.

The key relationship I used was the distinction between original physical items involved in the event and records or reports about those items. I correctly noticed that a photo is only a recorded image of a scene, a tape recording preserves testimony rather than being the material object connected to the offense, and an identification report is a professional conclusion based on physical traces rather than the trace itself. One useful constraint was that material evidence must be something whose own physical existence has probative value. I did not rely on superficial wording like “taken by police” or “at the scene,” which could have been misleading shortcuts.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the evidentiary role of each item, not just whether it was tangible. In similar problems, I should first separate primary evidence from representations and interpretations of evidence. A transferable rule is: when a definition centers on direct physical traces or objects, choose the item whose probative force comes from its own physical characteristics, not from a recording, statement, or expert processing of it.

item.context: That the policy of nuclear deterrence has worked thus far is unquestionable. Since the end of the Second World War, the very fact that there were nuclear armaments in existence has kept major powers from using nuclear weapons, for fear of starting a worldwide nuclear exchange that would make the land of the power initiating it uninhabitable. The proof is that a third world war between superpowers has not happened.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, indicates a flaw in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continuing to produce nuclear weapons beyond the minimum needed for deterrence increases the likelihood of a nuclear accident.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The major powers have engaged in many smaller-scale military operations since the end of the Second World War, while refraining from a nuclear confrontation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maintaining a high level of nuclear armaments represents a significant drain on a country's economy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot be known whether it was nuclear deterrence that worked, or some other factor, such as a recognition of the economic value of remaining at peace.

response:
Reasoning: The argument treats the absence of a superpower world war as proof that nuclear deterrence caused peace. That is a causal flaw: other factors could explain the same outcome. If we cannot know whether deterrence, rather than something else, prevented war, the argument’s conclusion is unsupported.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a causal-analysis approach: I looked for whether the argument was inferring that one factor caused an outcome simply because the outcome occurred alongside it. The key clue was that the argument treated the absence of a third world war as “proof” that nuclear deterrence was the reason, without ruling out alternative explanations. My success came from identifying this as a classic correlation/causation problem with possible omitted causes. For similar questions, test any claimed proof by asking whether the same evidence could be explained by a different cause the argument never eliminated.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for a statement that exposes a logical weakness in the argument, not one that merely raises a concern about nuclear weapons policy. My strategy was to identify the argument’s structure: it inferred that deterrence caused peace because no superpower world war occurred after nuclear weapons existed. That pointed to a causal reasoning pattern based on correlation or temporal coexistence, so I looked for an answer showing that the observed outcome could have been produced by other causes. This was an appropriate strategy because flaw questions often turn on whether the evidence uniquely supports the conclusion. The key evidence I used was the gap between “war did not happen” and “deterrence is the reason war did not happen.” I recognized that the argument treated absence of an event as proof of one specific explanation, while ignoring rival explanations.

I did not rely on irrelevant policy considerations such as cost, accident risk, or the frequency of smaller conflicts, because those do not directly undermine the inference offered as proof. A possible shortcut was noticing the classic “post hoc / alternative cause” pattern quickly, but in this case that shortcut fit the structure exactly. I also implicitly considered whether the argument confused necessary and sufficient conditions, but the more precise flaw was failure to rule out other causes. What made the reasoning successful was matching the credited response to the exact inferential gap rather than to the topic. In similar problems, I should first separate the conclusion, evidence, and hidden causal assumption before reading choices. General rule: when an argument claims one factor explains an outcome solely because the outcome occurred in that factor’s presence, test whether plausible alternative explanations would leave the same evidence intact.

item.context: According to the WHO, there are 120 million people worldwide who suffer from depression, and almost 1 of 4 people will experience mental or behavioral problems at a certain stage of their life. By 2020, depression will rank second in the global disease list, next to heart disease. About 26 million people in China are suffering from depression of varying degrees, but in contrast to the high incidence rate of depression, 90% of people with depression fail to seek medical attention because they are not aware that they may be suffering from depression.
item.question: According to this passage, which of the followings can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The number of people suffering from depression in the world is up to 1/4 of the total population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At present, heart disease ranks first in the global disease list.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reason for the high incidence rate of depression is not timely medical treatment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There are no more than 3 million Chinese patients with depression who seek medical treatment in time.

response:
Reasoning: “1 in 4” refers to mental or behavioral problems, not depression, so A is false. The passage does not say untreated depression causes high incidence, so C is false. D adds “in time,” which is not stated. Since depression will rank second next to heart disease, heart disease can be inferred to rank first.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used elimination based on whether each option was directly supported or overreached the passage. The key numerical clue was that China has about 26 million people with depression and 90% fail to seek medical attention, which implies only about 10% do seek it. My mistake was rejecting the option because of the phrase “in time” while accepting a ranking inference that relied on treating “next to” as definite proof of current first place; that was a weaker inference than the explicit percentage calculation. For similar problems, prefer conclusions that follow from stated numbers or proportions over broader status/ranking assumptions based on ambiguous wording.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task as asking for the safest statement that follows from the passage, but I applied an overly strict standard to one option and a looser one to another. My strategy was to eliminate answers by matching each one against explicit wording in the text, which is generally appropriate for inference questions, but I failed to compare how strongly each remaining choice was actually supported. I correctly noticed that “1 in 4” referred to mental or behavioral problems rather than depression, so rejecting that option was sound. I also correctly rejected the claim that lack of treatment causes the high incidence of depression, because the passage gives no causal link of that kind. The key error was dismissing the China option because of the phrase “in time,” even though the passage’s statement that 90% fail to seek medical attention supports the numerical inference that only about 10% do seek treatment, i.e., roughly 2.6 million, which fits “no more than 3 million.” I treated “in time” as a fatal addition instead of asking whether it materially changed the core inference. At the same time, I accepted the heart-disease option too quickly: “next to heart disease” in a future ranking does not necessarily justify a present ranking claim. I should have tested each option for degree of support, not just for literal overlap. A better approach is to prefer answers grounded in explicit quantities and direct complements when the passage provides percentages and totals. General rule: in inference questions, prioritize conclusions that follow from exact numerical or logical implications, and be cautious about temporal or ranking claims that extend beyond what the text directly anchors.

item.context: Phenology phenomenon in which undergo corresponding seasonal changes with the cyclical changes of the climate throughout the year. The factors that affect phenology phenomenon mainly include differences in altitude, differences in longitude, differences in latitude, and differences in time.
item.question: Which of the following verses reflects the phenological phenomenon affected by altitude differences?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sun rises from the surface of the river, illuminating the flowers on the riverside more red than fire, and the emerald river water is greener than blue grass

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two or three peach blossoms were first released outside the bamboo forest, and ducks were playing in the water. They were the first to notice the warming of the river in early spring

choices.label: C
choices.text: In April on earth, a hundred flowers withered, and the peach blossoms in the ancient temples in Gaoshan just bloomed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Why use the Qiang flute to blow the lamentable Yang Liu Qu to complain about the delay of the spring, the spring breeze can't blow outside Yumen Pass at all

response:
Reasoning: Altitude affects temperature: higher places warm later, so flowering is delayed. “In April on earth... peach blossoms in the ancient temples in Gaoshan just bloomed” shows lower areas already faded while high mountains are just blooming.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a causal-matching approach: identify the environmental factor named in the question, then find the option whose imagery shows seasonal timing shifting because of that factor. The key clue was the contrast between lowland spring already ending and a mountain temple’s blossoms only beginning, which directly signals later phenological development at higher elevation. My success came from linking altitude to lower temperature and delayed flowering, rather than just spotting a general spring scene. For similar problems, first translate each geographic factor into its typical phenological effect, then choose the option that explicitly shows that pattern through a comparison.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking which verse shows seasonal timing differences caused specifically by elevation, not just any seasonal scene. My strategy was to map each option to one of the listed phenology drivers: altitude, longitude, latitude, or time/seasonal sequence. That was an appropriate approach because the poem lines are descriptive, and the key is identifying the environmental variable implied by the imagery. The decisive evidence I used was the contrast between lowland spring already ending and flowers at a mountain temple only beginning to bloom, which matches the known relationship that higher elevations are cooler and phenological events occur later. I also used a causal constraint: if two places are compared at the same calendar time but show different flowering stages, altitude is a strong candidate when one place is explicitly mountainous.  

A potentially risky assumption was treating “Gaoshan” as a real elevation clue rather than merely a poetic name, but in this context that assumption is justified by the explicit contrast in blooming times. I correctly rejected alternatives that described ordinary spring scenery or regional climatic differences without an elevation comparison. One important success factor was distinguishing direct phenological evidence, such as flowering time, from indirect seasonal atmosphere. What made the reasoning successful was linking a biological response to a specific environmental gradient, rather than choosing based on poetic vividness. In similar problems, I should explicitly identify the observed biological event, the compared locations, and the environmental factor that can explain the timing difference. General rule: when a question asks for a cause of phenological variation, select the option that contains both a seasonal biological marker and a clear geographic or climatic contrast that mechanistically explains its timing.

item.context: The workers at Bell Manufacturing will shortly go on strike unless the management increases their wages. As Bell' s president is well aware, however, in order to increase the workers' wages, Bell would have to sell off some of its subsidiaries. So, some of Bell' s subsidiaries will be sold.
item.question: The conclusion above is properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bell's workers will not accept a package of improved benefits in place of their desired wage increase.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The workers at Bell Manufacturing will not be going on strike.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bell's management will refuse to increase its workers' wages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bell Manufacturing will begin to suffer increased losses.

response:
Reasoning: The argument needs “the workers will not go on strike.” Since they’ll strike unless wages are increased, assuming no strike means wages must be increased. And if wages are increased, Bell must sell some subsidiaries. Therefore, some subsidiaries will be sold.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a conditional-chain approach: “unless” set up a link from no wage increase to a strike, and the second premise linked any wage increase to selling subsidiaries. The key factor was recognizing that the conclusion required a trigger forcing the wage increase, since the premises alone only said what would happen if wages were increased, not that they would be. My success came from adding the assumption that no strike will occur, which, combined with the “unless” statement, guarantees the wage increase and thus the sale. For similar problems, identify the missing event needed to activate a conditional chain and look for the assumption that forces that event to happen.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stimulus as an argument with a conditional chain leading to a concrete prediction: strike unless wages increase, and wage increase only if subsidiaries are sold, therefore subsidiaries will be sold. The key task was not to prove the conclusion directly from the given facts, but to identify the missing assumption that forces the chain to activate. My strategy was to translate the first claim into a conditional: if there is no wage increase, then there will be a strike. I then noticed that to conclude anything about selling subsidiaries, I first needed to guarantee a wage increase, because selling subsidiaries was stated as necessary for that increase. The assumption I selected supplied exactly that by ruling out the strike, which, through the contrapositive of the first conditional, implies wages must increase.

The reasoning succeeded because it used the correct logical form rather than relying on plausibility or business context. A tempting mistake would have been to focus on management’s preferences or on what workers would accept, but those ideas are not logically required. I also avoided confusing a necessary condition with a sufficient one: selling subsidiaries was required for raising wages, not automatically predicted unless wages were independently established. In similar problems, I should continue mapping “unless” statements carefully and then ask which answer makes the required intermediate condition unavoidable. A general rule is: when a conclusion depends on a necessary condition, the missing assumption often must guarantee the event for which that condition is necessary.

item.context: The lifespan is either determined by genetic factors or acquired dispositions. Xu's longevity is affected by genetic factors and has nothing to do with acquired dispositions.
item.question: Which of the following one has the same argument structure as the topic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wu Song passed Jingyang hill, either killing the tiger or eaten by it. However, Wu Song killed the tiger, so he was not eaten by the tiger.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There are only two roads from this small mountain village to the county, the road and the path. The road is further, so Xiao Liang walked down path rather than the road.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reasons why students are not good at schoolwork are that either they don't listen carefully in class or they don't revise their lessons after class. Xiao Ming listened carefully in class, so he did not revise carefully after class.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By rule of the college, the first-year students must take at least one foreign language course, either English or French. Xiaohua choose English, so he cannot take French.

response:
Reasoning: The stem uses an exclusive disjunction: either genetic factors or acquired dispositions; genetic factors apply, so not acquired dispositions. This is “Either P or Q; P; therefore not Q.” Only A matches that exact form.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I matched the stem to the formal pattern “either P or Q; P; therefore not Q,” treating the first statement as an exclusive either-or. The key factor I focused on was the negation of the second option after affirming the first, but I ignored whether the alternatives were logically exhaustive and mutually exclusive in the same way. My mistake was selecting the option that looked formally similar while overlooking that the stem’s “either…or…” was being used normatively like a forced-choice rule, which D mirrors better than A. For similar problems, I should compare both the logical form and the exclusivity/obligation context of the alternatives, not just the surface sentence pattern.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the stem as a pure formal pattern: “either P or Q; P; therefore not Q.” That interpretation was too shallow, because I treated every “either…or…” as the same kind of disjunction. My strategy focused on symbolic similarity and ignored the role that the disjunction played in the sentence. In the stem, the two options were presented as an exclusive classification of one item under a stated framework, and the conclusion denied the unchosen category on that basis. Choice D mirrors that classification/selection structure: a rule sets up two alternatives within one requirement, one is chosen, and the other is excluded.  

I was misled by choice A because it also looked like “P not Q,” but I did not ask whether its conclusion depended on the same kind of institutional or categorical exclusiveness. In A, the negation follows more from the incompatibility of the outcomes themselves than from membership in a rule-governed two-option scheme. I also failed to distinguish “formal skeleton” from “argument structure,” which often includes the type of relation between premises, not just symbol order. A better method would be to compare not only logical form but also whether the disjunction is classificatory, causal, normative, or merely descriptive. The specific error was collapsing distinct kinds of exclusivity into one template. General rule: when matching argument structure, preserve both the inferential pattern and the semantic role of the alternatives, not just the surface connective words.

item.context: Among the employees of a software company, there are three Cantonese, one Beijinger and three northerners. Four are only responsible for software development and two are only responsible for product sales.
item.question: If the above introduction involves all employees of the company, which of the following statements about employees of the company is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There may be at least 7 people and at most 12 people.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There may be at least 7 people and at most 13 people.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There could be at least 6 people and at most 12 people.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There could be at least 6 people and at most 13 people.

response:
Reasoning: By region, employees total is 6 to 7: 3 Cantonese + 3 northerners, with the 1 Beijinger possibly counted among northerners. By job, there are 6 distinct people: 4 only developers and 2 only sales. Total employees can overlap completely with these 6, or be disjoint from up to 7 regional people, giving 6 to 13.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a set-overlap counting approach, treating the regional groups and the job groups as categories whose totals could partially coincide. The key factor was whether “one Beijinger” could also be included among “three northerners,” since that determines the regional total range. My error was allowing the Beijinger to overlap with the northerners; in these counting statements, separately listed subgroups should be treated as distinct unless overlap is explicitly indicated, so I overstated the maximum. For similar problems, first decide which categories are mutually exclusive by language or grammar before computing minimums and maximums.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task as a maximum/minimum overlap problem between two ways of classifying the same employees: by origin and by job role. That overall interpretation was appropriate, but I mishandled one key classification relationship. My strategy was to compute a possible headcount from the regional description, compute another from the job description, and then combine them by considering full overlap for the minimum and no overlap for the maximum. That framework is valid for this kind of problem, but it only works if the category counts themselves are modeled correctly first.  

The main fact I used incorrectly was treating “the Beijinger” as possibly separate from “the northerners,” which inflated the regional total by one. In context, “Beijinger” is a specific case within the broader “northerner” group, so those labels are not independent unless the wording explicitly separates them. I also implicitly assumed that all role counts were exact individuals and that overlap across role and region descriptions was unrestricted, which was reasonable here. The real error came from missing a containment relation, not from the overlap method itself.  

A better approach in similar problems is to first classify whether listed groups are disjoint, overlapping, or subset-related before doing any arithmetic. Then compute the true range for each description separately, and only after that combine ranges across different descriptions. A precise transferable rule is: when multiple labels describe the same population, never add category counts until you determine whether one category can include another.

item.context: Mr. Zhang put the four treasures of the study in a cabinet with four drawers, and asked the students to guess which floor the pen, ink, paper and inkstone were on. According to the order of pen, ink, paper and inkstone, Xiao Li guessed that the four treasures were installed on the first, second, third and fourth floors, Xiao Wang guessed that the four treasures were installed on the first, third, fourth and second floors, and Xiao Zhao guessed that the four treasures were installed on the fourth, third, first and second floors, Xiao Yang guessed that the four treasures were installed on the fourth, second, third and first floors in turn. Mr. Zhang said that Xiao Zhao didn't guess right, Xiao Li and Xiao Wang guessed right one, and Xiao Yang guessed right two.
item.question: Which of the followings can be infered:

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first drawer is filled with ink

choices.label: B
choices.text: The second drawer is filled with paper

choices.label: C
choices.text: The third drawer is not filled with pens

choices.label: D
choices.text: The third drawer is not filled with inkstone

response:
Reasoning: From Xiao Zhao: pen≠4, ink≠3, paper≠1, inkstone≠2. Xiao Yang has 2 right; since pen≠4, his two correct must be ink=2 and inkstone=1 or paper=3. Matching Xiao Li/Xiao Wang counts gives the only arrangement: pen=3, ink=2, paper=4, inkstone=1. So drawer 3 is not inkstone.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a constraint-satisfaction approach: translate each student’s guess into position claims, then use the stated numbers of correct guesses to eliminate possibilities systematically. The key factor was combining Zhao’s “none correct” statement with Yang’s “exactly two correct,” which sharply limited which item-floor pairings could still be true before checking Li and Wang’s “exactly one correct” conditions. The successful step was cross-validating all guess counts instead of stopping after a partial fit. For similar problems, convert each person’s statement into explicit true/false constraints and verify every candidate arrangement against all counts, not just the strongest clue.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a constrained assignment problem: each object had to occupy a different drawer, and the students’ guesses gave exact-match counts rather than partial information. My strategy was to convert each student’s statement into positional constraints and then combine them, which was appropriate because the data were discrete and mutually restrictive. A key successful step was using Xiao Zhao’s “none correct” statement first, since that immediately eliminated four placements and sharply reduced the search space. I then used Xiao Yang’s “two correct” statement conditionally, checking which of his placements were still possible after Zhao’s eliminations instead of treating all four as equally plausible. The next good move was to enforce the “exactly one correct” condition for both Xiao Li and Xiao Wang simultaneously; that cross-check prevented choosing a placement that satisfied one count but violated the other. I also implicitly used the one-to-one mapping constraint among drawers, which is essential in permutation problems like this. One assumption that worked here was that systematic elimination would be faster and safer than testing answer choices directly. An alternative I could also have considered was a grid or table to track allowed and forbidden placements, which would make the exact-count logic more transparent. The reasoning succeeded because I prioritized the strongest negative information first and then applied exact-count conditions globally rather than locally. General rule: in permutation problems with “exactly k correct” clues, first record all impossible placements from zero-match clues, then test remaining possibilities against all exact-count constraints together, always preserving the one-to-one assignment structure.

item.context: A, B, C, D four fans have a conversation. A said: Team Y can make it to the final. B said: If Team X can make it to the final, then Team Y can also make it to the final. C said : I think team Y cannot enter the finals, but team X can enter the finals. D said: Team X cannot enter the finals.
item.question: If only one of the four is right, which of the following can be introduced?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both Team X and Team Y can reach the finals

choices.label: B
choices.text: Team X cannot enter the finals, team Y can enter the finals

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither Team X nor Team Y can enter the finals

choices.label: D
choices.text: Team X can enter the finals, team Y cannot enter the finals

response:
Reasoning: Let X = “Team X reaches the finals,” Y = “Team Y reaches the finals.”  
A: Y; B: X→Y; C: ¬Y and X; D: ¬X.  
Check options:  
A) X,Y gives A and B true.  
B) ¬X,Y gives A, B, D true.  
C) ¬X,¬Y gives B and D true.  
D) X,¬Y gives only C true.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a truth-table style approach by translating each person’s statement into propositional logic and testing each answer choice against those statements. The key factor was recognizing that the conditional statement “if X, then Y” is still true whenever X is false, which affects how many speakers are counted as correct in each scenario. The successful step was checking every option systematically instead of relying on intuition about the teams. For similar problems, convert each statement into precise logical form first, then count truths case by case, especially treating conditionals with their formal truth conditions.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the problem correctly as a propositional logic consistency check: translate each fan’s statement into conditions on two variables, then test which answer choice makes exactly one statement true. That interpretation was appropriate because the phrase “only one of the four is right” imposes a truth-count constraint, not a probability or sports-knowledge judgment. My strategy was to symbolize the statements as \(X\), \(Y\), \(X \to Y\), \(X \land \neg Y\), and \(\neg X\), then evaluate each answer choice systematically. This was the right method because the answer choices already enumerate all relevant combinations of whether Team X and Team Y reach the finals.

The key evidence I used was the logical form of the conditional statement from B: “If Team X can make it, then Team Y can also make it,” which must be handled by implication truth rules rather than everyday causal intuition. A common pitfall would have been to treat \(X \to Y\) as false whenever \(X\) is false, but I correctly applied the fact that it is true when \(X\) is false. I also correctly recognized that C’s statement is a conjunction, so both parts must hold simultaneously for C to be right. Another strength was checking all four options instead of stopping when one looked plausible, since the condition is “exactly one true,” which requires ruling out all others.

What made the reasoning successful was matching each option against all four statements, not just against the most obvious ones. For similar problems, I should continue converting verbal claims into symbolic form before evaluating choices. item.context: Some people take their moral cues from governmental codes of law; for them, it is inconceivable that something that is legally permissible could be immoral.
item.question: Those whose view is described above hold inconsistent beliefs if they also believe that
