Reasoning: Their view implies: if an action is legally permissible, it cannot be immoral. Choice D says law fails to cover some cases where one person morally wrongs another, implying some immoral actions are legally permissible. That directly contradicts the view described.

reflections.simple: I used a direct consistency check: I translated the stimulus into a conditional claim that anything legally permissible cannot be immoral, then tested each option for contradiction. reflections.complex:

A general rule: when testing consistency, formalize the stated belief first, then look for an option that supplies a direct counterexample to that exact conditional rather than merely discussing related ideas.

item.context: Generalization means that after a conditioned response to a specific stimulus formed, other similar stimuli will also induce the same conditioned response. The more similar the new stimulus is to the original stimulus, the greater the possibility that the conditioned response will be induced.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings can be called generalization phenomenon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Overly fearful

choices.label: B
choices.text: State of extreme nervousness

choices.label: C
choices.text: Be besieged on all sides

choices.label: D
choices.text: Once bitten by a snake, ten years afraid of the well rope

response:
Reasoning: Generalization is when a response learned to one stimulus also occurs to similar stimuli. “Once bitten by a snake, ten years afraid of the well rope” fits: after fear of snakes is formed, a similar object (rope) also triggers fear. The others are not conditioned-response generalization examples.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-to-example matching approach: identify the core structure of generalization, then test which option shows a learned response extending from the original stimulus to a similar one. The key factor was the similarity requirement—there must be an initial conditioned response and then the same response triggered by a new but resembling stimulus. My answer was correct because I focused on that transfer pattern rather than on options that merely described strong fear or anxiety. For similar problems, extract the precise logical components in the definition and check that each candidate satisfies all of them, especially causal sequence and similarity.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for an example that matches a psychological definition, not just a proverb with a similar emotional tone. My strategy was to extract the core conditions from the definition: there must be an original learned response, a new stimulus, similarity between the new and original stimuli, and transfer of the same response. That was the right approach because the answer required matching a structured relationship, not identifying a general feeling like fear or anxiety. I used the key evidence that the response must first be conditioned to one specific stimulus and then appear when a similar stimulus is encountered. In my reasoning, I correctly distinguished between mere emotional states and an actual stimulus-generalization pattern. I also implicitly used the fact that the new stimulus has to resemble the original one in some meaningful way, which ruled out broad metaphorical options. A possible shortcut I took was relying on familiarity with the proverb, but in this case that shortcut aligned with the formal definition rather than replacing it. I should still note that other options needed to be rejected explicitly for lacking the original-stimulus/new-similar-stimulus structure. What made the reasoning successful was mapping each answer choice against the definition’s necessary components instead of choosing by intuition alone. For similar problems, I should continue converting abstract definitions into a checklist of required elements. General rule: when classifying an example under a definition, test whether every defining condition is present, and eliminate choices that match only the surface theme but not the underlying relational structure.

item.context: Aspiration level refers to the psychological need to achieve a certain quality standard for their work. Before an individual engages in a practical job, his heart will pre-estimate the achievement goal that can be achieved, and then he will make every effort to work towards this goal. If the quality and quantity of the work meet or exceed the standards set by himself, there will be a sense of success, otherwise there will be a sense of failure and frustration.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings meets the aspiration level?

choices.label: B

response:
Reasoning: Aspiration level involves setting a personal achievement standard before doing a task, then striving to meet it and feeling success if it is reached. FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach, looking for an example that seemed to show a person working toward a standard and completing tasks accordingly. The key factor I overweighted was “meeting requirements on time,” but the definition emphasizes a pre-set achievement goal plus an outcome that reaches or exceeds that expected standard. My mistake was treating routine compliance with external work arrangements as equivalent to an internally anticipated performance target and realized achievement. For similar questions, I should check that every part of the definition is present, especially the internal goal-setting and the attained result, not just diligent behavior.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the definition too narrowly by focusing almost exclusively on the explicit presence of a scheduled requirement and timely completion. The question was asking which option best reflects a person’s prior expectation of a quality level, followed by effort directed toward reaching that level, not merely which option shows discipline or responsibility. My strategy was to look for evidence of a standard plus sustained effort, but I treated an external schedule as if it were the same thing as an internally anticipated achievement standard. That was the key mismatch. I used one valid element from the definition—working toward a standard—but I underweighted the phrases about “quality standard” and “pre-estimate the achievement goal.” I also missed that the successful outcome in one option strongly implies cultivation directed toward a target level of performance or yield. By contrast, the option I chose mainly showed punctual task completion, which is compliance with routine requirements, not necessarily aspiration level in the psychological sense defined. I assumed that any consistent meeting of work demands qualified, which is too broad. I should have compared all options by mapping each element of the definition: prior goal, self-directed striving, and achieved quality standard. A better method is to reject choices that show only moral character, legality, patriotism, or routine diligence unless the internal goal-setting structure is present. General rule: when a definition includes a mental process plus an outcome, select the option that best exhibits both, not one that merely shows a superficially related behavior.

item.context: Third-party liability insurance is responsible for insuring the insured vehicle for accidents that cause the third party to suffer personal injury or death or direct property loss. The so-called third party refers to the insured, his property, and all persons and property on the insured vehicle, as well as others and other things. The so-called all persons refers to the driver and all passengers in the car. However, these people can be regarded as third parties except the driver after getting off the car.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings falls within the scope of compensation for third party liability insurance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A drove his own private vehicle, and the vehicle broke down on the way. A got off the car for repairing, the vehicle then suddenly slid backwards, and the foot of A was crushed by the vehicle. In this accident, A's medical expenses totaled 5,000 yuan.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A drove a truck to transport goods to a city. Due to the slippery snowy road, a rollover accident occurred while avoiding pedestrians. After inspection, the total cost of vehicle damage and cargo damage in this accident was 19,000 yuan.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A was a long-distance bus driver. During the driving of the vehicle, a fire broke out in the compartment. Passenger B was burned and his property was burned out. B asked A to pay a total of 10,000 yuan for medical expenses and property damage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A drove a bus to send a group of tourists to visit the places of interest. When arriving at the tourist site, passenger B who was going around behind the car was injured when A was reversing, and then B made a claim of 20,000 yuan from A.

response:
Reasoning: Third-party liability excludes the insured, the insured vehicle/property, the driver, and passengers while they are on the vehicle. After getting off, passengers may count as third parties, but the driver still does not. Thus only the former passenger injured after alighting is covered.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I identified who is excluded from “third party” and tested each option against those exclusions. The key factor was the clause that passengers are not third parties while on the vehicle, but can become third parties after getting off, whereas the driver never does. My success came from applying that status change carefully to each scenario instead of focusing on the severity or type of damage. For similar problems, first translate the definition into a checklist of included and excluded categories, then evaluate each option strictly by that checklist.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a classification task: identify which scenario matches the policy definition by checking who counts as a “third party” at the moment of the accident and what kind of loss is covered. That interpretation was correct, because the key issue was not general traffic fault or seriousness of injury, but whether the claimant was legally outside the excluded categories. My strategy was to convert the verbal definition into exclusions: the insured, the insured vehicle and its property, the driver, and persons/property still on the vehicle are not covered; a passenger may become a third party after leaving the vehicle. That was the right approach because each answer choice can be tested directly against those status rules.

I used the crucial temporal relationship in the definition: status can change depending on whether a person is still in the car or has gotten off. I also correctly distinguished bodily injury to the driver from bodily injury to others, and property damage to the insured vehicle/cargo from property damage belonging to an external claimant. One helpful assumption I made was that “all persons on the insured vehicle” includes passengers while they remain aboard, which excluded the in-vehicle passenger scenario. I also checked that damage to the truck and cargo belonged to the insured side, so it did not satisfy third-party loss.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on the claimant’s legal role rather than on sympathy, negligence, or accident type. In similar problems, I should continue translating prose definitions into a checklist of necessary and excluded conditions before comparing options. A general rule: when a legal or insurance definition contains explicit exclusions and status changes, decide coverage by the claimant’s status at the time of loss, not by who was harmed in ordinary language.

item.context: Astronauts who experience weightlessness frequently get motion sickness. The astronauts see their own motion relative to passing objects, but while the astronauts are weightless their inner ears indicate that their bodies are not moving. The astronauts' experience is best explained by the hypothesis that conflicting information received by the brain about the body' s motion causes motion sickness.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, provides the strongest additional support for the hypotheses above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During rough voyages ship passengers in cabins providing a view of the water are less likely to get motion sickness than are passengers in cabins providing no view.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some automobile passengers whose inner ears indicate that they are moving and who have a clear view of the objects they are passing get motion sickness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many people who are experienced airplane passengers occasionally get motion sickness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: People who have aisle seats in trains or airplanes are as likely to get motion sickness as are people who have window seats.

response:
Reasoning: The hypothesis says motion sickness comes from conflict between visual cues and inner-ear cues. On a ship, passengers without a view may see a seemingly still cabin while their inner ears detect motion, creating conflict. Passengers who can see the moving water get matching visual information and are less likely to get sick.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used hypothesis-testing by looking for the choice that most directly matched the proposed mechanism: motion sickness results from conflict between visual information and inner-ear signals. The key factor was whether an option compared situations with and without sensory mismatch, and showed motion sickness increasing when the mismatch was greater. My success came from mapping the ship example onto the same causal pattern as the astronauts: no outside view means visual stillness while the inner ear detects motion, whereas seeing the water reduces that conflict. In similar problems, I should test each option by asking whether it strengthens the specific causal link by varying the cause and observing the predicted change in the effect.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for evidence that would strengthen a specific causal hypothesis: motion sickness results from a mismatch between visual information and inner-ear information about motion. My strategy was to test each answer choice against that mechanism rather than against motion sickness in general, which was the right approach for a strengthen question. The key relationship I used was that support should show sickness increasing when the two sensory systems conflict and decreasing when they agree. Choice A fit that pattern well: no outside view means vision may suggest stability while the inner ear detects motion, whereas a view of the water gives visual motion cues that better match the vestibular input. That directly tracks the proposed cause, so it is strong confirmatory evidence.

A useful feature of my reasoning was that I did not just look for an answer mentioning motion; I looked for one that manipulated the presence or absence of sensory conflict. I also implicitly ruled out weaker options because they discussed people getting sick without clearly linking sickness to conflicting signals. One assumption I handled properly was that “additional support” does not require proof, only evidence predicted by the hypothesis. In similar problems, I should explicitly compare each option by asking: if the hypothesis were true, would this outcome be especially expected? The transferable rule is: for causal hypotheses involving two inputs, the strongest support is evidence showing the effect varies systematically with the presence versus absence of the predicted interaction.

reflections.simple: I used a contradiction-based weakening approach: first identifying the argument’s conclusion, then looking for a choice that directly undermines it rather than merely describing hibernation. The key factor was the claim that after hibernation animals wake with heightened movement, appetite, and renewed vigor, so evidence of slow recovery attacks that benefit claim. My success came from targeting the conclusion’s strongest, most specific assertion instead of getting distracted by background facts about duration, body temperature, or reproduction. reflections.complex: I interpreted the argument as having a specific conclusion about the internal state of animals during hibernation: despite reduced metabolism, their nervous system and muscles supposedly remain fully active, supported by claims that hibernation is beneficial and that animals wake vigorous and rejuvenated. My strategy was to look for the choice that most directly undermined that claimed benefit or post-hibernation vitality, because the conclusion depended on those observations as evidence. That was an appropriate weakening strategy, since the passage moved from physiological facts to a broad positive claim and then to the stronger statement about continued activity during hibernation. I used the key relationship that if animals do not emerge vigorous or immediately improved, then the argument’s support for “fully active” systems is weakened. I also noticed that some choices merely described who hibernates, how long they hibernate, or reproductive facts, which are largely irrelevant unless they challenge the causal chain in the argument. One assumption in my reasoning was that evidence of prolonged weakness after hibernation is enough to attack the premise that hibernation is straightforwardly beneficial; that assumption fits the structure of the argument. I should also have explicitly recognized that the conclusion overgeneralizes from selective physiological observations to a broad functional claim. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on attacking the most vulnerable inferential bridge, not on side details. In similar problems, I should identify the exact evidential role each premise plays and target the answer choice that breaks that link most directly. A transferable rule is: when an argument infers a broad functional conclusion from claimed beneficial outcomes, the best weakening evidence is often a case showing those outcomes do not reliably occur.

reflections.complex:

My strategy was to separate the policy into two parts: first, certain situations should not be entered into the violation system; second, for records already entered, objection-handling procedures should be improved. item.context: Whether it is a nation or a country, its culture can never be static, but is changing all the time. The main evidence I used was the author’s emphasis on “personality and characteristics” and the statement that weakening or assimilation can be reduced if people are vigilant. item.context: After the recent court rulings, commercial shark fishing and shark hunting will resume in Diamond Bay . item.question: In the argument given, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?

My strategy was to paraphrase the first boldface as a policy change and the second as a reason to doubt the policy’s benefit, which captured the topic but not the logical function each statement played. The key fact I underused is that the first boldface is not itself an evaluation; it is a factual development that other people treat as support for their prediction about fish populations. I also missed that the ecologists’ statement is not merely counterevidence against the citizens’ view; it expresses the argument’s own central point about what will happen if shark numbers fall. Because I collapsed “reason against a benefit” into “calls the evaluation into question,” I ignored the distinction between evidence, conclusion, and background context. That shortcut led me to choose a role description centered on policy appraisal rather than argument architecture. I should also have considered whether either boldface was a conclusion explicitly endorsed by the speaker, rather than by reported groups within the stimulus. The error came from tracking the subject matter correctly but failing to identify whose claim each sentence represented and whether it functioned as premise or conclusion. In similar problems, I should label each statement by speaker, attitude, and logical role before matching choices. General rule: in boldface questions, first map the argument’s hierarchy—background fact, reported support, intermediate claim, main conclusion, objection—before evaluating answer wording.

item.context: Through hundreds of years of natural evolution, human beings have developed unique intelligence such as intuition and multi-level abstraction. Although modern computers have a certain learning ability, but this ability still needs human guidance, complete self-learning ability has yet to be further developed. Therefore, it is impossible for a computer to reach or even exceed the level of human intelligence.
item.question: Which of the following is most likely the presupposition of the above argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is difficult for computers to truly understand human language, let alone human emotions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Understanding the complexity of human social relationships requires self-learning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a computer is fully self-learning, it can form intelligence such as intuition and multi-level abstraction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intuition, multi-level abstraction, and other unique human intelligence cannot be learned.

response:
Reasoning: The argument links computers’ lack of complete self-learning to their inability to reach human intelligence. So it presupposes that only with full self-learning could a computer develop human-like abilities such as intuition and multi-level abstraction. That is exactly option C.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a causal-gap approach: I looked at the claim that computers lack complete self-learning and inferred the argument must assume that self-learning would be the key condition for reaching human intelligence. The key clue I focused on was the sentence connecting current machine learning limits with the conclusion about never matching humans. My mistake was treating a possible enabling condition as the necessary presupposition, while overlooking that the argument actually depends on human traits being unlearnable in the first place. For similar assumption questions, I should test which statement must be true for the conclusion to hold, rather than choosing a statement that merely strengthens the argument’s mechanism.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument as: computers currently lack complete self-learning, therefore they cannot reach human intelligence. That reading captured the surface structure, but I focused too narrowly on the explicit mention of “self-learning” and treated it as the central hidden premise. My strategy was to connect the stated deficiency directly to the conclusion by selecting an assumption that made self-learning the key enabling condition. That strategy was inappropriate because an assumption question asks what must be true for the conclusion to hold, not what would make the reasoning more plausible or sufficient.

The critical evidence I underused was the opening claim that humans possess “unique intelligence” developed through evolution, specifically intuition and multi-level abstraction. The conclusion depends not just on computers lacking one mechanism, but on whether those uniquely human capacities are in principle learnable by computers at all. I assumed the argument required a bridge from “full self-learning” to “human-like intelligence,” which turned a necessary-assumption task into a causal-enabler task. I should also have tested my choice with the negation method: if my option were false, the argument could still survive, because computers might still fail for other reasons. By contrast, the actual needed premise is one whose denial would directly weaken the move from “current learning limits” to “impossible to match humans.” The specific error was confusing a possible route to intelligence with a required premise excluding that route. In similar problems, I should identify the conclusion’s strongest modal claim—here, “impossible”—and ask what hidden premise makes that impossibility defensible. General rule: in assumption questions, prefer the premise that is indispensable to ruling out alternatives, not one that merely explains a mechanism mentioned in the stimulus.

item.context: In order to develop the strategy of strengthening the city with culture, a city built two libraries successively in 2008 and 2010. More than 70,000 citizen library cards were handled by the end of 2008 and 130,000 citizen library cards were handled by the end of 2010. In 2011, the city established a third Library in the new area, which was completed and opened in early 2012. By the end of 2012, the city had handled more than 200,000 citizen library cards. The municipal government believes that the strategy is effective, because in just four years, the number of citizens patronizing the library has nearly tripled.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, weakens the above conclusion most?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The library should constantly purchase new books, and the maintenance cost is also very high, which will affect the construction of other cultural facilities in the city.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There are two colleges and universities in the city, and many students have also handled the library cards of the three libraries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many citizens who have applied for the library card of the first library have applied for the library card of the other two libraries.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The construction of the new area of the city has developed rapidly, and a large number of outsiders have poured into the new area in the past four years.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion equates growth in library cards with growth in the number of citizens using libraries. If many people got multiple cards across the three libraries, the total cards seriously overcount unique citizens, so the claimed tripling is not supported.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a weaken-the-argument approach by identifying the conclusion’s key assumption: that the number of library cards equals the number of distinct citizens using the library. The decisive clue was the shift from counting “cards handled” to claiming growth in the number of “citizens patronizing” the libraries. My reasoning succeeded because I looked for an option that exposed double-counting and showed the statistic could be inflated without any real tripling in unique users. For similar problems, always test whether the evidence’s metric matches the conclusion’s metric, and prefer choices that show the data may count the same people multiple times.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a weaken-the-conclusion problem, not a general criticism of libraries or city policy. The key conclusion was that the strategy of “strengthening the city with culture” was effective because the number of citizens using libraries had nearly tripled in four years. My strategy was to test whether the evidence actually measured unique citizens, since the argument moved from “library cards issued” to “citizens patronizing the library.” That was the right approach because weakening is strongest when it attacks the link between the cited data and the stated conclusion.

The crucial relationship I used was that card totals are not necessarily the same as the number of distinct users. If the same person can hold cards for multiple libraries, then aggregate card counts inflate usage and do not support the claimed growth in citizens served. I correctly rejected options that were merely about costs or unrelated background, because they do not directly challenge the inference from card numbers to patron numbers. I also should explicitly note that another plausible weakening route is showing that growth came from population inflow rather than cultural strategy, but that is less direct than showing the metric itself is distorted.

What made the reasoning successful was identifying a counting problem: total registrations can double-count people. For similar problems, I should always examine whether the argument shifts between “units counted” and “entities concluded about.” A general rule is: when an argument infers growth in people, behavior, or impact from administrative totals, first test whether the totals represent unique cases or contain overlap.

item.context: Etiquette and music culture is a great creation of pre-Qin Confucianism, unfortunately, it has been experiencing the process of marginalization. Probably since the Han Dynasty, etiquette has been unilaterally interpreted by the ruling class as the dignity of hierarchical order, including the clothing, chariots, palaces and utensils of officials of different grades. The result of this misreading is that the Confucian thought of etiquette has lost its leading position in the way of governing the country, and has become increasingly marginalized, so that when people mention ancient etiquette, they immediately think of the strict royal ceremonies and civil and military officials who lie on the ground, but the original meaning of etiquette is increasingly forgotten by people.
item.question: Which of the following is the most accurate summary of the main point of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Appeal to attach importance to etiquette culture

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sigh about the situation that etiquette has been misread

choices.label: C
choices.text: Emphasize the important position of etiquette

choices.label: D
choices.text: Describe the history of the marginalization of etiquette

response:
Reasoning: The passage focuses on how “etiquette” was historically misinterpreted by rulers as hierarchical ceremony, causing its true Confucian meaning to be forgotten and marginalized. Its core is lamenting this misreading, not mainly appealing, emphasizing status, or recounting history.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach: I tracked the author’s evaluative language and asked whether the passage was primarily explaining, advocating, or lamenting. The key factor was the repeated contrast between the original Confucian meaning of etiquette and its later reduction to rigid hierarchy, which showed the author’s focus was the distortion itself and its consequences. What helped was separating the central claim from secondary content like historical background and social effects. For similar questions, first identify the author’s attitude toward the subject, then choose the option that captures that stance rather than a detail, consequence, or broader theme.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s central communicative purpose, not merely its topic or one supporting detail. That was the correct framing, because the choices were all plausible at the level of subject matter, but differed in rhetorical focus: appeal, lament, emphasis, or historical description. My strategy was to identify the author’s evaluative stance by tracking emotionally loaded phrases such as “unfortunately,” “misreading,” “lost,” “marginalized,” and “forgotten.” This was appropriate because main-point questions are often resolved by distinguishing between neutral description and the author’s attitude toward the facts presented. I used the causal chain in the passage—misinterpretation by rulers leading to loss of true meaning and marginalization—to see what the author most wanted readers to notice. I also correctly rejected the trap of choosing an option that matched background content but not the passage’s dominant intention. For example, the passage includes historical reference, but it does not mainly narrate a full history; history is used as support for a complaint. Likewise, it implies etiquette matters, but it does not primarily argue for its importance in abstract terms. The reasoning succeeded because I prioritized tone and function over keywords alone. In similar problems, I should continue asking: is the passage mainly defining, narrating, arguing, or lamenting? A transferable rule is: when several options share the same topic, choose the one that best matches the author’s attitude and the role each detail plays in serving that attitude.

item.context: In a poll of a representative sample of a province' s residents, the provincial capital was the city most often selected as the best place to live in that province. Since the capital is also the largest of that province' s many cities, the poll shows that most residents of that province generally prefer life in large cities to life in small cities.
item.question: The argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that what is true of the residents of the province may not be true of other people

choices.label: B
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that most people may have voted for small cities even though a large city received more votes than any other single city

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes for granted that when people are polled for their preferences among cities, they tend to vote for the city that they think is the best place to live

choices.label: D
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that the people who preferred small cities over the provincial capital did so not because of their general feelings about the sizes of cities, but because of their general feelings about capital cities

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion infers a general preference for large cities from the fact that one large city got the most votes. But “most often selected” could mean only a plurality; the combined votes for many small cities could exceed the votes for the capital. So the poll may not show most residents prefer large cities.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-identification approach, checking whether the evidence actually supported the broad conclusion. The key clue was the shift from “the city most often selected” to “most residents generally prefer life in large cities,” which treats a plurality for one option as if it were a majority for a category. My reasoning succeeded because I noticed that votes could be split among many small cities, so the total support for small-city living could still exceed support for the single large city. In similar problems, I should test whether the argument improperly moves from the leading individual choice to a claim about overall preference for a broader group.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the flaw in an argument that moves from a poll result about one city to a broad claim about preferences for city size. My strategy was to compare the evidence stated in the premise with the stronger conclusion and look for a gap between “most often selected” and “most residents generally prefer.” That was appropriate because flaw questions often hinge on whether the conclusion overgeneralizes from limited or differently structured evidence. The key fact I used was that the capital was the single city with the most votes, which establishes only a plurality, not a majority. I also used the structural fact that the province has many cities, so votes for several small cities could collectively exceed votes for the large city. That directly undermines the inference from “top vote-getter” to “most people prefer large cities.”

A shortcut I implicitly relied on was treating the poll as otherwise legitimate and representative, which was fine because the flaw was in interpretation of results, not sampling. I correctly rejected alternatives that focused on other populations or on whether respondents answered sincerely, since those issues were not central to the argument’s leap. The reasoning succeeded because it distinguished between support for one option and support for a category of options. In similar problems, I should explicitly test whether the conclusion shifts from an individual winner to a grouped preference. A general rule is: when evidence identifies the most popular single item, do not infer majority support for that item’s broader class unless the votes for all competing items in other classes are accounted for.

item.context: People who quit smoking tend to gain more weight than before they quit. The opposition argues that smoking cannot lead to weight loss, because smokers often try to relieve tension by smoking, but it is impossible to fundamentally remove tension, which leads to weight loss. After quitting smoking, people can adopt other more effective methods
item.question: Methods relieve the nervous mood. Which of the following debate strategies should the opposing side use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cite arguments that question the accuracy of the pro's evidence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Give another fact and make a new interpretation of the causal link between the two sides.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rely on scientific knowledge to refute fallacies apt to confuse people.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The argument and conclusion that reveal the right side are inverted cause and effect.

response:
Reasoning: The opposition accepts the phenomenon but reinterprets the causal chain: weight change is tied to tension and coping methods, not smoking itself. By proposing alternative, more effective tension-relief after quitting, they offer a new fact and causal explanation rather than attacking evidence or claiming reversed causation.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a causal-analysis approach: I identified that the opposition was not denying the observed pattern but offering a different mechanism to explain it. The key factor was that their argument introduced an alternative variable—tension relief methods—and used it to reinterpret why weight changes occur, shifting causation away from smoking itself. My success came from distinguishing “challenge the evidence” from “accept the evidence but explain it differently.” For similar problems, first decide whether the rebuttal attacks the facts, reverses causation, or preserves the facts while proposing a third-factor causal explanation.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking about the *type of rebuttal strategy* the opposition was using, not whether the opposition’s substantive claim about smoking and weight was medically true. That interpretation was important, because the answer choices focused on debate methods such as attacking evidence, introducing alternative causation, invoking science, or alleging reversed causality. My strategy was to classify the structure of the opposition’s argument: it accepted the observed correlation but proposed a different mechanism linking the variables. That was appropriate because the wording emphasized “which debate strategy” rather than “which claim is true.”

The key evidence I used was that the opposition did not deny the phenomenon that quitters often gain weight; instead, it explained the phenomenon through tension relief and replacement behaviors. I also noticed that the opposition introduced an additional consideration—other methods of relieving nervous mood—which shifts the causal interpretation away from smoking itself. A useful assumption I made was that answer choices should be matched to argument form, not domain knowledge about physiology. I correctly rejected the option about questioning evidence because the opposition was not attacking data quality. I also rejected inverted causation because the argument did not claim weight change causes smoking behavior.

What made the reasoning successful was focusing on whether the rebuttal preserved the facts while revising the causal story. In similar problems, I should first ask: does the response deny the evidence, deny the causal link, reverse it, or replace it with a third-factor explanation? General rule: when an argument accepts an observed association but explains it via another mechanism or intervening factor, classify it as a reinterpretation of causality, not an evidential attack or reversal.

item.context: A company wants to select two employees from Zhao, Qian, Sun, Li, Zhou and Wu to go abroad to discuss the project. During the selection, he noticed the following situation: (1) Wu and Qian cannot go together; (2) only when Sun goes, Qian can go; (3) if Li goes, Zhou also goes; (4) either Zhao or Li goes; (5) if the Qian does not go, Zhao cannot go either; (6) for some reason, Sun cannot go.
item.question: Based on this, it can be concluded that which of the following is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Zhao and Zhou will go

choices.label: B
choices.text: Li and Wu will go

choices.label: C
choices.text: Li and Zhou will go

choices.label: D
choices.text: Qian and Wu will go

response:
Reasoning: Since Sun cannot go, and Qian can go only if Sun goes, Qian cannot go. If Qian doesn’t go, Zhao cannot go. But either Zhao or Li must go, so Li must go. If Li goes, Zhou also goes. Thus the two selected must be Li and Zhou.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a chain-of-constraints approach, translating each condition into implications and then propagating what must follow from the fixed fact that Sun cannot go. The key step was combining the dependence involving Qian with the rule about Zhao when Qian is absent, which forced Zhao out and then made Li necessary because at least one of Zhao or Li had to be chosen. From there, Li’s presence forced Zhou, and since exactly two employees are selected, that determined the pair. For similar problems, I should systematically start from absolute exclusions, convert “only if” and “if…then” statements into clear one-way implications, and follow the resulting forced chain before checking options.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the problem correctly as a constraint-satisfaction question: determine which option must follow from the six conditions, not merely which option is possible. My strategy was to propagate the hard constraints step by step, starting from the strongest unconditional statement, which was that Sun cannot go. That was appropriate because condition (2) links Qian’s eligibility to Sun, so eliminating Sun immediately restricts Qian as well. From there, I used condition (5) to eliminate Zhao once Qian was out, and then applied condition (4) to force Li, since at least one of Zhao or Li had to go. Finally, condition (3) forced Zhou once Li was included, which completed the pair because exactly two employees were to be selected.

The reasoning succeeded because I treated the implications as a chain and respected directionality: “only when Sun goes, Qian can go” means Qian implies Sun, not the reverse. I also correctly used the fact that the selection size is exactly two, so once two people were forced, no further alternatives mattered. A potential pitfall would have been to overuse condition (1) about Wu and Qian, but that condition becomes irrelevant after Qian is eliminated. Another possible mistake would have been to confuse “either Zhao or Li goes” with exclusive-or; the argument only needed at least one, not exactly one. In similar problems, I should identify impossibilities first, then propagate implications, then use cardinality constraints last. General rule: in logic-selection problems, prioritize absolute constraints and one-way implications, and convert each forced exclusion into downstream deductions before comparing answer choices.

item.context: Many large cities in the primary and secondary schools, in the morning and evening rush hour, can see pick-up and drop-off team. Some people believe that driving children to school is the cause of serious traffic jams.
item.question: Which of the following, if true, can best weaken the above argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Due to the low utilization rate of school buses in primary and secondary schools, many parents choose to drive their children to school

choices.label: B
choices.text: During the summer and winter holidays, morning rush hour traffic congestion was reduced by 20 percent and air pollution levels were also reduced

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most primary and secondary schools in large cities are located in the core of the city, the flow of cars and people itself is very large

choices.label: D
choices.text: With the introduction of a national policy to designate school districts, many children can attend schools closer to home

response:
Reasoning: The claim is that parents driving children causes serious jams. C offers an alternative cause: schools are in already high-traffic city centers, so congestion may mainly come from existing heavy car and pedestrian flow rather than school pick-up/drop-off itself.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a weakening-by-alternative-cause approach: instead of denying that parents drive children, I looked for a choice showing that congestion could be explained mainly by another factor. The key clue was the causal claim that school drop-offs are the cause of serious traffic jams, which is weakened if those schools are already in areas with inherently heavy traffic flow. The successful step was matching the answer choice to the exact weakness pattern: preexisting urban core congestion reduces confidence that drop-offs are the primary cause. For similar problems, test causal arguments by asking whether an option provides an independent explanation for the effect rather than merely describing related circumstances.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a weakening task: the goal was not to find a true statement about school traffic, but the option that most undermines the causal claim that parents driving children is responsible for serious congestion. My strategy was to look for an alternative explanation that could account for the same traffic pattern without relying on the claimed cause. That is the right strategy for causal-weaken questions, because showing a rival cause directly reduces confidence that the cited factor is the main driver. I focused on whether any option explained why congestion would be heavy even if school drop-off behavior were not the primary reason. The key evidence I used was the relationship between school location and preexisting traffic volume: if schools are concentrated in already crowded urban cores, congestion may arise from baseline conditions rather than parent vehicles.

I also implicitly rejected choices that merely explained why parents drive, described correlated time periods, or suggested future policy effects, because those do not directly challenge the causal link. One shortcut that helped was distinguishing between “cause of the behavior” and “cause of the congestion”; those are different questions. A weaker reasoner might be drawn to seasonal traffic reductions, but that only shows school activity matters somehow, not that parental driving is the main cause. What made the reasoning successful was prioritizing the strongest alternative cause over background or indirect facts. In similar problems, I should systematically classify options as alternative cause, no-impact detail, premise support, or scope shift. A general rule is: when weakening a causal argument, prefer evidence that shows the effect would likely occur for another reason even when the proposed cause is present.

item.context: Positive reinforcement, also known as positive reinforcement, refers to the process in which an individual makes a certain behavior or reflection, and then or at the same time receives a certain reward, so as to increase the intensity, probability or speed of the behavior or reflection. It can also be said that positive reinforcement is to increase the probability of events by adding a favorite stimulus.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following is positive reinforcement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Xiao Ming thinks the astronaut uncle on TV is cool. He is determined to study hard and go to space when he grows up.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The teacher encouraged the students to review the exam well and promised that students with more than 95 points in mathematics could not do holiday homework.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A middle school stipulates that students who play mobile phones in class will have their mobile phones confiscated. After the implementation of the regulations, almost no one dares to play mobile phones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In order to encourage his son to study hard, his father promised to take him abroad if he could be admitted to the top three in the class.

response:
Reasoning: Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant reward after desired behavior to increase it. D fits: father promises an enjoyable trip abroad if his son achieves top-three results, encouraging studying. A has no reward, B removes homework (negative reinforcement), C is punishment.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I checked each option against the core structure of positive reinforcement, namely “desired behavior followed by adding a pleasant stimulus to increase that behavior.” The key factor was distinguishing adding a reward from removing an unpleasant task or imposing a penalty. My success came from eliminating distractors that involved no explicit reinforcement, punishment, or negative reinforcement, and selecting the one that clearly offered a desirable reward contingent on performance. For similar problems, I should first identify the behavior, then ask whether the consequence adds something desirable afterward to increase that behavior.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as a definition-matching problem: identify the option where a desirable stimulus is added contingent on a behavior, thereby increasing that behavior. My strategy was to translate the definition into its core elements: target behavior, added reward, and the intended increase in future behavior. That was an appropriate approach because these psychology-style multiple-choice items are usually decided by checking each option against all parts of the definition rather than by surface similarity. I used the key distinction between positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, and punishment: adding something pleasant versus removing something unpleasant versus imposing a cost. That distinction let me reject the option about confiscating phones, which clearly suppresses behavior through punishment, and the option about admiration for astronauts, which lacks any external contingent reward. I also noted that exempting students from homework involves removal of an aversive condition, so it aligns with negative reinforcement rather than positive reinforcement. An important assumption I made was that the reward could be promised in advance as long as it was contingent on later performance, which is standard in reinforcement contexts. I briefly considered whether the exam-review option might count because it motivates performance, but the mechanism matters more than the general idea of encouragement. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the structure of the contingency, not just whether the outcome sounded motivating. For similar problems, I should systematically ask: what behavior is targeted, what consequence follows, is that consequence added or removed, and is the goal to increase or decrease the behavior? A transferable rule is: classify behavior-management examples by the sign of the consequence (added vs. removed) and the direction of behavioral change (increase vs. decrease), not by the everyday emotional tone of the example.

item.context: There is such a phenomenon in nature: when a plant grows alone, it appears short and monotonous. When it grows with many similar plants, it has deep roots and lush leaves and full of vitality. People call this phenomenon of mutual influence and mutual promotion in similar plant circles as symbiotic effect.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following is most consistent with the symbiotic effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In a dormitory of a university, six students' admission scores were different. For four years, six students studied together every day. Finally, they were admitted to graduate students in key universities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Living with wolves, you can only learn to howl. Get in touch with good people and you'll be well influenced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In order to get rid of the limitations of individual operation, a brand adopts chain operation to expand its business scope, and the sales volume increases greatly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Being close to villains and alienating virtuous officials are the reasons for the decline of the Post-Han Dynasty.

response:
Reasoning: Symbiotic effect means similar individuals growing together, mutually influencing and promoting each other positively. A fits best: students with different starting points study together for years and all improve significantly. B is one-way influence, C is business expansion, D is negative influence.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I extracted the core elements of “symbiotic effect” and checked which option fit all of them. The key factor was the combination of similar individuals, sustained mutual influence, and a positive promoting outcome, rather than just any influence or any group success. My success came from rejecting options that had only partial overlap, such as one-way influence, negative influence, or organizational expansion instead of peer mutual promotion. For similar problems, I should explicitly list the necessary conditions in the definition and eliminate any choice that misses even one essential condition.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the definition as requiring four elements: participants of the same kind, proximity within a group, mutual influence, and a positive, growth-promoting result. That interpretation was correct, because the plant example emphasizes not just any influence, but reciprocal promotion among similar members of a group. My strategy was to convert the verbal definition into a checklist and compare each option against it, which is appropriate for definition-matching questions. The key evidence I used was that the best option involved people of the same status category studying together over time and all achieving better outcomes, which mirrors the “similar plants grow better together” structure. I also correctly noticed that some distractors contained only partial matches: one-way moral influence, business expansion without peer mutuality, and negative association rather than promotion.  

A useful assumption I made was that “similar plant circles” should transfer to “similar individuals” rather than to any cooperative arrangement whatsoever. However, I did simplify one detail: the students began with different admission scores, so they were not identical, only similar in role and environment. That shortcut was acceptable because definition questions usually require the closest analog, not a perfect literal match. I should still explicitly test whether each candidate satisfies reciprocity, similarity, and positive co-development, rather than relying on a general impression of “working together.” The reasoning succeeded because I rejected options that matched only the surface idea of influence but violated the deeper structure of the definition. A transferable rule is: in analogy or definition questions, identify the necessary relational features—who interacts, how the influence flows, and whether the outcome matches—and eliminate options that preserve only the topic but not the structure.

item.context: Cross-species studies of animal populations have shown that cubs who are isolated from their mothers within a month of birth often show strong aggression. For example, when looking for food, he is aggressive and fighting for food, while other cubs give in and he is still fighting for food. The hypothesis that explains this phenomenon is that the aggressive problem is due to the lack of social training guided by parents at the newborn stage.
item.question: Which of the following options, if true, will most strongly strengthen the above argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antelope isolated from its mother in the early stage showed great aggressiveness in the conflict to establish its dominant position in the population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chimpanzees who grew up in the socialized training environment of their parents were much less aggressive in mating conflicts than chimpanzees who did not grow up in this environment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Babies who are adopted in the first three months of life often behave aggressively in childhood.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many polar bears are more aggressive in food conflicts than in mating conflicts.

response:
Reasoning: The claim is that early parental social training reduces later aggression. Option B directly compares same species with parental socialized training vs without it and shows less aggression in the trained group, strongly supporting causation. A is only another example, C shifts to humans/adoption, and D is irrelevant.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a causal-strengthening approach: identify the hypothesis being supported, then choose the option that most directly links the proposed cause to the observed effect. The key factor was whether an option compared animals with parental social training against animals without it while holding the species context relatively constant. My success came from preferring evidence with a direct contrast group, which supports the claim better than a loose anecdote or an irrelevant comparison. In similar problems, I should prioritize answer choices that test the stated causal mechanism through a clear comparison between exposed and unexposed groups.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a strengthen-the-argument task, asking which new fact most increases support for the causal hypothesis that early aggression results from missing parental social training. That interpretation was correct because the stimulus did not merely describe a correlation; it explicitly proposed an explanation for the correlation. My strategy was to look for an option that most directly linked the presence or absence of parental socialization to later aggression while minimizing alternative explanations. That was appropriate for a causal-strengthening question, since the best support usually comes from a controlled comparison between otherwise similar groups.

The key evidence I focused on was whether an answer compared animals with parental social training against animals without it, and whether the outcome was reduced aggression in the trained group. I correctly recognized that a within-species comparison is stronger than simply adding another anecdote from a different species, because it reduces the possibility that species differences explain the behavior. I also discounted options that shifted to humans or changed the context without isolating the proposed cause. An important assumption in my reasoning was that “grew up in the socialized training environment of their parents” is a reasonable proxy for receiving the relevant early social guidance.

I should also note that I implicitly preferred evidence bearing directly on causation over evidence that merely repeated the pattern. That was the right shortcut here. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the answer choice to the exact mechanism proposed by the argument, rather than to surface similarity alone. For similar problems, I should systematically ask: does this option test the stated mechanism, rule out alternatives, or only restate the phenomenon? General rule: in strengthen questions about causal explanations, favor evidence that compares groups differing mainly in the proposed cause and showing the predicted difference in effect.

item.context: A long time ago, potatoes were called ghost apples in France, and farmers were reluctant to introduce them. An agronomist came up with a way to plant potatoes on a piece of land and was guarded by an armed King's guard in military dress. At night, the guard deliberately withdrew. As a result, people came to steal potatoes and introduced them into their own fields. In this way, potato planting has been rapidly promoted in France.
item.question: Which one of the followings is the most appropriate conclusion that can be inferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some things can arouse people's interest if they are forbidden. For example, some movies and books become more and more popular because they are forbidden.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People are curious.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People tend to break rules and restrictions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The emergence of new things is unpopular at first.

response:
Reasoning: The guarded potato field made potatoes seem valuable or forbidden, which increased people’s desire to get them. The story best supports the idea that prohibition or restriction can stimulate interest more than the other broader choices.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an analogy-based approach, matching the guarded potato field to the broader idea that restriction increases desire. The key clue I focused on was that the guard presence made the potatoes seem forbidden or special, which pushed me toward a “forbidden things become attractive” conclusion. My mistake was choosing a conclusion that added an extra causal claim about interest and popularity, instead of sticking to the more directly supported behavior: people stole them when the restriction was removed. For similar inference questions, choose the option that stays closest to the observed actions in the passage and avoids adding broader psychological explanations unless the text clearly supports them.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the broad principle illustrated by the story, and that part was basically right. My strategy was to identify the mechanism in the anecdote—guards created the appearance of restriction or special value, which motivated theft—and then match that mechanism to the most abstract option. That strategy was reasonable, but I leaned too hard on an analogy I imported myself: the idea that banning books or movies increases interest. The passage itself does not emphasize popularity through prohibition; it emphasizes that people took something specifically because access seemed restricted and then acted against that restriction. I used the “forbidden increases desire” frame, but I missed that the behavior described was not just heightened interest but deliberate violation of a boundary. That distinction matters because one option focused on motivation, while another focused on conduct.

I also failed to compare the answer choices at the right level of precision. I treated my choice as stronger because it sounded insightful, but I should have tested which option is most directly entailed by the facts given. A better alternative analysis would have asked: what happened in the story that must be true, regardless of extra examples or emotional explanations? The error came from choosing an option that added an external generalization rather than one that stayed closest to the observed behavior. In similar problems, I should separate “why people wanted it” from “what they actually did” and prefer the inference that is explicitly demonstrated. General rule: when multiple abstractions fit a passage, choose the one that is most directly supported by the stated actions, not the one that depends on an extra psychological theory or analogy.

item.context: Economist: If minimum wage levels are low, employers have a greater incentive to hire more workers than to buy productivity-enhancing new technology. As a result, productivity growth, which is necessary for higher average living standards, falls off. Conversely, high minimum wage levels result in higher productivity. Thus, raising our currently low minimum wage levels would improve the country' s overall economic health more than any hiring cutbacks triggered by the raise would harm it.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Productivity growth in a country usually leads to an eventual increase in job creation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Productivity-enhancing new technology tends to quickly become outdated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The economist's country has seen a slow but steady increase in its unemployment rate over the last decade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The economist's country currently lags behind other countries in the development of new technology.

response:
Reasoning: The argument concedes possible hiring cutbacks but claims higher productivity will more than offset them. Choice A directly strengthens this by linking productivity growth to eventual job creation, showing the long-term benefits of a higher minimum wage can outweigh short-term employment losses.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a causal strengthening approach: I identified the argument’s main chain—higher minimum wage leads to more productivity-enhancing investment, which improves economic health—and then looked for a choice that reinforced the weakest link. The key factor was that the conclusion explicitly weighed productivity gains against possible hiring cutbacks, so the best support had to connect productivity growth back to employment or overall welfare. My success came from focusing on that tradeoff rather than on background facts about technology or unemployment. For similar questions, isolate the exact objection the argument concedes and prefer the choice that directly shows why that objection is less damaging than the claimed benefit.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as a strengthen task: the economist’s conclusion was not merely that higher minimum wages increase productivity, but that the resulting gains to economic health outweigh any employment losses from hiring cutbacks. My strategy was to identify the argument’s main vulnerability, which was the gap between “higher productivity” and “net overall benefit despite fewer hires.” That was the right place to look, because a strengthening answer should connect the stated cause-and-effect chain to the economist’s comparative conclusion. I focused on the concession in the stimulus—possible hiring cutbacks—and looked for a choice showing that productivity growth can compensate for or reverse that downside. The selected option did exactly that by adding a further link: productivity growth tends to produce later job creation. That evidence supports the claim that the long-term gains are broader than just efficiency and can offset short-term labor-market harm.

I avoided being distracted by answers about technology becoming outdated or the country lagging in technology, because those facts do not directly establish that raising the minimum wage improves overall economic health. I also correctly rejected the unemployment-trend option because a rising unemployment rate does not show that this policy would help. The reasoning succeeded because it tracked the argument’s structure rather than matching keywords like “technology” or “unemployment.” In similar problems, I should continue identifying the exact comparison or tradeoff in the conclusion and prefer answers that bridge that specific inferential gap. General rule: in strengthen questions, the best support often links an acknowledged cost to a later compensating benefit, thereby reinforcing the argument’s net-benefit claim.

item.context: New Age philosopher: Nature evolves organically and nonlinearly. Furthermore, it can best be understood as a whole; its parts are so interconnected that none could exist without support from many others. Ttherefore, attaining the best possible understanding of nature requires an organic, holistic, nonlinear way of reasoning rather than the traditional linear reasoning of science, which proceeds through experiments on deliberately isolated parts of nature.
item.question: The reasoning in the New Age philosopher's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that the overall structure of a phenomenon is not always identical to the overall structure of the reasoning that people do about that phenomenon

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to distinguish adequately between the characteristics of a phenomenon as a whole and those of the deliberately isolated parts of that phenomenon

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes for granted that a phenomenon that can best be understood as having certain properties can best be understood only through reasoning that shares those properties

choices.label: D
choices.text: takes for granted that if a statement must be true for the argument's conclusion to be true, then that statement's truth is sufficient for the truth of the conclusion

response:
Reasoning: The argument moves from “nature is organic, holistic, nonlinear” to “therefore reasoning about nature must also be organic, holistic, nonlinear.” That assumes the best method of understanding something must share the same properties as the thing understood, which is not justified.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a flaw-identification approach: I traced the argument from its descriptive premises about nature to its prescriptive conclusion about the proper method of reasoning. The key factor was the shift from “nature is holistic and nonlinear” to “understanding nature requires reasoning that is also holistic and nonlinear,” which exposed an unsupported similarity assumption. My success came from spotting that the argument treats shared properties between object and method as necessary for understanding. For similar problems, I should test whether the argument illegitimately infers that the best way to study something must resemble the thing being studied.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for the flaw in the philosopher’s reasoning, not whether the philosopher’s conclusion might be true in some broader sense. My strategy was to track the argument’s shift from descriptive claims about nature to a methodological claim about how humans ought to reason about nature. That was appropriate because flaw questions often turn on whether the conclusion introduces a stronger principle than the premises support. The key evidence I used was the move from “nature is organic, holistic, and nonlinear” to “the best understanding of nature requires reasoning that is also organic, holistic, and nonlinear.” I recognized that this move assumes a kind of resemblance principle: to understand something best, one’s reasoning must share the same properties as the object of study. That assumption is exactly the vulnerable step, since the premises never establish that matching structure between subject matter and method is necessary.

I did not rely on irrelevant distinctions, and I avoided being distracted by the criticism of science’s use of isolated experiments, which is secondary to the core inference. A weaker analysis might have chosen an answer about part-whole confusion, but the deeper issue is not misunderstanding nature’s parts; it is inferring that method must mirror object. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the logical bridge between premise and conclusion rather than on the surface vocabulary repeated in the stimulus. In similar problems, I should continue identifying when an argument illegitimately transfers properties from what is being studied to the tool used to study it. General rule: when an argument says a phenomenon has feature F, therefore the best way to analyze it must also have feature F, test whether that “method must resemble subject” principle is actually supported.

item.context: A chimp who displays feelings of affection toward the other members of its social group is more likely to be defended by these group members from raiders outside of the group -- even at the risk of harm to these defenders -- than are those chimps who rarely or never display feelings of affection toward their associates. This shows that, from a sociological perspective, affection plays the same role in chimp communities as in human communities, since humans are more willing to face risks to protect those toward whom they have feelings of affection.
item.question: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expression of affection in chimps is limited to members of the social group to which they belong.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Feelings of affection are the only reason humans protect each other.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chimps express their emotions behaviorally whenever they feel them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Feelings of affection in chimp communities are at least sometimes reciprocated.

response:
Reasoning: The evidence is about chimps who display affection being defended, but the conclusion compares this to humans protecting those they feel affection toward. So the argument must assume the defended chimps are themselves objects of affection from defenders—i.e., affection is at least sometimes reciprocated.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-gap approach: I compared the premise about chimps who display affection being defended with the conclusion that affection plays the same social role in chimps as in humans. The key factor was the mismatch between “showing affection toward others” in the evidence and “being protected by those toward whom one feels affection” in the conclusion. My success came from identifying the needed bridge: the argument requires that affection shown by one chimp is at least sometimes returned by group members, so the defenders’ behavior can be explained by affection. For similar problems, explicitly test whether the premise and conclusion use the same relationship in the same direction, and if not, look for an assumption that links them.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as an assumption problem asking what unstated claim must be true for the author to move from the chimp evidence to the human comparison. That interpretation was correct, because the conclusion was not merely about correlation in chimp behavior but about affection serving the same social function in both species. My strategy was to identify the gap between the evidence and the conclusion: the evidence described chimps who display affection receiving protection, while the conclusion required that protectors act because of affection, parallel to humans. That was the right strategy for an assumption question, since the task is to find the hidden bridge from observed pattern to causal or functional claim.

The key fact I used was that the evidence only mentions one chimp’s displayed affection toward others, not the defenders’ feelings toward that chimp. Without some link back from the group to the protected chimp, the argument cannot say affection motivates the defenders in the same way it does among humans. I implicitly tested whether the choice supplied that missing relational link, and reciprocal affection does. I correctly rejected stronger or irrelevant assumptions, such as affection being the only reason humans protect others or chimps always behaviorally expressing internal feelings. A useful alternative to consider was whether any answer merely strengthened the argument versus being strictly necessary; this helped distinguish a real assumption from extra detail. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on directionality: who feels affection toward whom matters. The general lesson is that when an argument infers a shared social function from correlated behavior, check whether the evidence tracks the relevant motivation on both sides of the relationship rather than only one side.

item.context: Attention can be divided into two types: seemingly attentive and seemingly inattentive. Attention seems to mean paying attention to something on the surface, but actually thinking about something else in mind. Inattention seems to mean that you don't seem to pay attention to something but actually pay great attention to it in your heart.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the followings does not seem to pay attention to?

choices.label: A
choices.text: People who come to the seaside for the first time are often attracted by the magnificent scenery unconsciously

choices.label: B
choices.text: The students were in the classroom when suddenly a man came in from outside, and the students couldn't help looking at him

choices.label: C
choices.text: Near lunchtime, the meeting is not over yet. Although many attendees appear to be listening carefully to the content of the meeting, they are thinking about what to eat for lunch

choices.label: D
choices.text: The scout found the suspect in the crowd, pretended not to see it, and then crept up and caught him unexpectedly

response:
Reasoning: “Seemingly inattentive” means appearing not to pay attention while actually paying close attention. A and B are obvious attention. C is seemingly attentive but actually inattentive. D matches appearing not to notice while secretly focusing on the suspect.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used direct definition matching: I translated “seemingly inattentive” into the pattern “outwardly not noticing, inwardly closely focused,” then checked which option fit that structure. The key factor was the contrast between external appearance and actual internal attention, not just whether attention existed. My success came from separating the two categories clearly and eliminating distractors that involved obvious attention or the opposite mismatch. For similar problems, first rewrite each definition into a simple behavior pattern, then test each option against both the outward appearance and the inner state before choosing.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for the option that fits the definition of “seemingly inattentive,” meaning outwardly not paying attention while inwardly focusing closely. That interpretation was correct because the stem did not ask for general attention, but specifically for the case where apparent inattention masks real attention. My strategy was to classify each option against the two definitions and eliminate those that represented either ordinary attention or the opposite pattern, “seemingly attentive.” This was appropriate because the problem is fundamentally a definition-matching task, not a causal or inferential one.

The key evidence I used was the contrast between external appearance and internal mental focus. I correctly identified that the seaside and classroom examples describe direct, spontaneous attention, with no mismatch between outward behavior and inner focus. I also used the important constraint that one option described people who look attentive but are mentally elsewhere, which belongs to the other category and therefore had to be excluded. The decisive clue in the remaining option was the deliberate pretense of not noticing combined with concealed tracking and action.
