One assumption that helped, rather than harmed, was treating “seemingly” as referring to observable behavior and “actually” as referring to mental state. I still should have considered whether any option involved unconscious attention versus deliberate concealment, because subtle wording can blur categories. What made the reasoning successful was comparing all options to both halves of the definition instead of just searching for a loosely related example. A transferable rule is: when a problem defines categories by an outer-inner mismatch, evaluate each choice on both dimensions separately before matching it.

item.context: The peaceful development of the world is conducive to the integration of the world economy. Only when the world economy is integrated and new norms recognized by the world have been established can there be human democracy.
item.question: According to the above definition, which of the following options is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Without human democracy, there would be no world economic integration

choices.label: B
choices.text: There would be no human democracy without new global norms

choices.label: C
choices.text: Without human democracy, there can be no peaceful development in the world

choices.label: D
choices.text: Without the integration of the world economy, there will be no new globally recognized norms

response:
Reasoning: “Only when A and B can C” means C requires both A and B. So if there are no new global norms, there can be no human democracy. This matches B. The others wrongly reverse or add unsupported implications.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a conditional-logic approach, translating “only when the world economy is integrated and new norms … have been established can there be human democracy” into a necessary-conditions structure. The key factor was recognizing that “only when A and B can C” means C requires both A and B, so denying either condition blocks C. The successful step was testing each option against that direction of implication rather than treating it as reversible. For similar problems, explicitly rewrite “only if/only when” statements as necessity relationships and check answer choices by valid contrapositive, not by inverse or converse.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the key sentence as a conditional claim about necessary conditions: “Only when the world economy is integrated and new norms recognized by the world have been established can there be human democracy.” That means human democracy depends on both conditions being present, so my task was to identify an option that preserved necessity rather than reversing it. My strategy was to translate the statement into formal logic: if human democracy occurs, then world economic integration occurs and new global norms exist. That was the right strategy because the answer choices tested common conditional errors such as reversal and unsupported chaining.

The crucial evidence I used was the phrase “only when,” which signals a necessary-condition structure. I also correctly treated the two conditions as conjunctive requirements, meaning the negation of either one blocks the result. That is why the option denying new global norms and then denying human democracy was valid by contraposition on one conjunct. I avoided the common mistake of inferring that the absence of human democracy implies the absence of the prerequisite conditions, which would reverse the conditional. I also rejected options that tried to derive new causal relationships not stated in the passage, such as claims from democracy back to peace or from integration to norms.

What made the reasoning successful was precise parsing of “only when” and disciplined use of necessity versus sufficiency. In similar problems, I should continue converting verbal conditionals into symbolic form before evaluating choices. A transferable rule is: when a statement says “only when A can B,” treat A as necessary for B, so valid inferences go from B to A, and from not-A to not-B, but not the reverse.

item.context: A scientific theory is a good theory if it satisfies two requirements: It must accurately describe a large class of observations in terms of a model that is simple enough to contain only a few elements, and it must make definite predictions about the results of future observations. For example, Aristotle' s cosmological theory, which claimed that everything was made out of four elements -- earth, air, fire, and water -- satisfied the first requirement, but it did not make any definite predictions. Thus, Aristotle' s cosmological theory was not a good theory.
item.question: If all the statements in the passage are true, each of the following must also be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prediction about the results of future observations must be made by any good scientific theory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Observation of physical phenomena was not a major concern in Aristotle's cosmological theory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aristotle's cosmological theory described a large class of observations in terms of only four elements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A scientific model that contains many elements is not a good theory.

response:
Reasoning: The passage says Aristotle’s theory satisfied the first requirement, so it did describe many observations simply, but failed because it made no definite predictions. Nothing says observation was not a major concern. Thus A, C, and likely D follow; B does not.

FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used an elimination approach, testing each choice against what the passage explicitly stated versus what it merely suggested. The key factor was the two-part definition of a good theory: satisfying only one requirement was not enough, and Aristotle’s theory was said to meet the simplicity/coverage requirement but fail the prediction requirement. The successful step was distinguishing a supported inference from an unsupported claim about Aristotle’s priorities, since the passage never discussed what was or was not a “major concern.” For similar problems, map each answer choice to exact textual support and reject any choice that adds a new claim about motives, emphasis, or causation not stated in the passage.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the task correctly as an “EXCEPT” question: identify the one option that is not logically forced by the passage, while the others are. My strategy was to translate the passage into a conditional standard for a good scientific theory: it must satisfy both the simplicity/observational-range requirement and the definite-prediction requirement. That was an appropriate method because the argument is explicitly structured around necessary conditions and then applies them to Aristotle’s theory. I used the key fact that Aristotle’s theory satisfied the first requirement but failed the second, so any option denying the prediction requirement could not be right, while options restating the first requirement were likely supported. I also noticed that the passage says nothing about Aristotle’s level of concern with observation, only that his theory described observations in a certain way. That distinction between “describes observations” and “was concerned with observation” was the critical inference boundary.

One subtle point is that choice D is broad, and I treated it as following from the requirement that a good theory be “simple enough to contain only a few elements.” That was acceptable because the wording sets few elements as a requirement for goodness. The main reason my reasoning succeeded was that I checked each answer against what was strictly entailed rather than what sounded plausible. In similar problems, I should continue converting verbal criteria into necessary-condition statements and then test each option for direct support versus unsupported interpretation. A useful general rule is: when a passage gives explicit requirements, conclusions must preserve those requirements exactly and must not introduce claims about motives, priorities, or attitudes unless the text states them.

item.context: Based on studies by the state health department, the Surgeon General has formulated tables that list standard exercise requirements for various age groups. People whose activity level falls within the range given for their age experience fewer cardiovascular problems than those whose activity level falls below the given range. Ttherefore, if people whose activity level falls below their given range increased their time exercising to fall within that range, their cardiovascular health would improve.
item.question: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Surgeon General intended her table to help motivate people to increase their activity level and improve their cardiovascular health.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who follow the Surgeon General's table guidelines have better overall health than those who do not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing the activity level would not itself cause cardiovascular health problems for people.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some individuals would be willing to increase their activity level solely to improve their cardiovascular health.

response:
Reasoning: The argument infers that moving from below-range activity to within-range activity will improve cardiovascular health. That requires assuming the increase itself won’t create cardiovascular problems that offset or defeat the benefit. A, B, and D are about intent, overall health, or willingness, not the causal link needed.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a necessary-assumption approach: identify the conclusion’s causal move, then ask what must be true for that move to hold. The key factor was that the argument goes from an observed correlation—people within the recommended range have fewer cardiovascular problems—to a prediction that increasing exercise into that range will improve health. The successful step was noticing that this prediction depends on the increase itself not introducing cardiovascular harm, which would undermine the claimed improvement. For similar problems, isolate the gap between comparison data and an intervention claim, then test which choice must be true to let that intervention produce the predicted effect.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as an argument-assumption problem asking what unstated premise is necessary for the conclusion to work, not what would strengthen it most or merely be relevant. The argument moved from an observed correlation or comparison—people within the recommended activity range have fewer cardiovascular problems than those below it—to a causal prescription that increasing exercise into the range would improve cardiovascular health. My strategy was to test what had to be true for that causal transition to hold. That was appropriate because assumption questions require identifying a claim whose denial would seriously weaken or break the reasoning.

The key evidence I used was the gap between “people in group X are healthier” and “if others move into group X, they will become healthier.” I recognized that this inference can fail if the act of increasing exercise has its own cardiovascular risks. I implicitly applied a negation test: if increasing activity itself could cause cardiovascular problems, the conclusion would no longer follow. I also correctly rejected distractors that addressed motive, intention, or broader health because those points are not required for the cardiovascular-health conclusion. One assumption I avoided was treating the Surgeon General’s tables as automatically causally valid just because they were official. I also did not need to assume willingness to follow the advice, since the conclusion concerned what would happen if people increased activity, not whether they would. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the causal vulnerability in the argument rather than peripheral facts. A transferable rule is: when an argument infers that moving from a lower-performing group into a higher-performing group will produce the better outcome, check whether it assumes the transition itself has no countervailing harms.

item.context: It is reported that the global temperature has been rising continuously for more than 150 years due to the massive emission of greenhouse gases by human beings. However, compared with 1970-1998, the rise rate of the global surface average temperature has slowed down significantly since 1999, and the rise rate of the average temperature has not been obvious in the past 15 years, so the global warming is not so serious.
item.question: Which of the followings, if true, weakens the above argument most?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The adjustment process of ocean and climate system makes the ocean surface heat transport to the deep sea.

choices.label: B
choices.text: This phenomenon appeared in the 1950s and 1970s, and then began to accelerate warming.

choices.label: C
choices.text: UN climate experts pointed out that the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air is at the highest level in 800000 years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Natural disasters caused by climate warming have occurred in recent years.

response:
Reasoning: The claim infers “less serious warming” from a slowdown in surface temperature rise. A directly undercuts this by showing the heat may still be accumulating, just moving from the ocean surface to the deep sea, so global warming has not actually weakened.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a causal weakening approach, looking for an option that explained why slower recent surface warming would not mean reduced overall warming severity. The key clue I focused on was the argument’s reliance on surface temperature trends, which made the ocean-heat-transfer explanation seem relevant. My mistake was choosing an option that challenges the mechanism indirectly, instead of the stronger weakness: evidence that the same slowdown pattern has happened before and was followed by faster warming, which directly undermines the conclusion drawn from the recent trend. For similar problems, I should prefer evidence that attacks the argument’s inference from trend to conclusion by showing the trend is temporary or historically misleading.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the argument as concluding that global warming is “not so serious” because the recent rate of increase in global surface average temperature has slowed. My strategy was to look for an option that directly challenged the link between slower observed surface warming and weaker overall warming, which is why I chose the option about heat moving into the deep ocean. That reasoning was relevant, but it targeted a narrower premise about where heat is stored rather than the stronger inferential weakness in the argument. I missed that the argument relies heavily on a short recent time window and treats a temporary slowdown as evidence about the long-term seriousness of the trend. The stronger weakening option shows that similar pauses or slowdowns occurred before and were followed by renewed acceleration, which directly undermines the inference from “recent slowdown” to “warming is not serious.”  

My main faulty assumption was that exposing a hidden mechanism behind surface temperatures was always the strongest rebuttal. In fact, when an argument generalizes from a short-term fluctuation to a broad long-term conclusion, the best weakening evidence often shows that the fluctuation is historically recurring and therefore not probative. I should also have compared how each option attacks the conclusion’s logic, not just whether it is scientifically compatible with continued warming. A useful rule is: when an argument draws a sweeping conclusion from a recent trend change, prioritize evidence that shows the change is temporary, cyclical, or previously observed without altering the long-term pattern.

item.context: The consumer market in social life is one of the important areas that embody the market concept. Strive to improve product quality, service quality is the manufacturer, there is no denying the responsibility of the business and the concept of customer supremacy is also an indisputable marketing concept. But it is indeed a common prejudice that the customer is God. Because one side pays the money between the consumer and the consumer provider, the other side provides the corresponding product, or the other side provides the service, of course, the other party has to pay the equivalent price. In essence, there is no distinction between high and low.
item.question: Which of the following is what the passage is intended to emphasize?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The discussion of the concept that the customer is God has its background and limitations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is more reasonable to introduce a new consumption concept than the customer is God.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shows that not all the habitual consumption concepts in people's life are correct.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is emphasized that there is an equal trading relationship between consumers, manufacturers and merchants.

response:
Reasoning: The passage argues against the prejudice that “the customer is God,” stressing that consumers and providers are in an exchange: one pays, the other supplies goods/services. Thus neither side is inherently higher or lower; the relationship is essentially equal.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a main-idea approach: identify the author’s stance, then match the option that most directly restates the passage’s concluding claim. The key factor was the contrast between acknowledging “customer supremacy” in marketing and rejecting the stronger claim that “the customer is God,” followed by the explicit statement that the two sides are equal in essence. My success came from prioritizing the passage’s final, abstract conclusion over background remarks about marketing concepts. For similar questions, first separate supporting context from the author’s ultimate claim, and choose the option that captures that core conclusion most directly.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the passage’s central emphasis, not just a point it mentioned in passing. That was the right framing, because the passage contrasts a widely accepted marketing slogan with the author’s deeper claim about the nature of exchange. My strategy was to identify the thesis by tracking the argumentative structure: concession first, then refutation, then a statement of essence. This was appropriate because phrases like “but,” “in essence,” and “there is no distinction between high and low” usually signal the author’s main conclusion. I used the key evidence that one party pays and the other provides goods or services, which defines a reciprocal transaction rather than a superior-subordinate relationship. I also noticed that the text acknowledges duties of manufacturers and merchants, but only as a setup before rejecting the exaggerated idea of customer divinity. A possible trap was choosing an option about “background and limitations,” since the passage does mention both, but that would describe the discussion rather than the author’s main point. Another tempting but weaker alternative was the broad claim about mistaken consumption concepts, which is too general compared with the passage’s specific conclusion. The reasoning succeeded because I prioritized the final normative claim over the introductory framing. In similar questions, I should distinguish between supporting context, objections, and the actual thesis. General rule: when a passage critiques a slogan and then states the “essence” of a relationship, the correct answer is the reconstructed principle, not the surrounding commentary.

item.context: Perceptual constancy is that the perceptual system can maintain a stable knowledge of objective things within a certain range, and does not change with the change of perceptual conditions or sensory imaging patterns.
item.question: Which of the following is perceptual constancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It was the first time for the 5-year-old Mingming to fly on an airplane. He saw people on the ground as small as ants in the air. It was very strange that How did people become so small?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The same water was poured from the big cup into the small cup, and Ming Ming felt there was more water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Obviously when I was in the car, I saw the trees on both sides of the road running, and I was very puzzled.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mom changed her clothes today and her hair was dyed, but Ming Ming still recognized her at a glance.

response:
Reasoning: Perceptual constancy means recognizing an object as the same despite changes in appearance, viewing conditions, or sensory input. Only D shows this: even though Mom changed clothes and hair color, Mingming still identified her as the same person. The others reflect perceptual confusion, not constancy.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I compared each option to the core idea of perceptual constancy, which is stable recognition despite changes in appearance or sensory conditions. The key factor was whether the observer maintained the same object identity under altered external cues, rather than being misled by changing perspective or context. My success came from separating true constancy from perceptual illusions or misunderstandings in the other choices. For similar problems, first extract the precise defining condition of the concept, then eliminate options that show distortion, error, or instability instead of preserved recognition.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for an example where perception remains stable even when superficial sensory conditions change, rather than an example of misperception or visual illusion. That interpretation was correct because the definition emphasizes preserving knowledge of the same objective object across variations in appearance. My strategy was to compare each option against the defining criterion: does the observer treat the object as unchanged despite altered perceptual input? This was an appropriate elimination approach because the answer choices contrasted stable recognition with classic failures of perception.

The key evidence I used was the distinction between “same object under changed conditions” and “changed judgment caused by changed context.” The non-selected options all involved size distortion, quantity illusion, or apparent motion, which are cases where perception varies with conditions rather than staying constant. I implicitly relied on the assumption that constancy includes person recognition despite changes in clothing or hairstyle, which is a valid application of object identity constancy. One alternative I should still consciously check in similar problems is whether a choice reflects a different kind of constancy, such as size, shape, or color constancy, rather than only identity recognition.

The reasoning succeeded because I matched the formal definition to the functional pattern in each option instead of focusing on surface wording. A possible failure mode would have been choosing an option with changing appearance but overlooking that the observer was confused rather than stable. In similar problems, I should explicitly classify each distractor as either constancy, illusion, or motion misattribution. A transferable rule is: when a concept is defined by invariance, select the option where the observer preserves the same judgment of the object despite altered sensory presentation.

item.context: Adam: Marking road edges with reflecting posts gives drivers a clear view of the edges, thereby enabling them to drive more safely. Ttherefore, marking road edges with reflecting posts will decrease the annual number of road accidents. Aiesha: You seem to forget that drivers exceed the speed limit more frequently and drive close to the road edge more frequently on roads that are marked with reflecting posts than on similar roads without posts, and those are driving behaviors that cause road accidents.
item.question: Aiesha responds to Adam's argument by

choices.label: A
choices.text: raising a consideration that challenges the argument's assumption that facilitating safe driving will result in safer driving

choices.label: B
choices.text: providing additional evidence to undermine the claim that safer driving does not necessarily reduce the number of road accidents

choices.label: C
choices.text: questioning Adam's assertion that reflecting posts give drivers a clear view of road edges

choices.label: D
choices.text: presenting a possible alternative method for decreasing road accidents

response:
Reasoning: Adam assumes that because reflecting posts make safer driving possible, drivers will in fact drive more safely and accidents will drop. Aiesha counters that the posts may encourage riskier behavior—speeding and driving closer to the edge—so facilitating safe driving need not lead to safer driving overall.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an assumption-based analysis: I looked for the gap between Adam’s premise about making driving safer and his conclusion about fewer accidents. The key factor was Aiesha’s point that improved road visibility can change driver behavior in a compensating way, leading them to take more risks rather than actually drive more safely. My answer was correct because I identified that she was not disputing the visibility benefit itself, but attacking the hidden assumption that enabling safer driving will cause safer driving behavior. For similar problems, isolate the conclusion’s unstated behavioral link and ask whether the response challenges that link rather than the explicit premise.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as asking for the role of Aiesha’s response in the structure of Adam’s argument, not for whether reflecting posts are good policy overall. That was the right framing, because the task was essentially an argument-function question: identify which assumption or inference Aiesha attacks. My strategy was to separate Adam’s reasoning into steps: the posts improve visibility, improved visibility enables safer driving, and therefore accidents will decrease. I then looked for where Aiesha intervenes, and noticed that she does not deny the visibility benefit itself; instead, she argues that drivers may respond behaviorally in a way that offsets or reverses the benefit. The key evidence I used was her mention of more frequent speeding and driving nearer the edge, which shows a gap between making safe driving easier and people actually driving more safely. That let me identify the hidden assumption that increased capacity for safe driving leads to safer behavior in practice. I avoided the trap of treating her response as contradictory evidence about accident rates directly or as a challenge to the factual claim about visibility. One alternative I needed to rule out was the possibility that she was proposing another safety measure, which she clearly was not. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on the causal link being attacked rather than on surface keywords. In similar problems, I should explicitly map each premise and conclusion, then ask which exact inferential bridge the response weakens. General rule: when a rebuttal introduces compensating or counterproductive behavior, it is usually targeting an assumption that an enabling condition will produce the intended outcome.

item.context: During the 1980' s Japanese collectors were very active in the market for European art, especially as purchasers of nineteenth-century Impressionist paintings. This striking pattern surely reflects a specific preference on the part of many Japanese collectors for certain aesthetic attributes they found in nineteenth-century Impressionist paintings.
item.question: Which one of the following, if true, most strongly supports the explanation above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several nineteenth-century Impressionist painters adopted certain techniques and visual effects found in Japanese prints that are highly esteemed in Japan.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impressionist paintings first became popular among art collectors in Europe at the beginning of the twentieth century.

choices.label: C
choices.text: During the 1980s, the Japanese economy underwent a sustained expansion that was unprecedented in the country's recent history.

choices.label: D
choices.text: During the 1960s and 1970s, the prices of nineteenth-century Impressionist paintings often exceeded the prices of paintings by older European masters.

response:
Reasoning: The explanation says Japanese buyers preferred specific aesthetic features in Impressionist works. Choice A directly links Impressionist techniques to Japanese prints already highly valued in Japan, supporting that aesthetic preference. The other choices concern timing, economic capacity, or prices, not preference for artistic attributes.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a strengthen-the-explanation approach: first identified the claim to support, then looked for the choice that most directly connected Japanese collectors’ buying pattern to an aesthetic preference. The key factor was the causal link between features in Impressionist paintings and visual techniques already admired in Japanese prints, since that makes the collectors’ preference intelligible. My success came from rejecting tempting but weaker alternatives about wealth, dates, or prices because they explain ability or market conditions, not why these works were especially appealing. For similar problems, match the answer to the exact explanatory gap in the stimulus and prefer evidence that directly ties the observed behavior to the proposed motive.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for evidence that would support a particular causal explanation, not merely any fact associated with Japanese buying patterns. The explanation to be supported was narrow: Japanese collectors were drawn to Impressionist works because of specific aesthetic qualities in those paintings. My strategy was to match each answer choice against that exact causal claim and ask whether it connected Japanese tastes to attributes of Impressionist art. That was the right strategy for a strengthen question centered on a proposed motive, because relevant support must tie the observed behavior to the stated preference rather than to wealth, market trends, or chronology.

The key evidence I used was that one choice directly linked Impressionist artistic techniques to visual features from Japanese prints that were already esteemed in Japan. That relationship supports the idea that Japanese buyers would find those paintings aesthetically appealing for culturally grounded reasons. I also correctly rejected choices about economic expansion and high prices because they could explain ability to purchase or market prominence, but not a preference for particular visual attributes. An important assumption I avoided was treating any explanation of increased buying as support; the prompt required support for this explanation specifically. The main reason the reasoning succeeded was disciplined attention to the distinction between demand based on taste and demand based on external market conditions. In similar problems, I should continue to identify the exact causal mechanism in the stimulus and require the answer to strengthen that mechanism directly. General rule: when evaluating support for an explanation, prefer evidence that links the proposed cause to the observed effect through the same variable named in the explanation, and discount choices that merely provide alternative causes or background context.

item.context: Aggression refers to the behavior that intentionally harms others. Aggression is an intentional and explicit behavior, and does harm to the physical and mental health of others. The behavior that lacks any of the above two characteristics cannot be called an aggression.
item.question: Which of the followings is an aggression?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In a golf competition, a golfer hit a spectator with a ball, causing injury to the spectator.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mr. Wang was very dissatisfied with Mr. Zhang and cursed him in his room, which was not heard by anyone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A policeman shot the gangster during the hunting and made him wounded and then captured.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The doctor performed an operation on the patient and connected his broken bones. The operation made the patient very painful.

item.context: Plant scientists have used genetic engineering on seeds to produce crop plants that are highly resistant to insect damage. Unfortunately, the seeds themselves are quite expensive, and the plants require more fertilizer and water to grow well than normal ones. Thus, for most farmers the savings on pesticides would not compensate for the higher seed costs and the cost of additional fertilizer. However, since consumer demand for grains, fruits, and vegetables grown without the use of pesticides continues to rise, the use of genetically engineered seeds of this kind is likely to become widespread.
item.question: In the argument given, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first and the second each provide evidence to support the argument's main conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first supplies a context for the argument; the second is the argument's main conclusion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first provides evidence to support a prediction that the argument seeks to defend; the second is that prediction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first presents a development that the argument predicts will have a certain outcome; the second acknowledges a consideration that weighs against that prediction.

response:
Reasoning: The conclusion is the final sentence: these seeds are likely to become widespread. The first boldface states the relevant development/innovation being discussed. The second boldface gives a drawback showing why widespread use might not occur for most farmers, i.e., a consideration weighing against the prediction.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I identified the argument’s main conclusion by locating the predictive claim in the final sentence, then mapped each boldface statement relative to that conclusion. The key factor was the contrast structure: the first boldface introduces the new development under discussion, while the second states an economic obstacle that counts against the eventual prediction of widespread adoption. My success came from separating background, counterconsideration, and conclusion instead of assuming every boldface sentence supported the conclusion directly. For similar boldface questions, first pinpoint the main conclusion, then classify each boldface as setup, support, objection, or concession based on how it functions in the argument’s logic.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the task correctly as a boldface-role question: identify how each highlighted statement functions within the structure of the argument, not whether the claims are true. My strategy was to locate the main conclusion first, using the indicator “However” and the predictive language “is likely to become widespread,” which signaled the author’s ultimate claim. Once that conclusion was fixed, I evaluated each boldface sentence by its relationship to that conclusion rather than by its standalone content. The first boldface introduced the subject matter—a new agricultural development—and therefore functioned as the development whose future effect the argument was assessing. The second boldface clearly did not support the conclusion; instead, it described economic drawbacks that would normally discourage adoption, so I treated it as a counterconsideration. That distinction was crucial, because some answer choices tempt you to label any stated fact as “evidence” without checking whether it supports or opposes the conclusion. I avoided that trap by tracking argumentative direction: support, background, or objection. I also used the contrast structure of the passage—problem, then “However,” then prediction—to infer that the author was acknowledging a negative factor before overriding it with another consideration. The reasoning succeeded because I focused on discourse markers and inferential roles rather than surface topic. In similar problems, I should always map the argument as conclusion, support, and concession before reading the answer choices. A transferable rule is: in boldface questions, classify each statement by its function relative to the main conclusion, especially whether it advances, frames, or resists the author’s final claim.

item.context: A company has a six-story office building. The company's finance department, planning department, administration department, sales department, human resources department, R & D department and other six departments work here, each department occupies one floor. It is known that: (1) the floors of the human resources department and the sales department are not adjacent; (2) the finance department is on the lower floor of the planning department; (3) the floor of the administration department is above the planning department, but below the human resources department.
item.question: If the finance department is on the third floor, which of the following may be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The R & D department is on the fifth floor

choices.label: B
choices.text: The R & D department is on the upper floor of the sales department

choices.label: C
choices.text: The administration department is not on the upper level of the planning department

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sales department is on the upper floor of the planning department

response:
Reasoning: If finance is 3rd, planning must be above it. Since administration is above planning and below HR, the only possible arrangement is planning 4th, administration 5th, HR 6th. Then sales and R&D are on 1st and 2nd; HR and sales are not adjacent automatically. So R&D may be above sales.
FINAL ANSWER: B

reflections.simple: I used a constraint-chaining approach: I fixed finance on the third floor, then propagated the ordering rules to determine where planning, administration, and human resources could go. The key factor was noticing that administration had to be both above planning and below human resources, which forced those three departments into a tight vertical order and left only the lower floors for the remaining departments. The success came from converting verbal relations into a single ordered block, which sharply reduced the possibilities. For similar problems, first lock in any department with a fixed floor, then immediately build all forced relative-order chains before testing answer choices.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as a constrained arrangement problem asking for a possibility, not a certainty: with one department fixed on the third floor, I needed to test which option was consistent with all remaining constraints. That interpretation was correct, and it mattered because “may be true” requires finding at least one valid layout rather than proving an option must occur. My strategy was to propagate the positional constraints from the fixed finance floor: planning had to be above finance, administration had to be above planning, and human resources had to be above administration. That chain-of-order reasoning was appropriate because the inequalities forced a very narrow vertical sequence.

The key evidence I used was the strict ordering finance < planning < administration < human resources, combined with the fact that there are only six floors. From that, I correctly concluded that once finance is fixed on floor 3, the three departments above it are forced into consecutive higher floors. I also checked the nonadjacency condition between human resources and sales, which then restricted sales to the lower remaining floors. One shortcut I took was saying the nonadjacency was “automatic”; more precisely, it followed only after the upper floors were fixed. I should also have explicitly tested each answer choice against the forced arrangement instead of relying mainly on the one that fit. The reasoning succeeded because I converted verbal conditions into a strict order and used the limited capacity of remaining floors. A transferable rule is: in ordering puzzles, first compress all relational clues into chains, then combine them with any fixed positions to see whether the domain forces a near-unique structure before evaluating options.

item.context: R Hospital topped the list of my most satisfied hospitals in City C for five years in a row, and the head of the hospital said this was due to the fact that the hospital provided better guidance services than other hospitals.
item.question: Which of the following is true and best supports the opinion of the person in charge of the hospital?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All the major hospitals in C city have invested a lot of energy in the guidance service, trying to improve the quality of guidance service

choices.label: B
choices.text: The survey of my most satisfied hospital in C city has been carried out for 20 years, and all the public hospitals are at the top of the list

choices.label: C
choices.text: There are more than 200 hospitals in R city, not all of which participated in the survey

choices.label: D
choices.text: The medical level is equivalent to that of R hospital, but the rankings of poor guidance services are not as good as R hospitals

response:
Reasoning: The claim is that R Hospital’s top satisfaction ranking is due to better guidance services. The strongest support is a comparison showing hospitals with similar medical standards rank worse when their guidance services are poorer. That isolates guidance service as the key factor.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a causal-support approach: identify the claim’s proposed cause and look for evidence that isolates that cause from other competing explanations. The key factor was the comparison between hospitals with similar medical quality but worse guidance service and worse satisfaction rankings, because that controls for medical level and links the ranking difference to guidance. The successful step was choosing the option that held other major variables relatively constant instead of picking a statement that was merely related to hospitals or surveys. For similar problems, I should prefer evidence that compares cases while controlling alternative causes, since that most directly strengthens a causal explanation.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question as a weakening/strengthening task focused on causal support: the hospital head claimed that repeated top satisfaction rankings were caused specifically by superior guidance services. That interpretation was correct, because the task was not to identify a generally positive fact about the hospital, but to find evidence that best links the ranking outcome to that one proposed cause. My strategy was to look for an option that controlled for alternative explanations, especially overall medical quality, reputation, or survey bias. That was the right strategy for a causal-support question, because strong support usually comes from a comparison where the alleged cause varies while other important factors stay similar. The key evidence I used was the comparative structure showing similar medical capability but worse results when guidance was weaker. That matters because it reduces the likelihood that medical skill alone explains the ranking. I correctly treated broad statements about investment, long survey history, or participation rates as weak, since they do not isolate the role of guidance services. An important assumption in my reasoning was that patient satisfaction can be influenced by both clinical quality and service experience, so controlling for medical level is highly probative. I also implicitly considered alternatives such as prestige, public-hospital status, and sample-selection issues, and rejected options that pointed in those directions without supporting the claimed cause. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the evidence type to the claim type: causal explanation requires comparative evidence that rules out rivals. A transferable rule is: when evaluating support for a causal claim, prefer evidence that holds major competing variables constant and shows the proposed factor tracking the outcome.

item.context: A company decided to reduce the number of salesmen to tide over the temporary economic crisis. The company's board of directors plans to first dismiss the less efficient salesmen, rather than simply deciding which salesmen to dismiss based on the salesmen's business volume.
item.question: Which of the following is a prerequisite for the board of directors to make this decision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The compensation of the salesman is based on the volume of business.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The salesman with the most business experience is the best salesman.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The efficiency of one salesman will not be the same as that of another salesman.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The board of directors has a more accurate way of judging the efficiency of the salesmen.

response:
Reasoning: To dismiss the less efficient salesmen, the board must be able to assess efficiency independently of mere sales volume. Without a better way to judge efficiency, they could not base layoffs on it. A, B, and C are not required for making that decision.
FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a necessary-condition approach: I asked what must be true for the board to choose efficiency rather than sales volume as the basis for layoffs. The key factor was the contrast in the prompt between “less efficient” and “based on business volume,” which implies the board needs some independent and better measure of efficiency. My success came from identifying that a decision criterion is only usable if the decision-maker can assess it reliably. For similar prerequisite questions, test each option by negation: if the option were false, ask whether the decision or plan could still reasonably be carried out.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for a necessary condition for the board to implement its stated layoff criterion, not merely a fact that might support it. That was the right framing because “prerequisite” signals something that must be true before the decision can be meaningfully carried out. My strategy was to test each option by asking: if this were false, could the board still reasonably choose to dismiss based on efficiency rather than business volume? That necessity test was appropriate for this kind of assumption question.

The key relationship I used was that choosing employees by efficiency requires some method of assessing efficiency that is distinct from, and better suited than, raw sales volume. I correctly recognized that compensation structure is irrelevant to whether efficiency can be judged, and that experience does not have to correlate with performance for the board’s policy to be possible. I also saw that differences in efficiency among salesmen are not the central issue; even if there are differences, the board still needs a reliable way to identify them. The crucial constraint is operational: a criterion cannot guide a decision unless it can be measured or judged with sufficient accuracy.

What made the reasoning successful was separating “possibly helpful” facts from “required enabling” facts. In similar problems, I should continue converting each answer into a negation test: if the option is absent, does the plan collapse? A general rule is: for prerequisite questions, look for the condition that makes the proposed distinction usable in practice, not for facts that merely make it attractive or plausible.

item.context: The socialization of occupation means the process of individuals choosing occupation according to social needs, mastering the knowledge and skills of a certain occupation, or renewing the knowledge and retraining the skills after engaging in a certain occupation.
item.question: Which of the following is the socialization of occupation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Xiao Zhang is a technician in a unit. When he saw a great need for translators in many fields, he studied in his spare time. After obtaining the translation qualification certificate, he left his post and took up a position with another company.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After joining the army, Xiao Liu was assigned to a car class and learned the exquisite repair skills. He opened his own garage after he retired.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because of his love of cooking, Xiao Li, an accountant, took part in a training class in his spare time to learn about nutrition and improve his cooking skills.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Xiao Chen has accumulated rich knowledge and experience in raising children. He later opened a kindergarten on the advice of a friend.

response:
Reasoning: Occupational socialization emphasizes choosing or shifting into an occupation based on social needs and acquiring/retraining for that job. A clearly shows recognizing market demand, learning professional skills, gaining certification, and changing occupations accordingly. C is hobby-related; D lacks occupational training; B is less directly about social-need-driven occupational choice.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a definition-matching approach: I broke the concept into key elements—occupation choice guided by social needs, acquisition of occupational knowledge/skills, and possible retraining when changing jobs—and checked which option satisfied all parts. The decisive clue was the explicit link between market demand and deliberate retraining for entry into a new profession. My success came from requiring both motivation by social need and concrete occupational transition/training, rather than accepting any skill learning or career outcome. For similar problems, convert the definition into a checklist of necessary conditions and eliminate options that meet only some but not all elements.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the definition as requiring three linked elements: orientation to social demand, acquisition or renewal of occupational knowledge and skills, and actual connection to a job choice or job transition. That interpretation was correct because the stem was not merely about learning a skill; it was about the broader process by which a person becomes fitted for an occupation in response to social needs. My strategy was to turn the definition into necessary conditions and test each option against them, which is the right approach for a concept-definition question. The key evidence I used was the phrase “according to social needs” and the requirement of “mastering” or “retraining” for an occupation, not just personal enrichment. This helped me reject the hobby-based case and the experience-based case that lacked clear occupational training tied to social demand. I also noted that one option involved skill acquisition within military service and later self-employment, but it did not foreground a socially driven occupational choice in the same direct way. A useful assumption I made was that when a definition includes multiple clauses, the best match is the option satisfying all of them explicitly, not one that only partially overlaps. What made the reasoning successful was prioritizing the most distinctive criterion rather than being distracted by any example involving work or skill learning. In similar problems, I should continue separating core conditions from incidental details and ask whether each option meets the full definition, not just part of it. A transferable rule is: for definitional multiple-choice questions, identify the necessary conditions in the stem and eliminate any choice that lacks even one essential condition, especially the most discriminating one.

item.context: A non-local tourist asked the head of the local meteorological department, is it true that many people say that there will be typhoons in recent days? The head of the meteorological department said: according to our observation, it is not necessary to have a typhoon recently. The tourist said, is it certain that there won't be a typhoon in the near future? The person in charge said the tourists were wrong.
item.question: Which of the following options is closest to the meaning of the head of the meteorological department?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There will be no typhoons in the near future

choices.label: B
choices.text: There may not be typhoons these days

choices.label: C
choices.text: There may be a typhoon recently

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is impossible to have a typhoon in the near future

response:
Reasoning: “Not necessary to have a typhoon” means “not necessarily” or “not certain.” When the tourist concluded “so there certainly won’t be a typhoon,” the head said that was wrong. So the head meant a typhoon is still possible in the near future.

FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a modal-logic/paraphrase approach: I interpreted “not necessary to have a typhoon” as denying certainty and then inferred the opposite possibility. The key clue was the head rejecting the tourist’s stronger conclusion that there “certainly won’t” be a typhoon, which led me to focus too much on possibility rather than on the original statement’s weaker meaning. My mistake was treating “not necessary to have” as equivalent to “may have,” when it is closer to “it is not definite / there may not be.” For similar problems, I should first map each statement to its exact modal strength and polarity, and choose the option that preserves that wording most directly rather than jumping to the converse possibility.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the key phrase “it is not necessary to have a typhoon recently” as if it meant “a typhoon is not certain,” and from there I jumped to the idea that a typhoon remained possible. That interpretation captured part of the logic about uncertainty, but it missed the direction of the speaker’s response to the original rumor. The question was asking for the option closest to the department head’s intended meaning, not for the strongest inference that could be squeezed from rejecting certainty. My strategy focused too much on the tourist’s follow-up error and too little on the head’s first statement, which was a weakening of the claim that typhoons were expected. I used the valid fact that “not certain no typhoon” does not entail “certain typhoon,” but I overlooked that the answer choices were about the closest paraphrase, not strict formal equivalence. I also assumed that rejecting the tourist’s conclusion should push me toward the opposite possibility, which is an overcorrection. The better comparison is between “uncertainty about occurrence” and “uncertainty about non-occurrence,” since natural-language test items often reward the milder paraphrase. What caused the error was collapsing two distinct moves: denying necessity and affirming possibility. In similar problems, I should track whether a statement is weakening a positive claim, weakening a negative claim, or merely rejecting certainty. General rule: when a speaker denies that something is necessary, infer only a weaker modal claim in the same direction unless the context explicitly supports the opposite possibility.

item.context: The Municipal Women's Federation conducted a questionnaire survey on 8100 children aged 9 to 12 in this city. Statistics show that 75% of children are willing to do homework, while only 12% think that homework takes up time to play. As for the answers to these good children, one parent's view is that either the children are not telling the truth, or their playful nature has been distorted.
item.question: Which of the following statements is the hypothesis on which the parent's inference depends?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If children could tell the truth, not so many children would say that they are willing to do homework, while only a few children think that homework takes up time to play

choices.label: B
choices.text: Under the education of school and family, children have agreed with the psychological orientation of good students and good children, and they are no longer used to revealing their true thoughts

choices.label: C
choices.text: The heavy pressure of study makes the children immerse themselves in study all day, and gradually get used to the life of lack of entertainment, thus losing the nature of love to play

choices.label: D
choices.text: Children who are naturally playful are more likely to play than to do homework, and doing homework will certainly reduce the time they spend playing

response:
Reasoning: The parent infers from the survey that either children aren’t truthful or their playful nature is distorted. This requires assuming that if children were truthful and normal/playful, the results would not show such high willingness to do homework and such low concern about lost playtime. That is exactly A.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a negation-style assumption approach, trying to identify what must be true for the parent’s either/or conclusion to follow from the survey results. The key clue was the gap between children’s reported willingness to do homework and the small number saying homework reduces playtime, but I treated that gap too globally instead of tying it to the parent’s specific claim about “playful nature.” My mistake was choosing a statement that restated the suspicious survey pattern rather than the underlying behavioral premise connecting playfulness, homework preference, and reduced play time. In similar assumption questions, I should test whether the option supplies the causal or psychological link needed for the conclusion, not just a stronger paraphrase of the evidence.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as an assumption-strengthening problem: identify what must be true for the parent’s inference to hold. That interpretation was correct, but my execution blurred the difference between a required premise and a statement that merely restates the observed survey pattern. My strategy was to look for an assumption saying, “if children were truthful and normal, the data would look different,” and that pushed me toward a meta-level statement about the survey results rather than the underlying psychology the parent relied on. The key evidence in the parent’s claim was the phrase “playful nature has been distorted,” which implies a baseline model of what normal children are like. I failed to extract that baseline explicitly.

The missing constraint was: for the parent to infer distortion from the survey, the parent must assume that naturally playful children ordinarily prefer play and that homework competes with playtime. Without that link, the survey answers would not conflict with normal child nature at all. My chosen option was too close to the conclusion; it summarized what the parent would expect to observe, but did not explain why those observations would indicate either dishonesty or distortion. I also overlooked that a necessary assumption often connects a descriptive fact to the conclusion’s core concept, rather than commenting on response patterns directly. In similar problems, I should identify the conclusion’s hidden causal or normative benchmark and test whether each option supplies that bridge. General rule: in assumption questions, prefer the statement that makes the conclusion conceptually possible, not one that simply paraphrases the evidence or predicted outcome.

item.context: Market forecaster: The price of pecans is high when pecans are comparatively scarce but drops sharply when pecans are abundant. Thus, in high-yield years, growers often store part of their crop in refrigerated warehouses until after the next year' s harvest, hoping for higher prices then. Because of bad weather, this year' s pecan crop will be very small. Nevertheless, pecan prices this year will not be significantly higher than last year, since __.
item.question: Which of the following most logically completes the market forecaster's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the last time the pecan crop was as small as it was this year, the practice of holding back part of one year's crop had not yet become widely established

choices.label: B
choices.text: pecan yields for some farmers were as high this year as they had been last year

choices.label: C
choices.text: pecan prices have remained relatively stable in recent years

choices.label: D
choices.text: last year's pecan harvest was the largest in the last 40 years

response:
Reasoning: If this year’s crop is small, prices would usually rise. But if last year’s harvest was exceptionally large, growers likely stored substantial pecans from that surplus. Those stored pecans increase this year’s supply, preventing a sharp price increase despite the bad harvest.

FINAL ANSWER: D

reflections.simple: I used a causal supply-and-demand approach: a small current crop would normally raise prices, so I looked for a choice that introduced an offsetting source of supply. The key clue was the prompt’s explanation that growers store pecans from high-yield years for later sale, which means a previous bumper crop could moderate this year’s scarcity. My success came from linking that storage behavior to the unusually large prior harvest, rather than focusing only on this year’s production. For similar problems, identify the argument’s expected effect first, then choose the option that provides a concrete mechanism that counteracts it.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the question correctly as asking for a premise that would reconcile two facts: this year’s crop is very small, yet prices are predicted not to rise much. The key reasoning strategy I used was supply smoothing over time, which was appropriate because the stimulus explicitly mentioned that growers store pecans from high-yield years for later sale. I focused on the economic relationship between current crop size and total market supply, recognizing that current-year production is not the only determinant of current-year prices. The decisive evidence was the statement that in abundant years growers refrigerate part of the crop until after the next harvest, which implies that a previous surplus can offset a current shortage. My successful assumption was that an unusually large prior harvest would likely have generated unusually large stored inventories, increasing this year’s available supply. I correctly rejected lines of thought that concerned only some farmers, general price stability, or comparisons to past small-crop years without linking them to present supply. What made the reasoning successful was matching the conclusion’s “nevertheless” structure with a mechanism that directly counteracts the normal price effect of scarcity. In similar problems, I should keep asking what hidden variable mediates the apparent contradiction—in this case, inventory carried over from prior periods. A transferable rule is: when a prediction seems to defy a standard cause-effect pattern, look for stockpiles, lag effects, or reserve capacity that alter the effective supply or demand actually entering the market.

item.context: Giselle: The government needs to ensure that the public consumes less petroleum. When things cost more, people buy and use less of them. Ttherefore, the government should raise the sales tax on gasoline, a major petroleum product. Antoine: The government should not raise the sales tax on gasoline. Such an increase would be unfair to gasoline users. If taxes are to be increased, the increases should be applied in such a way that they spread the burden of providing the government with increased revenues among many people, not just the users of gasoline.
item.question: As a rebuttal of Giselle's argument, Antoine's response is ineffective because

choices.label: A
choices.text: he ignores the fact that Giselle does not base her argument for raising the gasoline sales tax on the government's need for increased revenues

choices.label: B
choices.text: he fails to specify how many taxpayers there are who are not gasoline users

choices.label: C
choices.text: his conclusion is based on an assertion regarding unfairness, and unfairness is a very subjective concept

choices.label: D
choices.text: he mistakenly assumes that Giselle wants a sales tax increase only on gasoline

response:
Reasoning: Giselle’s argument is about reducing petroleum consumption by raising gasoline prices, not about generating government revenue. Antoine attacks the tax increase as if its purpose were to raise revenue and distribute that burden fairly, so he misses Giselle’s actual reasoning.

FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used an argument-analysis approach: I identified Giselle’s stated conclusion and the premise supporting it, then checked whether Antoine’s rebuttal addressed that actual rationale. The key factor was the mismatch in purpose: Giselle argued for a gasoline tax to reduce petroleum consumption, while Antoine objected as though the proposal were mainly about raising revenue and distributing tax burdens. The success came from spotting this shift in issue, which shows Antoine is not engaging the original argument. For similar problems, first isolate the exact basis of each speaker’s claim and test whether the response answers that basis rather than a different motive or issue.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question correctly as asking for a flaw in Antoine’s rebuttal, not a flaw in Giselle’s original argument. My strategy was to identify each speaker’s main conclusion and, more importantly, the purpose behind each argument. Giselle’s reasoning was causal and behavioral: raise the price of gasoline to reduce consumption of petroleum. Antoine shifted the discussion to tax fairness and the distribution of revenue burdens, which addresses a different policy objective. That mismatch was the key evidence, and recognizing it made the reasoning successful.

The crucial relationship I used was that a rebuttal must engage the original argument’s actual premise-conclusion structure. I did not get distracted by whether Antoine’s fairness concern might be reasonable in general, because relevance to the target argument matters more than plausibility on its own. One assumption I properly avoided was treating every tax argument as if it were about raising revenue. I also implicitly checked alternatives: the issue was not the number of non-gasoline taxpayers, not the subjectivity of fairness, and not an assumption that only gasoline would be taxed. The success came from comparing stated goals rather than comparing surface topics like “tax increases.” In similar problems, I should explicitly ask: “What exact problem is the first speaker trying to solve, and does the rebuttal address that problem?” General rule: when evaluating a rebuttal, test whether it attacks the original argument’s actual rationale rather than substituting a different rationale that was never claimed.

item.context: All scholars have the habit of staying up late, and Zhang Mu often stays up late, so Zhang Mu must be a scholar.
item.question: Which of the following fully reveals the error in the above form of reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All smart people are short-sighted, Jiang Lang is very short-sighted, so Jiang Lang is very smart

choices.label: B
choices.text: All pigs have four legs, but this animal has eight legs, so it is not a pig

choices.label: C
choices.text: All prime numbers are natural numbers, 91 is a natural number, so 91 is a prime number

choices.label: D
choices.text: I'm a fool, because all smart people are short-sighted, and my eyesight is quite good

response:
Reasoning: The error is: “All S are P; x is P; therefore x is S,” which is affirming the consequent/converse error. Option A has the same form: all smart people are short-sighted; Jiang Lang is short-sighted; therefore Jiang Lang is smart.
FINAL ANSWER: A

reflections.simple: I used a formal-logic matching approach: I looked for the pattern “All S are P; x is P; therefore x is S.” The key factor I relied on was the converse error, but I focused too much on the broad structure and not enough on whether the terms matched exactly. My mistake was choosing an option where the predicate shifted from “short-sighted” to “very short-sighted,” so it did not fully mirror the original reasoning form. For similar problems, I should require a strict one-to-one correspondence of terms and logical structure, rejecting choices that only look similar but add or alter conditions.
reflections.complex: I interpreted the original argument correctly at a high level: it moved from “all scholars have a trait” and “this person has the trait” to “therefore this person is a scholar,” which treats a necessary condition as if it were sufficient. My strategy was to look for the same abstract form, “All S are P; x is P; therefore x is S,” and that was the right general approach. However, I stopped at the surface pattern and failed to check whether the candidate preserved the terms exactly enough to count as a full parallel. In choice A, the predicates are not cleanly matched: it shifts from “smart” to “very smart” and from “short-sighted” to “very short-sighted,” which introduces degree changes not present in the original structure. That means A is only approximately analogous, not a fully exact exposure of the flaw. I missed that “fully reveals” requires the most precise logical isomorphism, not just a roughly similar mistake. Choice C preserves the category relation more cleanly, with no extra modifiers or psychological connotations. My error came from prioritizing the named fallacy over fidelity of term structure. In similar problems, I should compare not only the formal schema but also whether quantifiers, degrees, and predicates are preserved exactly. A useful rule is: when matching flawed reasoning, prefer the option that reproduces the inferential form with the least added semantic baggage or term distortion.

item.context: It is difficult to grow cacti in a humid climate. It is difficult to raise orange trees in a cold climate. In most parts of a certain country, it is either easy to grow cacti or easy to raise orange trees.
item.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be false?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most of the country is hot.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is not possible to raise cacti in the country.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Half of the country is both humid and cold.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most parts of the country are humid.

response:
Reasoning: If cacti are difficult in humid places and orange trees are difficult in cold places, then any part where either is easy cannot be both humid and cold. Since this is true in most parts of the country, most parts are not both humid and cold. So at most less than half can be both.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a constraint-combination approach: I translated each “difficult” condition into a limitation on where each plant can be easy to grow, then compared that with the statement about what is easy in most parts of the country. The key relationship was that any region that is both humid and cold blocks both favorable possibilities at once, so such regions cannot make up “most parts” if one of the two activities is easy in most parts. My success came from identifying the overlap condition that makes both options fail simultaneously. For similar problems, explicitly map each statement onto regions or cases, then test which answer choice creates a direct contradiction with the required majority/minority distribution.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the question as asking for a statement that cannot coexist with the three premises, so the task was to identify a necessary contradiction rather than a merely unlikely option. That interpretation was correct, and it led me to focus on what conditions make both kinds of cultivation difficult at the same time. My strategy was to combine the two conditional constraints: humid climates make cacti difficult, and cold climates make orange trees difficult, so any region that is both humid and cold is a region where neither activity is easy. Then I contrasted that with the premise that in most parts of the country, at least one of the two activities is easy. That was the key evidence: “most parts” satisfying an “either/or easy” condition excludes “most parts” from belonging to the overlap where both are difficult.  

The crucial inference was set-based: the set of humid-and-cold regions must be outside the set of regions where at least one activity is easy, so it cannot occupy too large a portion of the country. I did use one shortcut by moving quickly from “most parts are not both humid and cold” to rejecting a claim about half the country; that is valid here because “most” implies strictly more than half, leaving strictly less than half for the complement. I correctly avoided assuming converses such as “if not humid, then cacti are easy” or “if not cold, then orange trees are easy,” which would have overreached the premises. I also correctly treated the other options as not necessarily contradictory, since they could still be true under some arrangement of climates. What made the reasoning successful was translating verbal conditions into mutually exclusive regional categories instead of thinking about agriculture directly. In similar problems, I should keep mapping each premise to a set relation and ask which answer conflicts with a quantity claim like “most,” “some,” or “all.” General rule: when a premise says that most members of a population satisfy condition P, any answer requiring at least half to satisfy a condition incompatible with P must be false.

item.context: Brand X, which currently markets luxury watches via billboards and advertisements in popular magazines, is considering saving money by advertising its newest line of luxury watches only in niche publications read by the wealthy. A recent study shows that most purchasers of Brand X's luxury watches have only recently become wealthy, and purchase the watches because Brand X is highly coveted by those aspiring to wealth, who learn about Brand X watches via advertising. Ttherefore, Brand X should not implement its new advertising strategy because __.
item.question: Which of the following best completes the passage below?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the money saved by implementing the strategy will be outweighed by the reduction in revenue from the less expensive line of watches

choices.label: B
choices.text: consumers who are newly wealthy prefer to purchase products that are purchased regularly by the non-wealthy

choices.label: C
choices.text: newly rich consumers will not buy the watches if the watches are not advertised to people who are not yet wealthy who will then hold the watches in high regard

choices.label: D
choices.text: most purchasers of Brand X's luxury watches do not read magazines regularly

response:
Reasoning: The argument says Brand X is coveted by people aspiring to wealth, and those people learn about it through broad advertising. If ads appear only in niche wealthy publications, aspiring consumers who are not yet wealthy won’t see them, so the brand may lose its aspirational appeal to the newly rich who later buy it.
FINAL ANSWER: C

reflections.simple: I used a causal/assumption approach: I linked the proposed shift in advertising audience to the stated reason people buy the watches. The key clue was that buyers are mostly newly wealthy and that the brand’s desirability comes from being coveted by people aspiring to wealth who learn about it through advertising. My success came from tracing that chain forward: if advertising no longer reaches aspiring consumers, the aspirational status that motivates later purchases weakens. For similar problems, identify the argument’s causal chain and test whether the proposed change breaks a necessary earlier link in that chain.
reflections.complex:
I interpreted the prompt as a weaken-the-proposed-strategy question: the blank had to supply a premise showing why limiting ads to wealthy-only publications would undermine sales. That interpretation was correct because the stimulus linked current buyers to an aspirational pathway, not merely to direct exposure among the already wealthy. My strategy was to trace the causal chain in the passage: broad advertising reaches people who aspire to wealth, those people come to covet the brand, and later, when they become wealthy, they buy it. That was the right approach because the conclusion depended on preserving the mechanism that creates demand, not on comparing ad costs in isolation.

The key evidence I used was the distinction between current wealth status and prior exposure: “most purchasers” only recently became wealthy, and they learned the brand through advertising before joining the target niche. I also correctly noticed that the brand’s value is socially aspirational, so prestige depends on being admired by nonowners, not just seen by affluent readers. I avoided a common bad assumption that luxury advertising should target only those with current purchasing power. I should also note that alternative choices failed because they introduced unsupported claims about other product lines, reading habits, or unrelated consumer preferences. The reasoning succeeded because I matched the answer to the exact causal vulnerability implied by the study. For similar problems, I should explicitly map each step from evidence to conclusion and ask which answer preserves or breaks that chain. General rule: when an argument recommends narrowing marketing based on audience wealth, test whether demand actually originates earlier through broader aspirational exposure.

item.context: All students from Australia are living in the Eastern International Student Apartment. All students living in the Eastern International Student Apartment are required to attend the international exchange meeting this year. Some students from Australia join the Chinese language club; Some civil engineering students also join the Chinese club; None of the civil engineering students attended the international conference this year.
item.question: Which of the following can't be inferred from this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All Australian students attended this year's international conference

choices.label: B
choices.text: Not a single civil engineering student lives in the East International Student Apartment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some Australian students are majoring in civil engineering

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some Chinese club members did not attend the international exchange meeting this year

response:
Reasoning: Australians are in the Eastern apartment, and those residents attend the exchange meeting, so Australians attend it. Civil engineering students did not attend, so they can’t live there; thus some Chinese club members didn’t attend.
